Humpbacks recovered after the 1985 whaling moratorium; in 2016 NOAA found 9 of 14 populations no longer needed listing.

concepts.title: Coral bleaching
concepts.description: Most corals house algae (zooxanthellae) that are their main food and color. Stressed corals, above all by warmer water, expel the algae and turn white; they can recover if the stress eases, or die if it lasts.

concepts.title: Coral is a colony of animals
concepts.description: A coral is hundreds to thousands of tiny animals called polyps, each building a limestone skeleton. Corals are animals because they catch food instead of making it, using stinging nematocysts like their jellyfish relatives.

concepts.title: Salt glands and saltwater crocodiles
concepts.description: Alligators lack salt glands and stay mostly in fresh water; crocodiles have salt glands in their tongues, which lets the saltwater crocodile, the largest living crocodilian, travel far out to sea.

concepts.title: Telling crocodiles from alligators
concepts.description: Crocodiles have narrow, V-shaped snouts and show some lower teeth with the mouth closed; alligators have broad, U-shaped snouts with lower teeth tucked inside, the big fourth tooth hidden in a socket.

concepts.title: Crocodilians, built to lurk
concepts.description: Crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials form the crocodilians; eyes, ears and nostrils on top of the head let them watch and breathe while hidden underwater.

concepts.title: New Caledonian crows make tools
concepts.description: Wild New Caledonian crows make standardized hook tools from twigs and pandanus leaves (Hunt, 1996). In a 2002 Oxford study, Betty bent a straight wire into a hook to lift food from a tube.

concepts.title: Crustaceans and their armor
concepts.description: Crabs, lobsters, shrimps and wood lice are crustaceans, with two pairs of antenna-like feelers and an outer skeleton stiffened with calcium carbonate.

concepts.title: Molting to grow
concepts.description: A rigid outer skeleton cannot grow, so crabs and lobsters molt: they climb out, stretch a soft new skeleton with water or air, and hide while it hardens. Lobsters often eat the old shell to regain calcium.

concepts.title: Darwin's voyage on the Beagle
concepts.description: From 1831 to 1836, the young Charles Darwin sailed around the world on HMS Beagle, collecting animals, plants and fossils. In South America he dug up giant ground sloths like Megatherium, extinct giants related to living sloths.

concepts.title: Island-to-island differences in the Galápagos
concepts.description: In the Galápagos, Darwin noticed mockingbirds differed from island to island. John Gould later showed they were separate species, and that Darwin's mixed bag of birds were all ground finches, which set Darwin wondering how they diverged. He published his theory in 1859.

concepts.title: Deep-sea animals that make light
concepts.description: Most deep-sea animals can glow: a 2017 MBARI study found three quarters of animals from the surface to 4,000 meters in Monterey Bay make light. Female anglerfish use a glowing lure lit by bacteria.

concepts.title: The dark, hungry deep sea
concepts.description: Below about 1,000 meters no sunlight reaches the ocean. Darkness, cold, pressure and distance from the sunlit plankton at the base of the food chain limit deep-sea life.

concepts.title: Armor, spines and spray
concepts.description: Some animals defend themselves with armor (the three-banded armadillo rolls into a ball), spines (porcupine quills that detach in an attacker) or chemicals (the skunk's aimed spray, announced by a warning).

concepts.title: Surviving with little water
concepts.description: A camel's hump is fat, not water; it drinks huge amounts at once and can then go nearly a week without. A kangaroo rat makes water from dry seeds and wastes almost none.

concepts.title: Sorting animals, and diets that change with age
concepts.description: Backbone, heat source and diet sort most animals, but some answers change with age: gray tree frog tadpoles eat algae and debris, while adults eat insects.

concepts.title: Herbivores, carnivores and omnivores
concepts.description: Herbivores eat mainly plants, carnivores mostly meat, and omnivores regularly eat both; teeth often reveal which.

concepts.title: A diet label is not a family name
concepts.description: The giant panda belongs to the order Carnivora and kept a carnivore-like gut, yet it eats mostly bamboo: diet and classification answer different questions.

concepts.title: Why dinosaurs became so varied
concepts.description: Dinosaurs began on one supercontinent, Pangaea. As it split apart, dinosaurs on separate continents evolved independently and became more diverse, from Jurassic sauropods to Cretaceous titanosaurs.

concepts.title: Dinosaur eggs and nests
concepts.description: In 1978 a Maiasaura nesting site near Choteau, Montana, turned up nests of eggs, eggshells and babies; the babies could not yet walk but had worn teeth, so parents likely fed them. Dinosaurs laid eggs like the reptiles they were.

concepts.title: Naming the dinosaurs
concepts.description: After William Buckland described Megalosaurus in 1824, Richard Owen proposed the group Dinosauria in 1842, from Greek deinos ('terrible' or 'fearfully great') and sauros ('reptile' or 'lizard'); dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles.

concepts.title: What made a dinosaur a dinosaur
concepts.description: Dinosaurs held their legs straight under the body like pillars instead of sprawling like lizards, and had a hole through the hip socket; pterosaurs and sea reptiles such as plesiosaurs were reptiles on separate branches.

concepts.title: The Oberkassel puppy
concepts.description: About 14,000 years ago a sick puppy buried with two people at Oberkassel, Germany, survived for weeks only with human care: the earliest known evidence of dogs treated as pets.

concepts.title: Dogs came from ancient wolves
concepts.description: Dogs came from an ancient gray wolf population not well represented by wolves alive today, at least 15,000 years ago; where and how many times is still debated.

concepts.title: How cattle and horses were domesticated
concepts.description: All domestic cattle trace back to about 80 aurochs domesticated about 10,500 years ago in the Near East; the wild aurochs died out in 1627. Modern domestic horses come from the lower Volga-Don steppe around 2200 BCE and carry changes linked to docility and a stronger backbone.

concepts.title: Domestication versus taming
concepts.description: Domestication changes a line of animals by selective breeding over generations, often choosing calmer animals; taming changes only one animal's behavior. Dogs were the first animals domesticated, by hunter-gatherers.

concepts.title: Earthworm bodies breathe through skin
concepts.description: Earthworms have no lungs and breathe through moist skin; their bodies are chains of ringlike segments.

concepts.title: How earthworms help the soil
concepts.description: Earthworms eat decaying plants and soil, open burrows for air, water and roots, and leave casts richer than the surrounding soil. Darwin’s 1881 book estimated they move more than ten tons of earth per acre each year.

concepts.title: What an ecosystem is
concepts.description: An ecosystem is a place where living things and nonliving parts such as rocks, temperature and humidity work together; it can be as small as a tide pool, and every part depends on the others.

concepts.title: Elephant families and the matriarch's memory
concepts.description: African elephants live in female-led herds under a matriarch, usually the oldest female. Families led by older matriarchs are better at telling strangers' calls from familiar ones.

concepts.title: The elephant and its trunk
concepts.description: Elephants, in three living species, are the largest land animals. The trunk is a boneless fusion of nose and upper lip with about 150,000 muscle bundles, used to smell, breathe, trumpet, drink and grab.

concepts.title: Why species become endangered
concepts.description: Habitat loss is the most pervasive threat to species, alongside introduced species, climate change, pollution, overhunting and disease. The giant panda's biggest threat is habitat destruction; in 2016 IUCN moved it from Endangered to Vulnerable.

concepts.title: The 10 percent rule
concepts.description: On average only about 10 percent of the energy at one food-chain level passes to the next; the rest is lost as waste, heat and uneaten dead, which is why most ecosystems have at most five levels.

concepts.title: What "theory" means in science
concepts.description: In everyday talk a theory is a hunch; in science it is a comprehensive explanation of part of nature backed by a vast body of evidence. The National Academy of Sciences says there is no scientific controversy about the basic facts of evolution.

concepts.title: The dodo and the passenger pigeon
concepts.description: The dodo, a flightless relative of pigeons found only on Mauritius, was hunted and preyed on by animals sailors brought, and was gone by the late 1600s. Passenger pigeons numbered 3 to 5 billion but were slaughtered for markets; the last, Martha, died in 1914.

concepts.title: The thylacine
concepts.description: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, was the largest meat-eating marsupial of recent times. Hunted as a threat to sheep, with a bounty from 1888 to 1909, it was protected in July 1936; the last known one died at Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936.

concepts.title: Where farm animals came from and what they give
concepts.description: Chickens come from the red junglefowl and may first have been kept for fighting or religion. Cattle give meat, milk, hides and pulling power; high milk yields came from later breeding. Cattle, sheep and goats are ruminants that chew cud because they cannot digest cellulose directly.

concepts.title: Farm animals outweigh wild ones
concepts.description: By carbon mass, livestock make up about 60% of Earth's mammals, people about 36% and wild mammals about 4%; domestic poultry has almost three times the mass of all wild birds (2018 estimate).

concepts.title: Fins and scales
concepts.description: Paired pectoral fins steady and steer a fish, working with its back and tail fins; the scales of bony fishes are thin overlapping plates of bone that keep growing all its life.

concepts.title: How fish breathe with gills
concepts.description: Fish breathe through gills: water flows over blood-rich gill filaments, oxygen dissolved in the water passes into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes out.

concepts.title: The warm-blooded opah
concepts.description: Most fish species are cold-blooded, but the opah is warm-blooded, keeping warm with a heat-exchange system in its gills.

concepts.title: Fish: nearly half of all vertebrates
concepts.description: Of about 76,000 described vertebrate species in IUCN's 2025 table, about 37,000 are fish: nearly half of the backbone family.

concepts.title: Food chains and webs
concepts.description: A food chain runs from producers, which make their own food, through primary, secondary and tertiary consumers to apex predators, with decomposers recycling the dead; overlapping chains form a food web.

concepts.title: How fossils form
concepts.description: Fossils are rare: most dead things rot away. Quick burial in sediment is key, which is why around 99% of fossils are sea animals. In petrification, minerals left by water turn buried bones to stone. Body fossils are remains; trace fossils are signs like footprints.

concepts.title: Reading the age of fossils from rock layers
concepts.description: In undisturbed rock, lower layers were laid down first, so their fossils are older (superposition). Radiometric dating of volcanic ash above and below a fossil brackets its age, and comparing layers worldwide built the geologic timescale.

concepts.title: From tadpole to frog
concepts.description: A tadpole has gills and a finned tail and no legs; during metamorphosis hind legs sprout first, then lungs and front legs, the tail is absorbed, the mouth turns froglike and the gills disappear.

concepts.title: Thyroid hormone drives metamorphosis
concepts.description: In 1912 Friedrich Gudernatsch found that feeding tadpoles horse thyroid, and no other organ, sped up metamorphosis; removing a tadpole's thyroid stops it. Thyroid hormone directs the change.

concepts.title: The Grants' finches: selection seen in two years
concepts.description: On Daphne Major, Peter and Rosemary Grant saw a 1977 drought kill most medium ground finches; birds with larger beaks, able to crack big seeds, survived, and their offspring inherited larger beaks. Later rains reversed the trend.

concepts.title: Do bears truly hibernate?
concepts.description: Bears cool only a few degrees and wake fairly easily, so Britannica does not count them as true hibernators; a 2011 study found black bears cut metabolism to about 25 percent and called it hibernation.

concepts.title: Hibernation and torpor
concepts.description: Hibernation is a long, deep drop in metabolism and body temperature, with brief wake-ups every few weeks; torpor is the same slowdown on a shorter scale, sometimes just a few hours.

concepts.title: The hummingbird's engine
concepts.description: A ruby-throated hummingbird's heart runs from about 225 beats a minute at rest to more than 1,200 in flight. Hummingbirds are the only vertebrates that can hover for long, beating their wings about 70 times a second.

concepts.title: Hummingbird energy and torpor
concepts.description: Weighing 2 to 20 grams, with poor insulation and huge metabolic demands, hummingbirds can drop into torpor on cold nights; a black metaltail cooled to 3.3 °C in a 2020 study.

concepts.title: How many insects there are
concepts.description: About 1 million insect species have been described, and the Smithsonian estimates some 10 quintillion individual insects are alive at any one time. Both are estimates.

concepts.title: The insect body plan
concepts.description: An insect’s body has three parts: a head with a pair of antennae, a thorax carrying six legs and usually wings in adults, and an abdomen; its skeleton is on the outside.

concepts.title: What makes a species invasive
concepts.description: An invasive species causes ecological or economic harm in a place where it is not native. Most are moved by people. Invasives can compete with natives, change habitats and drive native species extinct.

concepts.title: Cane toads and brown treesnakes
concepts.description: Cane toads released in Queensland in 1935 to eat cane beetles barely affected the beetles but spread in the millions and poison native predators. Brown treesnakes that reached Guam in cargo helped wipe out 9 of its 11 native forest bird species.

concepts.title: Most animals are invertebrates
concepts.description: Invertebrates, animals without a backbone, are about 95 percent of described animal species; many wear a hard outer skeleton instead.

concepts.title: A body with no brain or heart
concepts.description: A jellyfish is about 95 percent water, with no brain, blood or heart; a nerve net senses its world, and one opening serves as mouth and anus.

concepts.title: How jellyfish sting
concepts.description: Jellyfish sting with nematocysts: capsules holding coiled harpoons that fire in about 700 nanoseconds, hard enough to pierce a crustacean shell.

concepts.title: Keystone species
concepts.description: A keystone species holds its ecosystem together, like the wedge stone at the top of an arch. Robert Paine showed it by removing sea stars from a Washington shore: mussels took over and variety collapsed.

concepts.title: The largest animal ever
concepts.description: The blue whale, a living mammal, is the largest animal known to have lived: up to about 33 meters and more than 150 metric tons, feeding almost only on tiny krill.

concepts.title: Egg, pouch or placenta
concepts.description: Mammals start life three ways: monotremes lay eggs, marsupials finish growing in a pouch, and placental mammals, everyone else, grow in the womb fed by a placenta. Elephants carry their young up to about 22 months.

concepts.title: How many mammal species there are
concepts.description: The Mammal Diversity Database (July 2026) lists about 6,800 living mammal species, a tiny share of all described animal species.

concepts.title: What makes a mammal
concepts.description: Mammals breathe air, make their own heat, have hair at some point in life and feed their young milk from mammary glands; they also share three middle ear bones. Linnaeus named the class after the milk.

concepts.title: Marsupials: born early, raised in a pouch
concepts.description: Marsupial young are born tiny and embryo-like and finish developing outside the womb, usually in a pouch. A red kangaroo is born after about 33 days at the size of a jellybean.

concepts.title: Where marsupials live
concepts.description: Most marsupials live in Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands; the rest live in the Americas, and the Virginia opossum is the only one north of Mexico.

concepts.title: When dinosaurs lived
concepts.description: Non-bird dinosaurs lived from about 245 to 66 million years ago, in the Mesozoic Era: the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods. The span was so long that Stegosaurus was long extinct before Tyrannosaurus appeared.

concepts.title: Fuel and navigation for migration
concepts.description: Migrants fuel long flights with stored fat (some double their weight; B6 fattened up in Alaska) and find their way using the sun, the stars and Earth's magnetic field.

concepts.title: Record-breaking bird migrations
concepts.description: In 2022 a juvenile bar-tailed godwit flew about 13,560 km nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania in 11 days. Tracked Arctic terns fly about 70,900 km a year (2010 study), with one Farne Islands tern estimated at 96,000 km (2016).

concepts.title: Batesian and Müllerian mimicry
concepts.description: In Batesian mimicry a harmless species copies a dangerous one (Bates, 1862); in Müllerian mimicry harmful species share one pattern (Muller, 1878). The viceroy turned out to be Müllerian.

concepts.title: Monotremes: mammals that lay eggs
concepts.description: The platypus and the echidnas are monotremes, the only mammals that lay eggs. The first platypus skin in Europe was suspected to be a hoax.

concepts.title: How egg-laying mammals raise their young
concepts.description: Platypus eggs hatch in about ten days and the young lick milk from fur-covered patches, since monotremes have no nipples. A young echidna suckles in the pouch until its spines grow.

concepts.title: Only female mosquitoes bite
concepts.description: Only female mosquitoes bite, because they need a blood meal to produce eggs; both sexes drink nectar and fruit juices. Anopheles mosquitoes develop in water from egg to larva to pupa to adult.

concepts.title: Mosquitoes carry deadly germs
concepts.description: Mosquitoes pick up germs from infected people and animals and spread them by biting; malaria parasites travel this way. WHO estimated 610,000 malaria deaths in 2024, and the CDC calls the mosquito the world’s deadliest animal.

concepts.title: How natural selection works
concepts.description: Natural selection needs three things: variation among individuals, differences in how many offspring they leave, and heredity. Given those, advantageous traits become more common over generations.

concepts.title: Seeing in the dark
concepts.description: Nocturnal animals are active after dark to hunt, mate or avoid daytime heat and predators. Many have enlarged eyes, and many have a tapetum lucidum, a mirror behind the retina that causes eyeshine; tarsiers lack one and have huge eyes instead.

concepts.title: An octopus thinks with its arms
concepts.description: The common octopus has about 500 million neurons, as many as a dog, and about two thirds are in its arms, so arms can work on problems while the brain does other things. Octopuses open wired-shut clams, run mazes and remember solutions.

concepts.title: Three hearts and blue blood
concepts.description: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood past the gills and one pumps it to the body (and stops when the octopus swims). Its blood is blue because its oxygen carrier, hemocyanin, uses copper instead of iron.

concepts.title: Owls' silent flight
concepts.description: Serrated leading edges, a velvety surface and soft trailing fringes on owl feathers muffle flight, so prey can't hear the owl and the owl can keep hearing its prey.

concepts.title: Owls hunt by ear
concepts.description: Barn owls can strike prey in total darkness by sound alone (Payne and Drury, 1958). Lopsided ears let them find a sound's height as well as direction, and the facial disc funnels sound to the ears.

concepts.title: Alex the African grey parrot
concepts.description: Irene Pepperberg's African grey parrot Alex learned to identify 50 objects, 7 colors, 5 shapes and quantities up to 6.

concepts.title: How penguins stay warm
concepts.description: Dense waterproof feathers, a thick fat layer and a countercurrent heat exchanger in the legs and feet keep penguins warm; emperor males fast for 9 weeks through the Antarctic winter on their fat.

concepts.title: Penguins are built to swim
concepts.description: Penguins' wings became flippers, and their limb bones are dense with almost no air spaces, cutting buoyancy for diving. Emperor penguins dive to about 550 m, deeper than any other bird.

concepts.title: Majerus's experiment confirms bird predation
concepts.description: After critics questioned earlier experiments, Michael Majerus released 4,864 moths near Cambridge over six years. Birds ate dark moths more often, enough to explain their decline. Colleagues published his results in 2012, the most direct evidence yet for camouflage and bird predation.

concepts.title: The peppered moth and industrial soot
concepts.description: Dark peppered moths, first noticed in Manchester in 1848, took over as soot blackened trees and killed pale lichens, because birds found light moths more easily. After the air was cleaned up, the dark form declined.

concepts.title: The peregrine falcon's dive
concepts.description: In 1999 a trained peregrine named Frightful was clocked at 242 mph diving from nearly three miles up; Audubon says wild peregrines may possibly reach 200 mph.

concepts.title: Phytoplankton make oxygen
concepts.description: Phytoplankton photosynthesize like plants, so they live near the sunlit surface. Roughly half of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean, mostly from plankton.

concepts.title: Plankton: the ocean's drifters
concepts.description: Plankton are living things carried by tides and currents because they cannot swim against them. Phytoplankton are plant drifters; zooplankton are animal drifters such as krill, young fish and jellyfish, which rise to the surface at night to feed.

concepts.title: Surviving polar cold
concepts.description: Polar bears keep warm with thick fur over black skin, a fat layer and furred soles; penguins trap air in tight feathers over fat, and swap heat between leg arteries and veins so little is lost through the feet.

concepts.title: Our closest living relatives
concepts.description: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives, with about 1.2 percent DNA difference. Humans did not evolve from any living primate: we share ancestors.

concepts.title: What makes a primate
concepts.description: Primates have forward-facing eyes with overlapping views, flat nails instead of claws, and large brains for their body size.

concepts.title: Birds of prey and how they kill
concepts.description: All birds of prey have hook-tipped beaks and talons. Eagles and hawks kill mainly with their feet, squeezing prey; falcons kill with a bite, using the tomial tooth on the beak.

concepts.title: The IUCN Red List
concepts.description: The IUCN Red List sorts assessed species from Least Concern to Extinct; Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered count as threatened. In version 2025-1, 47,187 of 169,420 evaluated species were threatened, including about 41% of amphibians; only about 1% of insects had been evaluated.

concepts.title: The amniotic egg
concepts.description: A reptile embryo grows inside the amnion, a fluid-filled sac, within a leathery or hard shell that holds water in, so reptiles can lay eggs on dry land; most amphibians still lay soft, jelly-like eggs in water.

concepts.title: The living reptile groups
concepts.description: Today's reptiles are turtles, the tuatara, lizards and snakes, and crocodilians: more than 12,500 species, most of them ectotherms.

concepts.title: Reptile scales keep water in
concepts.description: Most reptiles wear a continuous coat of scales made mostly of keratin; with waxy lipids, this skin cuts water loss and helped reptiles live on land.

concepts.title: Salamander or lizard?
concepts.description: Salamanders look like lizards but are amphibians: smooth, moist skin, no claws, no ear openings and eggs in jelly, versus a lizard's dry scales, claws and leathery-shelled eggs. Many salamanders even breathe without lungs.

concepts.title: How salmon find their home stream
concepts.description: Before heading to sea, young salmon imprint on the smell of their home stream, and adults follow those odor memories back; they also imprint on Earth's magnetic field where they enter the sea.

concepts.title: A salmon's round trip
concepts.description: Sockeye salmon hatch in fresh water, go to sea to grow, then swim upstream to spawn where they were born, turning red. All die within weeks, and their bodies feed the river and the next generation.

concepts.title: Senses we lack
concepts.description: Sharks and rays sense electric fields, pit vipers sense infrared heat, sea turtles navigate by Earth's magnetic field, and reindeer see ultraviolet light.

concepts.title: Shark bites are rare
concepts.description: The International Shark Attack File confirmed 65 unprovoked shark bites worldwide in 2025, in line with recent years and, in its words, extremely low.

concepts.title: Sharks: boneless and older than trees
concepts.description: Sharks are cartilaginous fishes with no bones, only lightweight, flexible cartilage like that in your ear; they have been around for about 400 million years, longer than trees (about 350 million).

concepts.title: How sharks sense their world
concepts.description: NOAA counts eight shark senses. Sharks smell blood from far off, and a lateral line of pores from snout to tail lets sensory cells detect pressure changes in the water.

concepts.title: The smallest animal record holders
concepts.description: The smallest known vertebrate is the Brazilian flea toad (males about 7.1 mm, 2024 study), just below Paedophryne amauensis (7.7 mm); the smallest known adult insects are male fairyfly wasps, as small as 0.139 mm.

concepts.title: Snails, slugs and the mollusks
concepts.description: Snails and slugs are gastropods, the largest group of mollusks (soft-bodied invertebrates, usually in a shell made by the mantle). They move on one muscular foot over mucus; slugs are snails whose shells shrank or vanished in evolution.

concepts.title: The radula
concepts.description: Snails and slugs eat with a jaw and a radula, a flexible band of thousands of microscopic teeth that rasps food like sandpaper.

concepts.title: How snakes move without legs
concepts.description: Limbless snakes move in four main ways: serpentine loops that push against rocks and twigs, rectilinear creeping on belly scales, concertina and sidewinding.

concepts.title: How snakes swallow big prey
concepts.description: A snake's two lower jaw halves are not joined at the chin, so they spread wide and move independently, and stretchy skin widens the gape; most snakes swallow prey whole.

concepts.title: Snakes smell with their tongues
concepts.description: A snake's flicking tongue carries scent particles to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of its mouth; the two tips of the fork give it directional, stereo smell.

concepts.title: Animals that flew before people
concepts.description: Fruit flies went up first, in 1947, and came back alive. Laika became the first living creature to orbit Earth in 1957 and died within hours. Belka and Strelka orbited and came home in 1960, and Ham the chimpanzee flew in January 1961, months before Yuri Gagarin.

concepts.title: Why animals went to space first
concepts.description: Nobody knew whether living bodies could survive spaceflight: weightlessness and radiation were unknowns. Fruit flies tested radiation and came back without mutations; Ham tested whether tasks could be done in space.

concepts.title: How many animal species are named
concepts.description: About 1.5 million animal species have been described, according to IUCN's 2025 table; about 1 million of them are insects. The figure is a snapshot, not an exact count.

concepts.title: How many species may exist
concepts.description: A 2011 study by Camilo Mora and colleagues used patterns in how species sit inside better-known higher groups to estimate about 8.7 million eukaryote species, about 7.8 million of them animals; most are still undescribed.

concepts.title: Spiders are arachnids, not insects
concepts.description: Spiders are arachnids: two body parts (cephalothorax and abdomen), eight legs and no antennae. Nearly all are predators, mostly of insects.

concepts.title: How spiders make silk and webs
concepts.description: Spider silk starts as a liquid protein in abdominal glands and hardens as it leaves through the spinnerets. Many night-hunting orb weavers eat their webs at dawn, recycling the protein, and rebuild each night.

concepts.title: Ranks of classification
concepts.description: Species sit inside ever-larger groups: today's ranks run domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Close relatives share a genus, like the big cats of Panthera.

concepts.title: Life between the tides
concepts.description: The intertidal zone lies between high and low tide; its middle floods and drains twice a day. Residents survive low tide by closing up in shells or moving to water that stays; hermit crabs reuse empty shells.

concepts.title: Sea stars: tube feet and an outside stomach
concepts.description: Sea stars are not fish (no gills, scales or fins). They move and grip on tube feet, regrow lost arms, and eat mussels by pulling the shell open and pushing their stomach inside.

concepts.title: Tiktaalik as a confirmed prediction
concepts.description: Evidence suggested vertebrates moved onto land about 375 million years ago, so Shubin's team searched rocks of that age from an ancient river delta and found Tiktaalik. The National Academy of Sciences cites it as a prediction of evolutionary theory that came true.

concepts.title: Tiktaalik: from water toward land
concepts.description: Tiktaalik, a 375-million-year-old fish from Arctic Canada, had scales, gills and fin rays, but also a neck, shoulders, thick ribs and sturdy wrist bones. It shows the transition from fish to four-legged vertebrates.

concepts.title: Every tortoise is a turtle
concepts.description: 'Turtle' covers the whole shelled order of more than 350 species; tortoises are the land-only branch, while other turtles live in fresh water or the sea.

concepts.title: A turtle's shell is its skeleton
concepts.description: The carapace is built from the turtle's backbone and ribs fused to bony plates; with the plastron it forms a rigid box the turtle can neither leave nor shed.

concepts.title: Nest temperature sets a sea turtle's sex
concepts.description: Sea turtle eggs below about 27.7 °C hatch male and above about 31 °C female; warming beaches in the northern Great Barrier Reef now produce almost only females.

concepts.title: What venom does
concepts.description: Venom is a mixture of toxic enzymes and proteins; neurotoxins attack the nervous system, up to paralysis that stops breathing, and hemotoxins attack blood and blood vessels.

concepts.title: Venom versus poison
concepts.description: Venom is injected through a wound by a fang, stinger or spine; poison harms when it is eaten or absorbed through the skin.

concepts.title: Vertebrates have a backbone
concepts.description: A vertebrate has a backbone, a column of vertebrae that partly encloses the central nervous system. The five vertebrate groups are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

concepts.title: Warning colors
concepts.description: Bold warning coloration (aposematism) advertises that an animal is toxic or dangerous. Monarchs keep milkweed poison in their bodies, and predators learn to avoid the pattern.

concepts.title: Clues to whales' land ancestry
concepts.description: Pakicetus looked like a land mammal but had a whale-like inner ear region. Whales beat their tails up and down because their land-mammal ancestors' backbones bent that way, and hippos are their closest living relatives, cousins rather than ancestors.

concepts.title: Whales evolved from land mammals
concepts.description: Whales' ancestors walked on land about 50 million years ago. Pakicetus lived at the water's edge on four legs; Ambulocetus had paddle-like feet and swam with its tail; Dorudon had flippers and tiny hind legs and lived entirely in water.

concepts.title: The wood frog freezes and thaws
concepts.description: Wood frogs survive winter with about 65 percent of the body frozen: glucose keeps the inside of the cells unfrozen while the water outside turns to ice, the heart stops, and the frog thaws in spring.

concepts.title: What modern zoos try to do
concepts.description: AZA says conservation is central to accredited zoos; its Species Survival Plans (since 1981) combine breeding, habitat protection, education and research. The Arabian oryx, Extinct in the Wild by 1972, was brought back from zoo and royal herds and moved to Vulnerable in 2011.

concepts.title: The debate over zoos
concepts.description: AZA argues accredited zoos are conservation centers. Animal-welfare groups such as the Born Free Foundation argue most zoo species are not threatened, few zoo animals return to the wild, space is restrictive, and a handful of successes can't justify keeping large numbers of animals.

concepts.title: The Alhambra: tiles and carved plaster
concepts.description: Tiles cover the lower walls; above them, carved stucco runs in bands of curving patterns and calligraphy, once brightly painted.

concepts.title: The Alhambra: courtyards and water
concepts.description: Rooms open onto courtyards like the Court of the Myrtles and its reflecting pool; a royal canal brought river water to the hill.

concepts.title: The Alhambra: fortress outside, palace inside
concepts.description: Built chiefly 1238-1358 by the Nasrids, its plain rammed-earth fortress walls ('the red') hide ornate rooms and patios.

concepts.title: How Angkor's stone arrived
concepts.description: Angkor Wat is laterite cased in Kulen Hills sandstone; a 2012 study traced a canal route from the quarries much shorter than the overland one.

concepts.title: Angkor Wat as Mount Meru
concepts.description: Suryavarman II's 12th-century temple to Vishnu models the Hindu cosmos: five towers for Meru's peaks, a moat for the oceans.

concepts.title: Angkor, a capital built around water
concepts.description: Angkor, the Khmer capital from the 9th to the 15th century, had a vast system of reservoirs, canals and moats.

concepts.title: What an architect does
concepts.description: An architect (from Greek 'chief builder') designs a building for a client and turns the design into drawings and specifications builders can price and build from, then guides approvals and can inspect the work.

concepts.title: From defense to comfort and display
concepts.description: Late castles added more rooms and big windows on inner courtyards; under the Tudors, English barons stopped building castles and moved into country houses.

concepts.title: Castles: homes designed for defense
concepts.description: A castle was a lord's or king's home built to be attacked: towers project so defenders can shoot along the wall, and machicolations let them drop missiles straight down.

concepts.title: Guns end the age of castles
concepts.description: French guns took castle after castle in Italy in 1494, ending the medieval castle; defense moved to modern fortification.

concepts.title: Mining: attacking a castle from underneath
concepts.description: Attackers dug a tunnel under a wall, propped it with timber and burned the props, bringing the masonry down, as King John did at Rochester in 1215.

concepts.title: Why castle towers turned round
concepts.description: Square towers and keeps were vulnerable to mining at their corners, so castle towers became round; Rochester rebuilt its lost corner semicircular.

concepts.title: Brasília
concepts.description: A capital built in the interior, opened in 1960: Costa's airplane-shaped plan and Niemeyer's buildings, praised and criticized.

concepts.title: Transport, cars and suburbs
concepts.description: Suburbs follow transport: ferries, trolleys, then cars and the 1956 interstate highways; Levittown became the symbol.

concepts.title: Central Park by design
concepts.description: Olmsted and Vaux's Greensward plan: a hand-built landscape for a crowded city, with crosstown roads sunk out of sight.

concepts.title: Cerdà's Eixample
concepts.description: Barcelona's walls came down and Cerdà's chamfered grid, meant to hold gardens, spread over the old field of fire.

concepts.title: The first subways
concepts.description: London's Metropolitan Railway (1863) ran steam trains in cut-and-cover trenches; electric deep tubes followed in 1890.

concepts.title: Grid street plans
concepts.description: Grids are ancient (Mohenjo-daro), named for Hippodamus, used by Roman towns and spread across America because they divide land simply.

concepts.title: Incremental housing
concepts.description: Aravena's 'half of a good house': build the hard half on well-located land and let families finish the rest.

concepts.title: Informal settlements
concepts.description: UN-Habitat: over 1.1 billion people in slums or informal settlements, defined by five household deprivations and insecure tenure.

concepts.title: Manhattan's 1811 grid
concepts.description: New York's commissioners gridded Manhattan to 155th Street because right-angled houses are cheapest to build.

concepts.title: Metro-land: railways build suburbs
concepts.description: The Metropolitan Railway marketed 'Metro-land' and built housing on its own land to create commuters.

concepts.title: Public housing: Karl-Marx-Hof
concepts.description: Red Vienna's kilometer-long Karl-Marx-Hof built on only about 18% of its site, around courtyards and shared facilities.

concepts.title: The first public parks
concepts.description: Paxton's Birkenhead Park (1847), paid for by the houses around it, inspired Olmsted's 'People's Garden' ideal.

concepts.title: Public squares
concepts.description: Siena's Campo: a shell-shaped meeting place whose nine paving sections point to the town hall.

concepts.title: The sprawl debate
concepts.description: UN-Habitat sees car-driven sprawl as wasteful of land; historian Robert Bruegmann argues it brings mobility, privacy and choice.

concepts.title: What makes streets and plazas work
concepts.description: Whyte's sitting space, Jacobs's eyes upon the street, and Copenhagen's car-free Strøget.

concepts.title: Why towns built walls
concepts.description: Walls meant security, paid for by taxes like murage; gates funnelled carts and walkers through arches.

concepts.title: Uruk, an early city
concepts.description: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia: the largest settlement of its time, with mosaic-clad mud-brick buildings, a wall and the first ledgers.

concepts.title: From walls to boulevards
concepts.description: Walls cramped growing cities, so many came down; boulevards and Vienna's Ringstrasse took their place.

concepts.title: L'Enfant's Washington
concepts.description: A capital chosen by law and drawn in 1791: diagonal avenues over a grid, the Capitol on its 'pedestal'.

concepts.title: What makes a city
concepts.description: Childe's checklist for the earliest cities: size, big public works, writing and full-time specialists.

concepts.title: The Forbidden City: who built it and why forbidden
concepts.description: Commissioned by the Yongle emperor in 1406 and occupied in 1420, it barred most subjects for five centuries and became the Palace Museum in 1925.

concepts.title: The Forbidden City: a plan that ranks
concepts.description: Behind a wall and moat, buildings line a north-south axis facing south; the Outer Court held government halls on marble terraces, the Inner Court the living quarters.

concepts.title: The Forbidden City: timber post-and-lintel halls
concepts.description: Its halls are timber buildings with post-and-lintel frames under tiled roofs.

concepts.title: Maasbommel's amphibious houses
concepts.description: At Maasbommel, 32 amphibious and 14 floating houses rise with the river on mooring posts; in 2011 they floated as designed.

concepts.title: Ascent: a timber high-rise
concepts.description: Milwaukee's 25-story Ascent, certified by CTBUH in 2022 as the tallest timber building, pairs mass timber with a concrete base and cores.

concepts.title: Cross-laminated timber
concepts.description: CLT panels are boards stacked in crossing layers and glued, which makes them stable, strong and stiff in both directions; they appeared in the early 1990s.

concepts.title: The curb cut
concepts.description: Curb cuts, pushed for by disabled activists (Berkeley, 1972), turned out to help parents, workers and travelers too.

concepts.title: Why a concrete house floats
concepts.description: A floating building sinks until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as it does; a hollow concrete base displaces enough water to float.

concepts.title: Green roofs
concepts.description: A green roof is a planted layer on a rooftop; light extensive roofs have a few inches of growing medium, while heavier intensive roofs can hold parks and trees.

concepts.title: Heat recovery ventilation
concepts.description: A heat recovery ventilator swaps stale air for fresh air through a heat exchanger, so the outgoing air warms the incoming air in winter.

concepts.title: Patrick Blanc's soil-free living walls
concepts.description: Botanist Patrick Blanc grows vertical gardens with no soil: roots grip felt on a PVC sheet on a metal frame, fed with water from the top.

concepts.title: ESA's printed lunar base study
concepts.description: In 2013 ESA and Foster + Partners studied a lunar base: an inflatable dome under a robot-printed regolith shell shaped as a catenary dome.

concepts.title: Why the Moon is hard to build on
concepts.description: The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so no shield from radiation or meteoroids, huge temperature swings and one-sixth gravity.

concepts.title: The inside-out lunar building
concepts.description: A pressurized Moon habitat is pushed outward by the air inside, so it is mainly in tension, unlike buildings on Earth.

concepts.title: Rebuilding Notre-Dame's spire
concepts.description: After the 2019 fire, Notre-Dame's spire was rebuilt as an exact replica of Viollet-le-Duc's 1859 spire, and the cathedral reopened in December 2024.

concepts.title: The Passive House
concepts.description: A Passive House keeps heat in with insulation, good windows and airtightness; the first was finished in Darmstadt in 1991.

concepts.title: Passive solar design
concepts.description: Passive solar design uses a building's windows, walls and floors to collect winter sun, store its heat and shade out summer sun.

concepts.title: Buildability of printed concrete
concepts.description: Printing concrete must flow through the nozzle, then hold the weight of the layers above without sagging.

concepts.title: Printing without formwork
concepts.description: Formwork is the temporary mold for wet concrete and a big share of its cost; a concrete printer extrudes walls layer by layer with no formwork.

concepts.title: Reinforcing printed concrete
concepts.description: Steel reinforcement has to cross the printed layers, which the nozzle's path makes hard; the joints between layers are also weak points.

concepts.title: The Eindhoven printed house
concepts.description: In 2021 the first Dutch 3D-printed concrete home got its tenants: 24 printed elements set on a foundation.

concepts.title: The 1:12 ramp
concepts.description: US accessibility standards cap ramp slopes at 1:12: every inch of rise needs at least 12 inches of run.

concepts.title: Reading a building
concepts.description: Historic England's method: take a quick overview of functions and phases first, then read clues like masonry joints and blocked openings.

concepts.title: Restore or protect?
concepts.description: Viollet-le-Duc restored buildings and often added his own designs; William Morris's SPAB (1877) asked for protection and daily care instead.

concepts.title: A power station turned gallery
concepts.description: Tate Modern reused Giles Gilbert Scott's Bankside Power Station, closed in 1981, as an art museum opened in 2000.

concepts.title: How thick timber survives fire
concepts.description: Big timbers char on the outside; the char insulates the wood inside, which burns slowly and predictably, so the member keeps carrying load.

concepts.title: Universal design
concepts.description: Universal design, championed by Ronald Mace, means designing for all people from the start, without special adaptations.

concepts.title: Milan's Vertical Forest
concepts.description: Bosco Verticale in Milan holds 800 trees on its balconies; wind tunnel tests, safety cables and steel cages keep them in place.

concepts.title: The flying buttress
concepts.description: A half arch that carries a vault's thrust from the upper wall across an aisle to an outer pier, often weighted by a pinnacle.

concepts.title: Gothic walls of glass
concepts.description: With ribs, piers and buttresses carrying the vault, Gothic walls opened into large windows; Chartres (after 1194) enlarged its clerestory.

concepts.title: Iron hidden in Gothic walls
concepts.description: Notre-Dame de Paris (iron staples from the 1160s) is the first known Gothic cathedral to use iron massively; mid-13th-century builders embedded iron chains in wall tops.

concepts.title: Why Gothic builders used the pointed arch
concepts.description: Unlike a round arch, a pointed arch can be made to rise to the same height over different spans, so vault ribs meet neatly; Saint-Denis (about 1135-44) combined it with the rib vault.

concepts.title: Plate tracery and bar tracery
concepts.description: Plate tracery cut openings through a stone slab; bar tracery (after 1220, early at Reims) used thin stone bars, so windows held more glass.

concepts.title: The Great Wall: many materials
concepts.description: The wall used rammed earth, brick, granite and marble in different places, and the Ming bound bricks with lime mortar containing sticky rice.

concepts.title: The Great Wall: built over centuries
concepts.description: Not one wall: Qin Shi Huang joined older border walls around 220 BCE, and the Ming (1368-1644) built the most extensive, best-preserved version.

concepts.title: The Great Wall from space: a myth
concepts.description: The wall looks like the stone and soil around it, so it is hard to see even from low Earth orbit; NASA says it is not visible from the Moon.

concepts.title: Hagia Sophia's windows and half domes
concepts.description: 40 windows at the dome's base make it seem suspended, while two half domes east and west act as buttresses against its outward push.

concepts.title: Hagia Sophia's pendentives
concepts.description: Hagia Sophia (532-537) sets a round dome over a square using pendentives, curved triangles that gather the dome's weight onto four piers.

concepts.title: Hagia Sophia's rebuilt, taller dome
concepts.description: Part of the first, too-shallow dome fell in 558; Isidorus the Younger raised the new dome's crown by about 6 m to reduce its thrust, finishing in 562.

concepts.title: The garbhagriha
concepts.description: The heart of a Hindu temple is the garbhagriha, the small innermost sanctuary housing the deity's image or emblem, under the main tower.

concepts.title: The temple tower as a mountain
concepts.description: The Kandariya Mahadeva Temple (11th century, for Shiva) rises like a mountain range, referring to Mount Meru.

concepts.title: Northern and southern temple towers
concepts.description: Northern (Nagara) towers curve; southern (Dravida) vimanas are pyramids of receding stories, as at Thanjavur (1003-1010); later southern gateways (gopuras) grew huge.

concepts.title: Adobe and Taos Pueblo
concepts.description: Adobe is unfired earth mixed with water and straw. The Tiwa-speaking people of Taos Pueblo have built and kept up multi-story adobe homes for centuries.

concepts.title: Why cities stack homes into apartments
concepts.description: Crowding and rising land values push cities to stack homes; in 19th-century Paris, apartments got smaller and cheaper the higher you climbed.

concepts.title: Architecture Without Architects (MoMA, 1964)
concepts.description: Bernard Rudofsky's 1964 MoMA exhibition celebrated non-pedigreed architecture: old building traditions evolved and upheld by ordinary people.

concepts.title: Vitruvius: climate decides the style of a house
concepts.description: Vitruvius taught that a house must suit its climate: sheltered and closed in the cold north, open and turned away from the sun in the hot south.

concepts.title: The Eames House: a home from catalog parts
concepts.description: Charles and Ray Eames built their 1949 home from prefabricated catalog parts; its foundation and steel frame went up in 16 hours.

concepts.title: The Mongol ger, a portable home
concepts.description: The ger is a round, felt-covered wooden home that Mongolian herding families take down, carry and put up again.

concepts.title: A yurt roof: compression ring and tension band
concepts.description: Yurt roof poles meet in a center ring held in compression; their outward thrust at the wall is held by a tension band, so the roof can span without inner supports.

concepts.title: The Inuit snow house
concepts.description: Iglu means house in Inuktitut. Inuit builders cut blocks of hard snow and lay them in an inward-leaning spiral that closes into a dome.

concepts.title: Why an igloo stays warm
concepts.description: Hard-packed snow insulates better than ice, tiered floors put sleepers in the warmest air, and a lamp and body heat do the rest.

concepts.title: Log building, from Colchis to New Sweden
concepts.description: Log houses stack whole trees crossed at the corners. Vitruvius described them among the Colchians; Scandinavian settlers brought the log cabin to America in 1638.

concepts.title: The prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps
concepts.description: From about 5000 to 500 BC, farming communities around the Alps built wooden houses on piles in or near lakes, rivers and bogs.

concepts.title: The Roman domus and its atrium
concepts.description: A wealthy Roman's domus centered on the atrium, open to the sky through the compluvium, with the impluvium basin below; bigger houses added a peristyle.

concepts.title: The Roman insula, an apartment block
concepts.description: In crowded Roman cities most people lived in insulae: brick-and-concrete apartment blocks of five or more stories with shops below and worse conditions higher up.

concepts.title: Pitched roofs and flat roofs
concepts.description: Sloped roofs shed rain; flat roofs are traditional where the climate is arid.

concepts.title: Row houses and the Royal Crescent
concepts.description: Row houses share side walls in one continuous group; Bath's Royal Crescent put 30 of them behind one palace-like front.

concepts.title: The Rietveld Schroder House's open plan
concepts.description: Truus Schroder and Gerrit Rietveld's 1924 house in Utrecht had an upper floor of sliding walls: one open space by day, three rooms at night, with a corner window that opens away.

concepts.title: Why stilt houses stand on stilts
concepts.description: Stilt houses such as South Sumatra's rumah panggung let floodwater pass beneath and let air under the floor to cut damp.

concepts.title: Thermal mass: walls that store heat
concepts.description: Heavy walls of earth and masonry store heat, so the inside warms hours after the outside and swings less, especially where days are hot and nights cool.

concepts.title: Timber-framed houses and wattle and daub
concepts.description: In a timber-framed house the frame carries the load, and the panels between the timbers, often wattle and daub, only keep out the weather.

concepts.title: Vernacular building
concepts.description: ICOMOS defines vernacular building as the traditional and natural way communities house themselves, with skills passed on informally.

concepts.title: Machu Picchu: walls without mortar
concepts.description: An Inca estate, probably for Pachacuti, whose main walls are blocks fitted almost perfectly and held together by gravity, not mortar.

concepts.title: Machu Picchu: walls that ride out earthquakes
concepts.description: Interlocking blocks can move in place, which is suggested to make the walls tougher in earthquakes; the evidence is anecdotal.

concepts.title: Machu Picchu: the hidden half
concepts.description: Kenneth Wright estimates 50-60 percent of the building effort went underground into foundations, site preparation and drainage.

concepts.title: Beam, arch and suspension bridges
concepts.description: A beam bridge bends; an arch bridge works in compression and needs strong foundations; a suspension deck hangs from curved cables in tension.

concepts.title: The Brooklyn Bridge's caissons and caisson disease
concepts.description: Workers dug inside bottomless boxes kept dry by compressed air; coming up too fast caused the bends.

concepts.title: The Brooklyn Bridge's steel cables and record span
concepts.description: Opened in 1883, it had the world's longest main span and was the first bridge to use steel cable wire.

concepts.title: The Roeblings: the family who built the Brooklyn Bridge
concepts.description: John Roebling designed it and died in 1869; Washington directed it by telescope after the bends; Emily carried his instructions.

concepts.title: Cable-stayed bridges
concepts.description: Nearly straight diagonal cables run from the deck directly to the towers; France's Millau Viaduct is one.

concepts.title: Sea-level canals and lock canals
concepts.description: Suez is an open cut with no locks; at Panama, de Lesseps's sea-level plan failed and the US built locks up to Gatun Lake.

concepts.title: How dams hold back water
concepts.description: Water pressure grows with depth, so dams are thickest at the base; gravity dams use weight, arch dams push into the valley sides, embankment dams are mounds of earth or rock.

concepts.title: The Eddystone lighthouses and Smeaton's tower
concepts.description: After two towers were lost, Smeaton's 1759 granite tower, shaped like an oak with dovetailed blocks, stood until its rock cracked.

concepts.title: How the Eiffel Tower was designed and built
concepts.description: Engineers Koechlin and Nouguier conceived a 300 m iron pylon; Sauvestre dressed it; about 18,000 prefabricated pieces were riveted together.

concepts.title: The 1887 protest against the Eiffel Tower
concepts.description: Leading artists called it useless and monstrous in Le Temps before it was built.

concepts.title: How radio saved the Eiffel Tower
concepts.description: Eiffel's 20-year permit was extended by 70 years because the tower proved useful for wireless telegraphy.

concepts.title: Cantilevers and the Forth Bridge
concepts.description: A cantilever is a beam supported at one end; the Forth Bridge (1890) joins three steel cantilevers with suspended spans.

concepts.title: Shallow foundations and piles
concepts.description: Shallow foundations spread the load near the surface; piles carry it through weak soil to firmer ground.

concepts.title: The Fresnel lens
concepts.description: Fresnel's 1822 lens focused light that would scatter into one intense beam.

concepts.title: Hoover Dam: an arch-gravity dam poured in columns
concepts.description: Its weight and arch action carry the water; it was built in columns cooled by pipes, since one pour would have taken 125 years to cool.

concepts.title: How ships tell lighthouses apart
concepts.description: At night each light has its own flash pattern, its characteristic; by day, painted daymarks.

concepts.title: Beating disease at Panama
concepts.description: Mosquito-borne yellow fever and malaria crippled the French; Gorgas's mosquito control let the US finish in 1914.

concepts.title: Why the Leaning Tower of Pisa leans
concepts.description: Begun in 1173 on a shallow footing in soft ground, it began to lean by 1178; a near-century pause let the ground firm up.

concepts.title: Straightening the Leaning Tower of Pisa
concepts.description: 1990-2001: soil removed from under the raised side pulled it back about 45 cm; stable by 2008.

concepts.title: Base isolation
concepts.description: Rubber-and-steel isolators let the ground move beneath a building; Utah's Capitol has 265 of them.

concepts.title: Why unreinforced brick buildings are dangerous in earthquakes
concepts.description: Brick with little or no steel collapses inward and outward, even in small quakes.

concepts.title: Retrofitting brick buildings for earthquakes
concepts.description: Tying roof and walls together and bracing chimneys keeps old brick buildings intact so people can get out.

concepts.title: Galloping Gertie: the Tacoma Narrows collapse
concepts.description: In 1940 wind twisted apart a narrow, girder-stiffened suspension bridge; it spurred aerodynamic research.

concepts.title: Drill and blast: tunnelling through rock
concepts.description: Drill, load explosives, blast, ventilate, clear the muck, repeat; Mont Cenis pioneered air drills.

concepts.title: Immersed-tube tunnels
concepts.description: Prefabricated sections are floated out, sunk into a dredged trench and covered; Øresund is an example.

concepts.title: A tunnel as an arch all the way round
concepts.description: Ground pushes on a tunnel from every side, so its shape is a continuous arch.

concepts.title: Breuer's tubular steel chair
concepts.description: Marcel Breuer's 1925 tubular steel club chair, inspired by bicycle handlebars, suited industrial production.

concepts.title: The Bauhaus building in Dessau
concepts.description: Gropius's Dessau building (opened 1926) wraps its workshop wing in steel and glass, and the school's own workshops made its lamps and furniture.

concepts.title: The Bauhaus school
concepts.description: Founded by Gropius in Weimar in 1919, the Bauhaus taught art and craft equally in two-teacher workshops, aimed design at mass manufacture, and was closed in 1933.

concepts.title: Designing the Guggenheim Bilbao
concepts.description: Gehry's museum (1997) used CATIA aerospace software to turn complex curves into structure, and is skinned in about 33,000 thin titanium sheets.

concepts.title: The Bilbao effect, and its skeptics
concepts.description: About 20 million visitors in 20 years gave rise to the 'Bilbao effect'; Witold Rybczynski argued eye-catching museums don't reliably repeat it.

concepts.title: Why people argue about Brutalism
concepts.description: Brutalism is loved and loathed: fans see post-war ambition, critics a dystopian landscape-destroyer, as Portsmouth's Tricorn Centre showed.

concepts.title: The New Brutalism: honest materials
concepts.description: Reyner Banham named 'The New Brutalism' in 1955, holding up the Smithsons' Hunstanton school as made of what it appears to be made of.

concepts.title: Brutalism's name: béton brut
concepts.description: Brutalism's name probably comes from béton brut, French for raw concrete; Le Corbusier's later concrete kept the marks of its formwork.

concepts.title: The Dom-ino frame
concepts.description: Le Corbusier's 1914 Dom-ino system (three slabs, six posts, a staircase) did away with load-bearing walls, freeing plans and facades.

concepts.title: Le Corbusier's five points and the Villa Savoye
concepts.description: Pilotis, roof garden, free plan, long horizontal windows and free facade (theorized 1927), best shown in the Villa Savoye (1928-31).

concepts.title: A house as a machine for living in
concepts.description: Le Corbusier's 1923 line 'a house is a machine for living in' meant a house should serve the body efficiently; the Villa Savoye even curves to fit the car.

concepts.title: Gaudí's Barcelona: the Sagrada Família and trencadís
concepts.description: Gaudí took over the Sagrada Família in 1883 and worked on it until his death in 1926; his broken-tile trencadís mosaics cover curves such as Park Güell's bench.

concepts.title: Gaudí's upside-down hanging models
concepts.description: Gaudí hung weighted cords to find shapes in pure tension, then turned them upside down to get arches and columns in pure compression.

concepts.title: Standing like a tree: Gaudí's tilted columns
concepts.description: Gaudí's structures stand without external buttresses, on piers and columns that tilt to carry diagonal thrusts, branching like a forest in the Sagrada Família.

concepts.title: Hadid's flowing later buildings
concepts.description: Later Hadid buildings flow: the Heydar Aliyev Center (2012) seems to lift and fold out of its plaza, blurring floor, wall and roof.

concepts.title: Zaha Hadid, from paper architect to Pritzker
concepts.description: Hadid, born in Baghdad, explored designs through painting; long called a 'paper architect', she became the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize in 2004.

concepts.title: The Vitra Fire Station: movement frozen
concepts.description: Hadid's first major built work (1993) is a layered series of sharply angled concrete planes, described by her office as 'movement frozen'.

concepts.title: The Barcelona Pavilion
concepts.description: Mies and Lilly Reich's 1929 German Pavilion: slender steel columns carry the roof, so walls of glass and stone stand freely; dismantled 1930, rebuilt 1983-86.

concepts.title: The Farnsworth House
concepts.description: Mies's glass box (designed 1945, built 1950-51) on the Fox River floodplain, raised above the highest flood then known, has since flooded badly.

concepts.title: Mies van der Rohe: less is more
concepts.description: Mies's motto 'less is more' and his 'skin and bones' architecture of exposed structure; he directed the Bauhaus from 1930 to 1933.

concepts.title: The Pritzker Architecture Prize
concepts.description: Founded in 1979 by the Pritzker family, the prize honors a living architect's built work each year; Gehry (1989), Utzon (2003) and Hadid (2004) won it.

concepts.title: The Sydney Opera House's spherical solution
concepts.description: Utzon found that every shell could be cut from one sphere, so the roof could be made of standard precast parts; the orange eureka story is a myth.

concepts.title: Utzon's resignation and the Opera House's completion
concepts.description: Utzon resigned in 1966 after a dispute with the New South Wales government and never returned; Peter Hall's team completed the building in 1973.

concepts.title: How a cantilever works
concepts.description: A cantilever is a beam supported at one end; unlike a simple beam, its upper half is stretched and its lower half squeezed.

concepts.title: Fallingwater and organic architecture
concepts.description: Wright set Fallingwater (1935-37) over the falls of Bear Run as stacked concrete trays anchored to a stone chimney, an example of his organic architecture.

concepts.title: Fallingwater's sagging cantilevers and their repair
concepts.description: Fallingwater's terraces sagged for decades; in 2001-2002 tightened high-strength steel cables stopped them.

concepts.title: How Córdoba's Great Mosque grew
concepts.description: Córdoba's prayer hall of rows of columns (784-786) was extended by moving its qibla wall; 9th- and 10th-century extensions doubled it to some 850 columns.

concepts.title: The qibla, mihrab, minbar and minaret
concepts.description: A mosque is built around the qibla, the direction of Mecca, marked by the mihrab; the minbar is a pulpit and the minaret is for the call to prayer.

concepts.title: Sinan and the Süleymaniye
concepts.description: Sinan, Ottoman chief architect for about 40 years, based the Süleymaniye (1550-1557) on Hagia Sophia and planned it around its central dome.

concepts.title: Neuschwanstein: a knight's castle from a stage set
concepts.description: Begun 1869 for Ludwig II, it copies no real castle: stage-set designs mixing the Wartburg with book illustrations, a style called historicism.

concepts.title: Neuschwanstein: modern technology in medieval guise
concepts.description: Brick walls clad in limestone, a steel Throne Hall, central heating, running water, electric bells and telephones; a retreat opened to the public after 1886.

concepts.title: The shinbashira
concepts.description: The pagoda's central column (shinbashira) at Hōryū-ji carries only the top spire; it keeps the roofs from sliding far in a quake.

concepts.title: Why pagodas ride out earthquakes
concepts.description: Hōryū-ji's stories are independent frames, its ground columns untied, and its wooden joints can rub and slide; no five-story pagoda is recorded as toppling in an earthquake.

concepts.title: The pagoda, from the stupa
concepts.description: The pagoda grew out of the Indian stupa, built to hold relics; five-story pagodas reached Japan in the 6th century, and Hōryū-ji's was rebuilt about 711.

concepts.title: What a palace is for
concepts.description: A palace is a royal residence that is sometimes also a seat of government or a religious centre; in Rome and Constantinople palaces were centres of power.

concepts.title: Two ways to plan a palace
concepts.description: After the Middle Ages, Western European palaces tended to be single buildings; East Asian palaces are many low, decorated wooden pavilions in vast walled gardens.

concepts.title: The word palace and Rome's Palatine Hill
concepts.description: Palace comes from Rome's Palatine Hill, where Augustus's house stood and Nero later built a splendid residence.

concepts.title: The Romanesque barrel vault and thick walls
concepts.description: A barrel vault is a row of arches; it pushes outward along its whole length, so Romanesque churches needed massive walls with few windows.

concepts.title: Durham Cathedral's rib vaults
concepts.description: Durham Cathedral (begun 1093) is the earliest known example of stone ribs forming pointed arches under a vault; the ribs allow thinner, lighter filling.

concepts.title: The groin vault
concepts.description: Two barrel vaults crossing at right angles make a groin vault, whose thrust gathers at four corners.

concepts.title: Which way holy buildings face
concepts.description: Orientation is a building's position on the east-west axis: churches usually put the altar east (Old St. Peter's faced west), mosques face Mecca, and Angkor Wat faces west.

concepts.title: Core-first construction
concepts.description: A concrete core with stairs, elevators and risers is cast in a self-climbing form, and the steel frame follows it up.

concepts.title: Building a skyscraper, step by step
concepts.description: Dig a pit, sink piles to bedrock, raise the steel frame by crane, pour floors on steel decking, bolt on the outer wall and fit out, with phases overlapping.

concepts.title: Burj Khalifa's Y plan and buttressed core
concepts.description: A Y-shaped plan from a desert flower, with three wings bracing a six-sided core, and wings that step back in a spiral to confuse the wind.

concepts.title: Burj Khalifa: the tallest building
concepts.description: As of 2026 the CTBUH ranks Burj Khalifa (2010, 828 m), designed by SOM's Adrian Smith and William F. Baker, as the world's tallest.

concepts.title: Chicago after the 1871 fire
concepts.description: The 1871 fire cleared central Chicago and set off a land rush; the first skyscrapers, with steel frames, elevators and new foundations, followed 10 to 15 years later.

concepts.title: The Chicago school
concepts.description: Jenney, Burnham, Root, Adler and Sullivan developed the skyscraper in late 19th-century Chicago, starting with frame buildings like the Home Insurance Building.

concepts.title: The curtain wall
concepts.description: A nonbearing outer wall of glass, metal or masonry hung on the structural frame.

concepts.title: From attic to penthouse
concepts.description: Elevators made upper floors as easy to reach as lower ones, turning the poor's attic into the prized penthouse and helping shape modern cities.

concepts.title: The safety elevator
concepts.description: Otis's 1854 brake gripped the guide rails if the rope failed; the 1857 passenger elevator made buildings over four or five stories practical.

concepts.title: The Empire State Building's design
concepts.description: Art Deco, 1,250 feet with a spire meant for airships, and the world's tallest building until 1971.

concepts.title: How the Empire State Building was built so fast
concepts.description: Overlapping design and construction, digging while demolishing, just-in-time deliveries and a site railway.

concepts.title: The Empire State Building's record build
concepts.description: The 102-story Empire State Building went up in about 410 days (1930-31), its frame rising about four and a half stories a week.

concepts.title: Glass and the sun
concepts.description: Glass buildings struggle with solar heat, from the Crystal Palace to the Walkie-Talkie's focused glare.

concepts.title: The rise of the glass tower
concepts.description: Air conditioning and cheap postwar energy made all-glass towers practical; Lever House (1952) led the way in New York.

concepts.title: The hard hat
concepts.description: Bullard's steamed-canvas Hard Boiled Hat, modeled on WWI helmets for miners, spread to construction; Hoover Dam first required it.

concepts.title: The Chrysler Building's secret spire
concepts.description: In 1929 Van Alen hoisted a secretly assembled spire in about 90 minutes to beat 40 Wall Street; the Chrysler held the title until 1931.

concepts.title: What counts as the top
concepts.description: The CTBUH measures to the architectural top: spires count, antennas don't, which is how the Petronas Towers outranked the Sears Tower in 1998.

concepts.title: The race to the top: a timeline
concepts.description: The tallest-building title passed from New York to Chicago, Kuala Lumpur, Taipei and Dubai.

concepts.title: Falls and fall protection
concepts.description: Falls are the leading cause of construction deaths; US rules require fall protection from six feet: guardrails, harnesses and nets.

concepts.title: Lunch atop a Skyscraper
concepts.description: The staged 1932 photo of real ironworkers eating lunch on a beam 850 feet up the RCA Building.

concepts.title: Sullivan: form follows function
concepts.description: Sullivan's 1896 essay: a tall building's outside should show its uses, from shops at the base to identical office floors to a closing attic; the Wainwright Building reads like a column.

concepts.title: Taming the wind: shape and dampers
concepts.description: Changing shape with height confuses the wind; softened corners, openings, wind tunnels and dampers like Taipei 101's steel sphere help too.

concepts.title: Wind vortices and resonance
concepts.description: Vortices shed alternately from a tower's sides push it across the wind; timed to its natural frequency, like pushes on a swing, they make it sway harder.

concepts.title: Where the word skyscraper comes from
concepts.description: A sailors' word for a mast-top sail (1794) became the name for very tall buildings in 1888 Chicago.

concepts.title: New York's 1916 zoning and the wedding-cake tower
concepts.description: After the Equitable Building's seven-acre shadow, the 1916 Zoning Resolution shaped slender towers and tiered wedding-cake buildings.

concepts.title: Poleni, the hanging chain and St. Peter's dome
concepts.description: In 1743 St. Peter's dome was cracking; Poleni showed with a weighted hanging chain (1748) that it was safe, and iron rings were fitted by 1748.

concepts.title: Rebuilding St. Peter's
concepts.description: St. Peter's replaced Constantine's basilica: begun 1506 (Bramante), Michelangelo from 1546, dome finished 1590, Maderno's Latin cross, consecrated 1626.

concepts.title: How an arch works
concepts.description: Wedge-shaped voussoirs, locked by a keystone, are squeezed together by the load; built on centering, an arch of small blocks spans wider than a stone lintel.

concepts.title: An arch's thrust
concepts.description: An arch also pushes outward at its feet (thrust), so it needs massive supports to carry that push into the foundation.

concepts.title: Plans, sections, elevations and scale
concepts.description: A plan is a horizontal cut, a section a vertical cut, an elevation a face seen straight on; all are drawn to scale so builders can measure from them.

concepts.title: Why beams bend, and why stone beams stay short
concepts.description: A loaded beam is squeezed on top and stretched underneath; brittle stone is weak in tension, so stone lintels must be short and posts close together.

concepts.title: How blueprints were made
concepts.description: The cyanotype (1842) turned treated paper blue where light hit it, giving white lines on blue; it was used for copying drawings from the 1870s until diazo prints replaced it.

concepts.title: Mud brick and fired brick
concepts.description: The first bricks were sun-dried mud; firing in a kiln makes them strong and hard. Bricks were sized for one person to handle.

concepts.title: How building changed: a timeline
concepts.description: From sun-dried mud brick and post-and-lintel stone, through Roman concrete domes and Florence, to iron-and-glass and the steel skeleton.

concepts.title: The Crystal Palace
concepts.description: A gardener's iron-and-glass building for 1851, sketched on blotting paper and built within six months from prefabricated parts.

concepts.title: A dome: the arch turned in a circle
concepts.description: A dome evolved from the arch and pushes outward all around its rim, so large domes need heavy support.

concepts.title: A dome's hoop forces
concepts.description: Horizontal hoop forces let a dome rise ring by ring without centering; they squeeze near the top but turn to tension toward the base, where masonry domes crack into slices.

concepts.title: Florence's dome and its tie rings
concepts.description: Florence Cathedral's dome (completed 1436) is still the largest masonry dome in the world; Brunelleschi bound it with tie rings of stone and oak.

concepts.title: Load-bearing walls versus a frame
concepts.description: In a load-bearing building the walls carry the floors; in a frame building a skeleton of columns and beams does, so the outer wall bears only itself and can be light, even glass.

concepts.title: Hooke's hanging chain
concepts.description: A hanging chain is in pure tension along its curve; turned upside down, the same shape stands as an arch in pure compression (Hooke, 1675).

concepts.title: Self-healing Roman concrete (2023 findings)
concepts.description: A 2023 MIT-led study found that lime clasts from hot mixing with quicklime can let Roman concrete seal its own cracks.

concepts.title: The load path
concepts.description: Every load needs a continuous route from where it is applied, through the structure and foundation, into the soil.

concepts.title: Dead loads and live loads
concepts.description: A building carries permanent dead loads (its own structure and fixed parts) and changing live loads (people, furniture, weather, wind).

concepts.title: Stone and wood: strengths and weaknesses
concepts.description: Stone is strong when squeezed and resists fire but is weak when stretched; wood is strong for its weight and spans farther but burns.

concepts.title: The post-and-lintel system
concepts.description: Two upright posts carry a horizontal lintel across their tops: the system of Stonehenge and of doors and windows today.

concepts.title: Modern and reinforced concrete
concepts.description: Portland cement (1824) binds modern concrete; concrete is weak in tension, so steel bars take the stretch, an idea credited to Joseph Monier's 1867 patent.

concepts.title: Roman concrete
concepts.description: The Romans made concrete of lime, volcanic ash and rock; it set in seawater, and the Pantheon's dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome.

concepts.title: Why steel suits the frame
concepts.description: Unlike stone or brittle cast iron, steel has high tensile strength, so it handles the stretch in beams; an iron and steel skeleton held up the Home Insurance Building.

concepts.title: Tension and compression
concepts.description: Compression pushes and squeezes; tension pulls and stretches. A post carrying weight is squeezed; a cable holding a hanging weight is stretched.

concepts.title: Keeping the line of thrust inside the masonry
concepts.description: Engineers treat masonry as having no tensile strength; if a line of thrust fits entirely inside it, an arch or dome can be shown to be safe.

concepts.title: The Taj Mahal: symmetry, minarets and inlay
concepts.description: Four matching facades, a twin building for balance, outward-leaning minarets, and semiprecious stones inlaid in white marble.

concepts.title: The Taj Mahal: who built it, for whom
concepts.description: Shah Jahan built it as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal (died 1631) from about 1632, with 20,000+ workers; some famous stories about it are legends.

concepts.title: The Hall of Mirrors
concepts.description: Built 1678-1684 by Hardouin-Mansart: 357 mirrors on 17 arches facing 17 windows, a boast of French wealth when mirrors were a luxury.

concepts.title: Versailles: a palace to control a court
concepts.description: A hunting lodge turned by Louis XIV into an immense palace; from 1682 it housed the whole court, keeping the nobility under the king's eye.

concepts.title: Vitruvius's three conditions of good building
concepts.description: Vitruvius's De architectura, the only complete architecture book to survive from antiquity, says good building needs firmness, commodity and delight.

concepts.title: Keeping an aqueduct flowing downhill
concepts.description: Gravity-fed aqueducts had to hold a gentle slope (about 25 cm per km at Nîmes); they ran mostly underground, crossing valleys on arches like the Pont du Gard.

concepts.title: Surveying a level: the chorobates
concepts.description: Vitruvius's chorobates: a twenty-foot straightedge on legs whose plumb lines, or water in a groove, show level.

concepts.title: Moving the Colosseum crowd
concepts.description: At least 80 entrances, 76 of them numbered to match tickets; class seating zones; vomitoria passages that disgorged the spectators.

concepts.title: How the Colosseum is built
concepts.description: A freestanding oval with a travertine framework, tufa and concrete, barrel and groin vaults, and three stories of arcades framed by the Greek orders.

concepts.title: The plan of an Egyptian temple
