concepts.description: Pylon, open court, hypostyle hall and sanctuary: darker, more enclosed and higher toward the god, recreating the mound of creation.

concepts.title: The first houses: Çatalhöyük and Skara Brae
concepts.description: Çatalhöyük packed mud-brick houses together with no streets, entered through the roof; Skara Brae kept its stone furniture for 5,000 years.

concepts.title: Göbekli Tepe: a monument before farming
concepts.description: Hunter-gatherers raised Göbekli Tepe's pillar enclosures about 11,500 years ago; long read as a temple, it turns out people lived there too.

concepts.title: Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall
concepts.description: A hypostyle hall's roof rests on columns: at Karnak, 134 of them under stone lintels, with a taller central aisle lit by clerestory grilles.

concepts.title: The Pantheon's cracked dome
concepts.description: Meridional cracks split the lower dome into slices that work as arches sharing the uncracked upper dome as keystone (Mark and Hutchinson, 1986).

concepts.title: Lightening the Pantheon
concepts.description: Materials graded from heavy basalt below to pumice at the top of the vault, over walls 6 m thick braced by brick arches.

concepts.title: Building the Parthenon without mortar
concepts.description: Hand-trimmed marble blocks with near-invisible joints, locked by iron clamps sealed in lead; unleaded iron from 1898 cracked the marble, so restorers use titanium.

concepts.title: The Parthenon's refinements
concepts.description: A base that curves up, columns that swell (entasis) and lean inward, thicker corners: few straight lines, for reasons still debated.

concepts.title: The Great Pyramid's stones
concepts.description: Yellowish limestone core, finer limestone casing and passages, and a King's Chamber built, lined and roofed with granite.

concepts.title: The Great Pyramid's relieving compartments
concepts.description: Five compartments above the King's Chamber, separated by granite slabs and topped by a gabled roof, probably shield its flat ceiling from the weight above.

concepts.title: How six wonders were lost
concepts.description: Fire, earthquakes and stone recycling destroyed six wonders; the Hanging Gardens may never have been at Babylon at all.

concepts.title: The Seven Wonders of the ancient world
concepts.description: Two tombs, two statues, a temple, gardens and a lighthouse, listed by Greek writers of the 2nd century BCE; only the pyramids survive.

concepts.title: Trabeated and arcuated building
concepts.description: Trabeated building uses beams or lintels (Egypt, Greece); arcuated building uses arches (Rome).

concepts.title: The ziggurat: a solid stepped temple tower
concepts.description: A ziggurat was a stepped temple tower of Mesopotamia with no rooms inside; at Ur, three staircases led to a temple on top.

concepts.title: Reed reinforcement in ziggurats
concepts.description: At Aqar Quf, layers of reed matting and plaited reed ropes run through the brickwork as reinforcement.

concepts.title: The ziggurat's waterproof skin
concepts.description: A mud-brick core wrapped in baked brick mortared with bitumen; weeper holes let water evaporate from the core.

concepts.title: Pollock and action painting
concepts.description: Abstract Expressionism began in New York in the late 1940s. Pollock poured and dripped paint on canvas laid on the floor, and critics called the canvas an arena in which to act.

concepts.title: Rothko and color-field painting
concepts.description: Rothko painted soft-edged rectangles of color on wall-sized canvases to express basic human emotions, and made dark paintings for a chapel in Houston.

concepts.title: Ancient Aboriginal rock art
concepts.description: A kangaroo painted on a Kimberley rock-shelter ceiling about 17,300 years ago is Australia's oldest known intact rock painting, dated from wasp nests beneath and on top of the paint.

concepts.title: Hilma af Klint
concepts.description: Hilma af Klint painted abstract works in Stockholm from as early as 1906, before Kandinsky, but asked that they stay unseen until at least 20 years after her death in 1944.

concepts.title: Kandinsky's abstraction
concepts.description: Kandinsky saw one of his paintings on its side at dusk and decided objects harmed his paintings; he wanted color, line and shape to work like music.

concepts.title: Mondrian's grid
concepts.description: Mondrian's mature paintings use only straight horizontal and vertical lines, the primary colors and black, white and gray; he cofounded De Stijl in 1917.

concepts.title: Masks in masquerade
concepts.description: In many African traditions a mask is one part of a masquerade of costume, music and dance in which performers may embody spirits or ancestors, as in Yoruba Egungun.

concepts.title: African sculpture and modern art
concepts.description: Matisse, Derain and Vlaminck collected African sculpture; after studying masks at the Trocadéro in 1907, Picasso gave figures in Les Demoiselles d'Avignon mask-like faces.

concepts.title: The makers behind the objects
concepts.description: African works reached Paris largely through colonial collecting and were labeled by people, not artist; named masters like Olowe of Ise were famous in their own lifetimes.

concepts.title: The Alexander Mosaic
concepts.description: A Pompeii floor of about 100 BCE, made of more than a million tesserae, showing Alexander fighting Darius, likely a copy of a lost Greek painting.

concepts.title: The Alhambra
concepts.description: The Nasrid palace-fortress in Granada, named "the red one", with the Court of the Lions, muqarnas ceilings and the motto "There is no victor but God" repeated on its walls.

concepts.title: The lost colors of ancient art
concepts.description: Greek and Roman statues and the Terracotta Army were brightly painted; most of the color has since been lost.

concepts.title: The 1913 Armory Show
concepts.description: The 1913 Armory Show brought European modern art to American crowds in New York, Chicago and Boston; it was mocked and even hanged in effigy, yet about 300,000 people saw it.

concepts.title: Baroque to Neoclassicism on the art clock
concepts.description: On Level 1's one-day clock of art history, everything from Caravaggio to David happens in the last ten minutes before midnight.

concepts.title: What counts as art?
concepts.description: People have disagreed over whether art must imitate nature or may express ideas; the Brancusi case shows the old and new definitions colliding.

concepts.title: The big eras of art
concepts.description: Western art history is told as a run of eras (Stone Age, ancient, medieval, Renaissance, Baroque, modern), each partly answering the one before.

concepts.title: What makes a painting priceless
concepts.description: The Salvator Mundi went from a damaged auction find in 2005 to $450.3 million in 2017, mainly because it was attributed to Leonardo, a disputed attribution.

concepts.title: How auctions set record prices
concepts.description: At auction a price climbs only while rivals keep bidding; the Salvator Mundi sale came down to two bidders, and fame can set records too.

concepts.title: Art to stir faith
concepts.description: After the Council of Trent (1545-63), the Catholic Church wanted clear, dramatic art to strengthen ordinary people's faith, which drove the Baroque.

concepts.title: Pozzo's painted dome
concepts.description: In 1685 Andrea Pozzo painted a fake dome on a flat surface in Sant'Ignazio, Rome; a disc in the floor marks where the illusion works.

concepts.title: Baroque drama
concepts.description: Baroque art, from Italy about 1600, used movement, diagonals and emotion to grab the viewer; the name began as an insult meaning a misshapen pearl.

concepts.title: The 1897 looting and the return debate
concepts.description: British forces looted thousands of works from Benin City in 1897; in 2022 Germany and the Smithsonian transferred ownership of Benin Bronzes to Nigeria, while other museums still hold large collections.

concepts.title: The Benin Bronzes
concepts.description: Court art of the Kingdom of Benin (Edo State, Nigeria): brass plaques for the oba's palace pillars and heads for royal ancestral altars, cast by lost wax by the Igun Eronmwon guild, which still works today.

concepts.title: Bernini's marble in motion
concepts.description: Bernini froze stories mid-action in marble: David about to throw, with the viewer in Goliath's place, and Daphne turning into a tree.

concepts.title: The oldest known drawing
concepts.description: A crosshatch drawn in red ochre on a stone flake at Blombos Cave, South Africa, about 73,000 years old; whether it is art is debated.

concepts.title: The Book of Kells
concepts.description: An illuminated Gospel book of about 800 made by Columban monks at Iona and Kells, famous for its Chi-Rho page, now at Trinity College Dublin.

concepts.title: Bird in Space on trial
concepts.description: In 1926 US customs taxed Brancusi's Bird in Space as metal because it did not look like a bird; in 1928 a court ruled it a work of art.

concepts.title: Showing the Buddha
concepts.description: Early Buddhist art showed the Buddha only through symbols; around the 1st century CE Gandhara and Mathura began showing him in human form.

concepts.title: Byzantine gold mosaics
concepts.description: Byzantine mosaics like Justinian and Theodora at San Vitale set flat, stylized holy and imperial figures against gold glass, read as a spiritual realm rather than a real place.

concepts.title: Byzantine icons and Iconoclasm
concepts.description: An icon is an image of a holy figure, usually painted on a wooden panel; believers honored the person shown, and Byzantine emperors banned icon veneration from about 726 until 843.

concepts.title: Calligraphy as China's highest art
concepts.description: Chinese calligraphy (shufa) has been ranked supreme among China's visual arts since the 3rd century CE; it uses the Four Treasures, allows no touching up and is thought to reveal the writer's character.

concepts.title: Caravaggio's light and real people
concepts.description: Caravaggio's Calling of Saint Matthew uses a beam of light to tell the story, and his saints were modeled on ordinary people, dirty feet and all.

concepts.title: Mary Cassatt
concepts.description: The American Cassatt joined the Impressionists at Degas's invitation and painted women and children with unsentimental directness.

concepts.title: Chauvet
concepts.description: Chauvet Cave in France: about 35,500 years old, full of dangerous animals, drawn with scraped walls, strong outlines and shading.

concepts.title: Chiaroscuro and tenebrism
concepts.description: Chiaroscuro (light-dark) uses light and shadow to make things look solid; tenebrism, its harshest form, was pioneered by Caravaggio.

concepts.title: The color wheel and primary colors
concepts.description: Newton bent the spectrum into a circle; painters' primaries are red, yellow and blue, and mixing two gives a secondary color.

concepts.title: Complementary colors
concepts.description: Complements sit opposite on the color wheel; side by side they make each other look more intense (Chevreul's simultaneous contrast), mixed they make brown.

concepts.title: Balance
concepts.description: Balance is the spread of visual weight in a picture: symmetrical, asymmetrical or radial.

concepts.title: Emphasis and movement
concepts.description: Emphasis creates a focal point by contrast; movement is the path the eye takes, as along the diagonal in Bruegel's Hunters in the Snow.

concepts.title: The rule of thirds
concepts.description: The rule of thirds, named by John Thomas Smith in 1797, places key elements on the lines of a 3 by 3 grid rather than dead center.

concepts.title: Kosuth's One and Three Chairs
concepts.description: Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs (1965) shows a chair as an object, a photo and a dictionary definition.

concepts.title: LeWitt: the idea makes the art
concepts.description: In conceptual art the idea matters most; Sol LeWitt's wall drawings are instructions that other people carry out.

concepts.title: Constable
concepts.description: John Constable painted his native Stour valley, studied skies outdoors, and won a Paris gold medal for The Hay Wain.

concepts.title: The Great Mosque of Córdoba
concepts.description: Begun about 785, its prayer hall is a forest of reused Roman columns carrying two tiers of arches striped in red brick and white stone.

concepts.title: Courbet and Realism
concepts.description: Realism (about 1850-80) showed contemporary, ordinary life without prettying it; Courbet painted a village funeral at history-painting size.

concepts.title: Picasso, Braque and Cubism
concepts.description: Picasso and Braque created Cubism in Paris between 1907 and 1914; a critic's 1908 jibe about 'cubes' named it, Cézanne inspired it, and after 1912 it added collage.

concepts.title: Cubism's many views
concepts.description: Cubism showed several views of an object at once, broken into overlapping planes, and threw out traditional perspective and shading.

concepts.title: Cylinder seals
concepts.description: Mesopotamians carved small stone cylinders that printed a continuous picture when rolled on wet clay, used like a signature.

concepts.title: Duchamp's Fountain and the readymade
concepts.description: In 1917 Duchamp submitted Fountain, a porcelain urinal signed R. Mutt; as a readymade, it became art by the artist's choice, and in 2004 experts voted it the most influential modern artwork.

concepts.title: Dada
concepts.description: Dada began in 1916 at Hugo Ball's Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich, out of disgust with middle-class values and despair over World War I; its name, dada, is French for 'hobby-horse'.

concepts.title: How cave art is dated
concepts.description: Radiocarbon dates once-living material like charcoal; uranium-series dates mineral crusts over paint, giving a minimum age.

concepts.title: Little Dancer Aged Fourteen
concepts.description: Degas's wax Little Dancer (1881) wore a real tutu, ribbon and hair, and outraged viewers used to idealized marble.

concepts.title: Degas and modern life
concepts.description: Degas, who preferred to call himself a realist, painted dancers backstage and Paris cafés from unusual, off-center viewpoints.

concepts.title: AARON
concepts.description: Harold Cohen's AARON, begun in 1973, was a program that made drawings on its own from rules he wrote.

concepts.title: NFT art
concepts.description: In 2021 Beeple's Everydays sold as an NFT, a blockchain token certifying ownership of a digital item, for $69.3 million.

concepts.title: The first computer art
concepts.description: Georg Nees showed computer-drawn graphics in Stuttgart in 1965; his Schotter uses randomness to turn order into chaos.

concepts.title: Painting for the open market
concepts.description: Dutch painters sold ready-made pictures to ordinary households and specialized in subjects like still life to find a niche.

concepts.title: No pictures in Dutch churches
concepts.description: Calvinist teaching banned images in Dutch churches, so painters lost the church commissions that fed art elsewhere.

concepts.title: Egypt's rules: grid and scale
concepts.description: A shared 18-unit grid and size-shows-importance kept Egyptian art consistent for about 3,000 years.

concepts.title: The composite view
concepts.description: Egyptian artists drew each body part from its most complete angle: head in profile, eye and shoulders frontal, legs in profile.

concepts.title: Art for the ka
concepts.description: Egyptians filled tombs with pictures and models of food and daily life so the ka, the life force, would be fed forever.

concepts.title: Tomb models and shabtis
concepts.description: Figures like Meketre's models and shabtis were buried to provide for and work for the dead in the afterlife.

concepts.title: The elements of art
concepts.description: The building blocks of any artwork: line, shape, color, texture and space (many lists add form).

concepts.title: Expressionism
concepts.description: Expressionism shows the emotions things arouse in a person rather than how they objectively look, through distortion and exaggeration; Van Gogh, Munch and Ensor paved the way, and Die Brücke formed in Dresden in 1905.

concepts.title: Munch's The Scream
concepts.description: Munch's The Scream (1893) grew from his account of sensing 'an infinite scream passing through nature' at sunset; its figure covers its ears under a blood-red sky.

concepts.title: Fan Kuan's Travelers among Mountains and Streams
concepts.description: A hanging scroll of about 1000, over 2 meters tall, where a huge mountain dwarfs a tiny mule train; Fan Kuan's signature was found hidden in the leaves in 1958.

concepts.title: Materials betray forgers
concepts.description: Lab tests find materials that did not exist at a painting's supposed date: Bakelite and cobalt blue for van Meegeren, titanium white for Beltracchi.

concepts.title: Han van Meegeren's fake Vermeers
concepts.description: Van Meegeren sold a fake Vermeer to Göring, confessed in 1945 and proved it by painting another under watch.

concepts.title: Fragonard's The Swing
concepts.description: In The Swing (about 1767-68) a woman in pink flies up between an older man and a hidden lover, her slipper in the air: Rococo at its most playful.

concepts.title: Giotto's Arena Chapel
concepts.description: About 1305 Giotto painted the Arena (Scrovegni) Chapel in Padua in fresco, with blue skies instead of gold; Dante noted his fame.

concepts.title: Giotto's solid, feeling figures
concepts.description: Giotto replaced flat Byzantine saints with rounded, weighty bodies that show emotion, as in the Lamentation.

concepts.title: Göbekli Tepe
concepts.description: Carved T-shaped stone pillars built by hunter-gatherers about 11,500 years ago, before farming.

concepts.title: Saint-Denis and the Gothic name
concepts.description: Gothic began with Abbot Suger's choir at Saint-Denis, dedicated in 1144 and meant to fill with light; Renaissance writers later used "Gothic" as an insult.

concepts.title: How Gothic churches soar
concepts.description: Pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses carried the roof's weight to piers and outside supports, so Gothic walls could be thin and full of windows.

concepts.title: Goya's dark turn
concepts.description: Goya rose to first court painter, went deaf after an 1792 illness, and turned to biting satire and, at the end, the Black Paintings on his own walls.

concepts.title: The Third of May 1808
concepts.description: Goya's 1814 painting of French soldiers executing Madrid citizens: a lit man in a white shirt faces a faceless firing squad.

concepts.title: Black-figure vases
concepts.description: Greek painters put figures in black on the red clay and scratched details through the black.

concepts.title: Contrapposto
concepts.description: Greek sculptors learned to rest a figure's weight on one leg, tilting hips and shoulders so the statue looks alive.

concepts.title: The kouros
concepts.description: Archaic Greek statues of young men stood stiff and frontal, left foot forward, in a pose that reflects Egyptian traditions.

concepts.title: The three Greek orders
concepts.description: Greek columns come in three styles: plain Doric, scrolled Ionic and leafy Corinthian.

concepts.title: Red-figure vases
concepts.description: About 530 BCE Athenian painters reversed black-figure: black background, red figures, details painted with a brush.

concepts.title: Hagia Sophia: one building, two faiths
concepts.description: Built as Justinian's church in 532–537, Hagia Sophia became a mosque in 1453, a museum from 1934 and a mosque again in 2020; its mosaics and calligraphy share the space.

concepts.title: Hand stencils
concepts.description: How hand stencils were made by blowing pigment around a hand, and how the Muna stencil's fingers were narrowed into a claw.

concepts.title: Hokusai's Great Wave
concepts.description: Hokusai's Under the Wave off Kanagawa (about 1830–32), from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji: a claw-like wave over three boats, with Fuji small in its hollow.

concepts.title: The hunting magic idea
concepts.description: The idea that animal images were magic for successful hunts, and the Lascaux reindeer problem.

concepts.title: The first Impressionist show
concepts.description: In 1874 painters shut out of the Salon held their own show; a critic mocking Monet's Impression, Sunrise gave them their name.

concepts.title: How Impressionists painted
concepts.description: Impressionists painted outdoors in front of the scene, in dabs of pure color, with complementary colors in the shadows, to catch light at a given moment.

concepts.title: Inca stonework and cloth
concepts.description: Inca builders fitted stones without mortar so tightly a knife blade cannot slip between them, walls that survived Cusco's 1650 earthquake; the finest cloth, qompi, was prized above gold.

concepts.title: Installation art and Kusama's mirror rooms
concepts.description: Installation art fills a whole room you walk into; Kusama's first Infinity Mirror Room (1965) used mirrors to make repeated forms seem endless.

concepts.title: Islamic calligraphy
concepts.description: Calligraphy is the most highly regarded Islamic art because Muslims believe the Qur'an, God's revelation, came in Arabic; the script decorates buildings and objects too.

concepts.title: Islamic geometric pattern
concepts.description: Islamic geometric patterns are built from circles and straight lines with compass and ruler; repeated units can extend without end, which many read as suggesting infinity.

concepts.title: Figures and the mosque
concepts.description: Islamic religious spaces avoid images of people and animals, from the belief that creating living forms belongs to God; figures are common in secular Islamic art.

concepts.title: Japonisme
concepts.description: After Japan reopened to Western trade in the 1850s, Japanese prints flooded Europe; the craze, named Japonisme in the early 1870s, taught artists flat color, bold stylization and asymmetric framing.

concepts.title: Monet, Degas and Van Gogh borrow from Japan
concepts.description: Monet hung over 200 Japanese prints at Giverny and built a print-like bridge; Degas borrowed asymmetry and framing; Van Gogh copied a Hiroshige print in 1887.

concepts.title: Kahlo's self-portraits
concepts.description: Injured in a 1925 bus accident at 18, Kahlo taught herself to paint in bed from a mirror; she painted 55 self-portraits exploring identity, the body and death.

concepts.title: Symbols in Kahlo's paintings
concepts.description: The Two Fridas (1939) pairs European and Tehuana selves joined by an artery; the 1940 thorn-necklace self-portrait uses thorns, a dead hummingbird, a cat and a monkey, symbols read in several ways.

concepts.title: Land art and Spiral Jetty
concepts.description: Land art is made in the landscape itself; Smithson's Spiral Jetty (1970) is a rock coil in Great Salt Lake that sinks and reappears with the water.

concepts.title: Landscape's low rank
concepts.description: The academies ranked subjects: history painting at the top, landscape and still life at the bottom because they lacked human subject matter.

concepts.title: Las Meninas
concepts.description: Velázquez's 1656 painting of the young infanta, her maids of honor and the painter himself at a huge canvas, by the king's own painter.

concepts.title: The mirror in Las Meninas
concepts.description: A mirror reflects the king and queen, leaving open what Velázquez is painting and where the viewer stands: a painting about painting.

concepts.title: Lascaux
concepts.description: The Lascaux cave paintings in France: found in 1940, about 17,000 years old, the Hall of the Bulls, and closed in 1963 after visitors damaged them.

concepts.title: New readings keep art alive
concepts.description: Art lasts when it survives, stays seen and keeps getting new readings, as Auden's and Williams's poems on the Icarus painting show.

concepts.title: The Lion-Man
concepts.description: A mammoth-ivory figure with a lion's head and upright human body, about 40,000 years old, from Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in Germany.

concepts.title: Feldman's four steps
concepts.description: Edmund Burke Feldman's method for looking at art: describe, analyze, interpret, then judge, with judgment held to the end.

concepts.title: Landscape with the Fall of Icarus
concepts.description: In the Icarus painting credited to Bruegel, Icarus is only a pair of legs in the sea while ordinary life goes on; it rewards slow looking and invites several readings.

concepts.title: Slow looking
concepts.description: Museum visitors spend on average only about 27 seconds with each artwork; close looking takes longer.

concepts.title: How manuscripts were illuminated
concepts.description: Medieval books were handwritten on vellum, mostly in monasteries; strictly, illuminated means decorated with gold or silver leaf that was glued down and polished to shine.

concepts.title: Maya stelae
concepts.description: Classic Maya stelae are free-standing carved stone slabs with rulers' portraits and hieroglyphic texts naming them and recording dates and deeds; Copán's are famous.

concepts.title: The Mexica Sun Stone
concepts.description: The basalt Sun Stone, probably carved 1502–1521, found buried in Mexico City in 1790: its central face is debated, it shows the current era 4 Movement, and despite its nickname it cannot tell the date.

concepts.title: Mexican muralism
concepts.description: From 1921 education minister José Vasconcelos commissioned murals on public buildings to teach history to a largely illiterate population; led by los tres grandes, Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros.

concepts.title: Millet's Gleaners
concepts.description: Millet's The Gleaners (1857) shows three peasant women picking up leftover grain, painted with a grandeur that unsettled wealthy viewers.

concepts.title: Carl Andre's bricks
concepts.description: Carl Andre's Equivalent VIII (1966), 120 firebricks bought by the Tate in 1972, set off a public row about Minimalism in 1976.

concepts.title: Minimalism
concepts.description: Minimalism, from 1960s America, used simple geometric shapes, often industrially made, that refer to nothing but themselves.

concepts.title: The dematerialization of art
concepts.description: From the late 1940s on, art moved from paint on canvas toward ideas and instructions; in 1968 critics called this the dematerialization of art.

concepts.title: Monet's series
concepts.description: Monet painted the same motif again and again, grainstacks and then Rouen Cathedral, to catch changing light.

concepts.title: Monet's water lilies
concepts.description: Monet's last subject was his own water-lily pond at Giverny: almost 300 paintings, the largest hung in oval rooms at the Orangerie.

concepts.title: Berthe Morisot
concepts.description: A founding Impressionist, Morisot painted private moments of women and children, like The Cradle, and once outsold Monet and Renoir.

concepts.title: How mosaics are made
concepts.description: Mosaics are pictures built from small closely set pieces called tesserae; Romans laid them on floors across the empire.

concepts.title: How public museums began
concepts.description: From the Tradescants' Ark (1634) to the Ashmolean (1683), the British Museum (1753) and the public Louvre (1793).

concepts.title: What museums do today
concepts.description: ICOM's 2022 definition: a museum researches, collects, conserves, interprets and exhibits heritage for society.

concepts.title: Space and negative space
concepts.description: Space is the area around and between things; the empty part, negative space, has a shape too. Space also means the feeling of depth.

concepts.title: Why Neoclassicism looked back
concepts.description: Digs at Herculaneum and Pompeii and Winckelmann's praise of Greek art turned artists from Rococo toward calm, clear ancient models.

concepts.title: Guimard's Métro entrances
concepts.description: From 1900, Hector Guimard's cast-iron Paris Métro entrances turned plant forms into street furniture; 86 of 141 survive, many lost when the style fell out of fashion.

concepts.title: Art Nouveau's line
concepts.description: Art Nouveau (about 1890–1910) was a deliberate new style of undulating, asymmetrical, plant-like lines, found mostly in architecture, interiors, jewelry, glass, posters and illustration.

concepts.title: The Oath of the Horatii
concepts.description: David's 1784 painting of three Roman brothers swearing to fight for Rome became a manifesto for stern, clear Neoclassical art.

concepts.title: The oldest known art
concepts.description: The oldest reliably dated cave art is a hand stencil on Muna island, Indonesia, at least 67,800 years old; art is far older than writing.

concepts.title: Wang Xizhi's Orchid Pavilion Preface
concepts.description: Wang Xizhi, the Sage of Calligraphy, wrote the Preface to the Orchid Pavilion in 353; legend says the original was buried with Emperor Taizong, so it survives only in copies.

concepts.title: Papunya and Western Desert dot painting
concepts.description: Paintings of Jukurrpa (the Dreaming); the 1971 Honey Ant Dreaming mural at Papunya began the Western Desert movement, where dots came to veil sacred designs; dots are a Western Desert style, not all Aboriginal art.

concepts.title: The Paris Salon
concepts.description: The Salon was France's official, jury-selected art show; rejected artists answered with the Salon des Refusés and independent exhibitions.

concepts.title: The Parthenon
concepts.description: Athena's marble temple in Athens, the high point of the Doric order, built with subtle curves whose purpose is still debated.

concepts.title: Who paid for art, 1600 to 1800
concepts.description: In this chapter three kinds of buyer shaped what got made: the Catholic Church, the Dutch open market, and kings and courtiers.

concepts.title: Ansel Adams and photography in the museum
concepts.description: Adams took Moonrise, Hernandez in 1941 and reprinted it for years with more contrast; in 1940 MoMA founded a department of photography with his help.

concepts.title: Photography arrives
concepts.description: Niépce made the oldest surviving photo in 1826 or 1827; Daguerre's faster daguerreotype was announced in 1839, and painting had to rethink its job.

concepts.title: Muybridge's galloping horse
concepts.description: In 1878 Muybridge's row of cameras showed a galloping horse lifts all four hooves with legs tucked under, disproving painters' "flying gallop".

concepts.title: From Pictorialism to straight photography
concepts.description: Early art photographers made photos look like paintings; in 1932 Group f/64 championed sharp, straight photography instead.

concepts.title: Pop Art's sources
concepts.description: Pop Art, from the 1950s in Britain and America, took its images from ads, packaging, films and comics, and turned away from Abstract Expressionism's personal feelings.

concepts.title: Lichtenstein's comic paintings
concepts.description: Roy Lichtenstein painted single comic panels, imitating cheap printing with black outlines, primary colors and Benday dots, as in Whaam! (1963).

concepts.title: Cézanne's structure
concepts.description: Cézanne turned from Impressionism's effects of light to the underlying structure of natural forms, advising painters to treat nature by the cylinder, the sphere and the cone.

concepts.title: Gauguin's imagined color
concepts.description: In Vision of the Sermon (1888) Gauguin used flat, unnatural color, a red field, to show a vision in the praying women's imagination rather than a real scene.

concepts.title: Post-Impressionism: one name, many directions
concepts.description: Roger Fry named Post-Impressionism in 1910 for painters, including Cézanne, Gauguin, Seurat and Van Gogh, who each took Impressionism in a different direction.

concepts.title: Prussian blue: influence both ways
concepts.description: Prussian blue, invented in Berlin around 1705, reached Japan as bero and colored Hokusai's Fuji series; Europeans then admired it as a Japanese blue. Influence runs in both directions.

concepts.title: Art to record the world
concepts.description: Ideas that early art came from a basic urge to record the world, or served as records such as counts and seasonal calendars.

concepts.title: The Night Watch
concepts.description: Rembrandt's 1642 militia company portrait, named for darkened varnish, turned a stiff group portrait into a scene of light and action.

concepts.title: Rembrandt's self-portraits
concepts.description: About 80 Rembrandt self-portraits survive from 40 years; suggested reasons include practicing expressions, testing light and selling to collectors.

concepts.title: The dome nobody could build
concepts.description: Florence Cathedral, begun in 1296, needed an eight-sided dome about 45 metres wide by 1418; Brunelleschi, a goldsmith, won the job in 1420.

concepts.title: How Brunelleschi built the dome
concepts.description: Brunelleschi built the dome (1420-36) without centering, using a double shell and self-supporting herringbone brickwork; it is still the largest masonry dome.

concepts.title: Dürer's Rhinoceros
concepts.description: Dürer's 1515 Rhinoceros, made without seeing the animal, gave it armor plates and stayed Europe's standard rhino image into the 1700s.

concepts.title: Why the Renaissance began in Florence
concepts.description: Florence, rich from cloth and banking, launched the Renaissance; its 1401 contest for Baptistery doors, won by Ghiberti over Brunelleschi, is often seen as a starting point.

concepts.title: High Renaissance balance
concepts.description: The High Renaissance (1490s-1520s) aimed at balance and harmony, as in Raphael's triangle-based Madonna in the Meadow.

concepts.title: Renaissance humanism
concepts.description: Humanists studied classical Greek and Latin texts and made human nature and dignity their subject, part of the Renaissance's rebirth of antiquity.

concepts.title: Leonardo's notebooks
concepts.description: Thousands of pages of Leonardo's notes survive, in left-handed mirror writing, on anatomy, machines and flight, with drawings leading the words.

concepts.title: Leonardo's painting
concepts.description: Leonardo's Mona Lisa uses sfumato, soft shading with no outlines; his experimental Last Supper began deteriorating in his lifetime.

concepts.title: Linear perspective
concepts.description: Parallel lines receding into a picture converge at one vanishing point on the horizon line; Brunelleschi demonstrated it about 1415 and Alberti wrote it down in 1435.

concepts.title: Masaccio's Holy Trinity
concepts.description: Masaccio's Holy Trinity (1425-27) used linear perspective so a painted vault seems to open a chapel into a flat wall.

concepts.title: The Medici as patrons
concepts.description: The Medici, rich from banking and cloth, paid for art that sometimes pictured them, and Lorenzo took the young Michelangelo into his household.

concepts.title: Michelangelo's David
concepts.description: Michelangelo carved the David (1501-04) from an abandoned block; it shows David before the battle and became a symbol of Florence's republic.

concepts.title: Oil paint versus tempera
concepts.description: Egg tempera dries fast and is shaded by crosshatching; slow-drying oil lets tones blend in thin glazes, a technique van Eyck perfected.

concepts.title: Patrons and contracts
concepts.description: Renaissance art was usually paid for by patrons who set pay, materials, deadline and subject by contract, down to the price of ultramarine blue.

concepts.title: Prints spread images
concepts.description: A block or plate prints the same picture again and again; after Gutenberg's press, prints like Dürer's carried images across Europe.

concepts.title: Woodcut and engraving
concepts.description: A woodcut prints from a raised design left after cutting away wood; an engraving prints from ink held in lines cut into a metal plate.

concepts.title: Naming the Renaissance
concepts.description: Vasari's Lives (1550) described a rinascita of art; 'Renaissance' as the name of an era came from Michelet in 1855.

concepts.title: Raphael's School of Athens
concepts.description: Raphael's School of Athens gathers Greek philosophers in a classical hall, with Plato and Aristotle at the central vanishing point.

concepts.title: The Sistine Chapel ceiling
concepts.description: Michelangelo, a sculptor at heart, painted the Sistine ceiling (1508-12) standing on scaffolding; it includes the Creation of Adam's nearly touching fingers.

concepts.title: Van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait
concepts.description: Van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait (1434) shows a couple in Bruges, a convex mirror reflecting the room, and the signature 'Jan van Eyck was here'.

concepts.title: The Ghent Lamb
concepts.description: Removing 16th-century overpaint from the Ghent Altarpiece in 2019 revealed the van Eycks' strikingly human-faced Lamb.

concepts.title: Reversible conservation
concepts.description: Modern conservators make every treatment reversible; Borja's 2012 amateur touch-up shows what happens without training.

concepts.title: Cleaning varnish
concepts.description: Old varnish discolors into a yellowish fog; conservators remove it to reveal the colors underneath.

concepts.title: Rivera's murals
concepts.description: Rivera's fresco The History of Mexico (1929–35) in the National Palace stairwell, and his 1933 Rockefeller Center mural, destroyed in 1934 after he refused to remove Lenin.

concepts.title: Rococo
concepts.description: Rococo began in early-1700s Paris as a lighter reaction to Louis XIV's Baroque: shell-like curves, pastels and playful love scenes, later attacked as frivolous.

concepts.title: Rome copies Greece
concepts.description: Romans admired Greek art and copied it; some Greek masterpieces survive only as Roman copies.

concepts.title: The Pantheon's dome
concepts.description: Hadrian's Pantheon spans about 43 m in unreinforced concrete, lit by one opening, the oculus.

concepts.title: Verism: warts and all
concepts.description: Roman portrait busts recorded every wrinkle, because an aged face signaled dignity and authority.

concepts.title: Pilgrimage and the Conques tympanum
concepts.description: Pilgrimage churches like Sainte-Foy at Conques drew crowds to relics; its early-12th-century tympanum carves the Last Judgment over the door.

concepts.title: Romanesque churches
concepts.description: Romanesque ("Roman-like") churches of about 1000 to 1150 used round arches and stone barrel vaults, whose outward push demanded thick walls and small windows.

concepts.title: The sublime
concepts.description: Edmund Burke (1757) described the sublime: awe mixed with terror at things vast, rugged and powerful. Romantic painters sought it in nature.

concepts.title: Romanticism
concepts.description: From the late 1700s to the mid-1800s, Romantic artists put emotion, imagination and the individual first, reacting against Enlightenment reason and Neoclassical order.

concepts.title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
concepts.description: Seurat's huge La Grande Jatte (1884–86), about 2 by 3 meters and two years in the making, shows Parisians relaxing on an island in the Seine, built from small strokes of color.

concepts.title: Pointillism: mixing in the eye
concepts.description: Seurat placed small dots of pure, unmixed color side by side so they blend in the viewer's eye from a distance, a method he called chromo-luminarism, now known as pointillism.

concepts.title: Chinese landscape painting
concepts.description: Shan shui ("mountain-water") painting flowered in the Northern Song; painters combined several viewpoints and used unpainted silk for mist.

concepts.title: The spirit world idea
concepts.description: The idea that cave art was symbolic or religious, perhaps tied to shamans and part-human, part-animal beings.

concepts.title: Bernini's St. Peter's Square
concepts.description: Bernini's curving colonnades (1656-67) wrap St. Peter's Square like embracing arms; from two discs, four rows of columns line up as one.

concepts.title: How stained glass was made
concepts.description: Glass was colored with metal oxides while molten, cut into pieces, painted with dark paint fired onto the glass, and held together with strips of lead called cames.

concepts.title: Windows that teach
concepts.description: Chartres' Belle Verrière survived the fire of 1194; Pope Gregory the Great's defense of pictures as books for those who cannot read became the standard Western defense of religious images.

concepts.title: Stonehenge
concepts.description: How Stonehenge was built: dates, where the stones came from, the woodworking joints and the hundreds of people needed.

concepts.title: Gatherings at Stonehenge
concepts.description: Stonehenge's solstice alignment and the midwinter feasts at Durrington Walls, with animals brought from across Britain.

concepts.title: Banksy
concepts.description: Banksy, an anonymous British street artist, works with stencils for speed; in 2018 his Girl with Balloon shredded itself just after it sold at auction.

concepts.title: Street art moves indoors
concepts.description: Keith Haring drew in chalk in the subway and Basquiat wrote SAMO graffiti before both became gallery artists.

concepts.title: The oldest picture story
concepts.description: A scene of three human-like figures and a wild pig at Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi, at least 51,200 years old, dated from mineral crusts over the paint.

concepts.title: Dalí's melting watches
concepts.description: Dalí's small painting The Persistence of Memory (1931) shows soft, melting pocket watches on the Catalan coast, painted realistically so the impossible looks real.

concepts.title: Surrealism and the unconscious
concepts.description: André Breton's 1924 manifesto launched Surrealism, which grew out of Dada and, drawing on Freud, sought art in the unconscious and in dreams.

concepts.title: Magritte's pipe
concepts.description: Magritte's The Treachery of Images (1929) shows a pipe over the words 'This is not a pipe': a picture of a pipe is not a pipe.

concepts.title: Lilies and dogs
concepts.description: White lilies stand for purity and the Virgin Mary; dogs can stand for faithfulness; symbols are clues to interpret, not a fixed code.

concepts.title: Skulls and memento mori
concepts.description: A skull is a memento mori, a reminder of death; vanitas still lifes add symbols of passing pleasures; Holbein hid one in The Ambassadors.

concepts.title: The Terracotta Army
concepts.description: About 8,000 life-size clay soldiers, each with its own face, guard the tomb of China's first emperor.

concepts.title: The Gardner Museum theft
concepts.description: In 1990 thieves dressed as police stole 13 works from Boston's Gardner Museum; unsolved, with empty frames still hanging.

concepts.title: The 1911 Mona Lisa theft
concepts.description: A former Louvre worker stole the Mona Lisa in 1911; the sensation made it world-famous before it was recovered in Florence in 1913.

concepts.title: Turner
concepts.description: J.M.W. Turner painted storms, steam and speed so loosely that sea, sky and light merge.

concepts.title: Ukiyo-e woodblock prints
concepts.description: Ukiyo-e, "pictures of the floating world", were Edo-period Japanese prints of actors, courtesans and landscapes, made cheaply by a team of publisher, artist, carver and printer, with a block per color.

concepts.title: Van Gogh's impasto
concepts.description: Van Gogh laid paint on thickly, squeezing it straight from the tube, so his strokes stand up from the canvas as impasto.

concepts.title: Van Gogh's color for feeling
concepts.description: Van Gogh used color to express emotion, as in The Night Café (1888), where he set red against green to express 'the terrible human passions'.

concepts.title: The Starry Night
concepts.description: Van Gogh, who painted some 900 paintings in about ten years and sold little, painted The Starry Night in 1889 at the Saint-Rémy asylum, from memory of the view from his barred window.

concepts.title: Ice Age figures of women
concepts.description: Small Ice Age carvings of women such as the Venus of Hohle Fels and the Venus of Willendorf, and why their meaning and name are uncertain.

concepts.title: Did Vermeer use a camera obscura?
concepts.description: Vermeer's blurred light spots match what a camera obscura shows, but no document proves he used one, so it stays a debated idea.

concepts.title: Vermeer and The Milkmaid
concepts.description: Only about 36 Vermeers survive; The Milkmaid shows a still kitchen lit from a window, with light built from hundreds of colored dots.

concepts.title: The Factory and the artist as machine
concepts.description: Warhol ran his studio, the Factory, like a production line and said in 1963 that he wanted to be a machine.

concepts.title: Warhol's repeated images
concepts.description: Warhol repeated consumer goods and celebrities, from 32 soup cans to 50 Marilyns, using photographic silkscreen to print the same image again and again.

concepts.title: Ziggurats
concepts.description: Mesopotamian cities built stepped temple towers of mud brick, like the ziggurat of Ur, with a temple on top.

concepts.title: The sky as the first calendar
concepts.description: Ancient cultures tracked the Sun, Moon and stars to mark seasons, plan farming and hold ceremonies.

concepts.title: Andromeda, our big neighbor
concepts.description: Andromeda is the nearest large spiral galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away.

concepts.title: The Apollo Moon landings
concepts.description: Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during six Apollo landings between 1969 and 1972, bringing back 382 kg of samples.

concepts.title: Asterisms: patterns within constellations
concepts.description: Familiar star patterns like the Big Dipper are asterisms, not official constellations.

concepts.title: The asteroid belt
concepts.description: A wide ring of rocky and metallic asteroids between Mars and Jupiter that never formed a planet.

concepts.title: The astronomical unit
concepts.description: The average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km, is the yardstick of the solar system.

concepts.title: The atmosphere gets in the way
concepts.description: Earth’s moving air blurs starlight (stars twinkle) and blocks much of the spectrum, which is why some telescopes go to space.

concepts.title: The Big Bang
concepts.description: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in a hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since.

concepts.title: Binary stars
concepts.description: Many stars orbit partners; watching their orbits lets astronomers weigh stars.

concepts.title: Black holes
concepts.description: A region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape; formed when very massive stars collapse.

concepts.title: Stars that never set
concepts.description: Stars close to the celestial pole circle it and, from mid-northern latitudes, never dip below the horizon.

concepts.title: Galaxy clusters and gravitational lenses
concepts.description: Galaxies gather in clusters whose gravity bends and magnifies the light of galaxies behind them.

concepts.title: The cosmic microwave background
concepts.description: The Big Bang’s leftover light, released about 380,000 years after it began and stretched into microwaves by the expansion.

concepts.title: Comets
concepts.description: Comets are icy bodies that grow a glowing head and tails when they near the Sun; their tails always point away from it.

concepts.title: Constellation stars aren’t neighbors
concepts.description: Stars in the same constellation are usually at very different distances and only line up from our viewpoint.

concepts.title: What constellations are
concepts.description: Constellations are patterns of stars and, officially, 88 regions that together cover the whole sky.

concepts.title: Futures of the Sun, Earth and universe
concepts.description: Earth’s axis will point away from Polaris, the Sun will brighten and swell, galaxies will merge, and accelerating expansion will carry distant galaxies from view.

concepts.title: From atoms to galaxies
concepts.description: Big Bang gas formed stars; stars forged heavier elements and returned them to space, where they built new stars, planets and people.

concepts.title: The cosmic web
concepts.description: On the largest scales, galaxies form a web of filaments and sheets around vast, nearly empty voids.

concepts.title: Dark energy
concepts.description: In 1998 astronomers found the expansion of the universe is speeding up; the unknown cause is called dark energy.

concepts.title: Dark matter
concepts.description: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible matter; an unseen mass, dark matter, outweighs ordinary matter about five to one.

concepts.title: Dwarf planets and Pluto
concepts.description: In 2006 the IAU defined a planet as clearing its orbital neighborhood; Pluto doesn’t, so it’s a dwarf planet.

concepts.title: A year is one orbit
concepts.description: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once, moving at about 30 km per second.

concepts.title: What protects life on Earth
concepts.description: Earth’s magnetic field deflects charged particles from the Sun, and its atmosphere and ozone layer shield the surface.

concepts.title: Earth’s spin makes day and night
concepts.description: Earth rotates on its axis about once every 24 hours; the side facing the Sun has day.

concepts.title: Earth is the third planet
concepts.description: Our solar system has eight planets; Earth is the third from the Sun.

concepts.title: The 400× coincidence
concepts.description: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.

concepts.title: Solar vs lunar eclipses
concepts.description: A solar eclipse is the Moon blocking the Sun; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.

concepts.title: The ecliptic
concepts.description: The Sun’s yearly path across the sky; the Moon and planets stay close to it because the solar system is flat.

concepts.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.description: Visible light is one small band of a spectrum that runs from radio waves to gamma rays; all of it is light traveling at the same speed.

concepts.title: Eratosthenes measures Earth
concepts.description: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes compared noon shadows in two Egyptian cities to estimate Earth’s circumference.

concepts.title: Escape velocity
concepts.description: To leave Earth completely, a spacecraft must reach about 11.2 km per second.

concepts.title: The event horizon
concepts.description: The boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can return; the EHT imaged a black hole’s shadow in 2019.

concepts.title: How we know what we know
concepts.description: Most astronomical knowledge comes from reading the light and other signals the universe sends us.

concepts.title: Finding exoplanets
concepts.description: Most exoplanets are found by the dips in starlight they cause (transits) or the wobble they give their stars.

concepts.title: The first stars and galaxies
concepts.description: After the cosmic dark ages, the first stars, made of only hydrogen and helium, lit up within a few hundred million years.

concepts.title: Galaxy collisions
concepts.description: Galaxies collide and merge; the Milky Way and Andromeda are expected to merge in about 4.5 billion years.

concepts.title: Kinds of galaxies
concepts.description: Galaxies come as spirals, ellipticals and irregulars, a scheme Edwin Hubble introduced.

concepts.title: Galileo’s telescope discoveries
concepts.description: From 1609–1610 Galileo turned a telescope to the sky and found evidence that not everything circles Earth.

concepts.title: The Earth-centered model
concepts.description: For centuries, most scholars placed a motionless Earth at the center, with Ptolemy’s model using small circles (epicycles) to fit planetary motion.

concepts.title: Why an Earth-centered view made sense
concepts.description: We don’t feel Earth moving, and no one could detect stars shifting as Earth orbited.

concepts.title: Gas giants and ice giants
concepts.description: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

concepts.title: Gravitational waves
concepts.description: Ripples in spacetime predicted by Einstein and first detected by LIGO in 2015 from merging black holes.

concepts.title: The habitable zone
concepts.description: The range of distances from a star where a planet could have liquid water on its surface; closer in for dim stars.

concepts.title: The Sun-centered model
concepts.description: Copernicus placed the Sun at the center, with Earth as one of the planets orbiting it.

concepts.title: The heliosphere
concepts.description: The solar wind blows a bubble around the solar system; Voyager 1 crossed its edge in 2012.

concepts.title: Helium was found in the Sun first
concepts.description: Helium was discovered in the Sun’s spectrum in 1868, before it was found on Earth; its name comes from the Greek word for Sun.

concepts.title: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram
concepts.description: A chart of stars’ luminosity against temperature; most fall on a diagonal band, the main sequence.

concepts.title: Hubble’s expanding universe
concepts.description: Hubble showed that other galaxies lie far beyond the Milky Way and that they are moving away from us, faster the farther they are.

concepts.title: The Hubble Space Telescope
concepts.description: Launched in 1990, Hubble orbits above the atmosphere and has made some of astronomy’s sharpest images.

concepts.title: Uranus and Neptune up close
concepts.description: Uranus is tipped on its side; Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system; methane makes both blue.

concepts.title: Infrared astronomy
concepts.description: Infrared light passes through dust, revealing hidden star birth, and captures light from the most distant galaxies.

concepts.title: Jupiter outweighs every other planet combined
concepts.description: Jupiter is the largest planet and has more than twice the mass of all the others put together.

concepts.title: Jupiter’s storms and moons
concepts.description: Jupiter’s Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth; its four large moons are worlds in their own right.

concepts.title: Kepler’s laws
concepts.description: Planets orbit in ellipses, sweep equal areas in equal times, and take longer to orbit the farther out they are.

concepts.title: The Kuiper Belt
concepts.description: A vast ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, home to Pluto and the source of many comets.

concepts.title: Why leap years exist
concepts.description: The extra quarter-day in each orbit adds up, so the calendar adds a day about every four years.

concepts.title: A light-year is a distance
concepts.description: A light-year is how far light travels in a year: about 9.46 trillion km.

concepts.title: The Local Group
concepts.description: The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group, dominated by the Milky Way and Andromeda, with dozens of smaller galaxies.

concepts.title: Brightness versus luminosity
concepts.description: How bright a star looks depends on its true output and its distance; brightness fades with the square of distance.

concepts.title: Lunar craters
concepts.description: The Moon’s craters were blasted out by impacts and survive for billions of years because the Moon has no air, water or plate tectonics to erase them.

concepts.title: The Moon’s dark “seas”
concepts.description: The dark patches on the Moon are maria: huge plains of ancient solidified lava, not water.

concepts.title: A star’s mass sets its life
concepts.description: On the main sequence, more massive stars are hotter and brighter but burn out far faster.

concepts.title: Why Mars is red
concepts.description: Mars looks red because iron oxide, better known as rust, coats its dust and rocks.

concepts.title: Mars once had water
concepts.description: Dry river valleys and lake beds show that liquid water once flowed on Mars; today its water is frozen.

concepts.title: Mercury: extremes without air
concepts.description: The smallest planet and closest to the Sun, Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so it swings from scorching days to frigid nights.

concepts.title: Meteoroids, meteors and meteorites
concepts.description: A meteoroid is space debris, a meteor is its streak of light in our sky, and a meteorite is what reaches the ground.

concepts.title: The Milky Way is our galaxy
concepts.description: The Sun is one of more than a hundred billion stars in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy.

concepts.title: The Milky Way is ~100,000 light-years across
concepts.description: Our galaxy is about 100,000 light-years from edge to edge.

concepts.title: The structure of the Milky Way
concepts.description: A barred spiral with a central bulge, spiral arms, and a halo; the Sun orbits the center about every 230 million years.

concepts.title: The giant-impact origin of the Moon
concepts.description: The leading explanation is that the Moon formed from debris after a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth.

concepts.title: What causes Moon phases
concepts.description: Phases show how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces us; the cycle takes about 29.5 days.

concepts.title: Evidence from Moon rocks
concepts.description: Moon rocks are chemically very similar to Earth’s mantle and the Moon has only a small iron core, consistent with the giant impact.

concepts.title: The Moon always shows us the same face
concepts.description: The Moon is tidally locked: it rotates once per orbit, so the same side always faces Earth.

concepts.title: Each kind of light tells a different story
concepts.description: Astronomers combine radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet and X-ray views, each revealing different objects.

concepts.title: The nearest star after the Sun
concepts.description: Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away, is the closest star to the Sun.

concepts.title: Neptune found by mathematics
concepts.description: Irregularities in Uranus’s orbit led astronomers to predict Neptune’s position; it was found there in 1846.

concepts.title: Neutron stars
concepts.description: The collapsed core left by a supernova: about 20 km across yet more massive than the Sun.

concepts.title: Newton’s law of gravity
concepts.description: One force, universal gravitation, explains falling objects, the Moon’s orbit and Kepler’s laws.

concepts.title: The night sky changes with the seasons
concepts.description: As Earth orbits the Sun, the night side faces different directions in space, so different constellations are visible in different seasons.

concepts.title: The observable universe
concepts.description: We can only see as far as light has traveled since the Big Bang; expansion makes that region about 93 billion light-years across.

concepts.title: Ocean worlds
concepts.description: Some icy moons, like Europa and Enceladus, hide oceans of liquid water beneath their ice, kept liquid by tidal heating.

concepts.title: The Oort Cloud
concepts.description: A vast, distant shell of icy bodies thought to surround the solar system, the source of long-period comets.

concepts.title: The big open questions
concepts.description: Dark matter, dark energy, the Hubble tension, what came before the Big Bang, and life elsewhere remain unsolved.

concepts.title: An orbit is falling around
concepts.description: A spacecraft in orbit is falling toward Earth but moving sideways so fast that it keeps missing.

concepts.title: Measuring star distances with parallax
concepts.description: Nearby stars shift slightly as Earth orbits; the smaller the shift, the farther the star.

concepts.title: Planets wander against the stars
concepts.description: Planets shift position against the background stars from night to night; “planet” comes from the Greek for wanderer.

concepts.title: The North Star marks north
concepts.description: Polaris sits almost directly above Earth’s North Pole, so it barely moves and marks north.

concepts.title: Earth’s wobble changes the pole star
concepts.description: Earth’s axis slowly wobbles over about 26,000 years, so the pole star changes over millennia.

concepts.title: Pulsars
concepts.description: Rapidly spinning neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse.

concepts.title: Quasars and active galaxies
concepts.description: When a galaxy’s central supermassive black hole feeds, its glowing disk can outshine the whole galaxy: a quasar.

concepts.title: Radio astronomy
concepts.description: Radio telescopes detect long-wavelength radio waves, which pass through dust and can be observed day and night.

concepts.title: Red giants and planetary nebulae
concepts.description: When a Sun-like star’s core runs low on hydrogen, it swells into a red giant, then sheds its outer layers as a glowing planetary nebula.

concepts.title: Redshift
concepts.description: Light from receding galaxies is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths; the farther the galaxy, the bigger the redshift.

concepts.title: Three stellar remnants
concepts.description: White dwarfs are Earth-sized, neutron stars city-sized, and black holes have no surface at all.

concepts.title: Retrograde motion
concepts.description: Planets sometimes appear to move backwards against the stars because Earth overtakes or is overtaken by them.

concepts.title: The four rocky planets
concepts.description: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the small, rocky inner planets.

concepts.title: Ancient scholars knew Earth is round
concepts.description: Greek thinkers had evidence Earth is a sphere, such as its curved shadow on the Moon during lunar eclipses.

concepts.title: The black hole at the center of the Milky Way
concepts.description: Sagittarius A* holds about 4 million times the Sun’s mass; stars orbiting it revealed it.

concepts.title: Saturn's rings are ice
concepts.description: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of water ice, with some rock.

concepts.title: The search for life
concepts.description: Scientists look for biosignatures on Mars and ocean moons and in exoplanet atmospheres, and SETI listens for signals.

concepts.title: Seasons aren't about distance
concepts.description: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter.

concepts.title: Seasons come from Earth's tilt
concepts.description: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun.

concepts.title: Every sky motion has a cause
concepts.description: Daily motion comes from Earth’s spin, yearly changes from Earth’s orbit, and the Moon’s motion and gravity drive phases, eclipses and tides.

concepts.title: Why everything rises in the east
concepts.description: Earth spins west to east, so the Sun, Moon, planets and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

concepts.title: How the solar system formed
concepts.description: About 4.6 billion years ago a spinning cloud of gas and dust collapsed into the Sun and a flat disk that built the planets.

concepts.title: The size of the solar system
concepts.description: The planets span about 30 astronomical units; sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune.

concepts.title: Solar storms and space weather
concepts.description: The solar wind and eruptions like flares and coronal mass ejections cause auroras and can disrupt technology.

concepts.title: Spectral fingerprints
concepts.description: Each element absorbs and emits its own set of colors, so a spectrum reveals what a star is made of.

concepts.title: Spring and neap tides
concepts.description: When the Sun and Moon line up tides are larger (spring); at right angles they are smaller (neap).

concepts.title: A star's color is its temperature
concepts.description: Blue stars are the hottest; red stars are the coolest.

concepts.title: Where stars are born
concepts.description: Stars form in cold, dense clouds of gas and dust, where gravity pulls clumps together until fusion ignites.

concepts.title: Stars are born, age and die
concepts.description: Stars form in clouds of gas and dust. The Sun will swell into a red giant and end as a white dwarf; massive stars can explode as supernovae.

concepts.title: Navigating by the stars
concepts.description: Before instruments, navigators crossed oceans by memorizing where stars rise and set.

concepts.title: Mass decides a star’s fate
concepts.description: Low-mass stars end as white dwarfs; the most massive leave neutron stars or black holes.

concepts.title: Proof that Earth moves
concepts.description: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured stellar parallax, direct evidence that Earth orbits the Sun.

concepts.title: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old
concepts.description: The Sun formed roughly 4.6 billion years ago.

concepts.title: The Sun runs on nuclear fusion
concepts.description: In its core the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, releasing the energy that becomes sunlight.

concepts.title: The Sun is a star
concepts.description: The Sun is an ordinary star (the closest one to Earth), not a special category of object.

concepts.title: Inside the Sun
concepts.description: Energy made in the Sun’s core travels out through the radiative and convective zones to the photosphere; the corona above is far hotter.

concepts.title: The Sun holds almost all the mass
concepts.description: About 99.8% of the solar system's mass is in the Sun.

concepts.title: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth
concepts.description: Light from the Sun takes roughly eight minutes to cross the distance to Earth, so we always see the Sun slightly in the past.

concepts.title: Sunspots and the solar cycle
concepts.description: Sunspots are cooler, magnetically active regions whose number rises and falls over an ~11-year cycle.

concepts.title: Supernovae and star stuff
concepts.description: Massive stars explode as supernovae, scattering elements forged inside stars, including those in our bodies.

concepts.title: Bigger is better
concepts.description: A telescope’s light-gathering area sets how faint it can see and how fine the detail it can show.

concepts.title: Refractors and reflectors
concepts.description: Refracting telescopes use lenses; reflecting telescopes use mirrors, and all the largest telescopes are reflectors.

concepts.title: The Moon drives the tides
concepts.description: The Moon’s gravity pulls Earth’s oceans into two bulges, so most coasts get two high tides a day.

concepts.title: Titan
concepts.description: Saturn’s largest moon has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.

concepts.title: Billions of galaxies, 13.8 billion years
concepts.description: The observable universe holds billions of galaxies and is about 13.8 billion years old.

concepts.title: The discovery of Uranus
concepts.description: William Herschel found Uranus in 1781, the first planet discovered with a telescope.

concepts.title: Venus is the hottest planet
concepts.description: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.

concepts.title: Venus: Earth’s twin in size only
concepts.description: Venus is nearly Earth’s size but has crushing pressure, acid clouds and a backwards rotation.

concepts.title: The Voyager probes
concepts.description: Launched in 1977, the twin Voyagers toured the giant planets; Voyager 1 is now in interstellar space.

concepts.title: The James Webb Space Telescope
concepts.description: Launched in 2021, Webb is a huge infrared telescope with a 6.5-meter gold-coated mirror, orbiting the Sun about 1.5 million km from Earth.

concepts.title: White dwarfs
concepts.description: The leftover core of a Sun-like star: about the size of Earth, with much of the Sun’s mass, slowly cooling.

concepts.title: What makes an acid
concepts.description: Acids taste sour (the word comes from Latin for sour) and, in water, hand off hydrogen ions (protons): lemons, vinegar and stomach acid all contain acids.

concepts.title: What causes acid rain, and how it was cut
concepts.description: Acid rain, first described by Robert Angus Smith in 1852, comes mostly from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fossil fuels; it harms lakes, forests and stone. US power plant SO2 fell 96 percent from 1990 to 2023.

concepts.title: How acidic acid rain is
concepts.description: Normal rain is already slightly acidic (about pH 5.6) from carbonic acid; acid rain usually measures 4.2 to 4.4, more than ten times as acidic.

concepts.title: Strong and weak acids
concepts.description: A strong acid such as hydrochloric acid ionizes almost completely in water; a weak acid such as the acetic acid in vinegar ionizes only a little.

concepts.title: What alchemists were trying to do
concepts.description: Alchemists tried to turn base metals such as lead or copper into gold or silver, hoped to make a philosophers' stone that would do it, and sought cures and longer life.

concepts.title: What alchemy left to chemistry
concepts.description: Alchemists never made gold, but they built and described laboratory apparatus and techniques (distillation, sublimation, filtration, the alembic, the hot-water bath) and left chemistry its name and several words.

concepts.title: Alkalis, from plant ashes
concepts.description: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, such as sodium or potassium hydroxide. The word first meant plant ashes; strong alkalis are caustic.

concepts.title: 1886: electricity frees aluminum
concepts.description: In 1886 Hall and Heroult independently found how to make aluminum by electrolysis of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite; by 1891 it cost under $1 a pound.

concepts.title: Aluminum: plentiful but locked away
concepts.description: Aluminum is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust, about 8 percent, but it is so chemically active that it never occurs as a metal in nature. It is about one-third as dense as iron or copper.

concepts.title: When aluminum outshone gold
concepts.description: In the mid-1800s aluminum was more valuable than gold; Napoleon III gave his most important guests aluminum cutlery while others ate with silver.

concepts.title: Antacids neutralize stomach acid
concepts.description: Antacids are bases: milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide) and calcium carbonate neutralize some of the stomach's hydrochloric acid.

concepts.title: The electron cloud
concepts.description: Electrons do not circle the nucleus like planets. Since Schrodinger (1926), they are described as waves occupying orbitals: regions where an electron is most likely to be found.

concepts.title: Electron shells
concepts.description: Electrons can sit only at certain energy levels, called shells (Bohr, 1913). The first shell holds up to 2 electrons and the second up to 8, and electrons fill the lowest-energy shell first.

concepts.title: The atom is mostly empty space
concepts.description: The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller across than the atom: a blueberry in a football stadium. Electrons fill almost all the volume, yet the nucleus holds nearly all the mass.

concepts.title: Atoms and the void
concepts.description: Democritus pictured atoms moving through empty space, differing only in shape, arrangement, position and size, like letters that build every word.

concepts.title: The ancient Greek idea of atoms
concepts.description: Leucippus and Democritus reasoned, without experiments, that cutting matter must stop at uncuttable particles, atoms. Aristotle disagreed, and a scientific atomic theory came only in the 1800s.

concepts.title: Why light microscopes cannot see atoms
concepts.description: A light microscope cannot separate details closer than about half the wavelength of light, about 200 nanometers at best, a limit set by physics. Atoms are about 2,000 times smaller.

concepts.title: The nucleus holds the mass
concepts.description: Protons and neutrons have almost the same mass and are far heavier than electrons, so nearly all of an atom's mass is in its nucleus.

concepts.title: How small an atom is
concepts.description: An atom is on the order of a ten-billionth of a meter across: about 50 million in a row make a centimeter.

concepts.title: The scanning tunneling microscope
concepts.description: The STM (Binnig and Rohrer, IBM, 1981) maps single atoms by scanning a one-atom-wide tip just above a surface and tracking a tunneling current. In 1989 it spelled IBM in 35 xenon atoms.

concepts.title: Protons, neutrons and electrons
concepts.description: Atoms are built from positive protons and neutral neutrons in the nucleus, with negative electrons around it. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, and the proton count identifies the element.

concepts.title: The outer shell
concepts.description: Neon's 10 electrons fill two shells exactly; sodium's 11 are arranged 2, 8, 1. The outermost (valence) shell decides how an atom behaves chemically.

concepts.title: What makes a base
concepts.description: Bases taste bitter and feel slippery; soap, baking soda, ammonia cleaners and lye are bases. A base accepts hydrogen ions, often by releasing hydroxide ions into water.

concepts.title: Acids and bases inside batteries
concepts.description: A car's lead-acid battery uses sulfuric acid and an alkaline battery uses potassium hydroxide as the electrolyte, which carries ions inside the battery; in a lemon battery the lemon's acid plays that role.

concepts.title: A battery is a reaction split in two
concepts.description: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy: electrons leave the anode, travel through the outside circuit and are taken up at the cathode. Recharging runs the reaction backward.

concepts.title: Boiling points depend on pressure
concepts.description: Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at sea-level pressure. Boiling happens when the vapor pushes back as hard as the air pressing down, so with less air pressure (up a mountain) water boils cooler, about 90 °C in Leadville, Colorado.

concepts.title: Reading bonds from properties
concepts.description: A solid's properties hint at its bonding: ionic solids are hard, brittle, high-melting and conduct only melted or dissolved; metals conduct as solids and bend; molecular substances are often gases, liquids or low-melting solids.

concepts.title: Boyle and experimental chemistry
concepts.description: In The Sceptical Chymist (1661) Boyle attacked older Aristotelian ideas about what matter is made of; his reliance on experiment earned him the name 'father of chemistry', though he also pursued alchemy all his life.

concepts.title: Boyle's law
concepts.description: At constant temperature, the volume of a trapped gas is inversely proportional to its pressure: double the pressure and the volume halves. Boyle published it in 1662 after air-pump experiments with Robert Hooke.

concepts.title: The Bronze Age
concepts.description: The Bronze Age saw the first widespread use of metal, bronze, for tools and weapons; from about 1000 BCE iron working brought it to an end.

concepts.title: Bronze: copper plus tin
concepts.description: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, first made deliberately about 3500 BCE. It is harder than copper and melts more readily, so it casts well; bell metal has extra tin.

concepts.title: Diamond and graphite: one element, two forms
concepts.description: Diamond and graphite are the two most common allotropes of carbon: both pure carbon, with the atoms arranged differently.

concepts.title: Carbon, the element of life
concepts.description: All living things are made mostly of carbon compounds. Organic molecules have carbon as their main element, bonded to hydrogen and other carbon atoms.

concepts.title: Carbon's enormous family of compounds
concepts.description: Carbon is only a trace in Earth's crust, yet it forms more compounds than all other elements combined: close to ten million known, and perhaps 10^60 possible.

concepts.title: What carbon dating can and cannot date
concepts.description: Carbon dating works only on once-living things, from about 500 to 50,000 years old. Dinosaurs are far too old.

concepts.title: How carbon dating works
concepts.description: Cosmic rays make carbon-14 in the air; living things take it in through the food chain. After death the intake stops and carbon-14 decays with a half-life of about 5,730 years, so what remains tells the time since death.

concepts.title: Carbon links to four atoms
concepts.description: A carbon atom can form up to four strong bonds, including bonds to other carbon atoms, so carbon builds chains, branched chains and rings of many sizes.

concepts.title: How catalysts work
concepts.description: A catalyst opens a different route for a reaction with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed. It does not change the reactants or products.

concepts.title: Catalysts
concepts.description: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up, so it can keep working. Berzelius named the effect catalysis in 1835. Substances in a wound make hydrogen peroxide foam as it rapidly breaks down.

concepts.title: Catalytic converters
concepts.description: Gasoline cars carry catalytic converters in which metals such as platinum and rhodium turn carbon monoxide, unburned fuel and nitrogen oxides into carbon dioxide, water vapor, nitrogen and oxygen.

concepts.title: Chemistry, the central science
concepts.description: Chemistry is called the central science because it connects to so many other fields, from biology (through biochemistry) to medicine, materials and the environment.

concepts.title: Gray areas between the two kinds of change
concepts.description: The line between physical and chemical change is not perfectly sharp. Dissolving salt is usually called physical, yet some chemists argue otherwise; and reversibility is no sure test, since a rechargeable battery reverses a chemical change.

concepts.title: Chemical change
concepts.description: In a chemical change at least one new substance forms: rusting, burning, cooking meat, a banana browning. Chemical changes are often harder to undo.

concepts.title: What chemistry studies
concepts.description: Chemistry is the study of matter: what it is made of (composition), how it looks and behaves (properties) and how it changes when it meets other matter (interactions).

concepts.title: Chemistry began in kitchens and workshops
concepts.description: People practiced chemistry long before it was a science: controlling fire to cook, fire pottery and smelt metals, and fermenting food and drink.

concepts.title: Combustion
concepts.description: Burning (combustion) is a reaction between a fuel and oxygen that gives off heat and usually light. Fuels made of carbon and hydrogen burn mainly to carbon dioxide and water; with too little oxygen they can make toxic carbon monoxide. In a candle, it is the wax vapor that burns.

concepts.title: The fire triangle
concepts.description: A fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat at once. Remove any one and it goes out: water removes heat, smothering removes oxygen, a firebreak removes fuel.

concepts.title: Copper, the first metal
concepts.description: Copper occurs as free metal, so it was one of the first metals people used, around 8000 BCE. It is second only to silver as a conductor and mostly goes into electrical uses.

concepts.title: Strong inside, loose outside
