concepts.description: Covalent bonds inside a molecule are strong, but the pulls between molecules are much weaker, so covalent substances melt and boil far lower than ionic ones. Melting or boiling water separates whole molecules; the bonds inside stay intact.

concepts.title: Single, double and triple bonds
concepts.description: Atoms can share one, two or three pairs of electrons. Hydrogen has a single bond, oxygen gas a double bond and nitrogen gas a triple bond, so strong that nitrogen, about 78 percent of the air, barely reacts.

concepts.title: Covalent bonds: sharing electrons
concepts.description: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. Identical atoms share equally; different atoms share unequally, making a polar bond. Hydrogen, nitrogen, water and all organic compounds are held this way.

concepts.title: What makes a crystal
concepts.description: A crystal is a solid whose particles sit in a pattern that repeats in every direction, and its outside often shows it: salt grains are cubes, and snowflakes have six-fold symmetry from ice's hexagonal arrangement.

concepts.title: How crystals grow
concepts.description: Crystals grow as particles join the pattern, from a solution, a cooling melt or a vapor (frost). Slow growth makes larger crystals: Naica's 11-meter gypsum crystals grew for hundreds of thousands of years in water at a steady temperature.

concepts.title: Marie Curie's new elements
concepts.description: Curie named radioactivity, found pitchblende more radioactive than uranium, and with Pierre Curie announced polonium and radium in 1898; she won Nobel Prizes in physics (1903) and chemistry (1911).

concepts.title: Isolating radium
concepts.description: To prove radium was a real element Curie needed it in a demonstrable amount; tracking radioactivity through her separations, she got a tenth of a gram of almost pure radium chloride from several tons of ore.

concepts.title: Dalton's atomic theory
concepts.description: Dalton proposed that all matter is made of atoms, that each element has its own kind of atom with a characteristic mass, that compounds join atoms in small whole-number ratios, and that chemical changes rearrange atoms without creating or destroying them.

concepts.title: Dalton's road from weather to atoms
concepts.description: Dalton kept daily weather records for 57 years; studying the gases of the air, and how each gas in a mixture acts independently, led him to atomism.

concepts.title: Density
concepts.description: Density is mass divided by volume: how much mass is packed into each bit of space. Water is about 1 gram per cubic centimeter.

concepts.title: Float or sink
concepts.description: An object floats if its average density is less than the liquid's and sinks if it is denser. Weight alone does not decide it: a big log floats while a small iron nail sinks.

concepts.title: Why diamond is so hard
concepts.description: In diamond every carbon atom is bonded to four others in a three-dimensional network, making it the hardest known natural substance. Diamonds form deep in the mantle.

concepts.title: The elements inside a phone
concepts.description: Old phones hold recoverable metals: a million recycled phones can yield about 35 thousand pounds of copper, 772 pounds of silver and 75 pounds of gold. Gold plates contacts because it conducts well and never tarnishes.

concepts.title: What an explosion is
concepts.description: An explosion is a rapid release of energy that makes a large volume of expanding gas in a very short time. Many are combustion sped up: the difference from a fire is speed.

concepts.title: Dust explosions
concepts.description: Ordinary combustible materials like sugar, flour or wood can burn rapidly when finely divided and explode when the dust hangs in air, because every grain is exposed. A 2008 sugar dust explosion in Georgia killed 14 workers.

concepts.title: Deflagration and detonation
concepts.description: In a deflagration the reaction moves through the material slower than sound (gunpowder, a low explosive, burns this way). In a detonation a supersonic shock wave sets the material off as it goes (high explosives).

concepts.title: Why each metal glows its own color
concepts.description: The heat of the burning firework gives electrons in the metal atoms extra energy; as they drop back they release light, and the size of the drop, which differs for each element, sets the color.

concepts.title: Firework colors come from metals
concepts.description: Fireworks began more than a thousand years ago, most likely in China, and were long only orange. In the 1800s chemists added compounds for color: strontium red, barium green, copper blue, sodium yellow. Blue is the hardest.

concepts.title: One atom changes the substance
concepts.description: Change one count and you change the substance: O2 is the oxygen you breathe, O3 is ozone, an irritating toxic gas; H2O is water, H2O2 is a bleach and antiseptic. Salt's formula NaCl is a ratio of ions, not a molecule.

concepts.title: Reading a chemical formula
concepts.description: A formula names each kind of atom by its symbol and counts it with a subscript; no subscript means one. H2O is two hydrogens and one oxygen; CO2 is one carbon and two oxygens.

concepts.title: Credit for DNA's structure
concepts.description: Wilkins showed Photo 51 to Watson without Franklin's knowledge; her own paper ran in the same 1953 issue of Nature as Watson and Crick's; she died in 1958, before the 1962 Nobel, which is not awarded after death.

concepts.title: Photo 51
concepts.description: In May 1952 Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling made Photo 51, a 62-hour exposure whose X-shaped pattern showed DNA's strands are helical.

concepts.title: X-ray diffraction
concepts.description: Rosalind Franklin used X-ray diffraction at King's College London: X-rays scatter off the atoms of a crystal at angles that reveal how the atoms are arranged.

concepts.title: Gold and silver as money
concepts.description: Some of the earliest coins, from Lydia, used electrum, a natural gold-silver mix; King Croesus switched to pure gold and silver coins.

concepts.title: Gold ignores oxygen and sulfur
concepts.description: Gold is one of the least reactive metals: unaffected by oxygen or sulfur, it never corrodes or tarnishes, is found fairly pure in nature, and is the most malleable element.

concepts.title: Why graphite is soft and slippery
concepts.description: Graphite's carbon atoms lie in flat sheets of hexagons held together only weakly, so the sheets slide apart: soft, good for pencils, and able to conduct electricity.

concepts.title: Atom economy
concepts.description: Atom economy asks that a reaction's final product contain as much of the starting materials as possible; BHC's ibuprofen route cut six steps to three and raised atom use from under 40 to about 80 percent.

concepts.title: Green chemistry: prevent, don't clean up
concepts.description: Green chemistry designs chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances, preventing pollution at its source rather than cleaning it up afterward.

concepts.title: Half-life
concepts.description: A half-life is the time for half the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay. After two half-lives a quarter remain. Half-lives range from seconds to billions of years.

concepts.title: Baking soda and baking powder
concepts.description: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when moistened and heated, much more with an acidic ingredient; baking powder packs its own acid with the soda.

concepts.title: Yeast makes bread rise
concepts.description: Yeast ferments sugars in dough into carbon dioxide and alcohol; gluten traps the gas, the oven expands it, kills the yeast and drives off most of the alcohol.

concepts.title: Caramelization
concepts.description: Heat alone breaks sugar down into new brown, flavorful compounds; unlike the Maillard reaction, no protein is involved.

concepts.title: Why bleach must never be mixed
concepts.description: Household bleach (sodium hypochlorite) mixed with ammonia makes toxic chloramine gases; mixed with acids, it releases chlorine gas. Both harm the eyes, nose, throat and lungs.

concepts.title: Safe habits with cleaners
concepts.description: Health agencies advise never mixing bleach with other cleaners, ventilating and following labels; after breathing fumes, get to fresh air and call a poison center.

concepts.title: How dyes make color
concepts.description: A dye colors a material by absorbing some colors of light and reflecting the rest; the reflected light is the color you see.

concepts.title: Mordants fix dyes
concepts.description: Some dyes need a mordant, a metal salt that soaks into the fiber and reacts with the dye to form a less soluble form held to the cloth. The name comes from Latin mordere, to bite.

concepts.title: Perkin's mauve, the first synthetic dye
concepts.description: In 1856 the 18-year-old William Henry Perkin, trying to make quinine from coal-tar chemicals, made mauve instead: the first commercialized synthetic dye. Before that, dyes came from plants and animals.

concepts.title: Fuels store chemical energy
concepts.description: Fuels store chemical energy in the bonds of their molecules; burning converts it to heat. Natural gas is odorless, so a smelly chemical is added to reveal leaks.

concepts.title: Hydrocarbon fuels
concepts.description: Gasoline and natural gas are hydrocarbons, compounds of only carbon and hydrogen. Natural gas is mostly methane (CH4). Gasoline is made from crude oil, first separated by distillation.

concepts.title: Glass is an amorphous solid
concepts.description: Molten glass is cooled too fast for crystals to form, so its particles freeze in a disordered jumble: an amorphous solid. Old panes thicker at the bottom are not proof that glass flows.

concepts.title: Making glass from sand
concepts.description: Glass is mostly sand (silica), which melts only above 1,700 °C. Soda lowers the melting point but makes glass that dissolves in water; lime makes it insoluble again: soda-lime glass.

concepts.title: Hard water and soap scum
concepts.description: Calcium and magnesium in hard water react with soap to form insoluble scum, wasting soap. Detergents work like soap but are made from petroleum and don't form scum, so they work in hard water.

concepts.title: The Maillard reaction
concepts.description: When food is heated, its sugars react with the amino acids of proteins, browning it and creating new flavors and aromas. A wet surface stays near water's boiling point, so browning waits until it dries.

concepts.title: How plastic is recycled
concepts.description: Recycling sorts plastics by type, grinds them into flakes, washes them, separates them by density in water and melts them into pellets. Heat and grinding shorten polymer chains, so quality drops.

concepts.title: Plastics that remelt and plastics that don't
concepts.description: Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be remelted and reshaped, so they recycle readily. Thermosets cross-link as they harden and cannot be remelted.

concepts.title: Diffusion carries smells
concepts.description: Molecules spread from where they are concentrated to where they are sparse (diffusion). Gas molecules are fast but collide constantly, so a smell's journey is a slow zigzag.

concepts.title: Smells are airborne molecules
concepts.description: Smelling is detecting chemicals in the air, so only substances that release molecules into the air (volatile ones) have a smell. Warmth helps more molecules escape.

concepts.title: Micelles carry grease away
concepts.description: Soap tails dive into grease while heads face the water; soap molecules surround the grease in clusters called micelles, which stay suspended and rinse away.

concepts.title: The two-ended soap molecule
concepts.description: Water alone can't lift grease. A soap molecule has a water-attracting head and an oil-attracting tail, so it can hold both; soap itself is made from fats or oils and an alkali.

concepts.title: Hydrangeas and soil pH
concepts.description: Hydrangeas bloom blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil, because acidic soil makes aluminum available and aluminum turns the flowers blue.

concepts.title: Hydrogen, the lightest gas
concepts.description: Hydrogen gas is the lightest of all gases, about 14 times less dense than air, so it rises fast and can escape from the top of Earth's atmosphere.

concepts.title: Hydrogen, the universe's most common element
concepts.description: Hydrogen is the simplest and most abundant element in the universe: more than 90 percent of all atoms and about three-quarters of ordinary matter by mass.

concepts.title: Hydrogen, the water maker
concepts.description: On Earth most hydrogen is bound in water. Cavendish showed in 1766 that it is a distinct substance; it burns with oxygen to form water, hence Lavoisier's name, meaning maker of water.

concepts.title: Why ice floats
concepts.description: Frozen water molecules lock into an open, spread-out pattern, so ice is only about 90 percent as dense as liquid water, and it floats. Salty seawater is denser still.

concepts.title: Acid-base indicators
concepts.description: An indicator changes color with pH. Red cabbage anthocyanins run from red (acid) through purple (neutral) to greenish-yellow (base); litmus, from lichens, turns red in acid and blue in base.

concepts.title: Ionic bonds: a trade of electrons
concepts.description: In table salt, each sodium atom gives one electron to a chlorine atom, making a positive sodium ion and a negative chloride ion. The attraction between opposite charges is the ionic bond.

concepts.title: Salt: a grid of ions, not molecules
concepts.description: Sodium chloride has no molecules: its ions form a three-dimensional grid, each surrounded by six of the opposite charge. It melts only at 801 °C, but water pulls its ions apart when it dissolves.

concepts.title: Iron in your blood
concepts.description: Most of the body's iron is in hemoglobin, the blood protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body.

concepts.title: Iron: the planet's metal
concepts.description: Iron is the most abundant element in Earth as a whole (about 35 percent), mostly in the core; it is fourth in the crust and the most-used, cheapest metal.

concepts.title: Steel: iron plus a little carbon
concepts.description: Pure iron is soft. Steel is iron with up to about 2 percent carbon, far harder and the world's main building material; cast iron, with 2 to 4 percent carbon, is brittle.

concepts.title: Isotopes
concepts.description: Isotopes are atoms of one element (same protons) with different numbers of neutrons, and so different masses: carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14.

concepts.title: Isotopes share their chemistry
concepts.description: Isotopes of an element behave almost identically in chemistry, because they have the same protons and electrons. Their name, Greek for "same place", dates from 1913.

concepts.title: Lavoisier's names and list of elements
concepts.description: In 1787 Lavoisier and colleagues published a naming method still at the base of chemical names; oxygen and hydrogen replaced old names; his 1789 textbook listed 33 elements, including light and caloric.

concepts.title: Lavoisier overturns phlogiston
concepts.description: Phlogiston theory said burnable things lost phlogiston when they burned. Lavoisier showed that burned metals gain mass because oxygen from the air combines with them.

concepts.title: From willow bark to aspirin
concepts.description: Willow bark was an ancient remedy; chemists isolated salicin, modified salicylic acid into gentler acetylsalicylic acid in 1897, and learned in 1971 that it blocks prostaglandin production.

concepts.title: Energy in small change: ATP
concepts.description: Cells release food's energy in small steps instead of one burst, capturing it in ATP, the cell's energy currency.

concepts.title: The big four elements of life
concepts.description: Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen make up about 96 percent of the human body's mass and are common to all living things.

concepts.title: Carbohydrates and glucose
concepts.description: Carbohydrates are built from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen with the general formula (CH2O)n; glucose, C6H12O6, is an important fuel for the body.

concepts.title: Cellular respiration
concepts.description: Cells combine glucose with oxygen, mostly in mitochondria, releasing energy and giving off carbon dioxide and water; the carbon you breathe out came from your food.

concepts.title: The dose makes the poison
concepts.description: Paracelsus taught that whether a substance harms depends on the dose; by that principle even water is poisonous in a large enough amount.

concepts.title: Designing and testing medicines
concepts.description: Chemists can design a drug to fit a target enzyme's shape, as with HIV protease inhibitors (first used in 1995); new drugs are then tested in people in phases, starting with safety and dosage.

concepts.title: Active sites: a fit, not a force
concepts.description: A substrate binds in the enzyme's active site, so each enzyme is specific; the picture moved from Fischer's lock and key (1894) to Koshland's induced fit (1958). Heat and extreme pH can denature enzymes.

concepts.title: Enzymes, the catalysts of life
concepts.description: Enzymes are catalysts, nearly all proteins, that speed up reactions by lowering the energy needed to start them and are left unchanged; salivary amylase breaks starch into sugars.

concepts.title: Why the body needs fat
concepts.description: Fat stores the most energy per gram, insulates, builds cell membranes and carries the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

concepts.title: What a fat is
concepts.description: A fat is glycerol with three fatty acids. Fats do not dissolve in water; straight saturated chains pack into solids, kinked unsaturated chains stay liquid.

concepts.title: Oxygen by mass, hydrogen by headcount
concepts.description: Oxygen is the body's top element by mass because it sits in the body's water and its atoms are heavy; counted atom by atom, light hydrogen is the most common.

concepts.title: The photosynthesis equation
concepts.description: Using light captured by chlorophyll, plants turn six carbon dioxide and six water molecules into one glucose and six oxygen molecules; the oxygen comes from the water.

concepts.title: Plants are built from air
concepts.description: Van Helmont's willow gained 164 pounds while its soil lost about 2 ounces; he credited water, but most of a plant's building material is carbon taken from carbon dioxide in the air.

concepts.title: Plants respire too
concepts.description: Plant cells have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts: plants make sugar by photosynthesis and burn some of it in cellular respiration for ATP.

concepts.title: Poison or medicine: the foxglove
concepts.description: Foxglove is toxic, yet in 1785 William Withering showed that small, carefully adjusted doses treated the swelling of heart failure; digitalis drugs are still prescribed.

concepts.title: Proteins are chains of amino acids
concepts.description: A protein is a chain of hundreds or thousands of amino acids drawn from 20 types, in an order set by a gene.

concepts.title: A protein's shape is its job
concepts.description: Proteins fold into shapes that set their jobs, from keratin in hair to enzymes; heat and chemicals can unfold them for good (denaturation).

concepts.title: Starch, glycogen and cellulose
concepts.description: Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all chains of glucose. Plants store starch and animals store glycogen, but human enzymes cannot break the links in cellulose.

concepts.title: Mass is not weight
concepts.description: Mass is the amount of matter in something; weight is the pull of gravity on it. On the Moon an astronaut weighs one-sixth as much but has the same mass.

concepts.title: Nylon
concepts.description: Wallace Carothers's DuPont team invented nylon in 1935 as a synthetic silk made from widely available compounds; nylon stockings launched in 1939, and in the war nylon went into parachutes.

concepts.title: Teflon, found by accident
concepts.description: In 1938 Roy Plunkett found that tetrafluoroethylene gas in a cylinder had turned into a white solid: no gas came out, but the cylinder weighed the same. The solid, Teflon, is heat resistant, inert and slippery.

concepts.title: What counts as matter
concepts.description: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space: an ant, a truck, a galaxy, and invisible air too.

concepts.title: What melting and boiling do to particles
concepts.description: Heating gives particles more energy. Enough energy frees them from fixed places (melting) or from their neighbors entirely (boiling). While a substance changes state, its temperature holds steady.

concepts.title: Why metals conduct and bend
concepts.description: Free electrons let metals conduct electricity; solid salt can't, because its ions are locked in place. Hammered, a metal's layers slide while the electron sea keeps them bonded, but a salt crystal's shifted layers push like charges together and it shatters.

concepts.title: Metallic bonds: a sea of electrons
concepts.description: In a metal, atoms pack tightly and their outer electrons roam freely through the whole piece, a sea of electrons around positive ions. The attraction between the ions and that shared sea is the metallic bond.

concepts.title: Mixtures and pure substances
concepts.description: A mixture is two or more kinds of matter mingled in amounts that can vary, and it can be separated by physical means. A heterogeneous mixture, like a chocolate chip cookie, is not the same all the way through.

concepts.title: What a molecule is
concepts.description: A molecule is two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds: the smallest piece of a pure substance that is still that substance. Split a water molecule and you get hydrogen and oxygen, not smaller water.

concepts.title: A molecule's fixed recipe
concepts.description: Every water molecule holds exactly two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom; that fixed makeup separates a compound from a mixture. Some molecules pair identical atoms, like the oxygen and nitrogen in air.

concepts.title: Why a molecule's shape matters
concepts.description: Shape decides behavior. Straight CO2's polar bonds cancel, so it is nonpolar; bent water's don't, so it is polar. Carvone's two mirror-image forms smell of spearmint and caraway because each fits different receptors in the nose.

concepts.title: Electron pairs set a molecule's shape
concepts.description: Around a central atom, electron pairs repel and spread as far apart as possible, which sets the molecule's shape: methane's four hydrogens point to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart.

concepts.title: The 'chemical-free' myth
concepts.description: Everything we eat, drink and live in is made of chemicals, natural and synthetic, so no product is chemical-free; the RSC's 2008 million-pound offer and a blank 2014 'overview' made the point.

concepts.title: Natural and synthetic molecules
concepts.description: A molecule is the same whether it comes from a plant or a factory: natural and synthetic vitamin C are chemically identical.

concepts.title: Neutralization
concepts.description: An acid and a base cancel each other out: hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions join into water, and the leftover ions form a salt. New substances form, so it is a chemical change.

concepts.title: Why the ocean is acidifying
concepts.description: The ocean absorbs about 30 percent of the CO2 released into the air; dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions.

concepts.title: How far ocean pH has fallen
concepts.description: Since the Industrial Revolution surface-ocean pH has dropped by about 0.1, roughly 30 percent more hydrogen ions, though seawater is still basic. The IPCC (2021) finds such low pH unusual in 2 million years.

concepts.title: Acidification and shell builders
concepts.description: Extra hydrogen ions use up carbonate ions, the building blocks of shells and coral skeletons, so oysters, clams, urchins and corals struggle; Northwest oyster hatcheries fought back by adding a base.

concepts.title: Oxygen feeds flames and cells
concepts.description: Oxygen reacts with practically every element. Burning usually combines a fuel with oxygen, and cells combine oxygen with food molecules to release energy.

concepts.title: Discovering and naming oxygen
concepts.description: Scheele (about 1772) and Priestley (1774) discovered oxygen independently. Lavoisier named it acid former, wrongly believing all acids contain it; the name stuck.

concepts.title: How much oxygen there is
concepts.description: Oxygen makes up 21 percent of the air by volume and is the most plentiful element in Earth's crust, nearly half of it by weight, bound up in rocks.

concepts.title: Particles explain the states
concepts.description: Matter is made of tiny particles. In a solid they are packed tight and vibrate in place; in a liquid they are close but slide past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move freely.

concepts.title: Each pH step is ten times
concepts.description: The pH scale is logarithmic: each whole step is a tenfold change in acidity, so lime juice (pH 2) is about a thousand times as acidic as coffee (pH 5).

concepts.title: The pH scale
concepts.description: pH, introduced by Sorensen in 1909, puts acidity on one scale, usually 0 to 14: 7 is neutral, lower is acidic, higher is basic. More hydrogen ions mean a lower pH.

concepts.title: Physical change
concepts.description: In a physical change, matter changes form or state but stays the same substance: melting, boiling, tearing, grinding. Boiling water bubbles, but it is still water.

concepts.title: Plasma, the fourth state
concepts.description: Plasma is a gas so energized that electrons are torn from its atoms, leaving a mix of electrically charged particles that conducts electricity. Heat or high voltage, like lightning, makes it.

concepts.title: Plasma fills the universe
concepts.description: The Sun and other stars are mostly plasma, so nearly all the visible matter in the universe is plasma, even though on Earth we meet it mainly in lightning and auroras.

concepts.title: Polymers: molecules as chains
concepts.description: A polymer is a giant molecule built from many small repeating units (monomers). Polyethylene, the most widely used plastic, is ethylene linked into long chains, and chain length and arrangement make plastics strong, light and flexible.

concepts.title: Nature's polymers
concepts.description: Living things are full of polymers: cellulose, starch, proteins, natural rubber and DNA. DNA's links come in four kinds (A, C, G, T); the human genome is about 3 billion bases, and one cell's DNA would stretch about 6 feet.

concepts.title: The alkali metal family
concepts.description: Group 1 alkali metals (lithium to francium) are soft, silvery and so reactive they occur only in compounds; each has one outer electron it gives up easily.

concepts.title: Alkali metals and water
concepts.description: Alkali metals react with water to make hydrogen gas and a hydroxide (an alkali), releasing heat; the reaction grows more violent down the group.

concepts.title: Atomic number identifies an element
concepts.description: Every atom of an element has the same number of protons, its atomic number, and that number decides which element the atom is.

concepts.title: The Big Bang's elements
concepts.description: The Big Bang made all the hydrogen, most of the helium and some lithium: elements 1, 2 and 3. Nearly everything else was built later.

concepts.title: Reading an element's box and symbol
concepts.description: Each box shows an element's atomic number, symbol and name, usually with its atomic mass. Symbols are one or two letters; some come from Latin names.

concepts.title: What an element is
concepts.description: An element is a pure substance that no chemical process can break down into simpler substances. Elements are the building blocks of all matter; compounds such as water are elements joined together. 118 are known.

concepts.title: Groups and periods
concepts.description: The periodic table has 7 rows (periods) and 18 columns (groups). Properties recur along the rows (the periodic law), so elements in the same group behave alike.

concepts.title: The halogens
concepts.description: Group 17 halogens (fluorine to tennessine) are "salt formers": very reactive nonmetals one electron short of a full shell. Fluorine is the most reactive element; reactivity falls down the group. They range from gas to liquid to solid.

concepts.title: Halogens at work
concepts.description: Chlorine disinfects drinking water (routine in the US since Jersey City, 1908), fluorine compounds help prevent tooth decay, and iodide in salt prevents iodine deficiency.

concepts.title: Where the heaviest natural elements came from
concepts.description: Fusion in stars stops at iron; heavier elements such as gold come from supernovas and neutron star mergers.

concepts.title: How Mendeleev arranged the elements
concepts.description: In 1869 Mendeleev ordered the known elements by atomic weight and grouped those with similar properties, revealing a repeating pattern; Lothar Meyer found it independently. Today the order is by atomic number.

concepts.title: Mendeleev's gaps and predictions
concepts.description: Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties; gallium, scandium and germanium later filled them, germanium matching closely.

concepts.title: Reading behavior from position
concepts.description: Metallic character is strongest at the left and increases down a group, so the most metallic elements are at the lower left and nonmetallic character peaks at the upper right; an element's position predicts how it behaves.

concepts.title: Metals
concepts.description: About three-quarters of the elements are metals: shiny, malleable, ductile and good conductors of heat and electricity, and solid at room temperature except mercury.

concepts.title: How neon lights glow
concepts.description: Electricity turns the gas in a neon tube into glowing plasma; neon glows reddish orange, and other colors come from other gases.

concepts.title: Noble gases
concepts.description: The group 18 noble gases barely react because their outer electron shells are complete; argon was found in air in 1894, and neon and argon are separated from liquid air.

concepts.title: Nonmetals, metalloids and the map
concepts.description: Nonmetals are dull, brittle when solid and poor conductors, and sit at the upper right; metalloids with in-between properties lie along the staircase line; mercury and bromine are the only liquid elements.

concepts.title: Stars forge the elements
concepts.description: Stars fuse lighter elements into heavier ones, such as carbon and oxygen, up to iron, and exploding stars scatter them into new stars, planets and people.

concepts.title: Building superheavy elements
concepts.description: The heaviest elements are made by fusing nuclei in accelerators: element 118 came from calcium (20 protons) plus californium (98). IUPAC's 2016 names completed row seven.

concepts.title: Elements beyond uranium
concepts.description: Elements beyond uranium (92) are transuranium elements, all radioactive and made by people; neptunium, the first, was made in 1940.

concepts.title: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation
concepts.description: Alpha particles are 2 protons and 2 neutrons (a helium nucleus), beta particles are small fast particles, often electrons, and gamma rays are high-energy photons.

concepts.title: Radioactive decay
concepts.description: Unstable nuclei break down on their own, giving off radiation and sometimes becoming a different atom. Becquerel discovered it in 1896 when uranium salts fogged wrapped photographic plates without sunlight.

concepts.title: Reactions rearrange atoms
concepts.description: A reaction breaks the bonds holding the reactants together and reassembles the same atoms into new combinations, so no atoms are made or destroyed; only their arrangement changes.

concepts.title: Conservation of mass in reactions
concepts.description: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. When products seem lighter or heavier, matter has slipped in or out unseen, usually as a gas: ash is light because gases escape, and a metal gets heavier as it combines with oxygen.

concepts.title: Where reaction energy comes from
concepts.description: Breaking bonds takes energy in; forming bonds gives energy out. A reaction is exothermic when the new bonds release more energy than breaking the old ones took, and endothermic when it is the other way round.

concepts.title: Exothermic and endothermic
concepts.description: An exothermic change releases heat (fire, a hand warmer rusting iron powder); an endothermic change absorbs heat (an instant cold pack).

concepts.title: Lavoisier's sealed-vessel experiment
concepts.description: Antoine Lavoisier, an 18th-century French chemist, weighed everything in his reactions. He heated tin sealed in a vessel with air: the solid gained exactly as much mass as the air lost, so the total stayed the same.

concepts.title: Oxidation at different speeds
concepts.description: Rusting and burning are both oxidation, originally meaning combining with oxygen. They differ in speed: rust creeps, fire races, an explosion is faster still.

concepts.title: Reactions need good collisions
concepts.description: Particles react only when they collide in the right orientation and with at least a minimum energy, the activation energy. Anything that makes such collisions more frequent speeds a reaction up.

concepts.title: Surface area, concentration and reaction speed
concepts.description: A solid reacts only at its surface, so smaller pieces react faster: a log smolders, sawdust burns explosively. Higher concentrations of reactants usually speed reactions up too.

concepts.title: Temperature and reaction speed
concepts.description: Reactions usually go faster when warmer: particles move faster, collide more often and more of them clear the activation energy. For many reactions, 10 °C roughly doubles the rate. A fridge slows spoiling.

concepts.title: Reactants and products
concepts.description: In a chemical reaction, the starting substances (reactants) turn into new substances (products). Chemists write reactants on the left of an arrow and products on the right. Burning wood: wood and oxygen become carbon dioxide, water vapor and ash.

concepts.title: How iron rusts
concepts.description: Rust is reddish-brown iron oxide. Iron rusts when it meets oxygen and water together, and salts speed it up. Because oxygen joins the iron, rust weighs more than the iron it came from.

concepts.title: Why rust spreads, and how to stop it
concepts.description: Unlike copper's protective coat, rust flakes off and exposes fresh iron, so corrosion keeps going. Paint blocks oxygen and water; galvanizing coats iron with zinc, which corrodes first.

concepts.title: Rutherford finds the nucleus
concepts.description: In the gold foil experiment (1909), most alpha particles passed straight through but a very few bounced back. In 1911 Rutherford explained it with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus in mostly empty space.

concepts.title: Distillation
concepts.description: Distillation heats a liquid to vapor and cools the vapor back to liquid somewhere else. Because parts of a mixture turn to vapor at different temperatures, it can make fresh water from seawater.

concepts.title: Filtering and evaporating
concepts.description: Mixtures are separated by physical differences. A filter holds back solid bits like sand but lets dissolved salt through with the water; evaporating the water then leaves the salt behind.

concepts.title: Silicon chips
concepts.description: Doped silicon makes transistors, tiny switches that computer chips are built from. Chip silicon must be extremely pure, with fewer than 1 stray atom per 10 billion.

concepts.title: Silicon: the crust's second element
concepts.description: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, more than a quarter of it by weight. It never occurs free, but combined with oxygen as silica in rocks and sand.

concepts.title: Silicon, the tunable semiconductor
concepts.description: Silicon is a semiconductor, between a conductor and an insulator. Doping it with about 10 boron atoms per million raises its conductivity about a thousandfold.

concepts.title: Silver: best conductor, easy tarnish
concepts.description: Silver has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of all metals, but sulfur compounds in air tarnish it with a dark coating.

concepts.title: Solutions
concepts.description: A solution is a homogeneous mixture, the same all the way through. The dissolved substance is the solute and the one doing the dissolving is the solvent. Solutions can be liquids, gases (air) or solids (brass).

concepts.title: How the stomach survives its own acid
concepts.description: A thick bicarbonate-rich mucus neutralizes acid at the lining, keeping the cell surface near neutral; tight junctions seal the lining, and it is replaced every 3 to 6 days. Heartburn is acid in the esophagus.

concepts.title: Stomach acid and its jobs
concepts.description: Parietal cells in the stomach lining make hydrochloric acid, giving stomach contents a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5; the acid kills much of the bacteria in food and unravels proteins.

concepts.title: Sublimation and deposition
concepts.description: Some solids turn straight into gas (sublimation): dry ice at normal pressure, and snow slowly even below freezing. The reverse, gas straight to solid, is deposition, as in frost. Both are physical changes.

concepts.title: Thomson finds the electron
concepts.description: In 1897 J.J. Thomson showed that cathode rays are particles far lighter than atoms, found in all matter: electrons. He pictured atoms as positive spheres with electrons embedded, the plum pudding model.

concepts.title: Solid, liquid and gas
concepts.description: A solid is rigid with a definite shape and volume; a liquid flows and takes its container's shape but keeps its volume; a gas takes both the shape and volume of its container.

concepts.title: Water is both acid and base
concepts.description: Water is amphiprotic: it can donate or accept a hydrogen ion. A tiny fraction of water molecules trade, making equal numbers of hydronium and hydroxide ions, which is why pure water is neutral, pH 7 at 25 C.

concepts.title: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules
concepts.description: The slightly positive hydrogen of one water molecule is drawn to the oxygen of its neighbor: a hydrogen bond. Breaking these is why water boils at 100 °C instead of about −80 °C; they also give water surface tension and hold ice's open lattice.

concepts.title: Water, a polar molecule
concepts.description: Oxygen pulls water's shared electrons harder than hydrogen does, so the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends slightly positive. The hydrogens sit at an angle of about 104.5°, so the molecule is polar.

concepts.title: How accounts get attacked
concepts.description: Most account break-ins rely on phishing, reused leaked passwords (credential stuffing) and guessing predictable passwords.

concepts.title: Protecting your accounts
concepts.description: Current NIST and CISA guidance: long passwords or passphrases, a different one for every account, a password manager, and multifactor authentication.

concepts.title: What AI is
concepts.description: Artificial intelligence is a computer doing tasks we associate with intelligent beings; early wins like Deep Blue's 1997 chess victory came from brute-force speed.

concepts.title: Machine learning
concepts.description: Machine learning trains a model on examples instead of hand-written rules; the model learns what its data teaches, including its gaps and biases.

concepts.title: AC and DC
concepts.description: Direct current flows one way; alternating current keeps reversing, 60 cycles a second on the US grid, one cycle per turn of a two-pole generator.

concepts.title: How antibiotics kill bacteria
concepts.description: Antibiotics hit structures bacteria have and human cells lack; penicillin, found by Fleming in 1928, stops bacteria building cell walls so they burst. They don't work on viruses.

concepts.title: Antibiotic resistance
concepts.description: Resistance means the bacteria, not your body, learn to beat a drug: resistant survivors multiply. WHO: about 1 in 6 lab-confirmed bacterial infections resisted antibiotics in 2023.

concepts.title: Augmented reality
concepts.description: Augmented reality adds computer-made images to your view of the real world instead of replacing it, from TV's first-down line to Pokemon GO.

concepts.title: How a battery works
concepts.description: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy, sending electrons from anode to cathode through the outside circuit; it dies when its reactants are used up.

concepts.title: How 3D printing began
concepts.description: Hull's 1983 stereolithography hardened liquid polymer with UV light layer by layer (SLA-1, 1987); Crump's glue-gun frog led to FDM in 1989.

concepts.title: Additive manufacturing
concepts.description: 3D printing builds an object layer upon layer from a digital model instead of cutting material away, which suits prototypes and one-person custom parts.

concepts.title: The Bessemer process
concepts.description: From 1856, blowing air through molten iron burned out extra carbon in minutes, using the reaction's own heat, and made steel cheap.

concepts.title: Arch and suspension bridges
concepts.description: An arch carries loads by compression into massive supports; a suspension bridge hangs its deck from cables in tension; the longest span is dated and changes.

concepts.title: Concrete and reinforced concrete
concepts.description: Concrete is sand and gravel bound by cement that hardens by reacting with water; weak in tension, it gets steel bars inside.

concepts.title: The elevator counterweight
concepts.description: A counterweight about equal to the car half full hangs on the other end of the cables, so the motor lifts only the difference.

concepts.title: The industrial robot
concepts.description: Unimate, the first factory robot, went to work at General Motors in 1961 handling hot die-cast parts; about 5 million robots worked in factories in 2025.

concepts.title: Mass production and its costs
concepts.description: Making Model Ts in huge numbers cut the price from $850 to as little as $260, but the repetitive line drove workers away until the $5 day.

concepts.title: The moving assembly line
concepts.description: Ford's 1913 line brought the car to workers who each did a small repeated task, cutting Model T assembly from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes.

concepts.title: Teaching a factory robot
concepts.description: A programmer teaches a robot its task with a teach pendant and it repeats it precisely; robots took dangerous, repetitive jobs and are fenced off from workers.

concepts.title: Roman concrete
concepts.description: The Pantheon's dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome; a 2023 MIT-led study found lime clasts that can help Roman concrete heal cracks.

concepts.title: The safety elevator
concepts.description: Otis's brake gripped the guide rails when the rope lost its pull; the safe passenger elevator made tall buildings practical.

concepts.title: The skyscraper frame
concepts.description: A steel skeleton, not the walls, carries a tall building's weight, so walls stop thickening with height and hang on as curtain walls.

concepts.title: Iron, carbon and steel
concepts.description: Steel is iron with up to about 2 percent carbon; cast iron, with 2 to 4 percent, is brittle and weak in tension.

concepts.title: The tallest building record
concepts.description: Height records change, so they carry a date: as of 2026 CTBUH ranks Burj Khalifa (2010, 828 m) the tallest.

concepts.title: Tension and compression
concepts.description: Structures resist two basic forces: tension pulls and stretches, compression pushes and squeezes; a bending beam has both.

concepts.title: The climbing tower crane
concepts.description: A tower crane grows with its building by jacking up its top and lifting in a new mast section; counterweights on its short arm balance the load.

concepts.title: Tunnel boring machines
concepts.description: A TBM cuts the face with a rotating cutterhead and lines the tunnel with concrete rings as it goes; tunnel records are dated.

concepts.title: Brunel's tunnelling shield
concepts.description: Inspired by shipworms, Brunel's shield let miners dig small patches while the tunnel behind was lined; it built the first tunnel under a navigable river.

concepts.title: How a camera forms an image
concepts.description: A camera is a dark box: light through a small opening or lens forms an image on a light-sensitive surface, as in the camera obscura.

concepts.title: Film and digital sensors
concepts.description: Film records light with silver salts that darken when developed; a digital sensor turns light at each pixel into an electric current that is measured and stored.

concepts.title: Cells and base stations
concepts.description: A cellular network splits land into cells, each with a base station that talks to phones by radio; low-power signals let frequencies be reused.

concepts.title: Handoff between cells
concepts.description: As a phone moves from one cell to another during a call, the network automatically passes the call to the new cell.

concepts.title: Confidently wrong
concepts.description: Because a language model predicts likely-sounding text rather than checking facts, it can state false things confidently: a hallucination.

concepts.title: How language models write
concepts.description: A large language model splits text into tokens and writes by predicting a likely next token, adding it and repeating; it learned this from huge amounts of text.

concepts.title: Circuits and switches
concepts.description: Current flows only around a closed loop of conductors; a switch opens or closes a gap in that loop.

concepts.title: Series and parallel circuits
concepts.description: In series, devices share one path and fail together; homes are wired in parallel so each device has its own branch.

concepts.title: How CO2 warms the planet
concepts.description: CO2 traps heat; burning coal, oil and gas has raised it more than 50%, and the IPCC finds humans have unequivocally warmed the planet.

concepts.title: Emissions by power source
concepts.description: Coal emits the most CO2 per kilowatt-hour, gas about half as much, and wind, solar, nuclear and hydro far less over their whole lives.

concepts.title: Debating the energy path
concepts.description: Countries set the Paris goal; named groups such as OPEC and Greenpeace disagree sharply on how fast to move away from fossil fuels.

concepts.title: What the cloud is
concepts.description: The cloud is on-demand access over the network to shared computers and storage in data centers.

concepts.title: Data centers and energy
concepts.description: Data centers used about 415 TWh (around 1.5% of world electricity) in 2024; most of it ends up as heat, and cooling can take up to 40%.

concepts.title: Signals: electricity as a messenger
concepts.description: In communication technology, electricity carries information in the pattern of a current or wave: on-off pulses, or a continuous copy of a sound wave.

concepts.title: Algorithms
concepts.description: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that solves a problem in a finite number of steps; a program is an algorithm written in code.

concepts.title: Letters and pictures as numbers
concepts.description: Computers store text, pictures and sound as binary: each letter gets a number (lowercase a is 01100001 in ASCII), and each pixel's color is stored as numbers.

concepts.title: Counting in binary
concepts.description: Binary uses only 0 and 1 because a transistor switch is either on or off; each place is worth double the one before, and 8 bits make a byte.

concepts.title: What a computer is
concepts.description: A computer is a programmable machine for processing, storing and displaying information; the word once meant a person who calculated.

concepts.title: The first computers
concepts.description: There is no single first computer: Babbage's mechanical designs, the ABC, Zuse's Z3, Colossus and ENIAC were each first by a different measure.

concepts.title: The instruction cycle and clock speed
concepts.description: A CPU runs one loop, fetch, decode, execute, from start-up to shutdown, paced by a clock that ticks billions of times a second.

concepts.title: Input, processing, memory, output
concepts.description: Every computer takes input, processes it in the CPU, holds data and instructions in memory, and sends out output.

concepts.title: Memory and storage
concepts.description: RAM is fast working memory that forgets without power; storage (hard drives and SSDs) keeps files for the long term with the power off.

concepts.title: From rooms to pockets
concepts.description: Transistors and then microprocessors shrank computers from 30-ton room-fillers to desktop personal computers to handheld smartphones.

concepts.title: Moore's law
concepts.description: Moore's law is Gordon Moore's observation (1965, revised 1975) that chip transistor counts double about every two years; it is a trend the industry chased, not a law of nature.

concepts.title: Operating systems
concepts.description: An operating system manages a computer's resources, shares processor time among programs in tiny slices, and is loaded into memory at start-up.

concepts.title: Software and code
concepts.description: Software is the instructions that tell hardware what to do; programmers write code in high-level languages that a compiler or interpreter translates into binary machine code.

concepts.title: Sorting algorithms
concepts.description: Different algorithms can solve the same problem with very different effort: selection sort work quadruples when the list doubles, merge sort work only slightly more than doubles.

concepts.title: Transistors and the microchip
concepts.description: A transistor is a tiny semiconductor switch flipped by a small electrical signal; an integrated circuit puts many of them, and their wiring, on one piece of silicon.

concepts.title: Casgevy, the first CRISPR medicine
concepts.description: Casgevy, approved in the UK in November 2023 and the US in December 2023, edits a sickle cell patient's own blood stem cells to make fetal hemoglobin.

concepts.title: The gene-editing line
concepts.description: Editing body cells affects one patient; editing eggs, sperm or embryos could pass changes to future generations, which the 2023 genome editing summit called unacceptable at this time.

concepts.title: How CRISPR edits genes
concepts.description: CRISPR-Cas9, borrowed from a bacterial defense against viruses, uses a guide RNA to lead the Cas9 enzyme to a matching DNA sequence and cut it; the cell's repair machinery then makes the edit.

concepts.title: Encryption basics
concepts.description: Encryption uses an algorithm and a key to turn plaintext into ciphertext; Caesar's shift cipher is a simple, easily broken example.

concepts.title: Public-key encryption
concepts.description: Diffie and Hellman (1976) showed how to keep messages secret with no prearranged key; public-key cryptography uses one key to lock and another to unlock.

concepts.title: How a quadcopter flies
concepts.description: A quadcopter's four propellers push air down for lift; two spin each way so their twisting forces cancel, and it steers only by changing propeller speeds under a flight computer's control.

concepts.title: What drones are used for
concepts.description: Drones carry out jobs such as delivering blood to hospitals in Rwanda (from 2016) and counting birds and watching volcanoes for the USGS.

concepts.title: Radar
concepts.description: Radar sends out radio pulses and times their echoes; half the round trip at the speed of light gives the distance, and the Doppler shift gives speed.

concepts.title: Sonar
concepts.description: Sonar times echoes of sound pulses in water, where sound travels far and fast, to find the seafloor or objects.

concepts.title: Electric current
concepts.description: Current is moving charge, counted in amperes. Electrons already in the wire drift slowly, but the push travels almost at light speed.

concepts.title: The electric motor
concepts.description: A motor spins a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field, reversing the current each half turn to keep it going; Faraday built the first in 1821.

concepts.title: Watts and kilowatt-hours
concepts.description: Power is how fast energy flows: a watt is a joule per second, volts times amps; bills charge for energy in kilowatt-hours.

concepts.title: Electromagnetic induction
concepts.description: A changing magnetic field through a coil induces a current, as Faraday found in 1831.

concepts.title: Electricity makes magnetism
concepts.description: An electric current makes a magnetic field, as Ørsted saw in 1820; a coil of wire becomes a switchable electromagnet.

concepts.title: What energy is
concepts.description: Energy is the ability to do work. It is stored (potential) or working (kinetic) and is measured in joules.

concepts.title: Energy changes form
concepts.description: Energy is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another; in most conversions a lot of it ends up as heat.

concepts.title: The four forces of flight
concepts.description: Weight, lift, drag and thrust act on every plane; in steady flight lift balances weight and thrust balances drag.

concepts.title: How a wing makes lift
concepts.description: A wing turns the passing air downward, so the air pushes it up; seen as pressure, faster air above the wing means lower pressure there. The equal-transit story is a myth.

concepts.title: A fridge moves heat
concepts.description: A refrigerator does not make cold: it forces heat out of its cold inside and releases it into the room, which is why an open fridge door warms a kitchen.

concepts.title: The refrigerant loop
concepts.description: A fridge's refrigerant evaporates inside, soaking up heat, then is compressed so it condenses in outside coils and gives that heat up; the loop repeats.

concepts.title: Why fusion is hard
concepts.description: Positively charged nuclei repel, so fusion fuel must be heated to about 150 million degrees C, becoming a plasma that has to be held by magnetic fields or squeezed by lasers.

concepts.title: NIF's 2022 ignition
concepts.description: On December 5, 2022, NIF's lasers delivered 2.05 MJ to a fusion target and got 3.15 MJ back: gain on the target, while the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid.

concepts.title: Fusion versus fission
concepts.description: Fusion joins very light nuclei, such as the hydrogen isotopes deuterium and tritium, into helium; fission splits heavy nuclei such as uranium.

concepts.title: Gas turbines and combined cycle
concepts.description: Gas turbines spin directly on hot gases; combined-cycle plants reuse the exhaust heat to make steam for a second turbine, getting more electricity from the same fuel.

concepts.title: The generator
concepts.description: A generator is a motor run in reverse: turbines spin a rotor inside coils to turn motion into electricity.

concepts.title: GPS clocks and relativity
concepts.description: GPS works only because its satellites carry very precise atomic clocks, corrected for relativity: a millionth of a second means about 300 meters.

concepts.title: How GPS finds you
concepts.description: GPS receivers only listen: they time one-way signals from at least four satellites, turn the delays into distances, and solve for position and time.

concepts.title: Balancing the grid
concepts.description: Grid operators must match electricity supply to demand at every moment, or blackouts can happen.

concepts.title: How power reaches your socket
concepts.description: Electricity is stepped up to high voltage for long transmission lines, then stepped down at substations and near homes; the lower 48 US states run on three main grids.

concepts.title: Germ theory
concepts.description: Germ theory says microorganisms that invade and multiply in the body cause infectious disease; Pasteur and Koch established it, and it underpins disinfection, vaccines and antibiotics.

concepts.title: Air conditioning
concepts.description: Air conditioners work like a fridge for a whole house, moving heat from indoors to outdoors; Carrier's 1902 system was built to control humidity at a printer.

concepts.title: Heat pumps
concepts.description: A heat pump moves heat either way: out of the house in summer and in from the cool outdoors in winter, delivering about 3 kWh of heat per 1 kWh of electricity.

concepts.title: Head and flow
concepts.description: A hydro plant's output depends on how much water flows and how far it falls; hydropower is a much bigger share of the world's electricity than of US electricity.

concepts.title: How a dam makes electricity
concepts.description: Water falling from a reservoir through a penstock turns a turbine and generator, turning gravitational energy into electricity.

concepts.title: MRI scans
concepts.description: MRI lines up protons in the body's water with a powerful magnet, knocks them with radio pulses and reads the energy they release; no ionizing radiation.

concepts.title: X-rays and CT scans
concepts.description: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by calcium-rich bone, which shows white; CT spins an X-ray beam around the body to build slices and 3D images.

concepts.title: The incandescent bulb
concepts.description: An incandescent bulb makes light by heating a tungsten filament until it glows, wasting most of its energy as heat.

concepts.title: How the internet began
concepts.description: ARPANET, funded by the US Defense Department, sent its first message ("lo") in 1969 and grew into an internet now used by about 6 billion people.

concepts.title: Light in glass fibers
concepts.description: Undersea cables carry data as laser light in hair-thin glass fibers inside a cable about as wide as a garden hose.

concepts.title: How long the internet takes
concepts.description: Light in optical fiber covers about a kilometer every 5 millionths of a second, so 1,000 km takes about 5 thousandths of a second.

concepts.title: Where packets came from
concepts.description: Paul Baran (RAND) and Donald Davies (NPL) independently invented packet switching; Baran wanted a network that survived damage, and Davies named the packets.

concepts.title: Packet switching
concepts.description: Data is chopped into small addressed packets that travel independently by any available route and are reassembled at the destination.

concepts.title: TCP/IP: the network of networks
concepts.description: Cerf and Kahn's TCP (1974) let separate networks join into one; ARPANET switched to TCP/IP in 1983, and TCP resends lost packets.

concepts.title: Undersea internet cables
concepts.description: Over 99% of intercontinental data crosses the oceans in cables; anchors and fishing, not sharks, cause most faults, so traffic is spread across many cables.

concepts.title: The jet engine
concepts.description: A jet engine squeezes air in a compressor, burns fuel in it, spins a turbine that drives the compressor, and blasts the gas out of a nozzle. Airliners use turbofans.

concepts.title: The LED
concepts.description: An LED makes light directly from a semiconductor junction, with no hot filament, using far less energy.

concepts.title: How a microwave oven heats food
concepts.description: A magnetron fills a metal box with microwaves whose field tugs food's water molecules back and forth about 2.45 billion times a second; their jostling is heat.

concepts.title: Microwaves are non-ionizing
concepts.description: Microwaves, like visible light and radio waves, are non-ionizing: too weak to knock electrons out of atoms. Their energy becomes heat and doesn't make food radioactive.

concepts.title: The world's electricity mix
concepts.description: In 2025 coal and renewables each made about a third of the world's electricity, gas about a fifth, and low-emissions sources more than 40%.

concepts.title: Why some bikes balance themselves
concepts.description: A moving riderless bike can steer itself into a lean and recover; in 2011 a bike with neither gyroscopic effect nor trail still did, so the full reason is a subtle mix of effects.

concepts.title: Balancing a bike by steering
concepts.description: A rider stays up by steering the wheels back under the falling bike, the way a hand moves under a balanced broom; a stopped bike cannot do this.

concepts.title: How an electric car works
concepts.description: An all-electric car drives its wheels with an electric motor powered by a battery pack; counting from the plug, over 77% of the energy reaches the wheels.

concepts.title: Factories and the Industrial Revolution
concepts.description: The Industrial Revolution moved work from homes into powered factories with divided labor; steam freed mills from riversides so they could grow in towns.

concepts.title: The four-stroke cycle
concepts.description: Intake, compression, power and exhaust: only the power stroke pushes, and a crankshaft turns the piston's up-and-down motion into rotation.

concepts.title: Friction
concepts.description: Friction resists surfaces sliding over each other; rough surfaces catch, starting to slide takes more force than keeping going, and friction lets you grip the ground.

concepts.title: How brakes stop a car
concepts.description: Friction brakes press pads on a spinning disc and turn the energy of motion into heat; energy of motion grows with the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples braking distance.

concepts.title: Gear ratios
concepts.description: Meshing gears cannot slip, so their tooth counts set the speed ratio: a driven gear with twice the teeth turns at half the speed.

concepts.title: Gears trade speed for force
concepts.description: A small gear driving a big one gives more turning force at lower speed; a big gear driving a small one gives speed instead, like a bike's low and high gears.

concepts.title: Horsepower
concepts.description: James Watt set one horsepower at 33,000 foot-pounds per minute, about 746 watts, more than an average horse can keep up over a working day.

concepts.title: Hydraulic force multiplication
concepts.description: Equal pressure on a piston with 10 times the area gives 10 times the force, but the small piston moves 10 times as far; car brakes work this way.

concepts.title: Factory work and the first factory laws
concepts.description: Factory work meant long, clock-driven shifts, often for children; Britain's 1833 Factory Act banned under-9s from textile mills and sent inspectors to enforce it.

concepts.title: The internal combustion engine
concepts.description: A car engine burns fuel inside its cylinders, where a spark ignites fuel and air; only about 12%-30% of the fuel energy moves the car, and most of the rest is lost as heat.

concepts.title: Trading force for distance
concepts.description: A pulley system shares a load among its rope strands, cutting the force needed, but you pull proportionally more rope: no machine puts out more work than goes in.

concepts.title: Newcomen's steam engine
concepts.description: Newcomen's 1712 engine pumped water from mines: it condensed steam under a piston to make a partial vacuum, and air pressure pushed the piston down.

concepts.title: Pascal's principle
concepts.description: Press on a liquid at rest in a closed container and the pressure rises equally everywhere in it; liquids barely compress, so they pass a push along.

concepts.title: Regenerative braking
concepts.description: When an electric car slows, the turning wheels drive its motor as a generator, recharging the battery instead of wasting all the energy of motion.

concepts.title: Simple machines
concepts.description: Levers, wheels and axles and pulleys are simple machines: a lever multiplies a push by the ratio of its arm lengths, a wheel and axle by the ratio of its radii.

concepts.title: Watt's steam engine
concepts.description: James Watt's separate condenser (1765, patented 1769) kept the cylinder hot and cut fuel costs; from 1781 his engines turned a shaft, and the watt is named for him.

concepts.title: How nuclear power works
concepts.description: Neutrons split uranium-235 atoms in a controlled chain reaction; the heat makes steam to spin a turbine, with no CO2 released while running.

concepts.title: The nuclear debate
concepts.description: Spent fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years; groups such as the IEA and Greenpeace weigh nuclear power's role very differently.

concepts.title: How oil forms and is found
concepts.description: Crude oil formed from ancient marine life under heat and pressure, sits in tiny spaces in rock, and is reached by drilling wells.

concepts.title: Refining and using oil
concepts.description: Refineries separate crude by boiling point and crack heavy molecules into fuels like gasoline; oil mostly powers transport, not the grid.

concepts.title: Why plastic lasts
concepts.description: Microbes' enzymes don't recognize plastic's bonds, so plastic doesn't rot: it breaks into smaller pieces, down to microplastics under five millimeters.

concepts.title: What plastic is
concepts.description: Plastics are polymers, long chains of repeating units, mostly built from fossil-fuel carbon; Baekeland's 1907 Bakelite was the first fully synthetic plastic.

concepts.title: Gutenberg's printing system
concepts.description: Gutenberg combined reusable metal type, oil-based ink and a press into a system that printed pages again and again; movable type itself came first in China and Korea.

concepts.title: Printing spreads ideas
concepts.description: Cheap printed copies multiplied Europe's books into the millions by 1500 and let ideas such as Luther's theses spread in weeks.

concepts.title: Pumped-storage hydropower
concepts.description: Pumped storage pumps water uphill with spare electricity and lets it run back through turbines when power is needed.

concepts.title: Qubits
concepts.description: A qubit can be 0, 1 or a mix of both (superposition), but measuring it always gives a plain 0 or 1.

concepts.title: What quantum computers are (and aren't) for
concepts.description: Quantum computers are expected to help with specific jobs such as simulating molecules and factoring huge numbers, not to replace ordinary computers; qubits are fragile and error-prone.

concepts.title: Who invented radio
concepts.description: Hertz made radio waves; Marconi, Popov and Tesla all have claims on radio, and even a 1943 US Supreme Court case weighed priority.

concepts.title: How radio sends sound
concepts.description: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves made by changing currents in antennas; stations carry sound by varying a carrier wave (AM or FM).

concepts.title: Electric trains
concepts.description: Most modern trains are driven by electric motors: electric trains take current from an overhead wire or third rail, and diesel-electrics make it on board.

concepts.title: Maglev trains
concepts.description: A maglev train is lifted by magnets so no wheels touch its guideway, and guideway coils that keep changing polarity pull it along.

concepts.title: Goddard's rockets
concepts.description: Robert Goddard flew the first liquid-fueled rocket in 1926, after a 1920 newspaper editorial claimed rockets could not work in a vacuum.

concepts.title: How rockets work in space
concepts.description: A rocket pushes on its own exhaust, not on air, and carries its own oxidizer, so it works in a vacuum where jet engines cannot.

concepts.title: Pixels and LCD screens
concepts.description: A screen image is a grid of pixels, millions on an HD or 4K screen; an LCD makes no light and uses liquid crystals to let a backlight through or block it.

concepts.title: Mixing red, green and blue light
concepts.description: The eye has three kinds of cones, so screens can make a broad range of colors by mixing red, green and blue light.

concepts.title: Crawling and indexing
concepts.description: Search engines send crawlers along links and build an index, like a book's, that searches look through instead of the live web.

concepts.title: Ranking search results
concepts.description: BackRub, which became Google, treated links as votes; ranking today weighs many signals such as meaning, relevance, quality and location.

concepts.title: SAE levels of driving automation
concepts.description: SAE J3016 sorts driving automation into Levels 0 to 5, by who is driving: you at Levels 0-2, the system at Levels 3-5 when engaged.

concepts.title: How self-driving cars sense the road
concepts.description: Self-driving cars combine cameras, radar, lidar, GPS and detailed maps into a 3-D picture, and computers steer, brake and accelerate from it.

concepts.title: London's sewers and the Great Stink
concepts.description: The Great Stink of 1858 pushed Parliament to fund Bazalgette's sewers, built to remove 'bad air'; the 1866 cholera outbreak hit only unconnected areas, proving Snow right.

concepts.title: How a sewage plant cleans wastewater
concepts.description: Gravity carries sewage to a plant; screens and settling tanks remove solids, microbes eat the organic material, and the water is disinfected and released.

concepts.title: Archimedes' principle
concepts.description: Water pushes up on a ship with a force equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside; a ship settles until that water weighs as much as the ship.

concepts.title: The Plimsoll line
concepts.description: A mark on a ship's hull shows the deepest it may safely sit; separate marks allow for fresh water, which is less dense than seawater.

concepts.title: Inside a smartphone
concepts.description: A smartphone packs a phone, radio, camera and screen together with a speaker, a vibration motor and a rechargeable lithium-ion battery.

concepts.title: Capacitive touchscreens
concepts.description: A capacitive touchscreen senses where a conducting finger disturbs its electric field; insulators like plastic have no effect.

concepts.title: Solar DC and inverters
concepts.description: Solar cells make direct current, so inverters convert it to the grid's alternating current.

concepts.title: How solar cells work
concepts.description: Sunlight knocks electrons loose in a semiconductor cell, making current with nothing spinning; panels have grown far more efficient since 1954.

concepts.title: Space spinoffs
concepts.description: NASA research gave everyday life technologies such as the CMOS image sensor in phone cameras and memory foam, recorded in NASA's yearly Spinoff report since 1976.

concepts.title: Spinoff myths
concepts.description: Tang, Teflon and Velcro are not NASA inventions; astronauts used them, which made people link them with space.

concepts.title: Why storing electricity is hard
concepts.description: Storage must convert electricity to another form and back, losing some on the way; big batteries now shift midday solar to the evening.

concepts.title: Rules matched to risk
concepts.description: The EU's AI Act, in force since August 2024, bans a few AI uses, strictly regulates high-risk ones like hiring and leaves most everyday AI, such as spam filters, free of new obligations.

concepts.title: The Collingridge dilemma
concepts.description: David Collingridge's 1980 dilemma: early on, a technology is easy to change but its effects are hard to foresee; once the effects are clear, it is entrenched and hard to change.

concepts.title: Weighing a new technology
concepts.description: Every technology trades benefits against costs; asking who benefits, who bears the risk and who supplies the evidence helps judge it, as leaded petrol and the War of the Currents show.

concepts.title: What technology is
concepts.description: Technology is knowledge put to work on the practical jobs of daily life, from stone tools to light switches.

concepts.title: Inventions that changed daily life
concepts.description: A few big inventions, from stone tools and the wheel to printing and the electric light, reshaped everyday life; nearly all of them are very recent.

concepts.title: Morse code
concepts.description: Morse code spells letters with dots and dashes, giving the commonest letters the shortest codes; Morse and his partner Vail share the credit.

concepts.title: The electric telegraph
concepts.description: A telegraph key opens and closes a circuit, sending pulses of current that switch an electromagnet at the far end; Morse in the US and Cooke and Wheatstone in Britain built working systems.

concepts.title: Who invented the telephone
concepts.description: Bell received the patent, but Gray filed on a similar idea the same day and Meucci had filed a caveat earlier, so the credit is still argued.

concepts.title: How a telephone carries a voice
concepts.description: A telephone turns sound into a current that rises and falls like the sound wave, then turns it back into sound with an electromagnet and a diaphragm.

concepts.title: Steam power plants
concepts.description: Coal and many gas plants burn fuel to boil water; the steam spins a turbine and generator, and most of the fuel's energy is lost as heat.

concepts.title: Roundabouts
concepts.description: Roundabouts cut the points where drivers' paths cross from 32 to 8, remove right-angle and head-on crashes, and slow traffic, so far fewer crashes injure anyone.

concepts.title: Traffic signals
concepts.description: Traffic lights take turns so conflicting movements never both get green, and wire loops in the road tell a signal when a car is waiting.

concepts.title: Action and reaction push vehicles
concepts.description: Every engine that moves a vehicle accelerates a working fluid backward, and the reaction pushes the vehicle forward: Newton's third law.

concepts.title: The propeller
concepts.description: A propeller is a spinning wing: its blades make lift pointed forward, throwing air or water backward, so it needs a fluid to push and cannot work in space.

concepts.title: Television's pioneers
concepts.description: Baird's mechanical system, Farnsworth's electronic camera tube and Zworykin's work at RCA all shaped television; no one person invented it.

concepts.title: Scanning a picture
concepts.description: Television sends a picture as a signal by scanning it spot by spot and line by line, then rebuilding it in the same order fast enough to look whole.

concepts.title: Vaccines: history and safety record
concepts.description: Jenner's 1796 smallpox vaccine led to smallpox's eradication in 1980; vaccines pass clinical trials before use and are monitored after, and WHO calls them very safe.

concepts.title: How vaccines train the immune system
concepts.description: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form, piece or blueprint of a germ; it makes antibodies and remembers, so a later infection is stopped fast.

concepts.title: Voltage
concepts.description: Voltage is the energy given to each coulomb of charge: one volt is one joule per coulomb.

concepts.title: Volta's first battery
concepts.description: Galvani's twitching frog legs led Volta to build the voltaic pile in 1800, the first reliable battery.

concepts.title: How a VR headset works
concepts.description: A VR headset shows each eye a slightly different image for depth and uses motion sensors to redraw the view as your head moves; mismatched signals can cause motion sickness.

concepts.title: Why AC won
concepts.description: AC beat Edison's DC because transformers can raise its voltage for efficient long-distance transmission and lower it for homes.

concepts.title: Germs in water, and killing them
concepts.description: Snow showed in 1854 that cholera spread through contaminated water; today plants disinfect with chlorine or chloramine, a practice US cities began in 1908.

concepts.title: How tap water is treated
concepts.description: Treatment plants clump dirt with coagulation and flocculation, let the clumps settle, filter the water through sand, gravel or charcoal, and then disinfect it.

concepts.title: Inventing the World Wide Web
concepts.description: Tim Berners-Lee invented the web at CERN in 1989 using HTML, URLs and HTTP; CERN gave the software away in 1993.

concepts.title: The web versus the internet
concepts.description: The internet is the infrastructure; the web is one service that runs on it, like email.

concepts.title: Wi-Fi bands
concepts.description: Routers use a 2.4 GHz band (longer reach, better through walls) and a 5 GHz band (faster, shorter range); 2.4 GHz is 2.4 billion cycles a second.

concepts.title: What Wi-Fi is
concepts.description: Wi-Fi carries data by radio over the short hop between your devices and the router; the modem links the home network to the provider.

concepts.title: Where wind works best
concepts.description: Wind power rises with the cube of wind speed, so turbines go on windy plains, hilltops, water and tall towers.

concepts.title: How a wind turbine works
concepts.description: Wind turns wing-shaped blades and a rotor that drives a generator in the nacelle atop a tall tower.

concepts.title: The 27th Amendment and Gregory Watson
concepts.description: A congressional pay amendment proposed in 1789 was ratified in 1992 after a campaign begun by a student, Gregory Watson, whose 1982 paper arguing it was still pending got a C.

concepts.title: How constitutions are amended
concepts.description: Most constitutions make amending harder than ordinary lawmaking (supermajorities, referendums, double decisions, approval by states) to balance flexibility against protection; some provisions cannot be amended at all.

concepts.title: Aristotle: humans as political animals
concepts.description: Aristotle held that humans are by nature political animals; the city-state comes into being for the sake of life but exists for the sake of the good life.

concepts.title: Aristotle's six forms of government
concepts.description: Aristotle classified constitutions by who rules (one, few, many) and whether they serve the common advantage or the rulers' own.

concepts.title: Auditing public money
concepts.description: Supreme audit institutions check how public money was actually spent, the last stage of the budget cycle. The 1977 Lima Declaration, the 'Magna Carta of government auditing', calls for independent government auditing.

concepts.title: Problems no country can solve alone
concepts.description: The UN calls climate change a global emergency beyond national borders. No nation can cut emissions enough alone, and each can be tempted to free ride on others' efforts: a collective action problem.

concepts.title: The Montreal Protocol
concepts.description: The Montreal Protocol (1987) phases out ozone-depleting chemicals. It was the first treaty in UN history ratified by every country; 99 per cent of those chemicals are gone and the ozone layer is recovering.

concepts.title: The Paris Agreement
