concepts.description: The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to hold warming well below 2 degrees C and pursue 1.5 degrees C. Each country sets its own national plan (an NDC) and updates it every five years.

concepts.title: The four-stage budget cycle
concepts.description: The budget cycle usually has four stages: the executive prepares the plan, the legislature debates, amends and approves it, the government carries it out, and auditors check the actual spending. The stages of different years overlap.

concepts.title: Budget: from a leather bag to a spending plan
concepts.description: 'Budget' comes from Old French bougette, a little leather bag; in 1733 a pamphlet mocking Walpole's tax plans, The Budget Opened, gave it its money meaning. A government budget sets out the revenue it expects and the spending it plans.

concepts.title: Checks and balances
concepts.description: Checks and balances empower each branch to block actions by the others. Montesquieu: power should be a check to power. The Federalist No. 51: if men were angels, no government would be necessary.

concepts.title: A check in action: South Korea 2016-2017
concepts.description: South Korea's National Assembly impeached President Park Geun-hye on 9 December 2016; the Constitutional Court unanimously upheld it on 10 March 2017, removing her from office.

concepts.title: Citizenship by birth: soil and blood
concepts.description: Jus soli grants citizenship by birthplace; jus sanguinis by a parent's citizenship. Nearly every Western Hemisphere country uses jus soli; Japan uses descent.

concepts.title: What citizenship is
concepts.description: Citizenship is a relationship between a person and a state: the person owes allegiance and is entitled to the state's protection.

concepts.title: Naturalization
concepts.description: Adults can become citizens by applying, usually after residence and a test of language or knowledge; Canada asks for 1,095 days in five years.

concepts.title: The end of apartheid
concepts.description: Apartheid ('apartness'), set up in South Africa in 1948, classified people by race and used pass laws; it was repealed in the early 1990s, and the 1994 elections brought a government led by Nelson Mandela.

concepts.title: What civil rights are
concepts.description: Civil rights are guarantees of equal opportunity and equal protection under the law regardless of race, religion or other characteristics; unlike civil liberties (restraints on government), they usually need positive government action.

concepts.title: The U.S. civil rights movement
concepts.description: Rosa Parks's 1955 arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott; courts struck down bus segregation; the Civil Rights Act (1964) banned discrimination and the Voting Rights Act (1965) outlawed literacy tests.

concepts.title: What a constitution is
concepts.description: A constitution is a state's fundamental organizing principle and supreme law: it sets up the system of government, distributes and constrains power, and protects rights. Aristotle called it the arrangement of the offices.

concepts.title: The U.S. Constitution
concepts.description: Signed in Philadelphia on 17 September 1787 to replace the Articles of Confederation, the U.S. Constitution took effect in 1789 and is the oldest written national constitution in use. It opens 'We the People'.

concepts.title: Inside the U.S. Constitution
concepts.description: Its seven articles set up Congress, the President and the courts, and Article VI makes it 'the supreme Law of the Land'. The first ten amendments, ratified in 1791, are the Bill of Rights.

concepts.title: Written and unwritten constitutions
concepts.description: Some constitutions, like the US one, are a single written document; the UK's is a collection of documents, statutes and practices. Nearly every state claims a constitution, but not all follow theirs.

concepts.title: Germany's constitutional complaint
concepts.description: Anyone in Germany can ask the Federal Constitutional Court to protect their fundamental rights; thousands do each year and few succeed.

concepts.title: Judicial review
concepts.description: Courts can strike down laws that break the constitution: all U.S. courts since Marbury v Madison, special constitutional courts in countries like Germany; UK courts can only declare incompatibility.

concepts.title: Constitutional monarchy
concepts.description: A monarch shares power with a constitutional government and acts as a symbolic head of state: in Thiers's phrase, the king reigns but does not govern.

concepts.title: Constitutional monarchy in Sweden and Japan
concepts.description: Sweden abolished royal absolutism in 1809 and made the King's role entirely ceremonial in 1974; Japan's Emperor is a symbol with no governmental powers.

concepts.title: What corruption is and how it is measured
concepts.description: Transparency International defines corruption as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. Its 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index scored 182 countries from 0 to 100; the average was 42 and Denmark topped it with 89.

concepts.title: Fighting corruption: Hong Kong's ICAC
concepts.description: In early-1970s Hong Kong, bribes were demanded even for ambulances. After police officer Peter Godber fled in 1973, Hong Kong set up the independent ICAC in 1974, using enforcement, prevention and education.

concepts.title: What courts do
concepts.description: Courts settle disputes peacefully: they find the facts, apply the law to them, and appeal courts check that the law was applied correctly.

concepts.title: Valencia's Water Tribunal
concepts.description: A court of elected farmers that has settled irrigation disputes at Valencia Cathedral's door since al-Andalus: oral, impartial and final.

concepts.title: Criminal versus civil cases
concepts.description: Criminal cases are brought by the state and can end in punishment; civil cases settle disputes between parties, with a lower standard of proof.

concepts.title: Deficits, surpluses and how debt builds up
concepts.description: A government's fiscal balance is revenue minus spending: a deficit when spending is higher. Governments borrow, mostly by selling bonds, to cover deficits, and recurring deficits pile up as debt. In 2023 the average OECD deficit was 4.6% of GDP.

concepts.title: How much debt, and how much is too much
concepts.description: The IMF projects global public debt above 100% of GDP by 2029, the highest since 1948. Rich countries with deep bond markets carry high debt at moderate risk; poorer ones can be in distress at lower levels. The IMF and OECD stress different sides.

concepts.title: Democracy's Athenian roots
concepts.description: Democracy is Greek for rule by the people. In Athens, Cleisthenes' reforms (508-507 BCE) based political rights on the local deme, but only free adult male citizens took part.

concepts.title: Churchill's 'worst form of government'
concepts.description: On 11 November 1947 Churchill told the Commons that no one pretends democracy is perfect, and that 'it has been said' democracy is the worst form of government except all the others tried.

concepts.title: Of, by and for the people
concepts.description: At Gettysburg on 19 November 1863, Lincoln resolved that government of the people, by the people, for the people shall not perish from the earth.

concepts.title: Dictatorship and how it keeps power
concepts.description: Dictatorship is absolute power without effective constitutional limits, gained by force or fraud and kept by terror and propaganda; the Roman dictator was a temporary crisis office.

concepts.title: Totalitarianism
concepts.description: Totalitarian states seek control of every part of life; Mussolini coined the term, and Stalin's USSR and Nazi Germany are classic cases.

concepts.title: Diplomatic immunity and its limits
concepts.description: Embassy premises are inviolable and diplomats cannot be arrested or tried in the host country's criminal courts, so that missions can do their work. The host can declare a diplomat persona non grata at any time.

concepts.title: Embassies and what diplomats do
concepts.description: A diplomatic mission represents its country, protects its interests and citizens, negotiates, reports home and promotes friendly relations. Relations are set up by mutual consent, under rules written down in the 1961 Vienna Convention.

concepts.title: Assemblies of citizens
concepts.description: Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden's Landsgemeinde and New England town meetings let voters decide in person.

concepts.title: Direct democracy
concepts.description: In direct democracy citizens decide issues themselves rather than electing representatives; it is hard to run at the scale of a large state.

concepts.title: Arguing in good faith
concepts.description: Rapoport's rules (restate, agree, credit, then criticize) and Graham's hierarchy (from name-calling to refuting the central point) describe how to disagree well.

concepts.title: Mill: know the other side
concepts.description: In On Liberty (1859), Mill argued you cannot prefer your view without knowing and answering the other side at its strongest.

concepts.title: Compulsory voting in Australia
concepts.description: Australia made voting at federal elections compulsory in 1924; turnout rose from under 60% in 1922 to over 91% in 1925.

concepts.title: Rights come with responsibilities
concepts.description: Citizenship guides pair rights with responsibilities: some are legal duties (obeying the law, jury service when called), others civic ones (voting, helping others).

concepts.title: What campaigns do: Lazarsfeld's findings
concepts.description: Lazarsfeld's 1940 Erie County study (The People's Choice, 1944) found radio and print had only minor direct effects on votes; people decided mainly through conversations, and ideas flowed through opinion leaders in a two-step flow.

concepts.title: Campaign spending rules
concepts.description: Countries set different rules for campaign money: the UK caps party spending in the year before a general election, while the US Supreme Court in Buckley v. Valeo (1976) allowed contribution limits but struck down spending limits.

concepts.title: Counting in the open
concepts.description: Votes are counted where candidates' agents can watch. In the UK, agents observe the verification and count, may request a recount, and a genuine tie is settled by drawing lots.

concepts.title: Checking the count
concepts.description: Paper records let counts be checked: India's VVPAT shows each voter a paper slip for 7 seconds. Philip Stark's risk-limiting audits hand-check random ballots and escalate to a full hand count if needed.

concepts.title: First-past-the-post
concepts.description: Under first-past-the-post each district elects the candidate with the most votes. It is simple and gives a local member and often single-party government, but can exclude smaller parties and tends toward two parties (Duverger).

concepts.title: Gerrymandering
concepts.description: Gerrymandering is deliberately drawing district lines to help or hurt a political interest, named after Elbridge Gerry's 1812 salamander district. Packing and cracking waste a group's votes; the efficiency gap measures wasted votes, while Chen and Rodden show geography alone can create bias.

concepts.title: Criteria for free and fair elections
concepts.description: The IPU's Declaration on Criteria for Free and Fair Elections (Paris, 26 March 1994) grounds authority in the will of the people and lists a secret vote, equal weight, equal campaigning and an honest, observed count.

concepts.title: Lateral reading
concepts.description: Wineburg and McGrew found fact checkers read laterally, leaving a site to see what others say about it, while historians and students read vertically and were fooled by logos and domain names.

concepts.title: Margin of error
concepts.description: A margin of plus or minus 3 points at 95% confidence (about 1,067 random interviews) means the result would land within 3 points of the truth 95 times in 100. The margin on a lead is about double, and sampling is only one source of error.

concepts.title: Mill's case against the secret ballot
concepts.description: John Stuart Mill (1861) argued a vote is power over others and so a public trust, to be exercised under the eye and criticism of the public; secrecy, he feared, invites selfish voting.

concepts.title: Misinformation, disinformation, malinformation
concepts.description: Wardle and Derakhshan (Council of Europe, 2017) separate false information shared without intent to harm (misinformation), false information shared to harm (disinformation) and genuine information shared to harm (malinformation).

concepts.title: Poll samples: who you ask matters
concepts.description: In 1936 the Literary Digest's 2.4 million replies wrongly predicted Landon because its sample leaned to the well-off and few replied; Gallup's scientific sampling called Roosevelt's win.

concepts.title: Proportional representation
concepts.description: Proportional representation turns each party's share of votes into a matching share of seats, using multi-member districts. It wastes few votes and admits smaller parties but often brings coalitions. New Zealand adopted MMP after a 1986 Royal Commission.

concepts.title: What elections are for: choosing and removing
concepts.description: Schumpeter (1942) saw democracy as a competitive struggle for the people's vote, in which voters choose who rules; Popper (1945) saw its test in the ruled dismissing rulers without bloodshed.

concepts.title: Ranked voting
concepts.description: Ranked systems let voters number candidates. The Alternative Vote (Australia's House of Representatives) transfers votes until someone has a majority; the Single Transferable Vote (Ireland) does so in multi-member districts. Arrow (1951) proved no ranking method meets every fairness condition.

concepts.title: Drawing district boundaries
concepts.description: Where members are elected by district, where the lines fall can change results. Boundaries are redrawn as populations change; Canada has used independent commissions chaired by judges since 1964.

concepts.title: The referendum debate
concepts.description: Elliot Bulmer's IDEA primer weighs referendums: they let people vote on a single measure, but voters may respond to unrelated factors, tire of frequent votes, and rulers may use them for false legitimacy, though Pinochet lost one in 1988. The Venice Commission requires clear, non-leading questions.

concepts.title: Referendums and initiatives
concepts.description: A referendum puts a specific question referred by governing institutions directly to voters; a citizens' initiative is started by the people through a petition. Results may be binding or advisory. New Zealand chose MMP by binding referendum in 1993.

concepts.title: The secret ballot
concepts.description: Open voting invited intimidation and bribery. Victoria introduced the modern secret ballot in 1856, South Australia added the X, and Britain adopted it in 1872, so no one can punish a voter for their choice.

concepts.title: The SIFT method
concepts.description: Mike Caulfield's SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims, quotes and media to the original context, since much online content has been stripped of context.

concepts.title: The will of the people as the basis of authority
concepts.description: Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) makes the will of the people the basis of government authority, expressed in periodic and genuine elections held by secret vote.

concepts.title: How the EU makes laws
concepts.description: Everything the EU does rests on treaties its members agreed. The Commission proposes laws; the directly elected European Parliament and the Council of national ministers adopt them; member countries implement them.

concepts.title: How the EU began: coal, steel and peace
concepts.description: In 1950 Robert Schuman proposed pooling coal and steel to make war between France and Germany materially impossible. Six countries signed the coal and steel treaty in 1951, the first step toward today's 27-member EU.

concepts.title: Losing the confidence of parliament
concepts.description: A prime minister can be removed whenever they lose the confidence of a majority of parliament. On 28 March 1979 the Callaghan government lost a no-confidence vote 311 to 310.

concepts.title: Parliamentary and presidential systems
concepts.description: In a parliamentary system the legislature selects the prime minister; in a presidential system the president is elected to a fixed term and is also head of state. France is semi-presidential.

concepts.title: Failed and fragile states
concepts.description: A failed state loses control of its territory and the monopoly of legitimate force and provides only minimal services; the Fragile States Index tracks the pressures.

concepts.title: Somalia's collapse
concepts.description: After Siad Barre's overthrow in 1991, Somalia descended into state collapse under rival warlords and decades of civil war.

concepts.title: Federal systems
concepts.description: Federalism divides power between the center and the regions under a constitution that neither can change alone.

concepts.title: Why a free press matters
concepts.description: Press freedom is the right to report news without government control, giving citizens informed access to political information. Carlyle called the press gallery a Fourth Estate.

concepts.title: Sweden's 1766 press freedom law
concepts.description: On 2 December 1766 Sweden's Riksdag passed what is regarded as the world's first law for press freedom and freedom of information, abolishing censorship and opening government documents.

concepts.title: Expression and assembly in international law
concepts.description: The UN's International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966) protects opinion and expression (Article 19) and peaceful assembly (Article 21), with limits only by law where necessary.

concepts.title: Speakers' Corner
concepts.description: At Speakers' Corner in Hyde Park anyone may speak on any subject if it is lawful. After an 1866 protest broke down the park railings, an 1872 act set rules for meeting and speaking there.

concepts.title: What government is and does
concepts.description: Government is the system by which a country or community is run: it makes laws, keeps order, defends, provides services and raises taxes. The word comes from the Greek for steering a ship.

concepts.title: Why governments arose
concepts.description: While humans were few there was hardly any government; in Sumer, sharing irrigation water called for a central authority. Today the UN has 193 member states.

concepts.title: The Code of Hammurabi
concepts.description: Around 1750 BCE, Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 legal rulings engraved on a stone stela, written as if-then rules, including 'an eye for an eye'.

concepts.title: Ways countries pay for healthcare
concepts.description: Countries finance healthcare mainly through government schemes funded by taxes (Nordic countries, UK), compulsory health insurance funded by contributions (France, Germany, Japan), and out-of-pocket payments; most mix them. The WHO's goal is universal health coverage.

concepts.title: How much countries spend on health
concepts.description: OECD countries spent on average 9.3% of GDP on health in 2024; the United States spent 17.2% and Germany 12.3%. Health took 15.1% of government spending in 2023.

concepts.title: Infrastructure must be maintained: Genoa's bridge
concepts.description: Genoa's Morandi bridge (1967) collapsed on 14 August 2018, killing 43. Its replacement, the San Giorgio bridge (2020), has robots that check it for weathering and erosion.

concepts.title: Paying for roads: user taxes and partnerships
concepts.description: Governments pay for roads with taxes, user charges and partnerships. The US Highway Trust Fund (1956) runs on road-user taxes such as fuel tax; PPPs have a private partner fund and deliver a public asset, with mixed audit results.

concepts.title: Trying individuals: Nuremberg and the ICC
concepts.description: The Nuremberg tribunal held that crimes against international law are committed by people. The International Criminal Court, in The Hague since 2002, tries individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression, as a court of last resort.

concepts.title: The International Court of Justice
concepts.description: The ICJ, the UN's principal judicial organ, sits in the Peace Palace in The Hague. Only states can be parties, its jurisdiction rests on their consent, and its 15 judges are elected by the General Assembly and Security Council.

concepts.title: Judicial independence
concepts.description: Judges must be free from pressure: England's Act of Settlement (1701) ended dismissal at the king's pleasure, and the UN's 1985 Basic Principles set a worldwide standard.

concepts.title: What judges do
concepts.description: In a trial the judge keeps it fair, rules on the law, directs the jury and passes sentence.

concepts.title: Bushel's Case and jury independence
concepts.description: In 1670 jurors who acquitted William Penn were punished; Bushel's Case ruled that jurors cannot be punished for their verdict.

concepts.title: How juries work
concepts.description: Ordinary citizens chosen at random decide guilt while the judge handles the law; countries such as Japan mix citizens and judges on one panel.

concepts.title: Lady Justice's symbols
concepts.description: Justice's scales stand for impartial weighing, her sword for power, and her blindfold (from the 16th century) for impartiality; the Old Bailey's statue has none.

concepts.title: What makes a rule a law
concepts.description: A law is a rule of conduct that a community recognizes as binding, enforced through a controlling authority.

concepts.title: What a bill is
concepts.description: A bill is a proposal for a new law or a change to an existing one; once both Houses agree and it receives Royal Assent, it becomes an Act.

concepts.title: The stages of a bill
concepts.description: A UK bill passes first reading, second reading, committee, report and third reading in each House, with ping-pong until both agree its exact wording; a US bill must pass both chambers in identical form.

concepts.title: Committees and bills
concepts.description: Most detailed lawmaking happens in committees: bills are referred to them, most die there, and the rest go through hearings and mark-up.

concepts.title: How lawmakers debate
concepts.description: Debate on a bill's principles happens at second reading, under rules that keep it about ideas: no names, and no accusations of lying.

concepts.title: The filibuster and cloture
concepts.description: The US Senate allows extended debate, so long speeches can delay a bill (a filibuster); cloture ends debate, by two-thirds from 1917 and three-fifths since 1975.

concepts.title: Civil law and common law
concepts.description: Civil law, from Roman law, starts from written codes such as the Napoleonic Code; common law, from medieval England, builds on judges' precedents.

concepts.title: Legal traditions around the world
concepts.description: Beyond civil and common law are customary and Muslim law, and many countries mix traditions, like bijural Canada.

concepts.title: The word legislator
concepts.description: A legislator is literally a "proposer of a law", from Latin legis lator.

concepts.title: Byelaws: local laws
concepts.description: A byelaw is a local law made by a local authority for its own area, using powers granted by Acts of Parliament.

concepts.title: Where local lawmaking power comes from
concepts.description: Local governments can make only the laws a higher government allows: Canada's municipalities are "creatures" of the provinces, and US states follow Dillon's Rule or home rule.

concepts.title: Secondary legislation
concepts.description: In the UK, ministers make secondary legislation, mostly statutory instruments, under powers in an Act, to fill in its details.

concepts.title: US rulemaking
concepts.description: US agencies write regulations under authority from laws enacted by Congress, through an open notice-and-comment process that is not a vote.

concepts.title: Select committees
concepts.description: In the UK, a Commons select committee shadows each government department, examining its spending, policies and administration.

concepts.title: Civil disobedience: Thoreau and King
concepts.description: Thoreau argued you should break a law that makes you an agent of injustice; King held there is a moral responsibility to disobey unjust laws, openly and accepting the penalty.

concepts.title: Obeying, and repealing, unjust laws
concepts.description: Socrates, in Plato's Crito, chose to obey a sentence he thought unjust because of his implicit agreement with Athens; the legal route out of a law is repeal.

concepts.title: What a veto is
concepts.description: A veto is an executive's power to reject a bill; the word is Latin for "I forbid", from the protests of Rome's tribunes.

concepts.title: Veto overrides around the world
concepts.description: Override thresholds vary: two-thirds is most common, Poland needs three-fifths and Brazil an absolute majority; a veto changes the majority a bill needs.

concepts.title: The US veto and override
concepts.description: The US President has 10 days (Sundays excepted) to sign or veto a bill; Congress can override by two-thirds of each chamber, but not a pocket veto.

concepts.title: Gideon and the right to a lawyer
concepts.description: Clarence Earl Gideon's handwritten petition led the U.S. Supreme Court in 1963 to require lawyers for poor felony defendants.

concepts.title: Prosecution and defence
concepts.description: A prosecutor brings the case for the state; a defence lawyer represents the accused, and England's cab-rank rule means barristers can't pick clients by their opinions.

concepts.title: National, regional and local government
concepts.description: Many countries split government into layers. In Canada the federal level handles defence, foreign affairs, currency and passports; provinces and territories run education and health care; municipalities handle local services like waste, water and fire protection.

concepts.title: India's panchayats
concepts.description: India's 1992 73rd constitutional amendment made panchayats institutions of self-government at village, block and district levels, alongside the Union and state governments.

concepts.title: The debate over lobbying and its regulation
concepts.description: Supporters say lobbying brings expertise and voice; critics say it can make influence unequal. Governments respond mainly with registration and disclosure.

concepts.title: What lobbying is
concepts.description: Lobbying is trying to influence government decisions; the word comes from the lobbies where people waited for lawmakers, and many kinds of groups do it.

concepts.title: How city councils are organized
concepts.description: In US cities, the council-manager form has the council hire a professional manager; the mayor-council form has a separately elected mayor with executive power.

concepts.title: Local government in public view
concepts.description: English council meetings are open to the public, with agendas published five clear days ahead; India's gram sabha includes every village voter.

concepts.title: Magna Carta's key clauses
concepts.description: Clause 39: no imprisonment without lawful judgment. Clause 40: justice not sold, denied or delayed. Clause 12: no scutage or aid without general consent. Clause 61: 25 barons could enforce it.

concepts.title: Magna Carta: the king under the law
concepts.description: On 15 June 1215 at Runnymede, King John agreed to Magna Carta under pressure from rebel barons. Its 63 clauses established that the sovereign is subject to the rule of law.

concepts.title: Who controls the military
concepts.description: In a democracy the armed forces are subordinate to elected civilian authorities, who decide missions, size, budget and purchases; parliaments oversee them through laws, hearings and the purse. Costa Rica's 1949 constitution abolished the army.

concepts.title: Military spending around the world
concepts.description: SIPRI counts world military spending of $2887 billion in 2025, 2.5% of global GDP; the US, China, Russia, Germany and India made up 58%. NATO members agreed in 2025 to aim for 5% of GDP by 2035.

concepts.title: Absolute monarchy and divine right
concepts.description: Absolutism is unlimited central authority; Louis XIV (1643-1715) is the classic example, defended by the divine right of kings.

concepts.title: Monarchy: rule of one
concepts.description: A monarchy is the undivided rule of one person, the monarch, usually by heredity; Malaysia elects its paramount ruler for five years.

concepts.title: Myth: every new government brings new officials
concepts.description: The UK Civil Service Code requires civil servants to serve any elected government equally well and keep their own politics out of their advice.

concepts.title: Myth: a higher tax bracket taxes all your income
concepts.description: With marginal brackets, as in US and UK income tax, only income inside a higher bracket pays its rate.

concepts.title: Nation versus state
concepts.description: A nation is a people with a shared identity; a state is a political organization with territory, laws and the means to enforce them. Their borders usually only partly overlap, as with the Kurds and the United Kingdom.

concepts.title: Headlines versus stories
concepts.description: Many shared links are never read (59% in a 2016 study); press codes forbid headlines not supported by the text, so read past the headline.

concepts.title: Signs of reliable reporting
concepts.description: Journalism codes ask for clearly identified sources, labeled opinion, and prompt, prominent corrections: clues a reader can check.

concepts.title: Oligarchy: rule by the few
concepts.description: Oligarchy is rule by a privileged few for their own ends, typically the wealthy; Aristotle set it against aristocracy, rule by the best.

concepts.title: Michels's iron law of oligarchy
concepts.description: Robert Michels argued that every organization, even a democratic one, ends up ruled by an elite few.

concepts.title: Venice's closed Great Council
concepts.description: Over about a century from 1297, Venice's Great Council closed to a fixed hereditary group, and the republic lasted into the late 18th century.

concepts.title: Parliaments: old roots, one or two chambers
concepts.description: Parliament means a place for talking. Iceland's Althing, founded around 930, is one of the oldest national parliaments and has one chamber; the UK Parliament has two, the elected Commons and the mainly appointed Lords.

concepts.title: What a parliament does
concepts.description: A parliament makes laws, controls taxes and spending, and holds the government to account. In the UK, the Commons alone imposes taxes and a prime minister needs its majority.

concepts.title: What political parties are and do
concepts.description: A political party is a group organized to acquire and exercise political power. Parties recruit candidates, organize voters, form governments and provide opposition, though Washington warned against the spirit of party in 1796.

concepts.title: Whig and Tory: insults turned names
concepts.description: Britain's first party names began as terms of abuse in 1679: Tory meant an Irish outlaw, and Whig probably came from a Scottish word for a horse drover.

concepts.title: Ageing and the rising pension age
concepts.description: Across the OECD, people aged 65+ per 100 aged 20-64 rose from 22 in 2000 to 33 in 2025 and may reach 52 by 2050. Retirement ages are rising; Denmark confirmed 70 from 2040, a move its government and unions argued over.

concepts.title: Public pensions: a big bill
concepts.description: Germany's 1889 state pension began at 70. Public pensions now average 8.1% of GDP across the OECD and 18% of government spending, from about 16% of GDP in Greece and Italy to under 3% in Iceland and Ireland.

concepts.title: What police do: policing by consent
concepts.description: Modern policing began in London in 1829 with unarmed officers; British policing rests on public consent and the prevention of crime.

concepts.title: Limits on police power
concepts.description: Police powers are limited by law: time limits on detention, rights in custody, the Miranda warnings, and in England and Wales few officers are armed.

concepts.title: Power versus authority
concepts.description: Power is the ability to exercise your will over others; authority is power that people accept as legitimate and agree to follow.

concepts.title: The presumption of innocence
concepts.description: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt: Woolmington's 'golden thread', Blackstone's ratio and Article 11 of the UDHR.

concepts.title: Data protection and its limits
concepts.description: In the EU, data protection is a fundamental right and the GDPR has applied since 25 May 2018, with rights to see and erase your data. Privacy is balanced against free expression and national security.

concepts.title: The right to privacy
concepts.description: Warren and Brandeis (1890) called privacy 'the right to be let alone'. The Universal Declaration's Article 12 protects it; the US Constitution never names it, but courts built it from amendments such as the Fourth.

concepts.title: Public goods and free riders
concepts.description: Public goods are nonexcludable and nonrival, like national defense; people can free ride on them, and taxes required by law overcome the free rider problem.

concepts.title: Public services
concepts.description: Public services such as schools, transport, mail, police, fire and help for people in need are provided for everyone and paid for by taxes. In 2024, 1 in 4 people lacked safely managed drinking water.

concepts.title: The punishment debate
concepts.description: Retributivists like Kant say punishment is deserved; Bentham said it is justified only if it prevents greater harm; Beccaria stressed certainty over severity.

concepts.title: Prisons in numbers
concepts.description: About 11.7 million people were in prison worldwide in 2023, around 30 per cent of them not yet sentenced.

concepts.title: The purposes of punishment
concepts.description: Punishment is justified by retribution, deterrence, incapacitation or rehabilitation; Norway's normality principle leans toward rehabilitation.

concepts.title: Who is a refugee
concepts.description: Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, a refugee is outside their own country because of a well-founded fear of persecution on one of five grounds. Refugee status is declaratory. Most forcibly displaced people (UNHCR, end-2025) stay inside their own countries.

concepts.title: Nansen and the first refugee passport
concepts.description: In 1921 the League of Nations made Fridtjof Nansen its first High Commissioner for Refugees. His 1922 Nansen passport let stateless refugees travel to find work; he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922.

concepts.title: Asylum and non-refoulement
concepts.description: Asylum is protection a state grants to people fleeing persecution or serious harm; UNHCR calls seeking it a human right. Non-refoulement forbids returning refugees to where their life or freedom would be threatened.

concepts.title: Freedom of religion: belief and practice
concepts.description: Everyone may hold, adopt or change a religion or belief, and no limits on belief are allowed; showing it in practice may be limited, but only by law and where necessary for safety, order, health, morals or others' rights.

concepts.title: Debate: France's 2004 school symbols law
concepts.description: France's 2004 law banned conspicuous religious symbols for public school pupils. The Stasi Commission and President Chirac backed it as secularism; Human Rights Watch called it an unwarranted infringement on religious practice.

concepts.title: Religion and the state
concepts.description: Countries arrange religion and state differently: the US bars Congress from establishing a religion, France's 1905 law separated churches and state, and England has an established church with the monarch as supreme governor.

concepts.title: Contacting your representative
concepts.description: A UK MP represents everyone in the constituency, voters or not, handles constituents' issues, and holds surgeries to meet them.

concepts.title: Petitions to parliament
concepts.description: UK Parliament petitions get a government response at 10,000 signatures and are considered for debate at 100,000; Canadian e-petitions need 500 signatures.

concepts.title: Republics
concepts.description: A republic, from res publica, 'the public thing', is ruled by representatives of the citizens and has no hereditary monarch; Rome's began in 509 BCE.

concepts.title: Madison's case for representation
concepts.description: In Federalist No. 10, Madison argued that delegating government to elected representatives lets a republic span more citizens and territory than a pure democracy.

concepts.title: Suffrage and who had it
concepts.description: Suffrage is the right to vote. In 18th- and 19th-century Britain it required property ('a stake in the country'), and some countries once excluded voters by race.

concepts.title: Universal suffrage
concepts.description: The Universal Declaration's Article 21 makes the will of the people, expressed in genuine elections by universal and equal suffrage, the basis of government's authority. The line keeps moving: Austria votes at 16.

concepts.title: Voting amendments in the U.S. Constitution
concepts.description: Amendments widened the U.S. vote: the 15th (1870) on race, the 24th (1964) against poll taxes, the 26th (1971) for citizens 18 and over.

concepts.title: Rules as a common code
concepts.description: Groups need shared rules so everyone plays the same game: in 1863 the Football Association was formed to set one definite code of football rules.

concepts.title: Rules that coordinate: Sweden's Dagen H
concepts.description: Some rules matter because everyone follows the same one. Sweden drove on the left while its neighbors drove on the right, then switched to the right on 3 September 1967.

concepts.title: Who runs schools: public and private
concepts.description: Public schools are typically funded and regulated by government; private schools are run by a private body. Government-dependent private schools get more than half their money from public sources. The Netherlands funds public and private schools equally.

concepts.title: Paying for schools: how much and which level
concepts.description: OECD governments spent 2.2% of GDP on primary and lower secondary schools in 2022. Some countries fund schools from the centre (Greece, Iceland, New Zealand); in Spain and Switzerland, regions or cantons do most of it.

concepts.title: Bagehot's fusion of powers
concepts.description: Walter Bagehot (The English Constitution, 1867) called the efficient secret of Britain's system the nearly complete fusion of executive and legislative powers, linked by the Cabinet.

concepts.title: Separation of powers
concepts.description: Separation of powers divides legislative, executive and judicial functions among separate bodies. Montesquieu (1748) warned that power tends to be abused and there is no liberty when the powers are united.

concepts.title: The social contract and Hobbes
concepts.description: A social contract is a real or imagined agreement setting out the rights and duties of rulers and ruled. Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) said people give up freedom to a sovereign to escape a state of nature that is nasty, brutish and short.

concepts.title: Locke: rights and consent
concepts.description: Locke held that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property; government rests on consent, and people may resist a government that violates their rights.

concepts.title: Rousseau: the general will
concepts.description: Rousseau's The Social Contract (1762) opens 'Man was born free, and he is everywhere in chains' and grounds legitimate laws in the general will.

concepts.title: South Africa's 1996 Constitution
concepts.description: Mandela signed South Africa's constitution at Sharpeville on 10 December 1996, Human Rights Day. It is the supreme law, and its Bill of Rights protects equality, religion, privacy and the vote.

concepts.title: Sovereignty
concepts.description: Sovereignty is a state's ultimate authority over its own decisions. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) is often seen as the foundation of the modern system of sovereign states. South Sudan, independent in 2011, is the UN's newest member.

concepts.title: What counts as a state: the Montevideo criteria
concepts.description: The 1933 Montevideo Convention lists four qualifications of a state: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. A state's existence does not depend on recognition.

concepts.title: Where the money goes: spending by function
concepts.description: Statisticians sort government spending into ten functions (COFOG). Social protection (pensions and sickness, disability and unemployment benefits) is the largest, 13.4% of GDP across the OECD in 2023; health is second.

concepts.title: How big government spending is
concepts.description: Across OECD countries, general government spending averaged 42.6% of GDP in 2023; Finland, France and Austria spent over 56% in 2024.

concepts.title: What a tax is
concepts.description: The OECD defines taxes as compulsory, unrequited payments to government: what you get back isn't in proportion to what you paid. Taxes fall on income and profits, social security, payroll, property, and goods and services.

concepts.title: How much countries tax
concepts.description: In 2024, taxes averaged 34.1% of GDP across OECD countries, from 18.3% in Mexico to 45.2% in Denmark.

concepts.title: Theocracy: rule by religion
concepts.description: Theocracy is government by divine guidance or divinely guided officials, often clergy applying religious law.

concepts.title: Theocracy today: the Vatican and Iran
concepts.description: The pope, elected by cardinals, holds all three powers in Vatican City; Iran's supreme leader, a jurist chosen by an elected assembly, stands above an elected president.

concepts.title: What a treaty is and why it binds
concepts.description: A treaty is a written agreement between states governed by international law, whatever it is called. Pacta sunt servanda: a treaty in force binds its parties and must be kept in good faith, and internal law is no excuse.

concepts.title: The Kadesh treaty: the oldest known peace treaty
concepts.description: Around 1269 BC the Hittite king Hattusili III and Egypt's Ramesses II made peace in writing: the oldest known peace treaty. A replica hangs at UN Headquarters.

concepts.title: Signing and ratifying a treaty
concepts.description: For treaties that need ratification, signing does not yet bind a state; ratification is the act by which a state consents to be bound. A signer must not defeat the treaty's purpose in the meantime.

concepts.title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
concepts.description: The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris on 10 December 1948, with no votes against. Eleanor Roosevelt chaired its drafting.

concepts.title: What the Declaration says
concepts.description: Its 30 articles begin 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights', apply without distinction of any kind, and promise life, liberty and security of person.

concepts.title: From declaration to law
concepts.description: The Declaration was proclaimed as a common standard and was not binding, which was first seen as a weakness; two covenants followed in 1966, and many countries wrote it into their constitutions.

concepts.title: The UN's founding, and what it is not
concepts.description: The UN Charter opens with a pledge to save future generations from war. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945. It is not a world government: it has no army, levies no taxes and depends on its members.

concepts.title: The General Assembly: one country, one vote
concepts.description: All 193 UN members sit in the General Assembly with one vote each, reflecting the Charter's sovereign equality of members. It makes recommendations; important questions need a two-thirds majority.

concepts.title: The Security Council and the veto
concepts.description: The Security Council has primary responsibility for peace. It has 15 members, 5 of them permanent with a veto: China, France, Russia, the UK and the US. Its decisions bind all UN members.

concepts.title: Unitary systems
concepts.description: In a unitary state the center holds the power and delegates it; the UK devolves power to Scotland but its Parliament remains sovereign.

concepts.title: What volunteering is
concepts.description: Volunteer work is unpaid and non-compulsory, done through organizations (formal) or directly for others (informal); informal volunteering is more than twice as common.

concepts.title: How much volunteering there is
concepts.description: About 862 million people aged 15 and over volunteer each month; the NSW Rural Fire Service shows volunteers delivering a public service.

concepts.title: How wars end: armistice and peace treaty
concepts.description: An armistice stops the fighting while peace terms are worked out; a peace treaty formally ends a war. The 1918 armistice was followed by the Treaty of Versailles; the 1953 Korean armistice was not a peace treaty.

concepts.title: Why wars start, and the rules on starting them
concepts.description: Clausewitz saw war as a continuation of state policy by other means. Rules tightened over time: the 1907 Hague Convention required a declaration, the 1928 Kellogg-Briand Pact renounced war but could not be enforced, and the 1945 UN Charter bans force except self-defence.

concepts.title: Weber's definition of the state
concepts.description: Weber (1919) defined the state as a community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory.

concepts.title: Weber's three types of authority
concepts.description: Weber named three sources of legitimate authority: traditional (custom), charismatic (a leader's exceptional qualities) and legal-rational (laws and offices).

concepts.title: New Zealand: women vote first
concepts.description: On 19 September 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in parliamentary elections, after Kate Sheppard's campaign and a petition of 31,872 signatures.

concepts.title: Britain: suffragists and suffragettes
concepts.description: British suffragists, led by Millicent Fawcett, used law-abiding methods; suffragettes, led by the Pankhursts, used radical action. Women over 30 first voted in 1918; equal votes at 21 came in 1928.

concepts.title: Women's suffrage in the U.S. and Switzerland
concepts.description: The 19th Amendment (1920) bars denying the vote on account of sex. Swiss men voted down women's suffrage in 1959; Swiss women won the federal vote in 1971.

concepts.title: The Antarctic Treaty: a continent run by agreement
concepts.description: Signed in 1959 by twelve countries, the Antarctic Treaty keeps Antarctica for peaceful purposes and science, freezes territorial claims and opens every station to inspection.

concepts.title: Youth parliaments
concepts.description: Youth parliaments let under-18s practice politics: the UK Youth Parliament elects members aged 11 to 18 and debated in the Commons chamber in 2009.

concepts.title: Children's right to be heard
concepts.description: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) gives children the right to express their views in matters affecting them (Article 12).

concepts.title: Advertising that informs
concepts.description: Advertising can tell buyers what exists and what it costs. Lee Benham found eyeglasses cost more in US states that banned advertising.

concepts.title: Advertising that persuades
concepts.description: Advertising also shapes preferences: people with strong ketchup favorites often cannot tell brands apart blindfolded, and De Beers's "A Diamond Is Forever" helped make the diamond solitaire the standard engagement ring.

concepts.title: Rival advertising can cancel out
concepts.description: A. C. Pigou argued in 1920 that when competing firms advertise against each other, the spending may simply cancel out.

concepts.title: Commodities, futures and gold
concepts.description: Commodities such as metals, grains and oil trade mostly through futures contracts, a practice pioneered at Osaka's Dojima rice market (1730). Gold pays no income, and precious metals are highly volatile.

concepts.title: Property as an investment
concepts.description: Real estate can pay through rent and through changes in its value. REITs own income-producing property and let investors share its income; non-traded REITs are hard to sell.

concepts.title: Income and price: where returns come from
concepts.description: An investment can pay through income, such as dividends, interest or rent, and through a change in its price. Total return is the income plus the price gain or minus the price loss.

concepts.title: How automation reshapes jobs
concepts.description: Machines take over tasks, but work often shifts rather than vanishing: US farm jobs fell from 41% of the workforce to 1.9%, and ATMs changed tellers' work instead of ending it.

concepts.title: The Luddites
concepts.description: From 1811, English textile workers known as Luddites smashed machines. They objected less to machines than to how owners used them to undercut skilled, fairly paid work.

concepts.title: Money as bank deposits
concepts.description: Most money today is bank deposits: records of what banks owe their customers, not physical cash.

concepts.title: Bank runs
concepts.description: Banks cannot pay all depositors at once, so a rush to withdraw can sink a bank, and fear of a run makes joining it rational.

concepts.title: Limits on bank money creation
concepts.description: Banks cannot create money without limit: they must lend profitably and manage risk, regulation constrains them, and central bank interest rates are the ultimate limit.

concepts.title: Banks as intermediaries
concepts.description: A bank accepts deposits and makes loans, standing between savers and borrowers.

concepts.title: Bank lending creates money
concepts.description: When a bank makes a loan it creates a matching new deposit; most money today is created this way, and repaying loans destroys it.

concepts.title: Money changers and the first banks
concepts.description: The word bank comes from the Italian banco, the bench of medieval money changers, who began taking deposits and lending them out.

concepts.title: How banks earn: the spread
concepts.description: A bank charges borrowers a higher interest rate than it pays depositors; the difference covers costs and profit.

concepts.title: Barter and the double coincidence of wants
concepts.description: Barter is trading goods or services directly; it only works when each side wants what the other offers.

concepts.title: Barter in history
concepts.description: No society that ran purely on barter has ever been described; barter tends to appear between acquaintances and when money runs short.

concepts.title: Barter has no common measure
concepts.description: Barter has no single unit for measuring value and makes saving for later hard.

concepts.title: The blockchain ledger
concepts.description: A blockchain is a shared, tamper-evident ledger in which each block of transactions is linked to the one before.

concepts.title: How a bond works
concepts.description: A bond is an IOU: you lend to a government, city or company, which pays interest on a schedule and repays the face value at maturity.

concepts.title: Bond risks and who gets paid first
concepts.description: Bonds can default, and a bond sold early may fetch less if interest rates have risen. If a company goes bankrupt, bondholders are paid before shareholders.

concepts.title: Britain's War Loan
concepts.description: Britain's 3.5% War Loan traced back to borrowing in 1917 for World War I. It had no fixed maturity, so the government chose when to repay: in 2015, when rates were low.

concepts.title: What a speculative bubble is
concepts.description: A bubble is a price far above what fundamentals justify for a long time, sustained by buyers expecting to sell higher; bubbles are hard to spot until they burst, and economists disagree about them.

concepts.title: The 50/30/20 rule
concepts.description: A common guideline: 50% of after-tax income to needs, 30% to wants, 20% to saving or paying down debt.

concepts.title: What a budget is
concepts.description: A budget is a written monthly plan: list expenses, note income, subtract, then track what you actually spend.

concepts.title: Booms, recessions and how they are dated
concepts.description: Economies swing irregularly between expansions and recessions, marked by peaks and troughs; the NBER dates US recessions after the fact.

concepts.title: Europe's butter mountains
concepts.description: The EU's Common Agricultural Policy held farm prices artificially high, farmers produced more, and by the 1980s huge surpluses of butter and wine piled up.

concepts.title: Who pays card fees
concepts.description: Merchants pay a fee on card sales, mostly interchange to the card issuer, set by the networks; the cost is passed on in prices, including to cash users.

concepts.title: How a card payment travels
concepts.description: A card payment links the cardholder, the merchant, the merchant's bank (acquirer) and the card issuer through a card network: authorize, then settle.

concepts.title: Paying by changing records
concepts.description: A card payment changes banks' records: the payer's balance goes down and the seller's goes up.

concepts.title: Paper money in China
concepts.description: Paper money began in China, from Tang-era flying money to Song-era notes in Sichuan, where heavy iron coins made paper convenient.

concepts.title: Why firms exist (Coase)
concepts.description: Ronald Coase argued in 1937 that firms exist because using markets has costs, now called transaction costs, such as finding prices and negotiating a contract for each deal. Inside a firm, managers direct the work.

concepts.title: What a coin's stamp did
concepts.description: A coin's stamp showed that an authority stood behind a standard weight of metal, so it no longer had to be weighed in every deal.

concepts.title: Ways to own a business
concepts.description: A sole proprietorship has one owner and a partnership two or more; in both, owners are personally liable for the business's debts. A corporation is a separate legal entity whose owners have limited liability.

concepts.title: Who runs a corporation
concepts.description: Shareholders own a corporation and elect a board of directors, which sets goals and policies and hires officers such as the CEO to run the firm.

concepts.title: Salomon and the company as a separate person
concepts.description: In the Salomon case, Britain's House of Lords ruled that a properly formed company is a separate person in law, so its owner was not personally liable for its debts.

concepts.title: What competition does for buyers
concepts.description: Competition pushes businesses to operate efficiently, keep prices down and keep quality up, and brings more choice and innovation.

concepts.title: Profits attract rivals
concepts.description: Profits draw new firms into a market; their extra supply pushes the price down until profits are squeezed away.

concepts.title: Price takers
concepts.description: In perfect competition, many firms sell identical products, so each must accept the market price.

concepts.title: Cowrie shell money
concepts.description: Cowrie shells served as money in parts of Africa and Asia because they were small, durable and hard to fake.

concepts.title: The consumer price index basket
concepts.description: The CPI tracks the cost of a representative, spending-weighted basket of goods and services, which is updated as habits change.

concepts.title: Why a fixed basket overstates living costs
concepts.description: Substitution bias and quality/new goods bias make a fixed-basket index overstate the rise in the cost of living.

concepts.title: What a credit score is
concepts.description: A credit score predicts how likely you are to repay on time, based on your credit reports; higher scores usually mean easier approval and better rates.

concepts.title: What goes into a credit score
concepts.description: A FICO score weighs payment history, amounts owed, length of history, new credit and credit mix; income isn't in it, and nobody has just one score.

concepts.title: Credit means trust
concepts.description: The word credit comes from Latin credere, 'to trust, entrust, believe': lending and borrowing run on trust.

concepts.title: What a cryptocurrency is
concepts.description: Cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin are digital tokens created and tracked by a network of computers, with no central issuer.

concepts.title: Why crypto prices swing
concepts.description: Bitcoin's price is set by supply and demand; with a nearly fixed supply and no issuer steadying it, the price swings sharply.

concepts.title: What drives the business cycle
concepts.description: Economists disagree about what drives booms and recessions: swings in spending, interest-rate moves, or shocks to productivity and tastes.

concepts.title: What deflation is
concepts.description: Deflation is a general fall in prices, usually a side effect of collapsing spending; falling prices in one sector are not deflation.

concepts.title: Why deflation hurts
concepts.description: Falling prices lead people to delay purchases and raise the real burden of debts, which can slow an economy for years.

concepts.title: Why buyers want less at higher prices
concepts.description: The substitution effect (switching to relatively cheaper goods) and the income effect (a higher price shrinks buying power) both cut the quantity demanded.

concepts.title: The law of demand
concepts.description: When a price rises, buyers want less; when it falls, they want more. The demand curve slopes downward.

concepts.title: What shifts demand
concepts.description: Income, tastes, prices of related goods, population and expectations shift the whole demand curve.

concepts.title: Deposit insurance
concepts.description: US deposit insurance (the FDIC, since 1933) guarantees deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, to keep public confidence.

concepts.title: What caused the Great Depression
concepts.description: Economists still disagree: the 1929 crash and falling spending, a shrinking money supply as banks failed (Friedman and Schwartz), and the gold standard all have advocates.

concepts.title: Enron's one-basket 401(k)
concepts.description: At the end of 2000, most of Enron's 401(k) plan assets were in Enron stock. When Enron went bankrupt in December 2001, many employees lost their jobs and much of their retirement savings.

concepts.title: Diversification
concepts.description: Diversification means spreading money among different investments, across and within asset classes, to reduce risk. Funds make it easy, but it can't prevent losses in a market-wide drop.

concepts.title: The dot-com bubble
concepts.description: In the late 1990s, money poured into internet start-ups; the Nasdaq peaked in March 2000 and fell more than 78% by October 2002.

concepts.title: Engel's law
concepts.description: The lower a household's income, the bigger the share of it spent on food; richer households spend more dollars but a smaller share.

concepts.title: Paper money reaches Europe
concepts.description: Marco Polo described Chinese paper money in the 13th century; Europe's first banknotes came from Sweden's Stockholms Banco in 1661.

concepts.title: Stock exchanges as meeting places
concepts.description: The NYSE traces its origins to the Buttonwood Agreement of 1792. An exchange gathers buyers and sellers so investors can nearly always buy or sell.

concepts.title: Bids, asks and orders
concepts.description: The bid is the highest price a buyer will pay, the ask the lowest a seller will take, and the gap is the spread. Orders are matched automatically; a market order trades now, a limit order only at your price or better.

concepts.title: Fiat money
concepts.description: Fiat money has no value of its own and no commodity backing; a government declares it legal tender.

concepts.title: Franklin's compound-interest bequest
concepts.description: Benjamin Franklin left £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia to be lent at 5% for 200 years, calculating that compounding would make it £131,000 in a century.

concepts.title: Exchange rates
concepts.description: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, set in the foreign exchange market; a stronger currency makes imports cheaper and exports dearer.

concepts.title: Why exchange rates move
concepts.description: Floating exchange rates move with supply and demand for a currency, driven by interest rates, inflation and expectations; some countries fix their rates instead.

concepts.title: What GDP measures
concepts.description: GDP is the market value of the final goods and services a country produces in a period; real GDP adjusts it for price changes.

concepts.title: What GDP misses
concepts.description: GDP leaves out unpaid work and ignores pollution, leisure and how income is shared; its pioneer Kuznets warned it is not a measure of welfare.

concepts.title: The 2008 financial crisis
concepts.description: A US housing bubble fed by risky mortgage lending burst, Lehman Brothers failed in 2008, and the Great Recession followed; economists still debate the causes.

concepts.title: The IMF and the World Bank
concepts.description: The 1944 Bretton Woods conference created the IMF, which lends to countries in crisis with conditions, and the World Bank, which funds development.

concepts.title: The World Trade Organization
concepts.description: The WTO, founded in 1995 from the 1947 GATT, sets trade rules, hosts negotiations and settles disputes between its members.

concepts.title: The gold standard
concepts.description: Under a gold standard, a currency's unit is fixed to a set amount of gold and paper money can be exchanged for it.

concepts.title: Leaving the gold standard
concepts.description: Countries left gold because its supply limited their money; the US ended its last gold link, for foreign governments, in 1971.

concepts.title: Rules for when sellers know more
concepts.description: When one side of a deal knows more about quality (asymmetric information), rules like food-safety and truth-in-advertising laws help buyers; The Jungle led to two such laws in 1906.

concepts.title: Capital rules for banks
concepts.description: Regulators make banks fund part of their lending with owners' money (capital), a cushion that absorbs losses before depositors are hurt; higher requirements make banks safer but may slow lending.

concepts.title: Central bank independence
concepts.description: Central banks are kept at arm's length from elected politicians so short-term election pressures do not push up inflation; critics question how much power unelected officials should hold.

concepts.title: What a central bank does
concepts.description: A central bank runs monetary policy, watches over banks and keeps payments safe. Sweden's Riksbank (1668) is the oldest; the US Federal Reserve dates from 1913 and aims for maximum employment and stable prices.

concepts.title: Budget deficits and surpluses
concepts.description: A government runs a deficit in a year when it spends more than it collects, a surplus when it collects more than it spends, and a balanced budget when the two are equal.

concepts.title: Fiscal policy and monetary policy
concepts.description: Fiscal policy is government spending and taxing, set in the US by Congress and the administration; monetary policy is what the central bank does with interest rates and money.

concepts.title: The free rider problem
concepts.description: When non-payers cannot be excluded, each person has an incentive to let others pay and enjoy the good for free, so a good everyone values may never be produced.

concepts.title: The lighthouse debate
concepts.description: Economists long used the lighthouse as a public good; Ronald Coase showed in 1974 that English lighthouses were privately run and paid for by light dues collected at ports, though critics note the dues were backed by the Crown.

concepts.title: Tax brackets and marginal rates
concepts.description: In a bracketed income tax, only the income inside a higher bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate, so a raise never lowers take-home pay.

concepts.title: Money growth and prices
concepts.description: If the amount of money grows faster than the goods and services it buys, prices rise; the link is real over long periods but not mechanical, because how fast money changes hands can shift.

concepts.title: The national debt
concepts.description: The national debt is the sum of past deficits and surpluses: governments cover deficits by selling bonds, and the debt is that borrowing plus interest. Economists weigh its costs and uses differently.

concepts.title: Pay-as-you-go pensions
concepts.description: US Social Security is pay-as-you-go: today's workers' taxes fund today's beneficiaries, so fewer workers per retiree (about four in 1965, 2.7 in 2023) strains the system.

concepts.title: How a central bank's rate moves the economy
concepts.description: A central bank sets a core short-term rate that feeds into loan and savings rates; raising it cools spending and price rises, cutting it encourages borrowing, spending and hiring, with long and variable lags.

concepts.title: The price revolution
concepts.description: In the 16th century, silver from American mines like Potosí flowed into Spain and across Europe while prices rose about sixfold; historians also point to population growth.

concepts.title: Public goods
concepts.description: A public good is nonexcludable and nonrival, like national defense; because non-payers cannot be kept out, governments usually fund such goods through taxes.

concepts.title: The first social insurance
concepts.description: Germany under Otto von Bismarck created the first old-age social insurance in 1889, paid for by workers, employers and the government, with benefits from age 70.

concepts.title: The main kinds of tax
concepts.description: Taxes fall on what people earn (income, payroll and corporate taxes), what they buy (sales taxes, VATs and excise taxes) and what they own (property and estate taxes).

concepts.title: Progressive, proportional and regressive taxes
concepts.description: A progressive tax takes a higher share of higher incomes, a proportional (flat) tax the same share from everyone, a regressive tax a smaller share of higher incomes. Flat taxes have supporters and critics.

concepts.title: What taxes pay for
concepts.description: Governments collect taxes to pay for what they provide: in the US, federal money goes mostly to defense, Social Security, healthcare and interest; states and cities spend most on education.

concepts.title: Unemployment insurance
concepts.description: Unemployment insurance gives temporary, partial wage replacement to workers who lose jobs through no fault of their own; economists weigh its support for families against effects on job search.

concepts.title: The Volcker rate hikes
concepts.description: Under Paul Volcker, the Federal Reserve let its key rate approach 20% in 1980 and 1981 to fight high inflation; inflation fell to 5% by late 1982, but a deep recession pushed unemployment near 11%.

concepts.title: The Great Depression and its legacy
concepts.description: The Great Depression (1929 to about 1941) was the deepest US downturn: output fell by a third, unemployment reached 25% and prices fell; it reshaped economic policy.

concepts.title: Hanoi's rat bounty
concepts.description: In colonial Hanoi, a bounty paid per rat tail led people to cut off tails, release rats to breed, and farm rats.

concepts.title: Hyperinflation and its causes
concepts.description: Hyperinflation is inflation above 50% a month, usually begun by governments creating money to pay for spending and fed by collapsing trust.

concepts.title: Loss aversion and the endowment effect
concepts.description: People tend to feel losses more strongly than equal gains, so owners value things more than non-owners: the endowment effect, shown in the 1990 mug experiment.

concepts.title: Mental accounting
concepts.description: Thaler's idea that people sort money into separate accounts in their heads and judge each decision on its own.

concepts.title: Coase and bargaining over externalities
concepts.description: Ronald Coase argued in 1960 that when deals cost little to make, affected parties can bargain to an efficient fix without government.

concepts.title: Market, command and mixed economies
concepts.description: In a market economy decisions are spread among buyers and sellers; in a command economy goals come from rulers; most real economies mix the two.

concepts.title: Externalities
concepts.description: An externality is the effect of a deal on a third party outside it; when costs like pollution are ignored, markets make too much of the product.

concepts.title: The Gini coefficient
concepts.description: A single number from 0 (everyone has the same) to 1 (one person has everything) that measures how unequally income is shared.

concepts.title: Hayek and prices as signals
concepts.description: Hayek argued that the knowledge an economy needs is scattered among many people, and that prices pass it along in a way no central planner could.

concepts.title: Keynes and spending in a slump
concepts.description: Keynes argued that unemployment comes from too little total spending, and that government should spend, even by borrowing, to fill the gap.

concepts.title: Keynes's 15-hour week
concepts.description: In 1930, Keynes predicted much higher living standards and a 15-hour work week a century later; longer lives and retirements delivered extra leisure instead.

concepts.title: Keynes's legacy and critics
concepts.description: Keynes helped design Bretton Woods and dominated Western policy until the 1970s, when monetarists led by Milton Friedman gained ground; Hayek never accepted his case.

concepts.title: Marx's critique of capitalism
concepts.description: Marx argued that labor creates value, that owners keep the surplus as profit, and that class struggle would end in the overthrow of capitalism.

concepts.title: Marx's reach and his critics
concepts.description: Marx's ideas inspired communist governments ruling about a third of the world, while critics such as the Austrian school rejected the labor theory of value.

concepts.title: Nudges and defaults
concepts.description: Behavioral economics shows that details like the default option steer decisions; Thaler and Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow lets people commit now to save more later.

concepts.title: Pigou's tax on externalities
concepts.description: In 1920, Arthur Pigou proposed taxing activities that impose costs on others and subsidizing those that spread benefits; a carbon tax is a modern example.

concepts.title: The prisoner's dilemma
concepts.description: A game in which each player does better by betraying whatever the other does, yet both end up worse off than if both had cooperated.

concepts.title: Cooperation in repeated games
concepts.description: When a game repeats with no known last round, cooperation can pay; tit for tat, which cooperates first and then copies, did well in Axelrod's tournaments.

concepts.title: Adam Smith's invisible hand
concepts.description: Smith's idea that many people pursuing their own interest through trade can produce outcomes that benefit society, though no one intends them.

concepts.title: Smith's limits and critics
concepts.description: Smith gave government real duties and distrusted collusion among traders; modern critics such as Joseph Stiglitz argue the invisible hand often fails.

concepts.title: The sunk cost effect
concepts.description: The tendency to keep going with something because of money, effort or time already spent; Arkes and Blumer showed it with theater season tickets.

concepts.title: Wealth versus income inequality
concepts.description: Income is a flow of money coming in; wealth is a stock of what you own. Wealth is far more unequally shared than income.

concepts.title: Incentives
concepts.description: Incentives are rewards (positive) and penalties (negative) that encourage or discourage choices; people respond to them in predictable ways. Prices are incentives too.

concepts.title: Four kinds of income
concepts.description: Land earns rent, labor earns wages, capital earns interest and entrepreneurship earns profit; wages are most people's main income.

concepts.title: The factors of production
concepts.description: Economists group the resources that make goods and services into land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship.

concepts.title: Index funds: from 'Bogle's Folly' to the majority
concepts.description: John Bogle's First Index Investment Trust (1976) raised about $11 million and was mocked as 'Bogle's Folly'. Most active large-cap funds have trailed the S&P 500 over 15 years, and US index-style funds overtook active funds in assets at the end of 2023.

concepts.title: How index funds work
concepts.description: An index fund tracks a market index such as the S&P 500 by holding all or a sample of its securities. It trades rarely, can cost less to run, and carries the same risks as its index.

concepts.title: Why prices rise, and the debate
concepts.description: Demand-pull, cost-push and expectations drive inflation; economists disagree about how much the money supply matters.

concepts.title: What inflation is
concepts.description: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise across an economy over time; it lowers the purchasing power of money.

concepts.title: Interest in ancient Mesopotamia
concepts.description: Mesopotamian laws, including Hammurabi's code in the 18th century BCE, set interest rates: 20% on silver and more on riskier barley loans.

concepts.title: Compound interest
concepts.description: Compound interest is paid on the original amount plus the interest already earned, so growth speeds up over time.

concepts.title: Interest: the price of borrowing
concepts.description: Interest is the price a borrower pays a lender for the use of money, usually stated as a rate; lenders charge it for giving up money now and for taking risk.

concepts.title: The Rule of 72
concepts.description: Dividing 72 by an annual interest rate estimates how many years compounding takes to double money.

concepts.title: Comparing homes for money: safety, growth and access
concepts.description: Every saving and investment product differs in how safe the money is, how fast it can grow and how readily you can get it back. A liquid asset can be turned into cash quickly.

concepts.title: Secured and unsecured loans
concepts.description: Secured loans are backed by collateral and usually cost less; unsecured loans have none, so lenders see more risk and may charge more.

concepts.title: The first coins
concepts.description: The first coins were probably made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, around 650 BCE; coinage also arose separately in China.

concepts.title: What a market is
concepts.description: A market is any way buyers and sellers get in contact to exchange goods and services, directly or through go-betweens. It need not be a place.

concepts.title: eBay's first sale
concepts.description: In 1995, the first item sold on AuctionWeb, the site that became eBay, was a broken laser pointer, for $14.83.

concepts.title: Markets for work and savings
concepts.description: Supply and demand apply to any market: goods and services, labor and financial capital.

concepts.title: Marshall's scissors
concepts.description: Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: price comes from both together.

concepts.title: Why metal made good money
concepts.description: Metal suits money because it is portable, does not perish and is hard to counterfeit.

concepts.title: Microcredit and Grameen Bank
concepts.description: Muhammad Yunus showed that small loans without collateral could work for the poor, founding Grameen Bank and sharing the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize.

concepts.title: Six traits of useful money
concepts.description: Useful money is durable, portable, divisible, uniform, limited in supply and acceptable.

concepts.title: The three jobs of money
concepts.description: Money is whatever works as a medium of exchange (a way to pay), a unit of account (a measure of value) and a store of value (a way to save).

concepts.title: Money runs on trust
concepts.description: Money is valuable because people trust that others will accept it; when that trust goes, its value goes too.

concepts.title: What a monopoly is
concepts.description: A monopoly is a single supplier of something with no substitute, protected by barriers to entry.

concepts.title: Why monopolies hurt buyers
concepts.description: A monopoly sells less at a higher price than a competitive market, and faces less pressure to improve.

concepts.title: Standard Oil and antitrust
concepts.description: Standard Oil dominated US refining until the Supreme Court broke it up in 1911 under the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890.

concepts.title: A mortgage: a loan pledged on a home
concepts.description: A mortgage lets the lender take the property if the loan isn't repaid; the word means 'dead pledge' because the pledge ends either way.

concepts.title: Why mortgages last decades
concepts.description: Longer mortgages mean lower monthly payments but more total cost; early payments are mostly interest (amortization).

concepts.title: Needs set by custom
concepts.description: Adam Smith counted as necessaries whatever local custom made shameful to go without, so the line between needs and wants moves with time and place.

concepts.title: Needs and wants
concepts.description: Needs are essential to survival and basic living; wants are for enjoyment. A need can come in a want-sized version.

concepts.title: Opportunity cost
concepts.description: Every choice costs the value of the next best alternative you give up, including time and lost earnings.

concepts.title: No such thing as a free lunch
concepts.description: Saloons once gave free lunch to drink buyers; the saying that no lunch is free became an economic maxim.

concepts.title: Paycheck deductions
concepts.description: Employers withhold payroll taxes and income tax, and may deduct retirement or health contributions, before pay arrives.

concepts.title: Gross and net pay
concepts.description: Gross pay is what you earn before deductions; net (take-home) pay is what you receive after them.

concepts.title: The division of labor and the pin factory
