concepts.description: In June 1215 rebel barons forced King John to agree to Magna Carta at Runnymede; its clauses 39 and 40 promised lawful judgment and justice for all.

concepts.title: Magna Carta's survival
concepts.description: The Pope annulled Magna Carta within ten weeks, but it was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225, and three of its clauses are still English law.

concepts.title: The empire of Mali
concepts.description: Founded by Sundiata about 1230, Mali grew rich on the gold and salt trade and under Mansa Musa took in Timbuktu and Gao.

concepts.title: What peasants owed the manor
concepts.description: Villeins paid for their holdings with week-work on the lord's demesne, produce, and fees such as merchet and heriot.

concepts.title: Mansa Musa's hajj
concepts.description: On his 1324 pilgrimage, Mansa Musa gave away so much gold in Cairo that, al-Umari reported, its value fell for about twelve years; 'richest person ever' is a popular claim that cannot be measured.

concepts.title: Marco Polo
concepts.description: The Venetian Marco Polo spent 1271-95 in Asia, 17 years in China, and dictated his Travels to Rustichello; parts are exaggerated, but evidence shows he was in China.

concepts.title: Weekly markets
concepts.description: An English market met once a week on a set day and place, by royal charter, and from 1200 only if it did not harm its neighbours.

concepts.title: Food by rank
concepts.description: Bread quality, meat and drink all marked rank: fine wheat for lords, coarse loaves for servants, meat rarely for peasants, and fish on fast days.

concepts.title: When the Middle Ages ended
concepts.description: Historians end the Middle Ages at different dates, most often 1453 (Constantinople falls), 1492 (Columbus) or 1517 (Luther), all near 'about 1500'.

concepts.title: Holy days and festivals
concepts.description: Free time followed the Church calendar ("holiday" means holy day); at York the craft guilds staged a 48-play cycle on Corpus Christi.

concepts.title: The medieval inquisition
concepts.description: Papal inquisitors from 1227 tried suspected heretics; most received penances or prison, and those who refused to recant were burned.

concepts.title: Medieval inventions we still use
concepts.description: Eyeglasses (Italy, about 1290) and mechanical tower clocks are medieval inventions still in daily use.

concepts.title: Water and wind power
concepts.description: Thousands of watermills ground England's grain by 1086; windmills, first known in Persia, appear in English records in the 1180s as timber post mills.

concepts.title: Why "Middle" Ages
concepts.description: Renaissance scholars invented the Middle Ages as a gap between classical antiquity and their own revival; medieval means "middle age".

concepts.title: Games and songs
concepts.description: Folk football was a rowdy all-comers game that kings banned again and again, in vain; songs like "Sumer is icumen in" survive from the 1200s.

concepts.title: Early, high and late
concepts.description: Historians divide the Middle Ages into early (about 500-1000), high or central (about 1000-1300) and late (about 1300-1500) periods.

concepts.title: When the Middle Ages were
concepts.description: The Middle Ages run from the collapse of Roman rule in the West in the 5th century to the Renaissance: roughly 500 to 1500, about a thousand years.

concepts.title: Spices as status
concepts.description: Spices were costly imports for the rich, used in strong sauces to show wealth; historians reject the myth that they hid rotten meat.

concepts.title: Coverture and its limits
concepts.description: In England a married woman's legal existence was suspended under coverture, while a single woman could contract and sue in her own name.

concepts.title: What medieval women did
concepts.description: Examples by class and region: Christine de Pizan wrote for a living in France, Margaret Paston ran and defended Norfolk estates, English brewsters and Paris silkwomen worked in trade.

concepts.title: The lord's mill
concepts.description: Lords claimed the right to grind all their tenants' grain and took a toll for it, which is why Abbot Samson destroyed a rival windmill in 1191.

concepts.title: The cloister
concepts.description: The cloister, a square of covered walkways, linked the church, refectory, chapter house and dormitory and was used for study, exercise and burial.

concepts.title: Monks and books
concepts.description: In the early Middle Ages, monks copied books by hand in scriptoria, and figures like Cassiodorus made sure pagan classics were copied too.

concepts.title: The cost of the Mongol conquests
concepts.description: Estimates of the dead are rough but enormous: roughly 40 million for Genghis Khan's conquests (Britannica); in 1258 the Mongols sacked Baghdad.

concepts.title: The Pax Mongolica
concepts.description: In the 13th and 14th centuries Mongol rule revived the Silk Road with unprecedented security, the yam relay stations and paiza passes.

concepts.title: Motte and bailey
concepts.description: Early castles were earth mounds topped by timber towers beside a fenced yard, quick to build with forced labour.
In 1066 Harold beat a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge, then lost to William of Normandy at Hastings; how Harold died is debated.

concepts.title: The Normans
concepts.description: The Normans were Vikings who settled in northern France after Rollo's 911 treaty, took up French language and Christianity, and later won lands in England and southern Italy.

concepts.title: Nuns and convents
concepts.description: Nuns lived by the Benedictine pattern under an abbess, in mostly small, enclosed houses.

concepts.title: Where the Ottomans came from
concepts.description: Founded about 1300 by Osman I, the Ottomans entered the Balkans as Byzantine allies, took Gallipoli in 1354 and built the Janissaries.

concepts.title: Near-collapse and recovery
concepts.description: In 1402 Timur defeated Bayezid I at Ankara and split Ottoman lands among his sons; after civil war Mehmed I reunited them in 1413.

concepts.title: Paper from China
concepts.description: Chinese craftsmen made the first paper from rags, first as medicine wrapping in the 2nd century BCE, and by the 3rd and 4th centuries CE wrote everything on it.

concepts.title: Paper's journey west
concepts.description: Paper reached Samarkand by trade, papermaking arrived there in 751 (the Talas prisoner story is a legend), Baghdad made paper by the 790s, and Europe had it by the 12th century.

concepts.title: The parish church in daily life
concepts.description: The parish church was normally the only place to receive the sacraments and be buried, and councils like Lateran IV (1215) set yearly duties for every believer.

concepts.title: The first parliaments
concepts.description: Parliaments grew from royal councils: León's assembly of 1188 included town representatives; in England the word appears in 1236, towns joined in 1265, the Model Parliament met in 1295 and the Commons sat apart from 1341.

concepts.title: Parliament and taxes
concepts.description: Parliament grew because kings needed its consent to extra taxes to pay for their wars.

concepts.title: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381
concepts.description: Angered by the Statute of Labourers and set off by the poll tax of 1380, rebels led by Wat Tyler and inspired by John Ball marched on London in 1381.

concepts.title: How the revolt ended
concepts.description: Richard II promised to abolish serfdom at Mile End; Wat Tyler was killed at Smithfield, the promises were forgotten, but no poll tax was levied for over 250 years.

concepts.title: Pilgrimage and its shrines
concepts.description: Medieval Christians made pilgrimages for penance, cures, vows and salvation, to Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela and other shrines.

concepts.title: Faith, fear and blame
concepts.description: The plague drove flagellant processions and the false blaming of Jews, who were massacred across Europe, as at Strasbourg in 1349, though they died of plague too.

concepts.title: Plague, wages and work
concepts.description: With workers scarce after the Black Death, wages rose and labour services gave way to wages and rents; England's Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to freeze wages.

concepts.title: Rats or people? The transmission debate
concepts.description: The rat-flea story is challenged by Dean et al. (2018), whose human flea and louse model fit death records better in seven of nine outbreaks; the question is still debated.

concepts.title: What caused the plague
concepts.description: Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, confirmed for the Black Death by ancient DNA from victims' teeth; bubonic plague spreads by flea bites, pneumonic plague person to person.

concepts.title: Portugal's voyages around Africa
concepts.description: Prince Henry sponsored voyages down West Africa for gold and enslaved people; Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 and da Gama reached India in 1498.

concepts.title: From thousands of books to millions
concepts.description: Printing turned Europe's few thousand manuscript books into more than 9 million printed books by 1500, in editions larger than whole monastic libraries.

concepts.title: The Renaissance begins in Italy
concepts.description: The Renaissance, 'rebirth', began in 14th-century Italy as a revival of classical learning, funded by rich city-states and families such as Florence's Medici.

concepts.title: How Robin Hood grew
concepts.description: Robin Hood is known from rhymes and ballads, not records; Marian and his noble rank were added centuries later.

concepts.title: Rome's three heirs
concepts.description: After Rome fell in the West, its world passed to three heirs: the western kingdoms, the Byzantine Empire and the caliphate.

concepts.title: Bosworth and the Tudors
concepts.description: Henry Tudor defeated Richard III at Bosworth in 1485, married Elizabeth of York and founded the Tudor dynasty; Richard's skeleton was found in Leicester in 2012.

concepts.title: The Wars of the Roses
concepts.description: From 1455 to 1485 the houses of Lancaster and York, both descended from Edward III, fought for England's crown; the rose name came long afterward.

concepts.title: A round Earth in the classroom
concepts.description: Medieval universities taught a spherical Earth from Sacrobosco's Sphere; the flat-Earth Middle Ages is a 19th-century myth.

concepts.title: The excommunications of 1054
concepts.description: In 1054 a papal legate and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other, the traditional date of the East-West split; the sentences were lifted in 1965.

concepts.title: Why East and West drifted apart
concepts.description: Disputes over papal authority, the Creed, celibacy and bread widened a gap that grew from the 5th to the 11th century.

concepts.title: What a serf was
concepts.description: A serf was bound to a hereditary plot and to his lord's will: not a slave, but not free to leave, marry or change work without permission.

concepts.title: How to attack a castle
concepts.description: Ladders, siege towers, rams, mines and counterweight trebuchets.

concepts.title: How sieges ended
concepts.description: Most sieges ended by treachery, starvation or disease; Rochester in 1215 fell to a pig-fat mine and then hunger.

concepts.title: The Silk Road
concepts.description: A network of routes about 6,400 km long, travelled in stages by middlemen; silk went west, wool, gold and silver east, and religions travelled too.

concepts.title: Gunpowder, compasses and paper money
concepts.description: Chinese gunpowder was used in fireworks and signals by the 10th century; the Song improved compasses for sea trade and pioneered paper money.

concepts.title: Kingdoms after Rome
concepts.description: Germanic kingdoms replaced Rome in the West: Ostrogoths in Italy, Visigoths in Spain, Vandals in North Africa, Franks in Gaul, Anglo-Saxons in Britain.

concepts.title: Sumptuary laws
concepts.description: Laws such as England's of 1363 set what each rank could wear, to stop people dressing above their station, but proved hard to enforce.

concepts.title: Sutton Hoo
concepts.description: The 1939 ship burial at Sutton Hoo, probably King Rædwald's, revealed a rich, well-connected Anglo-Saxon world.

concepts.title: Pray, fight, work
concepts.description: Early 11th-century bishops described society as three orders: those who pray, fight and work.

concepts.title: Charters and "city air"
concepts.description: Self-governing towns (communes) held charters from bishops, counts or kings, and many offered freedom to settlers who stayed a year and a day.

concepts.title: Town dwellers: the first bourgeois
concepts.description: Medieval France called a walled-town dweller a bourgeois, as distinct from a peasant; the word later named the middle class.

concepts.title: Why towns grew after 1000
concepts.description: Once raids ended, western European towns revived: Europe's population nearly doubled between 1000 and 1340, and new walled towns were founded.

concepts.title: Trial by combat
concepts.description: In trial by combat the two sides or their champions fought, trusting God to give victory to the right; it came to England with the Normans and was abolished only in 1819.

concepts.title: Trial by ordeal
concepts.description: Ordeals of hot iron and cold water asked God to reveal guilt; the Church's 1215 ban on priests blessing them ended them in England.

concepts.title: From Northmen to Normans
concepts.description: Charlemagne built defences against the Northmen, but Vikings raided and settled anyway, and a Viking leader's descendant, William, conquered England.

concepts.title: No horns
concepts.description: Vikings did not wear horned helmets: the best-preserved Viking helmet has none, no Viking-age writer mentions them, and the image came from 19th-century artists.

concepts.title: Viking longships
concepts.description: Clinker-built longships with a square sail and oars drew so little water that they could run onto beaches, go up rivers and be dragged overland.

concepts.title: Viking voyages
concepts.description: Vikings travelled east down Russian rivers to Kyiv and Constantinople, and west to Iceland, Greenland and Newfoundland, where they were present in 1021.

concepts.title: Who the Vikings were
concepts.description: The Vikings were Scandinavians who raided, traded and settled from the late 8th century; most were farmers, and the Age is dated from the Lindisfarne raid of 793.

concepts.title: Absolute pitch is rare
concepts.description: Absolute (perfect) pitch is naming or producing a note with no reference; it is estimated at under 1 in 10,000 in the US and Europe and does not guarantee better musicianship.

concepts.title: Perfect pitch and tone languages
concepts.description: Absolute pitch is more common with earlier music training and far more common among Mandarin-speaking conservatory students, whose language uses pitch for meaning.

concepts.title: The Zeng bells and China's eight sounds
concepts.description: The Marquis Yi of Zeng's bronze bells (about 2,400 years old, two notes per bell, music-theory inscriptions) and the ba yin classification by material.

concepts.title: Scat singing
concepts.description: Armstrong helped invent scat singing, using wordless syllables instead of lyrics; 'Heebie Jeebies' is one of the earliest scat recordings.

concepts.title: Louis Armstrong makes the solo central
concepts.description: On his Hot Five and Hot Seven records (1925-28), Armstrong broke from collective improvising and became the first great jazz soloist.

concepts.title: Single-impression printing
concepts.description: Pierre Attaingnant's Paris type (1528) combined each note with a piece of staff, printing music in one pass, halving the work.

concepts.title: Bach and the fugue
concepts.description: Bach's specialty, the fugue, passes one theme (the subject) from voice to voice; his Well-Tempered Clavier sets a prelude and fugue in every major and minor key.

concepts.title: Bach's life and revival
concepts.description: Bach led Leipzig's church music from 1723 until 1750 and was admired mainly as an organist; Mendelssohn's 1829 St. Matthew Passion began the Bach revival.

concepts.title: Basso continuo
concepts.description: The Baroque's foundation: a bass line played by a low instrument while a harpsichordist or organist improvised chords from figures written under it.

concepts.title: Baroque versus Classical
concepts.description: Late-Baroque music favored intricate polyphony over a continuo; the Classical style (the later 18th century) reacted with melody-led homophony, simplicity and clarity.

concepts.title: The Baroque era
concepts.description: Western music from about 1600 to about 1750, named after a misshapen pearl by critics who meant it as an insult; grand and dramatic, with a strong melody-bass polarity and new forms such as opera, oratorio and the concerto.

concepts.title: Beat and tempo
concepts.description: The beat is music's steady pulse; tempo is how fast it goes, counted in beats per minute or named with Italian terms like adagio and allegro.

concepts.title: Beatlemania
concepts.description: The Beatles, from Liverpool and steeped in American rock and roll, reached 73 million US viewers on February 9, 1964, and held the Hot 100's top five on April 4, 1964.

concepts.title: The studio as instrument
concepts.description: In 1966 the Beatles stopped performing live to concentrate on the studio; Sgt. Pepper (1967) took months at Abbey Road and ran its songs together.

concepts.title: Bebop's higher intervals
concepts.description: Charlie Parker built melodies from a chord's higher intervals (9th, 11th, 13th), and bebop players added substituted chords to older jazz harmony.

concepts.title: Bebop
concepts.description: Bebop took shape in early-1940s Harlem jam sessions: small groups, rapid tempos and solos built on the chords, made for listening rather than dancing.

concepts.title: Beethoven, the bridge
concepts.description: Beethoven kept Classical forms but stretched them to carry a personal vision (the Eroica, the Fifth's minor-to-major journey, the choral Ninth), bridging the Classical and Romantic eras.

concepts.title: Beethoven's hearing loss
concepts.description: Beethoven's deafness came on gradually: weakening hearing and ringing from about 1798, lost high notes by 1801, the private Heiligenstadt Testament of 1802, conversation books from 1818, profound deafness by the Ninth's 1824 premiere. He kept composing by inner hearing.

concepts.title: Blue notes
concepts.description: Blue notes lower the third, seventh and sometimes fifth by less than a semitone, landing between the major and minor pitches; guitarists bend or slide strings to reach them.

concepts.title: The 12-bar blues and its AAB verse
concepts.description: Most blues use a 12-bar form on three chords, with three-line stanzas: a line, its repeat, and a rhyming answer.

concepts.title: Where the blues came from
concepts.description: African Americans created the blues in the Deep South after the Civil War, out of work songs, field calls and spirituals; W.C. Handy helped bring it to a national audience.

concepts.title: The beat reaches movement areas
concepts.description: Listening to a regular beat engages movement-related brain areas even when the listener is still.

concepts.title: From ear to brain
concepts.description: Hair cells turn sound vibrations into electrical signals that the auditory nerve carries to the brain; an area at the top of each temporal lobe receives information from the ears.

concepts.title: The Mozart effect myth
concepts.description: The 1993 Mozart effect was a brief spatial-task boost; a 2010 meta-analysis found little evidence of any specific Mozart effect.

concepts.title: Music and the reward chemical
concepts.description: Pleasurable music that gives chills releases dopamine in the striatum, in one part while anticipating the peak and another at the peak itself.

concepts.title: Chopin and the piano
concepts.description: Chopin, born near Warsaw in 1810 and settled in Paris from 1831, wrote almost only for piano, including mazurkas and polonaises tied to his Polish feeling; he preferred intimate settings, and his heart was returned to Warsaw.

concepts.title: Chords and triads
concepts.description: A triad stacks three notes, a root, a third and a fifth; C-E-G is the C major triad.

concepts.title: The ear sorts pitch
concepts.description: Inside the cochlea, hair cells near the wide end respond to high pitches and those toward the center to low pitches, so each pitch has its own place.

concepts.title: A = 440 Hz
concepts.description: The international tuning standard sets the A above middle C at 440 Hz: agreed in 1939 and confirmed as ISO 16 in 1975, after decades of local pitches.

concepts.title: Consonance and dissonance
concepts.description: Consonant combinations sound stable, dissonant ones tense; music moves between them, and the preference for consonance depends heavily on what music you know.

concepts.title: From disco to house
concepts.description: Disco grew in early-1970s New York clubs on a four-on-the-floor kick; house grew from it in Chicago, named after Frankie Knuckles's Warehouse club.

concepts.title: Detroit techno
concepts.description: Techno came from young African American DJ-producers in Detroit in the mid-1980s: mostly instrumental, with synth melodies and more complex machine beats than house.

concepts.title: Digital sound and the CD
concepts.description: The CD (1982) stores sound as numbers, sampling 44,100 times a second, a little over twice the roughly 20 kHz top of human hearing.

concepts.title: MP3 compression
concepts.description: MP3, from Fraunhofer IIS, stores sounds the ear can't perceive with less precision, making files up to ten times smaller; Napster spread shared files in 1999.

concepts.title: The Divje Babe debate
concepts.description: A holed cave bear bone from Slovenia, claimed as a Neanderthal flute, that many scientists think was chewed by hyenas.

concepts.title: The turntable as an instrument
concepts.description: Herc's merry-go-round looped a record's drum break with two copies on two turntables (the breakbeat); Grand Wizzard Theodore added scratching.

concepts.title: The TR-808 drum machine
concepts.description: Roland's TR-808 (1980) synthesized its drum sounds from circuits; dismissed as fake and discontinued, it became central to hip-hop through records like Planet Rock.

concepts.title: Early music in India
concepts.description: The Samaveda set Vedic verses to fixed melodies for ritual singing; the Natyashastra, attributed to Bharata, treated music as part of theatre.

concepts.title: Earworms are common
concepts.description: Earworms (involuntary musical imagery) are reported weekly by about 9 in 10 people and are usually short snippets of a tune.

concepts.title: Evicting an earworm
concepts.description: Seeking out the tune and distraction are common, effective responses; chewing gum reduced earworms in a 2015 study.

concepts.title: What makes a song sticky
concepts.description: Earworm songs tend to be faster, with common melodic contours and an unusual interval or repetition.

concepts.title: The erhu
concepts.description: The erhu is China's most popular bowed fiddle: two strings over a snakeskin-covered resonator, no fingerboard, and a bow whose hair runs between the strings.

concepts.title: The koto
concepts.description: The koto is a long Japanese zither with 13 strings over movable bridges, plucked with tsume picks, long called Japan's national instrument.

concepts.title: The shakuhachi
concepts.description: The shakuhachi is a Japanese end-blown bamboo flute named for its length; Edo-period Fuke Zen monks, the komuso, played it as meditation called suizen.

concepts.title: How an electric guitar pickup works
concepts.description: A magnetic pickup turns a steel string's vibration into a voltage at the same frequency, which an amplifier makes loud through a speaker.

concepts.title: The solid-body electric guitar
concepts.description: Hollow electric guitars suffered distortion, overtones and feedback, so makers built solid bodies: Les Paul in the early 1940s, then Fender and Gibson by 1952.

concepts.title: Duke Ellington writes for his players
concepts.description: Duke Ellington led his band for more than 50 years and wrote for the particular sounds of its members, as his 'Mood Indigo' score shows.

concepts.title: The Cotton Club and segregation
concepts.description: Ellington's orchestra became the house band at Harlem's Cotton Club in 1927, a club that featured Black entertainers for a whites-only audience.

concepts.title: Musical anhedonia
concepts.description: Some healthy people with normal music perception get little pleasure from music, yet respond normally to other rewards such as money.

concepts.title: Why sad music can feel good
concepts.description: Music-evoked sadness is enjoyed when it is non-threatening, aesthetically pleasing and brings benefits such as mood regulation.

concepts.title: Music borrows the voice's emotional code
concepts.description: Voices and music express emotion with similar cues: sadness slow, soft and low; happiness fast, loud and high.

concepts.title: Music festivals
concepts.description: Woodstock (1969) drew about 400,000 people to a farm in Bethel, New York, and ended with Hendrix's anthem; Live Aid (1985) linked stadiums on two continents.

concepts.title: The Jaws motif
concepts.description: John Williams's Jaws theme alternates two neighboring notes, E and F, growing louder and faster as the shark nears; it stands in for a shark seldom seen.

concepts.title: Music changes what a scene means
concepts.description: In a 2001 study, the same ambiguous film clips were read more positively with positive music and more negatively with negative music, and memories shifted the same way.

concepts.title: Silent films had live music
concepts.description: Silent films were accompanied by live music from pianists, organists or, in big cities, orchestras.

concepts.title: The Fisk Jubilee Singers
concepts.description: In 1871 a student choir from debt-ridden Fisk University toured to raise money, bringing spirituals to audiences in the US and Europe.

concepts.title: Flamenco's compas
concepts.description: The compas is flamenco's 12-beat rhythmic cycle, with groups of three and two inside it, coordinating singers, guitarists and dancers in forms like soleares.

concepts.title: Flamenco: song, dance and guitar
concepts.description: Flamenco, from Andalusia with an essential Gitano (Roma) role, fuses cante (song, its essence), baile (dance) and toque (guitar), with handclaps and footwork.

concepts.title: Barbara Allen: one ballad, many versions
concepts.description: The ballad 'Barbara Allen', mentioned by Samuel Pepys in 1666, is one of the most collected folk songs, in so many versions that the Library of Congress issued a whole LP of them.

concepts.title: Folk songs and oral tradition
concepts.description: Folk music lives in oral tradition: learned by ear within families and communities, it changes as it passes on, as Cecil Sharp found in Appalachia.

concepts.title: Composing for a sound chip
concepts.description: Koji Kondo wrote Super Mario Bros. music for NES sound that offered three musical notes at a time plus one white-noise sound, with very little data.

concepts.title: Music that reacts to play
concepts.description: Game music can react to play: Kondo wrote Game Over jingles, goal fanfares and pieces that speed up as time runs short.

concepts.title: Game music gains recognition
concepts.description: The Super Mario Bros. theme became the first video game music in the National Recording Registry (2023), and the Grammys first awarded a video game score prize in 2023.

concepts.title: The gamelan ensemble and its gong cycles
concepts.description: Javanese gamelan combines gongs, metallophones, drums, strings, flute and voices, and it moves in cycles: the great gong ageng marks the end of each gongan.

concepts.title: Gamelan tuning: slendro and pelog
concepts.description: Each gamelan is tuned only to itself. A full Javanese set is a double set in two tunings: slendro (five near-equal steps) and pelog (seven unequal pitches, used in sets of five).

concepts.title: Afrobeats
concepts.description: Afrobeats is 2000s West African pop from Nigeria and Ghana, distinct from Fela Kuti's political Afrobeat; it reached global charts in the 2010s.

concepts.title: K-pop goes global
concepts.description: BTS topped the Billboard 200 in 2018 with an album sung mostly in Korean, the first K-pop act to do so, before their first English-language song.

concepts.title: Latin pop and Despacito
concepts.description: Despacito led the Billboard Hot 100 for 16 weeks in 2017, the longest No. 1 run for a mainly non-English song.

concepts.title: The Great Migration carries the music north
concepts.description: About six million Black Americans left the rural South between the 1910s and 1970, fleeing Jim Crow; the blues and jazz moved north with them, to Chicago and beyond.

concepts.title: Music in Greek life and thought
concepts.description: Mousike, the art of the Muses; Plato and Aristotle's belief that music shapes the soul; music and chorus at the heart of Greek drama.

concepts.title: Gregorian chant
concepts.description: Monophonic, rhythmically free liturgical chant of the Roman Catholic Church, sung for the Mass and the canonical hours.

concepts.title: Where Gregorian chant came from
concepts.description: Named after Pope Gregory I (590-604), the chant took its lasting shape when Charlemagne imposed it in Frankish lands and it merged with Gallican chant.

concepts.title: Guido's staff and syllables
concepts.description: Guido of Arezzo's four-line staff with letter clefs fixed pitch, and his ut-re-mi syllables from Ut queant laxis taught sight-singing.

concepts.title: Handel's Messiah
concepts.description: Messiah, set in 24 days in 1741 to a Bible text compiled by Charles Jennens, premiered in Dublin at Easter 1742; the King George II standing story is an unconfirmed legend.

concepts.title: Handel and the English oratorio
concepts.description: Handel, born in 1685 like Bach, wrote Italian opera in London until the fashion faded, then turned to the English oratorio: a sacred drama for soloists, chorus and orchestra, sung without stage action.

concepts.title: Haydn at Esterhaza
concepts.description: Haydn served the Esterházy princes for nearly 30 years, isolated enough to be 'forced to become original'; his Farewell Symphony asked the prince, in music, to let the musicians go home.

concepts.title: The Classical symphony
concepts.description: A symphony is a long orchestral work in several movements, typically four in the Classical era (fast, slow, minuet, fast); it grew from the Italian opera overture, and Haydn's 100-plus symphonies shaped it.

concepts.title: The range of hearing
concepts.description: Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and with age most people lose the highest pitches first.

concepts.title: Hip-hop begins in the Bronx
concepts.description: Hip-hop is commonly dated to DJ Kool Herc's August 1973 party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, and was built by the Bronx's Black and Latino youth, with Jamaican sound-system roots.

concepts.title: Hip-hop's four elements
concepts.description: Hip-hop is a culture of four core elements: DJing, MCing (rapping), breaking and graffiti; Herc named the break dancers b-boys and b-girls.

concepts.title: Sampling
concepts.description: Sampling builds new tracks from music and sounds extracted from other recordings; drum breaks such as Funky Drummer are favorite samples.

concepts.title: The oldest accepted instruments
concepts.description: Bone and ivory flutes from caves in southwestern Germany, over 35,000 years old at Hohle Fels and 42,000 to 43,000 at Geissenklösterle, made by early modern humans.

concepts.title: Raga
concepts.description: A raga is a melodic framework: a set of notes with a typical order and characteristic motifs, within which Indian classical musicians improvise, over a tambura drone.

concepts.title: Tala
concepts.description: Tala is the rhythmic cycle of Indian classical music: tintal has 16 beats in four groups, kept with claps and waves, played on tabla, and resolving on the sam, the first beat.

concepts.title: Buzzing lips and the harmonic series
concepts.description: Brass players buzz their lips into a cup mouthpiece; lip tension picks notes from the tube's harmonic series, whole-number multiples of the fundamental.

concepts.title: Valves and slides
concepts.description: Valves (about 1815) add tubing to lower the note and fill the gaps between harmonics; the trombone uses a slide.

concepts.title: How a guitar works
concepts.description: Frets shorten the vibrating string to change notes; the bridge passes the vibration to the top plate, which makes the sound.

concepts.title: The guitar's family tree
concepts.description: The guitar grew from a four-course Spanish instrument to six strings and Torres's classical guitar, and spread into relatives like the jarana, the charango and the ukulele.

concepts.title: Sorting instruments by what vibrates
concepts.description: The Hornbostel-Sachs system (1914) sorts instruments by what vibrates first: idiophones, membranophones, chordophones and aerophones.

concepts.title: The orchestra's four sections
concepts.description: An orchestra groups instruments into strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion; woodwinds and brass are both aerophones, and percussion gathers idiophones and membranophones.

concepts.title: Pipe length and pitch
concepts.description: Doubling an organ pipe's length drops its note an octave (8-foot normal pitch, 16-foot an octave down); pipes span 32 feet to under an inch, down to about 16 Hz.

concepts.title: Pipes, ranks and stops
concepts.description: An organ blows pressurized air into pipes, one pipe per key in each rank; flue pipes sound by an air jet, reed pipes by a reed; stops bring ranks into play.

concepts.title: Pitched and unpitched percussion
concepts.description: Some percussion (xylophones, timpani) plays definite pitches; some (cymbals, snare drums) has none; the family mostly marks rhythm.

concepts.title: Tuning a drum
concepts.description: A tighter drumhead sounds higher; timpani use this to play definite notes, usually in pairs.

concepts.title: Hammers, escapement and dampers
concepts.description: Piano hammers strike the strings harder when you press harder; the escapement lets them fall away at once; dampers stop the strings, and the right pedal lifts them.

concepts.title: Cristofori's soft-loud keyboard
concepts.description: Around 1700 in Florence, Cristofori replaced the harpsichord's plucking with hammers, making a keyboard that plays soft or loud by touch: the pianoforte.

concepts.title: How a string sets its note
concepts.description: A shorter, tighter or lighter string sounds higher; halving the length raises the note an octave.

concepts.title: Bows and bodies
concepts.description: A bow keeps a string vibrating by stick-slip; the string barely moves air, so the bridge drives the body, which makes the sound. The violin family: violin, viola, cello, double bass.

concepts.title: Timbre
concepts.description: Timbre (tone color) comes from which harmonics sound with the fundamental and how strong they are, so the same pitch sounds different on each instrument.

concepts.title: How the voice makes sound
concepts.description: Air from the lungs vibrates the vocal folds; their tension sets the pitch, and the throat, nose and mouth shape the sound.

concepts.title: Voice types
concepts.description: Four-part music uses soprano, alto, tenor and bass, with baritone between tenor and bass; men's ranges are typically about an octave below women's.

concepts.title: The air column and tone holes
concepts.description: In a woodwind the air column vibrates; opening tone holes acts like shortening the pipe and raises the note.

concepts.title: Edges and reeds
concepts.description: Woodwinds start the air vibrating with an edge (flutes), a single reed (clarinet, saxophone) or a double reed (oboe, bassoon); the metal saxophone is a woodwind because of its reed.

concepts.title: Call-and-response in jazz
concepts.description: Jazz players often answer each other, one instrument, voice or section replying to another, the same shape as spirituals and work songs.

concepts.title: New Orleans collective improvisation
concepts.description: Early New Orleans bands had a front line of cornet, clarinet and trombone improvising together; the first commercial jazz record (1917) was made by a white band.

concepts.title: Improvising over the changes
concepts.description: Jazz soloists invent melodies on the spot over a tune's chord progression, turning a familiar tune into something personal; hard progressions like 'Cherokee' tested them.

concepts.title: Jazz begins in New Orleans
concepts.description: Jazz was developed by African Americans in New Orleans from brass bands, blues, spirituals and West African, Caribbean and Spanish traditions; 1890s segregation laws pushed Black and Creole musicians together.

concepts.title: Josquin des Prez
concepts.description: Josquin (c. 1450-1521) worked between cathedrals, courts and the papal chapel; Luther called him the master of the notes.

concepts.title: Salsa and clave
concepts.description: Salsa ('sauce') is a hybrid built on Afro-Cuban music, especially the Cuban son, shaped in New York by Puerto Rican and Cuban musicians, and it runs on the clave pattern.

concepts.title: Samba
concepts.description: Samba de roda grew from the traditions of enslaved Africans in Bahia, Brazil, and, carried to Rio de Janeiro, shaped the urban samba that became a national symbol.

concepts.title: Tango
concepts.description: Tango grew around 1880 among the urban lower classes of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, mixing European, African-descended and criollo traditions, and took Europe by storm by 1915.

concepts.title: Copland's three planes of listening
concepts.description: In What to Listen for in Music (1939), Aaron Copland described listening on sensuous, expressive and sheerly musical planes, and urged active listening for something.

concepts.title: Safe listening
concepts.description: WHO: 80 dB is safe for up to 40 hours a week and 90 dB for only 4; keep devices at or under 60% volume. Human hair cells do not grow back, but noise-induced hearing loss is preventable.

concepts.title: Madrigals and word painting
concepts.description: The madrigal, a secular song for several voices, used word painting to act out its text; England built a strong madrigal tradition.

concepts.title: Is minor sad?
concepts.description: Hearing major as happy and minor as sad is largely learned: children pick it up around age 6, and it is weak where Western music is unfamiliar.

concepts.title: Major and minor chords
concepts.description: Major and minor triads share a root and a fifth; the minor third is one semitone lower (three semitones above the root instead of four).

concepts.title: Polyphony and organum
concepts.description: Polyphony is two or more independent melodic lines at once; it began as organum, a second voice added to chant, first described in Musica enchiriadis (c. 900).

concepts.title: Melodic contour
concepts.description: A melody has a contour, the shape it traces as it rises, falls or arches, moving by steps or by leaps.

concepts.title: A melody is a pattern
concepts.description: People recognize a melody by the relationships between its notes, so it survives new words and a new starting note: one tune carries Twinkle, the alphabet song and Baa, Baa, Black Sheep.

concepts.title: Heavy metal and the power chord
concepts.description: The power chord is a root plus fifth, neither major nor minor and clear under distortion; heavy metal, codified in the 1970s, built on it.

concepts.title: Meter
concepts.description: Meter groups beats into regular measures of strong and weak beats, usually in twos or threes; a waltz counts in threes (3/4 time).

concepts.title: Maqam
concepts.description: Maqam is the melodic system of the Middle East and parts of North Africa: pitches, characteristic motifs and rules of use, including three-quarter tones, explored in the taqsim.

concepts.title: The oud
concepts.description: The oud, a short-necked fretless lute with a pear-shaped body, is central to Middle Eastern music and is the parent of the European lute, whose name comes from Arabic al-'ud.

concepts.title: Motown, the hit factory
concepts.description: Berry Gordy founded Motown in Detroit in 1959 with an $800 family loan and ran it like an assembly line, with house writers, a house band and quality control.

concepts.title: Mozart's life and works
concepts.description: Mozart (1756-1791) was composing at five and touring Europe from 1763; he wrote more than 600 works, including Figaro, Don Giovanni and The Magic Flute, and died at 35 with his Requiem unfinished.

concepts.title: Mozart myths
concepts.description: Two popular Mozart stories are myths: Salieri did not poison him (the legend grew through Pushkin and Amadeus), and research finds no Mozart-specific 'Mozart effect' on intelligence.

concepts.title: Rhythm, melody and harmony
concepts.description: Music combines sounds, usually by cultural standards of rhythm (when), melody (which notes in a line) and, in most Western music, harmony (notes at once).

concepts.title: Music is universal
concepts.description: A 2019 Harvard-led study found music in every one of 315 societies it examined, with lullabies and dance songs everywhere.

concepts.title: Music and nations
concepts.description: Nationalism in Romantic music meant revealing and glorifying a nation's distinctive features, drawing on folk tunes, dances, folklore and village life: Smetana's Vltava paints a Czech river; Sibelius's Finlandia had to hide from Russian censors.

concepts.title: MTV and the music video
concepts.description: MTV (launched August 1, 1981) made image as important as sound; Michael Jackson's videos helped break racial barriers, and Thriller became the first music video in the National Film Registry.

concepts.title: The National Recording Registry
concepts.description: Each year the Librarian of Congress adds 25 recordings at least 10 years old to the National Recording Registry; this chapter's milestones are on it.

concepts.title: Neumes
concepts.description: Early chant signs that reminded singers of melodies they had memorized; heighted neumes hinted at the melody's shape.

concepts.title: Note values
concepts.description: A note's shape gives its length: each value lasts half as long as the one above, so a whole note equals two halves or four quarters.

concepts.title: Notre-Dame and the first great polyphony
concepts.description: Léonin's two-voice Magnus liber organi (c. 1170), Pérotin's three- and four-voice organa at Notre-Dame, and Machaut's four-voice Mass.

concepts.title: The octave
concepts.description: An octave up doubles the frequency (A 440 Hz to 880 Hz); notes an octave apart sound like the same note and share a letter name.

concepts.title: How opera began
concepts.description: Florence's Camerata tried to revive ancient Greek music and helped create monody; Peri's La Dafne (1598) was probably the first opera, and opera went public in Venice in 1637.

concepts.title: Recitative and aria
concepts.description: Opera sings its story in two modes: recitative follows the rhythm of speech and moves the plot; the aria pauses for emotion. Handel's Messiah uses the same tools.

concepts.title: Why orchestras got a conductor
concepts.description: Baroque ensembles were led from the keyboard or first violin; as the continuo vanished and orchestras grew, a standing conductor with a baton took over (widely from about 1820), stressing the beat for everyone.

concepts.title: How the orchestra grew
concepts.description: From Monteverdi's Orfeo and Lully's string-heavy court orchestra to Mannheim's four sections; the continuo dropped away after about 1770 and 19th-century orchestras added more winds and brass.

concepts.title: The Palestrina legend
concepts.description: A 1607 story that Palestrina's Pope Marcellus Mass saved church polyphony after the Council of Trent, a gross exaggeration.

concepts.title: The mechanical royalty
concepts.description: For 2026 the US statutory mechanical royalty for a CD, vinyl or download copy of a song is 13.1 cents (or 2.52 cents per minute, whichever is larger).

concepts.title: The US radio gap
concepts.description: In the US, the sound recording's performance right covers only digital transmissions, so AM/FM radio pays the musical work's owners (via PROs like ASCAP and BMI) but not the recording's.

concepts.title: A song holds two copyrights
concepts.description: A recorded song involves two copyrights: the musical work (notes and lyrics, by songwriters) and the sound recording (by performers and producers).

concepts.title: Petrucci prints polyphony
concepts.description: In Venice in 1501 Ottaviano Petrucci printed the Odhecaton, the first polyphonic music from movable type, using separate impressions for staff, notes and words.

concepts.title: The first recording nobody could play
concepts.description: Scott de Martinville's 1860 phonautograph drew sound on soot-covered paper but could not play it back; it was first heard in 2008.

concepts.title: Edison's phonograph
concepts.description: Edison's 1877 tinfoil phonograph was the first machine to both record and play back sound, by pressing vibrations into foil and tracing them back out.

concepts.title: Pitch is frequency
concepts.description: How high or low a note sounds (pitch) is how we hear frequency, the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.

concepts.title: Deliberate practice
concepts.description: In a 1993 Berlin study, the best student violinists reported the most solitary practice; Ericsson called focused, feedback-rich improvement work deliberate practice.

concepts.title: What practice explains
concepts.description: Practice matters but explains only part of the differences between musicians: about 21% in a 2014 meta-analysis; a 2019 Berlin-style replication found best and good violinists did not differ significantly.

concepts.title: Program music
concepts.description: Program music is instrumental music that carries a story, scene or idea beyond the notes; Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique (1830) came with a printed program and turned the beloved into a recurring melody, the idée fixe.

concepts.title: Punk
concepts.description: Punk came together in 1975-80 in New York and London (the Ramones, the Sex Pistols) with short, fast, minimal songs that rejected polished rock.

concepts.title: Pythagoras and musical ratios
concepts.description: Greek tradition credits Pythagoras with linking the octave, fifth and fourth to string-length ratios 2:1, 3:2 and 4:3; the hammer story is a legend.

concepts.title: Haydn, Mozart and the quartet
concepts.description: Haydn and Mozart played quartets together; in 1785 Mozart dedicated six quartets to Haydn, who told Leopold Mozart that Wolfgang was the greatest composer he knew.

concepts.title: Radio's national audience
concepts.description: Radio grew from KDKA's 1920 broadcast to 40.3 percent of US households by 1930, and networks like NBC sent one program to many cities at once.

concepts.title: Payola
concepts.description: Airplay was so valuable that record promoters secretly paid disc jockeys; the late-1950s payola scandal led Congress to amend the Communications Act in 1960.

concepts.title: Scott Joplin, King of Ragtime
concepts.description: Scott Joplin, an African American composer from Texas, became the King of Ragtime with 'Maple Leaf Rag' (1899), wrote an opera, and won a posthumous Pulitzer in 1976.

concepts.title: Ragtime's syncopation
concepts.description: Ragtime piano sets a syncopated right-hand melody against a steady left-hand beat; it led American popular music from about 1899 to 1917.

concepts.title: Rap, rhyme and flow
concepts.description: Rap is rhythmic, rhyming speech over music; flow is the rhythm and articulation of the delivery. Early rap rhymed on beat four; later rap scattered rhymes and accents.

concepts.title: Rap reaches the charts
concepts.description: Rap grew in African American communities in New York City and reached national prominence with the Sugarhill Gang's Rapper's Delight (1979), now in the National Recording Registry.

concepts.title: Bob Marley
concepts.description: Bob Marley and the Wailers carried reggae and its social message worldwide from the 1970s; at the 1978 One Love Peace Concert he joined rival leaders' hands.

concepts.title: Reggae and the offbeat
concepts.description: Reggae came from Jamaica in the late 1960s, after ska and rocksteady; its groove sets short guitar or keyboard chords on the offbeats. UNESCO listed it as heritage in 2018.

concepts.title: The first rock and roll record?
concepts.description: Rocket 88 (1951) is often billed as the first rock and roll record, but rock and roll grew gradually and has earlier contenders, such as Sister Rosetta Tharpe's 1944 recording.

concepts.title: Rock and roll's roots
concepts.description: Rock and roll arose in the mid-1950s US from rhythm and blues and country, with gospel influence; its first stars included Black artists, and Elvis Presley and Chuck Berry crossed the styles.

concepts.title: The Romantics revive Bach
concepts.description: On 11 March 1829 in Berlin, the 20-year-old Mendelssohn conducted Bach's St. Matthew Passion, its first performance since Bach's death, launching the 19th-century Bach revival.

concepts.title: Romantic music puts emotion first
concepts.description: Romanticism (late 18th to mid-19th century) exalted emotion over reason and the individual; in music it brought emotionalism, individualism, nationalism, richer harmony and new forms for personal expression.

concepts.title: Rubato
concepts.description: Rubato, 'robbed time', stretches some beats and hurries others for expression; in Chopin's style the left hand keeps a fairly steady tempo while the right hand bends the melody.

concepts.title: Scales
concepts.description: A scale picks notes inside the octave. Western music splits it into 12 semitones and the major scale follows tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone; other traditions use other ladders.

concepts.title: The Seikilos song
concepts.description: A Greek song carved with its melody on a marble tombstone from Tralles (1st or 2nd century CE), widely considered the oldest complete composition.

concepts.title: Soul music
concepts.description: Soul, an African American style of the 1950s to 1970s, returned to gospel and blues roots; Aretha Franklin's Respect (1967) became an anthem for civil rights and women's equality.

concepts.title: The speed of sound
concepts.description: Sound crosses about 343 meters of air per second at 20 C, far slower than light, so thunder lags lightning by about 3 seconds per kilometer.

concepts.title: Sound is vibration
concepts.description: Sound is a pressure wave: a vibrating object pushes air into compressions and rarefactions that pass outward through a medium, and cannot cross a vacuum.

concepts.title: Call-and-response in African American song
concepts.description: Spirituals and work songs are built for call-and-response: a leader sings a line and a group answers with a refrain.

concepts.title: Spirituals of enslaved African Americans
concepts.description: Spirituals are religious folk songs created by enslaved people of African descent in the American South, passed on only by live singing and often voicing a longing for freedom.

concepts.title: The staff and clefs
concepts.description: Music is written on a five-line staff that works like a graph (up is higher, left to right is time); a clef names the lines.

concepts.title: Streaming takes over
concepts.description: Streaming services such as Spotify (2008) replaced owning music; the RIAA reported streaming at 82% of US recorded-music revenue in 2025.

concepts.title: The string quartet
concepts.description: Two violins, a viola and a cello, one player per part and no conductor; developed largely by Haydn from about 1750 into an intimate conversation among equals.

concepts.title: Auto-Tune
concepts.description: Auto-Tune detects a note's pitch and moves it to the nearest semitone; used subtly it corrects, pushed hard it makes the robotic 'Believe' effect.

concepts.title: Reverb in the studio
concepts.description: Reverb is sound lingering after its source stops; studios record dry and add artificial reverb, and a drier sound seems closer.

concepts.title: Swing and the big bands
concepts.description: In the swing era (about 1935 to the mid-1940s) big dance bands played sections of brass, woodwinds and rhythm off against each other, with a forward momentum called swing.

concepts.title: Fletcher Henderson, Benny Goodman and the color line
concepts.description: Black bandleader Fletcher Henderson's arrangements shaped Benny Goodman's 'King of Swing' sound; Goodman's integrated small groups gave Black musicians visibility during segregation.

concepts.title: The Moog synthesizer
concepts.description: Robert Moog unveiled his modular synthesizer in 1964; Switched-On Bach (1968) made it famous, and the portable Minimoog followed in 1970.

concepts.title: How a synthesizer makes sound
concepts.description: A synthesizer builds sound electronically: an oscillator sets pitch, a filter removes harmonics to shape timbre (subtractive synthesis), and an envelope (ADSR) shapes loudness over time.

concepts.title: Tchaikovsky's ballets
concepts.description: Tchaikovsky wrote ballet music with symphonic drama: Swan Lake flopped in Moscow in 1877 and succeeded only in the 1895 Petipa-Ivanov revival after his death; The Nutcracker (1892) introduced the celesta as the Sugar Plum Fairy's voice.

concepts.title: How troubadour songs survived
concepts.description: About 2,600 troubadour poems survive but fewer than 300 melodies; the Comtessa de Dia's A chantar is the only trobairitz song with its music.

concepts.title: Troubadours
concepts.description: Poet-musicians of southern France and nearby lands (late 11th to late 13th century) who wrote words and music in Occitan, favored at courts.

concepts.title: Verdi and Italian opera
concepts.description: Verdi paired great drama with memorable melody; Nabucco (1842) made him Italy's operatic hero at 28, its chorus 'Va, pensiero' became an unofficial anthem, and he was still writing at 79 with Falstaff.

concepts.title: Paganini, Liszt and the virtuoso
concepts.description: Paganini's violin playing seemed so impossible that rumors of a pact with the devil spread; Liszt set out to do the same on piano, gave the first complete solo recitals (the word first used for his 1840 London concerts) and inspired 'Lisztomania'.

concepts.title: Vivaldi and the concerto
concepts.description: Vivaldi, the Red Priest who taught at Venice's Pietà, wrote about 500 concertos and fixed the concerto's fast-slow-fast shape, with orchestral refrains around solo passages.

concepts.title: The Four Seasons as program music
concepts.description: The Four Seasons (published 1725) paints scenes from sonnets printed with the music, an early example of program music; it was little known until Kaufman's 1947 recording.

concepts.title: Wagner's music drama
concepts.description: Wagner fused poetry and music into continuous music drama, built his own Bayreuth theater with a hidden orchestra, and staged the 15-hour Ring there in 1876. He also published antisemitic writing, a documented and disputed part of his legacy.

concepts.title: The bell time line in Ewe drumming
concepts.description: In Agbadza, the music of the Ewe of Ghana and Togo, a repeating bell phrase (2+2+1+2+2+2+1) is the time line that keeps every drum part in polyrhythmic alignment.

concepts.title: Griots
concepts.description: Griots (jeli or jali) are hereditary West African musician-historians who keep genealogies and oral history alive, many playing the 21-string kora.

concepts.title: Talking drums
concepts.description: West African talking drums such as the Yoruba dundun imitate speech: squeezing the drum's cords changes its pitch, following the tones of a tonal language.

concepts.title: Work songs and their legacy
concepts.description: Work songs kept laborers in rhythm and passed the time; out of them, during and after slavery, came spirituals and eventually the blues.

concepts.title: From West African bell to Afro-Cuban clave
concepts.description: West African bell patterns crossed the Atlantic with enslaved Africans: a pattern heard in Ghana would be called son clave in Afro-Cuban music.

concepts.title: Ethnomusicology
concepts.description: Ethnomusicology studies all the world's musics, each in its own context and largely through fieldwork; Smithsonian Folkways has documented the world's 'people's music' since 1948.

concepts.title: How musical traditions differ
concepts.description: Musical traditions differ in their scales, their ways of organizing time and their instruments, as the 1977 Voyager Golden Record's mix of gamelan, drumming, raga and shakuhachi shows.

concepts.title: Seawater stacks by density
concepts.description: Cold and salty water is denser than warm and fresh water, so the ocean sorts itself: light water on top, dense water below.

concepts.title: The five named oceans by size
concepts.description: The Pacific is by far the largest ocean, then the Atlantic, Indian, Southern and, smallest, the Arctic.

concepts.title: How deep sunlight reaches
concepts.description: Below about 200 m there is too little light for photosynthesis, and below 1,000 m no sunlight arrives at all.

concepts.title: Colors fade in order underwater
concepts.description: Water absorbs the longest wavelengths first: red and orange vanish within a few meters, then yellow and green; blue and violet reach deepest.

concepts.title: Why the ocean is blue
concepts.description: Water absorbs red light and scatters blue back, so a deep body of water looks blue. A glass looks clear, and sky reflection only matters at the surface.

concepts.title: How deep the ocean goes
concepts.description: The ocean averages about 3,700 m deep and reaches about 11 km at its deepest, yet on a 30 cm globe it would be a film under a tenth of a millimeter deep.

concepts.title: Why some seas look green
concepts.description: Particles, sediments and phytoplankton change the sea's color: light bounces off particles, and chlorophyll absorbs some colors, tinting water green.

concepts.title: Why all life depends on the ocean
concepts.description: The ocean supplies about half of Earth's oxygen, made by plankton, and almost all the rain that falls on land starts off as ocean water.

concepts.title: Pressure crushes air spaces
concepts.description: Water barely compresses but air does, so deep pressure crushes the air pockets in a foam cup, and would collapse air spaces like human lungs.

concepts.title: How salty the sea is
concepts.description: Seawater averages about 35 parts per thousand salt, mostly chloride and sodium, enough salt to bury the land about 40 stories deep.

concepts.title: Where sea salt comes from
concepts.description: Slightly acidic rain weathers rock, rivers carry the salts to sea, and evaporation leaves them behind. Hydrothermal vents and undersea eruptions add more from below.

concepts.title: The Southern Ocean: defined by a current
concepts.description: The Southern Ocean is bounded by the Antarctic Circumpolar Current at about 60° S. NOAA and National Geographic recognize it; the IHO's position has shifted.

concepts.title: The thermocline
concepts.description: Between warm surface water and cold deep water lies the thermocline, where temperature drops fast with depth. It varies from tropics to poles.

concepts.title: The fingerprint test for Earth's water
concepts.description: The ratio of heavy hydrogen (deuterium) in water is a clue to where it came from. Comet 67P seemed a mismatch in 2014; asteroid meteorites matched.

concepts.title: Earth's water: a debated mix
concepts.description: Newer work reopened the case: 67P's water may match Earth's after all, and Earth's own building blocks may have carried water. The shares remain debated.

concepts.title: Pressure grows with depth
concepts.description: Every 10 m of seawater adds about one atmosphere of pressure: double the surface pressure at 10 m, about 200 atmospheres at 2,000 m.

concepts.title: All Earth's water in one ball
concepts.description: Gathered into one sphere, all of Earth's water would be about 1,385 km across, well under half the Moon's width.

concepts.title: One world ocean
concepts.description: Earth has one connected global ocean, divided into named regions. It covers more than 70% of the surface and holds about 97% of Earth's water.

concepts.title: Africa across the Equator
concepts.description: The Equator nearly halves Africa, the only continent crossed by the Equator and both tropics, so its climate zones are largely mirrored north and south.

concepts.title: Africa's young population
concepts.description: About 19% of the world's people live in Africa, the youngest continent (median age about 19); Nigeria has the most people.

concepts.title: Africa, the second-largest continent
concepts.description: Africa is the second-largest continent, covering about one-fifth of Earth's land, and flat maps often undersell it.

concepts.title: Africa's great cities
concepts.description: Cairo, Lagos and Kinshasa are among Africa's largest cities; Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across the Congo River.

concepts.title: Africa's countries
concepts.description: Africa has 54 countries, more than any other continent; Algeria has been the largest since South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011.

concepts.title: The Alpide belt
concepts.description: A second great earthquake belt runs from the Atlantic through the Mediterranean and the Himalayas to Indonesia, along the Alpine-Himalayan ranges.

concepts.title: The Alps, Europe's crumpled water tower
concepts.description: The Alps are fold mountains pushed up by a fragment of the African plate colliding with Eurasia, and their water feeds rivers flowing to four seas.

concepts.title: Air cools as you climb
concepts.description: Near the surface, air cools by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m you climb, so a tall mountain stacks climates on top of each other.

concepts.title: Climbing through climate zones
concepts.description: Plant zones stack up a mountain like a trip toward the poles, as Humboldt showed on Chimborazo; trees stop at the timberline, and the zones are moving uphill.

concepts.title: The Amazon River
concepts.description: The Amazon rises in the Andes near the Pacific, flows east to the Atlantic, carries about a fifth of Earth's runoff, and drains the world's largest basin.

concepts.title: The Andes
concepts.description: The Andes run along South America's western edge through seven countries, the world's longest continental mountain range.

concepts.title: Claims on Antarctica
concepts.description: Seven countries claim parts of Antarctica, and the claims of Argentina, Chile and the United Kingdom overlap.

concepts.title: The Antarctic ice sheet
concepts.description: Antarctica is a rocky continent under an ice sheet up to 4.8 km thick that holds about 90% of the world's ice and makes it the highest continent.

concepts.title: The Antarctic Treaty
concepts.description: The 1959 Antarctic Treaty freezes territorial claims and keeps Antarctica for peace and science; the 1991 Madrid Protocol bans mining.

concepts.title: Antarctica's extremes
concepts.description: Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent: it holds the lowest measured temperature, gets so little snow it's a desert, and sends katabatic winds pouring off its ice.

concepts.title: Antipodes
concepts.description: A place's antipode is the point directly opposite it through Earth's center: opposite hemisphere, 180° of longitude away, about 12 hours off.

concepts.title: The shrinking Aral Sea
concepts.description: The Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake, shrank after its rivers were diverted in the 1960s to irrigate cotton, bringing harsher climate, toxic dust and collapsed fisheries.

concepts.title: The Arctic: an ocean ringed by land
concepts.description: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents, and sea ice floating on it covers the North Pole.

concepts.title: Arctic sea ice
concepts.description: Arctic sea ice grows to a maximum in March and shrinks to a minimum in September; the September minimum is shrinking about 12% per decade, and losing reflective ice speeds warming.

concepts.title: Most people on Earth live in Asia
concepts.description: About three-fifths of humanity lives in Asia, crowded into South Asia, eastern China and the Pacific coasts and islands.

concepts.title: Asia's regions and empty spaces
concepts.description: Asia, the largest continent, divides into East, South, Southeast, Central, West and North Asia, and much of its interior is thinly peopled.

concepts.title: How atolls form
concepts.description: A reef fringing a volcanic island keeps growing upward as the island sinks; when the island disappears, a ring of reef around a lagoon remains, as Darwin proposed and drilling confirmed.

concepts.title: Australians live on the coast
concepts.description: Most Australians live near the coast, especially the fertile east coast, beyond which the Great Dividing Range separates the cities from the Outback.

concepts.title: Australia: a dry continent-country
concepts.description: Australia is the smallest continent and one of the largest countries; except for Antarctica it's the driest continent, with a vast arid interior called the Outback.

concepts.title: What a biome is
concepts.description: A biome is a large area defined by its vegetation, soil, climate and wildlife; the five major types are forest, grassland, desert, tundra and aquatic.

concepts.title: How borders are drawn
concepts.description: Some borders follow natural features like mountains and rivers; others are straight lines such as the 49th parallel; borders drawn without regard to local communities often cause conflict.

concepts.title: The taiga (boreal forest)
concepts.description: The taiga is the largest land biome: a belt of water-saving, snow-shedding conifers across the far north.

concepts.title: Cardinal directions
concepts.description: North, east, south and west; Earth spins toward the east, so the Sun rises roughly in the east.

concepts.title: The Caribbean islands
concepts.description: The West Indies curve in a long crescent: the big Greater Antilles, led by Cuba, and the smaller Lesser Antilles.

concepts.title: The Central American isthmus
concepts.description: Central America is a narrow isthmus of seven countries linking North and South America, with a wetter Caribbean coast.

concepts.title: Climate normals
concepts.description: Climate is usually summarized as 30-year averages; NOAA updates its US normals every 10 years.

concepts.title: Climate shapes biomes
concepts.description: Temperature and precipitation decide which biome grows where, so similar climates grow similar-looking biomes, even from unrelated plants.

concepts.title: Where climate zones occur
concepts.description: Tropical climates sit near the Equator, big hot deserts about 15 to 30 degrees out, continental climates inside big landmasses, polar climates near the poles.

concepts.title: Mountains from colliding plates
concepts.description: When India hit Eurasia, neither plate could sink, so the crust crumpled upward into the still-rising Himalayas.

concepts.title: The Congo rainforest
concepts.description: The Congo Basin holds the world's second-largest rainforest; bonobos live only south of the Congo River.

concepts.title: The Congo River
concepts.description: The Congo crosses the Equator twice, so part of its basin is always in a rainy season and it flows steadily; only the Amazon carries more water.

concepts.title: Continents by size
concepts.description: Asia is the largest continent and Australia the smallest.

concepts.title: The Continental Divide
concepts.description: A ridge along the crests of the Rockies and the Andes separates rivers that flow to the Pacific from those that flow to the Atlantic side.

concepts.title: Continental drift and Pangaea
concepts.description: Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents were once joined in Pangaea; the idea was accepted once plate tectonics explained the motion.

concepts.title: Coordinates and 0°, 0°
concepts.description: A latitude and a longitude together fix one spot; the point 0°, 0° lies in open ocean in the Gulf of Guinea.

concepts.title: Corals are animals
concepts.description: Corals are animals: tiny polyps that build limestone skeletons and live in partnership with food-making algae.

concepts.title: Coral bleaching
concepts.description: Corals stressed by warm water expel the algae that feed and color them, turning white; prolonged bleaching kills them, and climate change is the reef's greatest threat.

concepts.title: The Coriolis effect
concepts.description: Earth's rotation deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.

concepts.title: Hurricane, typhoon or cyclone
concepts.description: The same storm is called a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone depending on the ocean where it forms.

concepts.title: The International Date Line
concepts.description: The date line roughly follows the 180° meridian; crossing it westward moves the calendar a day ahead.

concepts.title: The Dead Sea
concepts.description: The Dead Sea lies more than 400 m below sea level, Earth's lowest land, and is so salty that swimmers float.

concepts.title: Ocean dead zones
concepts.description: Nutrient runoff from farms and cities feeds algae; when they die and decompose they use up oxygen, creating dead zones such as the one off the Mississippi every summer.

concepts.title: Deciduous forests and autumn
concepts.description: Winter makes water scarce, so deciduous trees shed their leaves; autumn yellows appear when chlorophyll breaks down and reveals hidden pigments.

concepts.title: Deserts are defined by dryness
concepts.description: A desert is defined by very little precipitation, not by heat, so icy Antarctica is the largest desert and the Sahara the largest hot one.

concepts.title: How deserts form
concepts.description: Deserts form under belts of dry sinking air around 30° to 35° N and S, and in the rain shadows of mountains.

concepts.title: Evidence the continents were joined
concepts.description: Matching coastlines, matching rock layers and fossils like Mesosaurus show Africa and South America were once joined.

concepts.title: Earth's metal core
concepts.description: The core is iron and nickel: a liquid outer core that makes the magnetic field and a solid inner core, revealed by earthquake waves.

concepts.title: Crust and mantle
concepts.description: Earth's thin rocky crust sits on the mantle, a thick layer of solid rock that flows very slowly over long periods.

concepts.title: Earth's connected systems
concepts.description: Earth works as connected systems of rock, water, air, life and ice (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere, cryosphere) that constantly interact.

concepts.title: What causes earthquakes
concepts.description: Stuck plate edges build up force until rock suddenly slips along a fault, sending out seismic waves from the hypocenter.

concepts.title: Earthquake magnitude
concepts.description: Each whole step in magnitude means about 32 times more energy; the largest recorded earthquake was magnitude 9.5.

concepts.title: Elevation and contour lines
concepts.description: Heights are measured above sea level, and contour lines join points of equal elevation; close lines mean steep ground.

concepts.title: Equal-area maps
concepts.description: Equal-area projections show the true relative sizes of places but distort their shapes.

concepts.title: The Equator
concepts.description: The Equator is 0° latitude, halfway between the poles, splitting Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

concepts.title: Landforms carved by erosion
concepts.description: Waves carve caves, arches and sea stacks; wind shapes rock and dunes; glaciers widen valleys.

concepts.title: Europe, a peninsula of Eurasia
concepts.description: Europe is the western peninsula of Eurasia, bounded by the Urals and three bodies of water, and itself a peninsula of peninsulas.

concepts.title: Europe's four physical regions
concepts.description: From north to south Europe falls into the Western Uplands, the North European Plain, the Central Uplands and the Alpine Mountains.

concepts.title: The Rhine and the Danube
concepts.description: The Rhine runs from the Alps to the North Sea and the Danube from the Black Forest to the Black Sea; a canal now links them.

concepts.title: Where water vapor comes from
concepts.description: Most water vapor evaporates from oceans and other open water, plants add more by transpiration, and a molecule stays aloft only about 10 days.

concepts.title: Everest's sea-floor summit
concepts.description: The rock at Everest's summit is limestone from an ancient sea floor, full of marine fossils, lifted by the collision.

concepts.title: How much land feeds us
concepts.description: Almost half of the world's habitable land is farmed, and more than three-quarters of that farmland goes to livestock, which supply under a fifth of calories.

concepts.title: Five named oceans, one world ocean
concepts.description: The Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic are named regions of one connected global ocean; the Southern is the newest named.

concepts.title: Forced displacement
concepts.description: At the end of 2024, 123.2 million people were forcibly displaced; most stayed inside their own countries, and most refugees are hosted by neighbouring countries.

concepts.title: How little water is fresh
concepts.description: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is ice or groundwater; lakes and rivers hold a tiny fraction.

concepts.title: Scarce fresh water
concepts.description: Almost all of Earth's water is salty ocean, and most fresh water is locked in ice, so usable fresh water is a scarce resource.

concepts.title: Lakes dug by ice
concepts.description: Massive glaciers scoured and deepened old valleys in the middle of North America, making the basins the Great Lakes now fill.

concepts.title: How glaciers form and flow
concepts.description: Glaciers form where snow survives year after year and is squeezed into ice; they flow slowly downhill under their own weight.

concepts.title: Earth is warming
concepts.description: Burning fossil fuels has raised carbon dioxide by more than 50%, and Earth has warmed about 1°C, mostly because of human activity.

concepts.title: How GPS finds you
concepts.description: A receiver turns signal travel times into distances and needs four satellites: three for position, one to fix its clock.

concepts.title: The GPS constellation
concepts.description: At least 24 GPS satellites with precise clocks broadcast one-way signals of their position and time.

concepts.title: How the Grand Canyon was carved
concepts.description: The land was lifted into the Colorado Plateau, then the Colorado River cut down through it over the last 5 to 6 million years.

concepts.title: The canyon's rock record
concepts.description: The Grand Canyon exposes layers of rock with the oldest, nearly 2 billion years old, at the bottom and younger layers above.

concepts.title: Grasslands
concepts.description: Grasslands grow between forest and desert on the rainfall scale; fire, drought and grazing keep them open, and grass regrows from its base.

concepts.title: The Great Barrier Reef
concepts.description: The world's largest coral reef system stretches more than 2,000 km off northeastern Australia, built by colonies of tiny animals called polyps.

concepts.title: The Great Lakes
concepts.description: Five lakes, Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario, hold about a fifth of the world's surface fresh water and drain east to the Atlantic.

concepts.title: The Great Plains
concepts.description: East of the Rockies, the Great Plains form a dry, windy grassland that slopes gently down toward the east.

concepts.title: The Great Rift Valley
concepts.description: East Africa is being pulled apart as the Somali plate separates from the Nubian plate; the Red Sea is a rift the sea already flooded.

concepts.title: The green Sahara
concepts.description: About 11,000 years ago a wobble in Earth's axis pushed monsoon rains north and the Sahara held lakes, rivers and grasslands before drying out.

concepts.title: The greenhouse effect
concepts.description: Greenhouse gases trap some of the heat Earth gives off; without them Earth would average about -18°C.

concepts.title: Groundwater and aquifers
concepts.description: Groundwater fills pores and cracks in rock and soil, like water in a sponge; usable amounts sit in aquifers reached by wells.

concepts.title: Persian Gulf oil
concepts.description: The Persian Gulf countries hold about half the world's proved crude oil reserves, formed from ancient marine life.

concepts.title: Water scarcity and desalination
concepts.description: The Middle East and North Africa have very little fresh water, so Gulf countries desalinate seawater using their oil and gas.

concepts.title: The Hadley cell
concepts.description: A loop of air: rising and raining at the Equator, sinking and drying near 30 degrees, returning as the trade winds.

concepts.title: How the Himalayas rose
concepts.description: India collided with Asia 40 to 50 million years ago; the crust crumpled upward, lifting ancient seafloor to Everest's summit, and it is still rising.

concepts.title: The abode of snow
concepts.description: The Himalayas' snow and glaciers feed great rivers, including the Indus, the Brahmaputra and the Ganges.

concepts.title: Hokulea's 1976 voyage
concepts.description: In 1976 the canoe Hokulea sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti with no instruments, showing that Polynesians could have settled the Pacific by deliberate voyages.

concepts.title: Hotspots
concepts.description: Some volcanoes, like Hawaii's, form over a stationary hotspot in the mantle, far from plate boundaries.

concepts.title: Hurricane season
concepts.description: Hurricanes feed on warm tropical water, so the Atlantic season runs June to November and peaks in September, when the ocean is warmest.

concepts.title: Ice-age sea level
concepts.description: In the last ice age so much water was frozen on land that sea level fell by about 120 m, uncovering the Beringia land bridge between Asia and North America.

concepts.title: Earth's two ice sheets
concepts.description: Only Greenland and Antarctica have ice sheets today; together they hold over 68% of Earth's fresh water, and melting Antarctica would raise the sea about 58 m.

concepts.title: Iceland's rift
concepts.description: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, and over a hotspot.

concepts.title: International migrants
