levels.title: Frank Lloyd Wright
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Fallingwater and buildings that fit their landscape.
levels.summary: Wright set Fallingwater over a waterfall on concrete cantilevers echoing the rock ledges. Cantilevers are stretched on top, and the terraces sagged until steel cables fixed them.

cards.headline: A family wanted to look at their waterfall. Wright built their house over it.
cards.body: The Kaufmanns loved the falls on Bear Run, in Pennsylvania, and expected a house facing them, where they could admire the water from afar. Frank Lloyd Wright cantilevered the house directly over the falls instead. He designed it in 1935 as the family's weekend retreat, and it was finished in 1937. It's called Fallingwater.

cards.headline: A house that belongs to its rocks
cards.body: Wright called his approach organic architecture: a building in harmony with its site, joining people and nature. At Fallingwater he echoed the rock ledges along the stream. The house is a stack of concrete trays, each anchored to a central chimney built of local sandstone. Outside, the ledges are stone. The ones you stand on are concrete. From the living room, the stream isn't a view. It's underneath you.

mascot.line: Top stretched, bottom squeezed: the lintel's problem, upside down.

cards.headline: The cantilever: a beam held at one end
cards.body: A cantilever is a beam supported at only one end, with the other end free. (A diving board is one.) It bends the opposite way from Level 3's lintel. A lintel is stretched along its underside; a loaded cantilever is stretched along its upper half and squeezed along its lower half. Concrete handles stretching badly, so Fallingwater's concrete terraces carry steel reinforcing rods inside.

cards.fact: Fallingwater's terraces sagged.
cards.context: By 1955 the Kaufmanns had measured them tilting down about four inches. Decades later, in 2001 and 2002, engineers anchored bundles of high-strength steel cable into the concrete below the house, ran them along the big beams under the living room and tightened them. The sagging stopped. Level 7's lesson, applied late: when concrete is stretched, steel has to take the tension.

levels.title: Le Corbusier
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the idea of a house as a machine for living in.
levels.summary: Le Corbusier called a house a machine for living in. His Dom-ino frame freed walls, leading to five points: pilotis, roof garden, free plan, long windows, free facade, shown in the Villa Savoye.

cards.headline: In 1923, Le Corbusier wrote that a house is a machine for living in.
cards.body: The line comes from his book Vers une architecture: "La maison est une machine à habiter." It sounds cold. He meant that a house should first serve the body, giving comfort as efficiently as a good machine. Only then, he said, does it become a place for meditation and for beauty. So what does a living machine look like?

cards.headline: Dom-ino: a house as a kit
cards.body: In 1914 he drew the Dom-ino system: three concrete floor slabs, six posts and a staircase. That's the whole thing. As in Level 8's frame, the skeleton carries the floors, so no wall has to hold anything up. Walls can go anywhere, windows can run the full length of the front, and the module can be repeated again and again. The rest of his career grew out of this kit.

mascot.line: Most houses fit the car into the design. This design was shaped around the car.

cards.headline: Five points, and a garage built to fit the car
cards.body: In 1927 he set out five points for a new architecture: pilotis (posts that lift the house off the ground), a roof garden, a free plan, long horizontal windows and a free facade. Every one follows from the frame. The Villa Savoye at Poissy, France, built from 1928 to 1931, shows them best. Its ground floor even curves to match the turning radius of the family car, which drove in under the pilotis. A machine for living, with the car's needs designed right in.

cards.fact: Seventeen of Le Corbusier's works are World Heritage.
cards.context: UNESCO listed them together in 2016, spread across seven countries. Seven countries, one architect, one listing.

levels.title: The Bauhaus
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Bauhaus design.
levels.summary: Gropius's Bauhaus (1919-33) taught art and craft together, aimed design at factories, gave us Breuer's bicycle-inspired steel chair and built a Dessau home whose fittings came from its own workshops.

cards.headline: At the Bauhaus, every workshop had two teachers: an artist and a craftsman.
cards.body: Walter Gropius founded the school in Weimar, Germany, in 1919, by combining an academy of arts with a school of arts and crafts. Two teachers per workshop was the whole idea in miniature.

cards.headline: Art, meet the factory
cards.body: The Bauhaus set out to end the split between art and craft by training students equally in both. In each workshop, an artist called the Form Master taught theory while a craftsman taught technique. Then Gropius pointed the work at mass manufacture rather than one-off handmade pieces. The goal wasn't a single beautiful chair. It was a beautiful chair a factory could make thousands of.

mascot.line: Next time you park your bike, look at the handlebars. That's a chair, waiting.

cards.fact: A famous Bauhaus chair began with a bicycle.
cards.context: Marcel Breuer designed his tubular steel club chair in 1925, the year he became master of the school's cabinet-making workshop. The curved handlebars of his bicycle had shown him that bent steel tube was light, strong and suited to industrial production, just what the Bauhaus wanted. Today the chair is often called the Wassily chair.

cards.headline: A school that furnished itself
cards.body: In 1925 the Bauhaus moved to Dessau, and Gropius's office designed its new building, which opened in December 1926. Its workshop wing wears a steel and glass facade drawn around it like a curtain, so you can see into the workshops from outside. Inside, the lamps and tubular steel furniture came from the school's own workshops; Gropius designed the door handles. The school moved to Berlin in 1932, and the Nazi regime forced it to close in 1933.

levels.title: Less Is More
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Mies van der Rohe's minimalism.
levels.summary: Mies's motto was less is more. In his Barcelona Pavilion, thin steel columns hold the roof so stone and glass walls stand freely; his glass Farnsworth House met a river that ignored the plans.

cards.headline: Mies's Barcelona Pavilion was taken apart in 1930. Then it came back.
cards.body: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich designed it as Germany's pavilion for the 1929 Barcelona International Exposition. After the fair, it was dismantled. From 1983 to 1986 it was rebuilt on its original site. Why rebuild a building that was so small and held so little?

cards.headline: Less is more
cards.body: That was Mies's motto: less is more, an architecture of elegant simplicity. (He later ran the Bauhaus, from 1930 until the Nazi regime forced it to close in 1933.) In the pavilion, eight slender chrome-clad steel columns hold up a flat roof. That frees the walls, of glass, travertine, green marble and golden onyx, to stand wherever he wanted, like screens you wander between. Few parts, rich materials, nothing extra: the fewest, finest pieces doing all the talking.

mascot.line: Less wall, more view. Also, occasionally, more river.

cards.headline: A glass box on a floodplain
cards.body: The Farnsworth House near Chicago, designed in 1945 and built in 1950-51, is less at its purest: a glass box raised on steel on the floodplain of the Fox River. With glass on every side, the outdoors becomes the decoration. Mies set its floor one foot above the highest flood recorded at the time. The river didn't read the plans. In the 1996 flood, water stood more than five feet deep inside.

levels.title: The Sydney Opera House
levels.objective: After this level you can describe its sail-like roofs and how they were built.
levels.summary: Utzon's winning shells took years to make buildable, until every shell was cut from one sphere, so the roof could be made of standard parts. Utzon resigned in 1966; the building opened in 1973.

cards.headline: In 1957, Jørn Utzon won a competition with a roof nobody knew how to build.
cards.body: The Danish architect's design beat 233 entries in the international competition for a Sydney opera house. It showed a cluster of sail-like shells rising over the harbor. Beautiful, and for years, impossible.

mascot.line: When every curve is different, nothing repeats. Make them all one curve, and suddenly you have a kit.

cards.headline: Every shell, cut from one sphere
cards.body: To build a shell, the engineers at Arup needed its shape as mathematics. From 1958 to 1962, Utzon's team tried parabolas, then ellipses, and neither worked. By late 1961 Utzon saw the key: every shell could be cut from the surface of a single sphere. One shared curve meant the roof could be split into standard parts, prefabricated and assembled on site. Picture every piece of a peel coming from the same ball.

cards.fact: The famous orange story is a myth.
cards.context: Popular legend says Utzon peeled an orange and saw the roof. The Sydney Opera House itself calls that a popular myth. An orange can show how the geometry works, but the breakthrough was Utzon noticing that the shells were so alike that one form, a sphere, could produce them all.

cards.headline: The architect who never came back
cards.body: The shells were solved; the politics were not. In February 1966, after a dispute with the New South Wales government, Utzon resigned, and a team led by Peter Hall took over the design. Utzon left Australia that April and never returned to see his building finished. It was completed in 1973 and joined UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2007.

levels.title: Zaha Hadid
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Hadid's flowing buildings.
levels.summary: Long called a paper architect, Zaha Hadid designed through painting, built the angular Vitra Fire Station in 1993, and later folded whole plazas into buildings. In 2004 she won the Pritzker Prize.

cards.headline: For years, Zaha Hadid was labeled a paper architect.
cards.body: She kept winning competitions, starting with The Peak, a leisure club in Hong Kong, in 1983. But her winning designs often went unbuilt. In 2004 she became the first woman to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize. How do you get from paper to that?

cards.headline: Designing with paint
cards.body: Hadid was born in Baghdad in 1950, studied mathematics in Beirut, then trained as an architect in London. Especially early on, painting and drawing were how she investigated a design. Her work drew on Kazimir Malevich and the Suprematist painters, and it shared their sense of fragmentation, instability and movement. Her paintings weren't illustrations of buildings. They were how she found them.

mascot.line: Even standing still, it looks like it's about to leave. Which, for a fire station, is the job.

cards.fact: Her first major building was a fire station.
cards.context: The Vitra Fire Station in Weil am Rhein, Germany, was finished in 1993: a series of sharply angled, tilted planes of exposed concrete. Her office called it "movement frozen", a building tense and alert, ready to explode into action when the alarm rang. It no longer houses fire engines; it's used for exhibitions and events.

cards.headline: From shards to waves
cards.body: Her later buildings flow. Her office's Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, completed in 2012, seems to rise out of its plaza as if the ground itself had been lifted, curved and folded. Floor, wall, ceiling and roof blur into one surface. The sharp shards of the fire station had become long, continuous waves.

levels.title: Brutalism
levels.objective: After this level you can explain raw concrete buildings and why people argue about them.
levels.summary: Brutalism comes from béton brut, raw concrete, not from brutal. Banham praised buildings made of what they appear to be made of; fans see post-war ambition, critics a dystopia.

cards.headline: One building: 'elephant droppings' to a prince, Stonehenge to a writer.
cards.body: Portsmouth's Tricorn Centre opened in 1966, and the critic Ian Nairn cheered: "At last there is something to shout about in Portsmouth." Prince Charles later called it "a mildewed lump of elephant droppings"; the writer Jonathan Meades compared it to Stonehenge. It was demolished in 2004. Welcome to Brutalism.

cards.headline: Not brutal: raw
cards.body: The name doesn't come from brutal. It probably comes from béton brut, French for raw concrete, Le Corbusier's phrase while building his Unité d'Habitation in 1952. Yes, Level 73's machine-for-living man. From the 1950s he left his materials unfinished, including concrete still printed with the marks of the formwork it was cast in. You can read how a wall was made just by looking at it.

mascot.line: Brutalism's test is simple: if it looks like concrete, it had better be concrete.

cards.headline: Made of what it appears to be made of
cards.body: In a 1955 essay, the critic Reyner Banham named a trend in British architecture "The New Brutalism". His model was a school at Hunstanton by Alison and Peter Smithson: a building "made of what it appears to be made of". No decoration, nothing hidden. And it wasn't only concrete. The Smithsons wanted every material, brick, timber or glass, honestly expressed.

cards.headline: Loved and loathed
cards.body: Historic England calls Brutalism loved and loathed, one of the most controversial styles of the 20th century. To its fans, it shows the post-war drive to rebuild towns so they served people better. To its critics, it was a dystopian landscape-destroyer. The Tricorn's fans and foes were looking at the same raw concrete and seeing opposite things.

levels.title: The Guggenheim Bilbao
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how one museum changed a city.
levels.summary: Gehry's 1997 museum used aerospace software and titanium skin. Its crowds gave rise to the 'Bilbao effect', which critic Witold Rybczynski argued rarely repeats.

cards.headline: Can one building turn a city around? Bilbao bet a museum on it.
cards.body: The city of Bilbao grew on iron, steel and shipbuilding, and it went through a severe economic crisis in the 1970s and 1980s. In 1997 it opened a new art museum designed by Frank Gehry, a joint venture of the Guggenheim Foundation and the Basque regional government.

mascot.line: A test sample, pinned up and watched through the seasons. Very high-tech, and very patient.

cards.headline: Designed with aerospace software
cards.body: Gehry's curves were mathematically complex, so his team used CATIA, software first built for the aerospace industry, to turn his design into a structure and help the builders. Then the skin. Gehry chose titanium after watching how a sample pinned up outside his office behaved. About 33,000 thin titanium sheets now cover the museum, and they change color with the weather and the light.

cards.headline: The Bilbao effect
cards.body: The museum drew about 20 million visitors in its first 20 years, and the former industrial city became a major tourist destination. People began to talk of a Bilbao effect: the idea that one iconic building can transform a city's fortunes.

cards.headline: The skeptic
cards.body: The critic Witold Rybczynski wasn't convinced. In 2011 he argued that nobody had checked whether eye-catching museum architecture really brings the crowds, and that it doesn't, pointing to museums in Seattle and Denver. His title for it: the Bilbao anomaly. One spectacular success, in other words, doesn't make a rule.

cards.headline: Modern Masters finale: architecture has its own Nobel. Three of ours won it.
cards.body: Frank Gehry won the Pritzker Prize in 1989, Jørn Utzon in 2003 and Zaha Hadid in 2004, the first woman to win. What does the prize reward? And how do this chapter's ideas fit together?

cards.headline: The Pritzker Prize
cards.body: The Pritzker family of Chicago set up the prize in 1979, through their Hyatt Foundation. Each year it honors a living architect whose built work shows talent, vision and commitment. It's often called architecture's Nobel, and many of its procedures are modeled on the Nobel Prize. The winner receives $100,000 and a bronze medallion. Note the word built: Hadid, the former paper architect, won for buildings that stood.

levels.title: The First Cities
levels.objective: After this level you can describe early cities like Uruk.
levels.summary: Childe listed signs of the first cities: size, big public works, writing, full-time specialists. By about 3200 BCE Uruk had them all, and its first writing was bookkeeping.

cards.headline: Around 3200 BCE, the biggest settlement on Earth may have been in Iraq.
cards.body: It was Uruk, in southern Mesopotamia, in what is now southeastern Iraq. But a big crowd of houses isn't automatically a city. So what turns a settlement into one? Archaeologists have a checklist, and Uruk ticks the boxes.

cards.headline: A checklist for a city
cards.body: The archaeologist V. Gordon Childe listed 10 signs of the earliest cities. Among them: a bigger settlement than any village, large-scale public works, writing, and full-time specialists, people who do one job all day instead of farming. Think of it as a city's ID card. A village has houses. A city has houses plus a temple crew, a scribe and a wall builder.

mascot.line: Pushpins in a corkboard, but the corkboard is a temple. Somebody was very patient.

cards.headline: Mud brick, dressed up
cards.body: Uruk's public works were monumental buildings of mud brick. Their walls were covered in mosaics made from painted clay cones, pressed in like pushpins in a corkboard. Around the whole city ran brick walls about 10 km long. Legend says the hero Gilgamesh built them. Whoever did, it took a great many bricks.

cards.fact: The first writing was bookkeeping.
cards.context: The earliest written records in Sumerian are picture-sign tablets from Uruk, from about the end of the 4th millennium BCE. They aren't poems or prayers. They're lists and ledgers of goods, with numbers and names. A city full of specialists has to keep track of who handed over what. The first writers were, in effect, accountants.

learned: Childe's signs: size, public works, writing, specialists

levels.title: Grid Cities
levels.objective: After this level you can explain grid street plans from ancient cities to New York.
levels.summary: Grids are ancient (Mohenjo-daro), named for Hippodamus and used by Roman towns and Penn's Philadelphia. New York's 1811 grid was chosen because right-angled houses are cheapest.

cards.headline: In 1811, New York drew a grid over Manhattan, all the way to 155th Street.
cards.body: Look at a map of Manhattan today and you're looking at that decision. The commissioners who drew it later explained why, in one refreshingly blunt sentence. But first: they didn't invent the grid. Not even close.

cards.headline: Older than the Greeks
cards.body: Mohenjo-daro, the largest city of the Indus civilization (about 2600 to 1900 BCE), was laid out with remarkable regularity in about a dozen blocks. Much later, the Greek planner Hippodamus of Miletus, who laid out Athens's port of Piraeus, gave his name to grid plans. He didn't invent them; he just got the credit, like a band covering a song so well that people forget the original.

mascot.line: Right angles: loved by surveyors, landowners, and anyone who has ever tried to give directions.

cards.headline: Easy to measure, easy to divide
cards.body: Many Roman towns were laid out on a grid, with two main streets crossing at right angles. In 1682, William Penn gave Philadelphia a grid, and the idea traveled west with American pioneers for a practical reason: it was the simplest way to divide surveyed land. A grid turns a wild landscape into lots you can number, measure and hand out.

cards.fact: New York chose squares because squares are cheap.
cards.context: The 1811 commissioners wrote that straight-sided, right-angled houses "are the most cheap to build, and the most convenient to live in." No grand theory, no symbolism: a city is mostly homes, and boxy homes are the thriftiest. Manhattan's grid is a cost estimate you can walk around in.

levels.title: Walls and Gates
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why cities built walls and what happened when they came down.
levels.summary: Walls gave towns security, paid for by taxes like murage, with gates for carts and walkers. As cities grew, walls cramped them; many came down and became boulevards, like Vienna's Ringstrasse.

cards.headline: The word boulevard once meant the top of a city wall.
cards.body: It comes from French for the flat top of a rampart, a garbled borrowing of Middle Dutch bolwerc, the same word that gave English bulwark. So how does a wall turn into a wide, leafy street?

cards.headline: Security you paid for
cards.body: Fears of invasion, uprising and civil war made medieval town walls seem a necessary security. They weren't cheap: English towns could get royal permission to collect a tax called murage to pay for work on their walls. Carts and people came and went through the gates. A main gate could have several archways: a big one for carts and wagons, and one or two smaller ones for people on foot.

cards.headline: The wall becomes the problem
cards.body: But a wall doesn't grow when the town does. As cities filled up, walls caused overcrowding, blocked out air and light, and led to very poor sanitation. By the 18th century, walls and gates looked like an obstacle to growth and traffic, and gates were often pulled down as too narrow. It's a belt the town has outgrown, and nobody can loosen it.

mascot.line: Next time you see a ring road hugging an old town, look for the wall it replaced.

cards.headline: Wall down, boulevard up
cards.body: In the late 17th century, Louis XIV had an old Paris wall razed and replaced with a wide tree-lined promenade: a boulevard, for strolling along the line of the old wall. Vienna did it on a grand scale. On 20 December 1857, Emperor Franz Joseph ordered the city walls torn down for the Ringstrasse, a ring-shaped boulevard whose first section opened in 1865. The ring road is the ghost of the ring wall.

levels.title: Parks
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why cities build parks.
levels.summary: Paxton's Birkenhead Park (1847), paid for by houses around it, inspired Olmsted. His Central Park, with Vaux (1858), is a hand-built landscape for a crowded city, with crosstown roads hidden below.

cards.headline: The man who sketched the Crystal Palace also built a park that changed cities.
cards.body: Remember Level 8's Joseph Paxton, doodling the Crystal Palace on blotting paper? He also designed Birkenhead Park, opened in 1847, the first public park in the UK created at public expense. Why would a city pay for grass?

cards.headline: A park that paid for itself
cards.body: Birkenhead didn't just spend money on its park. It made money around it: the park was paid for from the profit on house plots sold around its edge. Houses on the rim paid for the green in the middle. A park that financed itself, which is the kind of gardening accountants enjoy.

cards.headline: The People's Garden
cards.body: In 1850, an American named Frederick Law Olmsted walked through Birkenhead Park. He wrote that democratic America had nothing comparable with this "People's Garden." Eight years later, in 1858, Olmsted and the architect Calvert Vaux won the competition to design New York's Central Park with their Greensward plan.

mascot.line: A park is a room with the ceiling left off. Someone still has to design the floor.

cards.headline: Nature, built by hand
cards.body: Central Park was planned as New York's population boomed and many immigrants lived in crowded, unhealthy conditions. It looks wild, but every bit of it is man-made and built by hand; workers planted 500,000 trees, shrubs and vines. Even the traffic is designed: the Greensward plan hid the crosstown roads below the landscape, out of sight. The meadow is as much architecture as any building.

levels.title: Streets and Squares
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how public squares bring people together.
levels.summary: Siena's Campo was built as a meeting place. Whyte found people sit where there's seating; Jacobs argued busy streets are safe streets; Copenhagen's car-free Strøget (1962) thrived.

cards.headline: Siena paved its main square to point at the government.
cards.body: Siena's Piazza del Campo is shaped like a shell, and its brick paving is divided into nine parts that all point toward the Palazzo Pubblico, the seat of government. What makes a public space pull people in?

cards.headline: A square made for meeting
cards.body: The nine parts recall the Government of the Nine, which ruled Siena from 1287 to 1355. But the Campo was made for everyone: a meeting place for citizens, with markets, games and political events. It still hosts the Palio horse race twice a year. A good square is the town's living room, with the town hall as the armchair everyone faces.

mascot.line: Years of careful filming to prove people like chairs. That's science: check the obvious, find the surprise.

cards.headline: Give people somewhere to sit
cards.body: How do you tell a good plaza from a bad one? William H. Whyte simply watched. Filming New York plazas with time-lapse cameras, he found that "people tend to sit where there are places to sit" (1980). It sounds obvious. It took cameras to prove it: sitting space mattered more than open space. A huge empty plaza loses to a small one with good ledges.

cards.headline: Eyes upon the street
cards.body: In The Death and Life of Great American Cities (1961), Jane Jacobs argued that a well-used street is apt to be a safe one. Her key ingredient: "eyes upon the street," from shops and homes whose windows face it. A blank wall watches nothing. A row of windows is a neighborhood watch that never signs up.

cards.fact: Copenhagen took the cars off its main street in 1962.
cards.context: Strøget was made car-free as an experiment, despite warnings that no cars would mean no customers. According to the Global Designing Cities Initiative, it succeeded and increased revenue for local shops. The street became what Siena's square always was: a place to be, not just a way through.

levels.title: Subways
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how subways changed cities.
levels.summary: London's Metropolitan Railway (1863) ran steam trains through cut-and-cover trenches; electric deep tubes followed in 1890. The railway then sold 'Metro-land' and built suburbs for its commuters.

cards.headline: In 1863, Londoners rode steam trains under the streets.
cards.body: The world's first underground railway, London's Metropolitan Railway, opened on 10 January 1863, hauled by steam locomotives. Picture a smoky train in a tunnel. How did they build it, and what did it do to the city above?

cards.headline: Dig up the street, then put it back
cards.body: The Metropolitan was built by cut and cover. Workers dug trenches along the streets, gave them brick sides, and roofed them over with iron girders or a brick arch. Then the street went back on top. It's the way you'd bury a garden hose: dig a trench, lay it in, cover it up. Just with a train, and a very inconvenienced London.

cards.headline: Deeper, and electric
cards.body: Cut and cover meant digging up whole streets. In 1890 London opened the first electric underground railway, the first deep "tube," dug by tunnelling instead of trenching. A deep tunnel runs far below the streets instead of in a trench just under them, so the street above can stay put.

mascot.line: Clever business: sell the house, then sell the ticket to work. Twice a day.

cards.fact: A railway that grew its own passengers.
cards.context: In 1915 the Metropolitan Railway began selling the countryside along its line as "Metro-land," a place for commuters to live. From 1919, a company it set up built housing estates on spare land the railway owned. The trains didn't just serve the suburbs; they created them. Build the line, then build the homes that fill the trains.

levels.title: Suburbs and Sprawl
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how cars shaped suburbs.
levels.summary: Suburbs follow transport: ferries, trains, then cars. Postwar highways (1956) and mass-built towns like Levittown spread them. UN-Habitat and Robert Bruegmann disagree about sprawl.

cards.headline: After World War II, a builder made a whole town like a product line.
cards.body: Levittown, New York, built by Levitt and Sons from 1946 to 1951, was an early completely preplanned, mass-produced housing development: more than 17,000 homes. It became a national symbol of suburbia. How do suburbs like it spread so far from the city? Follow the transport.

cards.headline: Suburbs follow the ride
cards.body: Suburbs have always grown along transport. Brooklyn Heights grew after an 1814 ferry to Manhattan; later came trolley-car suburbs, and in London, Level 86's Metro-land along the railway. Each new ride stretched how far from work people could live. After World War II, federal policy and highway construction sped up the growth of American suburbs.

cards.fact: 41,000 miles of new highway, mostly paid by Washington.
cards.context: The Federal-Aid Highway Act, signed on 29 June 1956, authorized 41,000 miles of interstate highways, with the federal government paying 90 percent. A ferry or a train line runs where it runs; a road network reaches much further. Highways were part of the postwar push that sped up the suburbs.

levels.title: Housing for Everyone
levels.objective: After this level you can explain informal settlements and public housing.
levels.summary: UN-Habitat counts over 1.1 billion people in slums or informal settlements. Vienna's Karl-Marx-Hof and Aravena's 'half of a good house' show two answers: city-built homes and homes families finish.

cards.headline: More than 1.1 billion people live in slums or informal settlements.
cards.body: That's UN-Habitat's count. It's a design problem, but not one about beautiful buildings. It's about whether a home is safe, big enough and truly yours. Architects have tried very different answers.

cards.headline: What counts as a slum?
cards.body: UN-Habitat counts a household as a slum household if it lacks one or more of five things: durable housing, enough living space, improved water, improved sanitation, or secure tenure (the right to stay). Informal settlements are areas where residents lack that secure tenure, basic services are often missing, and homes may not meet planning and building rules. A roof isn't enough. You also need the right to keep it.

cards.headline: A palace for tenants
cards.body: One answer is for the city to build. Vienna's Karl-Marx-Hof, designed by Karl Ehn in the Red Vienna social housing era (1919 to 1934), is about 1,100 meters long and originally held 1,382 apartments. Yet only about 18% of its site was built on. The rest is courtyards and green space, alongside laundries, baths and kindergartens. A very long building, wrapped around a lot of garden.

mascot.line: Half a house in the right place can beat a whole house in the wrong one.

cards.headline: Half of a good house
cards.body: Another answer: build half, and let families finish it. Alejandro Aravena's firm ELEMENTAL designs social housing it calls "half of a good house," leaving room for residents to finish their homes themselves. According to the Pritzker Prize, this "incremental housing" lets social housing be built on more expensive land, closer to jobs and opportunity. Aravena won the 2016 Pritzker Architecture Prize.

levels.title: Planned Capitals
levels.objective: After this level you can describe planned capitals like Brasília and Washington.
levels.summary: Washington was chosen by law (1790) and drawn by L'Enfant (1791): diagonals over a grid, the Capitol on a 'pedestal'. Brasília (1960) opened the interior; UNESCO praised it, critics didn't.

cards.headline: Some capitals were drawn on paper before a single street existed.
cards.body: In 1790, the Residence Act let President George Washington choose the site of a brand-new national capital. The city had to be invented from scratch, on paper first.

cards.headline: Diagonals over a grid
cards.body: Pierre L'Enfant's 1791 plan laid diagonal avenues radiating from the Capitol across a grid of streets, with circles, squares and parks where the avenues meet. It's Level 82's grid with shortcuts slashed across it. He put the Capitol on Jenkins' Hill, a site he called "a pedestal waiting for a monument."

mascot.line: Tip for future city planners: write it down.

cards.fact: The planner who wouldn't draw.
cards.context: L'Enfant refused to produce drawings for the Capitol, saying he carried the design "in his head," and he was dismissed in 1792. Level 1 said an architect's job ends in drawings builders can work from. A design in your head is a design nobody else can build.

cards.headline: A capital in the interior
cards.body: Brasília was built to promote settlement and development of Brazil's interior; the government began moving there from Rio de Janeiro on 21 April 1960. Lúcio Costa's plan is often compared to an airplane or a bird: a straight Monumental Axis for government buildings, crossed by a curved Highway Axis of homes. Oscar Niemeyer designed its landmark buildings.

cards.headline: Praised and criticized
cards.body: UNESCO listed Brasília as World Heritage in 1987 for its unique plan and architecture. Critics attacked its cost and architecture, and the writer Simone de Beauvoir found its housing districts sterile. A planned capital gets judged twice: once as a drawing, and again by the people who live in it.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Cities
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how streets, walls, parks and transport shape a city.
levels.summary: Barcelona tore down its walls and Cerdà spread a chamfered grid, with gardens in each block, over the old field of fire. Speculators filled the gardens; Cerdà gave us the word urbanization.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: the man who redrew Barcelona invented the word urbanization.
cards.body: Ildefons Cerdà is credited with coining it, in his General Theory of Urbanization (1867). His Barcelona pulls this whole chapter together: walls, grids, squares, gardens and traffic.

cards.headline: Walls down, grid out
cards.body: Barcelona's new district, the Eixample, was built on open land left clear to give a field of fire from the city walls. Level 83 showed walls cramping growing cities. In 1859, the engineer Ildefons Cerdà drew up a grid plan to extend Barcelona beyond its old walls, and it won royal approval. Level 82's grid, laid over the old killing ground.

mascot.line: Look at Barcelona from above: all those clipped corners are Cerdà's.

cards.headline: Corners cut, gardens planned
cards.body: Cerdà cut the corners of his blocks at 45 degrees so traffic could see along the crossing streets. Every crossing became a small open space, a bit like Level 85's squares. His blocks were also meant to leave open space and gardens in the middle, Level 84's idea of green for everyone, tucked inside every block.

cards.fact: Then the gardens filled up.
cards.context: The plan was not fully carried out: within 30 years the open areas had been built over and building density tripled. Birkenhead's houses paid for its park; in Barcelona, the buildings won and the gardens lost. A plan is a promise, and every city decides how much of it to keep.

levels.title: Green Buildings
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how buildings can save energy.
levels.summary: The first Passive House (Darmstadt, 1991) keeps heat in with insulation, good windows and airtightness. Overhangs admit winter sun. Heat recovery swaps air but keeps the warmth.

cards.headline: In 1991, four families moved into a house that barely needs heating.
cards.body: The row of four homes in Darmstadt, Germany, was the world's first Passive House, and the family of Wolfgang Feist, who developed the idea, lived in one of them. The trick is three plain ideas: keep the heat in, let the sun help, and never throw warm air away.

cards.headline: Wrap it like a flask
cards.body: The Passive House Institute lists five principles: very good insulation, highly energy-efficient windows, airtightness, no thermal bridges, and ventilation with heat recovery. The Darmstadt pioneers even had triple-glazed windows made specially for the job. Here's an analogy: a vacuum flask keeps tea hot for hours without heating it at all. It simply lets almost nothing escape.

cards.headline: Let the sun do some of the work
cards.body: Passive solar design uses the building itself, its windows, walls and floors, to collect and store the sun's heat. The US Department of Energy advises main windows facing within 30 degrees of true south. Then a roof overhang does something clever. The high summer sun hits the overhang and leaves the window in shade; the low winter sun slips underneath and warms the room. Heavy floors and walls, called thermal mass, store that warmth.

mascot.line: Out goes the stale air, in comes the fresh air, and the warmth stays home. Tidy.

cards.fact: Fresh air, without throwing the heat away.
cards.context: An airtight house still has to breathe. A heat recovery ventilator sends stale air out and fresh air in through a heat exchanger, where heat moves from the warmer stream to the cooler one. In winter, the warm air leaving your house warms the cold air coming in; in summer it works the other way round. The Darmstadt homes had four ventilation units doing exactly this.

levels.title: Living Walls
levels.objective: After this level you can explain green roofs and planted walls.
levels.summary: Green roofs come light (extensive) or heavy (intensive, with trees). Patrick Blanc's walls grow on felt with no soil. Milan's Vertical Forest holds 800 trees, tied down against the wind.

cards.headline: Two towers in Milan hold 800 trees on their balconies.
cards.body: Stefano Boeri's Vertical Forest, built from 2007 to 2014, packs greenery equal to about five hectares of parkland onto two apartment towers. Planting a building is harder than it sounds. Soil is heavy, and a tree high up has to stand up to the wind.

cards.headline: Two kinds of green roof
cards.body: A green roof is a layer of plants grown on a rooftop, and it comes in two weights. An extensive roof uses hardy plants in just 2 to 4 inches of growing medium: light, and needing little care. An intensive roof can be a whole park with trees, and it's heavier, so the building needs more structural support. Both earn their keep: their surfaces stay cooler than an ordinary roof, and they reduce and filter the rainwater running off it.

cards.headline: A garden with no soil
cards.body: The botanist Patrick Blanc grows his living walls without any soil. A metal frame holds a 1 cm sheet of PVC, and on that goes a layer of felt. Plant roots grow on and inside the felt, and water with added nutrients trickles down from the top. The whole thing, plants and frame included, weighs under 30 kg per square metre, so it can go on any wall. One covers the Quai Branly museum in Paris, completed in 2004.

mascot.line: Seatbelts for trees. Nobody wants one dropping in from upstairs.

cards.fact: Milan's trees wear seatbelts.
cards.context: Level 2 said wind is a live load that pushes sideways, and a tree on a balcony catches plenty of it. The engineers at Arup ran two wind tunnel test campaigns. Medium and large trees are tied on with safety cables in case a trunk breaks, and the biggest trees in the windiest spots sit in steel cages that hold their root-balls down.

levels.title: Tall Timber
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how new wood products allow wooden high-rises.
levels.summary: Cross-laminated timber glues boards in crossing layers, making stiff panels. Thick timber chars slowly, insulating its core. Ascent in Milwaukee (CTBUH, 2022) mixes mass timber with concrete.

cards.headline: In 2022, a 25-story tower was named the world's tallest timber building.
cards.body: The Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH) certified Ascent, in Milwaukee, at 86.6 meters. Remember Level 6: after the fire of 1666, London rebuilt in brick for protection from fire. So how does a wooden high-rise make sense?

cards.headline: Boards, crossed and glued
cards.body: The key product is cross-laminated timber, or CLT: layers of lumber boards stacked crosswise, typically at right angles, and glued together, at least three layers thick. It was introduced in the early 1990s in Austria and Germany. Crossing the layers is the whole point. A crossed panel is stable, strong and stiff in both directions, so it can make wide floor slabs and whole walls. Here's an analogy: a woven mat holds together far better than a pile of loose straws.

cards.headline: Why a thick timber survives a fire
cards.body: Wood burns, but thick wood burns slowly and predictably. Fire turns its surface to char, and that char insulates the wood inside, slowing the damage. In a standard fire test, wood chars at an average of about 0.6 mm per minute. A timber's strength depends on how much solid wood is left, so a thick one keeps much of its strength while its outside burns away. Here's an analogy: a big log on a campfire, black outside, solid inside.

mascot.line: London swapped wood for brick. Milwaukee brought wood back, and tested it in fire first.

cards.fact: Ascent's timber stands on concrete.
cards.context: Ascent is a hybrid. Its base and its elevator and stair shafts are concrete; 19 of its 25 stories are mass timber, built from CLT and glulam. Before it rose, the USDA Forest Products Laboratory worked with its designers to test how a three-hour fire would affect its glulam columns. Level 6 said wood is strong for its weight; tall timber puts that strength to work, and plans for the fire.

learned: CLT: boards in crossing layers, glued; early 1990s

levels.title: 3D-Printed Houses
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how houses can be printed layer by layer.
levels.summary: A concrete printer builds walls layer by layer with no formwork. The mix must flow, then carry the layers above. Steel reinforcement is hard to add. Eindhoven's first printed home got tenants in 2021.

cards.headline: On 30 April 2021, a couple got the keys to a house shaped like a boulder.
cards.body: It was the first 3D-printed concrete home in the Netherlands, in Eindhoven, and it met all of the country's strict building rules. Nobody poured its walls into a mold. A machine built them up, layer by layer.

cards.headline: No mold needed
cards.body: Ordinary concrete needs formwork: a temporary structure that holds the wet mix in shape until it hardens. It's the concrete cousin of Level 4's centering, the wooden frame that holds up an arch until the keystone is set. Formwork can take more than half the resources of a concrete structure. A construction printer skips it. Following a digital design, it squeezes concrete through a nozzle and builds the wall layer by layer.

cards.headline: Runny enough to squeeze, stiff enough to stack
cards.body: That makes the mix a balancing act. It has to flow well enough to push through the nozzle, then be strong enough to carry the weight of every layer printed on top of it without deforming. Engineers call this buildability. Here's an analogy: toothpaste that slides out of the tube but keeps its shape on the brush.

mascot.line: Every layer line on a printed wall is a joint. Engineers keep a close eye on those.

cards.fact: Printing still has Level 7's problem.
cards.context: Concrete is weak when stretched, so builders usually cast steel bars inside to take the tension. In a printed wall that's hard: building layer by layer makes conventional steel reinforcement difficult to add, and the joints between layers are weaker than solid cast concrete. The Eindhoven house was printed as 24 separate elements in a factory, then trucked to the site and set on a foundation.

levels.title: Floating Buildings
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how buildings can float on water.
levels.summary: A floating house sinks until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as it does. Maasbommel's amphibious houses sit on hollow concrete bases and rise on mooring posts; in 2011 they floated.

cards.headline: In 2011, a Dutch river rose, and the houses on its banks rose with it.
cards.body: At Maasbommel in the Netherlands, 32 amphibious houses and 14 floating ones were built in 2004 and 2005 outside the river dikes. In 2011 the River Maas rose high enough for the amphibious houses to float for the first time. No problems were found. So how does a house built on concrete float?

cards.headline: Archimedes moves in
cards.body: A floating object sinks until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as it does; then the water's upward push holds it up. That's why a lump of clay sinks but the same clay shaped into a boat floats, and why steel ships float too. Shape does the work. So each amphibious house at Maasbommel stands on a large, hollow concrete cube: plenty of room to push water aside.

Add a live load, like Level 2's piano, and it sinks a little deeper until the balance returns. Floating homes keep the heavy concrete below and build light on top.

levels.title: Building on the Moon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain plans for bases on the Moon.
levels.summary: The Moon has no shielding air and wild temperature swings. A pressurized habitat is mainly in tension. ESA's 2013 study proposed a printed regolith catenary dome over an inflatable.

cards.headline: On the Moon, the biggest push on a building comes from inside it.
cards.body: A Moon base has to hold Earth-level air pressure where there's no atmosphere outside. That outward push is several orders of magnitude bigger than the gravity and weather loads on buildings on Earth. It turns Chapter 1's rules inside out.

cards.headline: A tough building site
cards.body: The Moon has only a very thin atmosphere, so nothing blocks the Sun's radiation or incoming meteoroids. In full sunlight its surface reaches about 127 °C; in darkness it drops to about -173 °C. That's a swing of about 300 degrees between sunlight and shadow. Gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, so everything weighs less, but that's the only easy part.

cards.headline: The inside-out building
cards.body: On Earth, gravity squeezes buildings: Level 2's compression. A pressurized Moon habitat is mainly in tension instead, its walls pushed outward and stretched by the air inside. Here's an analogy: a balloon's skin, pulled tight by the air it holds. To protect it, engineers suggest a thick outer layer of regolith, the Moon's loose, broken soil and rock, to dampen temperature swings and shield against radiation.

mascot.line: Hooke's hanging chain, from 1675 all the way to the Moon. Good ideas travel well.

cards.fact: In 2013, ESA tested printing a Moon base from Moon soil.
cards.context: ESA and partners including the architects Foster + Partners studied whether a 3D printer could build a lunar base from regolith. The design: an inflatable, pressurized dome to shelter astronauts, covered by a robot-printed regolith shell. The shell was a weight-bearing catenary dome with hollow, closed cells like bird bones. A catenary is a hanging chain's curve: flip it and you get Level 10's arch. The team printed a 1.5-tonne demonstration block. It was a study, not a base.

levels.title: Saving Old Buildings
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how historic buildings are preserved.
levels.summary: Viollet-le-Duc restored and added; Morris's SPAB (1877) urged protection instead. After the 2019 fire, his Notre-Dame spire was copied exactly. Tate Modern gave a power station a new job.

cards.headline: On 15 April 2019, fire brought down Notre-Dame's spire. Who had designed it?
cards.body: The blaze in Paris destroyed most of the roof, some of the rib vaulting and the spire, a 19th-century addition by the architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, who was appointed to restore the cathedral. Rebuilding it meant taking a side in an old argument about how to save a building.

"Put Protection in the place of Restoration"

cards.headline: Notre-Dame chose the copy
cards.body: Its new timber spire, topped by a metal cross, rose again to 96 m, an exact replica of the one Viollet-le-Duc built in 1859. Carpenters cut and carved it in their workshops, then assembled it piece by piece inside the cathedral, which reopened in December 2024. So the restorer whose additions critics once attacked had his own addition restored, exactly.

mascot.line: Copy it, mend it, or give it a new life? Every old building makes somebody choose.

cards.fact: Sometimes saving a building means giving it a new job.
cards.context: Giles Gilbert Scott's Bankside Power Station in London opened in 1962 and shut down in 1981. Its machinery was removed, and the architects Herzog & de Meuron converted it into an art museum. It opened as Tate Modern on 11 May 2000, and its vast Turbine Hall now holds giant artworks.

levels.title: Design for Everyone
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how buildings are made usable for everyone.
levels.summary: Curb cuts, won by disabled activists, help everyone. Universal design means usable by all people without special adaptation. US rules cap ramps at 1:12.

cards.headline: In 1972, Berkeley cut a slope into one curb. Then everyone used it.
cards.body: Pressed by disabled activists, the city installed its first official curb cut at an intersection on Telegraph Avenue. (The very first curb cuts had appeared in Kalamazoo, Michigan, in 1945.) Then parents with strollers, workers pushing heavy carts and travelers wheeling luggage headed for them too.

cards.headline: Designed for all, from the start
cards.body: The architect Ronald Mace coined a name for that way of thinking: universal design. NC State's Center for Universal Design, founded in 1989 under his guidance, defines it as design usable by all people, to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation or specialized design. Its seven principles, published in 1997, start with Equitable Use: the same way of using a place for everyone, identical whenever possible, with nobody singled out.

mascot.line: Twelve to one: gentle enough for wheels, and your knees will quietly thank you too.

cards.headline: The one-in-twelve rule
cards.body: Some of it is plain arithmetic. The 2010 ADA Standards, the US accessibility rules, say a ramp run can be no steeper than 1:12: every inch of rise needs at least 12 inches of ramp. So a 6-inch step becomes a 6-foot ramp. Try it in your head with the front steps of your home.

cards.fact: Commodity, for everyone.
cards.context: Level 1's Vitruvius said good building needs commodity: usefulness to the people who use it. Universal design asks which people, and answers: all of them, as far as possible, without special adaptations. The curb cut shows why it pays. Built for wheelchair users, it helps parents with strollers, workers with carts and travelers with suitcases too.

levels.title: How to Look at a Building
levels.objective: After this level you can use a simple method to read any building.
levels.summary: Read a building in three steps: stand back and ask what it is for; find how it stands; read its changes, then ask what delights you. Firmness, commodity, delight still works.

cards.headline: That bricked-up window on an old building is a clue.
cards.body: Historic England's guide to recording buildings tells investigators to note blocked doorways, windows and fireplaces, along with joints in the masonry. Buildings change, and they keep the evidence. Here's a simple way to read any building, using Chapter 1 and this one.

cards.headline: Step 1: Stand back
cards.body: Start with a quick overview, Historic England advises: work out what the building is for and its main phases, so you see it as a working whole, not a pile of parts. Ask what it tells you about its origins, form, function, date and development. What it's for is Level 1's commodity: usefulness to the people who use it.

cards.headline: Step 2: Find how it stands
cards.body: Next, ask how it stands. Do thick walls carry the floors, or does a frame? A wall of glass is a giveaway: in a frame building, a skeleton of columns and beams carries the floors, and the outer wall bears only its own weight (Level 8). Spot an arch? Look for the massive supports resisting its outward thrust (Level 4).

mascot.line: Once you start spotting bricked-up windows, you can't stop. Consider yourself warned.

cards.headline: Step 3: Read the changes, then enjoy it
cards.body: Then look for the story. Historic England's clues to a building's phases include masonry joints, architectural styles, the plan, decoration, and fixtures and fittings. A seam where the stonework or brickwork changes may mark a later addition. Finally, ask what delights you. Firmness, commodity, delight: Vitruvius's three conditions still make a fine checklist.

levels.title: Art History in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the big eras of art from cave paintings to today.
levels.summary: The oldest known art is a hand stencil at least 67,800 years old, far older than writing. Art then moved through big eras, Stone Age to modern, each answering the last.

cards.headline: The oldest known artwork is a hand. It's at least 67,800 years old.
cards.body: Someone on Muna island, in Indonesia, pressed a hand to a cave wall and blew red ochre over it. Lift the hand away and its outline stays on the bare rock. It's still there. Art history starts with that hand, and this level runs from there to today.

mascot.line: Art had a 22-hour head start on writing. Honestly, that explains why pictures still say it faster.

cards.fact: If all of art history were one day, writing wouldn't show up until after 10 p.m.
cards.context: Squeeze the 67,800 years since that hand into 24 hours. Writing, invented about 5,200 years ago, appears just after 10 p.m.: for more than 22 hours, people made art but wrote nothing down. The Mona Lisa, begun about 1503, arrives about 11 minutes before midnight. Most of art's story happened before anyone could write about it.

cards.headline: Every era answers the one before
cards.body: Eras aren't just labels; they talk to each other. Renaissance is French for "rebirth": starting in 14th-century Italy, artists revived the ideas of ancient Greece and Rome. Centuries later, photography could record the world exactly, so painting no longer had to. Modern painters, starting in mid-1800s France, threw out the old rules. Each new era is partly a reply to the last one.

levels.title: What Counts as Art?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why people have disagreed about what counts as art.
levels.summary: In 1926 US customs taxed Brancusi's Bird in Space as metal because it didn't look like a bird. In 1928 a court ruled it art: art could express an idea, not just copy nature.

cards.headline: In 1926, US customs decided a famous sculpture wasn't art. Just metal.
cards.body: So they taxed it like any factory-made object. The fight that followed went all the way to court, where a judge had to settle a question people still argue about in galleries: what counts as art?

cards.headline: A bird with no wings
cards.body: The sculpture was Constantin Brancusi's Bird in Space. Picture a tall, slender strip of bronze, polished like a mirror. Brancusi left out the wings and feathers, stretched the body long and shrank the head and beak to a slanted oval. It doesn't show what one particular bird looks like. It's about the idea of flight.

cards.headline: Two ideas of art collide
cards.body: Customs followed the old rule: a sculpture was carved or shaped in the likeness of natural models, like people and animals. No likeness, no sculpture. So they charged a 40% duty on it as a manufacture of metal. Brancusi's side said art could capture an idea instead. The critic Frank Crowninshield testified that it suggested flight, grace and speed, just as a bird does.
cards.callout: Old test: does it look like something? New test: does it express something?

mascot.line: Next time someone says "my kid could make that", remember: that argument once needed a judge.

cards.fact: In 1928, a court ruled that Bird in Space was art.
cards.context: The court noted a new school of art whose artists tried to portray abstract ideas rather than imitate natural objects, and said it had to be recognized. The ruling even admitted it might be hard to associate the thing with a bird. It was still pleasing to look at, and a work of art. The idea of art had moved, and the law moved with it.

levels.title: The Artist's Toolkit
levels.objective: After this level you can name the basic elements of art: line, shape, color, texture and space.
levels.summary: Every artwork is built from the elements of art: line, shape, color, texture and space (many lists add form). Even empty space has a shape.

cards.headline: Every picture ever made uses the same few building blocks.
cards.body: A cave wall, a comic, the icon on your phone: artists build them all from what they call the elements of art. Learn five of them and you can take any picture apart.

cards.headline: Line and shape
cards.body: Start with line: a mark longer than it is wide. It can be straight or curved, thick or thin. Close a line into a loop and you have a shape. Shapes are flat and come in two families: geometric, like squares and circles, or organic, the free-form shapes you find in nature. A smiley face is one circle, two dots and a curve. Line and shape, doing all the work.

mascot.line: I once tried to pet a painted porcupine. Very smooth. Mildly embarrassing.

cards.headline: Color and texture
cards.body: Color is light reflected off things (Level 4 is all about it). Texture is how a surface feels, or looks like it would feel. It can be real, like thick paint you could touch, or only implied. A drawing of a porcupine can look prickly, but run your finger over it and the paper is smooth. The prickles are an illusion.

cards.fact: Empty space has a shape too.
cards.context: Space is the area around and between things. The empty part is called negative space, and it has a shape of its own: think of the hole in the letter O. Space also means the feeling of depth, when a flat picture seems to open up like a window. That's the five: line, shape, color, texture and space. Many lists add form, meaning 3D shapes like balls and boxes.

levels.title: How Color Works
levels.objective: After this level you can explain primary and complementary colors and how artists use them.
levels.summary: Newton bent the spectrum into a color wheel. Red, yellow and blue are the painter's primaries; complements sit opposite, look more intense side by side, and mix to brown.

cards.headline: In 1824, the royal tapestry works in Paris had a problem: weak colors.
cards.body: The new head of dyeing at the Gobelins, a chemist named Michel-Eugène Chevreul, went looking for bad dye. He found something much stranger. To see what, you need a color wheel.

cards.headline: Newton bends the rainbow
cards.body: In his book Opticks, in 1704, Isaac Newton took the colors of the spectrum and bent them into a circle: an early color wheel. Painters use the idea to this day. Three colors sit at the heart of a painter's wheel: red, yellow and blue, the primaries. Every other color is a mix of them. Mix two primaries and you get a secondary: orange, green or violet.

cards.headline: Opposites on the wheel
cards.body: Colors directly across the wheel from each other are complementary: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet. Each pair shares no primary. Red is a primary, and green is blue plus yellow, so between them they use all three. Mix complements in paint and they cancel each other out into brown.
cards.callout: Red ↔ green · Blue ↔ orange · Yellow ↔ violet

mascot.line: So if a color looks off, check the neighbors before you blame the paint.

cards.fact: A color changes depending on its neighbors.
cards.context: That was the Gobelins mystery. The dye was fine; the colors woven next to each other were changing how each one looked. Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839. Put complements side by side and each makes the other look more intense. His ideas went on to influence painters, including the Impressionists.

levels.title: The First Artists
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the oldest known cave art and how it was made.
levels.summary: The oldest finds go from lines (a 73,000-year-old ochre crosshatch at Blombos Cave) to hands (stencils blown in ochre) to scenes (a picture story at least 51,200 years old in Sulawesi).

cards.headline: The oldest known drawing looks like a hashtag.
cards.body: It's a crosshatch of red lines on a small flake of stone from South Africa, about 73,000 years old. The earliest finds tell a story in three steps: first lines, then hands, then whole scenes.

cards.headline: Step 1: lines
cards.body: The flake comes from Blombos Cave. Someone drew on it with a pointed crayon of red ochre, an earth pigment that gets its color from iron oxide. It's at least 30,000 years older than any other known drawing. Is it art? Researchers still disagree. The lines might mean something, or they might just be left over from sharpening the crayon.

cards.headline: Step 2: hands
cards.body: Remember Level 1's hand, at least 67,800 years old? To make a stencil, you press your hand to the rock and blow pigment over it, sometimes through a pipe. Lift your hand and its outline stays. On Muna island, someone later went back and narrowed the fingers, turning a human hand into something closer to a claw.

mascot.line: Three figures and a pig. Honestly, better plot than some movies I've seen.

cards.fact: The oldest known picture story is at least 51,200 years old.
cards.context: On a cave wall at Leang Karampuang, also in Sulawesi, three human-like figures interact with a wild pig. It's not one animal on its own: it's a scene, the earliest known narrative art. Its age comes from thin mineral crusts that formed on top of the paint, dated by the uranium in them.

levels.title: Lascaux and Chauvet
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the animal paintings in the caves of Lascaux and Chauvet.
levels.summary: Lascaux (about 17,000 years old) has huge black aurochs and closed in 1963 after visitors harmed it. Chauvet (about 35,500 years old) is full of lions, rhinos and mammoths.

cards.headline: In 1994, cave explorers in France felt a faint draft from a pile of stones.
cards.body: Behind it was a cave sealed by rockfalls for at least 21,000 years. On its walls: cave lions, woolly rhinos and mammoths. But first, meet an older discovery: Lascaux.

cards.headline: Lascaux: the Hall of the Bulls
cards.body: Four teenagers found Lascaux in 1940. Radiocarbon dating of its charcoal says about 17,000 years old. In its most famous room, four huge black bulls (aurochs) sweep across the rock, some about 5 meters long. Their bodies are drawn from the side, but their horns twist toward you, so you see both at once. The painters built scaffolding to reach the ceiling.

mascot.line: Sometimes the kindest way to love a painting is to stop breathing on it.

cards.fact: Lascaux lasted about 17,000 years in the dark, then about 15 years of tourists.
cards.context: It opened to visitors in 1948, up to 100,000 a year. Their traffic and the artificial lights faded the colors and brought algae, bacteria and crystals. In 1963 it closed. Since 1983, visitors have toured a replica nearby instead.

cards.headline: Chauvet: twice as old
cards.body: Radiocarbon dates put most of Chauvet's art at about 35,500 years old, roughly twice Lascaux's age. Its artists chose dangerous animals: among over 400 animals of 14 species are cave lions, woolly rhinos, mammoths and bears. They scraped walls clean, strengthened outlines and smudged charcoal to shade. In the End Chamber, a pride of lions hunts bison.

levels.title: The First Sculptures
levels.objective: After this level you can describe early carved figures and what they may have meant.
levels.summary: The Lion-Man, carved in mammoth ivory about 40,000 years ago, mixes lion and human. Small figures of women, like Hohle Fels and Willendorf, have unknown meanings.

cards.headline: About 40,000 years ago, someone carved a creature nobody had ever seen.
cards.body: It stands upright like a person, but it has the head of a cave lion, and it's carved from a mammoth's tusk. Meet the Lion-Man.

cards.headline: The Lion-Man
cards.body: He was found in Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in Germany and stands 31 cm tall, about the length of a school ruler. That makes him the largest known sculpture of Ice Age art. When a modern experimenter carved a copy with Ice Age-style stone tools, it took hundreds of hours. That's a lot of time to spend on something you can't eat, wear or hunt with.

cards.headline: Small women, carved to hold
cards.body: The Venus of Hohle Fels, from another German cave, is mammoth ivory, 6 cm tall and 35,000 to 40,000 years old. Instead of a head, she has a small pierced loop, so she may have been worn as a pendant. The Venus of Willendorf, found in Austria, is about 30,000 years old: 11.1 cm of limestone, tinted with red ochre. She has no face at all, only a pattern like a braid or a cap.

cards.fact: "Venus" isn't their name, and nobody knows what they meant.
cards.context: Modern scholars borrowed the name from the Roman goddess of love, a goddess from many thousands of years later. Ideas about Willendorf include a fertility figure, a good-luck charm and a mother goddess. And a 2022 study added a travel story: her stone likely came from near Lake Garda in northern Italy, across the Alps.

levels.title: Stonehenge and Great Stones
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what monuments like Stonehenge show about early societies.
levels.summary: Stonehenge took hundreds of workers, stones from Wales and feasts drawing people from across Britain. Göbekli Tepe, about 11,500 years old, was built by hunter-gatherers.

cards.headline: Stonehenge's builders joined giant stones the way a carpenter joins wood.
cards.body: Picture a ring of huge upright stones on a grassy plain, with stone beams laid across their tops. The beams are slotted on with joints you'd normally find in furniture. Monuments like this tell you who built them: how many people, how organized, and what mattered to them.

cards.headline: Built by hundreds, over centuries
cards.body: Stonehenge began as a circular ditch and bank about 3000 BC; the stones went up about 2500 BC. The giant sarsens, about 25 tons each on average, came from about 25 km away. The smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales, more than 200 km away. Moving, shaping and raising them took hundreds of people. That's not a weekend project. That's a society working together.

cards.fact: Some pigs at Stonehenge-era feasts came from as far as north-east Scotland.
cards.context: At Durrington Walls, near Stonehenge, archaeologists have found over 38,000 animal bones. Pig teeth show animals raised in west Wales, northern England and north-east Scotland, then slaughtered at midwinter. Stonehenge itself is lined up with the Sun: at midsummer the sun rises beside the Heel Stone, and at midwinter it set through the tallest arch. People came from far away, at special times of year.

cards.headline: Göbekli Tepe: older than farming
cards.body: In southeastern Turkey, hunter-gatherers began Göbekli Tepe about 11,500 years ago, more than twice Stonehenge's age and before farming. Its T-shaped limestone pillars reach over 5 meters and weigh up to 50 tons. Some are carved with foxes, scorpions and lions. Others have arms and hands carved down their sides, meeting in front over a belt: giant stone people. Building together may have led people to settle, not the other way round.

levels.title: Why Early People Made Art
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the main ideas about why early humans made art.
levels.summary: Why early people made art is debated. Main ideas: an urge to record the world, hunting magic (with a reindeer problem), a spirit world, and keeping records.

cards.headline: Nobody left a note explaining the cave paintings.
cards.body: So researchers work from clues, and they disagree. The purpose of this art is still debated. Here are the main ideas. Hold them as ideas, not answers.

cards.headline: Idea: because people need to
cards.body: One view skips usefulness altogether: humans have a basic need to record and recreate the world around them. On this view the first artists drew for the same deep reason you doodle in a meeting. The catch is that it's hard to test.

cards.headline: Idea: hunting magic
cards.body: Maybe painting an animal was a kind of spell, to make a hunt succeed or herds multiply. It has a big problem at Lascaux. The bones left behind show the painters mostly ate reindeer, yet reindeer are almost absent from the walls. If you're casting a spell for dinner, you'd paint dinner.

mascot.line: Notice the word "may". In this level, it's doing a lot of honest work.

cards.headline: Idea: a spirit world
cards.body: Most experts think cave art was symbolic or religious, sometimes both. One version: shamans entered trances to contact spirits, and the art shows that other world. Mixed creatures fit this idea, like Level 7's Lion-Man, or the Muna hand narrowed into a claw, which researchers think may reflect links between people and animals, or spiritual beliefs.

cards.fact: Some marks may be records, not pictures.
cards.context: Researchers suggest the patterns on an engraved ochre plaque from Blombos Cave may be a way of counting or storing information. Others wonder whether animals painted in their seasonal coats worked as an early calendar. The ideas don't have to compete: one cave could be a gallery, a temple and a notebook.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The First Artists
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the earliest known art and the main ideas about why it was made.
levels.summary: Radiocarbon dates charcoal back to about 50,000 years; uranium-series dates crusts over mineral paint, giving a minimum age. That's why records say 'at least'.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: how do you date a painting nobody signed?
cards.body: Every date in this chapter came from a lab, not a label. Here's the whole chapter in order, then how those numbers were found, and why so many of them start with "at least".

events.label: An ochre crosshatch at Blombos Cave
A hand stencil on Muna island
The Lion-Man, carved in ivory
Chauvet's lions and rhinos
Lascaux's great aurochs
Stonehenge's stones go up

cards.fact: Charcoal is a clock.
cards.context: Radiocarbon dating measures carbon-14 in things that were once alive, like the burnt wood in charcoal, and works back to about 50,000 years. Many of Chauvet's black lines are charcoal, so labs can date the drawings themselves: most are about 35,500 years old. At Lascaux, charcoal from the cave gives about 17,000.

mascot.line: "At least 67,800 years" is science being honest. The hand might be older still.

cards.headline: Why "at least"?
cards.body: Red ochre is iron oxide, a mineral, and many paintings have no organic material to date. So researchers date something else: thin mineral crusts that grew over the paint, using uranium, as at Leang Karampuang. The crust formed after the painting, so the paint must be older. That's a minimum age. The real one could be older, which is why records keep getting broken.

levels.title: Mesopotamia
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Mesopotamian art, from stepped temples to carved seals.
levels.summary: Mesopotamian cities raised stepped mud-brick ziggurats, like Ur's for the moon god Nanna, and carved tiny stone cylinder seals that printed pictures on clay.

cards.headline: The first cities built their temples out of mud.
cards.body: Mesopotamia is Greek for "between rivers": the land of the Tigris and Euphrates, where the world's earliest civilization grew up. Its builders worked in brick, and its artists often worked in something humbler still: clay. This level runs from a temple tower down to a picture about the size of your thumb.

cards.headline: A staircase for a god
cards.body: A ziggurat is a stepped temple tower. Picture a stack of ever-smaller brick platforms, like a giant wedding cake. The core was mud brick, wrapped in a tougher skin of baked brick. The best known, at Ur, went up about 2100 BCE under King Ur-Nammu for the moon god Nanna. Three staircases led up, and on the flat top sat a temple. The tower's whole job was to lift that temple up.

mascot.line: Carving a picture backward, in stone, the size of a thumb. Suddenly neat handwriting seems easy.

cards.fact: A cylinder seal prints a whole picture strip in one roll.
cards.context: Carve a design into a small stone cylinder, often no bigger than 5 cm tall, about the size of your thumb. Roll it across wet clay and the carving comes out raised, as one continuous band, the way a patterned paint roller works. Scholars count these tiny carvings among Mesopotamia's finest art.

cards.headline: A signature you could roll
cards.body: Seals weren't just decoration. Rolled onto clay, a seal marked what you owned or made a document legally binding: rolled on a tablet, it showed you had authorized the text, like a signature. Remember Level 1's writing, about 5,200 years ago? It was Sumerian cuneiform, wedge-shaped marks pressed into soft clay with a stylus. In Mesopotamia, words and pictures shared the same wet clay.

levels.title: The Rules of Egyptian Art
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the rules that kept Egyptian art so consistent for 3,000 years.
levels.summary: Egyptian artists drew each body part from its most complete angle, used a shared 18-unit grid, and made important people bigger. The style held for about 3,000 years.

cards.headline: Egyptian art kept one look for about 3,000 years.
cards.body: It did change, slowly, but it held its character so well that you can spot Egyptian art from across a museum. The secret is rules. Learn three and you can read almost any Egyptian painting.

cards.headline: Rule 1: every body part at its best angle
cards.body: Stand like a figure in an Egyptian painting and you'd need a very flexible neck. The head is in profile, but the eye looks straight at you. The shoulders face front, while the legs walk sideways. This wasn't clumsiness: artists combined viewpoints to show each part of the body in its most complete form. Level 6's aurochs did something similar, with bodies from the side and horns turned toward you.

mascot.line: Egyptian painters were using graph paper long before it was homework.

cards.fact: A standing figure measured 18 squares from the soles of the feet to the hairline.
cards.context: Artists laid a grid on the wall first, so a body came out with the same proportions whatever its size. Why stop at the hairline? Crowns and headdresses varied, so the top of the head didn't count. Every workshop sharing one grid is part of why the style stayed so steady.

cards.headline: Rule 3: bigger means more important
cards.body: In a tomb painting, the king or the tomb owner towers over everyone. His family is smaller, his servants smaller still. It isn't distance; it's rank. Remember Level 1: Egyptian art served the king and the gods, and size told you at a glance exactly who mattered.

levels.title: Art for the Afterlife
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Egyptians filled their tombs with art.
levels.summary: Egyptians believed the ka, a life force, needed food forever, and that images could magically provide it. So tombs held painted food, models like Meketre's and shabti workers.

cards.headline: In 1920, archaeologists opened a room nobody had entered in almost 4,000 years.
cards.body: It was in the tomb of Meketre, an Egyptian official. Robbers had stripped the tomb long ago, but they missed one small hidden chamber. Inside, packed tight, stood 24 painted wooden models. Why would anyone bury a miniature world?

mascot.line: Bread that never runs out and never goes stale. Egyptian tomb painters were very practical dreamers.

cards.headline: Food for the ka
cards.body: Egyptians believed each person had a ka, a life force that still needed food and drink after death. Real offerings run out. Pictures don't. So tombs were filled with scenes and models of food and food-making, which could feed the ka forever without ever being used up. A painted loaf is the one snack that never goes stale.

cards.headline: Meketre's model estate
cards.body: Meketre's models show boats, people carrying offerings, and workshops where craftsmen work and cooks make bread and beer. They look like toys. They weren't. Egyptians believed images could magically give the dead safe passage to the afterlife and food once there. Every tiny baker had a job: keep Meketre fed.

cards.fact: Some tomb figures were buried to do your chores.
cards.context: Shabtis were small figures of substitute workers, placed in tombs so they could do the dead person's labor in the afterlife. That fits the Egyptian dream: not a distant paradise, but daily life on Earth carried on, without the pain. Tomb art showed people as they wished to stay forever, which is why the tomb itself was called the ka house.
