levels.title: Festivals
levels.objective: After this level you can describe music festivals from Woodstock onward.
levels.summary: Woodstock (1969) drew about 400,000 to a farm in Bethel, New York, most without tickets, and ended with Hendrix's anthem. Live Aid (1985) linked London and Philadelphia for famine relief.

cards.headline: The Woodstock festival didn't happen in Woodstock.
cards.body: Woodstock ran August 15–18, 1969, on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, New York. The organizers kept the Woodstock name anyway. About 400,000 people showed up. What happens when that many people come to hear music in one field?

cards.headline: Mud, gate-crashers and a movie
cards.body: Not what anyone planned. Security was so thin that most people got in without paying, and rain turned the field to mud. The festival nearly bankrupted its four inexperienced promoters. What rescued them was a film: Michael Wadleigh's 1970 documentary was a commercial success that recouped their losses. The festival lost money; the movie of the festival made it back.

mascot.line: Text painting: the guitar doesn't just play the anthem's words, it acts them out.

cards.headline: 9 a.m. Monday: Hendrix plays the anthem
cards.body: Jimi Hendrix didn't take the stage until around 9 a.m. on Monday, August 18, by which time many festivalgoers had already left. His "Star-Spangled Banner" used the electric guitar to act out the words: rockets and bombs bursting, a siren-like wail. Musicians call this text painting, music that paints what the lyrics say.

cards.headline: From one field to the whole planet
cards.body: Sixteen years later, a festival didn't even need a single field. Live Aid, on July 13, 1985, ran at the same time at Wembley Stadium in London and JFK Stadium in Philadelphia, raising money for famine relief in Ethiopia, and it was broadcast worldwide. The audience was no longer just the people standing in front of the stage.

levels.title: Punk and Metal
levels.objective: After this level you can describe punk and heavy metal.
levels.summary: The power chord (root plus fifth, no third) drives heavy metal, codified in the 1970s by Zeppelin, Deep Purple and Sabbath, and punk (1975–80), which stripped rock down in New York and London.

cards.headline: Two of rock's loudest styles run on a chord with only two notes.
cards.body: Heavy metal and punk can sound like opposites: one heavy and virtuosic, the other short, fast and raw. Yet the power chord is a staple of both. Its trick is what it leaves out.

mascot.line: Leave out one note and you dodge the whole happy-or-sad question.

cards.headline: The power chord: a chord with a gap
cards.body: A power chord is just two notes: a root and the fifth above it. Remember Level 7? Major and minor chords differ in their middle note, the third. A power chord leaves the third out, so it's neither major nor minor. That's handy through heavy distortion, where full chords turn to mud but a power chord stays clear.

cards.headline: Heavy metal: rock, made heavier
cards.body: In the mid-1960s, British bands Cream and the Yardbirds and the guitarist Jimi Hendrix pushed rock toward a heavier sound. In the 1970s, Led Zeppelin, Deep Purple and Black Sabbath set the style: amplified distortion, heavy riffs and power chords, all on a blues-based foundation. The phrase "heavy metal" turned up in a 1968 Steppenwolf song before critics adopted it for the music.

cards.headline: Punk: rock, stripped to the bone
cards.body: Punk went the other way. It came together between 1975 and 1980, in New York and London at about the same time. At New York's CBGB club, the Ramones' 1976 debut album became the blueprint; in Britain, the Sex Pistols' 1977 hits made the country punk's epicenter. The songs were short, fast and minimal, a rejection of rock's polished production, and punk fueled a wave of independent record labels.

levels.title: Music Videos
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how music videos changed pop.
levels.summary: MTV launched on August 1, 1981, and made image as important as sound. Michael Jackson's videos helped break racial barriers, and Thriller became the first music video in the National Film Registry.

cards.headline: MTV's very first video was called "Video Killed the Radio Star."
cards.body: MTV went on the air just after midnight on August 1, 1981, and the first clip it played was that song by the Buggles. Remember Level 72, when radio made national hits? Now a TV channel wanted the job. Did pictures really change what a hit was?

cards.headline: Now a song needed a look
cards.body: MTV played music videos continuously, introduced by video disc jockeys, or VJs. Britannica sums up the effect: visual presentation became as important as the music in selling records. A band's look, its moves and its little movie now helped decide whether you bought the song.

cards.headline: Michael Jackson changes the channel
cards.body: At first MTV struggled. Its fortunes changed when it added rhythm and blues artists, and Michael Jackson's videos for "Billie Jean" and "Beat It" showed that MTV exposure could make an artist a huge star. Britannica credits "Beat It" with helping break down the barriers between Black and white artists on radio and in music videos.

mascot.line: Video killed the radio star. Then reality TV came for the video star.

cards.fact: In 2009, Michael Jackson's "Thriller" became the first music video added to the National Film Registry.
cards.context: Directed by John Landis, the 1983 video runs about 14 minutes, more short horror film than song clip. The twist: by the mid-1990s, most of MTV's own schedule wasn't music at all, but reality shows, game shows and cartoons.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: the sounds America decided never to lose.
cards.body: The Library of Congress keeps a list of recordings worth saving for good. Walk through it and you'll bump into this whole chapter, from a sheet of soot-covered paper to a Beatles album. Here's how the list works, and what it says about the road from phonograph to music video.

cards.fact: Each year the Librarian of Congress adds 25 recordings to the National Recording Registry.
cards.context: The registry comes from the National Recording Preservation Act of 2000. A recording must be at least 10 years old and "culturally, historically or aesthetically significant." So this year's biggest new hit, however huge, will have to wait its turn.

cards.headline: The chapter in one breath
cards.body: Edison's phonograph let sound be stored and played back. Radio sent one performance into millions of homes at once. Rock and roll merged rhythm and blues with country, led by Black pioneers. The electric guitar's pickup turned vibrating strings into a signal an amplifier could make loud. And MTV made how a song looked as important as how it sounded. Each new machine changed who could hear music, and how.

levels.title: Hip-Hop Begins
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how hip-hop began at Bronx block parties.
levels.summary: Hip-hop is commonly dated to Kool Herc's August 11, 1973 Bronx party. Built by Black and Latino youth with Jamaican sound-system roots, it has four elements: DJing, MCing, breaking, graffiti.

cards.headline: Hip-hop's birthday party raised money for back-to-school clothes.
cards.body: On August 11, 1973, Cindy Campbell threw a back-to-school jam in the rec room of her apartment building at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, to raise money for new school clothes. Her brother Clive, calling himself DJ Kool Herc, played the records. That night is the date most often given for the birth of hip-hop. So who was the DJ, and what did he start?

cards.headline: The DJ came from Kingston, Jamaica
cards.body: Herc was born in Kingston, Jamaica, and moved to the Bronx in 1967. Growing up, he'd soaked in Kingston's dance-hall parties and the powerful sound systems their deejays built, and he brought the idea north: his was the loudest sound system in the neighborhood. Jamaican deejays also "toasted," rapping improvised rhymes over the music. Hold on to that one. Talking over records is about to become an art of its own.

mascot.line: No studio, no record deal, no problem. Some of the biggest ideas in music started in a rec room.

cards.headline: Built by the Bronx's Black and Latino youth
cards.body: The South Bronx of the early 1970s was hit hard by poverty. That's where hip-hop grew, made by the neighborhood's Black and Latino young people. The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture traces it to African American, Afro-Caribbean and Afro-Latino traditions coming together in New York, and the Library of Congress describes the same thing: a new form of expression for Black and Latino youth. Nobody handed these kids a studio. They built a music out of parties.

cards.headline: Hip-hop is four arts, not one
cards.body: Hip-hop is a whole culture with four core parts: DJing, working the turntables; MCing, or rapping; breaking, the dance often called breakdancing; and graffiti. Herc even named the dancers. The ones who took the floor during a record's breaks, its percussive instrumental stretches, became break-boys and break-girls: b-boys and b-girls. So when someone says hip-hop, they might mean a song, a dance or a painted wall.

levels.title: DJs and Sampling
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how DJs and sampling build new music from old records.
levels.summary: Herc's merry-go-round looped drum breaks on two turntables (the breakbeat); Theodore found scratching in 1975. Sampling reuses recordings; Funky Drummer is the most sampled break.

cards.headline: The best part of a funk record lasted only a few seconds.
cards.body: Kool Herc noticed that the breaks, the percussive instrumental stretches of funk records, brought the most people out to dance. Then the break would end and the song would move on. His fix turned the record player into an instrument.

cards.headline: The merry-go-round: two copies, one endless break
cards.body: Herc set up two turntables and a mixer and played two copies of the same record. As the break finished on one, he started it on the other, then back again, looping those few seconds so the dancers could keep going far longer. He called it the merry-go-round. Today that looped drum section has a name of its own: the breakbeat.

mascot.line: Moral of the story: listen when your mom talks. You might invent something.

cards.headline: Scratching: a mistake worth keeping
cards.body: In 1975, a Bronx kid named Theodore Livingston was playing records in his bedroom when his mom came in to talk. Reaching to pause the record, he moved it back and forth under the needle, and he liked the rough sound it made. As Grand Wizzard Theodore, he's credited with inventing scratching, and one of his turntables is now in the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture.

cards.headline: Sampling: Herc's trick, done digitally
cards.body: Later, producers could grab sound electronically. Britannica defines digital sampling as music and sounds extracted from other recordings, and hip-hop's backing tracks often use it. The favorite ingredient is still a drum break. Clyde Stubblefield's 20-second drum solo on James Brown's 1970 single "Funky Drummer" has been called the most sampled drum break in music. The drummer's name may be new to you. His groove probably isn't.

levels.title: Rap
levels.objective: After this level you can explain rhyme and flow in rap.
levels.summary: Rap is rhythmic, rhyming speech over music; Rapper's Delight (1979) took it national. Flow is how words land on the beat: early rap rhymed on beat four, later rap roamed.

cards.headline: Rap turns the talking voice into an instrument.
cards.body: No strings, no keys, no singing required. Britannica defines rap as rhythmic, rhyming speech chanted to musical accompaniment. It sounds simple. The skill is in exactly where each word lands.

cards.headline: From Bronx parties to the national charts
cards.body: Remember Level 81's Jamaican toasting, deejays rapping improvised rhymes over the music? Rap grew up in African American communities in New York City. It reached the whole country with the Sugarhill Gang's "Rapper's Delight" in 1979, which climbed to No. 36 on the Billboard Hot 100. In 2011, the Library of Congress added it to its National Recording Registry.

cards.headline: Flow: where the words land
cards.body: Music theorist Kyle Adams defines flow as all the rhythmic and articulation choices in a rapper's delivery: where syllables fall against the beat, which ones get stressed, how crisp or smooth they sound. Remember Level 4: the beat ticks steadily underneath, and rhythm is the pattern laid over it. In rap, the words are that rhythm. Same beat, different flow, completely different song.

mascot.line: Try it: tap four beats and say a rhyme on every fourth tap. Now try landing it somewhere else.

cards.fact: Early-1980s rappers usually landed their rhymes on beat four.
cards.context: Analyses of early rap find rhymed line endings falling on or near the fourth beat, bar after bar, as regular as a clock chime. Later rappers broke the pattern: rhymes inside lines, rhymes off the beat, accents in surprising places. The rhymes got harder to predict, and more fun to chase.

levels.title: Synthesizers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a synthesizer makes sound.
levels.summary: A synth's oscillator sets pitch, its filter removes harmonics to shape timbre, and its envelope (ADSR) shapes loudness. Moog unveiled his modular synth in 1964; the Minimoog came in 1970.

cards.headline: A synthesizer makes a note out of electricity alone.
cards.body: No string vibrates, no pipe fills with air. Inside, circuits manipulate electrical currents to generate a sound, which a speaker finally turns into air pressure. Three parts do the shaping, and each is a knob you can learn to hear.

cards.headline: The oscillator sets the pitch
cards.body: An oscillator makes a repeating electrical wave. Remember Level 3: pitch is frequency, how many times per second something vibrates. On Robert Moog's synthesizer, pressing a key sent the oscillator a voltage that depended on which key you pressed, and that set the pitch. Some wave shapes are rich: a sawtooth wave contains all the harmonics of its note, higher frequencies stacked on top. That gives the next step something to carve.

cards.headline: The filter carves the tone
cards.body: Next comes the filter, which removes some of those harmonics. It changes the note's color, what musicians call timbre, while the oscillator keeps the pitch. Starting from a rich wave and filtering part of it away is called subtractive synthesis. Think of a sculptor with a block of marble: the sound is in there, and the filter chips away the rest.

cards.headline: The envelope shapes the note in time
cards.body: Last, an envelope controls how loud the note is from moment to moment, in four stages. Attack: the rise when you press the key. Decay: the fall to a steady level. Sustain: that level, held while your finger stays down. Release: the fade after you let go. Stretch out the attack and the note swells in gently instead of starting at full volume.

levels.title: Electronic Dance Music
levels.objective: After this level you can describe disco, house and techno.
levels.summary: Disco grew in early-1970s New York clubs on a four-on-the-floor kick; house grew from it in Chicago, named after the Warehouse; Detroit techno (1985) was instrumental and complex.

cards.headline: In 1979, Chicago tried to bury disco. Then Chicago brought it back.
cards.body: Disco Demolition Night, held in Chicago in 1979, became the symbol of a fierce backlash against disco. Yet within a few years, Chicago DJs were building a new dance music out of disco's parts. Follow the kick drum and you'll find three cities on one family tree.

cards.headline: New York: disco and the DJ
cards.body: Disco grew in underground New York City clubs in the early 1970s, rooms that welcomed mostly Black, Latino and gay dancers. DJs used extended 12-inch singles to build long mixes that kept people moving. Under it all ran the four-on-the-floor: a bass drum on every one of the four beats in a bar. Remember Level 4's beat, the steady pulse? Here you feel it in your chest.

mascot.line: A whole genre named after one club. Imagine your favorite hangout becoming a style of music.

cards.headline: Chicago: house, named after a club
cards.body: From 1977, DJ Frankie Knuckles played the Warehouse, a members-only Chicago club for Black gay dancers. He re-edited disco records on reel-to-reel tape to stretch out their grooves, and the music became known as house, after the club. In the early 1980s house blended disco's soul vocals and four-to-the-floor kick with synthesizer sounds. By 1986 it had reached Europe.

cards.headline: Detroit: techno
cards.body: In Detroit, three young African American DJ-producers, Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, began drawing attention in 1985. Inspired partly by the German electro-pop band Kraftwerk, their techno had glacial synth melodies and brisk machine rhythms. Unlike house, it was mostly instrumental, and its beats were more complex than house's steady kick. Same family, cooler temperature.

levels.title: Reggae
levels.objective: After this level you can describe reggae and Bob Marley.
levels.summary: Reggae came from western Kingston in the late 1960s, after ska and rocksteady, with choppy offbeat chords. Bob Marley carried it worldwide; UNESCO listed it as heritage in 2018.

cards.headline: UNESCO lists reggae as part of humanity's cultural heritage.
cards.body: In 2018, UNESCO added the reggae music of Jamaica to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage. The style itself was young: it was born in Jamaica in the late 1960s, in marginalized communities of western Kingston. How did it travel so far, so fast?

cards.headline: Ska, rocksteady, reggae: and the offbeat
cards.body: Reggae grew out of earlier Jamaican styles: ska became rocksteady, which became reggae. Its signature is the offbeat. Drums and bass drive a heavy four-beat rhythm, while the rhythm guitar or keyboard plays short, choppy chords on the offbeats instead of the main beats. Listen for that chunk off the beat. It's reggae's fingerprint.

cards.headline: Bob Marley carries it worldwide
cards.body: Bob Marley, born in 1945 in Nine Miles, Jamaica, formed the Wailers in Trench Town with Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer, writing songs for and about poor West Indians. Reggae's lyrics took on social and economic injustice, and through the Wailers it became linked with the Rastafari movement. After they signed with Island Records in 1972, their album Catch a Fire carried reggae worldwide. Marley died in 1981, at just 36.

cards.fact: In 1978, Bob Marley got two political rivals to join hands onstage.
cards.context: Jamaica was torn by political violence. At the One Love Peace Concert in Kingston, Marley brought Prime Minister Michael Manley and opposition leader Edward Seaga onstage and held their joined hands up high. For one night, a reggae concert was a peace summit.

mascot.line: Kingston to the Bronx: sometimes a genre's family tree crosses an ocean.

cards.headline: Echoes in the Bronx
cards.body: Remember Kool Herc, the Kingston-born DJ with the loudest sound system in his Bronx neighborhood? Britannica counts hip-hop among the styles reggae influenced, along with dancehall. Herc carried Jamaica's sound-system parties and toasting north, and Bronx kids turned them into something new.

levels.title: Global Pop
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how pop music from Korea, Nigeria and Latin America went global.
levels.summary: Pop crossed borders without English: BTS topped the Billboard 200 in 2018, Afrobeats (not Fela's Afrobeat) reached the Hot 100, and Despacito led the Hot 100 for 16 weeks.

cards.headline: In 2018, America's No. 1 album was sung mostly in Korean.
cards.body: BTS's Love Yourself: Tear topped the Billboard 200 album chart, the first time a K-pop act had done it. It's one of three stories in this level, from South Korea, Nigeria and Latin America, about pop crossing the world without switching to English.

cards.headline: K-pop: English came last
cards.body: BTS was assembled by producer Bang Si-Hyuk's Big Hit Entertainment, starting in 2010. They sang about self-love, individuality and empowerment, mostly in Korean, and topped the album chart that way. Their first English-language song, "Dynamite," only arrived in 2020, when it debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. The fame came first; the English came later.

mascot.line: One little letter, two different musics. Fela would want you to get it right.

cards.headline: Afrobeats: mind the "s"
cards.body: Afrobeats grew up in Nigeria and Ghana in the early 2000s, mixing highlife, dancehall and soca into upbeat dance pop about love, success and partying. Mind the "s": Afrobeat, without it, is Fela Kuti's 1960s and 70s blend of Yoruba music with jazz and funk, known for its political bite. In 2016 Drake's "One Dance," featuring Wizkid, topped the Hot 100 for 10 weeks, and in 2021 Nigeria's Burna Boy won the Grammy for Best Global Music Album.

cards.headline: Latin pop: the "Despacito" summer
cards.body: In 2017, Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee's Spanish-language "Despacito" (with a remix featuring Justin Bieber) led the Billboard Hot 100 for 16 weeks. That tied the record at the time, and no mostly non-English song had ever held the top spot longer. America's biggest singles chart no longer needed English to crown a winner.

levels.title: Studio Tricks
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what studio effects like Auto-Tune do.
levels.summary: Auto-Tune moves a sung note to the nearest semitone: a quiet fix, or a robot voice when pushed, as on Cher's Believe (1998). Studios add reverb; a drier voice seems closer.

cards.headline: Cher's robot voice came from a tool built to hide mistakes.
cards.body: On her 1998 hit "Believe," Cher's voice leaps from note to note like a machine. It was the first commercial recording to show off Auto-Tune's side effects on purpose. The tool was designed to fix singing quietly, and its inventor came from the oil business.

cards.headline: From oil fields to vocal booths
cards.body: Andy Hildebrand spent 1976 to 1989 interpreting seismic data for the oil industry. Later, his company Antares released Auto-Tune. It detects the pitch of each sung note and moves it to the nearest semitone: the smallest step on a keyboard, from one key to the very next, as you saw in Level 7. A slightly flat note gets nudged back into tune.

mascot.line: A bug, a feature, or a style? In music, sometimes all three.

cards.headline: Invisible fix or robot effect
cards.body: Used gently, pitch correction tidies a vocal and you never notice. Push it hard and the voice leaps from note to note while staying perfectly, unnaturally in tune: the "Believe" sound. Engineers realized the side effect could be a style. Today both uses, the quiet fix and the obvious robot, are common in recorded music.

cards.headline: Reverb: a room in a box
cards.body: Reverberation is sound that lingers after its source stops, built from reflections bouncing around a space. Studios often record in dry rooms lined with absorbent material, then add reverb afterward with metal plates, springs or digital algorithms. The balance sets the scene: the stronger the dry sound, the closer the singer seems. A voice recorded in a tiny booth can end up sounding like it's in a grand hall.

levels.title: From Records to Streaming
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how music moved from records to MP3s to streaming.
levels.summary: The CD (1982) samples 44,100 times a second to cover hearing up to 20 kHz; MP3 drops what you can't hear; streaming made up 82% of US recorded-music revenue in 2025.

cards.headline: In 2025, 82% of US recorded-music money came from streaming.
cards.body: That's the Recording Industry Association of America's count, measured at wholesale. Getting from discs on a shelf to songs that arrive through a phone took three big ideas.

cards.headline: Idea 1: turn sound into numbers
cards.body: Sony and Philips brought the compact disc to market in 1982. A CD stores sound as digital data, microscopic pits and flat spots read by a laser. It measures the sound wave 44,100 times every second. Why so many? To capture a frequency, you must sample more than twice as often, and remember Level 3: hearing tops out around 20 kHz. Twice that is 40,000, and the CD adds a little headroom.

cards.headline: Idea 2: throw away what you can't hear
cards.body: Researchers at Germany's Fraunhofer institute found a shortcut: store the parts of a sound your ear can't perceive with less precision. Their MP3 files came out up to ten times smaller, with virtually no audible difference. The team chose the name ".mp3" by email poll on July 14, 1995. In 1999, college student Shawn Fanning's Napster let people share music files over the internet, until a court fight with the record industry shut it down in 2001.

mascot.line: From a shelf of discs to a phone in your pocket, in about four decades.

cards.headline: Idea 3: stream it, don't store it
cards.body: Spotify, founded in Sweden, launched in 2008 and streamed songs instead of selling files: free with ads, or paid without them. That model won. The RIAA put streaming at 82% of US recorded-music revenue in 2025. Discs, then files, then streams: each step made music lighter to carry, until it weighed nothing at all.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Hip-Hop, Electronic and Beyond
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how turntables, synthesizers and computers changed music.
levels.summary: Roland's TR-808 (1980) synthesized drums from circuits; dismissed and discontinued, it powered Planet Rock (1982). Turntables, synths and computers remade music, often by accident.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: the drum machine the critics dismissed.
cards.body: Roland's TR-808 came out in 1980. Critics complained it didn't sound like real drums, and Roland stopped making it after selling about 12,000. Then hip-hop producers got hold of it. Its story ties together this whole chapter's machines.

cards.headline: Drums built from circuits
cards.body: The 808 didn't play recordings of drums. Roland's engineers used analog synthesis, manipulating electrical currents like Level 84's synthesizers, to make sounds that imitated hand-claps and bass notes. That's why critics called it fake, and why its thundering bass became famous. In 1982, Afrika Bambaataa and the Soul Sonic Force's "Planet Rock," made with an 808, became one of the decade's most influential records.

Computers turned songs into numbers small enough to stream. levels.title: Music and the Brain
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happens in the brain when we hear music.
levels.summary: Hair cells send signals up the auditory nerve to the temporal lobes. A steady beat stirs movement areas, chills release dopamine, and the Mozart effect was brief.

cards.headline: Your favorite song and a good meal share a brain chemical.
cards.body: When a piece of music gives you chills, your brain releases dopamine, a chemical also involved in the pleasure of rewards like food. Scientists caught it happening in 2011. But before a song can thrill you, it has to get into your head at all. Let's follow it in.

cards.headline: Your ears collect the sound; your brain hears it
cards.body: Remember Level 10's cochlea, where hair cells sort pitch like keys along a piano? Those hair cells turn the vibration into an electrical signal. The auditory nerve carries that signal to the brain, and the brain turns it into a sound you recognize. Its receiving desk is an area at the top of each temporal lobe. Until the signal arrives there, a song is just a pattern of electricity.

cards.headline: Sitting still, part of you is dancing
cards.body: Hearing is only the start. In a 2007 brain-imaging study, listeners heard different rhythms while lying still. Rhythms with a regular beat, the steady pulse from Level 4, drove extra activity in movement areas of the brain: the basal ganglia and the supplementary motor area. Nobody was moving. So when you say a song makes you want to move, your brain agrees. It has already started.

cards.headline: The chills are chemistry
cards.body: Back to the hook. In that 2011 study, music that gave listeners chills released dopamine in the striatum, deep in the brain. The timing was the surprise. At the peak moment, the release centered on one region, the nucleus accumbens. In the run-up, while listeners anticipated the peak, it came from another, the caudate. Your brain pays out twice: once for the big moment, and once for the wait.

mascot.line: Listen to Mozart because he's wonderful. That's reason enough.

cards.fact: Playing Mozart won't make you smarter.
cards.context: In 1993, students did better on a spatial-reasoning task right after hearing a Mozart sonata, but the boost faded within about 15 minutes. A 2010 analysis of nearly 40 studies found little evidence of any special Mozart effect, and other music did about as well. Music does remarkable things in the brain; this just isn't one of them.

levels.title: Why Songs Get Stuck
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why some songs get stuck in your head.
levels.summary: About 9 in 10 people get a weekly earworm, usually a looping snippet. Sticky tunes are faster, with a familiar shape and one odd leap. Listening, distraction or gum can help.

cards.headline: About 9 in 10 people get a song stuck in their head every week.
cards.body: That's from a survey of more than 12,000 people in Finland. Scientists call it involuntary musical imagery; everyone else calls it an earworm. So why does one tune move in and refuse to leave, while another never visits at all?

cards.headline: It's a loop, not a song
cards.body: Notice what actually plays in your head. It's rarely the whole track, start to finish. Most earworms are short snippets of a larger tune, a line or two that ends and starts again. That's part of why they're so hard to shake: a snippet has no ending to wrap things up, so round it goes, like a GIF of a song.

cards.headline: The recipe for a sticky tune
cards.body: In 2016, researchers asked 3,000 people which songs got stuck in their heads, then compared those songs with similarly popular ones nobody named. The earworms tended to be faster. Their melodies had a common overall shape, Level 5's contour, the kind your ear already knows. And they had something unusual too: a surprising leap or repetition. Familiar shape, one odd twist: that's the hook that catches.

cards.fact: The song people named most often: Lady Gaga's "Bad Romance."
cards.context: Next came Journey's "Don't Stop Believin'" and Kylie Minogue's "Can't Get You Out of My Head", a title that doubles as a confession. Sorry if one of them just moved in.

mascot.line: Some of that silent singing seems to lean on your mouth's planning. Gum gives it other work.

cards.headline: How to evict one
cards.body: In a 2014 study, the most popular and effective responses were surprisingly simple: listen to the tune itself, or distract yourself with other music or with words. Another option came from a 2015 University of Reading study: chew gum. It cut down on stuck songs, likely because chewing keeps busy the mouth-movement planning you use to sing a tune silently in your head.

levels.title: Music and Emotion
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why music can make us feel happy or sad.
levels.summary: Music borrows the voice's code: sad is slow, soft and low. Culture tunes cues like major and minor. Sad songs please when safe, and a few people get little joy from music.

cards.headline: A piece with no words can still sound heartbroken.
cards.body: Nobody in a cello solo sings "I'm sad." There are no words at all. So how can a few notes sound like grief? Part of the answer is older than any song. It's in the way people talk.

cards.headline: Music speaks in the voice's code
cards.body: A 2003 review pooled 104 studies of emotional voices and 41 of music performance, and found the two use similar cues. Sadness comes out slow, soft and low, in speech and in music alike. Happiness comes out fast, loud and high. So when a cello sounds heartbroken, it's doing what a sad voice does. You already speak this language; music just sings it.

cards.headline: Culture tunes some of the code
cards.body: Not every cue works that way. Remember Level 7: young children first judged happy and sad music by tempo alone, and only later by major and minor. And in Papua New Guinea, hearing major as happier was strongly tied to how much Western-style music people knew. Speed seems to speak early and widely; the mood of a minor key is partly learned.

cards.headline: Why a sad song can feel good
cards.body: Here's the puzzle: why would anyone choose to feel sad? A 2015 review found sadness from music is enjoyed when it feels non-threatening, when the music is beautiful, and when it helps, for example by easing a mood. The key is that in art, the real loss isn't there. A sad song lets you feel the storm from indoors.

mascot.line: If music leaves you cold, you're not broken. Brains differ, even in their favorite rewards.

cards.fact: Some people with normal hearing get little pleasure from music.
cards.context: A 2014 study described healthy people who heard music normally but got little pleasure from it, and their bodies showed no response to music others loved. Yet winning money pleased them just fine. Remember Level 91's musical chills? For them, music simply doesn't deliver that reward.

levels.title: Film Music
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how film scores shape what we feel.
levels.summary: Silent films had live music. Jaws's two neighboring notes, E and F, stand in for a shark we rarely see. In a 2001 study, music changed how viewers read the same scene.

cards.headline: Silent films were never silent.
cards.body: Through the silent era, a pianist, a theater organist or, in big cities, a whole orchestra played live beside the screen. Before movies could talk, they already had music. So what is music doing to you while you watch?

cards.headline: Two notes, one shark
cards.body: For Jaws (1975), John Williams built the shark's theme from just two notes, E and F, alternating over and over. Remember Level 6? Two neighboring keys like E and F make a second, the kind of interval traditional theory counts as dissonant: tension with no release. As the shark closes in, the two notes grow louder and faster. You feel it coming before you see a thing.

mascot.line: A shark that's mostly music. Scarier than rubber, as it turned out.

cards.fact: In Jaws, the shark doesn't appear until the film's 81st minute.
cards.context: The mechanical sharks kept breaking down, so for most of the film the shark is suggested rather than shown. Williams's two notes do the work: hear them, and you know it's there. The score won him an Academy Award.

cards.headline: Same scene, different story
cards.body: In a 2001 study, people watched ambiguous film clips with upbeat music, gloomy music or none. With upbeat music, they read the scenes more positively; with gloomy music, more negatively; with no music, fairly neutrally. A week later, their memories of the clips leaned the same way as the music. A score doesn't just decorate a scene. It tells you what the scene means.

levels.title: Video Game Music
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how game music grew from beeps to orchestras.
levels.summary: Koji Kondo wrote Super Mario Bros. for three notes at once, with music that reacts to play. It became the first game music in the National Recording Registry in 2023.

cards.headline: In 2023, a video game tune joined America's archive of sound treasures.
cards.body: The Library of Congress added Koji Kondo's Super Mario Bros. theme, from 1985, to its National Recording Registry: the first video game music ever chosen. Not bad for music written for a very limited machine. Here's how game music got from beeps to that honor.

cards.headline: Three notes and a hiss
cards.body: Kondo later described what he had to work with: just three musical notes at a time, plus one white-noise sound, and very little data for music at all. Remember Level 1's harmony, notes sounding together? A single three-note chord would have used every voice the machine had. So every note had to earn its place, and Kondo made it sound effortless.

mascot.line: Faster music, same game. Your pulse probably noticed before you did.

cards.headline: Music that plays along with you
cards.body: Film music follows a fixed story; game music has to follow you. Kondo wrote jingles to cheer players on after a Game Over, fanfares for reaching a goal, and pieces that sped up when time was running short. That last one is Level 4's tempo put to work: the clock is ticking, and the music makes sure you feel it.

cards.headline: From sound chip to concert hall
cards.body: Those three-voice tunes didn't stay in the console. Kondo's Super Mario Bros. music has been performed by orchestras around the globe. And in 2023 the Grammys handed out their first award for video game scores, won by Stephanie Economou for Assassin's Creed Valhalla: Dawn of Ragnarok. Game music had graduated.

levels.title: Who Gets Paid
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how songwriters get paid and what copyright protects.
levels.summary: A recorded song holds two copyrights: the musical work and the sound recording. US AM/FM radio pays only the songwriters' side. Each 2026 CD or download copy earns 13.1 cents.

cards.headline: Someone was charging for "Happy Birthday."
cards.body: For years, Warner/Chappell Music collected licensing fees for "Happy Birthday to You." Then filmmakers sued, and in 2015 a federal judge ruled the company held no valid copyright to the lyrics. So who really owns a song, and who gets paid when you hear it?

cards.headline: Every recorded song holds two copyrights

items.label: The musical work
points: The notes and the lyrics
Created by songwriters

items.label: The sound recording
points: The recording itself
Created by performers and producers

cards.headline: The song and the recording are different things
cards.body: US copyright splits every recorded song in two. The musical work is the song on paper: melody, harmony and lyrics, the stuff of Level 1, written by songwriters. The sound recording is one particular performance of it, captured by performers and producers. They're commonly owned and licensed separately. Cover a song and you make a new recording, but the song still belongs to its writers.

cards.headline: The radio gap
cards.body: A musical work's copyright includes public performance, like radio play, which songwriters usually license through organizations such as ASCAP and BMI. But in the US, the performance right for sound recordings covers only digital transmissions, like streaming and satellite radio. So when a hit plays on AM/FM radio, the songwriters' side gets paid, and the recording's side gets nothing.

cards.fact: In 2026, each CD, vinyl or download copy of a US song earns its owners 13.1 cents.
cards.context: That's the statutory "mechanical" royalty set by the Copyright Royalty Judges for copying the musical work. Songs longer than five minutes can earn more, at 2.52 cents per minute.

levels.title: Learning an Instrument
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what practice does for a musician.
levels.summary: The best Berlin student violinists reported the most solo practice. Deliberate practice is focused and feedback-driven, but practice explains only part of skill, about 21% in music.

cards.headline: Why are the best violinists better than the rest?
cards.body: In 1993, psychologists put that question to a Berlin music academy. They grouped violin students as the best, the good, or future music teachers, and asked each one to estimate how much they had practiced over the years. The answer made practice famous. Then it got more complicated.

cards.headline: The best had practiced the most
cards.body: The difference showed up in the hours spent practicing alone. By age 18, the best students reported about 7,400 hours; the future music teachers, about 3,400. That's more than twice as much. The researchers, led by Anders Ericsson, concluded that practice was a big part of what separated them.

mascot.line: Nobody's counting your hours. Pick the one bar that trips you up and give it some slow, careful attention.

cards.headline: Not all practice is equal
cards.body: Ericsson called the key ingredient deliberate practice: effortful work designed to improve, with well-defined tasks, set at the right difficulty, and informative feedback. That's different from play. Running your favorite piece top to bottom for fun is playing. Slowing down the one bar you keep fumbling, fixing it and checking it again: that's deliberate practice.

cards.headline: Practice matters. It isn't everything.
cards.body: Later research added a twist. A 2014 meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained about 21% of the differences in music performance. And a 2019 repeat of the Berlin study found no significant practice gap between the best and the good violinists. Practice clearly helps, and it's the part you control. It just isn't the whole story.

levels.title: Perfect Pitch
levels.objective: After this level you can explain perfect pitch and how rare it is.
levels.summary: Absolute pitch, naming a note with no reference, is under 1 in 10,000 in the US and Europe, and far more common among Mandarin speakers who trained early. Most people use relative pitch.

cards.headline: Play a random note, and a few people can simply name it.
cards.body: No piano to check against, no starting note: they hear it and say "that's an A." It's called absolute pitch, or perfect pitch: naming or singing a note without any reference note. How rare is it, and why do some people have it?

cards.headline: Rarer than you'd think
cards.body: In the US and Europe, absolute pitch is estimated at fewer than 1 in 10,000 people. And it isn't a musical superpower. Having it doesn't necessarily make someone better at other musical tasks. A person with perfect pitch might hear Level 3's 440 Hz tone and instantly call it A, and still struggle with rhythm. It's a rare ear, not a guarantee.

cards.headline: What the rest of us use
cards.body: Remember Level 5? You recognize "Twinkle, Twinkle" starting on any note, because you hear the relationships between notes. That's relative pitch, and nearly everyone uses it. Even without perfect pitch, most people have a surprisingly accurate long-term memory for pitch, as long as they don't need to name the note. You may not know it's an A. You still remember how it sounds.

mascot.line: Imagine a childhood where the pitch of a word decides what it means. Your ear would pay attention too.

cards.headline: The language clue
cards.body: A 2006 study tested music students at the Central Conservatory in Beijing, who spoke Mandarin, and at the Eastman School in New York. In both, absolute pitch was more common the earlier training began. But at every starting age, it was far more common among the Mandarin speakers. In Mandarin, pitch changes meaning: "ma" can mean mother, hemp, horse or a scolding, depending on its tone.

levels.title: How to Really Listen
levels.objective: After this level you can use a simple method to listen closely to any piece of music.
levels.summary: Copland's three planes: sensuous, expressive, sheerly musical. Listen in passes (beat, melody, harmony), and closely rather than loudly: WHO allows 80 dB for 40 hours a week.

cards.headline: Are you just listening, or listening for something?
cards.body: In 1939, the American composer Aaron Copland wrote a book called What to Listen for in Music. His goal was to turn passive listeners into active ones: not someone who is just listening, "but someone who is listening for something." Here is his map, a method built from this tree, and one rule to protect your ears.

items.label: Sensuous
points: The pleasure of the sound itself
Bathing in it, barely thinking

items.label: Expressive
points: What the music makes you feel

items.label: Sheerly musical
points: The notes themselves
Melody, rhythm, harmony, tone color

cards.headline: Listen in three passes
cards.body: Copland noticed that casual listeners catch the melody first, then the rhythm, and take harmony and tone color for granted. So give them turns. Pick one song. First pass: tap the beat (Level 4). Second: hum the melody (Level 5). Third: ignore the tune and follow the chords underneath (Level 6). Copland said we really hear on all three planes at once; the passes just train you to notice.

mascot.line: Close listening is a quiet sport. Your ears have a lot more music ahead of them.

cards.headline: Listen closely, not loudly
cards.body: WHO says 80 decibels is safe for up to 40 hours a week, but at 90 decibels safe time drops to four hours: ten decibels louder cuts your time to a tenth. It suggests keeping your device at no more than 60% of maximum. Remember Level 10's hair cells, sorting pitch in the cochlea? Human hair cells don't grow back. But noise-induced hearing loss is completely preventable.

levels.summary: Earth has one connected ocean covering more than 70% of the surface and holding about 97% of its water. It makes about half our oxygen and feeds our rain.

cards.headline: Take a deep breath. The ocean made about half of it.
cards.body: You might live hundreds of kilometers from the nearest beach, and the sea still reaches you, in every breath and every rain shower. Meet the biggest thing on the planet, and find out why nothing alive can do without it.

cards.headline: One ocean, many names
cards.body: A globe shows a Pacific, an Atlantic and more. But NOAA, the US ocean agency, says there is only one global ocean. The names mark regions of it, divided by lines people drew, not by walls of land. That one ocean covers more than 70% of Earth's surface and holds about 97% of all Earth's water. Every lake, river, glacier and cloud on the planet shares the leftovers.
cards.callout: One connected ocean · about 97% of Earth's water

mascot.line: Next time someone says they need some sea air, you can tell them they already have it.

cards.fact: About half of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean.
cards.context: It's made by plankton: drifting plants, algae and some bacteria that photosynthesize, soaking up sunlight and giving off oxygen. So when you thank a forest for fresh air, save some thanks for the sea. Roughly every other breath you take is on the ocean's tab.

cards.headline: The ocean waters the land
cards.body: The ocean supplies most of the water that evaporates into the air. Winds carry that vapor, sometimes far inland, and it falls again as rain and snow. The river you cross and the crops you eat all run on that rain and snow. The ocean is the planet's water tank, and the sky is the delivery van.

levels.title: The Blue Planet
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how much of Earth is ocean and how deep it goes.
levels.summary: Water covers about 71% of Earth. The ocean averages about 3,700 m deep, about 11 km at its deepest, yet on a 30 cm globe it would be under 0.1 mm deep.

cards.headline: In 1972, astronauts looked back and saw a blue marble.
cards.body: On December 7, 1972, the Apollo 17 crew, on their way to the Moon, photographed the whole Earth at once. The picture became known as the Blue Marble. Why so blue? And how deep does all that blue actually go?

cards.headline: Seven parts in ten
cards.body: The marble is blue because most of it is water: about 71% of Earth's surface, with the ocean alone covering more than 70%. Spin a globe, stop it with a finger, and most of the time you'll land in the sea. From space, the land is the exception, not the rule.

cards.fact: The ocean is about 3,700 m deep on average.
cards.context: NOAA puts the average at about 3,682 m. That's across the whole ocean: under a typical patch of open sea, there's more than three and a half kilometers of water between you and the bottom. Holding your breath won't cut it.

mascot.line: The deepest place on Earth, reduced to a scratch on a desk globe. Perspective is a wonderful thing.

cards.headline: Deep, and yet thin
cards.body: Now zoom out. Earth's radius is about 6,371 km, so shrink the planet to a globe 30 cm across and the average ocean becomes less than a tenth of a millimeter deep. Even the deepest known spot, Challenger Deep at about 11 km, would be a scratch about a quarter of a millimeter deep. The blue in the Blue Marble is a very thin coat of paint.

levels.title: Five Oceans
levels.objective: After this level you can name and compare the five oceans.
levels.summary: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic: biggest to smallest. The Southern Ocean is bounded by a current at 60° S; NOAA and National Geographic count it.

cards.headline: One ocean on the map has no coastline on its northern side.
cards.body: Its southern edge is Antarctica. Its northern edge is a line drawn across open water at 60° south. To see why, meet all five named oceans, biggest first.

cards.headline: The ocean drawn by a current
cards.body: Historically there were four named oceans: the Atlantic, Pacific, Indian and Arctic, each defined by the continents around it. The Southern Ocean is different. It is defined by a current that flows all the way around Antarctica, and its northern edge is set at 60° south. Its border is a line through moving water. Good luck putting up a fence.

cards.headline: Five oceans, one asterisk
cards.body: The US Board on Geographic Names has used the name Southern Ocean since 1999, NOAA counts it as the fifth ocean, and National Geographic began recognizing it on June 8, 2021. The International Hydrographic Organization, which publishes the standard limits of oceans and seas, dropped it in 1953. In 2023 it voted to recognize it again, while leaving each member country free to keep its own view. So: five oceans, most of the time.

levels.title: Where Earth's Water Came From
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the leading ideas for where Earth's water came from.
levels.summary: Deuterium is water's origin clue. Asteroid meteorites match Earth; comet 67P seemed not to, until 2024. Some water came from within Earth. The shares are debated.

cards.headline: Earth was born too hot to keep its water. Or was it?
cards.body: For a long time, scientists thought any water on the newborn Earth would have boiled off or blown away into space, so the oceans must have arrived later, on comets or icy asteroids. So who delivered the sea? The answer is still being argued over.

cards.headline: A fingerprint in every drop
cards.body: Water carries a clue. Its hydrogen comes in two kinds: ordinary hydrogen, and a rare, heavier form called deuterium. Deuterium forms more readily in cold places far from the Sun, so the share of it in water hints at where that water formed. The test is simple: find a space rock whose water has the same fingerprint as your bathtub.

items.label: Comets
points: 2014: ESA's Rosetta measures comet 67P
Its water has more than three times Earth's deuterium ratio
Verdict then: comets like it are unlikely suppliers

items.label: Asteroids
points: Meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites carry water
Their hydrogen fingerprint matches Earth's
A 2014 WHOI-led study: Earth got its water early from such bodies

mascot.line: A cold case with three suspects and no confession. Science at its most honest.

cards.headline: Case reopened
cards.body: In 2024, a NASA-led team found that dust had skewed Rosetta's readings, and that 67P's water looks much like Earth's after all. A 2020 study added a twist: meteorites like the stuff Earth formed from hold enough hydrogen to supply at least three times the water in the oceans. Today's picture is a mix. Some water came from inside Earth, vented by volcanoes, and much came from asteroids and possibly comets. How much from each is still debated.

levels.title: Why the Sea Is Salty
levels.objective: After this level you can explain where the salt in seawater comes from.
levels.summary: Seawater is about 35 parts per thousand salt, mostly chloride and sodium. Rain weathers rock, rivers carry the salt, evaporation leaves it, and vents add more.

cards.headline: Dry out the ocean and the leftover salt would bury every continent.
cards.body: Spread the ocean's salt evenly over all the land and it would form a layer about as tall as a 40-story office building. That's a lot of seasoning. Where did it all come from? Mostly from rocks on land.

cards.fact: Seawater is about 35 parts per thousand salt.
cards.context: In other words, dissolved salts make up about 3.5% of its weight. Most of it is chloride and sodium, the same two ingredients as table salt. That's why a gulp of sea tastes like a kitchen accident.

cards.headline: Rivers deliver, the sea keeps
cards.body: Rain holds a little dissolved carbon dioxide, which makes it slightly acidic, so over time it breaks down rocks on land. Streams and rivers carry the freed salts to the sea. River water has salt in it too, just far too little to taste. At sea, water evaporates but the salt is left behind, so delivery after delivery, it builds up. The river passes the salt along; the ocean hangs on to it.

cards.headline: Salt from below
cards.body: Rivers aren't the only suppliers. On the sea floor, seawater seeps into cracks, is heated by magma and gushes back out of hydrothermal vents carrying dissolved minerals. Undersea eruptions release minerals straight into the water too. So the ocean is salted from both ends: from the land above and the rocks below.

levels.title: Layers of Water
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how temperature and salt stack seawater in layers.
levels.summary: Cold and salty water is denser than warm and fresh, so the sea stacks itself: light water on top, dense below, with the thermocline's quick drop between.

cards.headline: A liter of seawater weighs about 26 g more than a liter of fresh water.
cards.body: That small difference is enough to sort the whole ocean into layers, like a drink that refuses to mix.

cards.headline: Two ways to get heavier
cards.body: Water gets denser in two ways. Cool it down: cold water is denser than warm water. Add salt: salty water is denser than fresh water. At 10°C, a liter of fresh water weighs 1,000 g and a liter of seawater about 1,026 g. So the heaviest water in the sea is the cold, salty kind, and the lightest is warm and fresh.

cards.headline: The ocean sorts itself
cards.body: When waters of different density meet, the ocean orders them: the lighter water rides near the surface and the denser water settles at depth. It's like oil floating on vinegar in a salad dressing, except here both layers are water. Warm water floats on top, and cold, dense water fills the deep.

mascot.line: Warm on top, cold below, and a sharp step between. The ocean keeps its layers neater than my desk.

cards.headline: The thermocline: a cold step down
cards.body: Between the warm, well-mixed surface water and the much colder deep water sits the thermocline, a layer where the temperature drops fast as you go down. It isn't the same everywhere. It's semi-permanent in the tropics, shifts with the seasons in temperate seas, and is shallow or missing altogether in polar seas.

levels.title: Why the Ocean Is Blue
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why seawater looks blue.
levels.summary: Water absorbs red light and scatters blue, so deep water looks blue while a glass looks clear. Sky reflection adds only at the surface; particles and plankton turn it green.

cards.headline: Scoop a glass from the bluest sea on Earth. The water is clear.
cards.body: Pour it back, and it's blue again. So which is it? Both. Water has a faint blue color of its own, far too faint to see in a glass. You need a lot of it.

cards.headline: Water eats the red
cards.body: Sunlight is a mix of every color. When it enters the sea, water absorbs the colors at the red end of the spectrum much more strongly than blue. Like a filter, it strips out reds and oranges and scatters the leftover blue back toward your eyes. The ocean isn't painted blue. It's blue because of what it takes away.

cards.headline: But isn't it just the sky?
cards.body: Partly, right at the surface. The sea does reflect the sky, which is why a big stretch of water looks gray on an overcast day. But the color of the sea and the color of the sky arise separately. The deep blue comes from water absorbing red light, the same reason a glass of it looks clear while a whole sea looks blue.

cards.headline: When the sea turns green
cards.body: Not every sea is blue. Where the water carries lots of sediment and particles, light bounces off them and the sea can look green or other colors. Where phytoplankton are plentiful, their chlorophyll absorbs some colors and tints the water green. A green sea isn't broken. Often it's just crowded.

levels.title: Light Fades Below
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how sunlight fades with depth.
levels.summary: Colors fade in order: red first, blue last. Below about 200 m there's too little light for photosynthesis, and below 1,000 m no sunlight at all.

cards.headline: Take a red fish 100 m down and it turns black.
cards.body: Nothing happened to the fish. At 100 m there's no red light left to bounce off it, so it looks blackish. Sunlight doesn't just dim as you sink. It loses its colors, one by one.

cards.headline: Colors switch off in order
cards.body: Remember Level 7: water absorbs red light most strongly. So a few meters down, most of the red and orange is already gone. Next to fade are yellow and green. Blue and violet travel deepest of all. That's why the underwater world turns bluer and bluer the deeper you go.

cards.fact: Below about 200 m, there isn't enough light for photosynthesis.
cards.context: Faint light can still be detected as deep as 1,000 m, but past about 200 m there's rarely any significant light, far too little to power anything that makes food from sunlight. So the ocean's sunlight-powered food makers all live near the top.

mascot.line: Most of the ocean has never had a sunny day. Bring a flashlight, and maybe a sweater.

cards.headline: The dark majority
cards.body: Below 1,000 m, no sunlight arrives at all. Now remember Level 2: the ocean averages about 3,700 m deep. So under a typical patch of sea, the floor lies about 2,700 m below the last glimmer of daylight, nearly three quarters of the way down in total darkness. The ocean is mostly a place where the Sun has never shone.

levels.title: Pressure
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how water pressure grows with depth.
levels.summary: Every 10 m of seawater adds about one atmosphere of pressure. Water barely squeezes but air does, so deep pressure shrinks a foam cup for good.

cards.headline: Send a foam cup to the deep sea and it comes back doll-sized.
cards.body: Oceanographers decorate foam cups and send them down with their deep-sea gear. The cups come back shrunken, and they stay that way. Nothing touched them but water. So what squeezed them?

cards.headline: A weight that stacks up
cards.body: The answer is pressure. At the surface, the air above you already presses on you with one atmosphere. Every 10 m of seawater adds about one atmosphere more. So at just 10 m down, the pressure on a diver is double what it is at the surface. You don't have to go deep to feel the ocean leaning on you.

cards.headline: Counting atmospheres
cards.body: Keep going and the atmospheres pile up in a steady stack. Water adds about 10 atmospheres at 100 m, and about 200 at 2,000 m. The rule is simple arithmetic: divide the depth in meters by 10, and you have the pressure the water adds, in atmospheres. Easy to count. Much harder to survive.

cards.headline: Why the cup shrinks
cards.body: Water itself barely squeezes, but air does. Foam is full of tiny air pockets, and deep-sea pressure crushes them, so the cup shrinks and never bounces back. Your lungs and the air spaces in your head are air pockets too, and enough pressure would collapse them. That shrunken cup is a warning in miniature.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Blue Planet
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the size, saltiness and layers of the ocean.
levels.summary: All Earth's water would make a ball about 1,385 km across. Dive in: warm over cold, colors fade, light ends at 1,000 m, pressure climbs. Salty all the way down.

cards.headline: Every drop of water on Earth would fit in a ball smaller than the Moon.
cards.body: Oceans, ice, rivers, clouds: all of it. Let's build that ball, then dive into the real ocean with everything this chapter taught.

cards.fact: All of Earth's water would make a ball about 1,385 km across.
cards.context: That's about 1,386 million cubic km of water, and the ball would be well under half as wide as the Moon. Tiny next to Earth, which fits Level 2: the ocean is a thin blue coat on a big rocky planet. About 97% of that ball would be seawater.

cards.headline: Take the plunge
cards.body: Now dive into the real thing. At the top, warm water floats over the thermocline, where the temperature drops fast. A few meters down, the red light is gone. By about 200 m there's too little light for photosynthesis, and past 1,000 m there's no sunlight at all. All the way, pressure climbs about one atmosphere every 10 m, until you reach the average sea floor about 3,700 m down.

cards.headline: Salty all the way down
cards.body: Every liter of that dive is salty: about 35 parts per thousand, mostly chloride and sodium, washed off the land by rivers and pushed up through sea-floor vents. Cold, salty water is dense, which is why it settles into the deep while warm water rides on top. Size, salt and layers: that's the blue planet in one dive.

levels.title: Planet Earth in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can name Earth's continents and oceans and say how much of the surface is water.
levels.summary: About 71% of Earth's surface is water. The land splits into seven continents, and the water into five named oceans that are really one.

cards.headline: We named our planet Earth. Most of it is water.
cards.body: About 71% of the surface is ocean. Spin a globe, stop it with a finger, and you'll land on water about seven times out of ten. Maybe we should have called it Ocean.

cards.headline: Seven big pieces of land
cards.body: Everything that sticks up out of all that water is split into seven continents: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia. People live on all of them, with one exception. Antarctica has no permanent population at all; the only people there are researchers and the staff who support them. Nobody grows up in Antarctica.
cards.callout: Asia · Africa · North America · South America · Antarctica · Europe · Australia

cards.fact: Your old atlas may show four oceans. Most countries now count five.
cards.context: The classic four are the Atlantic, Pacific, Indian and Arctic. The fifth is the Southern Ocean, the water that encircles Antarctica. It's the newest named ocean, and National Geographic started recognizing it in 2021. So if you learned four, you weren't wrong. You were just early.

mascot.line: One ocean, five name tags. The water has never once read them.

cards.headline: Five names, one ocean
cards.body: Here's the twist: those five oceans aren't separate bodies of water. They all flow into each other. As NOAA, the US ocean agency, puts it, there is only one global ocean. The five names are like rooms in one big house. The walls are lines that people drew on maps, and the water ignores them completely.

levels.title: Why Every Map Is Wrong
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why every flat map distorts the round Earth and compare two common projections.
levels.summary: A round Earth can't be flattened without distortion. Mercator's map keeps compass lines straight but inflates the far north and south; equal-area maps keep sizes true.

cards.headline: On many world maps, Greenland looks as big as Africa. Africa is 14 times bigger.
cards.body: Nobody drew it wrong on purpose. The mapmaker had an impossible job, and so does every mapmaker who ever lived.

cards.headline: The orange peel problem
cards.body: Peel an orange and try to press the peel flat on a table. It splits, stretches, or both. Maps have the same problem: Earth is round, paper is flat, and you can't get from one to the other without distorting something. A globe can keep size, shape, distance and direction all true at once. A flat map has to give some of them up.

cards.headline: Mercator's deal with sailors
cards.body: In 1569, Gerardus Mercator published a map built for navigation. On it, a straight line is a steady compass bearing: draw a line between two ports, hold that heading, and you're on course. The price was size. The farther a place is from the Equator, the more his map inflates it. Greenland sits far to the north, so it balloons.
cards.callout: Straight lines: great. Sizes: not so much.

cards.fact: Africa is about 14 times bigger than Greenland.
cards.context: On a Mercator map they look like rivals. An equal-area map fixes that: it shows every place at its true relative size, so Africa finally looks as huge as it is. The catch? Shapes come out stretched and squashed instead. No flat map wins at everything. Each one picks which truth to tell.

levels.title: Latitude and Longitude
levels.objective: After this level you can find any place on Earth using latitude and longitude.
levels.summary: Latitude measures north or south of the Equator, longitude east or west of the Greenwich prime meridian. Together they pin down one spot.

cards.headline: Two numbers can find your front door. Or anywhere else on Earth.
cards.body: No street name, no city, no country. Just two numbers. Here's how the whole planet got a grid.

cards.headline: Latitude: how far north or south
cards.body: Picture rings around the globe, stacked like the rungs of a ladder from bottom to top. That's latitude. It measures how far north or south of the Equator you are: 0° at the Equator, up to 90° at the North or South Pole. The rings are parallel to each other, so they never meet. That's why they're called parallels.
cards.callout: 0° at the Equator, 90° at the poles

cards.headline: Longitude: how far east or west
cards.body: Now slice the globe like an orange, from pole to pole. Those lines are meridians, and they measure longitude: how far east or west you are, from 0° up to 180°. Unlike parallels, meridians all meet at the poles. But which slice is zero? Countries used to pick their own. In 1884 an international conference settled on one: the meridian through Greenwich, England.

mascot.line: Null Island: population zero, lost data plenty. I'd visit, but I'd need a boat and a very good excuse.

cards.fact: At 0°, 0° there's nothing but ocean.
cards.context: Where the Equator crosses the prime meridian, you're bobbing in the Atlantic Ocean, in the Gulf of Guinea off West Africa. Yet mapping software sometimes gives records with missing locations exactly those coordinates, so mapmakers jokingly call the spot Null Island. Give a place two good numbers, a latitude and a longitude, and it lands exactly where it belongs.

levels.title: The Equator and the Tropics
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the Equator, the tropics and the polar circles mark and why they sit where they do.
levels.summary: The Equator splits the hemispheres. Earth's 23.5° tilt sets the tropics, the only zone with an overhead Sun, and the polar circles, where days can last 24 hours.

cards.headline: Twice a year in Hawaii, flagpoles lose their shadows at noon.
cards.body: The Sun stands straight overhead, and the shadow hides right under the pole. Anywhere else in the US? Never. A few imaginary lines on the globe explain why.

cards.headline: The Equator: Earth's belt
cards.body: Start in the middle. The Equator is 0° latitude, exactly halfway between the North and South Poles, and it splits the planet into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Twice a year, at the equinoxes, the Sun passes directly over it. Every latitude you met in Level 3 is counted from this line.

cards.headline: The tropics: where the Sun turns around
cards.body: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so the spot where the noon Sun stands directly overhead drifts north and south through the year. It reaches the Tropic of Cancer, about 23.5° N, around June 21. Then it turns back and reaches the Tropic of Capricorn, about 23.5° S, around December 21. Between those lines lie the tropics, the only places where the Sun is ever directly overhead. Hawaii is inside. The rest of the US is not.
cards.callout: Overhead Sun zone: 23.5° N to 23.5° S

cards.headline: The polar circles: days that last all day
cards.body: Now go about 23.5° from each pole: that same tilt again. You reach the Arctic Circle at about 66.5° N and the Antarctic Circle at about 66.5° S. On these lines the Sun stays up for a full day at least once a year, and stays down for a full day, too. Keep going toward a pole and it stretches to six months. Try explaining bedtime there in June.

levels.title: Time Zones
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the world has time zones and where the calendar date changes.
levels.summary: Earth turns 15° an hour, so the world uses 24 time zones counted from Greenwich. The date changes at the International Date Line, near 180°.

cards.headline: Call a friend on the far side of the world and you might be calling tomorrow.
cards.body: It's Monday evening where you are, and your friend is eating breakfast on Tuesday. Nobody's clock is broken. The planet is round, and it spins.

cards.headline: Every town had its own noon
cards.body: Earth turns 360° in about 24 hours, which is 15° of longitude every hour. So the Sun reaches its highest point at a slightly different moment in every town. For centuries, communities set their clocks by their own Sun. That worked fine until railways spread, and a timetable had to juggle a different local time at every stop.

cards.headline: Twenty-four slices of time
cards.body: The fix was standard time. Cut the globe into 24 zones along meridians 15° apart, counted from Greenwich, and make each zone one hour apart. The system was adopted at the same 1884 conference that picked the prime meridian. On a real map, though, the borders zigzag, bending to follow countries' borders.
cards.callout: 15° of longitude = 1 hour

mascot.line: Head east over the line and you get yesterday back. I'd use mine to finish yesterday's crossword.

cards.headline: Where tomorrow begins
cards.body: Keep adding hours as you travel around the world and the days stop adding up. Something has to reset the calendar. That's the International Date Line, which roughly follows the 180° meridian, halfway around the world from the prime meridian. Cross it heading west and your calendar jumps a day ahead; head east and you get yesterday back. It even bends around the islands of Kiribati, so the whole country shares one date.

levels.title: Compass and Directions
levels.objective: After this level you can use the cardinal directions and explain how a compass finds north.
levels.summary: North, east, south and west come from Earth's spin. A compass needle lines up with Earth's magnetic field, but magnetic north isn't true north.

cards.headline: Your compass doesn't point to the North Pole.
cards.body: It points somewhere nearby, and that somewhere keeps moving. The needle isn't broken. It's just loyal to a different north.

cards.headline: Directions for free, courtesy of the Sun
cards.body: North, east, south and west are the four cardinal directions, and east and west sit at right angles to north and south. The sky gives you a rough version for free: Earth spins toward the east, so the Sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west. Face the sunrise and north is on your left. Handy, but only roughly right, and no help at midnight.
cards.callout: N · E · S · W

cards.headline: A needle that feels the planet
cards.body: A compass needle is a tiny magnet, and Earth behaves like a giant one. Let the needle swing freely and it lines up with Earth's magnetic field. That's the big upgrade over the Sun: it works at noon or midnight, under clear skies or thick clouds. You're holding a sensor for the whole planet's magnetism in your palm.

cards.headline: Two norths
cards.body: Here's the catch. The Geographic North Pole sits at 90° N, the top of every meridian. The North Magnetic Pole is somewhere else, and it drifts over time. Your compass follows the magnetic one, so it's usually off from true north by an angle called magnetic declination. That angle changes depending on where you stand, so navigators look it up and correct for it.

levels.title: Reading the Land
levels.objective: After this level you can read elevation on a map and name landforms like plateaus, valleys and deltas.
levels.summary: Heights are measured above sea level, and contour lines join points of equal height. Plateaus, valleys and deltas are three landforms to spot.

cards.headline: A flat sheet of paper can show you how steep a mountain is.
cards.body: No shading, no 3D glasses. Just a bunch of wiggly lines, if you know how to read them.

cards.headline: Every height starts at the sea
cards.body: Every height on a map needs a zero, and the usual zero is mean sea level. So when you hear that Mount Everest, the world's highest mountain, stands about 8,849 m tall, that means 8,849 m above the sea. Your hometown has a number like that, too. It's just less likely to be on a postcard.

cards.headline: Lines that never go up or down
cards.body: A topographic map draws contour lines, each one joining points at the same elevation. Walk along one and you'd never climb or descend. The trick is the spacing: lines bunched close together mean the ground rises fast, a steep slope. Lines spread far apart mean gentle ground. A cliff looks like a traffic jam of lines.

levels.title: Continents and Oceans by Size
levels.objective: After this level you can rank the seven continents and five oceans by size.
levels.summary: Asia is the biggest continent and Australia the smallest. The Pacific is the biggest ocean, larger than all land combined; the Arctic is the smallest.

cards.headline: Every continent could fit inside the Pacific Ocean at once.
cards.body: All seven of them from Level 1, packed together, and the Pacific would still have room. Time to rank the whole planet.

cards.headline: The land league table
cards.body: Line the continents up by size and Asia wins easily, holding almost a third of the world's land. Next come Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica and Europe. Australia comes last: the smallest continent, and the flattest one, too. Last place, but it still gets to be a whole continent.
cards.callout: Asia › Africa › North America › South America › Antarctica › Europe › Australia

cards.fact: The Pacific covers about a third of Earth's surface.
cards.context: It's the largest and deepest ocean, and its area beats all the land on Earth combined. Then come the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern and, smallest of all, the Arctic. Remember, they're really one connected ocean. The Pacific just claims the biggest share.

cards.headline: Don't trust the wall map
cards.body: On a Mercator map, Antarctica looks gigantic. In the real ranking it's fifth, behind Asia, Africa and both Americas. Mercator inflates places the farther they are from the Equator, and Antarctica is about as far as you can get. When size is the question, trust the ranking, not the poster.

levels.title: How Your Phone Knows Where You Are
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how satellites let a phone pinpoint its location.
levels.summary: GPS satellites broadcast their position and time. Your phone times the signals, turns them into distances, and uses four satellites to find itself.

cards.headline: Your phone never tells GPS satellites where it is. It just listens.
cards.body: The satellites only broadcast; your phone does all the math itself. That's also why the service is free for anyone, anywhere.

cards.headline: A sky full of clocks
cards.body: About 20,200 km up, at least 24 GPS satellites circle Earth, each one twice a day. They're spread out so that from almost anywhere, at least four are in view. Each carries a very precise atomic clock and keeps repeating the same message: here's where I am, and here's exactly what time it is.

cards.headline: Time becomes distance
cards.body: Your phone notes when each message arrives. The signal travels at the speed of light, so the delay tells your phone how far away that satellite is. Know how far you are from three satellites, and there's enough information to work out where you are. It's like counting the seconds between lightning and thunder to judge how far away a storm is, only with radio waves and far better clocks.

cards.fact: It takes four satellites, not three.
cards.context: The satellites' clocks are superb; the one in your phone isn't. At light speed, a tiny timing slip turns into a big miss. So your phone uses a fourth satellite to correct its own clock. The answer comes out as latitude, longitude and altitude: Level 3's two numbers, plus your height.

cards.headline: GPS: decoded

levels.title: Checkpoint: Reading the Planet
levels.objective: After this level you can use maps, coordinates, directions and time zones together to describe where any place is.
levels.summary: A place's antipode is directly opposite through Earth's center: same latitude in the other hemisphere, 180° of longitude away, about 12 hours apart.

cards.headline: Dig straight down from the US. You won't reach China.
cards.body: Kids have been promised China for generations. Grab a shovel (a very long one), and let's check the claim with everything from Chapter 1.

cards.headline: The point exactly opposite
cards.body: Your antipode is the spot on the far side of Earth where a straight line through the center would pop out. Finding it takes Level 3's coordinates. Keep your latitude number but switch hemispheres, so north becomes south. Then go 180° of longitude around. Start from almost anywhere in the contiguous US and you surface in the Indian Ocean. Sorry, China.

cards.fact: Most of the world's land sits opposite ocean.
cards.context: Only about 15% of land has land on its far side. That's no shock after Level 1: about 71% of Earth's surface is water. Spain is one lucky exception. Most of New Zealand's North Island lies exactly opposite it.

cards.headline: Opposite in time, too
cards.body: Your antipode is 180° of longitude away, and Earth turns 15° an hour, so it's about 12 hours off from you. When it's noon where you stand, it's midnight there. Planning to call your antipode? One of you is going to be in pajamas.
