levels.title: Priests and Kings
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Egypt split between priests and kings.
levels.summary: After the New Kingdom, the high priests of Amun ruled the south from Thebes while kings ruled the north from Tanis. The priests also rescued robbed royal mummies.

cards.headline: After about 1069 BCE, kings ruled Egypt’s north and priests ran the south.
cards.body: The New Kingdom was over. Egypt didn’t fall; it split. And the most powerful man in the south wore a priest’s robes.

cards.headline: A priest takes the title
cards.body: Herihor was high priest of the god Amun at Karnak, in Thebes. Late in the 20th dynasty, as Egypt became disunited, he took the full title of a pharaoh and founded a line of priest-kings who ruled the south. Picture your local archbishop quietly adding “King” to his business card.

cards.headline: Two capitals
cards.body: In the 21st Dynasty the split settled in. Kings ruled Lower Egypt from Tanis, in the Delta, while the High Priests of Amun at Thebes grew more and more powerful. Remember Level 1’s valleys between the peaks? This is the third: the Third Intermediate Period, when the land was divided again. Later a Libyan leader, Shoshenq, founded a new dynasty at Tanis. The one who finally took all of Egypt would come from Kush, in the south.
cards.callout: North: kings at Tanis. South: priests at Thebes.

cards.headline: Rescuing the dead kings
cards.body: Meanwhile, the royal tombs at Thebes were being robbed. Priests and officials of the 21st Dynasty gathered damaged royal mummies, rewrapped them and hid several New Kingdom kings together in a secret cache at Deir el-Bahari. It worked: nobody found it until 1881. Among the kings inside was Ramesses II. Ramesses the Great, sharing a hiding place, saved by priests.

levels.title: The Nubian Pharaohs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the kings of Kush who ruled Egypt.
levels.summary: Kush, a Nubian kingdom south of Egypt, conquered Egypt in the 8th century BCE and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty. Driven out by Assyria, Kush lasted another thousand years.

cards.headline: In the 700s BCE, a kingdom from the south conquered Egypt.
cards.body: Many people have never heard of it. But Kush was no small neighbor. It was one of Africa’s earliest civilizations, and for nearly a century its kings ruled Egypt as pharaohs.

cards.headline: The kingdom up the river
cards.body: Kush was the southern part of Nubia, a region stretching south from near the Nile’s first cataract, in what is now Sudan. Remember Level 5’s rapids at Aswan, Egypt’s southern border? Kush lay beyond them, upstream. Its kings ruled from Napata, near Mount Barkal, and the cult of Egypt’s god Amun was strongly rooted there. Egypt’s new pharaohs would already know its gods.

cards.headline: Piye marches north
cards.body: In the 8th century BCE, King Piye marched into Egypt, ended its petty kingdoms and took Memphis. By about 715 BCE, under Piye and then Shabaka, all of Egypt was ruled from Kush. How do we know Piye’s side? He recorded his conquest on a great stone stela, found back home at Mount Barkal. The Kushite kings ruled as Egypt’s 25th Dynasty. The pharaohs now came from the south.

mascot.line: More pyramids than Egypt. Kush deserves a much bigger spot in the story.

cards.fact: Sudan has some 255 ancient pyramids, more than twice as many as Egypt built.
cards.context: Kushite kings were buried in pyramids. Their rule in Egypt ended after the Assyrians invaded in 671 BCE; by 654 BCE the Kushites were back in Nubia. But Kush didn’t fade. It lasted about another thousand years, later ruling from Meroe, until the king of Aksum destroyed Meroe in 350 CE. Losing Egypt was one chapter in Kush’s story, not the end.

levels.title: Persian Rule
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Persia conquered Egypt.
levels.summary: Persia’s Cambyses II conquered Egypt in 525 BCE and was crowned pharaoh. Egypt won back its independence in 404 BCE, but Persia returned in 343 BCE.

cards.headline: In 525 BCE, a Persian king put on the crown of the pharaohs.
cards.body: Kush had taken Egypt from the south. Now the Persian king Cambyses II took it, and he didn’t just seize the land. He took the job title too.

cards.headline: Crowned by the conqueror
cards.body: Cambyses II won the Battle of Pelusium in the Nile Delta, took Memphis, and Egyptian resistance collapsed. Then he had himself crowned as pharaoh. A later Persian king, Darius I, restored the priests’ privileges, had Egyptian law written down and completed or repaired a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea. Foreign rulers, wearing Egyptian titles.

mascot.line: When the writer is famous and the story is juicy, check it twice.

cards.headline: Don’t believe every travel writer
cards.body: Remember Herodotus from Level 2? His 5th-century BCE visit came while Egypt was Persian. He accused Cambyses of atrocities in Egypt and put them down to madness. But Egyptian sources from Cambyses’ own time suggest those accusations must largely be discounted. A famous writer with a great story still needs checking against the evidence.

cards.headline: The last native pharaoh
cards.body: Egypt rebelled near the end of Darius’s reign, and in 404 BCE it won its independence under Amyrtaeus of Sais. Egyptian kings ruled again, but not for long. The last of them, Nectanebo II, reigned from 360 until 343 BCE, when Persia reconquered Egypt. He fled south, and after that nothing more is known of him. The line of native pharaohs didn’t end with a funeral. It simply went quiet.

levels.title: Alexander in Egypt
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Alexander the Great took Egypt.
levels.summary: In 332 BCE Egypt welcomed Alexander the Great and the Persian satrap surrendered. Alexander was crowned at Memphis, hailed as son of Amun at Siwa, founded Alexandria and was buried there.

cards.headline: In 332 BCE, Egypt welcomed a foreign conqueror as its deliverer.
cards.body: Alexander the Great took Egypt without a real fight. Then he set about becoming a proper pharaoh.

cards.headline: No battle needed
cards.body: Egypt was still under Persian rule when Alexander, king of Macedonia, arrived in November 332 BCE. The Persian governor, the satrap Mazaces, surrendered, and the people welcomed Alexander as their deliverer. Picture tenants throwing a party for the new landlord. After Persia, the bar was low.

cards.headline: Playing pharaoh
cards.body: At Memphis, Alexander sacrificed to the sacred Apis bull and was crowned with the double crown of the pharaohs. Remember it from Level 6? White and red together: Upper and Lower Egypt under one king. Then he went to the oracle of Amun in the Siwa oasis, where the priest greeted him as “son of Amun,” the traditional greeting for a pharaoh. A Macedonian, hailed in the pharaohs’ own words.
cards.callout: Crowned at Memphis, greeted as son of Amun at Siwa

cards.headline: A city, and a body
cards.body: Alexander founded a new city near the Nile’s western arm, between the sea and Lake Mareotis, sheltered by the island of Pharos: Alexandria. He didn’t stay to see it grow. He died in Babylon in 323 BCE, and his general Ptolemy diverted his body to Egypt. It ended up in a golden coffin in Alexandria. Alive, Alexander left Egypt behind. Dead, he came back to stay.

levels.title: Alexandria
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Alexandria’s lighthouse and library.
levels.summary: Alexandria’s Pharos lighthouse was one of the Seven Wonders, and its library tried to collect every book in the world. The library faded slowly over centuries, not in one fire.

cards.headline: One city had antiquity’s most famous lighthouse and its most famous library.
cards.body: One burned a fire every night. The other, whatever you’ve heard, didn’t vanish in one great blaze.

cards.headline: A tower with a fire on top
cards.body: On the island of Pharos stood a lighthouse finished in about 280 BCE, one of the Seven Wonders of the World. It rose more than 110 metres; only the pyramids of Giza would have been taller. A spiral ramp led to the top, where a fire burned at night. It stood until an earthquake in the 1300s, and in 1477 a sultan, Qaitbay, built a fort from its ruins. Ancient recycling, on a grand scale.

cards.headline: All the books in the world
cards.body: Around 295 BCE, Ptolemy I had Demetrius of Phaleron found a library and the Mouseion, a research institute for scholars. The goal: all the books in the world. Ships entering Alexandria’s harbor were searched, and books found aboard were confiscated or copied for the collection. Imagine landing at an airport and having your paperback copied at customs.

mascot.line: Big fires make great stories. Slow neglect makes real history.

cards.headline: A slow goodbye, not one fire
cards.body: The popular story is one great fire. The evidence is messier. In 48 BCE, during Julius Caesar’s civil war, at least part of the library was damaged, yet scholars seem to have kept working there. Historians describe a slow decline through neglect and several blows over centuries, and they still debate the causes. A later tale blaming the Arab conquerors is, modern historians say, a myth. No single villain, no single night.

levels.title: The Ptolemies
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a Greek family ruled Egypt for 300 years.
levels.summary: Ptolemy, Alexander’s Macedonian general, founded a dynasty that ruled Egypt for almost 300 years. They appeared as pharaohs on temple walls while keeping their own Greek ways.

cards.headline: For almost 300 years, Egypt’s kings were Macedonian Greeks named Ptolemy.
cards.body: How does a foreign family hold a country that long? By being two kinds of ruler at once.

cards.headline: Ptolemy takes charge
cards.body: When Alexander died in 323 BCE, his Macedonian general Ptolemy became governor of Egypt, and in 305 BCE he proclaimed himself king. His dynasty ruled until 30 BCE. Naming the heirs was easy: the kings ran from Ptolemy I to Ptolemy XV. If you’ve ever lost track of which one is which, you’re in good company.

cards.headline: Two faces of one crown
cards.body: To their Egyptian subjects, the Ptolemies looked like proper pharaohs: they backed Egyptian temples and appeared on temple walls in the traditional pharaonic style. Ptolemy I also promoted Serapis, a god with Egyptian roots and Greek features, whose cult blended both religions. Remember Manetho from Level 9? He wrote his history of Egypt in Greek around 300 BCE, early in Ptolemaic rule.
cards.callout: Pharaohs on the temple walls, Greeks at home

cards.headline: Only one learned Egyptian
cards.body: Behind the temple images, the family kept its own ways. Ptolemy II married his full sister, Arsinoe II, and brother-sister marriage became a feature of the dynasty. And according to the ancient writer Plutarch, of all the Ptolemies only Cleopatra VII took the trouble to learn Egyptian. Nearly three centuries on the throne, and one ruler who could chat with Egyptians in their own language.

levels.title: Rome's Breadbasket
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Egypt became the grain supply of Rome.
levels.summary: From 30 BCE Egypt was the Roman emperor’s own province, closed to senators without permission. Its Nile-fed grain fed Rome for about four months a year.

cards.headline: For four months of every year, one ancient writer said, Rome ate Egyptian grain.
cards.body: No wonder the emperors kept Egypt on a very short leash.

cards.headline: The emperor’s own province
cards.body: In 30 BCE Egypt became a Roman province, but not an ordinary one. Octavian, the future emperor Augustus, treated it as his own private kingdom, as heir to the Ptolemies. A prefect he appointed ran it, and Roman senators were forbidden to visit without the emperor’s permission. Egypt wasn’t just conquered. It was fenced off.

cards.headline: Four months of bread
cards.body: Why the fuss? Grain. Egypt’s granaries now belonged to Rome, and Egypt became the empire’s breadbasket. The historian Josephus, writing in the 1st century CE, said Egypt sent Rome enough grain to feed it for four months of the year, on top of its tax money. Four months out of twelve: a third of the city’s year, from one province.
cards.callout: Egypt fed Rome a third of the year

mascot.line: Same river, same silt. Only the address on the grain sacks changed.

cards.headline: The Nile pays Rome’s bills
cards.body: Remember Level 2’s flood? Its silt was a natural fertilizer that let Egypt feed a dense population, and now Rome took the harvest. Josephus even noted that Egypt was walled round by near-impassable deserts and harborless seas, the defenses you met in Level 3, and still it submitted to Rome. The walls that guarded the pharaohs didn’t keep out the tax collector.

levels.title: The End of the Old Gods
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Christianity and later Islam replaced the old religion.
levels.summary: Christianity spread through Egypt, and the temples closed, the Serapeum in 391 CE and Philae under Justinian. After the Arab conquest of 640 to 642 CE, Egypt became Muslim gradually.

cards.headline: Egypt’s gods outlasted every conqueror. They didn’t outlast a change of faith.
cards.body: The old religion didn’t fall in one battle. It went quiet temple by temple, from the Serapeum in 391 CE to Philae in the 6th century.

cards.headline: A new faith
cards.body: Christianity, tradition says, was brought to Alexandria by St. Mark in the first half of the 1st century CE, and it spread quickly through Egypt. Egypt’s Christians came to be called Copts, and they spoke Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language. The old tongue lived on. It just had new prayers to say.

cards.headline: The temples close
cards.body: In 391 CE the patriarch of Alexandria and his followers destroyed the city’s Serapeum, the great temple of Serapis, with Emperor Theodosius I’s encouragement, and other temples fell too. One famous holdout was Isis’s temple on the island of Philae, where the last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in 394 CE. It wasn’t closed until Emperor Justinian’s reign, in the 6th century, and was then made into a church.
cards.callout: Serapeum destroyed 391 CE; Philae closed in the 6th century

cards.headline: Then, slowly, Islam
cards.body: Between 640 and 642 CE, Arab forces under ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ beat the Byzantine armies and entered Alexandria. Even then, change was slow. Egypt was mostly Christian at the conquest and became Muslim gradually over centuries; historians can’t pin down when Muslims became the majority. By the 12th century the Coptic church itself had adopted Arabic alongside Coptic. Faiths and languages rarely switch overnight.

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: Egypt beat the Sea Peoples and still came out weaker. It split between kings at Tanis and priests at Thebes, and outsiders stepped in: Kushites who worshipped Amun, a Persian crowned pharaoh, Alexander greeted as son of Amun, Ptolemies carved as pharaohs, Romans who shipped its grain home. Native kings returned only once, and Nectanebo II was the last. Libraries faded slowly and temples closed. The crown kept changing heads; the land kept feeding whoever wore it.

levels.title: Forgetting Hieroglyphs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how knowledge of hieroglyphs was lost.
levels.summary: The last known hieroglyphs were carved at Philae in 394 CE. Egyptians switched to a Greek-based alphabet, and later scholars like Horapollo misread the signs as symbols.

cards.headline: For more than 1,400 years, nobody on Earth could read a hieroglyph.
cards.body: The signs never went anywhere. They stayed carved on temple walls and tombs the whole time. What vanished was anyone who knew what they said. So how does a whole civilization’s writing get forgotten?

cards.headline: The last hieroglyph
cards.body: The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in 394 CE, at the Temple of Isis at Philae. That’s more than four centuries after Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE (remember the end of Level 1’s timeline?). The old script had outlived the pharaohs by a long way. Its final signs are roughly cut but still clear enough to read. There was just no one left to read them.

mascot.line: Same language, new letters. Hold on to Coptic: it comes back to help later in this chapter.

cards.headline: A new alphabet
cards.body: Why stop? As Christianity spread in Egypt, people dropped hieroglyphs for an adapted form of the Greek alphabet. The language itself lived on as Coptic, the final stage of Egyptian, written in Greek letters plus seven letters borrowed from demotic. So Egyptians kept speaking their ancestors’ language while the old signs fell silent. It’s like keeping your family’s recipes but losing the handwriting they were written in.

cards.headline: Reading riddles
cards.body: Without readers, people guessed. In the 5th century CE, a Greco-Egyptian scholar named Horapollo wrote the Hieroglyphica, explaining each sign as a symbol or an allegory. He couldn’t actually read hieroglyphs himself. Renaissance scholars loved his book anyway, and the idea stuck: hieroglyphs were picture riddles, not sounds. That one wrong idea kept the door locked until the 1820s.
cards.callout: Wrong assumption: pictures, not sounds

levels.title: The Rosetta Stone
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Rosetta Stone was found and why it mattered.
levels.summary: French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone in 1799. It carries one decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

cards.headline: In 1799, soldiers digging a fort’s foundations hit the key to a lost script.
cards.body: They were French troops of Napoleon’s campaign in Egypt, working near the port of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta. The broken slab they dug up was covered in writing, in three different scripts. That was the whole point.

cards.headline: One message, three scripts
cards.body: The stone carries the same decree three times. First in hieroglyphs. Then in demotic, the everyday Egyptian handwriting. Then in ancient Greek, the language of Egypt’s Macedonian Greek rulers. Nobody could read the first two, but scholars could still read Greek. So here was a lost script with a translation stapled on. Picture a menu printed in a language you can’t read, right beside one you can.
cards.callout: Hieroglyphs + demotic + Greek = one message

mascot.line: The key to a whole lost script is, word for word, a bit of priestly paperwork.

cards.headline: What it actually says
cards.body: Don’t expect a treasure map. The decree was issued in 196 BCE by priests of a temple in Memphis, confirming the Macedonian king Ptolemy V as a divine ruler. It’s official temple business. The words were never the exciting part. The exciting part was hearing the same thing said three ways.

cards.headline: From Rashid to London
cards.body: The French didn’t keep their find. After the French surrender in Egypt in 1801, the stone passed to the British. It has been on display in the British Museum since 1802, leaving only once, when it was moved to safety during the First World War. Whether it should stay there is a live argument, and it gets its own level later in this chapter.

levels.title: Champollion Cracks the Code
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Champollion deciphered hieroglyphs.
levels.summary: Thomas Young read the sounds of Ptolemy’s name; in 1822 Champollion showed that hieroglyphs mix sound signs with signs for ideas.

cards.headline: In 1822, a scholar burst in on his brother, cried “I’ve got it!” and fainted.
cards.body: In French, he said “Je tiens mon affaire!” The scholar was Jean-François Champollion, and what he’d got was the key to hieroglyphs. But he wasn’t the first to get a foot in the door. An English scientist had already shown that some signs spelled the sounds of a name.

cards.headline: Thomas Young’s head start
cards.body: Thomas Young was an English physicist, also famous for his work on light, who began studying the Rosetta Stone in 1814. He showed that some hieroglyphs on the stone spelled out the sounds of a royal name: Ptolemy. He also made major advances in reading demotic. That was a real crack in the wall. Most of the wall was still standing.

mascot.line: Sometimes the breakthrough isn’t a flash of genius. It’s just counting carefully.

cards.headline: Too many signs
cards.body: Champollion tried counting. The hieroglyphic text on the Rosetta Stone uses 1,419 signs, while the Greek version has only 486 words. If every sign were a whole idea, those numbers should be much closer. So many signs had to stand for sounds, mixed with others that stood for whole ideas or objects. Hieroglyphs weren’t picture riddles after all. They were writing down a spoken language.
cards.callout: 1,419 signs for 486 words: too many for pictures alone

cards.headline: Not just foreign names
cards.body: Maybe sound signs were only a trick for foreign names like Ptolemy? Champollion knew Coptic, the last stage of Egyptian, which helped him hear the sounds behind the signs. With it he read the name of Ramesses, a native Egyptian king. Egyptians had been writing sounds all along. On 27 September 1822 he announced it in Paris, with Thomas Young in the audience. The door locked since 394 CE was open.

levels.title: Egyptomania
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the craze for all things Egyptian in Europe.
levels.summary: Napoleon’s scholars and their Description de l’Égypte, then Champollion’s decipherment, set off Egyptomania: Egyptian-style buildings and real obelisks shipped to London and New York.

cards.headline: Napoleon invaded Egypt with an army and about 150 artists and scientists.
cards.body: The army’s campaign ended in surrender. The scholars did better: they helped set off a craze for ancient Egypt that swept Europe and America.

cards.headline: A country in picture books
cards.body: The 1798 invasion doubled as the first large-scale scientific expedition to Egypt. The scholars measured and drew everything they could. Back in France, their record became the Description de l’Égypte, published from 1809 with huge prints of pyramids, temples and other antiquities. For readers at home, it was like having Egypt delivered to the library in giant installments.

mascot.line: Next time you see an Egyptian-style gate or column far from Egypt, you’ve spotted a bit of Egyptomania.

cards.headline: Egyptomania
cards.body: Then came Champollion’s decipherment in 1822 (Level 93), and interest surged again. The craze got a name: Egyptomania. Architects mined the Description for Egyptian designs. In the United States the first wave was mostly buildings, including cemetery architecture and the Washington Monument, begun in 1848. Some of that craze is still standing in Washington.

cards.headline: Cleopatra’s Needles
cards.body: Some people wanted the real thing. Two granite obelisks, carved about 3,500 years ago for Thutmose III, were given away by Egypt’s government: one was raised in London in 1878, the other in New York’s Central Park in 1881. They’re called Cleopatra’s Needles because the Romans moved them to Alexandria, to a temple conceived by Cleopatra. They were already more than a thousand years old in her day.
cards.callout: Named for Cleopatra, carved for Thutmose III

levels.title: Finding Tutankhamun
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Howard Carter's discovery in 1922.
levels.summary: Funded by Lord Carnarvon, Howard Carter found Tutankhamun’s largely intact tomb in November 1922 and spent about ten years recording its 5,398 objects.

cards.headline: By 1922, the man paying for the dig was ready to give up.
cards.body: Lord Carnarvon had funded Howard Carter’s digging for years with little to show for it. Carter talked him into one final season. It began on 1 November 1922, and three days later, a step appeared.

cards.headline: A step under a hut
cards.body: On 4 November, Carter’s team found a step cut into the bedrock beneath the remains of ancient workmen’s huts, about four metres below the entrance of Ramesses VI’s tomb. Soon they had exposed a sealed doorway. Carter covered it back up and cabled Carnarvon in England: “At last have made wonderful discovery in Valley.” The tomb had spent centuries under a building site.

mascot.line: Even the most famous line in archaeology got a second draft.

cards.headline: Wonderful things
cards.body: On 26 November, with Carnarvon beside him, Carter made a small hole in a second sealed doorway, stamped with Tutankhamun’s seals, and held up a candle. Carnarvon asked if he could see anything. That night Carter’s journal recorded his reply: “Yes, it is wonderful.” His later popular account polished it into the line everyone quotes: “Yes, wonderful things.”

cards.headline: Ten years of homework
cards.body: The tomb was largely intact, the first known intact royal burial from ancient Egypt. Carter’s team numbered its 5,398 objects and spent about ten years clearing and recording them. Their notes, photographs and drawings are kept at the Griffith Institute in Oxford. The gold made the headlines. The paperwork made it science.

levels.title: Studying Egypt Today
levels.objective: After this level you can describe modern tools like scans and satellite images.
levels.summary: Muon detectors find hidden spaces in the Great Pyramid, CT scans unwrap mummies digitally, and infrared satellite images reveal buried mud-brick buildings.

cards.headline: Archaeologists can now look inside a pyramid without moving a single block.
cards.body: They can unwrap a pharaoh without touching a thread, and spot buried buildings from orbit. Egypt is still giving up secrets. What’s changed is the tools.

cards.headline: An X-ray lit by the sky
cards.body: Muons are particles made when cosmic rays hit our atmosphere, and they rain down constantly. Stone absorbs some of them, so detectors can map empty spaces inside a pyramid. In 2017 the ScanPyramids team reported a big void at least 30 metres long above the Great Pyramid’s Grand Gallery. In 2023, muons located a corridor about 9 metres long behind the north face, and a camera pushed inside confirmed it.

mascot.line: No scissors, no unrolling: just a scanner and a lot of patience.

cards.headline: Unwrapping without unwrapping
cards.body: Amenhotep I’s mummy was so finely wrapped, with flower garlands and a lifelike mask, that no one opened it in modern times. In 2021, radiologist Sahar Saleem and Egyptologist Zahi Hawass unwrapped it digitally with CT scans. Inside was a man about 35 years old, with good teeth and 30 amulets tucked into his wrappings. The mask stayed on. The secrets came out.

cards.headline: Archaeology from orbit
cards.body: Sarah Parcak of the University of Alabama at Birmingham processes satellite images to see in infrared, which your eyes can’t. In the desert, it picks up moisture differences in the ground above buried mud bricks, tracing the outlines of vanished buildings. Her team mapped the street grid of Tanis, once a capital in the Nile Delta, and tracked tomb looting after 2011. Some of the best new digging starts with no digging at all.

levels.title: Who Owns the Past?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain debates over returning ancient objects to Egypt.
levels.summary: Zahi Hawass wants the Rosetta Stone and Nefertiti bust returned; the museums in London and Berlin defend how they got them. Egypt opened the Grand Egyptian Museum in 2025.

cards.headline: The Rosetta Stone has sat in London since 1802. Many want it back.
cards.body: Who should keep objects taken from Egypt long ago? It’s a real argument, and both sides have reasons. Here are both cases, who makes them, and one very large new building.

cards.headline: The case for return
cards.body: In 2022, Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, launched a petition for the Rosetta Stone’s return that passed 100,000 signatures. He also wants the bust of Nefertiti back from Berlin and the Dendera Zodiac from the Louvre, saying these unique objects belong in Egypt. On Nefertiti he goes further: he argues the bust, found in 1912 and taken to Berlin in 1913, left Egypt illegally.

mascot.line: When two sides tell the same story differently, it helps to know exactly who is saying what.

cards.headline: The museums’ case
cards.body: The British Museum says the Rosetta Stone came to Britain under an 1801 treaty signed by a representative of Egypt. It adds that Egypt’s government has made no formal request, and that most known copies of the decree are already in Egypt. Berlin’s museum points out that the Nefertiti bust left through an official division of finds in 1913, overseen by an inspector of Egypt’s antiquities service. Same objects, very different stories.

cards.headline: A new home by the pyramids
cards.body: Egypt has also made its point in concrete. The Grand Egyptian Museum, near the Great Pyramid at Giza, officially opened on 1 November 2025 with about 100,000 artifacts. For the first time since its discovery, Tutankhamun’s entire collection is shown together. Remember Carter’s 5,398 numbered objects from Level 95? They’re finally all in one place.

levels.title: Myths About Egypt
levels.objective: After this level you can debunk common myths, like aliens building the pyramids.
levels.summary: Paid workers, not slaves, built the Giza pyramids; Merer’s logbook shows human crews at work; the curse and Cleopatra’s looks rest on thin evidence.

cards.headline: Ancient Egypt collects myths the way a pyramid collects sand.
cards.body: Take the famous curse on Tutankhamun’s tomb: Howard Carter, the man who opened it in 1922, lived until 1939. Some myths started with ancient writers, and some with Hollywood. The fix is always the same: check the evidence.

cards.headline: Myth: slaves built the pyramids
cards.body: The picture of whipped slaves comes from Herodotus (yes, Level 2’s “gift of the river” man), misreadings of the Bible’s book of Exodus, and Hollywood films. The ground tells another story. Near the Giza pyramids, archaeologists found workers’ districts with bakeries and workshops, and workers’ tombs close to the pyramids, some naming the dead. Most archaeologists now think paid laborers built them.

mascot.line: The best answer to a wild theory is often a very boring document.

cards.headline: Myth: aliens did it
cards.body: The builders left paperwork. In 2013, archaeologists at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea found the oldest known inscribed papyri, including the logbook of an official named Merer. His crew shipped limestone by boat from the Tura quarries to Giza for Khufu’s pyramid, and he logged the work in half-day entries. Aliens, as far as anyone knows, don’t fill in timesheets.

cards.headline: Myth: we know Cleopatra’s face
cards.body: People argue hotly about Cleopatra’s looks, but the evidence is thin. She belonged to a Macedonian Greek dynasty, yet even her mother’s identity is uncertain, and her coins and portrait busts don’t all agree. Plutarch, writing long after, said her beauty was “not altogether incomparable,” but that talking with her had “an irresistible charm.” Egypt’s most famous face is one of its least certain.

levels.title: Egypt's Legacy
levels.objective: After this level you can name what the modern world still owes to ancient Egypt.
levels.summary: Our calendar descends from Egypt’s solar calendar via Julius Caesar, the letter A from an ox-head sign, and the word paper from papyrus.

cards.headline: You use ancient Egypt daily: in your calendar, your alphabet and your paper.
cards.body: Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE, but pieces of it never left. Here are three hiding in plain sight.

cards.headline: Your calendar
cards.body: In 46 BCE, Julius Caesar reformed Rome’s calendar by adopting the Egyptian solar calendar, advised by Sosigenes, an astronomer from Alexandria. The year became 365 and a quarter days, with an extra day every fourth year. Pope Gregory XIII fine-tuned it in 1582, and his Gregorian calendar gradually replaced Caesar’s. Every leap day has an Egyptian ancestor.
cards.callout: Egypt, then Caesar, then Gregory, then your wall

mascot.line: A for ox. Once you see the horns, you can’t unsee them.

cards.headline: Your alphabet
cards.body: Look at the letter A. The inventors of the alphabet were influenced by Egyptian writing, and A goes back to a sign shaped like an ox’s head. Early Semitic writing in Sinai adopted it around 1500 BCE. The Phoenicians called it aleph, meaning “ox,” and the Greeks renamed it alpha and used it for a vowel. Turn a capital A upside down and imagine the horns.

cards.headline: Your paper
cards.body: The word “paper” comes from papyrus, the Egyptian writing material. The Greeks adopted papyrus, and the Roman Empire used it widely. Books and documents on papyrus were still being made, now and then, until about the 12th century. So whenever you ask for a sheet of paper, you’re naming an Egyptian invention.

levels.title: Ancient Greece in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the main eras of ancient Greece from the Bronze Age to Roman rule.
levels.summary: Greek history runs from Bronze Age palaces (to about 1200 BCE) through a Dark Age, the Archaic, Classical and Hellenistic ages, to Roman rule.

cards.headline: Ancient Greece wasn’t one moment. It was a relay race of eras.
cards.body: Palace kingdoms, a dark age, city-states and colonies, then Rome. Here’s the whole track before we run it lap by lap.

events.label: Bronze Age: palace kingdoms on Crete, then on the mainland
Dark Age: the palace kingdoms are gone

Classical age, ending with Alexander the Great’s death
Hellenistic age: Greek kingdoms, until Rome takes Egypt

cards.headline: The famous part came late
cards.body: Picture ancient Greece and you probably see the Classical age, 480 to 323 BCE: the Greece of the postcards. But the Bronze Age palaces had fallen roughly 700 years before it began. So that famous stretch is less than 160 years of a story that runs for well over a thousand. It’s like summing up your whole family history with last summer’s vacation photos.

cards.fact: Rome conquered mainland Greece in 146 BCE.
cards.context: That year a Roman army defeated the Greek Achaean League and destroyed the city of Corinth. The Greek kingdoms farther east held out a little longer: the last, Egypt, fell to Rome in 30 BCE. That’s the finish line. This chapter starts back at the very beginning, with palaces, myths and memory.

levels.title: Mountains and Sea
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how mountains and the sea shaped Greek life.
levels.summary: Mountains cover about four-fifths of Greece and split communities apart, while the sea was never far off and became the easiest road.

cards.headline: In Greece, the sea is never far away. Your neighbors often were.
cards.body: Mountains made the walk next door hard work, and the sea opened the way to far-off places. That odd combination shaped Greek life.

cards.headline: A land of mountains
cards.body: Mountains cover about four-fifths of Greece. They made travel over land hard, so communities in separate valleys grew up apart and developed independently. Athens and Thebes sit less than 100 km (60 miles) apart, yet they came to see each other as foreign rivals. Imagine the next town over treating you like a foreigner. In Greece, that was normal.

cards.headline: Never far from the sea
cards.body: Now look at the coastline. Arms of the sea reach so deep into the land that only a small wedge of the interior is more than 80 km (50 miles) from the coast. Today’s Greece also counts more than 2,000 islands. Mountains blocked travel over land, but the sea opened up wider horizons. For a Greek, the easiest road was usually water.

cards.fact: Only about one-fifth of Greece is lowland.
cards.context: Lowland is the best farmland, and in Greece there was never much of it. Picture a town boxed in by mountains, with only a small patch of good fields. Hold on to that picture: it comes back in Level 9.

levels.title: The Minoans
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the palace culture of Minoan Crete.
levels.summary: Arthur Evans dug Knossos on Crete from 1900, named its Bronze Age builders Minoans after King Minos, and rebuilt parts of the palace in concrete.

cards.headline: Greek myth put a monster in a maze on Crete. In 1900, a man went digging.
cards.body: He found a palace instead, and he gave a lost civilization the name it still goes by.

cards.headline: The palace at Knossos
cards.body: The myth: King Minos of Crete kept the Minotaur, half man and half bull, in a Labyrinth built by Daedalus. In 1900 the British archaeologist Arthur Evans began digging at Knossos, on Crete, and uncovered a great palace. Its twisting maze of rooms and corridors led some archaeologists to link it with the Labyrinth, though many now doubt it. A maze-like palace, right where the myth put the maze: you can see why the idea stuck.

cards.headline: Named after a myth
cards.body: Evans named the people who built the palace Minoans, after the legendary King Minos. The name is his, not theirs. Their own writing, a script called Linear A, has never been deciphered, so their records can’t speak for them. A whole civilization goes by a nickname borrowed from Greek myth.

cards.headline: A culture of sea and color
cards.body: The Minoans flourished on Crete from about 3000 BCE to about 1100 BCE. They traded across the Aegean and with Egypt and the Levant; remember Level 2’s sea road? Their palace walls were painted with dancing, sports and dolphins. By the mid-15th century BCE their palace culture was in decline, as influence from mainland Greece grew. Hold that thought for Level 4.

mascot.line: Ancient palace, modern concrete. Even ruins can get a renovation.

cards.headline: Rebuilt in concrete
cards.body: From the 1920s, Evans’s team rebuilt parts of the palace in reinforced concrete, and his artists completed its wall paintings from fragments. The philosopher R. G. Collingwood joked that the rebuilt architecture seemed to consist of garages and public lavatories. So walk Knossos with care: part of what you see is ancient, and part is Evans’s best guess.

levels.title: The Mycenaeans
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Mycenaean warrior kingdoms.
levels.summary: Mycenaean kings ruled from fortified palaces; their Linear B tablets, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952, are the oldest written Greek.

cards.headline: The oldest Greek anyone can read turned out to be paperwork.
cards.body: No songs of heroes, just palace records. Cracking them in 1952 still changed what we know about early Greece.

cards.headline: Warrior kings of the mainland
cards.body: On the Greek mainland, the Bronze Age belonged to the Mycenaeans. Their kings ruled from fortified palaces at places like Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns. The walls were built of stones so huge that later Greeks called them Cyclopean, believing only the one-eyed giants, the Cyclopes, could have moved them. When people credit your walls to giants, you built well.

cards.headline: A mask for a king who wasn’t there
cards.body: In 1876 Heinrich Schliemann dug into a grave at Mycenae and found a gold funerary mask. He believed it belonged to Agamemnon, the king of Mycenae who, in legend, led the Greeks against Troy. It doesn’t: the mask dates to about 1550–1500 BCE, roughly 300 years before Agamemnon would have lived, if he existed. The name stuck anyway. It’s still the Mask of Agamemnon.

cards.headline: Cracking Linear B
cards.body: The Mycenaean palaces kept records on clay tablets in a script called Linear B. In 1952 a British architect, Michael Ventris, working with John Chadwick, deciphered it and showed it was an early form of Greek: the oldest known written Greek. The tablets, from about 1400 to 1200 BCE, were used to run the palaces, mostly as inventories. The oldest Greek you can read is, basically, a stockroom list.

cards.fact: Linear B tablets turned up at Knossos, too.
cards.context: They were found on Crete as well as at Pylos, Mycenae and other mainland palaces. Remember Level 3’s Minoans, declining as influence from the mainland grew? Records in Greek inside the palace of Minos fit that story.

levels.title: The Trojan War
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what legend and archaeology tell us about Troy.
levels.summary: Legend tells of a ten-year siege of Troy. Troy was real, at Hisarlik in Turkey, and Troy VIIa fell around 1200 BCE, but the war as told may be legend.

cards.headline: Was the Trojan War real? Troy was. The war is a harder question.
cards.body: First the legend, then what the spades found, and then where the two meet.

cards.headline: The story Greeks told
cards.body: In legend, Paris, a prince of Troy, took Helen, the wife of Menelaus. A Greek army led by Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, sailed after them and besieged Troy for ten years. Later Greek writers dated the war to the 12th or 13th century BCE. It’s the ultimate family feud: one runaway couple, ten years of war.

cards.fact: The wooden horse isn’t in the Iliad.
cards.context: Homer’s great war poem never shows it. The horse is mentioned in the Odyssey and told in full in Virgil’s Aeneid. The most famous trick of the Trojan War is missing from the most famous poem about it.

cards.headline: Digging for Troy
cards.body: Troy was real. Its ruins lie at Hisarlik, in northwestern Turkey near the Dardanelles. Frank Calvert dug there first and persuaded Heinrich Schliemann, who excavated on a large scale from 1870. Schliemann was sure Homer’s Troy lay at the bottom of the mound. But the mound holds nine main layers, Troy I to Troy IX, and the gold he called “Priam’s Treasure” came from Troy II, about a thousand years too early.

mascot.line: A real place, a real fire, and a story that grew in the telling. That’s a lot of legends!

cards.headline: So, was it real?
cards.body: Scholars point to Troy VI or Troy VIIa as the city behind the legend, and Troy VIIa was destroyed around 1200 BCE, close to where later Greeks placed the war. Still, archaeology suggests a conflict on the scale of Homer’s ten-year siege may never have happened. The honest answer: a real city, a real destruction, and a legend wrapped around them whose size nobody can confirm.

levels.title: Homer
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Homer's Iliad and Odyssey and why Greeks learned them by heart.
levels.summary: The Iliad covers weeks of the Trojan War; the Odyssey, a ten-year journey home. They were the core of Greek education, and who composed them is still debated.

cards.headline: A dinner guest in ancient Greece could recite all of Homer. His dad made him.
cards.body: In Xenophon’s Symposium, Niceratus says his father had him learn the Iliad and Odyssey by heart so he’d grow up to be a good man. Why these two poems?

cards.headline: Two epics, two journeys
cards.body: The Iliad covers just a few weeks in the final year of the Trojan War. It centers on the anger of Achilles and ends with the funeral of Hector, before Troy falls. The Odyssey follows Odysseus, king of Ithaca, who spends 10 years trying to get home after the war. One poem is about a war that won’t end; the other is about a man who can’t get home.

cards.headline: Greece’s textbook
cards.body: For Greeks, these were far more than stories. Homer’s epics were the basis of Greek education and culture throughout the Classical age. That’s why Niceratus’s father set the whole of Homer as homework. If you wanted your son to grow up good, Homer was the textbook.

cards.headline: Who was Homer?
cards.body: Homer is thought to have lived in the 9th or 8th century BCE, if he was a single poet at all. That’s the Homeric question, and it’s still open. Some scholars think one poet composed both epics; others think many people retold and revised them. Either way, the poems grew out of a centuries-old oral tradition: singers inherited phrases, scenes and plots and reshaped them each time they performed.

cards.headline: Singing without writing
cards.body: In the 1930s the scholar Milman Parry showed how that could work. Homer repeats set phrases such as “swift-footed Achilles”: building blocks a singer could use while composing on the spot. In Yugoslavia, Parry recorded singers, including one who could not read, performing an epic about as long as the Odyssey. No page, no problem.

levels.title: The Greek Dark Age
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happened after the Bronze Age palaces fell.
levels.summary: Around 1200 BCE the Mycenaean palaces fell in a wider collapse with debated causes. Writing was lost and population fell, but Lefkandi shows life went on.

cards.headline: Around 1200 BCE, the palaces fell and Greece stopped writing.
cards.body: For about four centuries, no written records survive. So what brought the palaces down, and how do we know anything about the silence that followed?

cards.headline: A whole world breaks
cards.body: The fall wasn’t only Greek. Around 1200 BCE, collapse swept the eastern Mediterranean: the Mycenaean palaces fell, and so did the great Hittite Empire. The suspects include earthquakes, drought and raiders known as the Sea Peoples. No single cause explains it all, so many historians picture several blows landing at once. Think dominoes: you don’t need one giant push if every piece is already wobbling.

cards.headline: Why “dark”?
cards.body: Remember Level 4? Linear B was palace bookkeeping. With the palaces gone, writing was lost, and no written accounts from the next centuries survive. Population fell, and many settlements were abandoned. Even the metal changed: bronze needed long-distance trade, but iron could be mined in Greece, so iron came to replace it. “Dark” mostly means we can’t read about this age.

cards.headline: A light in the dark
cards.body: At Lefkandi, on the island of Euboea, archaeologists found a grave from about 1000 BCE that is rich by the standards of any period. Inside a large building lay gold and a bronze vessel from Cyprus. Somebody in the “Dark Age” had overseas connections and serious wealth. That’s why historians now think the age was less dark than once believed: Greek culture and trade carried on.

levels.title: The Greek Alphabet
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Greeks adapted the Phoenician alphabet.
levels.summary: Greeks borrowed the Phoenician alphabet by the 8th century BCE and turned five consonant letters into vowels. It’s the ancestor of European alphabets.

cards.headline: Try reading this: THS SNTNC HS N VWLS.
cards.body: You probably managed, with a little guessing. The alphabet the Greeks borrowed worked like that: no vowels. They fixed it.

cards.headline: Letters from the Phoenicians
cards.body: In the 8th century BCE at the latest, and probably earlier, the Greeks borrowed an alphabet from the Phoenicians, whom they met through trade. It had letters only for consonants; readers filled in the vowels themselves. Remember Level 7? Greece had lost writing when the palaces fell. Now writing came back, by way of the traders.

cards.headline: Old letters, new jobs
cards.body: The Greeks’ big change was vowels. They took five Phoenician consonant letters and gave them new jobs: aleph became alpha, he became epsilon, yod became iota, ayin became omicron and waw became upsilon. Even the name survives: alphabet comes from alpha and beta, which go back to Phoenician aleph, “ox”, and beth, “house”. Every time you say alphabet, you’re saying “ox, house”.

mascot.line: New letters, and the first thing we know of is a dance-off prize. My kind of people!

cards.headline: A prize for the best dancer
cards.body: The earliest datable Greek alphabet inscriptions, from about 725 BCE, come from Athens and from a Greek colony on Ischia, an island off Italy. The one from Athens is scratched on a wine jug, and it names the jug as a prize for the best dancer. So one of the first things Greeks wrote in their new letters was a party trophy.

cards.fact: You’re reading the Greek alphabet’s descendants right now.
cards.context: The Greek alphabet is the direct or indirect ancestor of all modern European alphabets, including the Latin letters of this sentence and Cyrillic.

levels.title: Colonies Around the Sea
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Greeks founded colonies from Spain to the Black Sea.
levels.summary: From the 8th to the 6th century BCE, Greeks short of land and resources founded independent colonies, from Marseille to the Black Sea.

cards.headline: Plato said people lived around the sea “like ants or frogs about a pond.”
cards.body: He meant his world, from Gibraltar to the Black Sea, and he had a point: Greek towns ringed the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. How did the frogs get all the way around the pond?

cards.headline: Why leave home?
cards.body: From the 8th to the 6th century BCE, Greeks founded new cities along the coasts of the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. Why go? Remember Level 2’s thin slice of lowland: as populations grew, towns ran short of farmland. Greece also lacked metals, timber and grain, and quarrels at home pushed people out. Trade usually came first, and settlers followed.

cards.headline: A new city, not a branch office
cards.body: A colony was founded by a mother city, but it didn’t take orders from it. Colonies were politically independent, though they modeled themselves on the cities that founded them. Think of a grown child moving out: same family habits, own front door.

cards.headline: From Sicily to France
cards.body: Corinth founded Syracuse, on Sicily, in 733 BCE. Greeks from Phocaea founded Massalia about 600 BCE; today it’s Marseille. So many Greek cities rose along southern Italy’s coast that the region was called Magna Graecia, “Great Greece”. The first, on the island of Ischia and at Cumae, date to about 750 BCE. Ischia? That’s where Level 8’s early inscription turned up.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Myth and Memory
levels.objective: After this level you can connect the land, the Bronze Age and Homer into the story of early Greece.
levels.summary: Myths and Homer kept memories of the Bronze Age alive; archaeology and Linear B let us test them, from Knossos and Mycenae to Troy.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: Greeks kept their past in song. We check it with spades.
cards.body: Myths, epics, tablets and trenches. Put them side by side and early Greece comes into focus.

cards.headline: A memory in a helmet
cards.body: Here’s how a story can carry a real memory. The Iliad describes a helmet covered in boar’s tusks. Archaeologists have found helmets like that in Mycenaean-era graves, from centuries before Homer. The palaces burned and writing was lost, but a piece of Bronze Age gear survived in song. Mycenaean culture left a lasting mark on later Greek myth and epic.

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: Put Chapter 1 together. Mountains split Greece apart, and the sea opened it up. Palace kingdoms rose on Crete and then on the mainland, keeping records on clay. Around 1200 BCE they fell, and writing went with them. Singers kept the old stories alive in performance, until an alphabet borrowed from the Phoenicians let Greeks write again, and colonists carried Greek cities around the sea.

levels.title: The Polis
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a Greek city-state was.
levels.summary: A polis was an independent town plus its countryside; there were over a thousand, most of them small, and the word lives on in “politics”.

cards.headline: Ancient Greece had no capital city. It had more than a thousand cities.
cards.body: No single king, no one government, no national flag. So what exactly was a Greek city, and why were there so many?

cards.headline: A town with its farms attached
cards.body: The Greek word is polis, usually translated “city-state”. A polis was a town plus the countryside for some miles around, villages and all. Picture your town, the farms beyond it, and a line where the next town’s fields begin. Now give that town its own government. Each polis was independent of its neighbors, and the Greek city-states never formed a permanent union.

cards.headline: Small by design
cards.body: Scholars have catalogued 1,035 Greek city-states, out of some 1,500 in all. Most were tiny by our standards: several hundred to a couple of thousand people, closer to a big school than a big city. The island of Lesbos alone held five of them. Imagine five countries sharing one island, each sure it was the best.

cards.headline: Why so many?
cards.body: Remember Level 2? Mountains made travel hard, so communities in separate valleys grew up apart and independently. The polis emerged around 750 BCE and stayed the main way Greeks organized themselves until the Roman Empire. It still lives in your vocabulary: politics comes from Greek politikos, “of citizens”, from polis. Talk politics and you’re talking city-state business.

levels.title: Acropolis and Agora
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the high city and the marketplace.
levels.summary: A Greek town had a fortified high city, the acropolis, for refuge and temples, and an open agora for politics, trials, worship and trade.

cards.headline: Every Greek town had two hearts: one up high, one down low.
cards.body: One was for safety and the gods. The other was for shopping, arguing and gossip. Meet the acropolis and the agora.

cards.headline: The high city
cards.body: Acropolis means “high city”. It was the town’s fortified high ground: the place to run to when enemies came, and home to its chief temples. Some were old strongholds. Remember Level 4’s palace kings? The Mycenaeans built a palace on the Acropolis of Athens. Think of it as the town’s castle and cathedral rolled into one.

cards.headline: The meeting place
cards.body: Down below lay the agora, an open space where citizens met for nearly everything: worship, politics, trials, business and plain socializing. Covered colonnades called stoas often ran along its edges, some with shops inside. Town square, mall and courthouse, all at once. The word survives in agoraphobia, the fear of open spaces, coined in 1871 from agora.

mascot.line: A sign that speaks in the first person. Very polite, and very Greek.

cards.headline: A stone that talks
cards.body: How do we know where Athens’ Agora ended? The stones tell us, literally. Around 500 BCE, Athenians set marble boundary stones at its edges, inscribed “I am the boundary of the Agora.” No arrows, no fine print: just a rock introducing itself. Handy, if a little chatty.

levels.title: Kings, Tyrants and the Few
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the kinds of government in Greek cities.
levels.summary: Greek cities were ruled by kings, aristocrats, oligarchs or tyrants; a tyrant seized power but wasn’t necessarily cruel, like Cypselus of Corinth.

cards.headline: Corinth’s first tyrant ruled without a bodyguard.
cards.body: He was that popular. So why do we call him a tyrant? Because Greek words for government didn’t mean quite what ours do.

items.label: Rule by one
points: Monarchy: “rule of one”, like Level 4’s palace kings

cards.headline: What made a tyrant
cards.body: A king inherited power. A Greek tyrant seized it. In the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, tyrants took over many city-states by rallying people fed up with rule by a few aristocrats. The title didn’t automatically mean cruel: Greeks judged a tyrant by how he ruled. Even the word was an import, probably borrowed from Lydian, a language of Asia Minor.

cards.headline: The Corinth story
cards.body: In the 8th and early 7th centuries BCE, an aristocratic family, the Bacchiads, ruled Corinth, and they founded colonies including Syracuse. They also ruled violently. Around 657 BCE, Cypselus overthrew them, with popular support and a favorable oracle from Delphi. Then he governed without a bodyguard. Rule by the few, then rule by one: same city, new system.

levels.title: Citizens and Outsiders
levels.objective: After this level you can explain who counted as a citizen and who did not.
levels.summary: Citizenship came by birth; only men had political rights. Metics, free resident foreigners, paid a special tax, needed a sponsor and rarely became citizens.

cards.headline: You could live in a Greek city all your life and still be a foreigner.
cards.body: So could your children, and theirs. Paying taxes and working there didn’t make you belong. Birth did.

cards.headline: Citizens: born, not made
cards.body: A citizen belonged to the polis: he could vote, and he owed it taxes and military service. Citizenship normally came by birth to citizen parents, and outsiders were only rarely granted it, even after generations. Only men had political rights, though women still counted as citizens legally, socially and religiously. Membership ran in families, like a surname.

cards.headline: Metics: the neighbors who stayed
cards.body: Most Greek states had metics: free resident foreigners, including freed slaves. The word comes from metoikos, “one who has changed his residence”. Athens had the most. There a metic paid a yearly tax, 12 drachmas for a man, and needed a citizen sponsor. He couldn’t own land or a house without a special grant. The law protected metics, but they always stood a step outside.

cards.fact: Pasion, a former slave, became a great banker in Athens as a metic.
cards.context: He built his fortune in 4th-century BCE Athens, and the city later granted him citizenship. That was the rare exception: most metic families stayed metics, however long they lived there.

levels.title: Slavery in Greece
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the role of slavery in Greek cities.
levels.summary: Slaves, mostly war captives and people seized by raiders, were legal property and did every kind of work, worst of all in the mines; freed slaves became metics.

cards.headline: In some Greek cities, up to a third of the people were owned by someone else.
cards.body: The same city-states that prized the free citizen ran on enslaved labor. It’s the other half of the story, and it deserves to be told plainly.

cards.headline: How people were enslaved
cards.body: War was the main road into slavery: captives could be sold. Pirates and raiders seized non-Greeks to the north and east and sold them in Greece. Greeks enslaved Greeks defeated in war too, just not members of their own polis. Chattel slavery spread after about 600 BCE. By law a slave was property: Aristotle called a slave “a live article of property”.

cards.headline: Every kind of work
cards.body: Enslaved people cooked, cleaned, fetched water, farmed, and worked beside potters and metalworkers. The worst fate was the mines: narrow tunnels, prone to landslides. The silver mines at Laurium, in Athens’ territory, used as many as 30,000 slaves. Some slaves belonged to the city itself: in Athens, public slaves certified that the city’s coins were genuine.

cards.headline: Free, but not a citizen
cards.body: Some slaves did win their freedom. Remember Level 14’s metics? A freed slave joined them: free to live and work in the city, but still not a citizen. Pasion made that journey from slave to banker. Freedom was one border crossed. Citizenship was another border altogether.

levels.title: Hoplites and the Phalanx
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how armored citizens fought shoulder to shoulder.
levels.summary: Hoplites, citizens who bought their own armor, fought in a phalanx about eight ranks deep, each sheltering behind his neighbor’s shield.

cards.headline: Greek armies marching into battle drifted to the right. All of them.
cards.body: The historian Thucydides noticed it and explained why. The answer lies in how Greek citizens fought: packed together, shield beside shield.

cards.headline: The hoplite
cards.body: A hoplite was a heavily armed foot soldier: metal helmet, breastplate, greaves on his shins, a shield on his left forearm, a sword, and a thrusting spear about 2 m (6 ft) long. Hoplites appeared probably in the late 8th century BCE. Remember Level 14: citizens owed military service. Hoplites paid for their own gear, so only men of some property could serve.

cards.headline: The phalanx
cards.body: Hoplites marched shoulder to shoulder in a rectangular block called a phalanx, normally eight ranks deep. Holding the line was everything. The poet Archilochus, in the 7th century BCE, praised a soldier who is “a short man firmly placed upon his legs”, not to be uprooted from his spot. Forget solo heroics: this was teamwork with spears.

cards.headline: Why the drift?
cards.body: Here’s Thucydides’ answer. The shield sat on the left arm, so each man’s right side was exposed. Nervous, he edged right to shelter behind the shield of the man beside him, and the whole block crept sideways. Your safety depended on your neighbor, and his on you. Hard to picture a better lesson in being a citizen.

levels.title: Coins and Trade
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Greek cities began minting coins.
levels.summary: Coins began in Lydia; Greek cities then minted their own, each with its own emblem, and the obol and drachma recall older spit-money.

cards.headline: Greek pocket change started out as kitchen skewers.
cards.body: Before coins, Greeks used metal spits as money. Here’s how cities went from skewers to silver stamped with their own badges.

cards.headline: Born next door
cards.body: The first coins were made in Lydia, in Asia Minor, in the second half of the 7th century BCE. They were electrum, a mix of gold and silver. Remember Level 13’s tyrant, a word probably borrowed from Lydian? Money came from the same neighborhood. A lump of precious metal with an official stamp: simple, portable, and nothing to roast.

cards.headline: Skewers and handfuls
cards.body: The names remember what came before. The small coin called an obol takes its name from obelos, “spit”. Six obols made a drachma, a name that probably meant “a handful”, from a Greek word for grasp. So a drachma was, originally, a fistful of skewers. Your pocket change once doubled as a barbecue set.

mascot.line: From sea turtle to land tortoise. Even the coins had to slow down.

cards.headline: Money as a flag
cards.body: Each city-state stamped its own identity on its coins. Aegina’s silver showed a sea turtle, a symbol of its naval strength. Athens’ “owls” were struck from Laurium silver and circulated throughout the Classical world. Aegina’s later coins show a land tortoise, which the Art Institute of Chicago reads as sea power lost to Athens. And in Athens, public slaves checked that coins were genuine.

levels.title: The Olympic Games
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the ancient Olympics and the truce that protected them.
levels.summary: Every four years Greeks met at Olympia to honor Zeus; the first event was a single sprint, winners got olive wreaths, and a truce guaranteed safe travel.

cards.headline: The first Olympic champion on record was a cook.
cards.body: Coroebus of Elis won the sprint in 776 BCE. After that, Greeks from rival city-states met every four years to race, and, remarkably, to hold their fire.

cards.headline: One race to start
cards.body: The Games were held every four years at Olympia, a sanctuary of Zeus. At first there was a single event, the stadion: a sprint of one length of the track, about 192 m (210 yards). Yes, it gave us the word stadium. Winners got no money, just a wreath of wild olive leaves. Bragging rights did the rest.

cards.headline: Who got in
cards.body: The Games were panhellenic: open to all Greeks, not just one city. In practice, that meant freeborn Greek men, who competed naked. Married women were not allowed to attend. So “all Greeks” meant some Greeks, a pattern you’ll recognize from Level 14.

cards.headline: A truce with teeth
cards.body: Getting to Olympia could mean crossing enemy land. So a truce of several weeks let athletes and spectators travel safely, even while wars went on. It wasn’t world peace; it was a safe road. And it was enforced. Thucydides reports that in 420 BCE Sparta was barred from the Games for sending hoplites into Lepreum during the truce, and fined two minae per soldier.

levels.title: The Oracle at Delphi
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Oracle advised cities and kings.
levels.summary: At Delphi the Pythia spoke for Apollo; colonists, cities and kings consulted her, and her ambiguous answers could mislead, as Croesus learned.

cards.headline: A king asked Delphi about war. The answer was true, and it ruined him.
cards.body: That’s the story of Croesus and the Greek world’s great advice service. Cities, colonists and kings all lined up to ask.

cards.headline: Ask Apollo
cards.body: At Delphi, in the mountains of central Greece, a prophetess called the Pythia spoke the will of the god Apollo, seated on a sacred tripod. The oracle worked only a limited number of days, and generous donors could jump to the head of the line. Even divine advice, it turns out, had a VIP queue.

cards.headline: Advice for cities
cards.body: Greeks planning a new colony most often asked Apollo at Delphi for approval first. Remember Level 9’s colonies? Delphi’s blessing was part of the send-off. And in Level 13, Cypselus took Corinth with a favorable oracle from Delphi. A yes from Apollo was a powerful thing to have on your side.

mascot.line: Lesson from Delphi: always ask a follow-up question.

cards.headline: Read the small print
cards.body: Priests wrote the answers down in verse that was often highly ambiguous. Herodotus tells how Croesus of Lydia, the kingdom that made the first coins, asked whether to attack Persia. He would destroy a great empire, came the reply. He attacked, and the empire he destroyed was his own. Treat it as a story Greeks loved to tell, not a transcript.

levels.title: Checkpoint: City-States
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Greek city-states were organized and connected.
levels.summary: Over a thousand independent city-states, each with its own rulers, citizens and coins, still saw themselves as one people through language, gods, Olympia and Delphi.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: over a thousand independent cities. One people?
cards.body: Each ran its own government and minted its own coins. Yet Herodotus could still speak of all Greeks as one people. What held them together?

cards.headline: What split them, what joined them

items.label: What split them
points: 1,035 catalogued, independent city-states
No permanent union

items.label: What joined them
points: A shared language, religion and culture
Panhellenic games at Olympia

cards.headline: In their own words
cards.body: Herodotus gives us a Greek definition of being Greek. In his history, the Athenians say all Greeks share kinship in blood and speech, shrines and sacrifices, and a like way of life. Notice what’s missing: a king, a capital, a single government. Greece was a family of cities, not a country.

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: Put Chapter 2 together. Mountains helped make small, independent city-states, each with a high citadel and a busy agora. Some were ruled by a few aristocrats, some by tyrants. Citizens, by birth, voted, paid taxes and fought, while metics and slaves stood outside. Each city stamped its own coins, yet all could meet at Olympia under a truce and ask Apollo at Delphi.

levels.title: Athens
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Athens and its patron goddess, Athena.
levels.summary: The Greeks told that Athena won Athens with an olive tree. Athens ruled all of Attica and honored her with the owl and the Panathenaia.

cards.headline: The Greeks said Athens got its goddess by holding a contest.
cards.body: Two gods wanted the city. One offered water, the other a tree. Guess which gift won, and why Athens never forgot it.

cards.headline: A spring or a tree?
cards.body: Here’s the myth. Poseidon, god of the sea, struck a rock and made a spring, but its water was salty. (In some versions he offered the first horse instead.) Athena planted the first olive tree. Her gift won, and the city took her name: Athens. A salty spring against olives, oil and shade? Not a hard call.

cards.headline: One city, a whole region
cards.body: Remember Level 2: mountains split Greece into valleys that grew up apart. Athens broke the pattern. It ruled the whole region of Attica, an area remarkably large for one city-state; it could have held several. Athenian myth said the hero Theseus had united Attica’s towns. By the fifth century BCE, citizens from every corner of Attica were Athenians, with the same rights and duties.

mascot.line: From one mythical tree to a whole city’s prize shelf. Athens really committed to the olive!

cards.headline: The goddess’s birthday party
cards.body: Athens never let the story go. Athena’s little owl became the city’s symbol. Every July, the Panathenaia festival celebrated her birthday and presented the goddess with a new embroidered robe; every fourth year it was held with great splendor. Winners at its games took home jars painted with Athena and filled with olive oil from her sacred trees. The prize for beating everyone? A jar of the goddess’s own gift.

levels.title: Solon's Reforms
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Solon eased debt and changed the laws.
levels.summary: About 594 BCE Solon cancelled debts and freed Athenians enslaved for debt, replaced Draco’s harsh code, and ranked citizens by wealth instead of birth.

cards.headline: In early Athens, an unpaid debt could make you a slave.
cards.body: Poor Athenians borrowed against their own bodies, and some were sold abroad. Around 594 BCE, one man was handed the job of fixing it.

cards.headline: Shaking off the burdens
cards.body: Before Solon, a poor Athenian could borrow with his own person as security. If he couldn’t pay, he could be enslaved, even sold abroad. Solon, archon (chief official) about 594 BCE, cancelled debts, freed the enslaved debtors and banned loans secured on a person. Athenians called it the “shaking off of burdens.” In a poem, Solon boasted of bringing home many who had been sold into slavery.

cards.fact: “Draconian” comes from Draco, whose laws punished even trivial crimes with death.
cards.context: Draco gave Athens that code around 621 BCE. Solon replaced it, keeping only Draco’s laws on homicide, and his own laws were written on wooden boards called axones, displayed for the public. The name of the harsh lawgiver lives on as an adjective; the laws themselves didn’t last.

cards.headline: Wealth, not birth
cards.body: Solon also sorted citizens into four classes by income, measured in farm produce; the top class harvested at least 500 measures a year. Higher classes could hold higher offices, and even the poorest, the thetes, kept their place in the Assembly. Political privilege now depended on wealth, not noble birth. Not democracy yet, but a rich farmer no longer needed a famous grandfather.

cards.headline: Then he left town
cards.body: Then Solon did something rare for a man with power: he left. He set off on a journey, saying he wouldn’t be back for ten years, rather than be pressed to change his laws. Imagine writing the house rules and then leaving the country so nobody can talk you into rewriting them.

levels.title: Cleisthenes and Democracy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Cleisthenes created democracy in 508 BCE.
levels.summary: After the tyrants fell, Cleisthenes (508-507 BCE) mixed Attica into ten new tribes and a Council of 500 chosen by lot: the start of demokratia.

cards.headline: In 508 BCE, one Athenian reshuffled every citizen in Attica.
cards.body: It sounds like paperwork. It’s the moment Athenian democracy began. First, how Athens got there.

cards.headline: From tyrants to a showdown
cards.body: After Solon, Athens fell under tyrants: Peisistratus, then his son Hippias. In 510 BCE the Spartan king Cleomenes marched in and expelled Hippias. Then two nobles fought for control. Isagoras, backed by Sparta, won the top office in 508, but his rival Cleisthenes had the people on his side. When Cleomenes came back to support Isagoras, the Athenians forced them both out.

cards.headline: Shuffle the deck
cards.body: Cleisthenes replaced Athens’ four old tribes, based on descent, with ten new ones. He split Attica into three zones (the city, the coast and the inland) and gave every tribe townships, called demes, from all three. Your rights now came from your deme, which kept its own list of citizens. Like sorting a school into teams that each mix every class, it made tribes less likely to follow local and family loyalties.

mascot.line: A council picked by drawing lots. Imagine your name coming up in the civic raffle!

cards.headline: People power, by lottery
cards.body: Each tribe sent 50 men to a new Council of 500. Councillors had to be at least 30 and were chosen by lot every year, and the Council prepared the proposals the Assembly voted on. Cleisthenes is regarded as the founder of Athenian democracy. The word came a little later: demokratia, from demos (people) and kratos (rule), was coined in the middle of the 5th century BCE.

levels.title: The Assembly
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Athenian citizens debated and voted.
levels.summary: The Assembly of male citizens met on the Pnyx about 40 times a year, heard any citizen who wished to speak and voted by show of hands.

cards.headline: In Athens you didn’t elect a lawmaker. You were one.
cards.body: If you were a male citizen aged 18 or over, that is. Here’s how the Assembly worked, from the hilltop to the show of hands.

cards.headline: A hill full of voters
cards.body: The Assembly, the ekklesia, was open to every male citizen aged 18 or over. It met in the open on the Pnyx, a rocky hill in Athens with room for about 6,000 people. In the 4th century BCE it met four times in every tenth of the year: 40 meetings a year. It had final control over policy, and it usually voted by a show of hands, with a simple majority deciding.

cards.headline: “Who wishes to speak?”
cards.body: Debate opened with a herald’s invitation, repeated again and again: “Who wishes to address the assembly?” Any citizen could answer it, even a man who earned his living at a trade. The Council of 500 prepared the proposals, but the final say belonged to the crowd on the hill. Picture a town meeting where the carpenter can outtalk the aristocrat.

cards.headline: A red rope, then a paycheck
cards.body: Turnout was a real problem. Aristophanes’ comedy the Acharnians opens with the Pnyx empty while citizens gossip in the marketplace, dodging a rope smeared with red dye. In the early 4th century BCE, Athens tried a carrot instead of a rope: because too few citizens came, it began paying them to attend. Even the first democracy had to get people off the couch.

levels.title: Ostracism
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Athenians voted to send a citizen away.
levels.summary: In an ostracism, citizens wrote names on potsherds; with enough votes, the man named most left Attica for 10 years, keeping his property.

cards.headline: Once a year, Athens could vote a man out of town.
cards.body: It was an election in reverse, and the ballots were bits of broken pottery.

cards.headline: An election in reverse
cards.body: Each midwinter, the Athenians voted, without debate, on whether to hold an ostracism a few weeks later. If they said yes, each citizen scratched a name on an ostrakon, a piece of broken pottery. If enough votes were cast (6,000, in Plutarch’s account), the man named most had to leave Attica within 10 days and stay away 10 years.

cards.headline: A safety valve
cards.body: Oddly gentle: the exile kept his property. Ostracism, credited to Cleisthenes, aimed at a leading citizen who might threaten the state, and Athens remembered how Peisistratus had made himself tyrant. It was first used in 488-487 BCE and faded out after an ineffective vote, probably in 417. Think of it as removing a player before he can take over the game.

cards.headline: Tired of “the Just”
cards.body: Plutarch tells a story about Aristides, nicknamed “the just.” An illiterate voter, not recognizing him, handed him a sherd and asked him to write “Aristides” on it. Had Aristides ever wronged him? “None at all,” said the man, “neither know I the man; but I am tired of hearing him everywhere called the just.” Aristides wrote his own name.

cards.headline: A well full of Themistocles
cards.body: Real ballots survive. A well on the north slope of the Acropolis held 190 ostraka naming Themistocles, written by just fourteen hands. They seem to have been prepared in advance, ready to hand out. Election-day leaflets, ancient style.

levels.title: Juries and Courts
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how huge citizen juries decided cases.
levels.summary: Athenian juries of hundreds, chosen by lot from 6,000 citizens over 30, heard timed speeches and voted with secret bronze ballots, with no judge.

cards.headline: Imagine a jury of about 500 people, and no judge.
cards.body: In Athens that was ordinary. Big juries, the thinking went, were hard to frighten or buy.

cards.headline: Six thousand jurors a year
cards.body: Each year 6,000 volunteers, male citizens at least 30 years old, were chosen by lot to serve as jurors. A court had about 500 jurors for public cases and about 200 for private ones. There was no judge: jurors decided both the law and the facts, and voted without discussing the case among themselves. Pericles introduced pay for jury service, and critics grumbled that it filled the courts with common people.

cards.headline: Speak for yourself, against the clock
cards.body: There were no lawyers as we know them. Litigants usually spoke for themselves, though others could speak for a defendant. A water clock, the klepsydra, timed each speech: water ran from one pot into another, and when it ran out, so did your turn. It was even stopped while laws and documents were read aloud. No filibusters in Athens.

cards.headline: A secret vote in your fist
cards.body: Each juror got two bronze ballots: one pierced, for the prosecutor, and one solid, for the defendant. They looked identical apart from the axle, so with your fingers over the ends, nobody could see which one you cast. A tie meant the defendant won. The whole system had one goal: large juries made intimidation and bribery harder.
