levels.title: Pericles
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Pericles' leadership of Athens' golden age.
levels.summary: Pericles led Athens by winning election as general year after year; Thucydides called it a democracy in name but rule by its leading man.

cards.headline: A democracy with a favorite: Athens kept electing the same man.
cards.body: His name was Pericles. How does one citizen come to lead a city that governs itself?

cards.headline: Elected, not drawn
cards.body: Most Athenian officials were picked by lot, but the ten generals (strategoi) were elected by vote. That was Pericles’ office. Born about 495 BCE, he rose to lead Athens, and after his chief rival was ostracized, Plutarch says, he was re-elected general every year for fifteen years. His power rested on that constant re-election and, as Thucydides saw it, on his intelligence and incorruptibility.

cards.headline: Democracy in name?
cards.body: In Pericles’ funeral speech, as Thucydides records it, Athens’ constitution “favours the many instead of the few; this is why it is called a democracy.” Yet Thucydides also judged that under Pericles, Athens was a democracy in name but in fact government by its leading man. Both were true at once: the people voted, and they kept voting for him.

mascot.line: Even the first citizen couldn’t escape the comedians. That’s democracy too.

cards.headline: Why the helmet?
cards.body: Look at a bust of Pericles and he’s wearing a helmet. Plutarch says his head was long and out of proportion, so almost all his portraits covered it, and comic poets called him “squill-head” (a squill is a sea onion). The most powerful man in Athens still got roasted on stage.

levels.title: The Parthenon
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how and why the Parthenon was built.
levels.summary: After the Persian sack, Pericles rebuilt the Acropolis; the Parthenon (447-438 BCE) honored Athena, held her gold and ivory statue and a league treasury, and was wrecked in 1687.

cards.headline: The Parthenon rose from the ashes of a sack.
cards.body: Enemy troops had wrecked the Acropolis. Athens answered with the most famous temple in Greece, and a fight about who paid for it.

cards.headline: Rebuilding the high city
cards.body: After the Acropolis was sacked during the wars with Persia, Pericles directed a magnificent rebuilding program. Work on the Parthenon began in 447 BCE; the temple was finished by 438, and its outside decoration went on until 432. Its pediments told Athena’s own stories: her birth, and her contest with Poseidon. Remember Level 21’s olive tree? It went up on the temple.

cards.headline: Whose money?
cards.body: The Parthenon also held the treasury of the Delian League, an alliance of Greek states led by Athens. Plutarch reports that Pericles’ enemies accused him of taking the Greeks’ common treasure from the island of Delos and spending it to gild and adorn Athens. It’s the oldest argument in public building: gorgeous, but who paid?

cards.headline: A temple with many lives
cards.body: Inside stood a great gold and ivory statue of Athena by the sculptor Phidias, dedicated in 438 BCE and now lost. The temple itself lived on as a Byzantine church, a Roman Catholic cathedral and then a mosque. In 1687, during fighting between Venice and the Ottomans, gunpowder stored inside exploded and destroyed the center of the building. Using a temple as a powder store: not its best career move.

levels.title: Who Was Left Out
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why women, slaves and foreigners could not vote.
levels.summary: Athenian democracy was for adult male citizens only; citizen women, metics (free foreigners) and enslaved people had no vote.

cards.headline: Athens called itself rule by the people. Which people?
cards.body: Only adult male citizens voted. Women, resident foreigners and enslaved people were left out, and each group was left out for a different reason.

cards.headline: Citizens, but not voters
cards.body: Athenian women could be citizens, and after 451 or 450 BCE that mattered more than ever: a law carried by Pericles limited citizenship to people with Athenian parents on both sides. Yet only men could vote in the Assembly. In Pericles’ funeral speech, as Thucydides gives it, widows are told that the greatest glory is to be least talked of among men.

cards.headline: Neighbors with no vote
cards.body: Metics were free foreigners living in Athens, including freed slaves, and they made up a large part of the city. They paid a special yearly tax, could not acquire land or a house, and had no direct part in politics. You could live in Athens, work there and pay its taxes, and still be a guest.

cards.headline: Owned, not represented
cards.body: Enslaved people had no voice at all. Athens practiced chattel slavery: people were owned as property, mostly foreigners captured in war or sold by slave traders, and children born to enslaved parents were enslaved too. Rule by the people was never meant to include them.

cards.headline: Why a lottery?
cards.body: Aristotle wrote that appointing officials by lot is thought democratic, and electing them oligarchic, meaning rule by the few. A lottery gives every eligible citizen the same chance, whoever his friends are. Athens used it for most offices from 487-486 BCE, and kept elections for jobs like general. That’s how a man like Pericles could win again and again, while councillors and jurors were simply drawn.

levels.title: Sparta
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Sparta's unusual society.
levels.summary: Sparta conquered Messenia and made its people helots, state-owned serfs whose labor let every Spartan citizen train for war; two kings ruled at once, and most of what we know comes from outsiders.

cards.headline: Sparta’s citizens didn’t farm, trade or build. Their job was war.
cards.body: Somebody still had to grow the food. The answer explains almost everything strange about Sparta.

cards.headline: Farmland next door
cards.body: Sparta lay in Laconia, in the southeastern Peloponnese, on the Eurotas river. Around 735–715 BCE it conquered its neighbor Messenia, gaining a large tract of fertile land and turning its people into helots. Remember Level 9’s colonists, leaving home short of farmland? Sparta found its farmland next door, and kept the farmers.

cards.headline: The helots
cards.body: Helots were serfs owned by the Spartan state, not by one master. They worked the land and handed over half of their produce, which left Spartan men free to train for war full-time. But helots greatly outnumbered Spartans, by some estimates about seven to one, and Spartans feared a revolt. Each year, officials called ephors formally declared war on the helots, so killing one carried no religious guilt. Sparta’s army wasn’t only for enemies abroad.

cards.headline: Two kings, and a vote by volume
cards.body: Sparta had two hereditary kings at the same time, from two separate royal families. Five ephors served one-year terms, a council of elders led the citizens’ assembly, and the assembly voted by shouting. Picture a company with two bosses, a board that changes every year, and decisions made by whoever cheers loudest.

mascot.line: Keep a pinch of salt handy for Sparta. Its fans and critics did most of the talking.

cards.fact: Most of what we know about Sparta was written by outsiders.
cards.context: Spartans wrote little about themselves. Our accounts come from non-Spartans such as Herodotus, Xenophon and Plutarch, and Plutarch lived from about 46 CE, centuries after Sparta’s great days. So this chapter keeps asking of each Spartan story: evidence, or legend?

levels.title: Growing Up Spartan
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the harsh training of Spartan boys.
levels.summary: At seven, Spartan boys left home for the agoge: barracks life to about thirty, short rations, stealing encouraged. A pit near Taygetus held no newborns.

cards.headline: At seven, a Spartan boy left home. The state raised him from then on.
cards.body: Some of what we’re told about Spartan childhood is well attested. Some of it, the bones have now tested.

cards.headline: Raised by the state
cards.body: From the age of seven, Spartan boys entered the agoge, the state’s training system. They lived in barracks, grouped by age, away from their families, and the training and barracks life lasted until a man was about 30. Picture boarding school, boot camp and a sports academy rolled into one, with no weekends home.

cards.headline: Hungry on purpose
cards.body: Boys in the agoge got little food and were encouraged to steal more. The Greek writer Xenophon says a boy caught stealing was beaten, not for the theft but for doing it badly: getting caught was the failure. The lesson was cunning. Few schools have made “don’t get caught” part of the curriculum.

mascot.line: This is how history gets checked: a famous story, a pit of bones, and someone patient enough to look.

cards.fact: Plutarch said Sparta threw away weak babies. The bones disagree.
cards.context: Plutarch wrote that elders inspected every newborn and had weak ones left at a chasm at the foot of Mount Taygetus. But in 2007 an anthropologist who studied bones from a pit near Mount Taygetus found adolescents and adults aged 18 to 35, and no newborns. A story told centuries later met the evidence, and lost.

levels.title: Spartan Women
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Spartan women had unusual freedom.
levels.summary: Spartan girls trained in athletics and Spartan women could inherit and own land and ran estates, unusual freedoms in Greece; they still had no vote, office or place in the assembly.

cards.headline: “Come back with your shield, or on it.”
cards.body: Later Greek writers put those words in the mouth of a Spartan mother sending her son to war. Legend or not, Spartan women had a reputation no other Greek women had.

cards.headline: Girls in training
cards.body: Spartan girls exercised like the boys: running, wrestling, throwing the discus and javelin. They weren’t trained for battle. Xenophon gives the reason: strong parents, Spartans believed, would have stronger children. So the freedom had a purpose, and the purpose was the army.

cards.headline: Owners and managers
cards.body: Spartan women could inherit and own land. And with the men so often away, they ran homes, farms and estates. Aristotle wrote that nearly two-fifths of Sparta’s land was owned by women, and he listed it among Sparta’s faults. He meant it as a complaint. Today it reads as one of the most surprising facts about the ancient Greek world.

cards.headline: Where the freedom stopped
cards.body: Spartan women still could not vote, hold public office or attend the citizens’ assembly. Freer than most Greek women, yes. Equal to Spartan men, no.

cards.fact: In 396 BCE a Spartan princess won at the Olympics.
cards.context: Cynisca’s team won the four-horse chariot race. Chariot victories went to the owner, so she became the first woman to win an Olympic victory without ever holding the reins.

levels.title: The Persian Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the empire that invaded Greece.
levels.summary: Persia’s Achaemenid Empire, begun by Cyrus around 550 BCE, ran from Egypt to the Indus with a Royal Road of relay couriers; when Athens helped the Ionian Revolt, Darius vowed revenge.

cards.headline: Every dinner, a servant told Persia’s king: “Master, remember the Athenians.”
cards.body: Herodotus says Darius ordered it. Why would the ruler of the largest empire the world had yet known brood over one Greek city?

cards.headline: The biggest empire yet
cards.body: Persia’s Achaemenid Empire began with the conquests of Cyrus the Great around 550 BCE. At its height it stretched from Egypt to the Indus River and westward into parts of Greece: the largest empire the world had yet known. It was divided into provinces called satrapies, each owing a fixed yearly tribute. Next to that, a Greek city-state was a dot on the map.

cards.headline: News at relay speed
cards.body: Darius I built the Royal Road, running more than 2,400 km (1,500 miles) from Susa, the Persian capital, to Sardis near the Aegean coast. Ordinary travelers took about three months. Royal messengers, handing off at relay stations, did it in nine days. Herodotus wrote that neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stopped them.

cards.fact: Herodotus’s line about Persian couriers is carved on a New York post office.
cards.context: An adapted version runs across the James A. Farley Post Office. Many people take it for the US Postal Service’s motto, but the Postal Service has no official motto. America’s most famous mail slogan was first written about Persia’s royal messengers.

cards.headline: The spark
cards.body: The Greek cities of Ionia, on the coast of what is now Turkey, lived under Persian rule. In 499 BCE they revolted. Athens sent help, and Sardis was burned. The revolt was crushed by 494 BCE, but Darius used Athens’s part in it as his reason to invade Greece in 490 BCE. Hence the dinner reminder.

levels.title: Marathon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Battle of Marathon and the legend of the runner.
levels.summary: In 490 BCE about 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans beat a larger Persian force at Marathon with strong wings; Pheidippides ran to Sparta, and the run to Athens is later legend.

cards.headline: Marathon is famous for a run. The real runner went the other way.
cards.body: In 490 BCE Athens faced Persia’s army almost alone. Here’s how it won, and what really happened to the runner.

cards.headline: Almost alone
cards.body: In September 490 BCE a Persian force landed on the plain of Marathon, about 40 km (25 miles) from Athens. Athens asked Sparta for help, but the Spartans said they could not march until the full moon. So about 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 men from little Plataea faced a larger Persian force by themselves.

cards.headline: Strong wings, thin middle
cards.body: The Athenian general Miltiades strengthened the two ends of his line and left the center thin. The Persians pushed back the center, and the Greek wings turned inward and surrounded them. Herodotus counted 6,400 Persian dead and 192 Athenians. Even if his count is generous, it was a rout.

cards.headline: Which run?
cards.body: Herodotus does record a runner: Pheidippides, sent from Athens to Sparta before the battle to ask for help, covering about 240 km (150 miles) in about two days. The famous dash from Marathon to Athens to announce victory isn’t in Herodotus; it’s a later legend. The modern marathon race honors the legend, not the longer run that happened.

cards.fact: The Spartans did come. After it was over.
cards.context: Herodotus says 2,000 Spartans reached Attica on the third day after leaving Sparta, too late for the battle. They went to see the Persian dead at Marathon, praised the Athenians and went home.

levels.title: Thermopylae
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the stand of the 300 Spartans.
levels.summary: In 480 BCE about 7,000 Greeks under the Spartan king Leonidas held Thermopylae for two days; after a local showed Persia a path, far more than 300 made the last stand.

cards.headline: “The 300” were never alone at Thermopylae.
cards.body: Legend remembers 300 Spartans. The real stand, in 480 BCE, had thousands of Greeks, a traitor and a mountain path.

cards.headline: A gate between mountain and sea
cards.body: In 480 BCE Xerxes, son of Darius, invaded Greece by land. Herodotus claimed he had more than 2.6 million fighting men; modern estimates run from about 70,000 to 300,000. Either way, the Greeks needed a place where a small force could block a large army. At Thermopylae the road squeezed into a line only a few dozen yards wide, between a steep hillside and the sea.

cards.headline: Two days, then a path
cards.body: Leonidas, a Spartan king, led about 7,000 Greeks, including 300 Spartans, and they held the pass for two days. Then a local Greek, Ephialtes, showed the Persians a mountain path around it. A wall of shields is only as good as its flanks.

cards.headline: Who stayed
cards.body: Leonidas sent most of the army away. Staying with him were his 300, some helots, and about 1,100 Boeotians from Thespiae and Thebes. They held one more day, and many, if not all, were killed. “The 300” makes a great title. It just leaves out more than a thousand people.

mascot.line: Spot the pattern? A later writer, a better-known name. Sparta’s stories keep doing this.

cards.fact: Told the Persian arrows would hide the sun, a Spartan said: then we’ll fight in the shade.
cards.context: Herodotus gives the line to a Spartan named Dieneces. Plutarch, writing centuries later, gave it to Leonidas. Good lines have a way of drifting toward famous people.

levels.title: Salamis
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Greek fleet won at Salamis.
levels.summary: Themistocles turned silver into 200 triremes; in 480 BCE, with Athens sacked, he lured Persia’s larger fleet into the strait of Salamis. Plataea ended the invasion.

cards.headline: In 480 BCE the Athenians abandoned their city. Then they won at sea.
cards.body: It started with a lucky strike in a silver mine and a man who didn’t want to share it out.

cards.headline: Silver into ships
cards.body: When Athens’s state-owned silver mines struck a rich vein, Themistocles persuaded the Athenians to spend the windfall on the navy. By 480 BCE Athens had 200 triremes: warships rowed by about 170 men in three tiers, with a bronze-covered ram at the bow. Think of a trireme as a torpedo powered by people.

cards.headline: A city made of ships
cards.body: After Thermopylae, Greece lay open. Athenians sent their women and children to the Peloponnese, and much of the population sheltered on the island of Salamis. The Persians sacked Athens itself. For a while, the city of Athens was its fleet.

cards.headline: The trap in the strait
cards.body: Themistocles sent Xerxes a false message, and the much larger Persian fleet attacked into the narrow strait between Salamis and the mainland. Packed together, its ships could hardly maneuver, and the Greek triremes rammed them. The Greeks sank about 300 Persian ships and lost about 40. Numbers help less when there’s no room to use them.

cards.fact: Xerxes watched it all from the shore.
cards.context: Herodotus says he sat at the foot of a hill facing Salamis, with scribes noting who fought well. Afterward he went home to Susa, and in 479 BCE a Greek victory on land at Plataea ended the invasion.

levels.title: The Delian League
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Athens turned an alliance into an empire.
levels.summary: Founded in 478 BCE against Persia, the Delian League paid for a fleet Athens led; Athens stopped members leaving and took the treasury, making the league an empire.

cards.headline: Athens’s allies paid for its navy. Then they found they couldn’t leave.
cards.body: An alliance against Persia slowly became an Athenian empire. Here’s how a club turned into a cage.

cards.headline: A league with an island bank
cards.body: In 478 BCE, with Persia beaten back but not gone, Athens and many Greek cities formed an alliance to protect themselves from Persia. Its treasury sat in the temple of Apollo on the island of Delos, which is why we call it the Delian League. Athens supplied the commanders and decided which members gave ships and which gave money.

cards.headline: Money in, ships out
cards.body: Over time most members paid money instead of sending ships, and the tribute built and maintained the fleet Athens led. Around 330 cities appear in the surviving tribute lists. Remember Level 37’s triremes? Now the allies were paying for them, while their own navies faded.

cards.headline: No exit
cards.body: When Naxos tried to leave, Athens attacked and forced it back in. In 454 BCE Athens moved the treasury from Delos to Athens, and the league became, in effect, an Athenian empire. League money even helped pay for Pericles’ rebuilding of Athens, including the Parthenon. The allies had joined a club. Now they were paying rent.

levels.title: The Peloponnesian War
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Athens and Sparta fought for 27 years.
levels.summary: From 431 to 404 BCE Athens’s navy fought Sparta’s army; Thucydides blamed Spartan fear of Athens. Plague hit Athens, and Sparta, with Persian aid, won.

cards.headline: The Greeks who beat Persia together fought each other for 27 years.
cards.body: And at the end, Persia helped decide who won.

cards.headline: Sea power against land power
cards.body: From 431 to 404 BCE Athens, leading the Delian League, fought Sparta, leading the Peloponnesian League. Athens had the stronger navy; Sparta’s alliance had the stronger army on land. Thucydides, who lived through the war and wrote its history, said the real cause was Athens’s growing power and the fear it caused in Sparta.

cards.headline: Safe behind the walls
cards.body: Under Pericles, Athens avoided Sparta’s army, kept its people inside the city walls and relied on its navy. Then, in 430 BCE, plague struck the crowded city. It killed tens of thousands, including Pericles. Thucydides caught it too, and survived to write about it. The plan to stay safe had packed everyone together for the disease.

cards.headline: Persian gold, Spartan ships
cards.body: Athens lost a huge expedition to Sicily in 415–413 BCE. Then, in 405 BCE, the Spartan admiral Lysander, with much aid from Persia, destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami. Athens surrendered in 404 BCE. Persia had lost to the Greeks at Salamis. In the end, it helped sink Athens anyway.

cards.fact: Athens’s walls came down to flute music.
cards.context: Xenophon says the victors tore them down to the music of flute girls, thinking that day the beginning of freedom for Greece. The Delian League was disbanded the same year.

cards.headline: A victory monument, with an argument built in
cards.body: After Plataea, 31 Greek cities dedicated a gold tripod at Delphi on a bronze column of three twisted snakes. The Spartan commander Pausanias first had it inscribed in his own name; the allies objected, and the cities’ names replaced it, with Sparta first, then Athens and Corinth. Constantine later moved the column to Constantinople. It still stands in Istanbul, minus its snake heads.

levels.title: The Twelve Olympians
levels.objective: After this level you can name the main Greek gods and what each ruled.
levels.summary: The Greeks said their twelve great gods lived on Mount Olympus, Greece’s highest peak; the lists of the twelve varied, and the gods looked and acted like people.

cards.headline: The Greek gods had a real address: the highest mountain in Greece.
cards.body: Who was said to live up there, what did each one rule, and who got a seat at the table?

mascot.line: Best view in Greece, and nobody upstairs to complain about the noise!

cards.headline: A home on the highest peak
cards.body: Remember Level 2? Mountains cover about four-fifths of Greece. The Greeks gave their gods the tallest one. Mount Olympus rises 2,917 m (9,570 feet), the highest peak in Greece, and they regarded it as the home of the gods and the site of Zeus’s throne. That’s why the great gods are called the Olympians. In a land full of mountains, the gods took the penthouse.

cards.headline: The twelfth seat
cards.body: Ask the Greeks to name all twelve and you’d get more than one answer. One common list runs Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes and Dionysus. Other lists seat Hestia, goddess of the hearth, or even Hades instead. Twelve chairs, and the guest list kept changing.

cards.headline: Gods who acted like people
cards.body: What made these gods feel so Greek? Greek religion pictured many gods in human form, with one supreme god over them. They looked like people, and they behaved like people too. In Greek stories Hera, queen of the gods, keeps appearing as Zeus’s jealous, vengeful wife, hounding the women he loved. Gods, yes, but with very human tempers.

levels.title: Zeus
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Zeus, king of the gods, and his thunderbolt.
levels.summary: In myth Zeus was hidden on Crete from Cronus, who swallowed his children, then overthrew the Titans, got his thunderbolt from the Cyclopes and drew the sky when the brothers split the world.

cards.headline: Zeus survived babyhood because his mother fed his father a rock.
cards.body: It’s one of the strangest family stories ever told, and the Greeks told it about their king of the gods, ruler of the sky.

cards.headline: A father who swallowed his children
cards.body: The Greeks told it like this. Cronus, king of the Titans, learned that one of his children was fated to overthrow him. His solution was brutal: each time his wife, Rhea, gave birth, he swallowed the baby. One child after another disappeared down his throat. Family dinners in that house were tense.

cards.headline: The stone in swaddling clothes
cards.body: When Zeus was born, Rhea made a swap. She hid the baby in a cave on Crete and handed Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes, and he swallowed it. Yes, Crete: the island of Level 3’s Minoans. Zeus grew up, forced Cronus to cough up his brothers and sisters, and with his brothers Hades and Poseidon beat Cronus and the Titans.

cards.headline: Thunder, made to order
cards.body: Where did the famous thunderbolt come from? The poet Hesiod said the Cyclopes forged it: three craftsmen named Thunder, Lightning and Bright Flash. They made Poseidon’s trident and a helmet of invisibility for Hades too. Remember Level 4’s Cyclopean walls? Same giants. Zeus became the sky and weather god, sender of thunder, lightning, rain and winds.

mascot.line: Sky, sea or underworld? I know which one I’d hope to draw.

cards.headline: Splitting the world
cards.body: After the victory, the three brothers divided the world, and they did it by drawing lots. Zeus got the sky, Poseidon the sea and Hades the underworld. The biggest inheritance in Greek myth was settled the way you’d decide who does the dishes.

levels.title: Poseidon
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes.
levels.summary: Poseidon drew the sea by lot; with his trident he also ruled earthquakes and horses, and myths said he punished Argos after losing it to Hera.

cards.headline: The Greek god of the sea was also the god of earthquakes.
cards.body: Sea, shaking ground and horses: an odd set of jobs for one god. Meet Poseidon.

cards.headline: Lord of the sea
cards.body: Remember Level 42’s lottery? When Zeus and his brothers split the world, the sea fell to Poseidon. In a land where the sea opened up wider horizons (Level 2), that was a big realm. His weapon and main symbol was the trident, perhaps once a fish spear. The Romans later matched him with their own sea god, Neptune. The mightiest weapon in the sea may have started as fishing gear.

cards.headline: The earth-shaker
cards.body: Poseidon ruled more than water. He was the god of earthquakes, and Greeks called him enosichthōn, “earth-shaker”. He was the god of horses as well; in some myths he created the horse. The same god who stirred the waves could rattle the ground under your feet. Wherever things heaved, rolled or galloped, Poseidon was in charge.

mascot.line: Lose a contest, dry up the rivers. Remind me never to beat him at anything.

cards.headline: A sore loser
cards.body: Poseidon wanted cities, too. He contested Argos with Hera, and lost. In one version he flooded the land in revenge. In the version the ancient writer Pausanias tells, he made the rivers of Argos disappear, which is why, Pausanias says, they give no water except after rain. A myth that doubles as a weather report.

levels.title: Athena and Apollo
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Athena and Apollo and what they stood for.
levels.summary: Athena, born armed from Zeus’s head, stood for war with a plan, crafts and practical reason; Apollo, Artemis’s twin, carried the bow and the lyre and was god of prophecy and healing.

cards.headline: One Greek goddess was born out of her father’s head, fully armed and shouting.
cards.body: That was Athena. Her half-brother Apollo arrived more quietly, carrying a bow in one hand and a lyre in the other. What did each of them stand for?

cards.headline: Born with a battle cry
cards.body: The Greeks said Athena burst from Zeus’s forehead fully grown, in armor, and giving a battle cry. One version explains how she got in there: Zeus had swallowed her pregnant mother, Metis, goddess of counsel. Remember Cronus in Level 42, swallowing his children? Swallowing relatives seems to run in the family.

cards.headline: War with a plan
cards.body: Athena was a goddess of war, handicraft and practical reason. Her kind of war was the thinking kind: strategy, not the violence and bloodlust of Ares. She was patroness of spinning and weaving too, and her owl became famous as the symbol of Athens. Ares brought the fury; Athena brought the plan.

cards.headline: The bow and the lyre
cards.body: Apollo and his twin sister, Artemis, were born on the island of Delos, children of Zeus and Leto. Apollo carried two symbols. His bow stood for distance, death, terror and awe; his lyre stood for joy through music, poetry and dance. He was a god of prophecy and healing as well. The same god could strike you from afar or play you a song.

cards.headline: The bright one
cards.body: Apollo had another name, Phoebus, meaning “bright” or “pure”, and in time he came to be connected with the Sun. So when a poem hails “Phoebus Apollo”, it’s calling him the bright one.

levels.title: The Underworld
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Hades and the Greek underworld.
levels.summary: Hades ruled the underworld that shared his name; Charon ferried the buried dead for a coin, Cerberus guarded the way, and Persephone’s months below explained winter.

cards.headline: In Greek myth, even the dead had to pay their fare.
cards.body: A ferryman, a guard dog and a god who shared his name with his kingdom. Welcome to the underworld.

cards.headline: One name, two meanings
cards.body: Hades was the god of the underworld, and his realm, the house of Hades, came to share his name. It fell to him by lot, remember, when Zeus drew the sky and Poseidon the sea. He was also called Pluto, “Wealth”, perhaps because he gathered every living thing into his treasury at death. Sooner or later, everyone ends up at his place.

cards.headline: The ferry fare
cards.body: To get in, a soul had to cross the water. Charon ferried the dead over the rivers Styx and Acheron, but only those who had received the rites of burial. His fare was the coin placed in the corpse’s mouth. No funeral, no ferry.

cards.headline: The dog at the door
cards.body: Waiting on the far side was Cerberus, the monstrous watchdog of the underworld. He usually had three heads, though the poet Hesiod gave him 50, and snakes grew from his back. His job worked in both directions: keep the living out, and devour any of the dead who tried to escape. The underworld had a one-way door.

cards.headline: Why winter comes
cards.body: Hades’ queen was Persephone, daughter of Demeter, Level 41’s grain goddess. The Greeks told how Hades carried her off while she was gathering flowers. Because she ate a pomegranate seed below, she had to spend a third of every year with him (more, in some versions). While she was gone, Demeter grieved and the fields lay barren. A myth that turns the seasons into a family story.

levels.title: Heracles
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Twelve Labors of Heracles.
levels.summary: Hounded by Hera, Heracles served Eurystheus at Tiryns to win immortality; he was set ten labors, but two were not counted, so they became twelve.

cards.headline: Heracles was set ten impossible jobs. His boss refused to count two of them.
cards.body: That’s how the Ten Labors became the famous Twelve. But why was a son of Zeus taking orders at all?

cards.headline: Hated from the cradle
cards.body: Heracles was the son of Zeus and a mortal woman, Alcmene, and Zeus’s wife, Hera, persecuted him for it. She sent two serpents to kill him in his cradle; the baby strangled them. Remember Level 41’s jealous Hera? This is her at full strength.

cards.headline: Why the labors
cards.body: Hera struck again when he was grown. She drove him mad, and he killed his wife, Megara, and their children. Afterwards he asked the oracle at Delphi where he should live. The answer: in Tiryns, serving Eurystheus for twelve years and performing ten labors; then he would become immortal. Tiryns? One of Level 4’s Mycenaean strongholds.

cards.fact: Heracles’ first labor was killing the Nemean lion. He wore its skin ever after.
cards.context: Then came the nine-headed Hydra of Lerna, a wild boar, man-eating birds and more. The last labor took him down to the underworld to fetch up Cerberus, Level 45’s three-headed watchdog. Of all the dogs in myth, that’s the one you’d least want to walk.

mascot.line: Two whole labors, disallowed on a technicality. I’d have asked for a referee.

cards.headline: Ten became twelve
cards.body: So why twelve? Eurystheus refused to count two. The Hydra didn’t count, he said, because Heracles’ companion Iolaus had helped. The Augean stables didn’t count either, because Heracles, who cleaned them in a single day by diverting two rivers, did the job for hire. Even myth has fine print. In the end, the Greeks said, his divine part rose to heaven and he became a god.

levels.title: Perseus and Medusa
levels.objective: After this level you can retell Perseus's quest.
levels.summary: Cast adrift because of a prophecy, Perseus beheaded Medusa by watching her reflection, killed his grandfather by accident and was said to have founded Mycenae.

cards.headline: A prophecy said a baby would kill his grandfather. So Grandpa set him adrift.
cards.body: The baby was Perseus. The sea didn’t stop the prophecy; it only postponed it.

cards.headline: Cast adrift
cards.body: Acrisius of Argos had been told his grandson would kill him. So when his daughter, Danaë, had a son, Perseus, he shut mother and baby in a chest and cast it into the sea. The chest grounded on the island of Seriphus, and Perseus grew up there. Problem postponed, not solved.

cards.headline: An impossible errand
cards.body: On Seriphus, King Polydectes wanted Danaë, and he tricked Perseus into promising to bring him the head of Medusa. Medusa was the most famous of the monsters called Gorgons, and the only one who could die. Her hair was snakes, and anyone who looked at her face turned instantly to stone. Some errand.

cards.headline: Don’t look
cards.body: Perseus went well equipped: winged sandals, the cap of Hades that made him invisible, and a curved sword. The real trick came from Athena, a shield: he guided himself by Medusa’s reflection and never met her eyes. From her neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus, and her head ended up on Athena’s aegis. Level 44’s goddess of strategy, wearing the proof.

cards.headline: The prophecy comes true
cards.body: Back on Seriphus, Perseus turned Polydectes and his supporters to stone. Later, throwing the discus, he accidentally struck and killed Acrisius. The prophecy came true after all. Perseus was also said to have founded Mycenae, Level 4’s stronghold, and Pausanias heard the name came from a mykes: the cap of his scabbard that fell there, or a mushroom.

levels.title: Theseus and the Minotaur
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the myth of the Labyrinth.
levels.summary: Theseus ended Minos’s tribute of young Athenians by killing the Minotaur, finding his way out with Ariadne’s thread, the clew that gave us the word clue.

cards.headline: Every time you look for a clue, you’re following a Greek myth.
cards.body: The word began as a ball of thread in the Labyrinth on Crete. Here’s how it got there.

cards.headline: A terrible tribute
cards.body: Remember Level 3’s myth: King Minos kept the Minotaur, half man and half bull, in a Labyrinth built by Daedalus. To avenge his son Androgeos, killed by Athenians, Minos made Athens send seven youths and seven maidens to be devoured by it: every ninth year in one version, every year in another. Fourteen young Athenians, fed to a monster.

cards.headline: Theseus volunteers
cards.body: When the third tribute came due, Theseus volunteered to go. He was the son of King Aegeus of Athens (or, in another version, of Poseidon). On Crete, Minos’s own daughter, Ariadne, helped him: with her thread, he found his way back out of the Labyrinth after killing the Minotaur. The enemy king’s daughter handed the hero the way home.

mascot.line: Next time you solve a mystery, tip your hat to a ball of yarn.

cards.fact: The English word “clue” comes from “clew”, a ball of thread.
cards.context: Its meaning shifted because of the clew Ariadne gave Theseus to guide him out of the Labyrinth. The spelling “clue” appears by the mid-1400s, and by the 1620s a clue could be anything that points the way, maze or no maze. Every detective story owes Ariadne a thank-you note.

cards.headline: The wrong sail
cards.body: Theseus had promised his father a signal: if he survived, his ship would come home under a white sail instead of the usual black one. He forgot. Seeing the black sail, Aegeus believed his son was dead and killed himself; in one version he drowned himself in the sea, which was called the Aegean ever after. The hero won, and his father never knew.

levels.title: The Voyage of Odysseus
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the monsters and trials of the Odyssey.
levels.summary: Odysseus tricked and blinded the Cyclops Polyphemus, earning Poseidon’s anger, heard the Sirens tied to the mast and lost six men passing Scylla and Charybdis.

cards.headline: Odysseus beat a one-eyed giant with a joke about his own name.
cards.body: Level 6 said the Odyssey follows Odysseus’s ten-year struggle to get home. Here are some of the monsters that made it take so long.

cards.headline: My name is Nobody
cards.body: Odysseus and his men were trapped in the cave of the Cyclops Polyphemus. Odysseus told the giant his name was “Noman”: Nobody. Then he blinded him with a heated olive-wood stake. When Polyphemus shouted to the other Cyclopes that Noman was killing him, they told him to pray to Poseidon and went away. Nobody ever used an alibi so well.

cards.headline: Poseidon’s grudge
cards.body: There was a catch. Polyphemus was Poseidon’s son, and he prayed to his father for revenge. Remember Level 43’s sore loser? Poseidon answered by delaying Odysseus’s homecoming with shipwrecks and other disasters, and Odysseus finally reached home as the only survivor. Blind the sea god’s son, and the sea itself turns against you.

cards.headline: A song to die for
cards.body: Then came the Sirens, part bird and part woman, whose sweet song lured sailors to destruction; Homer has two of them. Odysseus stopped his crew’s ears with wax and had himself tied to the mast, so he couldn’t steer the ship off course. He heard the deadliest song in the world, strapped in like a passenger.

cards.headline: Between Scylla and Charybdis
cards.body: Next, two monsters guarded narrow waters so close together that no ship could pass without meeting one or both. Odysseus steered closer to Scylla, lost six men to her, and got through. The pair was later placed in the Strait of Messina. We still say “between Scylla and Charybdis”: stuck between two equally bad choices.

levels.title: Milestone: Myth and City
levels.objective: After this level you can connect Greek myths, gods and city-states into one picture.
levels.summary: With no sacred books, Greeks learned their gods from poets like Homer and Hesiod, and their cities claimed heroes: Theseus for Athens, Perseus for Mycenae.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Greek myths weren’t set in never-never land.
cards.body: The gods had a real mountain, and the heroes had real hometowns. Let’s see how myth and city fit together.

cards.headline: Poets wrote the gods’ biography
cards.body: Greek religion had no sacred books. So who told Greeks what their gods were like? Herodotus had an answer: Homer and Hesiod, who he supposed lived no more than 400 years before him. They taught the Greeks the gods’ family tree, gave the gods their names, set their jobs and described their looks. Level 6 called Homer Greece’s textbook. For the gods, he was the encyclopedia too.

cards.headline: A legend on the city calendar
cards.body: The historian Thucydides wrote that before Theseus, Attica was a patchwork of independent towns, each with its own council. Theseus, he said, merged them into one council at Athens, and the Athenians kept a state-funded Feast of Union, the Synoecia, dating from him. A hero who fought a monster in a maze was also remembered as the man who made Athens one city.

levels.title: What Is Philosophy?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what Greek philosophers were trying to do.
levels.summary: Philosophy means love of wisdom. The first Greek philosophers, in 6th-century BCE Ionia, looked for causes in nature, and Xenophanes questioned Homer’s gods.

cards.headline: In the 6th century BCE, some Greeks started asking “why?” and wouldn’t stop.
cards.body: No labs, no telescopes, just arguments. This chapter follows the people who turned asking questions into a way of life. First: what were they after?

cards.headline: Love of wisdom
cards.body: The word philosophy is Greek: philosophia, “love of wisdom”. Philo- is the love part, and sophia is wisdom. Notice what the name doesn’t say. A philosopher isn’t someone who owns wisdom, like a trophy on a shelf. It’s someone who loves it and goes looking for it. You can love something you haven’t caught yet.

cards.headline: Causes inside nature
cards.body: The first Greek philosophers lived in Ionia, on the coast of what is now Turkey, in the 6th century BCE. Their big move was to look for causes within nature itself, not in the whims of gods who behaved like people. Thales, who gets Level 52 to himself, is counted as the first. Swap “the gods willed it” for “here’s how it works”, and you’ve got the idea.

mascot.line: A horse drawing a horse-shaped god. Once you picture it, you can’t unpicture it.

cards.headline: Xenophanes picks a fight with Homer
cards.body: Remember Level 6? Homer was the basis of Greek education: Greece’s textbook. In the 500s BCE the thinker Xenophanes attacked it: Homer and Hesiod, he complained, gave the gods theft, adultery and deceit, things people get blamed for. Then his sharpest jab: if horses or oxen had hands and could draw, they’d draw gods that looked like horses and oxen.

cards.fact: Ethiopians say their gods are snub-nosed and black; Thracians say theirs are blue-eyed and red-haired.
cards.context: That’s Xenophanes again, noticing that each people’s gods look like that people. Taking a story everyone grew up with and questioning it out loud, with reasons: that’s philosophy in action.

levels.title: Thales and the First Questions
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how early thinkers looked for natural explanations.
levels.summary: Thales of Miletus said everything comes from water and explained earthquakes without Poseidon; Anaximander and Anaximenes offered the boundless and air.

cards.headline: The first philosopher, the story goes, fell into a well while stargazing.
cards.body: In Plato’s telling, a Thracian servant girl mocked him for gazing at the sky while missing what was at his feet. So what was Thales looking for up there?

cards.headline: Everything is water
cards.body: Thales lived in Miletus, a Greek city on the coast of what is now Turkey, in the early 6th century BCE. According to Aristotle, he said water is the origin of all things, and that the earth rests on water. Why water? Aristotle guessed that Thales noticed the food of every creature is moist, and seeds are moist too. Look around your kitchen: it’s not a crazy guess.

mascot.line: Wrong answer, right question. Honestly, that’s how a lot of good science starts.

cards.headline: Earthquakes without Poseidon
cards.body: Now the bold part. The Roman writer Seneca reports that Thales used his floating earth to explain earthquakes: the land rides on water like a boat, and rough water rocks it. The old answer was an angry god, Poseidon, shaking the ground. Thales was wrong. But he offered a natural cause that people could argue about and improve, and that was new.

cards.headline: Arguing with the teacher
cards.body: Improving is exactly what happened next, in the same city. Anaximander, Thales’s pupil or associate, said the source of everything wasn’t water but the apeiron, “the boundless”. Anaximenes, a third thinker from Miletus, chose air: thin it and it becomes fire; thicken it and it turns to wind, cloud, water, earth and finally stone. One city, three thinkers, three answers.

levels.title: Pythagoras
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Pythagoras and his followers.
levels.summary: Pythagoras led a rule-bound community at Croton in southern Italy; his followers believed souls are reborn in animals and that all things are numbers.

cards.headline: “Stop beating that puppy!” said Pythagoras. “It has a dead friend’s soul.”
cards.body: That story comes from Xenophanes, the critic from Level 51, and he told it as a joke. But a joke needs a real target. What did Pythagoras believe?

cards.headline: Souls that move house
cards.body: Pythagoreans believed that after death a human soul is reborn in other animals, so all living things are kin. That’s what Xenophanes was mocking: a friend’s soul, now in a puppy. The belief came with a whole way of life, run by strict rules. Pythagoreans wore white, entered temples barefoot and, most famously, did not eat beans.

cards.headline: A brotherhood in Italy
cards.body: Pythagoras grew up on the island of Samos and, about 530 BCE, moved to Croton, a Greek city in southern Italy. There he gathered followers into a community. Later tradition says newcomers had to keep silent for five years. Pythagoras seems to have written no books, so what we know of him comes from other, mostly later, writers. Legends grow fast in that kind of silence.

cards.headline: All things are numbers
cards.body: Pythagoreans found numbers hiding in music. The central harmonies, the octave, the fifth and the fourth, match the simple whole-number ratios 2 : 1, 3 : 2 and 4 : 3. If something as moving as music runs on arithmetic, what else might? The Pythagoreans’ answer: everything. Numbers were the key to the world, summed up as “all things are numbers”.

cards.fact: The Pythagorean theorem is older than Pythagoras.
cards.context: Babylonian tablets from about 1900–1600 BCE already show knowledge of it, and there’s no evidence Pythagoras proved it himself. He got his name on it anyway. Some people have all the luck.

levels.title: Socrates
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Socrates' method of questioning.
levels.summary: Socrates wrote nothing and is known through Plato and Xenophon. He questioned people who seemed wise, testing their definitions, and turned philosophy toward how to live.

cards.headline: The oracle at Delphi said no one was wiser than Socrates. He set out to check.
cards.body: In Plato’s telling, his friend Chaerephon asked the question, and the answer puzzled Socrates, who didn’t think he was wise at all. His way of checking changed philosophy.

cards.headline: Known only through others
cards.body: First, a warning label. Socrates, who lived in Athens from about 470 to 399 BCE, wrote nothing. We know him mainly through two of his followers, Plato and Xenophon. So whenever you read “Socrates said”, it really means “Plato or Xenophon says Socrates said”. The most famous talker in philosophy never left us a single word of his own.

cards.headline: Testing the oracle
cards.body: Socrates went to people with a reputation for wisdom: politicians, poets, craftsmen. He questioned them and found they thought they knew things they didn’t. His verdict, in Plato’s Apology: he was wiser in only one small way. What he didn’t know, he didn’t think he knew. Knowing what you don’t know turns out to be a head start.

mascot.line: Ask “what is courage?” and keep asking. It gets harder, not easier. That’s the point.

cards.headline: How the questions worked
cards.body: His method, the elenchus, tested definitions until the contradictions showed. In Plato’s Laches, a general defines courage as staying at your post and not running away. But, Socrates asks, can’t a retreat take courage too? Try again: courage is endurance of the soul. Then is foolish endurance courage? The dialogue ends with no answer, and two men who know they don’t know.

cards.headline: Down from the heavens
cards.body: Remember Thales, gazing at the stars and asking what everything is made of? Socrates turned philosophy around. As the Roman writer Cicero put it, Socrates was the first to call philosophy down from the heavens and bring it into cities and homes, to ask about life, morals, good and evil. Not what the world is made of, but how you should live in it.

levels.title: The Trial of Socrates
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Athens sentenced Socrates to death.
levels.summary: In 399 BCE Socrates was tried for impiety and corrupting the young, amid suspicion over his companion Critias; convicted narrowly, he drank hemlock.

cards.headline: In 399 BCE, Athens put a philosopher of about 70 on trial for his life.
cards.body: His accusers said his questions had done real harm. How does asking questions become a crime?

cards.headline: The charges
cards.body: The charges were impiety, not honoring the city’s gods, and corrupting the young. The accusers were Meletus, Anytus and Lycon, and the case went to a jury of about 500 citizens. In his defense, as Plato tells it, Socrates called himself a gadfly stuck to Athens, a big, sluggish horse that needed stinging awake. Horses tend to swat gadflies.

cards.headline: Why then?
cards.body: Timing mattered. After Athens lost its war with Sparta, a group called the Thirty Tyrants, led by Critias, ruled the city in 404–403 BCE. Critias had been a companion of Socrates. An amnesty in 403 BCE had closed that chapter, and the formal charges were about gods and the young. But suspicion of Critias’s old companion hadn’t gone away.

mascot.line: Proposing a reward instead of a penalty. Bold move. Not a winning one.

cards.headline: A cheeky counter-offer
cards.body: Socrates was found guilty; in Plato’s Apology he says that if just 30 votes had gone the other way, he’d have been acquitted. Then he had to propose a penalty. His suggestion: free meals in the Prytaneum, the honor Athens gave Olympic victors. It was not a crowd-pleaser. The jury chose death.

cards.headline: The cup
cards.body: Friends planned to get him out of prison. In Plato’s Crito, Socrates refuses: he must not break Athens’ laws. So he was put to death by drinking hemlock. In Plato’s Phaedo, the numbness rises from his legs until it reaches his heart. Tried for his questions, he chose the laws over escape.

levels.title: Plato
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Plato's Academy and his allegory of the cave.
levels.summary: Plato, Socrates’ student, wrote dialogues and founded the Academy in the 380s BCE. His cave allegory shows prisoners taking shadows for reality.

cards.headline: Imagine you’d spent your whole life watching shadows on a wall.
cards.body: You’d think the shadows were everything. That’s the start of Plato’s most famous story. Before we step into the cave, meet the man who told it.

cards.headline: Socrates’ student
cards.body: Plato, born in Athens around 428 BCE, was a student of Socrates and was deeply affected by his death. He wrote dialogues, usually with Socrates as the main speaker. In the 380s BCE he set up a school outside the walls of Athens, at a grove called the Akademeia: the Academy. Every academy since, including the one on your local school sign, borrows its name.

cards.headline: The cave
cards.body: In the Republic, Plato imagines prisoners chained in a cave, facing a wall. Behind them a fire burns, and the objects moving in front of it cast shadows on the wall. The shadows are all the prisoners have ever seen, so to them, shadows are reality. Now free one prisoner. Dazzled by the fire, he is dragged up into sunlight, where he sees real things, and at last the sun itself.

cards.headline: The way out
cards.body: For Plato, our senses show us shadows: imperfect copies. Real knowledge means climbing toward the Forms, perfect models such as Justice, Beauty and Equality. The sun stands for the highest of all, the Good. Think of every wobbly circle you’ve ever drawn. You still know what a perfect circle is, though you’ve never drawn one.

cards.fact: The prisoners would kill whoever tried to lead them out.
cards.context: The freed man goes back down to tell the others, and they laugh at him. Plato has Socrates say they’d put to death anyone who tried to free them. Many readers hear an echo of Socrates’ own fate. Remember the hemlock in Level 55?

levels.title: Aristotle
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the huge range of things Aristotle studied.
levels.summary: Aristotle studied with Plato for 20 years, then founded the Lyceum. He built the first logic, catalogued over 500 animal species and defined virtue as a mean.

cards.headline: Logic, animals, politics, poetry, ethics: Aristotle wrote about all of them.
cards.body: And that’s the short list. How did one person cover so much? Start with where he learned.

cards.headline: Twenty years with Plato
cards.body: Aristotle was born in 384 BCE in Stagira, in northern Greece. He joined Plato’s Academy in 367 BCE, aged 17, and stayed 20 years as pupil and then colleague. He still argued with his teacher, above all about the Forms. As he put it, friends and truth are both dear, but it’s our duty to prefer the truth. In 335 BCE, back in Athens, he opened his own school: the Lyceum.

mascot.line: A fish story that turned out true. Rarest catch in the sea.

cards.headline: A mind without borders
cards.body: His range is dizzying: logic, physics, biology, ethics, politics, rhetoric, poetry. He created the first systematic logic, a theory of correct reasoning. On the island of Lesbos he studied animals, especially sea creatures, and more than 500 species appear in his works. Some of his unlikely-sounding fish stories were proved right many centuries later. Most fish stories go the other way.

cards.headline: Courage, again
cards.body: Remember Level 54, where the Laches ended without defining courage? Aristotle had a go. Each virtue, he argued, is a middle point between too much and too little. The coward flees every danger; the rash person charges at all of them. Courage sits in between: facing the dangers worth facing, with the right amount of fear.

cards.fact: Of perhaps 200 works by Aristotle, about 31 survive.
cards.context: And the survivors read like lecture notes and drafts, not polished books. Next time your notes look messy, take heart: so did Aristotle’s.

levels.title: Stoics and Epicureans
levels.objective: After this level you can compare two Greek schools about how to live well.
levels.summary: Around 300 BCE two schools opened in Athens: Zeno’s Stoics said virtue is the only good; Epicurus said the goal is pleasure, meaning freedom from pain and worry.

cards.headline: Around 300 BCE, two schools opened in Athens: one on a porch, one in a garden.
cards.body: Both asked the same question: how do you live well? Their answers could hardly be more different.

cards.headline: The porch
cards.body: Zeno of Citium came to Athens about 312 BCE and taught in the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch; his followers were named Stoics after it. Their core claim: virtue is the only true good. Live in harmony with nature, guided by reason. Strong emotions, they held, are errors of judgment, so reason can correct them. Stuck in traffic? A Stoic would say the traffic isn’t the problem; your judgment about it is.

mascot.line: The philosopher of pleasure, celebrating with a pot of cheese. I respect it.

cards.headline: The garden
cards.body: Epicurus opened his school, the Garden, in Athens around 306 BCE, and it admitted women and enslaved people. He called pleasure the goal of life, but defined it as the absence of pain in the body and trouble in the soul. His school lived mainly on barley bread and water. In one letter he asked for a little pot of cheese, so he could have a feast. Wild times.

levels.title: Diogenes and the Cynics
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Diogenes and why he searched for an honest man.
levels.summary: Diogenes of Sinope, called the Dog, lived in poverty and mocked empty customs. His lamp in daylight searched for a real human being; his pupil Crates taught Zeno.

cards.headline: A man walked through the streets in broad daylight, holding a lit lamp.
cards.body: As he went, he said, “I am looking for a man.” His name was Diogenes, and this was his idea of a lesson.

cards.headline: The Dog
cards.body: Diogenes came from Sinope, a Greek city on the Black Sea coast, and was said to have been exiled for adulterating the coinage. In Athens he lived in poverty, begged for food and slept in public places; later he lived in a large storage jar. He did everything in public, which is probably why people called him the Dog. His followers were the Cynics: in Greek, the dog-like ones.

cards.headline: Looking for a man
cards.body: So what was the lamp for? Diogenes taught that virtue meant living simply, according to nature, and throwing out empty customs and luxury. Tradition remembers his search as one for an “honest man”. But in Diogenes Laertius’s ancient account, he just says he is looking for a man. The jab, it seems: in a city full of people, he couldn’t find one living as a real human being should.

mascot.line: Poor Plato. You spend years on a definition and someone brings a chicken.

cards.headline: Nobody was safe
cards.body: Stories about him spare no one. When Plato defined a human as a featherless biped, Diogenes plucked a chicken, brought it in and said, “Here is Plato’s man.” When Alexander the Great offered him any favor, he replied, “Stand out of my light.” Asked where he came from, he answered: “I am a citizen of the world.”

cards.fact: Stoicism has Cynic roots.
cards.context: Diogenes taught Crates, and Crates taught Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism from Level 58. Living by nature runs through both schools. The Stoics just did it with fewer chickens.

levels.title: Euclid's Geometry
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what Euclid’s Elements did for mathematics.
levels.summary: Around 300 BCE in Alexandria, Euclid built the Elements: 13 books proving geometry step by step from a few stated starting points. It set the standard for proof for over 2,000 years.

cards.headline: Around 300 BCE, a Greek wrote a math book. It taught for 2,000 years.
cards.body: Euclid’s Elements didn’t last because it was packed with new facts. It lasted because of how it made you sure of them.

cards.headline: Start with almost nothing
cards.body: Euclid worked in Alexandria, in Egypt, around 300 BCE. Book I of his Elements opens with 23 definitions (“A point is that which has no part”), then five postulates and five common notions: starting points you accept without proof. Everything after that is proved, step by step, from them alone. Think of a recipe that lists every ingredient up front and never sneaks in a new one halfway through.

cards.headline: Old results, new building
cards.body: Euclid didn’t discover most of it. He compiled the Elements from the work of earlier mathematicians, but the design of the whole was his own. Across 13 books he moves from flat shapes to numbers to solid, three-dimensional figures, and each result rests on the ones proved before it. His real invention was the architecture: a heap of known results turned into one building where every brick holds up the next.

cards.fact: The Elements has had more than 1,000 editions since it was first printed in 1482.
cards.context: Its way of proving things and teaching geometry lasted, practically unchanged, for more than 2,000 years. If you’ve ever written a proof in a geometry class, you’ve worked in Euclid’s style.

mascot.line: No royal road, but plenty of footpaths. You’re on one right now.

cards.headline: No royal road
cards.body: Centuries later, the philosopher Proclus told a story: King Ptolemy asked Euclid for a shorter way to learn geometry than the Elements. Euclid replied that there is no royal road to geometry. True or not, it sums up the book. Every step has to be earned, even if you’re a king.

levels.title: Archimedes
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Archimedes’ discoveries about levers and floating.
levels.summary: Archimedes of Syracuse worked out the law of the lever and showed that an object in a fluid is lighter by the weight of the fluid it displaces. The naked “Eureka!” run is a later embellishment.

cards.headline: Archimedes ran naked through the streets shouting “Eureka!” Probably not.
cards.body: That part is later embellishment. But the science behind the story is real, and so is another idea of his you’ve used on every seesaw.

cards.headline: The seesaw rule
cards.body: Archimedes lived in Syracuse, on Sicily, from about 287 BCE until 212 or 211 BCE. He showed that weights balance on a lever at distances from the pivot in inverse proportion to the weights. That’s the seesaw trick: an adult twice your weight balances you by sitting half as far from the middle. Go far enough out, and a small weight can balance a huge one.

cards.headline: Move the Earth?
cards.body: So a famous line got pinned on him: “Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.” It comes from Pappus of Alexandria, writing around 340 CE, more than five centuries later, and it’s probably not Archimedes’ own words. But it is the lever rule, pushed to the limit. With a long enough lever, anything moves. Finding the place to stand is your problem.

mascot.line: Keep your clothes on for this one. The science works just as well.

cards.headline: Lighter in water
cards.body: In On Floating Bodies, Archimedes showed that a solid denser than a fluid, dipped into it, is lighter by the weight of the fluid it pushes aside. The Roman writer Vitruvius tells how he used water to test whether King Hiero’s gold wreath had been secretly mixed with silver. The test is probably true. The naked dash through the streets shouting “Eureka!” is later embellishment.

cards.fact: Archimedes died when Rome captured his city.
cards.context: His war machines long delayed the Roman capture of Syracuse. When the city finally fell, in 212 or 211 BCE, he was killed in the sack.

levels.title: Eratosthenes Measures the Earth
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Eratosthenes estimated Earth’s size.
levels.summary: Eratosthenes compared the noon Sun at Syene and Alexandria, used Euclid’s geometry of parallel lines, and multiplied by 50 to get Earth’s circumference: 250,000 stadia.

cards.headline: His nickname was “Beta”: second best. He measured the whole Earth anyway.
cards.body: No ship, no satellite, no trip around the world. Just a shadow, a rule from geometry and a little multiplication.

cards.headline: Second at everything
cards.body: Eratosthenes was born in Cyrene around 276 BCE, settled in Alexandria and became director of its great library. He worked in so many fields that people called him Beta: like an all-round athlete who takes second prize in every event. A backhanded compliment. But measuring a planet takes astronomy, geography and geometry at once, so a good all-rounder was exactly who you’d want.

cards.headline: Two cities, one Sun
cards.body: At noon on the summer solstice, the Sun shone straight down at Syene, in southern Egypt. At Alexandria it stood about 7° from vertical, about one-fiftieth of a circle. Eratosthenes assumed the Sun’s rays arrive parallel. Then a rule from Level 61’s Euclid does the work: a line crossing two parallel lines makes equal angles with them. So those 7° at Alexandria are also the angle at Earth’s center between the two cities.

mascot.line: Second best at everything, first to measure the planet. I’ll take that trade.

cards.headline: Times fifty
cards.body: If the angle is one-fiftieth of a circle, the distance from Syene to Alexandria is one-fiftieth of the way around the world. Multiply it by 50 and you have Earth’s circumference. His answer: 250,000 stadia. How close was that? It depends on how long his stadion was, so estimates of his error run from 0.5 to 17 percent. Not bad for second best.

levels.title: Greek Astronomy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Greek models of the heavens.
levels.summary: Eudoxus built an Earth-centered sky of 27 nested spheres; Aristarchus put the Sun at the center but couldn’t explain why the stars didn’t shift; Hipparchus measured stars and found precession.

cards.headline: The Greeks agreed the heavens moved in circles. They argued about the center.
cards.body: Most put Earth there. One put the Sun there instead. Here’s how Greek astronomers built a sky out of spheres, and why the Sun-centered idea lost.

cards.headline: A sky of nested spheres
cards.body: In the 4th century BCE, Eudoxus of Cnidus modeled the heavens with 27 spheres around Earth: one for the stars, three each for the Sun and Moon, and four for each planet. Picture nesting dolls, all turning around you. His rule that every heavenly motion is uniform and circular stuck: Aristotle endorsed it, and it stayed orthodox until Kepler in the 1600s.

cards.headline: The Sun in the middle
cards.body: Aristarchus of Samos (about 310 to 230 BCE) proposed something bolder: the Sun at the center, with Earth moving around it. The best surviving description of his idea comes from Level 62’s Archimedes, in a book called the Sand-Reckoner. Archimedes noted the catch: if it were true, the universe would be vastly larger than anyone believed.

cards.headline: Why the Sun lost
cards.body: If Earth moves, the stars should seem to shift as you watch from different points on its path. Nobody could see any shift, and backers of the Sun-centered idea couldn’t explain why. So it won little support. The Greeks weren’t being stubborn: they were following the evidence they could see.

cards.headline: Checking the old records
cards.body: In the 2nd century BCE, Hipparchus catalogued about 850 stars. Comparing his observations with ones from the 5th and 3rd centuries BCE, he found stars had shifted about 2°: the precession of the equinoxes. Old notes, compared carefully, revealed a slow drift of the stars. Around 150 CE, Ptolemy’s Almagest built on his work and kept Earth at the center.

levels.title: The Antikythera Mechanism
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the ancient Greek geared calculator.
levels.summary: Found in a shipwreck in 1901, the Antikythera mechanism (about 100 BCE) used 30 surviving bronze gears to show the Sun, Moon and eclipses. Nothing as complex is known for about a thousand years.

cards.headline: In 1901, divers raised lumps of bronze from a wreck. It was a sky calculator.
cards.body: Nothing as complex survives from the ancient world. Here’s what it did.

cards.headline: A wreck full of surprises
cards.body: The mechanism came from a trading ship that sank in the first half of the 1st century BCE, off the small island of Antikythera. Sponge divers found the wreck, and in 1901 the device came up in corroded fragments. It had been made around 100 BCE, give or take 30 years. From the outside it looked like junk. The inside was another story.

mascot.line: A whole sky in a box, run by a crank. I would never get any work done.

cards.headline: Thirty gears inside
cards.body: X-ray images showed that the fragments hold 30 bronze gear wheels. Turn a hand crank and the gears moved pointers that showed the Sun and Moon in the zodiac, the Moon’s phases on a half-silvered ball, and eclipses to come. Think of a clock that tells you not the hour but the sky.

cards.fact: It even knew when the Olympics were due.
cards.context: The mechanism showed when the Panhellenic games, including the ancient Olympic Games, would take place. The same bronze gears predicted eclipses and kept the sports calendar.

cards.headline: A thousand years ahead
cards.body: No geared mechanism as complex is known from the ancient world, or from anywhere until medieval cathedral clocks, about a thousand years later. That’s what makes it so startling. It isn’t just old. It’s a machine nobody else managed to match for a millennium.

levels.title: Hippocrates
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Hippocrates’ approach to medicine.
levels.summary: Hippocratic writers treated diseases as having natural causes, even epilepsy, the “sacred disease”, and recorded case histories. Most of the 60 writings under Hippocrates’ name aren’t by him.

cards.headline: Epilepsy was “the sacred disease.” One Greek medical book called that an excuse.
cards.body: That book belongs to a collection linked to Hippocrates. Its big idea: diseases have natural causes.

cards.headline: A name on a shelf
cards.body: Hippocrates lived from about 460 to 375 BCE and worked on the island of Cos. Plato mentions him as an admired physician and teacher, but facts about his life are hard to separate from later tales. About 60 medical writings carry his name, and most weren’t written by him. So “Hippocrates” is part man, part label on a whole shelf of Greek medicine.

cards.headline: Not sacred after all
cards.body: One of those writings, On the Sacred Disease, takes on epilepsy. Its author says it is “nowise more divine nor more sacred than other diseases, but has a natural cause”, and he places that cause in the brain. People who blamed the gods, he says, were using them as a screen for their own inability to cure it. Look for causes in the body, not in the heavens.

cards.headline: Natural, but not always right
cards.body: Hippocratic writers recorded case histories and cared about diagnosis and prognosis: what’s wrong, and what will happen next. Their natural explanations weren’t always correct. On the Nature of Man taught that health is a balance of four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. The idea was still current in Europe’s Middle Ages. Natural, yes. Right, no.

cards.fact: The Hippocratic Oath probably wasn’t written by Hippocrates.
cards.context: It dates to about 400 BCE. Doctors swore by Apollo and other gods to give only beneficial treatment and keep patients’ secrets. Revised versions are still used at many medical school graduations.

levels.title: The First Atoms
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Democritus’s idea that everything is made of atoms.
levels.summary: Leucippus and Democritus argued that everything is made of uncuttable atoms moving in the void. No one could see one to check, and Aristotle rejected the idea.

cards.headline: Cut a pebble in half. Then again. And again. Where does it stop?
cards.body: Two Greek thinkers said the cutting has to end somewhere, at a piece too small to cut. They called it the atom.

cards.headline: The uncuttable
cards.body: Leucippus and his pupil Democritus, a citizen of Abdera born about 460 BCE, built the theory. Everything, they said, is made of atoms: pieces too small to be divided, which is what the name means. Between the atoms is the void, empty space for them to move through. Atoms and void. That was the whole universe.

cards.headline: An alphabet of matter
cards.body: Atoms differ only in shape, arrangement, position and size. Water and iron differ by how their atoms are put together. Aristotle explained it with letters: A differs from N in shape, AN from NA in arrangement, and N from Z in position (turn an N on its side). A few letters make endless words. A few kinds of atoms make the world.

cards.headline: Sweet by convention
cards.body: So where do taste and color come from? Democritus put it bluntly: “by convention sweet and by convention bitter, by convention hot, by convention cold, by convention color; but in reality atoms and void.” Sweetness isn’t out there in the atoms. Only atoms and void are really there.

mascot.line: An idea you can’t see, defended by pure reasoning. Bold move.

cards.fact: No one could look at an atom to check.
cards.context: The atoms seemed far too small to perceive, so the theory stood on argument alone. Aristotle wasn’t convinced: he rejected atomism, refusing to believe that all of reality comes down to atoms.

levels.title: Mapping the Known World
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Greek maps of the world.
levels.summary: Anaximander drew the first Greek world maps on a drum-shaped Earth; Eratosthenes coined geography and drew a grid; Ptolemy listed about 8,000 places by latitude and longitude.

cards.headline: How do you map the world when you’ve only seen a slice of it?
cards.body: Greek mapmakers started with a drum-shaped Earth and ended with a grid of numbers. Here’s how the known world got drawn.

cards.headline: A world on a drum
cards.body: Anaximander of Miletus (about 610 to 546 BCE) drew a map of the known world, later corrected by his fellow Milesian Hecataeus. He pictured Earth as a squat cylinder, like a drum, one-third as thick as it is wide, held up by nothing at all. People lived on the flat top. Wrong shape, bold idea: a world that doesn’t need anything to stand on.

cards.headline: Eratosthenes draws a grid
cards.body: Remember Level 63’s Eratosthenes? He also invented geography as a subject, probably coining the word geographia itself. His Geographika placed some 400 places, from Thoule (probably Iceland) to Taprobane (Sri Lanka), on a grid of lines we’d call parallels and meridians. Now faraway places could be placed in relation to each other.

mascot.line: A map you can send as a list of numbers. The ancient world’s version of sharing your location!

cards.headline: A world made of numbers
cards.body: In the 2nd century CE, Ptolemy’s Geography went further: it gave the latitude and longitude, in degrees, of about 8,000 places. That’s a map written as a list, so anyone could redraw it. When it was translated into Latin between 1406 and 1409, its grid gave Renaissance mapmakers a framework to fill.

levels.title: Greek Inventions
levels.objective: After this level you can name Greek inventions, from the water mill to the steam toy.
levels.summary: Ctesibius improved the water clock; Hero’s aeolipile spun on steam but powered only toys; the water mill spread from Greece and freed people from grinding grain by hand.

cards.headline: The Greeks built a steam engine. They used it to spin toys.
cards.body: Other Greek machines did go to work: clocks, pumps and mills that ran on water, air and steam.

cards.headline: A clock that drips
cards.body: Ctesibius of Alexandria, working around 270 BCE, improved the water clock. Water dripped in at a steady rate and raised a float, and the float held a pointer that marked the hours. He also invented force pumps and a water organ, in which the weight of water forced air through the pipes. Time, pressure and music, all from plumbing.

cards.headline: Steam, just for fun
cards.body: More than three centuries later, around 62 CE, Hero of Alexandria described the aeolipile: a sphere with two bent nozzles. Steam rushing out of the nozzles spun it round. It counts as the first steam-powered engine, and it was used to power toys and amuse visitors. His Pneumatica also describes coin-operated machines, singing birds and a fire engine.

cards.headline: The mill that freed hands
cards.body: One Greek invention truly went to work. One of the oldest references to a water mill is a Greek poem celebrating that it freed the young women who ground grain in hand mills from their toil. Easy to build and able to run in any fast stream, the water mill spread from Greece and was in use throughout Europe by the end of the 3rd century CE.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Science and Math
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Greek thinkers used reason to study nature.
levels.summary: Greek thinkers studied nature through proof, measurement and argument, looking for natural causes. Archimedes prized a proof enough to want it on his grave.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: Archimedes built war machines. His tomb showed geometry.
cards.body: That choice says a lot about how Greek thinkers ranked their work, and how they went about studying nature.

cards.headline: A sphere in a cylinder
cards.body: Archimedes proved that a sphere has two-thirds the volume of the cylinder that just holds it, and he asked for a sphere in a cylinder on his tomb. About a century and a half later, Cicero found it, overgrown with plants. According to Plutarch, Archimedes thought so little of practical inventions that he wrote nothing about them. The proof, not the machine, was the prize.

cards.headline: Three ways to reason about nature

items.label: Proof
points: Euclid proved geometry from stated starting points
Archimedes worked out the law of the lever

items.label: Measurement
points: Eratosthenes turned a 7° angle into Earth’s size
Hipparchus compared star positions across centuries

items.label: Argument
points: Hippocratic writers sought natural causes of disease
Democritus argued for atoms no one could see

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: Put Chapter 7 together. Greek thinkers looked for natural causes, not divine ones, and trusted reasoning that could be checked: a proof, a measured angle, a star position in an old record. They got plenty wrong, from a drum-shaped Earth to the four humors. But checking was built in. Comparing old records is exactly how Hipparchus found the stars slowly drifting.
