levels.title: The Theater
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Greek theaters and the festivals they served.
levels.summary: Athens staged plays as contests at the City Dionysia, the spring festival of Dionysus; theaters set seats on a hillside around a round dancing floor.

cards.headline: In ancient Athens, the best seat at the play was saved for a god.
cards.body: Not for a king or a general, but for Dionysus himself. That tells you something important: a Greek play wasn’t a night out. It was a festival.

cards.headline: A holy day with a prize
cards.body: Athens staged its plays at the City Dionysia, the spring festival of Dionysus, in his theater on the south slope of the Acropolis. On festival days the god’s image was carried in from his nearby temple, so he could be present at the plays. And the plays competed: each chosen poet entered three tragedies and a satyr play, and a panel of judges picked the winner. Picture a film festival that is also a religious holiday.

cards.fact: Poor Athenians were given their theater money.
cards.context: At first, admission was free. When a charge came in later, poor citizens were handed the entrance money. Imagine your city covering your ticket because the show was part of a holy day.

mascot.line: Next time you hear an orchestra tune up, remember: the word first meant a patch of ground for dancing.

cards.headline: A seeing place on a hill
cards.body: Greek theaters grew out of a flat patch of ground in front of a natural hill, with the audience sitting on the slope. The words still carry the floor plan. Theatron meant “a place of seeing”. The orchestra was the flat, round dancing place in the middle. Actors dressed in the skene, a small tent at the back, which gave us the word “scene”. Go “behind the scenes” and you’re in a Greek changing tent.

cards.fact: Some Greek theaters still work.
cards.context: The theater at Epidaurus was built into a mountainside in the late 4th century BCE and is famed for its acoustics. Every summer, a festival still stages ancient drama there. You can sit on the same slope and hear the same plays.

levels.title: Tragedy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Greek tragedy and its great writers.
levels.summary: Tragedy grew from a chorus to three masked actors; Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides wrote about 300 tragedies, of which about 33 survive.

cards.headline: Three Athenians wrote about 300 tragedies. About 33 survive.
cards.body: Who were they, what did their plays look like on stage, and why did the least successful of the three end up with the most plays today?

cards.headline: One actor, then two, then three
cards.body: Tragedy started with a chorus. Tradition credits Thespis, in the 6th century BCE, as the first actor to speak apart from it; actors are still called thespians. Aeschylus added a second actor and Sophocles a third. That was the limit: never more than three speaking actors. All were men, all in masks, so one man could come back as a queen with a change of face. A chorus of up to 15 men sang and danced.

cards.headline: Stories the audience already knew
cards.body: Tragedies almost always took their plots from myth. The audience knew the outline, but not which version the playwright would tell. Aeschylus’s Oresteia, staged in 458 BCE, is the only complete Greek trilogy to survive. It opens with Agamemnon coming home from the Trojan War, and his wife, Clytemnestra, murdering him. Everyone knew the king would die. The suspense was in how.

mascot.line: Four wins in a lifetime, and still the most-read of the three. Some reviews just take a while to come in.

cards.headline: Lose the festival, win the library
cards.body: Aeschylus wrote about 90 plays and Sophocles about 123; seven of each survive. Euripides wrote 92, and 19 survive, counting one disputed. That’s about 33 plays out of some 300. Yet Euripides won only four first prizes in his lifetime, against perhaps 24 for Sophocles. His fame grew later and eclipsed both rivals, and that’s why more of his work made it to us.

levels.title: Comedy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Greek comedy and Aristophanes.
levels.summary: Aristophanes’s Old Comedy mocked real people with fantasy and satire; Menander’s New Comedy turned to everyday life and was recovered from papyrus.

cards.headline: In 405 BCE, a prize-winning comedy sent a god to fetch a dead playwright.
cards.body: Greek comedy could laugh at anyone: politicians, philosophers, even Dionysus, the god of the festival itself.

cards.headline: Old Comedy: nobody was safe
cards.body: Aristophanes is the master of Athens’s Old Comedy. He wrote about 40 plays, and 11 survive. They mix wild fantasy with political satire aimed at real, named people. In Knights (424 BCE) he went after the powerful politician Cleon. In Clouds (423 BCE) he mocked Socrates. Picture a sketch show roasting your country’s leaders by name.

cards.headline: Jokes with a point
cards.body: In Lysistrata (411 BCE), the women of Athens and Sparta go on strike: no sex until their husbands end the Peloponnesian War. In Frogs, which won first prize in 405 BCE, Dionysus goes down to the underworld to bring back Euripides, judges a contest between him and Aeschylus, and brings back Aeschylus instead. Remember Level 72’s tragedians? Comedy was already reviewing them.

cards.fact: Menander’s best-kept comedy was printed in 1958.
cards.context: Menander (about 342–292 BCE) was the star of New Comedy, which swapped politics for everyday life: stern fathers, young lovers, scheming slaves. He wrote over 100 plays, and they were long lost. The Dyskolos, about a grumpy old man, came back from a papyrus found in Egypt. It’s the only one of his plays to survive nearly complete. Family trouble, stock characters, happy ending: sound familiar?

levels.title: Greek Music
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the lyre and the aulos.
levels.summary: Greek music centered on the lyre, with its tortoise-shell sound box, and the aulos, a pair of reed pipes; Homer shows a singer performing to the lyre.

cards.headline: A blind singer took down his lyre and sang. One guest hid his tears.
cards.body: The guest was Odysseus, hearing a song about himself, in Homer’s Odyssey. For Greeks, stories came with music. So what were they playing?

cards.headline: The lyre: a tortoise that sings
cards.body: Greeks told a myth about it: the baby god Hermes made the first lyre from a tortoise shell, then stole Apollo’s cattle, and calmed Apollo by giving him the lyre. Real lyres kept the idea. The common kind had a tortoise-shell sound box, with two arms and a crossbar holding the strings. It was played alone or to accompany singing and poetry, and learning it was part of a Greek education. Its inventor, officially, was a cattle thief.

cards.headline: The aulos: pipes with bite
cards.body: Greece’s other great instrument was the aulos: a reed pipe, usually played in pairs, one in each hand. It’s often translated “flute”, but its reeds made it sound more like an oboe. Players often strapped a leather band across their cheeks. The aulos often accompanied choruses, and it played at the theater, in worship of Dionysus, at athletic contests and at drinking parties. Remember Level 71’s dancing chorus? The aulos was often its soundtrack.

cards.fact: Homer shows a singer performing to the lyre.
cards.context: In the Odyssey, the blind singer Demodocus takes his lyre from a peg at the Phaeacian feast and sings of a quarrel between Odysseus and Achilles. Odysseus, listening at the table, hides his tears. Level 6 said Homer’s poems grew out of singers performing. Here is Homer’s own picture of one.

levels.title: Sappho and Poetry
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Greek lyric poetry and Sappho.
levels.summary: Lyric poetry, named for the lyre, was sung and often personal; Sappho of Lesbos was its most admired poet, though her nine books survive only in fragments.

cards.headline: The ancients called her the Tenth Muse. Only one of her poems reached us whole.
cards.body: Nine books of poems, and time kept almost none of it. The rest is being pieced together from rubbish and a mummy’s wrappings.

cards.headline: Songs for the lyre
cards.body: Remember Level 74’s lyre? It gave its name to lyric poetry, which Greeks performed to its music, and which often spoke of personal feeling. It came in two kinds: solo songs, by poets such as Sappho and Alcaeus, and songs for a chorus, by poets such as Pindar. A lyric poem wasn’t read quietly. It was sung.

cards.headline: Sappho of Lesbos
cards.body: Sappho lived about 610–570 BCE on the island of Lesbos. She wrote about love and desire, weddings and the women of her circle, and her style was admired in every age. Scholars in Alexandria later gathered her poems into nine books. That edition was lost by the early Middle Ages. Only one poem, an ode to Aphrodite, came down to us complete. It’s like knowing a singer from one full track and a box of torn lyric sheets.

mascot.line: Somebody threw these poems away, and somebody else dug them up. Archaeology is a very slow recycling program.

cards.headline: Poems from the rubbish heap
cards.body: The rest comes from quotations by other ancient writers, and from papyrus. Many scraps were dug up at Oxyrhynchus, an ancient rubbish dump in Egypt; others had been recycled into the plaster-like wrapping of a mummy. In 2004 scholars published papyrus that almost completed her poem on old age, and in 2013 more fragments surfaced. Sappho is still arriving, one scrap at a time.

levels.title: Sculpture
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Greek sculpture became lifelike.
levels.summary: Greek statues moved from the stiff kouros to the relaxed Kritios Boy; most bronzes were melted down, so we know many through Roman marble copies and a few sea finds.

cards.headline: In 1972, two Greek bronze warriors came up from the sea off southern Italy.
cards.body: They had been lost at sea, and that’s exactly why we still have them. First, though: how did Greek statues learn to look alive?

cards.headline: From attention to at ease
cards.body: Early Greek statues stood at attention. Archaic kouroi, carved from about 615–590 BCE on, face stiffly forward, left foot slightly forward, arms at their sides. Then, just after 480 BCE, a marble youth from the Athenian Acropolis, the Kritios Boy, shifted his weight onto his left leg and bent his right knee. That relaxed stance is contrapposto. Weight on both feet looks like a statue; weight on one looks like a person waiting for a bus.

cards.headline: The lost bronzes
cards.body: Many famous Greek statues were bronze, and most full-size bronzes were later melted down. Polyclitus’s Spear Bearer, from about 450–440 BCE, is gone; we know it only through Roman copies. Marble is weaker than bronze, so those copies needed props, often carved as tree trunks. See a stump beside a marble god’s leg? You may be looking at a Roman copy of a Greek bronze.

cards.fact: The sea saved the Riace Bronzes.
cards.context: The two warriors were probably made in the mid-5th century BCE and spent the centuries since underwater off the coast of southern Italy, where no one could melt them down. Brought up in 1972, they are among the few full-size Greek bronzes to survive. Losing them was the best thing that ever happened to them.

levels.title: Painted Pottery
levels.objective: After this level you can explain black-figure and red-figure pottery.
levels.summary: Black-figure painted black figures and scratched in details; red-figure, from about 530 BCE, flipped the scheme; prize amphorae kept black-figure for centuries.

cards.headline: Win a contest in Athens, and your prize came in a painted jar of olive oil.
cards.body: Greek pots weren’t made for museum shelves. They mixed wine, stored oil and carried prizes, and on their sides painters reinvented how to draw a body.

cards.headline: Black-figure: paint the shape, scratch the detail
cards.body: The first great style was black-figure. It began in Corinth about 700 BCE. Painters filled in each figure in black on the bare clay, then scratched fine details through the black with a sharp point. Bold silhouettes, crisp lines, and not much room for a subtle expression.

cards.headline: Red-figure: the big flip
cards.body: About 530 BCE, painters in Athens flipped the system. Now the background was painted black, and the figures were left the red of the clay. Details went on with a brush instead of being scratched. A brush curves and flows, so painters had more freedom to show bodies, movement and faces. Red-figure became the dominant style.

cards.headline: Pots with jobs
cards.body: These were working pots. A krater was a big bowl for mixing wine with water. Prize amphorae at Athens’s Panathenaic Games came full of olive oil, with Athena on one side and the contest on the other. And they kept black-figure long after other pottery dropped it: one at Harvard dates to 340–339 BCE, nearly two centuries after red-figure arrived. A trophy doesn’t chase fashion.

levels.title: The Column Orders
levels.objective: After this level you can name the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders.
levels.summary: Greek columns come in three orders: Doric from the mainland, Ionic from Asia Minor, and Corinthian, the latest, first seen on a monument to a Dionysia victory.

cards.headline: A Roman architect traced a column style to a grave. Basket, tile, weeds.
cards.body: It’s a story, not a record. But it’s a good way into the three styles of Greek column, and where they came from.

cards.headline: Three orders, read from the top

items.label: Doric
points: No base; a plain, cushion-like capital
Began on the Greek mainland

items.label: Ionic
points: Scrolls curl at the capital; stands on a base
Began in the Greek cities of Asia Minor

items.label: Corinthian
points: Capital wrapped in acanthus leaves

cards.headline: Two shores, one wooden past
cards.body: Doric and Ionic grew up at nearly the same time on opposite shores of the Aegean Sea: Doric on the Greek mainland, Ionic in the Greek cities of Asia Minor. Both began in temples built of wood. The Roman architect Vitruvius even gave them bodies: Doric was proportioned like a man, Ionic like a woman, with its scrolls like curling hair. Sturdy and plain on one shore, slender and curly on the other.

mascot.line: A basket, a tile and a weed. Architecture has had worse origin stories.

cards.headline: The basket on the grave
cards.body: Corinthian came last. Vitruvius told how a basket was left on a Corinthian girl’s grave, covered with a tile. An acanthus plant grew up around it, and the sculptor Callimachus, passing by, turned the leafy basket into a capital. Treat that as legend. The hard evidence stands in Athens: the Monument of Lysicrates, built in 334 BCE to celebrate a victory at the City Dionysia, has the earliest surviving Corinthian columns.

levels.title: The First Historians
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what Herodotus and Thucydides set out to do.
levels.summary: Herodotus inquired into the Greco-Persian Wars and became the father of history; Thucydides, who lived through the Peloponnesian War, wrote it as a possession for all time.

cards.headline: “So that things done by man not be forgotten in time.”
cards.body: That’s how Herodotus opened the first great narrative history of the ancient world. Soon another Greek, Thucydides, set out to do the job differently.

cards.headline: Herodotus asks around
cards.body: Herodotus was born about 484 BCE in Halicarnassus, in Asia Minor. He called his work an inquiry: into the Greco-Persian Wars, and into their cause. He traveled widely, as far as Egypt, and wrote down the traditions people told him without vouching for all of them. That earned him the title “father of history”, and, from critics, a reputation for believing too much.

cards.headline: Thucydides was there
cards.body: Thucydides, an Athenian, lived through the war he wrote about: the Peloponnesian War. He caught the plague that struck Athens in 430–429 BCE. As a general in 424 BCE he failed to save the city of Amphipolis and was exiled for 20 years. His history breaks off in 411 BCE, before the war was over. He wasn’t collecting old stories; he was reporting on his own lifetime.

mascot.line: He said “for all time”, and here you are, still reading him. Fair claim.

cards.fact: Thucydides called his book “a possession for all time”.
cards.context: He admitted that the absence of romance might make it less appealing. But he wasn’t writing to win the applause of the moment, he said. In a chapter full of festival prizes, here’s a writer aiming past the judges, at you.

levels.objective: After this level you can explain Greek achievements in theater, art and writing.
levels.summary: Greek theater, music, poetry, sculpture, pottery and history reached us by lucky routes: later taste, Egyptian papyri, the sea and Roman copies.

cards.headline: Theater and the Arts finale: most of it is lost. What survived got lucky.
cards.body: Plays, poems, statues and pots each reached us by a different road. Follow the roads, and you’ve reviewed the chapter.

cards.headline: Four lucky roads
cards.body: Look at how the survivors got here. Later readers kept copying what they liked, which is why Euripides, with few festival wins, outlasted his rivals. Egypt gave back papyrus: Menander’s Dyskolos, and scraps of Sappho from a rubbish dump and a mummy’s wrapping. The sea hid the Riace warriors from anyone who wanted their metal. And Roman copies in marble kept lost bronzes alive. Survival wasn’t a prize for quality. It was taste and luck.

levels.title: Philip of Macedon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Philip conquered the Greek cities.
levels.summary: Philip II, once a hostage in Thebes, built an army around the long sarissa, beat Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, and was murdered in 336 BCE.

cards.headline: A hostage from Macedonia grew up to become master of Greece.
cards.body: As a young man, Philip was held in Thebes. In 338 BCE he beat Thebes and Athens in a single battle. What did he learn in between?

cards.headline: Schooled by the enemy
cards.body: Around 367 BCE, Philip, a young prince of Macedonia, was sent to Thebes as a hostage and stayed about three years. He used the time well: he studied under Epaminondas, Thebes’ great general. In 359 BCE, at 23, Philip became king of Macedonia. Imagine a rival team’s coach giving you private lessons, then sending you home.

cards.headline: A longer reach
cards.body: Philip rebuilt his army around the sarissa, a pike nearly one and a half times as long as the spear other Greeks carried. Think of a shoving match where your opponent’s pole is half again as long as yours: his point reaches you before yours reaches him. Greek armies were about to find out how that felt.

cards.fact: In 338 BCE Philip beat Athens and Thebes together at Chaeronea.
cards.context: His son Alexander, only 18, commanded the left wing. Remember Level 2’s Athens and Thebes, less than 100 km apart yet foreign rivals? They finally fought side by side, and lost side by side. In 337 BCE Philip gathered the Greek states into the League of Corinth, with himself as leader, and planned a war on Persia.

cards.headline: The war he never fought
cards.body: Philip never reached Persia. In 336 BCE, during celebrations of his daughter’s wedding in the theater at Aegae, his own bodyguard Pausanias stabbed him to death. Alexander, born in 356 BCE, became king at 20. He inherited the army, the league and the plan.

levels.title: The Education of Alexander
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Aristotle taught the young Alexander.
levels.summary: From 13 to 16, Alexander was taught by Aristotle at Mieza; he treasured Aristotle’s edition of the Iliad and traced his family back to Achilles.

cards.headline: Alexander slept with a dagger and a book under his pillow.
cards.body: So Plutarch says. The book was the Iliad, in an edition prepared by his teacher. Who teaches a future conqueror?

cards.headline: The best tutor in Greece
cards.body: Philip sent for Aristotle, in Plutarch’s words ’the most famous and learned of philosophers’, to teach his son. From age 13 to 16, Alexander studied with him in a quiet school in the precinct of the nymphs near Mieza. Aristotle inspired his interest in philosophy, medicine and scientific investigation. Not a bad homeschool.

cards.headline: The tuition fee was a town
cards.body: How do you pay the most famous thinker around? According to Plutarch, Philip rebuilt Aristotle’s hometown, Stageira, and brought back its citizens from exile or slavery. The awkward part: Philip was the one who had destroyed it. Tuition, with an apology built in.

mascot.line: Imagine studying a poem at school and finding your own family in it!

cards.headline: A soldier’s handbook
cards.body: Remember Level 6? Homer’s epics were the basis of Greek education. Alexander took that further. He called the Iliad a handbook of the art of war and carried Aristotle’s edition, the ’Iliad of the Casket’, on campaign. Plutarch says his mother’s family descended from Neoptolemus, son of Achilles. For most Greek boys, the Iliad was a school text. For Alexander, it was family history.

levels.title: Bucephalus
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the story of Alexander's horse.
levels.summary: Plutarch tells how young Alexander tamed Bucephalus by turning him from his shadow; the horse died in India in 326 BCE. The story comes from writers of about four centuries later.

cards.headline: Nobody could ride the horse. Then a boy noticed its shadow.
cards.body: It’s the most famous horse story in history. Here it is, and then the catch: who told it?

cards.headline: 13 talents of trouble
cards.body: Plutarch tells it like this. A horse dealer offered Philip a horse for 13 talents, a fortune. The horse was wild; no one could mount him. Young Alexander noticed the horse was frightened by his own shadow, so he turned him toward the sun, calmed him and rode off. Philip, Plutarch says, told him: ’seek thee out a kingdom equal to thyself; Macedonia has not room for thee.’

cards.headline: A horse with a city
cards.body: The horse’s name, Bucephalus, is Greek for ’bull-headed’. He carried Alexander all the way to India and died, aged 30, after the battle on the Hydaspes River in 326 BCE. Alexander named several cities Alexandria after himself. This one he named Bucephala, after his horse.

cards.fact: Our main accounts of Alexander were written about four centuries after he died.
cards.context: Plutarch was born around 46 CE, in Chaeronea of all places. He and Arrian drew on eyewitness histories, like one by Callisthenes, that are now lost. It’s like writing a biography today of someone who lived four centuries ago, from notes nobody can check. So treat the shadow story as a good story from a late source.

levels.title: Conquering Persia
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Alexander's campaign against Persia.
levels.summary: From 334 to 330 BCE Alexander crossed into Asia, beat Persia at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, and burned Persepolis.

cards.headline: In 334 BCE a young king crossed into Asia to take on Persia.
cards.body: He brought about 30,000 infantry and more than 5,000 cavalry. Four years later, the Persian king was dead. Here’s the road.

cards.headline: First stop: Troy
cards.body: Alexander crossed the Dardanelles, and before his first battle he visited Troy. Yes, Level 5’s Troy, near the Dardanelles. Plutarch says he anointed Achilles’ gravestone with oil and ran a race by it with his companions. A general heading to war, pausing at the setting of his favorite book.

cards.headline: Endings, real and legendary
cards.body: At Persepolis Alexander burned the palace of Xerxes, a sign that the Greek war of revenge on Persia was over. Some endings are harder to pin down. Legend said whoever loosed the Gordian knot would rule Asia, and most ancient writers say Alexander simply cut it with his sword. It may never have happened. It’s still a great story.

levels.title: To India and Back
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how far Alexander marched and why he turned back.
levels.summary: Alexander crossed the Indus in 326 BCE and beat Porus on the Hydaspes, but his army refused to go past the Hyphasis, and the march home through Gedrosia was a disaster.

cards.headline: Alexander’s army marched all the way to India. Then, at a river, it said no.
cards.body: No enemy stopped Alexander at the Hyphasis. His own soldiers did.

cards.headline: Farther east
cards.body: After Persia came years of fighting in Central Asia. There Alexander captured Roxana, daughter of a local noble, and married her to make peace. In spring 326 BCE he crossed the Indus into India.

cards.headline: ’Like a king’
cards.body: On the Hydaspes River in 326 BCE, Alexander met King Porus, whose elephants were unfamiliar to the Macedonians. Alexander won. Asked how he wished to be treated, Porus, Plutarch says, answered: ’like a king.’ Impressed, Alexander kept him as ruler and gave him more land. The same battle cost Alexander his horse: Level 83’s Bucephalus died there.

cards.headline: The army says no
cards.body: At the Hyphasis River, the army mutinied and refused to go any farther. Alexander, Plutarch says, shut himself in his tent in anger, then gave in. He set up 12 altars to the 12 Olympian gods to mark the spot. The conqueror of Persia was stopped by his own tired men.

cards.headline: The long way home
cards.body: The way back was worse. The march through the Gedrosian desert was a disaster of thirst and hunger. Plutarch wrote that not even a quarter of the fighting force came back from India. Getting there was glory. Getting home was survival.

levels.title: The Death of Alexander
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happened when Alexander died.
levels.summary: Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BCE, aged 32, with no adult heir; his family was killed off and his generals fought over the empire until 281 BCE.

cards.headline: Alexander conquered an empire. He never said who should get it.
cards.body: Asked on his deathbed, he may have given the most dangerous answer possible.

cards.headline: Babylon, 323 BCE
cards.body: In Babylon, Alexander fell ill after a long banquet and drinking bout. Ten days later, on June 13, 323 BCE, he died, aged 32. What killed him is still debated: malaria, typhoid fever and poison are the favorite theories. Plutarch thought the poison story a fabrication.

mascot.line: Three little words, and a very long fight over what they meant.

cards.headline: ’To the strongest’
cards.body: The historian Diodorus says the dying Alexander handed his ring to his general Perdiccas. Asked who should have his kingdom, he answered: ’to the strongest.’ Whether or not he said it, that’s exactly what happened. It’s like leaving your house to ’whoever grabs the keys first’.

cards.headline: Two kings, no king
cards.body: Alexander had named no heir, so his generals made two kings: his half-brother Philip Arrhidaeus and his son by Roxana, Alexander IV, born after his death. Neither truly ruled. In 310 BCE the general Cassander had the boy and his mother Roxana killed. Alexander’s family was gone; his generals, the Successors, fought on until 281 BCE.

cards.fact: Alexander’s death in 323 BCE ends the Classical age.
cards.context: Remember Level 1’s timeline? The Classical age runs to his death, and the Hellenistic age begins, lasting until Rome takes Egypt in 30 BCE. One man’s death marks the border between two eras.

cards.headline: One of Alexander’s generals traded land in India for 500 elephants.
cards.body: It turned out to be a bargain. The elephants helped decide who got Alexander’s empire.

cards.headline: Elephants decide it
cards.body: Seleucus gave up territory to the Indian ruler Chandragupta for 500 elephants. At Ipsus in 301 BCE, Seleucus and his allies faced another general, Antigonus. Seleucus had an estimated 400 elephants, and they made the difference. Antigonus was killed, and with him went any hope of putting Alexander’s empire back together.

In their kingdoms Greek became the language of government, and Greek culture mixed with the cultures of the peoples they ruled. Picture a head office where every memo is in Greek, whether the branch office sits on the Nile or in Syria.

levels.title: The Library of Alexandria
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Library and the Lighthouse of Alexandria.
levels.summary: In Greek-ruled Alexandria, the Ptolemies built a library meant to hold every book, mostly Greek, and a Greek architect built the Pharos lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders.

cards.headline: Athens lent its most precious books to a king. It never got them back.
cards.body: The borrower was building the greatest library of the Greek world, in a Greek city in Egypt.

cards.headline: All the books in the world
cards.body: About 295 BCE, Ptolemy I had Demetrius of Phaleron found a library and the Mouseion in Alexandria. Demetrius was an Athenian statesman and philosopher at Ptolemy’s court. The aim: collect, if possible, all the books in the world. Most of them were in Greek. A Greek king in Egypt, with an Athenian running the project.

cards.fact: Ptolemy III kept Athens’ official copies of its great tragedies.
cards.context: He borrowed the texts of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, leaving 15 talents of silver as security. Then he kept the originals, sent back copies, and let Athens keep the silver. Think of it as the grandest unreturned library book of all.

cards.headline: A catalog in 120 books
cards.body: Finding anything among that many scrolls took a system. The scholar Callimachus, who worked at the library, compiled the Pinakes: a catalog of its authors and their works, sorted by field of learning. It filled 120 books. The catalog alone was a library.

cards.headline: A Greek light on the harbor
cards.body: Out on the island of Pharos stood the lighthouse, built by the Greek architect Sostratus of Cnidus and finished about 280 BCE. It rose more than 110 metres, with a fire burning at the top at night, and it was one of the Seven Wonders of the World.

levels.title: Rome Conquers Greece

levels.summary: Rome ended Macedonia’s kingdom at Pydna in 168 BCE and destroyed Corinth in 146 BCE, enslaving its people, but Greek culture won over the Romans.

cards.headline: A Roman general shipped Greek masterpieces home: break one, and you replace it.

cards.headline: Pydna, 168 BCE

cards.headline: The hostage historian
cards.body: In Rome, Polybius became a friend of the general Scipio Aemilianus. He wrote his Histories, in Greek, to explain how the Romans had brought nearly the whole inhabited world under their rule in under 53 years. A Greek hostage, telling Greeks how they’d lost.

cards.fact: Rome destroyed Corinth in 146 BCE.
cards.context: That’s Level 1’s finish line. Most of Corinth’s men were killed and its women and children were enslaved. The general Mummius shipped the city’s art to Rome, warning the shippers that anything lost or damaged would have to be replaced with work of equal value. As if you could order another Greek masterpiece.

cards.headline: Captive Greece
cards.body: Rome won the wars. Greece won the Romans. The poet Horace put it in one line: captive Greece took her fierce conqueror captive and brought the arts to rustic Latium.

levels.title: Greek in Our Words
levels.objective: After this level you can name everyday English words that come from Greek.
levels.summary: Telephone ("far voice"), photograph ("light writing"), school ("leisure") and dinosaur ("terrible lizard") are all built from Greek parts.

cards.headline: Telephone, photograph, school, dinosaur. You speak more Greek than you think.
cards.body: Every one of those words is built from ancient Greek parts. Take them apart and some surprising meanings fall out.

cards.headline: A far-voice in your pocket
cards.body: Start with your phone. Telephone joins two Greek words: tele, “far”, and phone, “sound” or “voice”. The word first named something else: around 1830, a system that sent words using musical notes. So every time you say “phone”, you’re saying “voice” in Greek, and a telephone is, quite literally, a far-voice.

cards.headline: Writing with light
cards.body: In 1839 the English scientist John Herschel needed a name for pictures made by light. He built one from Greek: photo-, “light”, and -graph, “something written”. A photograph is light-writing. Greek gave the new invention a name that explained exactly what it did.

mascot.line: Technically, homework is just leisure with extra steps.

cards.headline: School meant spare time
cards.body: Here’s the surprise. School comes, through Latin, from Greek skhole, which meant “leisure” or “spare time”. Leisure was what Greeks spent on learned discussion, and the word came to mean the place for it. So school began as free time well spent. Try that argument on a Monday morning.

cards.fact: Greek still names brand-new things.
cards.context: In the 1840s the anatomist Richard Owen needed a word for giant fossil reptiles. He built dinosaur from Greek deinos, “terrible”, and sauros, “lizard”. Level 8’s alphabet was built from Greek parts too: alpha plus beta.

levels.title: Democracy Then and Now
levels.objective: After this level you can compare ancient and modern democracy.
levels.summary: Athenian democracy was direct but open only to adult male citizens; most modern democracies are representative, the kind of republic Madison argued suits a large country.

cards.headline: Athens called itself a democracy. So do many countries today.
cards.body: Same word, very different machine. Put the two side by side and see what changed.

cards.headline: Rule by the people, in person
cards.body: Democracy comes from Greek demos, “people”, and kratos, “rule”. In Athens that was meant literally: citizens voted on laws themselves in the Assembly. Most democracies today are representative: you vote for people who make the laws for you. In Athens you didn’t elect a lawmaker. If you were a citizen, you were one.

cards.headline: Who counted as “the people”?
cards.body: But “the people” was a small club. Only adult male citizens could take part; women, slaves and foreigners were shut out, so most people living in Athens had no vote. Modern democracies have widened the circle, slowly. In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to let women vote in national elections.

cards.headline: Madison’s big-country problem
cards.body: The new United States faced a problem Athens never had: size. In Federalist No. 10 (1787), James Madison described a pure democracy as a small number of citizens who assemble and govern in person. A republic, run by elected representatives, could cover a far larger country. Most modern democracies are closer to Madison’s republic than to Athens.

levels.title: The Modern Olympics
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Olympics were revived in 1896.
levels.summary: Pierre de Coubertin’s movement revived the Olympics in Athens in 1896; the marathon was new that year, and the torch relay only began in 1936.

cards.headline: The Olympics came back in 1896. Some of the oldest-looking parts were brand new.
cards.body: The revival borrowed a Greek name and a Greek stage. Then it invented traditions that look far older than they are.

cards.headline: A Frenchman’s revival
cards.body: The comeback was led by Pierre de Coubertin, a French educator. In 1894 a congress at the Sorbonne, in Paris, agreed to hold international Olympic Games and founded the International Olympic Committee. The first modern Games opened in Athens in 1896. A Greek festival, restarted by a Frenchman, back in Greece.

cards.headline: The newest old race
cards.body: The marathon was invented for those 1896 Games, inspired by the legend of a runner carrying news from Marathon to Athens. A Greek, Spyridon Louis, won it by more than seven minutes and became a national hero. The race that sounds most ancient was brand new, and the host country won it. Perfect ending.

cards.fact: The Olympic torch relay began in 1936, not in ancient Greece.
cards.context: It was created for the 1936 Berlin Games, staged by Nazi Germany. A flame was lit at Olympia with a mirror focusing the Sun’s rays, then runners carried it to Berlin. Ancient Greeks never ran a torch relay. It looks ancient because it was designed to.

levels.title: Greek Columns Everywhere
levels.objective: After this level you can spot Greek columns in modern buildings.
levels.summary: The 19th-century Greek Revival copied Greek temples: Philadelphia’s Second Bank borrowed from the Parthenon, and the Lincoln Memorial echoes democracy’s birthplace.

cards.headline: Why does a bank in Philadelphia look like a Greek temple?
cards.body: Because in the 1800s, Europe and America fell hard for Greek temples, and started building them for money and memory.

cards.headline: The Greek Revival
cards.body: In the first half of the 19th century a style called the Greek Revival spread through Europe and the United States. Its architects based their designs on Greek temples of the 5th century BCE, and the Parthenon in Athens was a favorite model. For a few decades, looking ancient was the most fashionable thing a new building could do.

cards.headline: A temple for money
cards.body: The Second Bank of the United States, in Philadelphia, was built from 1819 to 1824. Its architect, William Strickland, took the Parthenon as his model, borrowing its columns and its plain pediments. An ancient temple became the template for a bank. Next time a bank greets you with a row of columns, you’re looking at a Greek temple’s descendant.

mascot.line: Count them next time you visit. Thirty-six, and every one has a state’s name above it.

cards.headline: Democracy in stone
cards.body: The Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., dedicated in 1922, has a reason as well as a look. Its architect, Henry Bacon, modeled it on the Parthenon because he felt a memorial to a man who defended democracy should echo democracy’s birthplace. Its 36 columns stand for the 36 states in the Union when Lincoln died. The shape is Greek; the count is American.

levels.title: Myths on Screen
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Greek myths live on in books and films.
levels.summary: Joyce’s Ulysses, Harryhausen’s skeletons and Percy Jackson retell Greek myths; retellers have always added details, like Achilles’ heel.

cards.headline: Books and films keep changing Greek myths. That’s a very old tradition.
cards.body: From a Dublin novel to an Olympus in a skyscraper, the old stories keep getting retold, and remixed.

cards.headline: Odysseus in Dublin
cards.body: In 1922 James Joyce published Ulysses, a novel set in Dublin on a single day, June 16, 1904. It’s built as a modern parallel to Homer’s Odyssey, with an ordinary Dubliner, Leopold Bloom, as Odysseus. The title is the Latin-based name for Odysseus. Level 6’s ten-year voyage home shrinks to one long day around town.

cards.headline: Skeletons and skyscrapers
cards.body: Films and novels do it too. For Jason and the Argonauts (1963), animator Ray Harryhausen spent four months on one stop-motion battle: Jason and two Argonauts against an army of skeletons. In Rick Riordan’s 2005 novel The Lightning Thief, Percy Jackson learns he’s a son of Poseidon, and Mount Olympus sits on the 600th floor of the Empire State Building. The gods just moved to New York.

mascot.line: Achilles’ heel: famous weak spot, famous late arrival.

cards.headline: The heel Homer never mentioned
cards.body: Even famous details can be latecomers. The story that Thetis dipped baby Achilles in the River Styx, leaving only the heel she held vulnerable, isn’t in Homer; later tellers added it. Remember Level 6? Singers reshaped their stories every time they performed. A film that adds a twist is joining a very old habit.

levels.title: Science's Greek Roots
levels.objective: After this level you can name ideas in modern science that began in Greece.
levels.summary: Science still speaks Greek: the "uncuttable" atom, Rutherford’s alpha and beta rays, and a doctors’ oath descended from Hippocrates.

cards.headline: Atom means “uncuttable” in Greek. Then physicists found its parts.
cards.body: Modern science still talks in Greek words, letters and promises, even where the science has moved on.

cards.headline: The uncuttable atom
cards.body: Atom comes from Greek atomos, “uncuttable” or “indivisible”. It named an ancient Greek idea: matter is made of tiny pieces that can’t be divided. In 1897 the English physicist J. J. Thomson discovered the electron, the first known particle smaller than an atom. The Greek name survived the discovery. We still call it the uncuttable thing, and we know it has parts.

cards.headline: Alpha, beta, radiation
cards.body: Scientists borrow Greek letters as labels. In 1899 Ernest Rutherford found that radioactive substances give off more than one kind of radiation. He named the less penetrating rays alpha and the more penetrating ones beta, after the first two letters of the Greek alphabet. That alphabet, remember, was adapted from Phoenician letters back in Level 8.

cards.headline: A promise that lasted
cards.body: Medicine kept a Greek promise. The Hippocratic oath is an ethical code attributed to the Greek physician Hippocrates, and versions of it still appear in the graduation ceremonies of many medical schools. In 1948 the World Medical Association adopted the Declaration of Geneva, known as the oath’s modern version. The wording changed; the idea of a doctor’s public promise stayed.

levels.title: How Greek Books Survived
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Arabic and Byzantine scholars saved Greek texts.
levels.summary: Greek books survived through Byzantine copies like the Venetus A, Arabic translations such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq’s, and manuscripts carried west after 1453.

cards.headline: The oldest complete Iliad isn’t ancient. It’s about a thousand years old.
cards.body: So how did Greek books cross the centuries? Hand to hand, copy to copy, and sometimes by luck.

cards.headline: Copied in Byzantium
cards.body: The Venetus A, a Byzantine manuscript made toward the end of the 10th century CE, is the oldest complete text of the Iliad, more than 1,500 years after Homer. In the 15th century the Greek cardinal Bessarion acquired it and gave his whole collection of Greek manuscripts to Venice, where it still is. Level 6’s textbook of Greece reached us as a copy of a copy.

cards.headline: Saved in Arabic
cards.body: In 9th-century Baghdad, the scholar Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated works of Plato, Aristotle, Hippocrates and Galen from Greek. His Galen matters most: most of that doctor’s Greek manuscripts were lost, and some of his works survive only in Arabic. For those books, the original is gone and the translation is the survivor.

cards.headline: Back to the West
cards.body: In 1453 Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks, and Byzantine refugees brought more Greek manuscripts west. Scholars in Italy could now read original Greek, and older Latin translations made from Arabic versions began to look second-hand. Greek learning had travelled east and came back.

mascot.line: Recycled parchment, rescued genius. Always check under the prayers.

cards.headline: Math under a prayer book
cards.body: Some books survived by luck. A Byzantine copy of works by Archimedes was scraped and written over with prayers in the 13th century. A scholar spotted the faint math underneath in 1906, and modern imaging recovered it. It holds the only surviving copy of Archimedes’ Method.

cards.headline: Greek books: saved

levels.title: Myths About Greece
levels.objective: After this level you can debunk common myths, like statues always being plain white.
levels.summary: Greek sculptures were painted; the white look came from lost and scrubbed-off paint and 18th-century taste. And "Greek" is a Roman name: the Greeks called themselves Hellenes.

cards.headline: Picture a Greek statue. You probably see white marble. Its sculptor saw paint.
cards.body: Some of the most familiar ideas about Greece are later inventions. Here are two, starting with the color.

cards.headline: Painted, not plain
cards.body: Greek sculptures were painted in bright colors, a practice called polychromy. Researchers find surviving specks of pigment with infrared and ultraviolet light, then build full-color reconstructions. In 2023 a study found traces of Egyptian blue, white and purple paint on the Parthenon Sculptures in the British Museum. The marble was the canvas, not the finished look.

cards.headline: Where the white came from
cards.body: So why the white? Most of the paint simply wore away. In the 18th century the art historian Johann Joachim Winckelmann linked whiteness with beauty, writing that color should play a minor part in it. And restorers sometimes removed surviving paint to restore an assumed original whiteness. The myth wasn’t only an accident: people scrubbed away the evidence.

cards.headline: They didn’t call themselves Greeks
cards.body: Second myth: the name. The ancient Greeks called themselves Hellenes. “Greek” comes from Latin Graeci, the Romans’ name for them. One theory traces it to Greeks from Graia who helped found Cumae, in Italy, where Romans first met Greeks. Cumae? That’s one of Level 9’s first colonies. Greece’s official name today is still the Hellenic Republic.

levels.title: Why Greece Still Matters
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Greek ideas still shape the modern world.
levels.summary: Shelley’s "We are all Greeks" helped rally Europe behind Greek independence; the fuller truth is that Greece borrowed, excluded and handed on as well as invented.

cards.headline: “We are all Greeks,” the poet Shelley wrote in 1822. Was he right?
cards.body: He meant that Europe’s laws, literature, religion and arts had their root in Greece. This chapter lets you test that claim.

cards.headline: A poem for a war
cards.body: Shelley wrote those words in the preface to Hellas, a poem inspired by the Greek War of Independence, which began in 1821. The poet Lord Byron went further: he went to Greece to help, died of fever at Missolonghi in 1824, and became a Greek national hero. In 1830 Greece became an independent state. Love of ancient Greece helped cheer on a modern one.

cards.headline: Not a lonely origin
cards.body: Shelley’s line leaves things out. Greece borrowed: its alphabet came from the Phoenicians. Its learning was carried by others: some of Galen’s works survive only in Arabic. And its democracy shut out women and slaves. Greece matters less as a pure fountain than as a crossroads where ideas arrived, changed and moved on.

cards.headline: You meet it every day
cards.body: Look back over this chapter. Say “school” and you’re saying “leisure” in Greek. The Olympics were reborn in Athens. Banks and memorials wear Greek columns. Films keep retelling the myths, and doctors still make a promise that began with Hippocrates. That’s why Greece still matters: you use it without noticing.

levels.title: Rome in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the three big eras of Roman history and roughly when each began and ended.
levels.summary: Rome went from Kingdom to Republic (509 BCE) to Empire (27 BCE). It ringed the Mediterranean; the West fell in 476 and the East in 1453.

cards.headline: Rome tried kings, then a Republic, then emperors. Then it fell. Twice.
cards.body: That’s the whole plot. It took more than a thousand years to play out, and even the ending was in no hurry.

cards.headline: Kingdom, Republic, Empire
cards.body: Romans dated their city’s founding to 753 BCE, and at first it was ruled by kings: the Kingdom. In 509 BCE the Romans threw out their last king and ran things as a Republic instead. That lasted until 27 BCE, when Augustus took sole power and the Empire began. Same city, three very different answers to one question: who’s in charge here?
cards.callout: Kingdom → Republic (509 BCE) → Empire (27 BCE)

cards.headline: An empire around a sea
cards.body: At its height, Rome held every coast of the Mediterranean, stretching from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to the Middle East. Picture it on a map: a giant ring of land with a sea in the middle. So Romans simply called the Mediterranean Mare Nostrum, “our sea.” Sail anywhere on it, and wherever you landed, you were still in Rome’s empire.

cards.fact: Rome fell twice.
cards.context: The western half of the empire ended in 476 CE, when its last emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed. The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, kept going until 1453, almost a thousand years later. So if someone asks you when Rome fell, the honest answer is another question: which half?

levels.title: Romulus and Remus
levels.objective: After this level you can retell Rome’s founding legend and explain why Romans valued it.
levels.summary: Legend says twin sons of Mars, nursed by a she-wolf, founded Rome, and Romulus killed Remus. Historians treat it as legend, not history.

cards.headline: Rome’s origin story: twins, a wolf and a murder.
cards.body: Not exactly a bedtime story. Yet the wolf became a symbol of Rome itself.

cards.headline: Raised by a wolf
cards.body: In the legend, the twins Romulus and Remus were sons of the god Mars. They were abandoned as babies, and a she-wolf found them and nursed them. Rome turned that moment into its emblem: the she-wolf feeding the twins became one of the city’s best-known symbols. Most cities don’t put a wild predator in the family photo. Rome made it the cover shot.

cards.headline: A city named in blood
cards.body: The twins grew up, and their new city came between them. They quarreled over it, and Romulus killed Remus. The winner got the naming rights: the city was named Rome, after Romulus. Imagine your hometown being named after whichever sibling won the argument. Romans didn’t have to imagine it.

cards.headline: Legend, not history
cards.body: Romans had a second origin story, too. They traced their ancestry to Aeneas, a Trojan prince who, in legend, fled the fall of Troy to Italy. Historians treat both stories as legend, because they were written down centuries after the events they describe. So why learn them? Because they show how Romans saw themselves. A legend won’t tell you what happened, but it tells you who a people wanted to be.

levels.title: What the Ground Remembers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what archaeology shows about Rome’s earliest villages.
levels.summary: Latin farmers built huts on the Palatine by about the 8th century BCE. Hilltop villages merged, and the marshy Forum valley was drained.

cards.headline: Forget the wolf for a moment. What does the ground say?
cards.body: Under the ruins on Rome’s Palatine Hill lie traces of the city’s first huts. They tell a quieter story than twins and a she-wolf.

cards.headline: Huts on a hill
cards.body: The first Romans were Latins, a people of the region of Latium in central Italy. On the Palatine Hill, archaeologists have found traces of their Iron Age huts from around the 8th century BCE. Now hold that next to the traditional founding date, 753 BCE. The huts sit close to the traditional founding: the shovel and the storytellers land in the same century. Not bad for a tale with a wolf in it.

cards.headline: From villages to a town
cards.body: Early Rome wasn’t one city. It was a cluster of small hilltop villages that gradually merged into one community. Down between the hills lay a marshy valley. It was drained, and that soggy low ground became the Roman Forum, the center of Roman public life. Before it was famous, it was a bog.

cards.fact: Rome’s great drain still works.
cards.context: The Cloaca Maxima, Rome’s great drain, helped dry out that marshy Forum valley. Parts of it still carry water today. Somewhere under the modern city, a very old drain is still doing its job.

levels.title: Seven Hills and a River
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Tiber and the seven hills shaped where and why Rome grew.
levels.summary: Rome grew at a crossing of the Tiber on a trade route, on hills that were easy to defend and stayed dry. Ostia became its port.

cards.headline: Why build a city right here? Follow the river and the salt.
cards.body: Rome sits where it does for reasons you can still see on a map: a river you can cross, a road for salt, and hills that keep your feet dry.

cards.headline: A river crossing
cards.body: Rome grew where the Tiber River could be crossed, near an island in the river, about 25 km from the sea. An ancient salt route, later called the Via Salaria, passed right through, linking the coast with inland Italy. So anyone moving goods between the two came this way. Own the crossing, and trade has to walk past your front door.
cards.callout: River crossing + trade route = a place worth holding

cards.headline: Seven hills
cards.body: The city spread across seven hills beside the Tiber, among them the Capitoline and the Palatine, where those first huts stood. The hills made sense twice over. They were easier to defend, and they stayed dry when the Tiber flooded the low ground between them. Enemies and floods: the hills handled both.

cards.fact: Rome had its own port.
cards.context: Rome sat about 25 km inland, so its harbor was downstream. Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber, became Rome’s port. Grain and other goods came in there and traveled up the river to the city. The same river that gave Rome its crossing also delivered dinner.

levels.title: The Etruscans Next Door
levels.objective: After this level you can describe who the Etruscans were and what Rome borrowed from them.
levels.summary: The Etruscans of Tuscany were early Italy’s great power. Rome had Etruscan kings and borrowed the fasces and haruspicy from them.

cards.headline: Before Rome was a great power, it lived next to one.
cards.body: The Etruscans were among the most powerful peoples of early Italy. Rome borrowed a lot from them, even, tradition says, some of its kings.

cards.headline: Rome’s powerful neighbors
cards.body: North of Rome, in Etruria, mostly what is now Tuscany, lived the Etruscans. They weren’t one kingdom but a set of independent cities, and they were among the most powerful peoples of early Italy. Their language was unrelated to Latin, and it is still only partly understood. Rome’s big neighbors next door, and we still can’t fully read their mail.

cards.headline: Etruscan kings
cards.body: Here’s the twist. According to Roman tradition, the last three kings of Rome were Etruscans. Historians can’t vouch for every detail, but the bigger picture holds: young Rome grew up under strong Etruscan influence. For a while, the neighbors weren’t just next door. They were on the throne.

cards.headline: What Rome borrowed
cards.body: Some of Rome’s most Roman-looking things were imports. Take the fasces, a bundle of rods around an axe. Attendants carried it in front of officials as a sign of their authority, and it came from the Etruscans. So did haruspicy: reading omens in the organs of sacrificed animals. A way to show power and a way to read the gods, both borrowed from next door.
cards.callout: Fasces: rods and an axe, the symbol of authority

levels.title: The Seven Kings
levels.objective: After this level you can outline Rome’s age of kings and how kingship worked there.
levels.summary: Seven kings ruled from 753 to 509 BCE, each chosen with the Senate’s and people’s approval. Numa founded religion; Servius, the census.

cards.headline: Rome had seven kings, if you trust the legends. Not the kind you picture.
cards.body: No crown passed neatly from father to son. Most of the time, Rome had other ideas about who got the job.

cards.headline: Seven kings
cards.body: Roman tradition counted seven kings, from Romulus in 753 BCE to Tarquin the Proud in 509 BCE, the last three of them Etruscans. But this wasn’t a family business. Kingship was not simply inherited: tradition says most kings were chosen with the approval of the Senate and the people. Being the old king’s son didn’t get you the job. Getting approved did.

cards.headline: Remembered for different things
cards.body: Each king came with a reputation, like a line on a résumé. Numa Pompilius, the second king, was remembered as the founder of Rome’s religious institutions and its calendar. Servius Tullius, the sixth, was credited with the first census, which sorted citizens by wealth. Ask a Roman who started a custom, and there was often a king ready to take the credit.

cards.fact: The Senate started as the king’s advisers.
cards.context: It began as a council of elders who advised the king. Keep an eye on it. The kings would go, but the Senate would stay, long after the last king was gone.

levels.title: Gods of the Household and the State
levels.objective: After this level you can describe early Roman religion, from household spirits to state priests and omens.
levels.summary: Romans kept peace with the gods through correct ritual: household spirits at home, Jupiter on the Capitoline, Vesta’s fire and augury.

cards.headline: Romans rarely asked whether the gods existed. They asked what the gods wanted.
cards.body: Get the ritual right, and the gods stayed on your side. Get it wrong, and even a few birds could hold up the city’s business.

cards.headline: Keeping peace with the gods
cards.body: Roman religion was less about what you believed and more about doing the rituals correctly. The goal had a name: the pax deorum, peace with the gods. Think of it as a contract where the fine print really matters. It started at home. Every household honored the Lares and Penates, guardian spirits of the home and its food store, at a small shrine. Even the pantry had protection.

cards.headline: Gods of the state
cards.body: The city had its own gods to keep happy. On the Capitoline Hill stood Rome’s greatest temple, dedicated to Jupiter, king of the gods, together with Juno and Minerva. Meanwhile, the Vestal Virgins tended the sacred fire of Vesta, goddess of the hearth, day and night. That fire was never allowed to go out. Every home had its little shrine. Rome had a fire nobody was allowed to let die.

cards.fact: Birds could put Roman politics on hold.
cards.context: Before major public decisions, Romans consulted augurs, priests who read the will of the gods in the flight of birds. An unfavorable sign could delay public business. Imagine a big vote postponed because the wrong birds flew by.

levels.title: The Roman Family
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the power of the paterfamilias and how Roman families were organized.
levels.summary: The paterfamilias held legal power over his descendants, even adults. The familia included the whole household, enslaved people too.

cards.headline: In Rome, a 40-year-old could still be under his father’s legal power.
cards.body: Growing up didn’t make you your own boss. Meet the paterfamilias.

cards.headline: The father’s power
cards.body: Every Roman family had a paterfamilias: its oldest living male. He held legal power over his children and grandchildren, even when they were grown adults with children of their own. In early Roman law this power, patria potestas, in theory reached as far as life and death. So if your grandfather was alive, he wasn’t just your boss. He was your dad’s boss too.

cards.headline: More than relatives
cards.body: To a Roman, familia meant more than relatives. It meant the whole household, including the enslaved people who lived and worked in it. The family reached back in time, too. Noble families kept wax masks of their ancestors and carried them in funeral processions. At a noble Roman funeral, the ancestors came along.

cards.fact: Roman names came in three parts.
cards.context: Take Gaius Julius Caesar. Gaius was his personal name, Julius his clan name, and Caesar the name of his family’s branch of that clan. Say a Roman man’s full name, and you’ve recited a small family tree.

levels.title: The Last King
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rome overthrew Tarquin the Proud and why it rejected kings.
levels.summary: Tarquin the Proud ruled as a tyrant. After the Lucretia scandal, Brutus led the Romans to expel him in 509 BCE and swear off kings.

cards.headline: Rome’s kings ended with a crime, an uprising and an oath never to have another.
cards.body: The seventh king pushed too far. What came next left Romans with a lasting horror of one word: king.

cards.headline: A tyrant king
cards.body: The seventh king, Tarquin the Proud, was remembered as a tyrant who ruled by force and ignored the Senate, the very council that had begun as the king’s advisers. Then, according to tradition, the king’s son assaulted a noblewoman named Lucretia. That was the spark. The crime set off an uprising, and not just against one bad king, but against the monarchy itself.

cards.headline: No more kings
cards.body: According to tradition, the Romans, led by Lucius Junius Brutus, drove out their king in 509 BCE and ended the monarchy. Then Brutus had them swear never again to let anyone be king in Rome. Not just “no more Tarquin.” No more kings, ever.
cards.callout: The end of the monarchy: 509 BCE

cards.fact: Romans hated the word “king.”
cards.context: After the tyrant kings, the title rex, king, became so hated that even Rome’s most powerful later leaders avoided it. They could hold enormous power. They just couldn’t call it that.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Rome Began
levels.objective: After this level you can connect Rome’s geography, neighbors, legends and kings into one founding story.
levels.summary: Legend and evidence tell one story: a river-crossing site, Latin villages, Etruscan influence, and kings until 509 BCE.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: what Romans said, and what the ground says.
cards.body: Romans had a great story about how their city began. Archaeologists have shovels. Let’s see where they meet.

items.label: What legend says
points: Romulus founded Rome in 753 BCE
Seven kings ruled until 509 BCE

items.label: What evidence shows
points: Iron Age huts on the Palatine by the 8th century BCE, close to the traditional date
Hilltop villages merged, and a marshy valley was drained to become the Forum

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: Put it together and early Rome makes sense. The site sat on a crossing of the Tiber, on the route between the coast and inland Italy: a place worth holding. Latin villages on its hills merged into a town. Powerful Etruscan neighbors shaped it, and tradition says its last three kings were Etruscan. Founding legends told Romans who they were. Then, in 509 BCE, Rome drove out its seventh king and swore off kings for good. Which leaves a big question: what do you build instead?

levels.title: A Republic Is Born
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a republic is and what SPQR stood for.
levels.summary: After the kings, Rome became a res publica: elected magistrates with limited terms, the Senate and People of Rome, from 509 to 27 BCE.

cards.headline: Rome’s answer to tyranny was to share power, and keep it short.
cards.body: Rome had just sworn never to have another king. Now it needed a government where nobody could turn into one.

cards.headline: The public thing
cards.body: No king? Then who owns the state? Rome’s answer was res publica, Latin for “the public thing,” and the root of our word republic. Instead of a king, citizens elected officials called magistrates, and every one of them held power only for a limited term. Think of it as renting power, never owning it. The state belonged to the public, not to a king.

cards.headline: SPQR
cards.body: Romans called their state by four letters: SPQR, Senatus Populusque Romanus, “the Senate and People of Rome.” Read it again: there’s no king anywhere in the name. That arrangement lasted almost five centuries, from 509 BCE until Augustus took sole power in 27 BCE.
cards.callout: SPQR: the Senate and People of Rome

cards.fact: “The People” came with fine print.
cards.context: Only adult male citizens could vote. Women, enslaved people and foreigners had no vote at all. So when SPQR said “the People,” it meant a smaller crowd than everyone who lived in Rome.

levels.title: Two Consuls, One Year
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how consuls shared power and why their terms were short.
levels.summary: Two consuls led Rome for one year each, commanded its armies and could block each other. Emergencies allowed a dictator for six months.

cards.headline: Rome’s top job came with a partner and an expiry date.
cards.body: Rome wanted a leader strong enough to run the state, but never strong enough to become a king. Its fix was simple and sneaky.

cards.headline: Two at the top
cards.body: The Republic was led by two consuls, elected by the citizens every year. Each could block the other’s actions, so neither could rule alone. Picture a car with two steering wheels and two brake pedals: nobody goes on a joyride. And after one year, both stepped down. However good you were at the job, no one held supreme power for long.

cards.headline: Generals and calendars
cards.body: Consuls also commanded Rome’s armies in war. They were so central to Roman life that Romans didn’t count their years by number. They named each year after its two consuls. Imagine dating your birthday by who happened to be in charge that year. For a Roman, that was simply the date.

cards.fact: Emergencies came with a six-month limit.
cards.context: In a crisis, Rome could appoint a dictator with supreme power. Even that came with a timer: six months at most. Rome’s emergency brake had an expiry date too.

levels.title: The Senate
levels.objective: After this level you can describe who sat in the Senate and how it steered the Republic.
levels.summary: The Senate was about 300 former magistrates, usually serving for life. It only gave advice, but that advice was almost always followed.

cards.headline: The Senate couldn’t pass laws. It ran Rome anyway.
cards.body: Consuls came and went every year. So who remembered how things were done?

cards.headline: A council of former officials
cards.body: Remember the council of elders that advised the kings back in Level 6? It outlived them. In the Republic, the Senate was made up of former magistrates, men who had already held office, and they usually stayed senators for life. For most of the Republic there were about 300 of them. The only way into the room was to have helped run Rome already.

cards.headline: Advice that was obeyed
cards.body: Formally, the Senate only gave advice to the magistrates. In practice, its advice was almost always followed, especially on foreign policy and money. Why? A consul had one year. The senators facing him had all held office before and would sit there for life. When a room like that “suggests” something, you listen.

cards.fact: The Senate met in the middle of everything.
cards.context: Its usual home was the Curia, a building in the Roman Forum, the center of Roman public life. Rome’s most powerful advisers met a short walk from the markets and law courts.

levels.title: Patricians and Plebeians
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Conflict of the Orders between Rome’s old families and ordinary citizens.
levels.summary: Plebeians won rights from the patricians over two centuries, starting with a walkout in 494 BCE and ending with the Hortensian law of 287.

cards.headline: What if the workers and soldiers of a city simply walked out?
cards.body: In Rome, they did. It was the opening move in a fight over who got a say, and it lasted about two centuries.

cards.headline: Two kinds of citizen
cards.body: Every Roman citizen was one of two kinds. Patricians belonged to Rome’s old aristocratic families. Plebeians were all the rest. In the early Republic, patricians held the priesthoods and, by tradition, the magistracies too, though some historians think a few plebeians also held early offices. Either way, the top jobs belonged mostly to one side. Rome had thrown out its king, but not its old families.

cards.headline: The walkout
cards.body: In 494 BCE, according to tradition, the plebeians tried something bold: they walked out of Rome in protest. They refused to work or fight until they won concessions. A city nobody will work or fight for is just a pile of buildings. Their long struggle for political rights, about two centuries of it, is called the Conflict of the Orders.

levels.title: The Twelve Tables
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Rome wrote down its laws and what that changed.
levels.summary: Around 450 BCE Rome wrote its laws on the Twelve Tables in the Forum, so patrician judges could no longer bend unwritten custom.

cards.headline: A law you can’t read is a law someone else controls.
cards.body: The plebeians knew it. So they demanded that Rome’s laws be written down.

cards.headline: Law in public
cards.body: Roman law used to be unwritten custom, and patrician judges could interpret it as they pleased. Imagine playing a game where only the other team knows the rules. Plebeians demanded written laws, and around 450 BCE they got them: the Twelve Tables, Rome’s first written laws, displayed in the Forum. Now anyone could check the rules, at least in principle.

cards.headline: Everyday rules
cards.body: The Twelve Tables weren’t grand speeches about liberty. They covered ordinary life: debt, property, family and damage to others. In other words, the everyday arguments neighbors actually have. Centuries later, Cicero remembered memorizing them as a boy at school, then noted that boys no longer did. Kids these days.

cards.fact: The original tablets are lost.
cards.context: They were probably destroyed when the Gauls sacked Rome. The laws survive only because later writers quoted them. So the laws written down for everyone to read are the ones nobody today can read in the original.

levels.title: Tribunes of the Plebs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the tribunes’ power to protect plebeians, including the veto.
levels.summary: Tribunes, elected by plebeians, could veto other magistrates and were sacrosanct. Ten of them protected ordinary citizens.

cards.headline: The most powerful word in Roman politics meant “I forbid.”
cards.body: The plebeians had officials of their own, and those officials could stop the powerful with a single word.

cards.headline: Protectors of the plebs
cards.body: The tribunes of the plebs were officials elected by plebeians to protect them from abuses by magistrates. Their number eventually rose to ten: ten officials whose whole job was to take the plebeians’ side. And a tribune’s door was expected to stay open day and night, so any plebeian could come and ask for help. Think of a 24-hour help desk with real political muscle behind it.

cards.headline: I forbid
cards.body: Remember how each consul could block the other in Level 12? A tribune could block them both. He could stop the acts of other magistrates, consuls included, simply by declaring “Veto,” Latin for “I forbid.” (A dictator was probably out of reach.) So why didn’t an angry consul just arrest him? Tribunes were sacrosanct: harming one was a religious crime. And because plebeians elected them, tribunes answered to ordinary citizens rather than to the old families.

levels.title: Cincinnatus and the Citizen Ideal
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the story of Cincinnatus and explain the Roman idea of civic duty.
levels.summary: Called from his plow in 458 BCE to save Rome, Cincinnatus won and gave up power after 16 days: the model Roman citizen.

cards.headline: Rome handed a farmer supreme power. He gave it back in about 16 days.
cards.body: Remember the dictator’s six-month limit from Level 12? One man didn’t need anywhere near that.

cards.headline: Called from the plow
cards.body: In 458 BCE, according to tradition, a Roman army was trapped by its enemies. The Senate needed a rescuer, so it made Cincinnatus dictator, with supreme power. The messengers didn’t find him in a palace or a war tent. They found him plowing his farm. For the moment, the most powerful man in Rome was standing behind a plow.

cards.headline: Power returned
cards.body: Cincinnatus won the war. Then he resigned as dictator after about 16 days, far short of his six months, and went back to his farm. He gave up supreme power the moment the crisis was over. His story shows what Romans prized, the mos maiorum, “the custom of the ancestors”: duty, discipline and service to the state. Cincinnatus managed all three and still got the plowing done.

cards.fact: An American city carries his name.
cards.context: Cincinnati is named after the Society of the Cincinnati, which took its name from Cincinnatus. So a whole city is named, at one remove, after a man remembered for giving power back.

levels.title: The Gauls Sack Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Gallic sack of Rome and how it changed Roman defense.
levels.summary: Around 390 BCE Gauls under Brennus won at the Allia and sacked Rome. “Woe to the conquered.” Rome answered with a great stone wall.

cards.headline: Around 390 BCE, Rome learned it could be captured.
cards.body: It began with a battle at a river and ended with an enemy army inside the city.

cards.headline: Disaster at the Allia
cards.body: In about 390 BCE (387 by some counts), an army of Gauls led by Brennus crushed the Romans at the Allia River. Then came the unthinkable: the Gauls marched into Rome itself and sacked it. The damage reached even Rome’s laws. The original Twelve Tables from Level 15 were probably destroyed in the sack.

cards.headline: Woe to the conquered
cards.body: According to Livy, when the Romans protested the ransom, Brennus threw his sword onto the scales and said “Vae victis”: woe to the conquered. In other words, losers don’t get to argue. Legend gives Rome one bright moment: the sacred geese of Juno warned the defenders of the Capitoline of a night attack by the Gauls. Saved by geese. Rome would take it.

cards.fact: Rome’s answer: a wall.
cards.context: After the sack, Rome surrounded itself with a strong stone wall, later called the Servian Wall. A city that had just learned it could be captured gave itself a shell.

cards.headline: The sack: survived

levels.title: Conquering Italy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rome came to control the Italian peninsula, and the role of roads and alliances.
levels.summary: Rome beat the Samnites, built the Via Appia from 312 BCE and made defeated peoples allies. By about 264 BCE it controlled Italy.

cards.headline: Rome won Italy with armies, roads and allies.
cards.body: Swords can win land. Roads and allies help you keep it.

cards.headline: Wars in the hills
cards.body: From 343 to 290 BCE, Rome fought the Samnite Wars against the hill peoples of central and southern Italy, a struggle for control of the peninsula. Rome came out on top. By about 264 BCE it controlled nearly all of Italy south of the Po Valley. The little town on the Tiber now ran almost the whole boot, minus the top.

cards.headline: Roads and allies
cards.body: In 312 BCE Rome began the Via Appia, its first great road, built to move armies quickly to the south. But the smarter move was what Rome did with the people it beat. Defeated Italian peoples became allies who supplied soldiers instead of paying tribute, and some were granted citizenship. So every war Rome won made its next army bigger. Lose to Rome, and you ended up marching for it.
cards.callout: Via Appia: begun 312 BCE

cards.fact: A victory that cost too much.
cards.context: King Pyrrhus of Epirus beat Roman armies, but at such a cost that his name became a warning. A “Pyrrhic victory” now means a win that costs too much.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How the Republic Worked
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how consuls, Senate, assemblies and tribunes balanced one another.
levels.summary: Consuls led, the Senate advised, the assemblies elected and legislated, and tribunes could veto: a mixed constitution Polybius admired.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale. How do you stop anyone from becoming a king?
cards.body: You spread power around and let each part hold the others back. Here’s the whole machine.

items.label: Consuls
points: Two, elected every year, each able to block the other
Commanded the armies

items.label: Senate
points: Former magistrates, usually for life
Advice almost always followed

items.label: Citizens and tribunes
points: Assemblies elected magistrates and passed laws
Tribunes could veto other magistrates

cards.headline: Checks and balances
cards.body: It took an outsider to name the design. Polybius, a Greek historian taken to Rome as a hostage, wrote his history to explain how Rome came to dominate the Mediterranean world. Along the way he praised Rome’s government as a mix of three kinds of rule: the consuls were the monarchy, the Senate the aristocracy, and the assemblies the democracy. Each part checked the others, so none could take over. Rome kept a piece of a king, a piece of the nobles and a piece of the people, and let none of them win.

levels.title: Carthage, Queen of the Sea
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Carthage and why it clashed with Rome.
levels.summary: Carthage, founded by Phoenicians in 814 BCE, ruled the western seas. In 264 BCE it and Rome went to war over Sicily: the Punic Wars.

cards.headline: Once Rome held Italy, it looked across the water and found a rival.
cards.body: By about 264 BCE Rome controlled nearly all of Italy south of the Po Valley. Across the sea waited a city that was older than Rome and far better at sea.

cards.headline: A city of traders
cards.body: Carthage began as a colony. Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded it, traditionally in 814 BCE, on the coast of what is now Tunisia. It grew rich from trade, and it guarded that trade with ships, becoming the leading naval power of the western Mediterranean. Rome was a land power with a new peninsula. Carthage was a trading house with a fleet.

cards.headline: Sicily in between
cards.body: Look at a map and the trouble is obvious. Sicily sits between Italy and North Africa, like a stepping stone in the middle of a stream. Rome now held Italy and faced Carthage, the great sea power, across the water. In 264 BCE the two went to war over control of Sicily. Romans called these wars Punic, from the Latin Punicus, “Phoenician.” The name remembers where Carthage came from.
cards.callout: Punic = Phoenician

cards.fact: Carthage was older than Rome.
cards.context: Carthage’s traditional founding date, 814 BCE, comes 61 years before Rome’s own, 753 BCE. So when the two met in Sicily, Rome was the newcomer, taking on an older city that already ruled the western sea. The upstart against the old sea power: that’s the story of the Punic Wars.
