levels.title: The Pantheon
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Pantheon and its record-breaking dome.
levels.summary: Hadrian’s Pantheon has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, lit only by its oculus. As a church it survived intact.

cards.headline: The largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world was built by the Romans.
cards.body: Remember the volcanic concrete from Level 73? This is what it could do at full stretch.

cards.headline: A ball inside a building
cards.body: Pantheon means “of all the gods.” The building standing today is Hadrian’s rebuilding of Agrippa’s first Pantheon. Its dome, about 43 m across, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. And the proportions are perfect: the height from the floor to the top of the dome equals its diameter. So a complete sphere 43 m wide would fit inside, resting on the floor.

cards.headline: Light and lightness
cards.body: Look up and there’s a hole in the roof. The oculus, about 8 m wide, is the building’s only source of natural light. The dome itself slims down as it rises: it gets thinner toward the top, and lighter stone was mixed into the concrete higher up. Less weight up high means less weight pressing down on everything below.
cards.callout: Oculus: the open “eye” at the top

cards.fact: The Pantheon survived by changing religion.
cards.context: In 609 CE the temple “of all the gods” became a Christian church, which helped it survive intact. New job, same building.

levels.title: Running the Provinces
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how governors, taxes and local elites ran the provinces.
levels.summary: Governors ran provinces, split by Augustus between the Senate and himself. Taxes came from a census, and local elites did most of the work.

cards.headline: Rome ran a vast empire with surprisingly few officials.
cards.body: So who did all the work? Mostly, other people.

cards.headline: Who got which province
cards.body: Augustus split the provinces in two. Peaceful ones got governors chosen by the Senate. Frontier provinces, the ones with armies, were run by his own deputies. Notice which half he kept: the half with the soldiers. Either way, every province paid taxes on land and on people, and a census counted them for taxation. Being counted by Rome meant being charged by Rome.

cards.headline: Local help
cards.body: Here’s the few-officials secret. Rome relied on local elites to govern their own cities and collect taxes. Under the Republic, tax collection had often been contracted out to private companies of publicani instead, and they were notorious for abuses. Handing a for-profit company the job of squeezing your subjects: what could go wrong?
cards.callout: Publicani: private tax contractors

cards.fact: Pontius Pilate was a provincial governor.
cards.context: He was the Roman prefect who governed Judaea from 26 to 36 CE. A name most people know, in a job most people never think about.

levels.title: Becoming Roman
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Roman citizenship and how it spread to all free people in 212.
levels.summary: Citizenship brought legal privileges. It spread to Italy, then to towns, soldiers and individuals, until Caracalla gave it to almost all free people in 212 CE.

cards.headline: In 212 CE, one emperor made almost every free person a Roman citizen.
cards.body: For centuries, citizenship had been something you were granted or earned. What made it worth having?

cards.headline: What citizenship meant
cards.body: Roman citizens had legal privileges, such as the right to appeal to Rome and protection from certain punishments. Think of it as a passport that doubled as a shield. According to the Book of Acts, Paul of Tarsus, a Roman citizen, used exactly that shield: his right to appeal to the emperor.

cards.headline: How it spread
cards.body: Italy got it the hard way. During the Social War of 91–88 BCE, Rome granted citizenship to its Italian allies, which helped end the revolt. After that it spread through the provinces by grants to towns, to individuals and to soldiers. Non-citizen soldiers, the auxiliaries, received it after about 25 years of service. And as Level 62 showed, a person freed by a Roman citizen usually became a citizen too.

cards.fact: In 212 CE Caracalla made almost every free person a citizen.
cards.context: After centuries of grants, one town, one veteran at a time, being Roman became a status shared across the whole empire. The members’ club had opened its doors to nearly everyone.

levels.title: Roman Law
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the key ideas of Roman law and how they reached modern legal systems.
levels.summary: Jurists developed Roman law for a thousand years after the Twelve Tables. Justinian’s code carried it into the law of much of the world.

cards.headline: If you live in France or Brazil, your law has Roman roots.
cards.body: The trail runs through Roman lawyers’ opinions and one emperor’s giant collection.

cards.headline: Lawyers who shaped the law
cards.body: Rome first wrote its laws down around 450 BCE, in the Twelve Tables. Then its legal experts, the jurists, wrote opinions that developed and explained the law. Some of their ideas now feel like common sense. Take the burden of proof: it rests on the person who makes a claim, not on the one who denies it. If your neighbor says you owe him money, he has to prove it. You don’t have to prove you don’t.
cards.callout: Burden of proof: whoever claims must prove

cards.headline: Justinian’s code
cards.body: In the 6th century CE the emperor Justinian had Roman law collected into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the “body of civil law.” That code shaped the civil law systems used across continental Europe, Latin America and many other countries. So a court in Paris or São Paulo still runs on ideas an emperor had collected about 1,500 years ago.

cards.fact: Legal English is full of Latin.
cards.context: Many legal terms are Latin words, such as alibi, which means “elsewhere.” So “I have an alibi” really just says “I was elsewhere.”

levels.title: Money and Trade
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Roman coins, trade routes and the economy of the Mediterranean.
levels.summary: The silver denarius carried the emperor’s face everywhere. Amphorae carried wine, oil and fish sauce, and traders reached India.

cards.headline: In Rome there is a hill made entirely of broken jars.
cards.body: To see how it got there, follow the money, and the olive oil.

cards.headline: Coins with a message
cards.body: The denarius, a silver coin, was the standard Roman coin for centuries. It was also a tiny billboard: coins carried the emperor’s portrait and short messages, spreading his image across the empire. Every time you paid, you saw the boss. Then came the catch. Over time emperors reduced the silver in the denarius, and by the 3rd century CE it held very little. Same coin, same face, less and less silver.

cards.headline: Goods on the move
cards.body: Wine, olive oil and fish sauce moved around the Mediterranean in amphorae, clay jars made for shipping. Think of them as Rome’s cardboard boxes. And trade didn’t stop at the sea’s edge: Roman traders sailed to India, and Chinese silk reached Rome through many middlemen along the Silk Road.
cards.callout: Amphora: a two-handled shipping jar

cards.fact: Monte Testaccio is an artificial hill.
cards.context: It’s made of fragments of millions of broken olive oil amphorae, piled up in Rome itself. Picture how much olive oil that was, and then remember it’s only the empties.

levels.title: Life on the Frontier
levels.objective: After this level you can describe forts, soldiers and communities on the Roman frontier.
levels.summary: Auxiliaries held standard forts along the limes. Towns grew beside them, and the Vindolanda tablets let us read their letters.

cards.headline: At a fort in northern Britain, a commander’s wife sent a birthday invitation.
cards.body: Life on the edge of the empire wasn’t all marching and watching. So who actually lived out there?

cards.headline: Forts on the limes
cards.body: The fortified frontier of the empire was called the limes. Much of it was held by auxiliaries, non-citizen soldiers recruited from the provinces: the same soldiers who received Roman citizenship after about 25 years (Level 76). Their forts followed a standard plan: a rectangle with rounded corners, four gates and a headquarters building at the center. Seen one Roman fort? You could find your way around the next.
cards.callout: Limes: the fortified frontier

cards.headline: Towns beside the forts
cards.body: Where there were soldiers, other people followed. Civilian settlements grew up beside frontier forts, with traders, craftsmen and soldiers’ families. On Hadrian’s Wall, small forts stood about every Roman mile, with larger forts along its length. A frontier, it turns out, was also a neighborhood.

cards.fact: We can read letters written on the frontier.
cards.context: At Vindolanda, a fort near Hadrian’s Wall, archaeologists found more than a thousand wooden writing tablets. Among them is the invitation from the start of this level, from one commander’s wife to another. It’s everyday frontier life, in the frontier’s own words.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Rome Held an Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how roads, law, citizenship, the army and trade held the empire together.
levels.summary: Roads, a shared army, citizenship, law and trade held the empire together, and Roman ways spread through the provinces.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale. How do you hold together an empire from Britain to Egypt?
cards.body: Not with soldiers alone. You’ve already met most of the answer in this chapter.

cards.headline: More than force
cards.body: Rome held its empire together with roads, a shared army, citizenship, law and trade, not by force alone. It also ran its provinces with few officials: local elites ran their own cities and collected the taxes. And in 212 CE almost every free person became a citizen. The strongest glue wasn’t fear. It was citizenship and shared law: being Roman.

cards.headline: Becoming Roman
cards.body: Historians call the spread of Roman language, culture and ways of life in the provinces Romanization. You could see it: towns across the West built forums, baths and amphitheaters on the Roman model. You could hear it too, as Latin spread through the western provinces with soldiers, settlers and officials. In the East, Greek stayed the common language.
cards.callout: Romanization: provinces adopting Roman ways

levels.title: The Crisis of the Third Century
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the chaos of the third century, when emperors rose and fell rapidly.
levels.summary: From 235 to 284 CE, more than 20 emperors came and went, an emperor was captured, and the empire split in three before Aurelian reunited it.

cards.headline: More than 20 emperors in about 50 years. Most of them were murdered.
cards.body: Remember 69 CE, when the legions learned they could make and unmake emperors? For half a century, they did it again and again. Becoming emperor was a promotion with a very short life expectancy.

cards.headline: Everything at once
cards.body: From 235 to 284 CE, the Crisis of the Third Century, the empire suffered civil wars, invasions, plague and economic trouble, all at the same time. Even the money went bad. Emperors had kept reducing the silver in the denarius until the coin held very little, and prices soared. Imagine every new batch of coins holding a little less of the metal that made them worth anything. That was Roman money in the third century.

cards.headline: An emperor taken prisoner
cards.body: Then came the low point. In 260 CE the emperor Valerian was captured by the Persian king Shapur I. No Roman emperor had ever been taken prisoner by a foreign enemy before. The empire itself came apart, too. For a time it split into three: a breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, Rome in the middle, and Palmyra under Queen Zenobia in the east. One empire, three maps.

cards.fact: Aurelian put the pieces back together.
cards.context: In the 270s the emperor Aurelian reunited the three pieces into one empire. He also built new walls around Rome itself. A reunited empire whose capital needed fresh walls: that is the third century in a single picture.

levels.title: Diocletian Divides the Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Diocletian's reforms and the Tetrarchy.
levels.summary: Diocletian ended the crisis in 284 CE with four emperors, smaller provinces and price controls, then retired to his palace at Split.

cards.headline: One emperor wasn’t enough. Diocletian tried four.
cards.body: After half a century of murdered emperors, Diocletian’s fix was bold. If one ruler can’t guard everything, hire more rulers.

cards.headline: Rule of four
cards.body: Diocletian became emperor in 284 CE and ended the half century of crisis. His big idea was the Tetrarchy, “rule of four”: two senior emperors, called Augusti, and two junior ones, called Caesars. With four emperors, one could be near every threatened frontier. The junior Caesars also gave the empire a planned succession. That fixed an old problem: Rome never had a fixed law of succession, so every emperor had to pick his own heir. Now the next emperors were lined up in advance.
cards.callout: Tetrarchy: two Augusti and two Caesars

cards.headline: Smaller pieces, fixed prices
cards.body: Diocletian also split the provinces into smaller units and separated civil from military command, so the man running a province was no longer the man leading its troops. Then he took on inflation. In 301 CE his Edict on Maximum Prices tried to stop it by fixing prices by law. It failed. It turns out you can’t order a price to stay put.

cards.fact: Diocletian did what no emperor had done: he retired.
cards.context: In 305 CE he stepped down voluntarily, the first Roman emperor to do so, and moved to his palace at Split, in modern Croatia. After an age when most emperors left office by being killed, this one simply packed up and left.

levels.title: The First Christians
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how Christianity began and spread through the Roman world.
levels.summary: Jesus was crucified in Judaea under Pilate. Paul and others carried the faith to the cities of the empire along Roman roads.

cards.headline: A faith from a small province spread along roads that Rome had built.
cards.body: Rome built its roads to move armies. They turned out to be very good at moving a new faith, too.

cards.headline: From Judaea
cards.body: The story starts in Judaea, a Roman province. Jesus of Nazareth was a Jewish teacher executed there by crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judaea from 26 to 36 CE. Then Paul of Tarsus carried the faith to non-Jews, city by city, around the eastern Mediterranean. A movement born in one small province was on the road.

cards.headline: Roads, peace and Greek
cards.body: Rome helped, without being asked. Christianity spread mainly in cities, helped by Roman roads, peace and the common Greek language of the East. Roads built first for marching legions carried much more than soldiers. But the new faith came with a catch. Christians worshiped one God and refused to sacrifice to the Roman gods or to the emperor. In an empire of many gods, that got noticed.

cards.fact: Early churches looked after their own.
cards.context: Each Christian community was led by a bishop, and it cared for its own poor, widows and sick. A church wasn’t only a place to pray. It was a support network with someone in charge.

levels.title: Persecution
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why and when Christians were persecuted by the Roman state.
levels.summary: Persecution was local and sporadic until Decius in 250 CE. Diocletian’s Great Persecution from 303 CE was the harshest.

cards.headline: Why would a tolerant empire of many gods persecute one group?
cards.body: The answer isn’t really about what Christians believed. It’s about what they refused to do.

cards.headline: Why Christians were targeted
cards.body: Roman religion was about doing the rituals right to keep the pax deorum, the peace with the gods. So when Christians refused to sacrifice to the gods and the emperor, it looked like disloyalty, and Romans feared it would break the peace with the gods. Picture a neighbor refusing to help mend the dam everyone lives behind. Still, for most of the first two centuries persecution was local and sporadic, not constant. Even Nero, as Tacitus tells it, blamed the Christians of Rome for the fire of 64 CE, not Christians everywhere.

cards.headline: Empire-wide
cards.body: Then the crisis century changed the rules. In 250 CE the emperor Decius ordered everyone in the empire to sacrifice to the gods: the first empire-wide persecution. Refusing was no longer a local matter. The worst came last. The Great Persecution under Diocletian, from 303 CE, was the harshest the Christians faced. Yes, the same Diocletian who reorganized the whole empire.

cards.fact: Trajan told a governor not to hunt Christians.
cards.context: Pliny the Younger, governing a province, asked Trajan how to treat Christians. Trajan’s answer: don’t hunt them out, but if they are accused and refuse to recant, punish them. Don’t go looking, but don’t look away. Those who died were honored as martyrs, from a Greek word meaning “witness.”

levels.title: Constantine

levels.summary: Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge in 312 CE, gave Christians tolerance in 313, ruled alone from 324 and called the Council of Nicaea.

cards.headline: Ten years after the Great Persecution began, Christians were free to worship.
cards.body: What changed so fast? A new emperor, and a battle at a bridge.

cards.headline: The Milvian Bridge
cards.body: In 312 CE Constantine defeated his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome. Christian writers said he saw a sign before the battle and had his soldiers fight under a Christian symbol. Whatever he saw, he won. By 324 CE he had beaten his last rival too and ruled the whole empire alone. Diocletian’s rule of four had become rule of one.

cards.headline: A Christian-friendly emperor
cards.body: Then things moved fast. In 313 CE the Edict of Milan granted religious tolerance to Christians throughout the empire. Just ten years earlier, in 303 CE, Diocletian had launched the Great Persecution. In 325 CE Constantine went further and called the Council of Nicaea, a meeting of bishops that agreed a common statement of Christian belief. An emperor was now hosting the church’s biggest meeting.

cards.fact: Constantine was baptized only on his deathbed.
cards.context: The emperor who granted Christians tolerance and gathered the bishops at Nicaea was not baptized until 337 CE, as he was dying. He joined the church officially on his way out.

levels.title: Constantinople
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Constantine founded a new capital on the Bosporus.
levels.summary: In 330 CE Constantine dedicated a new Rome on the Bosporus, closer to the frontiers and between two continents. Today it is Istanbul.

cards.headline: Constantine built a second Rome where Europe meets Asia.
cards.body: Rome already had a capital. It was called Rome. So why build another one?

cards.headline: A new capital
cards.body: In 330 CE Constantine dedicated his new capital, Constantinople, on the site of the old Greek city of Byzantium. The location was the whole point. It stood on the Bosporus, the strait between Europe and Asia, controlling the route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Whoever held the city held the front door between two seas.
cards.callout: Bosporus: the strait between Europe and Asia

cards.headline: Why move?
cards.body: It was also closer than Rome to the threatened Danube and eastern frontiers, so an emperor there was nearer the trouble. And it was built as a new Rome, with its own senate, forums and a great hippodrome for chariot racing. Its racing fans would make history too: in 532 CE Blues and Greens rioted together in the Nika revolt and nearly toppled the emperor Justinian.

cards.fact: Constantinople is today Istanbul.
cards.context: The city Constantine founded is in Turkey today, still on the Bosporus where Europe meets Asia. Same strait, same city, new name.

levels.title: Julian the Apostate

cards.headline: One emperor tried to turn the clock back to the old gods.
cards.body: Half a century after the Milvian Bridge, Constantine’s own nephew set out to undo his uncle’s work.

cards.headline: The last pagan emperor
cards.body: Julian, Constantine’s nephew, became sole emperor in 361 CE. His uncle had backed Christianity; Julian rejected it, and tried to restore worship of the traditional gods. He was the last Roman emperor to follow the old gods. The old religion got one more emperor on its side, and then no more.

cards.headline: A short reign
cards.body: Christians gave him the name he’s still known by: Julian the Apostate. An apostate is someone who abandons their faith. His revival never got time to take root. He was killed on campaign against Persia in 363 CE, about two years after becoming sole emperor, and his religious program died with him.

cards.fact: Julian banned Christians from teaching classical literature.
cards.context: Picture a school where the old poets and philosophers are on the syllabus, but Christian teachers aren’t allowed to teach them. That was Julian’s rule for classical literature.

levels.title: A Christian Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Christianity became the empire's official religion under Theodosius.
levels.summary: In 380 CE Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the official religion; in the 390s temples closed. After his death in 395 the empire split.

cards.headline: Within a lifetime of the Great Persecution, Christianity became the law.
cards.body: From hunted faith to official religion. Here’s how the tables turned.

cards.headline: The official religion
cards.body: In 380 CE, under Theodosius I, Nicene Christianity became the official religion of the empire. Then the old religion was shut down. In the 390s Theodosius banned sacrifices and closed temples. Even the sacred fire of Vesta, which the Vestal Virgins had tended and never allowed to go out, was put out, and the Vestals were disbanded. The fire that must never go out: out.

cards.headline: Church and emperor
cards.body: The church could now challenge an emperor. After a massacre at Thessalonica, Bishop Ambrose of Milan made Theodosius do public penance. The ruler of the Roman world, saying sorry in public, on a bishop’s orders. Theodosius was also the last emperor to rule both halves of the empire. After his death in 395 CE, it was divided between his two sons.

cards.fact: The ancient Olympics ended in a Christian empire.
cards.context: They are traditionally said to have ended in 393 CE under Theodosius, in the same decade the temples were closed.

levels.title: Disaster at Adrianople
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Gothic victory at Adrianople and why it mattered.
levels.summary: Goths fleeing the Huns crossed the Danube in 376 CE, rebelled against mistreatment and destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople in 378.

cards.headline: In 378 CE a Roman emperor died on the battlefield against the Goths.
cards.body: It started with refugees at a river.

cards.headline: Refugees become rebels
cards.body: The trouble began far from Rome. The Huns, nomadic horsemen from the Eurasian steppes, were pushing west and driving other peoples before them. In 376 CE Goths fleeing the Huns were allowed to cross the Danube into the empire. Then Roman officials mistreated and exploited them, and the Goths rebelled. Rome had let them in, then given them a reason to fight.

cards.headline: The battle
cards.body: Two years later came Adrianople. In 378 CE the Goths destroyed a Roman army there, and the emperor Valens was killed. Gothic cavalry arriving during the battle played a decisive part in the defeat. Rome had lost armies before: in 9 CE, three legions under Varus were wiped out in the Teutoburg Forest. This time the emperor himself died.

cards.fact: Afterwards, the Goths stayed.
cards.context: Gothic groups settled inside the empire as allies under their own leaders. Rebels one year, allies the next, with their own commanders inside Rome’s borders. It was a new arrangement, and a risky one.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale. Would Augustus have recognized the empire of 395?
cards.body: Line up the empire of 395 CE against the one Augustus left. Four big changes made it a different world.

cards.headline: A different empire
cards.body: By 395 CE the empire was Christian. It was divided into East and West, with two capitals: Rome, and Constantinople, dedicated in 330 CE. After Theodosius died in 395 CE, his two sons divided it between them. And it was defended partly by Germanic allies under their own leaders, like the Goths who settled inside the empire after Adrianople. Three changes down.

cards.headline: Lord, not first citizen
cards.body: The fourth change was the emperor himself. Augustus had called himself princeps, “first citizen,” and avoided the title of king. Later emperors dropped the modesty and ruled openly as absolute monarchs, surrounded by elaborate court ceremony. Historians sometimes call this the Dominate, from dominus, “lord.” From first citizen to lord: Augustus might not recognize the job.

levels.title: The Sack of Rome, 410
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Alaric's sack of Rome and its shock to the Roman world.
levels.summary: In 410 CE Alaric’s Visigoths plundered Rome for three days, the first foreign capture in about 800 years. Augustine answered with The City of God.

cards.headline: In 410 CE, Rome fell to an enemy for the first time in about 800 years.
cards.body: The last time, it was Brennus and his Gauls, back in about 390 BCE. So how did the city that took the whole world end up taken?

cards.headline: Alaric at the gates
cards.body: The Visigoths weren’t strangers at the door. Since the years after Adrianople, Gothic groups had lived inside the empire as allies under their own leaders, a risky arrangement. For a while, the western empire’s leading general, Stilicho, held the Visigoth leader Alaric off. Then, in 408 CE, Stilicho was executed. In 410 CE Alaric’s Visigoths sacked Rome and plundered it for three days. The guard went first. Two years later, so did the city.

cards.headline: A shock to the world
cards.body: The scholar Jerome put it in one line: the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken. Then came the blame. Christianity had been the empire’s official religion since 380 CE, and some pagans said the sack was the price of abandoning the old gods. Augustine of Hippo wrote The City of God partly to answer them. One raid on one city, and the argument went all the way up to heaven.

cards.fact: The emperor wasn’t even home.
cards.context: By 410 CE the western emperor Honorius lived at Ravenna, a city protected by marshes, not in Rome. So while Alaric’s men plundered the old capital, the emperor sat safely behind a swamp. Not a glamorous address, but a hard one to storm.

levels.title: Attila and the Huns
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Huns under Attila and their impact on the empire.
levels.summary: Attila squeezed gold from the East, was stopped in Gaul in 451 CE and turned back from Italy in 452. His empire died with him in 453.

cards.headline: Christian writers called him the “Scourge of God.”
cards.body: Attila, king of the Huns, earned that name the hard way. Here’s how, and why his power didn’t outlive him.

cards.headline: King of the Huns
cards.body: Remember the Huns from Level 89, the steppe horsemen whose push west drove the Goths across the Danube? Attila ruled them from 434 to 453 CE, at first sharing power with his brother Bleda. He raided the Eastern Empire and forced it to pay him large amounts of gold. For once, the Romans were the ones handing over the treasure.

cards.headline: Stopped twice
cards.body: In 451 CE Attila invaded Gaul. A Roman and Visigothic army under the general Aetius stopped him at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains. Yes, Visigoths: 41 years after sacking Rome, they fought on Rome’s side. In 452 CE Attila invaded Italy instead. Pope Leo I met him, and Attila withdrew. A general stopped him in Gaul; a pope met him in Italy.

cards.fact: Attila’s empire died with him.
cards.context: Attila died in 453 CE, and his empire of many peoples soon fell apart. It had depended on Attila himself to hold it together. Without him, the Scourge of God’s empire lasted about as long as a sandcastle at high tide.

levels.title: 476: The Last Western Emperor
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happened in 476 and why historians debate its importance.
levels.summary: After the Vandal sack of 455 CE, Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 and ruled Italy as king. Historians debate how much changed.

cards.headline: The last western emperor bore the names of Rome’s founder and first emperor.
cards.body: Romulus, the founder, and Augustus, the name the Senate gave Octavian, Rome’s first emperor. And “Augustulus” means “little Augustus.” The empire ended on a diminutive.

cards.headline: The Vandals
cards.body: Before the last emperor, one more sack. In 455 CE the Vandals sacked Rome for two weeks. Alaric’s Goths had managed three days. The Vandals also left behind something that outlasted the damage: their name. It gave us the word vandalism. Every scribbled-on bus shelter carries a little fifth-century history.

cards.headline: 476 CE
cards.body: In 476 CE the Germanic commander Odoacer deposed the young western emperor Romulus Augustulus. Then he did something odd. He did not make himself emperor. He sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and ruled Italy as king. That’s the usual date given for the fall of the Western Empire. The crown jewels went east, and Italy got a king.

cards.fact: Did Rome really fall in 476?
cards.context: Many historians see 476 CE as a convenient marker rather than a sudden end, since life in Italy went on much as before for many people. An empire ended, and for many people the next day looked a lot like the one before.

levels.title: Why Did Rome Fall?
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the main explanations for the fall of the Western Empire.
levels.summary: Invasions, civil wars and the loss of Africa broke the West. Gibbon blamed Christianity and lost virtue; others see a transformation.

cards.headline: Historians have given many answers to why the West fell. Here are the big ones.
cards.body: The West fell in 476 CE. Fine. But why? Historians have proposed many answers, and one twist: maybe “fall” is the wrong word.

cards.headline: Outside and inside
cards.body: Start with the squeeze. From outside, pressure from Germanic peoples and the Huns stretched the western army beyond its limits. From inside, repeated civil wars between Roman generals weakened the West further. Then came the money. When the Vandals captured Carthage in 439 CE, the West lost its richest tax base and a major grain supply. Enemies at the door, fights in the house, and an empty pantry.

cards.headline: Fall or transformation?
cards.body: The classic answer came from Edward Gibbon, the historian who called the age of the Five Good Emperors the happiest (Level 60). His The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire blamed, in part, the rise of Christianity and a loss of civic virtue. Some historians today tell it differently: not a sudden collapse, but a transformation into the kingdoms of medieval Europe. Less a house falling down, more a house slowly remodeled by new owners.

cards.fact: The richer half survived.
cards.context: The East was richer and more populous than the West, which helps explain why it outlived the West by nearly a thousand years (you’ll meet it next level). Two halves of one empire, and the one with more money and more people was the one still standing.

cards.headline: The fall: debated
learned: Invasions stretched the western army
Civil wars weakened the West
Losing Africa cost taxes and grain
Some see transformation, not collapse

levels.title: The Empire That Didn't Fall
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Eastern Roman Empire lasted until 1453.
levels.summary: The Greek-speaking East called itself Roman. Justinian won back Italy and built Hagia Sophia; Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

cards.headline: The Roman Empire lasted until 1453, if you count the East.
cards.body: The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, outlived the West by nearly a thousand years. So when did Rome really end? Depends which half you ask.

cards.headline: Romans in the East
cards.body: Historians call the Eastern Roman Empire the Byzantine Empire. That’s our label, not theirs: its people called themselves Romans. Their capital was Constantinople, which Constantine dedicated in 330 CE. Over time, though, Greek replaced Latin as the language of its government. So picture it: Romans, running the Roman Empire, in Greek.

cards.headline: Justinian’s ambition
cards.body: In the 6th century CE, the emperor Justinian reconquered Italy and North Africa, for a time. The old West was briefly Roman again. He also had Roman law collected into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the “body of civil law.” And he built the great church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, finished in 537 CE. Land, law and a landmark: not a bad record for a “fallen” empire.

cards.fact: Constantinople fell in 1453 CE.
cards.context: Sultan Mehmed II led the Ottoman capture of the city, more than a thousand years after Constantine dedicated it in 330 CE. That’s the last page of Roman history, if you count the East. The city itself carried on under a new name: today it’s Istanbul.

levels.title: Integration: Rome in Our Laws and Governments
levels.objective: After this level you can connect Roman institutions to modern republics and legal systems.
levels.summary: Senates, capitols, vetoes and balanced constitutions come from Rome, and Justinian’s code underlies civil law across much of the world.

cards.headline: Every time a president vetoes a bill, they are speaking Latin.
cards.body: Veto is Latin for “I forbid.” And that’s just one of the things Rome left inside modern governments. Let’s count them.

cards.headline: Names we kept
cards.body: Start with the names. Rome’s Senate began as a council of elders advising the king, and the United States Senate takes its name from it. The US Capitol is named after Rome’s Capitoline Hill, home of its greatest temple, dedicated to Jupiter, king of the gods. And veto? A Roman tribune could block other magistrates by declaring “Veto.” Today the word still means the power to block laws, as when a US president vetoes a bill. Same word, same job.

cards.headline: Ideas we kept
cards.body: Names are easy to borrow. Ideas matter more. The Greek historian Polybius praised Rome’s government as a mix: consuls like monarchs, a Senate of aristocrats, and assemblies for the people, each checking the others. The framers of the US Constitution studied the Roman Republic and its balance between different parts of government. And Justinian’s code shaped the civil law systems of continental Europe, Latin America and many other countries. Rome’s rules still run courtrooms Rome never saw.

levels.title: Integration: Rome in Our Words, Calendars and Cities
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Rome's legacy in languages, calendars, architecture and city planning.
levels.summary: Roman towns became London and Paris, Roman columns became capitols and banks, and July and August still honor Caesar and Augustus.

cards.headline: You can see Rome in a city map, a bank front and a calendar.
cards.body: The empire is long gone. Its fingerprints aren’t. Let’s go looking for them.

cards.headline: Cities and buildings
cards.body: Many European cities grew from Roman towns or forts, including London, Paris, Cologne and Vienna. Many Roman towns were laid out on a grid, with two main streets crossing at right angles. Much later, neoclassical architecture copied Roman columns, domes and temple fronts in buildings across Europe and the Americas. Next time you pass a bank with columns out front, you’re looking at a Roman idea wearing a suit.

cards.headline: Words and time
cards.body: Everyday spoken Latin kept changing until it became Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian. English isn’t one of those Romance languages, but a large share of its vocabulary comes from Latin, much of it through French. Now check a calendar. July is named for Julius Caesar, and August for Augustus. Rome’s two most famous names, still sitting side by side every year.

cards.fact: “E pluribus unum”: out of many, one.
cards.context: Latin mottoes still appear on seals and coins. This one sits on the Great Seal of the United States: a modern country describing itself in Rome’s language.

levels.title: Integration: How We Know About Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how historians use texts, inscriptions, coins and archaeology to study Rome.
levels.summary: Ancient writers had biases, so historians test them against inscriptions, coins, letters and the archaeology of places like Pompeii.

cards.headline: A history of Rome is a detective story built from four kinds of clues.
cards.body: Texts, inscriptions, coins and the ground itself. Each clue tells part of the truth. None tells all of it.

cards.headline: Texts and their biases
cards.body: The obvious clue is the written word. Much of Roman history comes from ancient writers such as Livy, Tacitus and Suetonius. But each had his own sources, purposes and biases. Most accounts of Caligula come from later writers hostile to him, so historians treat the wildest stories with caution. And Rome’s founding stories were written down centuries after the events. Picture a witness who wasn’t there, and one who didn’t like the suspect.

cards.headline: Stone, metal and earth
cards.body: So historians check the writers against other clues. Huge numbers of Latin inscriptions carved in stone record laws, careers, dedications and epitaphs. Coins help date events and show how emperors wanted to be seen: each one a tiny press release in your pocket. Archaeology reveals the ordinary lives writers ignored, from houses and graves to rubbish heaps. Yes, Roman trash counts as evidence.

cards.fact: Ordinary Romans speak through the ground.
cards.context: Pompeii gives historians a rare snapshot of ordinary Roman town life. At Vindolanda, a fort near Hadrian’s Wall, archaeologists found more than a thousand wooden writing tablets, including a birthday invitation from one commander’s wife to another. The writers ignored lives like these. The ground kept them anyway.

levels.title: Integration: The Arc of Roman History
levels.objective: After this level you can connect the major turning points of Roman history into one story.
levels.summary: From 753 BCE to 1453 CE, Rome went from kings to republic to empire to a Christian, divided state. One thread: control of the army.

cards.headline: Two thousand years in one story. Ready?
cards.body: More than 2,000 years, six dates, and one pattern that ties them together.

events.label: Traditional founding of Rome
The Republic begins
Octavian becomes Augustus
Under Trajan, the empire reaches its greatest extent
The last western emperor is deposed
Constantinople falls to the Ottoman Turks

cards.headline: The thread through it all
cards.body: Now the pattern. Again and again, whoever controlled the army controlled the state. After Marius, soldiers looked to their general, not the Senate, for pay and for land when they retired. So their loyalty followed the paymaster. Sulla marched his army on Rome. Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his. Vespasian, a general, won a civil war and a throne. In Rome, the road to power ran through the camp.

cards.fact: Roman history spans more than 2,000 years.
cards.context: It runs from the traditional founding in 753 BCE to the fall of Constantinople in 1453 CE. From Iron Age huts on the Palatine Hill to a capital on the Bosporus: that’s the whole story you’ve just walked through.

levels.title: The Middle Ages in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the thousand years between Rome's fall in the West and the Renaissance.
levels.summary: The Middle Ages run from the collapse of Roman rule in the West to the Renaissance, roughly 500 to 1500, and split into early, high and late periods.

cards.headline: The Middle Ages lasted about a thousand years. That’s a lot for one name.
cards.body: Before the castles and the crusades, start with the frame: when the Middle Ages were, and how historians slice them.

cards.headline: From Rome to the Renaissance
cards.body: The Middle Ages is the period of European history from the collapse of Roman rule in the West, in the 5th century, to the Renaissance. In round numbers: about 500 to about 1500. The usual starting marker is 476, when the last emperor in the West lost his throne. The finish line is blurrier, because the Renaissance arrived in different parts of Europe at different times. Think of it like a sunrise: easy to see it has happened, hard to name the exact minute.
cards.callout: About 500 to about 1500: roughly a thousand years

events.label: The early Middle Ages begin
The high (or central) Middle Ages begin
The late Middle Ages begin
The Middle Ages give way to the Renaissance

mascot.line: A thousand years under one name. Imagine one label for everything from the 1020s to today!

cards.headline: Why slice it at all?
cards.body: Because a thousand years is far too long to be one thing. Someone living in 500 and someone living in 1500 were as far apart in time as you are from the 1020s. The early period, about 500 to 1000, was a time of frequent warfare, when town life in western Europe virtually disappeared. The centuries that followed looked very different. So historians split the age into early, high and late, the way you might split your own life into childhood, school and work.

levels.title: Why "Middle" Ages?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain where the name came from and why historians question the idea of "Dark Ages".
levels.summary: Renaissance scholars named the Middle Ages as a dark gap between antiquity and their own revival. Historians now rarely say "Dark Ages" because of the judgment it carries.

cards.headline: Nobody in the Middle Ages thought they lived in the middle of anything.
cards.body: The name was stuck on later, by people who saw the whole thousand years as a gap to hurry past. Who named it, and why do historians push back?

cards.headline: In the middle of what?
cards.body: Italian scholars of the Renaissance invented the idea. They admired ancient Greece and Rome and saw their own age as a revival of classical learning. Everything in between became a middle period: a thousand years of darkness and ignorance, in their telling. Our word medieval still carries the idea. It comes from Latin medium, “the middle”, and aevum, “age”. Picture a sandwich where the people who named it only cared about the bread.

cards.headline: Petrarch turns out the lights
cards.body: One of the first to paint it dark was the Italian scholar Petrarch, in the 14th century. He wrote of living in a dark time that had begun with the decline of the Roman Empire. For Petrarch, ancient Rome was the light, and the centuries since were the shadow it left behind. It was a powerful image, and a stubborn one.
cards.callout: Ancient Rome = light; everything after = dark, in Petrarch’s picture

mascot.line: Rule of thumb: when a whole era gets called “dark”, check who was holding the lamp.

cards.headline: Why historians dropped “Dark Ages”
cards.body: Historians now rarely use the term “Dark Ages” because of the value judgment it carries. Some defend it as meaning only that we have few written records from the period, but its usual sense is a time of ignorance and barbarity. And the evidence keeps turning on lights. In Level 9 you’ll dig up a ship burial that reshaped how historians see early England, showing a society far more sophisticated than “dark” suggests.

levels.title: After Rome Fell
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the kingdoms that replaced the Western Roman Empire.
levels.summary: In 476 Odoacer deposed the last western emperor but ruled as king. Germanic kingdoms (Ostrogoths, Visigoths, Vandals, Franks, Anglo-Saxons) took over, often keeping Roman ways.

cards.headline: Rome’s western empire ended in 476. Its new ruler still bowed to an emperor.
cards.body: A Roman one, in Constantinople. Not much of a revolution. So what actually changed when Rome fell in the West, and who took over?

cards.headline: 476: a convenient line
cards.body: In 476 the Germanic commander Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last emperor in the West. Then he didn’t crown himself emperor. He called himself king, and he recognized the eastern emperor, Zeno, as his overlord. That’s why 476 is traditionally the end of the Western Empire: it’s a tidy line drawn across a messy change. Nobody in Italy woke up the next morning and said, “Ah, the Middle Ages.” That name came centuries later.

Visigoths in Spain, ruling from Toledo
Vandals in North Africa, ruling from Carthage

items.label: In the north
points: Franks in northern Gaul

cards.headline: Theodoric: a Goth running Rome’s paperwork
cards.body: In 489 the Ostrogoth king Theodoric invaded Italy. In 493 he killed Odoacer, and he ruled Italy until 526. Yet the old Roman civil service carried on more or less unchanged. Only Goths served in the army; Romans ran the government. Theodoric and his Goths were Arian Christians, not Catholics, like the Visigoths in Spain. New king, new army, same paperwork: that’s what the fall of Rome often looked like on the ground.
cards.callout: Goths held the swords; Romans held the pens

levels.title: The Byzantine Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Eastern Roman Empire lasted another thousand years.
levels.summary: The eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, lasted until 1453. Its Greek-speaking people called themselves Romans; layered walls and a trusted gold coin helped it endure.

cards.headline: Rome didn’t end in 476. Half of it kept going for about another thousand years.
cards.body: The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, outlasted the West by almost a millennium, until 1453. How does an empire lose half of itself and carry on?

cards.headline: Romans, not Byzantines
cards.body: Historians call it the Byzantine Empire, after Byzantium, the old Greek town where Constantinople was founded in 330. Its people never called themselves Byzantines. They called themselves Romaioi: Romans. Over time, Greek replaced Latin as the language of government. So picture Roman emperors, running the Roman Empire, in Greek, and puzzled by the name we gave them.

mascot.line: Moat, wall, bigger wall. Constantinople did not believe in a welcome mat.

cards.headline: Three walls deep
cards.body: Constantinople’s best defense was its land walls, begun under Emperor Theodosius II in 412. An attacker faced a moat, then an outer wall, then a taller main wall studded with 96 towers. Those walls held firm through the early Middle Ages against Germanic, Hun, Avar, Slav and Arab attackers. The city fell only in 1453, to Ottoman forces armed with heavy cannon. Attackers had to win three times in a row; defenders only had to win once.

cards.fact: Its gold coin was trusted far beyond its borders.
cards.context: The solidus, which westerners called the bezant, weighed about 4.5 grams and was known for its purity for centuries. It dominated European trade until the 13th century. Think of it as the medieval world’s dollar: accepted far from the empire that minted it. Strong walls kept enemies out; good gold kept business coming in.

levels.title: Justinian and Hagia Sophia
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Justinian's law code and his great church.
levels.summary: Justinian (527-565) had Roman law sorted into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the root of today's civil law, and built Hagia Sophia (532-537) with its floating dome.

cards.headline: In 532 a riot burned Constantinople’s great church. Justinian built a finer one.
cards.body: It was finished by 537. Same emperor, same busy decade: he also had Rome’s tangled laws sorted out. Two projects, one of law and one of stone, both built to last.

cards.headline: The great legal spring clean
cards.body: Roman law had piled up for hundreds of years, and the rules often contradicted each other. Justinian, emperor from 527 to 565, had it sorted. Between 530 and 533 a commission of 16 lawyers led by Tribonian boiled centuries of legal writing down into the Digest, in 50 books. Contradictions were removed, and any law left out was repealed. It was the ultimate clear-out: if it isn’t in the book, it isn’t the law.

cards.headline: Law that outlived the empire
cards.body: Justinian’s collections came to be known together as the Corpus Juris Civilis, the “Body of Civil Law”. Through them, Roman law became the foundation of civil law, the legal system used today across continental Europe and Latin America. Remember Level 4’s Romans who spoke Greek? Their emperor’s rulebook is still in court every day, from Paris to Buenos Aires.

cards.headline: A dome on a ring of light
cards.body: Hagia Sophia, “Holy Wisdom”, was designed by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidorus of Miletus. Its main dome is about 32 meters across. Windows pierce its base, so in daylight the supports seem to vanish and the dome looks as if it floats. The historian Procopius wrote that it seemed “suspended from heaven by that golden chain”. Heavy stone, made to look weightless: that was the trick.

cards.fact: For nearly a thousand years, it was the largest cathedral in Christendom.
cards.context: Finished in 537, Hagia Sophia held that record for close to a millennium: roughly from Justinian’s day to the end of the Middle Ages.

levels.title: The Franks
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Clovis and the Franks built a kingdom in Gaul.
levels.summary: Clovis (481-511) united the Franks, took most of Gaul and made Paris his capital. His Catholic baptism won him the bishops and most of his subjects.

cards.headline: France takes its name from a Germanic people: the Franks.
cards.body: Its favorite royal name comes from one of their kings, Clovis, and a form of his name, Louis, became the most common name of French kings. The Franks went on to build the most powerful Christian kingdom in early medieval western Europe. It started with him.

cards.headline: Clovis takes Gaul
cards.body: Clovis became king of the Franks in 481. He forced the other Frankish groups to accept his rule, and in 486 he took over the last Roman-ruled territory in Gaul. In 507 he defeated the Visigoths and took Aquitaine, in southwestern Gaul. (Remember Level 3’s Visigoths ruling from Toledo? This is why their kingdom ended up in Spain.) Then he made Paris his capital.

mascot.line: Same church as the people you rule. Clovis made a smart move there.

cards.headline: The baptism that mattered
cards.body: The Goths had become Arian Christians, like Theodoric in Level 3. Clovis, whose wife Clotilda was a Catholic, was baptized a Catholic Christian at Reims by Bishop Remigius. The date is debated: sources give dates including 498 and 508. Either way, it put him on the same side as the church and the Catholic majority he ruled. That spared Gaul the long conflicts other Germanic kingdoms went through. Same faith as your subjects: a strong foundation for a kingdom.

cards.headline: Split four ways
cards.body: When Clovis died in 511, his kingdom was divided among his four surviving sons. Not the tidiest inheritance. Yet his family, the Merovingian dynasty, ruled for more than 200 years. The Franks’ story was far from over.

levels.title: Monasteries
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how monks copied books and kept learning alive.
levels.summary: Benedict's Rule balanced prayer, work and reading. Monks copied books by hand in scriptoria, and Cassiodorus had his monks copy pagan classics too.

cards.headline: Scribes often said: “Two fingers hold the pen, but the whole body toils.”
cards.body: They knew. In the early Middle Ages, books found refuge in monasteries, and every one was copied by hand, letter by letter. So why were monks the ones holding the pens?

cards.headline: A rule for living
cards.body: In 529 Benedict of Nursia founded a monastery at Monte Cassino in Italy. He wrote a Rule for it that balanced prayer, work and study: about five hours of manual work and four of reading scripture and spiritual writings a day, with enough food and sleep. Moderate, as monastic life goes. By the early 9th century his Rule had replaced most others across northern and western Europe. One man’s timetable became a continent’s.

cards.headline: Why monks copied
cards.body: Benedict didn’t set out to build libraries. But monks needed service books, Bibles and the writings of the Church Fathers, and the only way to get a book was to copy one. So monasteries set aside a writing room, the scriptorium, where scribes copied manuscripts onto parchment or vellum, made from animal skin. No printer, no photocopier: just a pen and a very long afternoon.

cards.headline: Saving the pagans
cards.body: Cassiodorus, who had served as a senior official under Theodoric (Level 3’s Gothic king of Italy), founded a monastery called Vivarium around 540. He had its monks copy pagan as well as Christian authors, and other monasteries later followed his example. It mattered, because books were scarce: a monastic library of 600 volumes counted as fairly large. A small-town library today would have looked like a miracle.
cards.callout: Copy it, or lose it: every book existed only as many times as someone wrote it out

levels.title: The Rise of Islam
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how Islam began and spread in its first century.
levels.summary: Muhammad (born about 570) preached in Mecca; Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed to him by God. After 622 and his death in 632, caliphs built an empire from Spain to the Indus.

cards.headline: In 622 Muhammad moved to Medina. Muslims still count their years from it.
cards.body: That journey from Mecca began a new calendar. By the early 8th century, the empire of his successors stretched from Spain to the Indus River. Here’s how that began.

cards.headline: A prophet in Mecca
cards.body: Muhammad was born around 570 in Mecca, in Arabia. By tradition, in 610 he had a vision of the angel Gabriel. Muslims believe the Qur’an is the word of God, revealed to Muhammad in stages through Gabriel. In 622 he moved from Mecca to Medina. That move, the hijra, marks the start of the Islamic calendar. Your calendar counts from one starting point; this one counts from a journey.

cards.headline: The successors
cards.body: Muhammad died in Medina in 632. The leaders who followed were called caliphs, from khalifah, “successor”. Under the first four caliphs, Arab Muslim armies beat the Byzantines at Yarmuk in 636, took Syria and Egypt from them, and defeated the armies of Persia. Remember Level 4? Byzantium lost Syria and Egypt, but Constantinople’s walls held against Arab attackers.

cards.headline: From Spain to the Indus
cards.body: The Umayyad caliphs, from 661, moved the capital from Medina to Damascus. Under them, Muslim forces took North Africa and, from 711, overran most of Spain, ending the Visigothic kingdom you met in Level 3. By the early 8th century the caliphate reached from Spain to Central Asia and the Indus valley. Conquered Christians and Jews, whom Muslims called People of the Book, could keep their religion as long as they paid taxes.
cards.callout: Within about a century of 632: from the Atlantic to the Indus

levels.title: Anglo-Saxon England
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and the treasure of Sutton Hoo.
levels.summary: Angles, Saxons and Jutes built kingdoms in Britain after Roman rule ended; England means "land of the Angles". The Sutton Hoo ship burial showed their wealth.

cards.headline: In 1939 a buried ship turned up in Suffolk. Its wood had long since vanished.
cards.body: Yet the ship was still there. Rows of iron rivets traced its ghost in the sand, some 27 metres long. Inside lay a treasure fit for a king. But first: whose England was this?

cards.headline: Land of the Angles
cards.body: Roman rule in Britain ended about 410. Germanic peoples, chiefly Angles, Saxons and Jutes, came to rule much of what is now England (archaeology suggests some had arrived even earlier). They built kingdoms, including Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Sussex, Wessex and Kent. The Angles gave the country its name: England comes from Old English Engla land, “land of the Angles”. The Anglo-Saxons ruled until the Norman Conquest of 1066.

mascot.line: The wood was gone, but the nails remembered exactly where it had been.

cards.headline: The ghost ship
cards.body: At Sutton Hoo, landowner Edith Pretty hired local archaeologist Basil Brown to dig the mounds on her land. In May 1939 he struck iron rivets. The ship’s wood had decayed, but the rivets and its outline in the sand showed a vessel some 27 metres long. No body was found; later chemical analysis suggested it had dissolved in the acidic soil. A ship made of nothing but its nails, and a grave with no one in it.

cards.headline: Treasure fit for a king
cards.body: The burial held 263 finds of gold, garnet, silver, bronze and more, including a famous helmet and objects from far-off Byzantium. It is usually thought to be the grave of Rædwald, a king of East Anglia who died around 624. Edith Pretty gave the whole treasure to the British Museum in 1939. And it changed minds: a period once dismissed as the “Dark Ages” turned out to be rich, skilled and connected to a wider world.

levels.title: Checkpoint: After Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Europe and the Mediterranean changed after Rome fell in the West.
levels.summary: Rome's world passed to three heirs: western kingdoms, the Byzantine Empire and the caliphate. A timeline from 476 to 711 ties the chapter together.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: Rome’s old world ended up with three heirs.
cards.body: A West of new kingdoms, a Greek-speaking Roman East, and a caliphate reaching from Spain to the Indus. Let’s put the whole chapter on one page.

events.label: Odoacer deposes the last western emperor

mascot.line: One empire, three heirs, and you just met all of them. Nicely done.

cards.headline: Three heirs, one inheritance
cards.body: Historians describe Rome’s old world as passing to three heirs. In the West, kingdoms looked to the Roman Church, kings like Theodoric kept Roman government running, and monasteries copied the books. In the East, the Byzantine Empire kept Rome going behind walls that held against attackers, Arabs included, and Justinian’s code carried Roman law into the future. To the south, the caliphate took Syria and Egypt from Byzantium. A dark age? Historians rarely call it that now. A crowded one, certainly.

levels.title: Charlemagne
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Charlemagne built an empire and revived learning.
levels.summary: Charlemagne, king of the Franks from 768 to 814, conquered much of western Europe and revived learning: Alcuin, schools, copied classics and a clear new script.

cards.headline: The small letters on this screen go back to Charlemagne’s scribes.
cards.body: Yet the king behind them never quite learned to write. Charlemagne conquered much of western Europe, then set out to fill it with schools and books.

cards.headline: Charles the Great
cards.body: Charlemagne means Charles the Great, and he was king of the Franks from 768 until his death in 814. His family was new to the throne: in 751 his father, Pippin, had taken it from the last Merovingian king. (Remember Clovis’s dynasty from Level 6? This is where its run ended.) Charlemagne spent much of his reign at war. He became king of the Lombards, in Italy, in 774, and fought the Saxons for about 30 years until they submitted in 804. By the end, his realm covered much of western Europe.

cards.headline: A school in the palace
cards.body: Conquest was only half the plan. In 781 Charlemagne invited Alcuin of York, an English scholar, to head the palace school at Aachen. Monasteries and other church institutions added schools of their own. Remember Level 7’s monks copying books by hand? Now scholars copied large numbers of classical Latin texts, many of which might otherwise have been lost. Historians call this revival the Carolingian Renaissance.

mascot.line: Tablets under the pillow for late-night practice. Even emperors do homework in bed.

cards.headline: The king who couldn’t write
cards.body: The copyists used a new handwriting, Carolingian minuscule, clear and easy to read. Centuries later, Renaissance scholars revived it, and it became the basis of the roman type you’re reading right now. The irony? His biographer Einhard wrote that Charlemagne kept writing tablets under his pillow to practise his letters, but he started too late in life and never mastered it. The man behind Europe’s handwriting struggled with his own.

levels.title: An Emperor in 800
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Pope crowning Charlemagne emperor mattered.
levels.summary: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor, the first in the West since Rome fell there. Byzantium called it usurpation; Verdun later split the empire.

cards.headline: On Christmas Day 800, Charlemagne went to church a king and left an emperor.
cards.body: No one in the West had held that title since Rome fell there. So who gave it to him, and why did it matter so much?

cards.headline: A pope on the run
cards.body: The story starts with a pope in trouble. In 799 Pope Leo III was attacked in Rome by his enemies. He escaped and fled north to Charlemagne, who had him restored as pope. So a conquering king and a pope who owed him his job were about to meet again in Rome.

cards.headline: Christmas Day, 800
cards.body: At Christmas mass in St Peter’s Basilica, Leo crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans. For the first time since the empire in the West dissolved in the 5th century (Level 1’s 476), the West had an emperor again. His biographer Einhard later claimed Charlemagne would not have set foot in church that day had he known the pope’s plan. Historians still argue over whether to believe him.

mascot.line: Two emperors both calling themselves Roman. Imagine the seating plan at that dinner.

cards.headline: Who gets to make an emperor?
cards.body: The coronation set a precedent: from then on, emperors in the West would be crowned by popes. Not everyone applauded. In Constantinople, whose people called themselves Romans (Level 4), the Byzantines saw Charlemagne as a usurper of their emperor’s title. A long rivalry between East and West followed. Two emperors, one Roman title. Awkward.

cards.headline: Split three ways
cards.body: The empire didn’t stay whole for long. In 843 the Treaty of Verdun split it among three of Charlemagne’s grandsons. Sound familiar? Clovis’s kingdom was divided among his four sons in Level 6. The lines drawn at Verdun foreshadowed the countries of western Europe, France among them.

levels.title: Who the Vikings Were
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Vikings as raiders, traders and settlers.
levels.summary: Vikings were Scandinavians who raided, traded and settled from 793. Most were farmers, and they never wore horned helmets.

cards.headline: Picture a Viking. Now take the horns off the helmet.
cards.body: They were never there. The real Vikings were raiders, yes, but also farmers, traders and settlers. Their story starts with a shock on an English island.

cards.headline: 793: terror from the sea
cards.body: The Viking Age is usually dated from 8 June 793, when raiders struck the monastery on Lindisfarne, an island off north-east England. It was the first documented Viking attack. Monasteries made tempting targets: they held church silver and were less well defended than trading towns. Alcuin, Level 11’s scholar, was at Charlemagne’s court when the news arrived. He wrote that never before had such terror appeared in Britain.

cards.headline: Farmers first
cards.body: So who were they? Vikings were Scandinavians, from what are now Denmark, Norway and Sweden, active from the late 8th century to the 11th. Most were farmers, living in villages of six or seven farms. Abroad they could be raiders, but also traders, explorers, settlers or soldiers for hire. Viking traders even brought home silver coins minted in Muslim Central Asia, carried along the rivers of Russia. The axe was one tool in a busy toolkit.

mascot.line: Horns on a crowded ship sound like a great way to annoy the rower behind you.

cards.headline: The helmet problem
cards.body: Now, those horns. The best-preserved Viking Age helmet, from a warrior’s grave at Gjermundbu in Norway, has no horns at all. No writer of the Viking Age mentions horned helmets, and horns would have snagged in a fight or on a crowded ship. The horned look was popularized by 19th-century artists. It’s a costume, not a clue.

levels.title: Viking Ships
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what made Viking longships so fast and flexible.
levels.summary: Clinker-built longships with a square sail and oars drew under a metre of water, so they could run onto beaches, go up rivers and be dragged overland.

cards.headline: “Nor was it thought that such an inroad from the sea could be made.”
cards.body: Alcuin wrote that after Lindisfarne. Viking ships could turn up where nobody expected a ship at all. Here’s how.

cards.headline: Built to take a beating
cards.body: A longship was clinker-built: its planks overlapped, like the shingles on a roof, and were fastened together. The result was sturdy enough for heavy seas. The hull was pointed at both ends, and the ship carried one large square sail plus oars. Sail when the wind helps, row when it doesn’t.

mascot.line: Under a metre! You could wade out to it without getting your shoulders wet.

cards.headline: Less than a metre of water
cards.body: A Viking ship museum built a full-size copy of a warship made near Dublin around 1042: the Sea Stallion, 30 metres long. It needs less than a metre of water. That shallow draught let Viking ships work in shallow water and on rivers. Crews could sail right onto a beach, and even drag their ships over land. No harbour? No problem.

cards.headline: Wind or no wind
cards.body: Under sail, the Sea Stallion has an estimated top speed of 17 knots. When the wind dies, its 60 oars keep it moving. In 2007 and 2008 a modern crew sailed it from Roskilde to Dublin and back to test what these ships could do. Put it together and you get Alcuin’s shock: a raid that arrives from the open sea, with no harbour needed.

levels.title: Vikings Across the World
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Viking voyages from Russia to North America.
levels.summary: Vikings went east along Russian rivers to Kyiv and Constantinople, and west to Iceland, Greenland and Newfoundland, where tree rings show they were in 1021.

cards.headline: Wood cut by Vikings in Newfoundland has been dated to one exact year: 1021.
cards.body: How do you date a wood chip to a single year? And how did Vikings reach North America at all? Follow them west, but first, east.

cards.headline: East: rivers to Constantinople
cards.body: Swedish Vikings controlled a trade route along the rivers of Russia. Around 882 the Viking Oleg, ruler of Novgorod, made Kyiv his capital, founding the state called Kyivan Rus. From Kyiv, merchants took convoys down the Dnieper River to Constantinople, hauling their ships overland around its rapids. Level 4’s great city sat at the end of a Viking trade road.

cards.headline: West: island by island
cards.body: Westward, Norse settlers, most from Norway, settled Iceland in about 870 to 930. About 985, Erik the Red, exiled from Iceland, founded the first European settlement on Greenland. He picked the name Greenland believing a good name would attract settlers. Medieval marketing. About 1000, his son Leif Erikson reached North America, and the sagas say he called part of it Vinland.

cards.headline: The year 1021
cards.body: At L’Anse aux Meadows, on the northern tip of Newfoundland, lies the first known evidence of Europeans in the Americas: a Norse camp of timber-and-sod buildings. In 2021 Margot Kuitems and colleagues studied wood cut there with metal tools, which local peoples didn’t make then. A cosmic-ray event in 993 left a spike in that year’s tree ring. Counting outward from it, wood from three trees all gave 1021: Vikings in the Americas, centuries before Columbus.
cards.callout: 1021: the first secure date for Europeans in the Americas

levels.title: Alfred the Great
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Alfred defended Wessex against the Vikings.
levels.summary: Alfred of Wessex (871-899) survived the Viking attack of 878, won at Edington, agreed a Danelaw border and defended Wessex with burhs, ships and learning.

cards.headline: In 878 a king of Wessex was hiding in a marsh. He became “Alfred the Great”.
cards.body: He is the only English monarch known as “the Great”. He had lost almost everything to a Viking army. Here’s how he won it back.

cards.headline: Down to the marshes
cards.body: A great Danish army arrived in England in 865. Alfred became king of Wessex, one of Level 9’s Anglo-Saxon kingdoms, in 871. In early 878 the Danes seized Chippenham, and the West Saxons submitted, all except Alfred. He withdrew to the Somerset marshes and fought on. The famous tale of him letting a peasant woman’s cakes burn there? A legend, first written down long after his death.

cards.headline: Edington, then a border
cards.body: In May 878 Alfred beat the Danes at Edington. Their leader, Guthrum, was baptized a Christian with Alfred as his godfather. In 886 Alfred and the Danes agreed a frontier along the old Roman road, Watling Street. The Danish-ruled north and east became known as the Danelaw, “Danes’ law”. The Vikings were no longer just raiders. They were neighbours.

mascot.line: Walls, ships and books. Alfred defended Wessex with all three.

cards.headline: Never more than 20 miles
cards.body: Then Alfred built. He covered Wessex with fortified towns called burhs, placed so that no part of the kingdom was more than 20 miles from one. He had a navy of fast new ships built. And he had Latin books translated into English, taking part in the work himself. Wessex was never again in such danger.

levels.title: The Normans
levels.objective: After this level you can explain who the Normans were and where they settled.
levels.summary: In 911 the Frankish king gave the Viking Rollo land around Rouen. His Northmen became French-speaking Christian Normans and later won lands as far as Sicily.

cards.headline: Normandy is named after Vikings: the Northmen who settled there.
cards.body: Yet their descendants spoke French and went to church. How did a band of raiders turn into a French duchy?

cards.headline: A deal on the Seine
cards.body: Viking raids battered the Frankish coasts in the 9th century, and by about 900 Vikings had a permanent base in the Seine valley. In 911 King Charles III, known as Charles the Simple, made a deal with their leader, Rollo: the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte. Rollo got the land around Rouen and the mouth of the Seine. In return, he stopped raiding, became a Christian and swore loyalty to Charles. The raider became a landholder.

cards.headline: Northmen into Normans
cards.body: Rollo’s Scandinavian countrymen followed in large numbers. Latin writers called them Nortmanni, “Northmen”, which gave us Norman and Normandy. The settlers adopted the French language, French customs and the Christian religion. The Vikings of the Seine became French-speaking Christians with a Norse family story.

mascot.line: From longships on the Seine to a crown in Sicily. Restless family.

cards.headline: Far beyond Normandy
cards.body: The Normans didn’t stay put. Norman adventurers won lands in southern Italy and Sicily, where Roger II became king of Sicily in 1130. And one duke of Normandy had his eye on an even bigger prize. That’s the next level.

levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Norman Conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings.
levels.summary: In 1066 Harold beat Norway at Stamford Bridge, then lost to William of Normandy at Hastings on 14 October. How Harold died is debated.

cards.headline: In 1066 England had three kings and fought two invading armies in three weeks.
cards.body: Edward, Harold and William all wore the crown that year. Harold had to fight in the north, then race to the south coast. Here’s how it unfolded.

cards.headline: One crown, three claimants
cards.body: Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066, and Harold Godwinson was crowned king. Two men disagreed. William, duke of Normandy, claimed Edward had promised him the throne. Harald Hardrada, king of Norway, invaded the north with Harold’s own brother, Tostig.

cards.headline: North, then south
cards.body: On 25 September Harold beat the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge, near York. Hardrada and Tostig were both killed. The battle is traditionally taken as the end of the Viking Age. Three days later, on 28 September, William’s fleet landed at Pevensey on the south coast. Harold marched south to meet him.

mascot.line: A famous arrow that may be mostly 19th-century thread. Always check the stitches!

cards.headline: Hastings, 14 October
cards.body: The armies met near Hastings on 14 October 1066 and fought all day. Late in the afternoon Harold was killed, and the English fled. How he died is debated. The Bayeux Tapestry, really an embroidery about 68 metres long, seems to show an arrow in his eye, but that arrow was added in 19th-century repairs. The accounts written nearest the battle suggest Norman knights cut him down.

cards.headline: Christmas Day, again
cards.body: William was crowned king in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066. Remember Charlemagne’s Christmas crowning in Level 12? And Level 9’s Anglo-Saxon rule was over.

levels.title: The Domesday Book
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why William the Conqueror surveyed all of England.
levels.summary: At Christmas 1085 William ordered a survey of who held England's land and what it was worth; the 1086 results became Domesday Book.

cards.headline: Nineteen years after Hastings, William wanted to count every pig in England.
cards.body: Or so it felt to the English. The result names more than 13,000 places, and most of them still exist.

cards.headline: Christmas 1085
cards.body: At Christmas 1085 William ordered a survey of England, and it was carried out the following year. Why? He needed to fix problems in how tax was raised and how defence was organised. That meant knowing who held what land, and what it was worth. Nearly twenty years into his reign, he still didn’t know exactly who held what.

cards.headline: Who? How many? What’s it worth?
cards.body: Commissioners asked the same questions everywhere. Who held this manor under King Edward, and who holds it now? How many plough teams and mills? What was it worth in 1066, and what now? The answers showed how England had changed since the Conquest. One writer of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle complained that not one ox, cow or pig was left out. Picture a tax inspector with a clipboard, times a whole kingdom.

mascot.line: A survey so final they named it after Judgement Day. Tough crowd.

cards.headline: A book with no appeal
cards.body: The results fill Domesday Book, which names more than 13,000 places, though London and Winchester were left out. People at the time called it the description of England. By the mid-12th century it had a scarier name: Domesday, after the Day of Judgement, because its record could not be appealed. It is kept today at The National Archives.

levels.title: Feudalism
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how lords, vassals and land were tied together.
levels.summary: Lords granted vassals fiefs, usually land, for service, sealed by homage and fealty. The word feudalism came centuries later, and the tidy pyramid is a simplification.

cards.headline: Nobody in the Middle Ages ever talked about “feudalism”.
cards.body: The word was coined centuries later. The deal it describes was real, though: land in return for loyalty and service. Here’s how it worked, and why historians argue about the label.

cards.headline: Land for service
cards.body: A lord granted a vassal a fief: a piece of property, usually land, held in return for service. The vassal owed his lord military service, counsel and financial support. The lord, in return, was expected to protect and respect him. In England the king granted land in return for “knight service”, because a knight’s armour and heavy horse were expensive to buy and keep. No wages, no payslip: you got land, and you turned up armed when called.

cards.headline: Becoming someone’s man
cards.body: The bond was sealed in a ceremony called homage, in which the vassal became the lord’s “man”. The word comes from Latin homo, “man”. He also swore fealty, a promise to be faithful. So this wasn’t a company hiring an employee. It was two people, bound by an oath.
cards.callout: Homage: becoming his man. Fealty: swearing to be faithful.

mascot.line: A tidy triangle is easy to draw. Medieval Europe was never quite that tidy.

cards.headline: Handle the pyramid with care
cards.body: You may have seen it drawn as a pyramid: king on top, then lords, knights and peasants. Treat that as a simplification, because arrangements differed widely across Europe. In 1974 the historian Elizabeth A. R. Brown argued that feudalism has no agreed definition and is misleading. In 1994 Susan Reynolds argued that words like fief and vassal had no precise technical meaning until lawyers defined them in the late 12th century. Many historians now avoid the term.
