levels.title: Serfs and Peasants
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the life of a medieval peasant.
levels.summary: A serf was bound to a hereditary plot and to his lord's will. Villeins worked the lord's demesne every week and paid in produce and fees, from the lord's mill to merchet and heriot.

cards.headline: A serf wasn’t a slave. He still couldn’t move house without permission.
cards.body: He was bound to a plot of land and to the will of his lord. So what exactly was a serf, and what did he owe?

mascot.line: Not owned, but not free to leave either. Serfdom lived in that awkward middle.

cards.headline: Tied to the land
cards.body: A serf held a hereditary plot of land, and he was bound to it and to his lord. That’s the difference from a slave: slaves were bought and sold without reference to land, while a serf went with his plot. He could not leave his holding or village for good, marry, or change his occupation without his lord’s permission. The ways out were few: being formally freed by the lord, or running away.

cards.headline: Working the lord’s land
cards.body: Every manor had a demesne, the part the lord kept for his own use, and serfs supplied the labour to work it. Week by week an unfree peasant, a villein, brought his own plough and oxen to plough the demesne, then harrowed, reaped, threshed and carried the crops. This duty was called week-work. His own holding, a cottage and some strips of land in the fields, had to fit around it. Picture paying your rent by doing your landlord’s gardening every single week.

cards.headline: A bill for everything
cards.body: A villein paid for his holding in money, labour and produce. A substantial share of the grain a serf grew went to his lord, and he had to use his lord’s mill. Marrying off a daughter cost a fee called merchet. And when he died, his family owed the lord a heriot, usually the best beast. Even dying came with a bill.

levels.title: Castles
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how castles were built and why.
levels.summary: A castle was a king's or lord's fortified home. Early motte-and-bailey castles were quick earth-and-timber works; by the 12th century lords built stone keeps.

cards.headline: Some early castle towers arrived more or less flat-packed.
cards.body: Timber towers were often made off-site, then put up on top of a mound of earth. So what was a castle for, and how did wood turn into stone?

cards.headline: A home that could fight back
cards.body: A castle was a medieval stronghold, generally the home of the king or lord of the land around it. Castles developed rapidly in western Europe from the 9th century. In England they were something new after the Norman Conquest of 1066: they housed Norman nobles and their families, as well as knights and soldiers, and helped the Normans control the land they had conquered. Part house, part barracks, part statement: we’re staying.

mascot.line: An upside-down pudding bowl with a tower on top. Not delicious, but very hard to attack.

cards.headline: A mound and a yard
cards.body: The common early design was the motte and bailey. The motte was an artificial mound of earth and stone, shaped like an upside-down pudding bowl and topped by a timber tower. Beside it lay the bailey, a fenced yard with houses and animal pens. Unskilled forced labourers could build one quickly from basic materials, and the towers were often prefabricated off-site, then put up like enormous flat-pack furniture. Some assembly required.

cards.headline: From timber to stone
cards.body: Stone gave better defence and more prestige, so earth and timber gave way to stone. By the 12th century lords were building stone keeps, much easier to defend than wooden towers, some with walls six metres thick. The keep was the strongest part of the castle, with a well, private rooms and supplies for a siege. It sent a message: this lord is rich, and he isn’t going anywhere.

levels.title: Castle Defenses
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how moats, walls, towers and gatehouses kept attackers out.
levels.summary: Moats, curtain walls and arrow loops held attackers off; gatehouses with portcullises and murder holes made the way in a trap; concentric castles like Beaumaris layered it all.

cards.headline: Murder holes: the name tells you exactly what they were for.
cards.body: Castle builders turned the way in into the most dangerous place to stand. Let’s walk through a castle’s defences from the outside in.

cards.headline: The outer ring
cards.body: Start with the moat, crossed by a drawbridge hinged at one end so it could be raised. Behind it rose the curtain wall, a fortified wall linking the towers together. Narrow vertical slits called arrow loops let archers shoot out while staying safe behind stone. Anyone attacking was out in the open. The defenders were not.

mascot.line: Castle rule: the friendlier the doorway looks, the more you should worry.

cards.headline: The gate is a trap
cards.body: The gate was a castle’s most vulnerable point, so gatehouses often became mini-castles in themselves. A portcullis, a heavy wooden or iron grille, could drop to seal the passage. Overhead were murder holes, openings through which defenders dropped heavy stones, hot sand or boiling water on anyone below. Get past the front door, and you were standing in the worst room in the house.

cards.headline: Walls within walls
cards.body: The most powerful design was the concentric castle: two rings of towered walls, one inside the other, each supporting the other. At Beaumaris in Wales, Edward I and his architect James of St George built four rings of defences, including a water-filled moat with its own dock. The outer walls alone had 300 arrow loops. Then the money ran out, and work petered out by the 1320s, unfinished. Remember Constantinople’s moat and layered walls in Level 4? Same idea: make attackers win again and again.

levels.title: Siege Warfare
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how armies besieged castles, from ladders to trebuchets.
levels.summary: Attackers used ladders, towers, rams, mines and trebuchets, yet most sieges ended by treachery, starvation or disease, as at Rochester in 1215 after a pig-fat mine.

cards.headline: In 1215 King John sent for 40 pigs too fat to eat.
cards.body: He wasn’t planning a feast. He was besieging Rochester Castle, held against him by rebels. To see why he wanted pig fat, start with the attacker’s toolkit.

cards.headline: Over, through or under
cards.body: Attackers could climb the walls with ladders, but this escalade rarely worked except by surprise or treachery. Wheeled wooden siege towers could roll up and drop a drawbridge onto the wall. Battering rams, sheltered by a wheeled shed, went for the gate. Or miners dug a tunnel under the wall, propped it with timber, packed it with fuel and set it alight, so the wall above collapsed.

mascot.line: Forty unappetising pigs, one collapsed corner. Medieval engineering could be very creative.

cards.headline: The pig-fat mine
cards.body: That was John’s plan. His siege engines bombarded Rochester’s keep with stones while miners attacked its south-east turret from below. They burned the fat of the 40 pigs to fire the timber props, and the south-east corner of the keep came down. Even then the rebels didn’t give up: they fell back into the northern half of the keep. The king had brought down the wall, but not the defenders.

cards.headline: The slowest weapon wins
cards.body: The trebuchet was a throwing engine powered by a falling counterweight. Counterweight engines appeared in the 12th century and could hurl stones weighing hundreds of kilograms. Yet medieval sieges were settled more often by treachery, starvation or disease than by broken walls. Rochester ended the same way: starvation soon forced the rebels to surrender. Sometimes the deadliest siege weapon was a calendar.

levels.title: Becoming a Knight
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a boy trained to become a knight.
levels.summary: A noble boy served as a page from about 7, joined his father's lord's household at about 12, and trained as a squire before being dubbed with the accolade, if he could afford the equipment.

cards.headline: Becoming a knight could start at about the age of 7.
cards.body: Long before a sword touched his shoulder, a boy of noble birth spent years serving, learning and carrying other people’s gear. Here’s the road, step by step.

cards.headline: Step one: page
cards.body: A boy destined for knighthood might serve as a page from about the age of 7. At around 12 he joined the household of his father’s lord for further training. At this stage he might be called a damoiseau, literally “lordling”. Think of it as boarding school with horses, where the head teacher was your father’s lord.

cards.headline: Step two: squire
cards.body: Next he served as a squire: a young man of noble birth, apprenticed in the duties of chivalry, who looked after a knight’s armour and weapons. The training went well beyond fighting, taking in hunting, music and dancing. The goal was a worthy knight, a just master and a sensible manager of an estate. Swordplay, dance steps and estate accounts: a demanding timetable.

mascot.line: Years of training, and the big moment is a tap on the shoulder. Knights did understatement well.

cards.headline: Step three: the accolade
cards.body: When he was skilled enough, and had the money, he was dubbed. The accolade was a touch on the shoulder with the flat of a sword blade. But he had to buy his own knightly equipment, and in France some squires waited for, or put off, the expensive dubbing. Many knights were vassals holding lands as fiefs from the lords they fought for. Remember Level 21’s land-for-service deal? These are the men who turned up.

levels.title: Armor
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how armor changed from chain mail to plate.
levels.summary: Mail of iron links gave way to plate from the late 13th century, fast after 1325. Field armour weighed about 20 to 25 kg, and the crane is a film myth.

cards.headline: Knights were never winched onto their horses by crane.
cards.body: That picture comes from films, such as the 1944 Henry V. Real armour had to let a man fight. So what was it made of, and how heavy was it?

cards.headline: A shirt of rings
cards.body: Before plate, the standard metal armour across Europe was mail: a flexible mesh of interlocking iron links, worn over a quilted garment. A mail shirt, or hauberk, contained thousands of links and was expensive and slow to make. It moved with the body and stopped sword cuts well, but it was less good against arrows and blows from maces. Think of a knitted jumper, made of iron.

cards.headline: Enter the plates
cards.body: Plate armour emerged in the late 13th century. Between 1325 and 1340 came a revolution: mail was replaced or reinforced with plates of iron or steel. Through the 14th century, plates spread to the rest of the body, until the complete suit, the harness, was developed. Rigid plates deflected glancing blows; a weapon got through only if it struck directly and with great force.

mascot.line: No cranes, no winches, no being stuck on your back like a beetle. Just practice.

cards.fact: A field armour usually weighed about 20 to 25 kg.
cards.context: That weight was spread over the whole body. Even a suddenly unhorsed knight could get up quickly, ready to fight, and modern tests show a man in properly fitted armour can mount a horse, lie on the ground and stand up again. Heavy, yes. Helpless, no.

levels.title: Chivalry
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the ideals of chivalry and how far knights lived up to them.
levels.summary: Chivalry first meant mounted knights, then an ideal of faith, loyalty and honour. In practice mercy was mostly for ransomable nobles.

cards.headline: “Chivalry” first meant men on horses, not good manners.
cards.body: In the Middle Ages the word meant knights: fully armed, mounted fighting men. Only later did it come to mean courtesy. The gap between those two meanings is this level’s story.

cards.headline: The ideal
cards.body: By the 12th and 13th centuries, chivalry meant the honourable, courteous conduct expected of a knight. A Christian ideal took hold: respect the Church, protect the poor and the weak, stay loyal to your superiors, and guard your personal honour. It’s the knight of the storybooks. And that’s the catch: it was an ideal.

cards.headline: The reality
cards.body: Real knights fought pragmatically. A captured enemy knight might be spared if he was worth land, gold or booty, not out of kindness, and ransoms and plunder could bring great profits. That protection didn’t reach peasants, who were often slaughtered when they got in the way. Chivalry was built around the noble warrior on horseback, and peasants weren’t in the club.

mascot.line: An ideal is worth knowing. Just check it against what people actually did.

cards.headline: Part of the problem
cards.body: Some historians go further. In 1999 Richard Kaeuper argued that chivalry was part of the problem of violence in medieval Europe, not merely its solution. Chivalric writing prized prowess, skill at violent deeds, so highly that it became almost a one-word definition of chivalry, even as the Church tried to regulate knightly violence. The code was real. So was the gap.

levels.title: Heraldry
levels.objective: After this level you can explain coats of arms and what they told people.
levels.summary: Heraldry took shape in the 12th century to tell armoured men apart. Coats of arms, named after the surcoat, used set metals and colours, a rule of contrast, and became hereditary.

cards.headline: In 1127 a king hung a shield of golden lions around a young man’s neck.
cards.body: Henry I of England gave the blue shield to Geoffrey of Anjou, his future son-in-law. It’s an early glimpse of heraldry. So why did knights need pictures on their shields?

cards.headline: Who’s in there?
cards.body: As armour came to cover the whole body, telling one armoured man from another got harder, and that sped the spread of heraldry. It took shape in the 12th century, and by about 1170 heralds appear in descriptions of tournaments. A design on a shield worked like a name tag you could read from across a field.

mascot.line: Gold on blue: easy to spot across a muddy field. Blue on black: good luck.

cards.headline: A coat of arms, literally
cards.body: The phrase “coat of arms” comes from the surcoat, a cloth tunic worn over armour that displayed the bearer’s arms. Heraldry had its own colour names: the metals gold (or) and silver (argent), and colours such as red (gules), blue (azure) and black (sable). A rule of contrast generally kept colour off colour and metal off metal, so a design stayed visible. Geoffrey’s gold lions on blue passed the test.

cards.headline: Handed down
cards.body: Over time, arms tended to become hereditary, passing down through families. A design that once said “this is the man” came to say “this is the family”. A shield had become a surname you could see.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Castles and Knights
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how land, castles and knights held medieval society together.
levels.summary: Medieval bishops described society as those who pray, fight and work. A timeline from the first castles to the plate revolution, plus five questions, ties land, castles and knights together.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: a medieval bishop sorted society into three kinds of people.
cards.body: Those who pray, those who fight and those who work. You’ve just spent a chapter with two of them. Let’s put land, castles and knights on one page.

events.label: Castles begin to spread across western Europe

mascot.line: Land, castles, knights and forty very unlucky pigs. That’s a chapter well earned.

cards.headline: Pray, fight, work
cards.body: In the early 11th century, bishops such as Adalbero of Laon described society as three orders: those who pray, those who fight and those who work. Like chivalry, it was an ideal, but a medieval one, unlike the modern pyramid. It maps this chapter well. Many knights held land as fiefs and fought for their lords. Serfs worked the lord’s demesne every week. And castles, the homes of kings and lords, held the land together. Fighters, workers, and the stone that kept them in place.

levels.title: The Medieval Church
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Church's power over daily life.
levels.summary: The parish church was the one place for the sacraments and burial, the tithe took a tenth of everyone's income, and the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) required yearly confession.

cards.headline: In a medieval village, the biggest building was often the church.
cards.body: It was also the one building that mattered to every parishioner, whatever their age or wealth. What made one building so central to ordinary life?

cards.headline: From the font to the grave
cards.body: Your whole life ran through that building. Apart from the last anointing of the dying, the parish church was normally the only place you could receive the sacraments, and it was where you would be buried. In the 12th century the theologian Peter Lombard, whose textbook became the standard one, counted seven sacraments, including baptism, marriage and the Eucharist. Baptized, married, buried: one address for all three.

mascot.line: One sheaf in ten, every year. Suddenly a phone bill looks rather gentle.

cards.headline: A tenth of everything
cards.body: The Church also took a share of your income. The tithe was a tenth of it, paid in money or in crops and farm animals. Church law required it from the 6th century, and from the 8th, kings’ law enforced it across Europe. It paid the clergy, kept churches standing and helped the poor. Picture handing over one sheaf of wheat in every ten you cut, every single year.

cards.headline: Once a year, by order
cards.body: In 1215 Pope Innocent III gathered more than 400 bishops and 800 abbots and priors at the Fourth Lateran Council. One of its rules reached every believer: each Catholic had to confess at least once a year and take Communion during Lent. The Church now set a date in everyone’s calendar. A yearly check-up for the soul, and not an optional one.

levels.title: Popes and Emperors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the struggle between popes and emperors over power.
levels.summary: In the Investiture Controversy, Gregory VII excommunicated Henry IV, who sought absolution at Canossa in 1077; the Concordat of Worms (1122) split the rights to install bishops.

cards.headline: In January 1077, a king crossed the Alps in winter to beg a pope’s forgiveness.
cards.body: He waited three days at a castle called Canossa before the pope let him back into the Church. How did a pope get that kind of power over a king?

cards.headline: Who hands over the ring?
cards.body: The fight was over investiture: who installs a new bishop. Traditionally the king did it, handing the bishop a ring and a crosier, the shepherd’s staff, with the words “receive the church”. Those objects stood for the spiritual office and for the lands and property that came with it. Whoever held the ring and staff held a lot of power. Kings wanted it. So did popes.

cards.headline: Pope against king
cards.body: In 1075 Pope Gregory VII set out sweeping claims for his office, including that a pope could depose emperors. In January 1076 the German king Henry IV and his bishops told Gregory to step down. Gregory struck back in February: he deposed Henry and excommunicated him, the first pope to depose a crowned ruler. Excommunication shut a person out of the sacraments, the very rites Level 31’s parish church existed to give.

cards.headline: Three days at Canossa
cards.body: So Henry submitted. He went to Canossa as a penitent and, as tradition tells it, stood barefoot in the snow for three days. On January 28 Gregory absolved him. Centuries later, during Prussia’s struggle with the Catholic Church, Otto von Bismarck declared, “We are not going to Canossa.” One castle had become shorthand for backing down.

mascot.line: Ring for the Church, land for the ruler. Every good compromise leaves both sides a little grumpy.

cards.headline: The deal at Worms
cards.body: The quarrel outlived both men. In 1122 the Concordat of Worms split the difference: the emperor Henry V gave up investing bishops with ring and crosier and accepted their free election, but kept the right to invest them with their lands. The Church got the ring. The ruler kept the real estate.

levels.title: Building Cathedrals
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how medieval builders raised huge cathedrals.
levels.summary: Rib vaults, pointed arches and flying buttresses let Gothic cathedrals rise and fill with windows; master masons and treadwheel cranes built them, partly paid for by tithes.

cards.headline: Cologne Cathedral was begun in 1248. It was finished in 1880.
cards.body: That’s 632 years from first stone to last, with a pause of centuries in the middle. How do you build something that takes longer than a lifetime?

cards.headline: Stone that pushes sideways
cards.body: A stone ceiling is heavy, and a vault pushes outward on the walls beneath it. Gothic builders answered with three tools. The pointed arch and the rib vault, where stone ribs carry the ceiling, let them cover taller, broader spaces. The flying buttress, a half arch, carried the vault’s thrust across an aisle to an outer pier. With the push handled outside, walls could open into huge windows. Tradition names Saint-Denis, rebuilt about 1135 to 1144 under Abbot Suger, as the first Gothic building.

cards.headline: The master mason’s building site
cards.body: A master mason ran the site. He made templates for every shaped stone and put a master craftsman in charge of each part of the job. Canterbury’s builders brought stone by boat from France, easier than hauling it over bad roads. On scaffolding, cranes and pulleys lifted it, some powered by a treadwheel: a “hamster wheel” big enough for two men. And the bills? Tithes were a prime source of money for many great cathedrals.

mascot.line: Nobody was taking the stairs that day. Engineering is learned, sometimes the hard way.

cards.headline: When the ceiling fell
cards.body: At Beauvais, builders raised the tallest Gothic stone vault in the world. In November 1284 its flying buttresses twisted and broke, and the choir vault came down, probably set off by a storm. Rebuilding took until about 1340. Gothic builders were pushing stone to its limits, and sometimes the stone pushed back.

levels.title: Pilgrimage
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why people went on pilgrimages and where they went.
levels.summary: Pilgrims travelled for penance, cures, vows and salvation, to Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela and Canterbury, where Becket's murder in 1170 created a great shrine.

cards.headline: A medieval traveller home from Spain might wear a scallop shell.
cards.body: Not a beach souvenir. The scallop was the emblem of St James and his shrine at Santiago de Compostela. Why did so many people set off on journeys like that?

cards.headline: Why go?
cards.body: Medieval Christians went on pilgrimage for many reasons: to seek salvation, to fulfil a vow, to do penance for their sins, or in hope of a miraculous cure. At the greatest shrines, Jerusalem and Rome, pilgrims could also gain indulgences, which the Church taught remitted the penalty of sin. One journey could be a prayer, a punishment and a hospital visit at once.

cards.headline: A shell to prove it
cards.body: After Jerusalem and Rome came Santiago de Compostela in Spain, where the apostle James’s body was believed to have been brought. Pilgrims wore badges from the shrines they reached, on their necks, clothes or bags, and the scallop was James’s. Many believed a saint’s power passed into a souvenir that had touched the shrine. Some even buried them in house foundations for protection.

cards.headline: A murder makes a shrine
cards.body: On December 29, 1170, Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral by four knights. By 1173 he was a saint, and a whole industry grew up around the pilgrims coming to his shrine. Two centuries later, Chaucer built The Canterbury Tales (1387–1400) around 30 pilgrims travelling there from Southwark, holding a storytelling contest on the way. A famous poem, and at heart a road trip.

levels.title: Monks and Nuns
levels.objective: After this level you can describe daily life in a monastery or convent.
levels.summary: Monks and nuns lived by the Divine Office, eight services from matins in the night to compline, around a cloister; nuns lived the same pattern under abbesses in small, enclosed houses.

cards.headline: Imagine an alarm that goes off eight times a day, starting in the night.
cards.body: For medieval monks and nuns, that was simply the timetable. Level 7 gave you Benedict’s Rule. Now step inside the day it made.

cards.headline: The Divine Office
cards.body: The backbone of the day was the Divine Office: psalms, hymns, prayers and readings at set hours. Matins, the longest, came at night. Prime came early, lauds and vespers were the great morning and evening prayers, terce, sext and none marked mid-morning, noon and mid-afternoon, and compline was the night prayer. Remember Benedict’s balance of prayer, work and reading? The Office was the prayer. The work and study fitted in between.

cards.headline: A world around a square
cards.body: Life centered on the cloister, a square enclosure ringed by covered walkways. In a Benedictine house the church stood on one side and the refectory, the dining hall, faced it; the chapter house sat on the east and the dormitory upstairs. Young members were taught in the cloister and elders studied there. It was also for exercise, and its walks were where the dead were buried. School, gym and graveyard, all around one square.

cards.headline: Nuns and abbesses
cards.body: Women lived this life too. An abbess was the superior of a community of nuns following the Benedictine Rule, and some abbesses even ruled double monasteries of monks and nuns. An English nun’s day had the same three parts: eight services, devotional reading and manual labour. Strict enclosure kept nuns inside the walls, and most English houses were small: only a minority had more than a dozen or so nuns.

levels.title: Hildegard of Bingen
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Hildegard's music, writing and science.
levels.summary: Hildegard of Bingen (born 1098), a German abbess, recorded her visions in Scivias, composed songs and the Ordo virtutum, wrote on medicine and corresponded with popes and an emperor.

cards.headline: In a 12th-century play, every character sings except one: the Devil.
cards.body: He only speaks, because the author believed the Devil had no divine harmony. She was Hildegard of Bingen, a German abbess who also wrote about medicine and traded letters with popes.

cards.headline: From pupil to leader
cards.body: Hildegard was born in 1098 and educated by a woman named Jutta at the Benedictine cloister of Disibodenberg. She took the Benedictine habit at 15, and in 1136 she succeeded Jutta as prioress. About 1147 she left with several nuns to found her own convent at Rupertsberg, near Bingen. Pupil, prioress, founder: three steps in one life.

cards.headline: Visions on the page
cards.body: At 43 she told her confessor about the visions she experienced. The result was Scivias (1141–52), a book describing 26 of them. She also travelled widely through Germany, preaching about her visions to large crowds. A nun, speaking in public, to anyone who would listen.

mascot.line: Poor Devil. All that scheming and not a single tune.

cards.headline: A composer with a Devil problem
cards.body: She collected 77 of her poems, each set to music she composed herself. Her Ordo virtutum, the Play of the Virtues, is the earliest known morality play: 17 Virtues, sung by women, fight for a human soul, while the Devil can only speak. In Hildegard’s world, evil is tone-deaf.

cards.headline: Healer, letter-writer, saint
cards.body: At Rupertsberg she cared for the sick and wrote two medical works: Causes and Cures, on theory, and Physica, full of remedies. About 390 of her letters survive, to popes, an emperor, kings, queens and ordinary lay people. In 2012 the Catholic Church made her a saint and a Doctor of the Church. Nine centuries on, still collecting titles.

levels.title: The First Universities
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the first universities began.
levels.summary: Universities began as guilds of students and masters: Bologna late in the 11th century, Paris between 1150 and 1170, and Oxford by 1200. They taught a spherical Earth from Sacrobosco's Sphere.

cards.headline: The first universities weren’t buildings. They were groups of people.
cards.body: Students and teachers banded together, a bit like a trade guild, and popes, emperors and kings gave them charters. How did a crowd of scholars become an institution?

cards.headline: Bologna: a union of outsiders
cards.body: The first true university in the West grew up at Bologna, in Italy, late in the 11th century, and it became the leading school of canon and civil law. Scholars who weren’t citizens of Bologna formed guilds by nationality to secure protections the city didn’t give them. In 1158 the emperor Frederick I granted them privileges, later extended to all Italian universities. Think of it as a union for out-of-towners.

cards.headline: Paris and Oxford
cards.body: Northern Europe’s first university, Paris, was founded between 1150 and 1170 and became famous for theology. Oxford was well established by the end of the 12th century. These were studia generalia: recognized places of study open to students from all over Europe. A student from Scotland and one from Sicily could sit in the same lecture.

mascot.line: Nobody in that lecture hall was worried about sailing off the edge.

cards.headline: A round Earth on the syllabus
cards.body: One thing they taught: the Earth is a sphere. Around 1230 Johannes de Sacrobosco, who taught at Paris, wrote The Sphere, which became the most popular university astronomy textbook. It argued at length that the Earth is round. It circulated in handwritten copies for 240 years, then was printed from 1476. The idea that medieval people thought the Earth was flat is a myth spread by 19th-century writers.

levels.title: The Great Schism
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Church split into East and West in 1054.
levels.summary: In 1054 a papal legate and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other, the traditional date of the East-West split, after centuries of drifting apart.

cards.headline: In 1054 a cardinal walked into Hagia Sophia and excommunicated a patriarch.
cards.body: It was July 16, and the pope who had sent him was already dead. Did one day in July really split Christianity in two?

cards.headline: Excommunication, returned
cards.body: Remember Justinian’s great church from Level 5? That’s where it happened. The papal legate Cardinal Humbert excommunicated Patriarch Michael Cerularius and his clergy. Cerularius called a synod and excommunicated the pope’s envoys right back. These mutual excommunications became a watershed in church history, the traditional date for the split between the Latin West and the Orthodox East. A slammed door, heard for centuries.

cards.headline: Drifting apart
cards.body: But the two churches had been drifting apart since the 5th century. The East never accepted Rome’s growing claim to lead the whole Church. Rome had added “and the Son” to the Creed without consulting the East. Easterners also resented Roman rules on celibate clergy and unleavened bread at the Eucharist. And Level 4’s eastern empire had swapped Latin for Greek in government. 1054 was less an explosion than the end of a long, slow drift.

mascot.line: Nine centuries to retract a letter. And you thought your inbox was slow.

cards.headline: Undoing 1054
cards.body: The excommunications themselves stood until 1965, when Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I held simultaneous ceremonies revoking them. That’s 911 years to take back one July’s work.

levels.title: Heresy and the Inquisition
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Church dealt with people who disagreed with it.
levels.summary: The Church condemned beliefs like Cathar dualism as heresy. From 1227 papal inquisitors tried suspects; most got penances or prison, and the unrepentant were burned.

cards.headline: An inquisitor arrives in your town with an offer: confess now, get off lightly.
cards.body: That was how a medieval inquiry often began. What came next depended on what you had believed, and what you said.

cards.headline: What counted as heresy
cards.body: Heresy was a belief that church authorities rejected as false. The best-known medieval example was the Cathars, who spread across western Europe in the 12th and 13th centuries. They believed in two principles, one good and one evil, and held that the material world was evil. Their leaders, the perfect, were set apart by a ceremony called the consolamentum. In 1209, under Pope Innocent III, a crusade against them began.

cards.headline: The inquisitors
cards.body: From 1227 Pope Gregory IX appointed the first inquisitors to investigate heresy; many were Dominican and Franciscan friars. An inquisitor opened with a period of grace, when those who confessed got light penances. Then came trials, where suspects usually weren’t told the charges or who had accused them. From 1252 Pope Innocent IV allowed stubborn suspects to be tortured by lay officials.

cards.headline: Penance, prison or the fire
cards.body: Those found guilty might be sent on penitential pilgrimages, made to wear yellow crosses sewn on their clothes, or imprisoned. Those who refused to recant were handed to the secular authorities and burned. At Verona in 1278, more than 150 Cathars were burned together. Such mass burnings were not the usual outcome, though: the inquisitors’ chief aim was to bring heretics back into the Church.

cards.headline: Counting the fires
cards.body: Film has made Bernard Gui, inquisitor of Toulouse, a byword for cruelty. His own records tell a smaller, grimmer story: of the hundreds of people he sentenced, a few dozen were burned. Fewer than legend suggests, and still people, each one, sent to the fire for what they believed.

mascot.line: Popes, pilgrims, masons and a tone-deaf Devil. That was quite a chapter. Well done.

cards.headline: Two teams, one Church
cards.body: Medieval thinkers pictured Christendom as two groups: the sacerdotium, the clergy, and the imperium, the rulers, with the pope supreme in the first and the emperor in the second. But the Church never stayed in its lane. It owned cities and armies and often tried to steer affairs of state, as Canossa showed. It dominated intellectual life, from convents to universities. And through the parish and the tithe, it reached every household. Power, learning and daily life: one Church, in all three.

levels.title: Why the Crusades Began
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Pope Urban II's call in 1095 and why so many answered it.
levels.summary: A Byzantine appeal against the Turks led Urban II to call knights east at Clermont in 1095. Those who went wore a cross and were promised remission of penance for sin.

cards.headline: In 1095 a pope called Western knights to march east. Why did so many go?
cards.body: The Crusades began with a request for help from an old empire and one famous speech at Clermont. Start there.

cards.headline: A request from Constantinople
cards.body: Remember Level 4’s Byzantine Empire, whose people still called themselves Romans? It now faced a dangerous enemy: the Seljuk Turks. So its emperor, Alexius I Comnenus, sent envoys to Pope Urban II with a request: help against the Turks. It was a call for soldiers, the kind of favor you ask a powerful friend. The pope turned it into something much bigger.

cards.headline: The speech at Clermont
cards.body: In November 1095, at a church council in Clermont, in France, Urban urged Western knights to go east and rescue the Holy Land from the Turks. His exact words are lost: the only accounts of the speech were written years later. But the reply was remembered. Cries of “God wills it” rang out, and those who agreed to go were to wear a cross. That cross gave the movement its later name.
cards.callout: Crusade comes from Latin crux, “cross”

cards.headline: Why so many said yes
cards.body: Urban’s council offered a powerful reward. Anyone who went to aid the Christians of the East received a plenary indulgence: the remission of all penance for their sins. Crusaders believed that fighting what they saw as a holy war was a way to win redemption. Imagine being told one hard journey could settle a lifetime of debts. For many who took the cross, that was the promise.

levels.title: The First Crusade
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the First Crusade and the capture of Jerusalem.
levels.summary: In 1096 crusaders massacred Rhineland Jews. The armies took Antioch in 1098 and, helped by divided rivals, stormed Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, killing many Muslims and Jews.

cards.headline: Before it reached the Holy Land, the First Crusade struck the Rhineland’s Jews.
cards.body: Before any army reached Jerusalem, crusader bands turned on the Jewish communities of the Rhineland in 1096. The road to Jerusalem in 1099 starts there.

cards.headline: Spring 1096: the Rhineland
cards.body: In May 1096, crusader bands attacked the Jewish communities of Rhineland towns including Speyer, Worms and Mainz. Many Jews were left only a choice between baptism and death, and some chose death. At Mainz, Jews sheltered in the bishop’s castle, but he fled before the attack, and more than 1,000 were killed. These massacres are traditionally seen as a turning point in Jewish-Christian relations and a pivotal moment in the history of antisemitism.

cards.headline: The long road east
cards.body: Not every band got far. The People’s Crusade, stirred up by the preacher Peter the Hermit, was ambushed and all but wiped out by the Turks in Anatolia in 1096. The main armies did better. After a long siege, they captured the great city of Antioch in June 1098. Jerusalem was next.

cards.headline: Divided rivals
cards.body: Here’s the surprise: the crusaders didn’t face one united Muslim world. The Seljuk empire never held together as a unit, and Shi‘i Fatimid Egypt and Sunni Baghdad were rivals. The Fatimids had even taken Jerusalem for themselves in August 1098. So the crusaders’ final push was against Egypt’s Fatimids, not the Turks that Alexius had asked for help against. Two quarreling neighbors are easier to beat than one.

cards.headline: Jerusalem, 15 July 1099
cards.body: On 15 July 1099 the crusaders stormed Jerusalem. In the slaughter that followed, many of its Muslim and Jewish men, women and children were killed. The city’s Jews had fought beside their Muslim neighbors; they sheltered in synagogues, which the attackers set on fire. Godfrey of Bouillon was chosen to govern and took a modest title, Defender of the Holy Sepulchre. Keep this day in mind: it returns in Level 44.

levels.title: The Crusader States
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the kingdoms the crusaders set up in the Levant.
levels.summary: Four crusader states, called Outremer, were ruled by a Christian minority. Bohemond kept Antioch despite his oath, and Edessa’s fall in 1144 set off a failed Second Crusade.

cards.headline: Europeans called the new crusader lands Outremer: “overseas”.
cards.body: Winning Jerusalem was one thing. Holding a strip of land far from home, surrounded by rivals, was another.

cards.headline: Four states
cards.body: After the First Crusade, the newcomers set up four states: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Tripoli. Europeans called them Outremer, French for “overseas”. Godfrey had settled for a modest title, Defender of the Holy Sepulchre. His brother Baldwin, who had first become ruler of Edessa, took the title of king of Jerusalem in November 1100, after Godfrey died.

cards.headline: A broken promise
cards.body: The Byzantines saw things differently. On the way east, Emperor Alexius had made each crusade leader swear to hand back any conquered land that had belonged to his empire before the Turkish invasions. Bohemond, who had led the capture of Antioch, ignored his oath and kept the city for himself. Alexius had asked for soldiers. He got new neighbors who kept the keys.

cards.headline: A ruling minority
cards.body: Outremer was a set of feudal lands, but its lords were a Christian minority ruling diverse local peoples, including Muslims and many kinds of Christians. Picture a few newcomers taking over a busy city where most people speak other languages and pray in other ways.

cards.headline: The first to fall
cards.body: In 1144 the Muslim ruler Zengi captured Edessa, the northernmost and weakest of the four states. Its loss set off the Second Crusade, led by Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany. It failed outside Damascus in 1148, and Edessa was never won back. From then on, the crusader states stayed on the defensive.

levels.title: Saladin
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Saladin united Muslim forces and retook Jerusalem.
levels.summary: Saladin, a Kurdish commander, united Egypt and Syria, destroyed the crusaders at Hattin in 1187 and took Jerusalem on ransom terms. The West later made him a legend.

cards.headline: In 1187 Jerusalem changed hands again. This time a Kurdish sultan took it.
cards.body: His name was Saladin. The West turned him into a legend of chivalry. The real man is more interesting.

cards.headline: From Tikrit to Cairo
cards.body: Saladin was born in 1137 or 1138 in Tikrit, in today’s Iraq, into a prominent Kurdish family. In 1169, aged 31, he became vizier of Egypt. In 1171 he abolished the Shi‘i Fatimid caliphate, the dynasty that had held Jerusalem in 1099, and returned Egypt to Sunni Islam. From 1174 he spent a dozen years uniting Egypt, Syria, northern Mesopotamia and Palestine. Egypt and Syria were the lands the first caliphs took from Byzantium in Level 8. The divided rivals of Level 42 now had one leader.

cards.headline: Hattin, 4 July 1187
cards.body: Saladin was intensely devoted to jihad, holy war, against the crusaders. On 4 July 1187, at Hattin in northern Palestine, he trapped an exhausted, thirst-stricken crusader army and destroyed it. He spared the captured King Guy and most of the lords. But he ordered the execution of almost all the captured Templars and Hospitallers, the knights of the military orders. Mercy and ruthlessness, on the same day.

cards.headline: Jerusalem, 2 October 1187
cards.body: Three months later, Jerusalem surrendered, after 88 years under the Franks. Saladin had planned to avenge the slaughter of 1099 by killing the city’s Christians. Instead he agreed to let the inhabitants buy their freedom. Several thousand were apparently not ransomed and were probably sold into slavery. Not a massacre, and not a free pass: set beside 1099, the difference is stark.

cards.headline: A legend in the West
cards.body: Western chroniclers praised Saladin as a gallant, chivalrous enemy, and for centuries Western novels and films celebrated his generosity. He died in Damascus in 1193, leaving too little money to pay for his grave. The legend is warm. The real Saladin was devout and determined, and ruthless when he chose to be.

levels.title: Richard the Lionheart
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Richard's role in the Third Crusade.
levels.summary: Richard I took Acre, executed its garrison and won at Arsuf, but never retook Jerusalem. He and Saladin, who never met, agreed a truce in 1192 that opened the holy places to pilgrims.

cards.headline: Richard the Lionheart and Saladin are history’s famous rivals. They never met.
cards.body: They fought each other’s armies and bargained through envoys, but never stood face to face. Here’s the Third Crusade without the legend.

cards.headline: Three rulers answer Hattin
cards.body: Saladin’s victory at Hattin set off the Third Crusade, from 1189 to 1192. The German emperor Frederick Barbarossa drowned crossing a river in 1190. Philip II of France and Richard I of England pressed on; on the way, Richard conquered Cyprus, which became a vital supply base. The crusaders took Acre in July 1191. The next month Philip went home, and Richard was left to lead.

cards.headline: Acre’s prisoners
cards.body: Acre shows the side of the Lionheart the legends leave out. Saladin had agreed to pay a ransom for the city’s Muslim garrison. When he failed to pay, Richard had all 2,700 prisoners executed in view of Saladin’s army. Remember the Templars killed after Hattin? Neither leader was above killing prisoners.

cards.headline: So close to Jerusalem
cards.body: Richard beat Saladin’s army at Arsuf in September 1191. Twice he led his forces to within a few miles of Jerusalem, and twice he pulled back; he never retook the city. All the while he bargained with Saladin and his brother al-Adil, with real mutual respect. In September 1192 they agreed a three-year truce: the coast from Jaffa north stayed Christian, and pilgrims had free access to the holy places.

mascot.line: A legend with the edges left in is still a great story. It’s just a truer one.

cards.headline: A king mostly away
cards.body: Sailing home, Richard was captured by Duke Leopold of Austria and handed to the German emperor, Henry VI. He was freed in 1194 for a ransom of 150,000 marks. Richard was king of England from 1189 to 1199 but spent little time there, and recent historians judge him less kindly than his own age did. A famous soldier; a mostly absent king.

levels.title: The Knights Templar
levels.objective: After this level you can explain who the Templars were and how they fell.
levels.summary: Founded around 1120 to protect pilgrims, the Templars were fighting monks and bankers. Philip IV had them arrested in 1307 on baseless charges; the pope suppressed them in 1312.

cards.headline: They took vows like monks, fought like knights and lent money to kings.
cards.body: The Knights Templar were one of the strangest creations of the Crusades, and one of the richest. So how did they fall so hard?

cards.headline: Guards for the pilgrim road
cards.body: In late 1119 or early 1120, eight or nine French knights led by Hugh de Payns vowed to protect pilgrims traveling to the Holy Land. King Baldwin II of Jerusalem housed them in the area of the former Temple of Solomon, and that gave them their name: the Templars. Within about ten years, the Church formally approved the order at the Council of Troyes.

cards.headline: Monks with swords
cards.body: Templars swore the vows of monks: poverty, chastity and obedience. But the knights fought, in a white surcoat marked with a red cross. The poverty was personal, not collective. Their military strength made them ideal bankers, to kings as well as to pilgrims. Picture a bank whose vault is guarded by the bankers themselves.

mascot.line: Charges invented, confessions forced. Historians read these trial records very carefully.

cards.headline: The arrests of 1307
cards.body: When Acre fell in 1291, the Templars lost much of their reason for being, while their wealth, lands in Europe and power bred resentment. Philip IV of France was chronically short of money. On 13 October 1307 he had every Templar in France arrested. They were accused of heresy and idol worship, and many confessed under torture. The charges are now recognized as baseless.

cards.headline: The end of the order
cards.body: Pope Clement V suppressed the Templars in 1312 and gave their property to another military order, the Hospitallers. In 1314 the last grand master, Jacques de Molay, was burned. The order that began by guarding pilgrims was destroyed by a Christian king who needed money.

levels.title: The Fourth Crusade
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how crusaders ended up sacking Christian Constantinople.
levels.summary: In debt to Venice, the Fourth Crusade took Christian Zara, then followed an exiled prince to Constantinople, sacked it in April 1204 and ruled it as a Latin empire until 1261.

cards.headline: In 1204 crusaders sacked a Christian city: Constantinople.
cards.body: Nobody set out to do that. A debt, a deal and an exiled prince took them there.

cards.headline: A bill in Venice
cards.body: Pope Innocent III called a new crusade in 1198. The crusaders hired Venice to ship them east for 85,000 marks. But when the army gathered in 1202, only about a third of the expected men turned up, and they couldn’t pay. To settle the debt, in November 1202 they attacked and took Zara (Zadar), a Christian city. Imagine booking a bus for thirty friends when only ten show up. The driver still wants the full fare.

cards.headline: A prince’s offer
cards.body: Then came a tempting offer. An exiled Byzantine prince, Alexius, promised the crusaders a huge payment, the Byzantine church’s submission to Rome and help on crusade, if they would put him on the throne in Constantinople. The fleet turned toward the city.

cards.headline: Over the walls from the water
cards.body: Remember Level 4’s walls, which held against attackers through the early Middle Ages? In 1204 the attack came from the water. On 12 April, men climbed from ships’ masts across catwalks onto the walls. For three days the army pillaged at will, defiling and stealing from the holy places. Justinian’s Hagia Sophia, from Level 5, was looted. The four bronze horses of St Mark’s in Venice were brought from Constantinople at this time.

cards.headline: A Latin empire
cards.body: The crusaders made Baldwin of Flanders emperor of a new Latin empire, and Hagia Sophia became a Roman Catholic cathedral. When Pope Innocent III heard how the crusaders had behaved, he was filled with shame and rebuked them. In 1261 Michael VIII Palaeologus retook a much diminished Constantinople. The Crusades had begun with a call to aid the Christians of the East. This one wrecked their capital.

levels.title: The Reconquista
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the centuries-long Christian conquest of Muslim Spain.
levels.summary: From Covadonga around 718 to Granada in 1492, Christian kingdoms retook Iberia from Muslim rule. It began as politics, turned religious, and the peoples stayed closely bound.

cards.headline: Level 8’s conquest of Spain began in 711. Undoing it took until 1492.
cards.body: Historians call it the Reconquista, the “reconquest”. It was the Crusades’ long western story, and more tangled than its name suggests.

cards.headline: Where it started
cards.body: Remember 711? Muslim forces overran most of the Iberian Peninsula, ending the Visigothic kingdom. The Reconquista was the series of campaigns by which Christian states took that land back. Its traditional starting point is the Battle of Covadonga, around 718, when Christians in Asturias, in northern Spain, first held off Muslim forces. The fight back began within ten years; the finish took nearly eight centuries.

events.label: Christians hold off Muslim forces at Covadonga

Ferdinand III takes Córdoba

cards.headline: Holy war, or politics?
cards.body: The Reconquista began as political expansion by Christian kingdoms. Popes were backing it by the 11th century, but it became explicitly religious only after Muslim power in Spain had been broken. All along, the Christian and Muslim peoples of Spain were tightly bound together, culturally and economically. Rivals on the battlefield were often neighbors everywhere else.

cards.headline: Granada, 1492
cards.body: After Las Navas de Tolosa, the last serious Muslim threat to Christian dominance was gone. One kingdom held out longest: Granada, home of the Alhambra palace, the last Moorish kingdom in Spain. In January 1492 it fell to Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic Monarchs. Nearly 800 years after 711, Muslim rule in Spain was over.

levels.title: What the Crusades Changed
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Crusades' effects on trade, ideas and relations between faiths.
levels.summary: After Acre fell in 1291, the Crusades left richer Italian trading cities, embittered Greeks, long memories among Jews and Muslims, and less effect on learning than once claimed.

cards.headline: In 1291 the last crusader stronghold on the mainland fell. What had changed?
cards.body: The Mamluks took Acre and destroyed it, along with the castles along the coast. The crusader states were gone. Their effects were not.

cards.headline: Winners at the market
cards.body: The clearest winners were Italian trading cities. They gained quarters in the crusader states, extended their trade with the Muslim world and set up trading posts, some lasting long after 1291. Crusading also expanded trade between Europe and the Muslim world, bringing new goods and tastes to European tables. For armies it was holy war. For merchants it was also a very long business trip.

cards.headline: A wound between Christians
cards.body: The Crusades, above all the Fourth (Level 47), so embittered the Greeks that any real reunion of the Eastern and Western churches was out of the question. The Byzantines had asked the West for help in 1095. By 1204 the West had sacked their capital.

cards.headline: Long memories
cards.body: Memories ran deep on every side. For Jews, the Rhineland massacres of 1096 (Level 42) became a turning point in relations with Christians. Muslim writers of the time called the crusaders Franks and saw them as cruel invaders. The same events looked very different depending on who told the story.

cards.headline: What they probably didn’t do
cards.body: Some changes get credited to the Crusades that likely came another way. Unlike Sicily and Spain (Level 48’s Spain), the crusader states do not seem to have been a route for Arabic science and philosophy to reach the West. That’s one reason historians now see the Crusades as one significant factor in Europe’s development, not its single driving force.

levels.title: Milestone: The High Middle Ages
levels.objective: After this level you can connect feudalism, the Church and the Crusades into one picture of medieval Europe.
levels.summary: From 1095 to 1291 the Crusades filled two centuries of the high Middle Ages and drew Rome’s three heirs into one story that also struck Jews and Christian Constantinople.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Let’s put the Crusades in one picture.
cards.body: From a pope’s speech in 1095 to the fall of Acre in 1291, crusading in the Holy Land lasted almost two centuries. Here’s how it fits the Middle Ages you met in Level 1.

mascot.line: Ten levels, three heirs of Rome, two centuries. That’s a milestone well earned.

cards.headline: Rome’s heirs, meeting again
cards.body: Level 1 split the Middle Ages into early, high and late. The Crusades, from 1095 to 1291, sit in the high Middle Ages, between the early period (to about 1000) and the late one (from about 1300). Remember Level 10’s three heirs of Rome? The Crusades pulled all three into one story: a Byzantine emperor asked the pope in the West for help against Muslim Turks. Along the way, crusaders also attacked the Rhineland’s Jewish communities in 1096 and sacked Christian Constantinople in 1204. It was never a simple two-sided war.

levels.title: The Growth of Towns
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why towns grew after the year 1000.
levels.summary: Once the raids ended, towns revived: Europe’s population nearly doubled from 1000 to 1340, new walled towns appeared, and charters offered freedom after a year and a day.

cards.headline: Stay in some medieval towns for a year and a day, and you could become free.
cards.body: Yet for centuries after Rome, town life in western Europe had almost vanished. Then, after about 1000, the towns came back, and people wanted in. Why?

cards.headline: The quiet centuries end
cards.body: Remember Level 1? In the early Middle Ages, about 500 to 1000, frequent warfare made town life in western Europe virtually disappear. Towns only began to grow steadily again once the raids by Vikings, Magyars and Saracens had stopped. Raiders, it turns out, are terrible for business. First came peace, then came the towns.

cards.headline: More people, more towns
cards.body: Then came the people. Between 1000 and 1340, Europe’s population nearly doubled. In the 10th and 11th centuries new towns were founded and old ones spread out, and once a town felt full, its people usually ringed it with a wall. Picture your own hometown doubling in size: new streets, new neighbours, and a wall to keep it all together.

mascot.line: Imagine a fresh start that came with your new address.

cards.headline: City air brings freedom
cards.body: Growing towns wanted settlers, and they had something to offer. Many became communes: self-governing towns whose citizens swore to help each other, holding a charter from a bishop, count or king. Emperor Henry V, who ruled from 1111 to 1125, wrote the principle “city air brings freedom” into charters for Speyer and Worms. New towns on lords’ lands offered freedom and land to settlers who stayed more than a year and a day.
cards.callout: Stadtluft macht frei: “city air brings freedom”

levels.title: Markets and Fairs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe medieval markets and trade fairs.
levels.summary: English markets met weekly by royal charter; fairs met yearly on saints’ days. The Champagne fairs linked north and south, and piepowder courts gave quick justice.

cards.headline: Medieval England had courts named after dusty feet.
cards.body: They sat right at the fairs, settling traders’ arguments on the spot. To see why anyone needed them, follow the money: first to the weekly market, then to the great fairs.

cards.headline: Market day
cards.body: A medieval market wasn’t open every day. In England it met once a week, on a set day and in a set place, and holding one took a royal charter. Towns, villages and monasteries all won them. From 1200 there was a catch: a new market was allowed only if it didn’t harm the markets nearby. Even medieval kings worried about the shop down the road.

cards.headline: Fair season
cards.body: A fair was bigger and rarer: once a year, usually on a saint’s feast day, lasting from a single day to a week or more. The greatest were the Champagne fairs in France, which rotated among four towns, Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube, Provins and Troyes, and peaked in the 13th century. Under the count’s protection, merchants swapped northern cloth for spices and dyes from the Mediterranean. North met south in a French field.

cards.headline: Credit and quick justice
cards.body: Big deals needed trust. At the Champagne fairs, bargains often ran on letters of credit rather than bags of coins, laying groundwork for modern credit. And when a deal went wrong in England, a piepowder court (from the French for “dusty feet”) settled disputes at fairs and markets fast and on the spot, before the traveller could dust off and leave.
cards.callout: A weekly market for the neighbourhood; a yearly fair for the wider world

levels.title: Guilds
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how guilds controlled crafts and trained apprentices.
levels.summary: Craft guilds grew in busy towns, held a monopoly, set quality and prices, and trained members from apprentice to journeyman to master.

cards.headline: A “masterpiece” was once a job application.
cards.body: In a medieval town, you couldn’t just hang out a sign and start making shoes. The trade belonged to a guild, and to join its top rank you had to prove yourself.

cards.headline: Two kinds of guild
cards.body: Merchant guilds brought together a town’s merchants. Craft guilds brought together the artisans of one trade: the bakers, say, or the weavers. Craft guilds arose soon after merchant guilds, in growing towns where work was splitting into many specialised trades. Once a town needed a baker, a butcher and a candlestick maker, it needed rules for all of them.

cards.headline: Rules of the trade
cards.body: A craft guild held a monopoly on its trade in town: if you weren’t in the guild, you didn’t sell. It set standards for the quality of goods and worked to keep prices stable. It also looked after its own, with a patron saint, a chapel in the parish church, charitable work and often a guildhall. Part quality inspector, part trade association, part social club.

mascot.line: Five to nine years of training. Suddenly a driving test looks quick.

cards.headline: Apprentice, journeyman, master
cards.body: Guild members climbed a ladder. An apprentice, usually a boy in late childhood or his teens, lived with the master’s family for a fixed term of five to nine years. Then he became a journeyman: the “journey” originally meant a day’s labour, and journeymen worked for wages, often by the day. To rise to master, a journeyman might have to prove his skill with a masterpiece.
cards.callout: Apprentice, journeyman, master: the ladder of a medieval craft

levels.title: Food and Feasts
levels.objective: After this level you can describe what rich and poor people ate.
levels.summary: Bread, meat and drink marked rank: white wheat for lords and coarse loaves for servants, meat rarely for peasants, fish on fast days. Spices were costly status symbols, not a cover for rotten meat.

cards.headline: A medieval dinner could tell you exactly who was sitting at the table.
cards.body: Not by name cards, but by the bread, the meat and the pepper. Let’s eat our way up the social ladder.

cards.headline: Your bread is your rank
cards.body: In a castle kitchen, the baker made fine white wheat rolls for the lady’s table and rough loaves of barley, oats or even peas and beans for the servants. At a feast, food was often served on a slice of bread that soaked up the juices, and you ate with your fingers: forks did not appear on medieval tables. Your plate could be dinner too.

cards.headline: Meat means money
cards.body: Meat on the table was a sign of status. Peasants ate it only rarely, mostly before winter, when livestock was culled so that fewer animals had to be fed through the cold months. Religious fasting banned meat on Fridays and many other days, so fish took its place. At a feast, lower-ranking guests got coarser bread and second-quality ale; wine was expensive, because it had to be imported.

mascot.line: Myth spotted: the rotten-meat story falls apart once you check the price of pepper.

cards.headline: Pepper for show
cards.body: Spices were costly imports, and lords served strong-tasting sauces with expensive foreign spices to show off their wealth. You may have heard that spices hid the taste of rotten meat. Historians reject that: spices cost far more than fresh meat, and salting and smoking preserved food better. Spices weren’t a cover-up. They were a boast.
cards.callout: If you could afford the pepper, you could afford fresh meat

levels.title: Clothes and Status
levels.objective: After this level you can describe medieval clothes and what they said about status.
levels.summary: Wool clothed almost everyone, from cheap russet to costly scarlet. England’s 1363 law set what each rank could wear, and a 1463 law capped pointed shoes, whose fashion shows up in medieval bones.

cards.headline: Your medieval neighbours could read your rank from across the street.
cards.body: No ID card needed: the cloth on your back did the talking. It talked so loudly that the law stepped in.

cards.headline: Wool for everyone, but not the same wool
cards.body: In 14th-century England, wool was the fabric people bought most, and linen came second. But “wool” covered a huge range, from cheap, coarse russet and blanket to costly scarlet. Two people could both wear wool and still look worlds apart, the way a cheap T-shirt and a designer one are both cotton.

cards.headline: Dressing by law
cards.body: In 1363 England passed a law setting what cloth each rank could wear, from servants and craftsmen up to merchants and knights. It blamed the “outrageous and excessive apparel” of people dressing above their “estate and degree”. The lowest ranks were limited to blanket and russet worth no more than 12 pence. Did it work? Laws like this have proved difficult or impossible to enforce over the long term.

mascot.line: Fashion leaves clues: sometimes in the wardrobe, sometimes in the skeleton.

cards.headline: The pointy-shoe problem
cards.body: Late-medieval fashion loved poulaines, shoes with long pointed toes. In 1463 King Edward IV limited the points in London to under two inches. The fashion left marks you can still measure: Cambridge researchers found bunions in 6% of people buried in the 11th to 13th centuries, but 27% of those buried in the 14th and 15th. The bones kept the receipts.

levels.title: Windmills and Watermills
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how mills changed medieval work.
levels.summary: England had thousands of watermills by 1086, and windmills from the 1180s. Lords claimed the right to grind their tenants’ grain, so Abbot Samson destroyed a rival mill.

cards.headline: In 1191 an abbot ordered a brand-new windmill torn down.
cards.body: Its builder, Herbert the dean, hadn’t asked permission. Why wreck a perfectly good machine? Because in the Middle Ages a mill meant power, in both senses.

cards.headline: Rivers at work
cards.body: Water came first. In 1086 a royal survey counted more than 5,000 water mills in England south of the rivers Severn and Trent. Their wheels ground grain into flour. Later, waterwheels would also drive saws, bellows for forges, trip-hammers and textile mills. For a medieval village, the river was the power socket.

cards.headline: Then the wind
cards.body: Windmills weren’t a European invention: the earliest-known references come from Persia, in 644 and 915. In England, the first written references that clearly mention windmills date from the 1180s. These were timber post mills: the whole body, millstones, gears and all, turned on one great post to face the wind. Imagine turning a wooden shed to catch the breeze.

cards.headline: The lord’s mill
cards.body: A lord could claim soke, or suit of mill: the right to grind all the grain used on his manor at his mill. The miller took his pay as a toll, a share of each person’s grain. So Abbot Samson saw the dean’s windmill as competition: the town’s burgesses would take their grain there instead. “I give you as many thanks as if you had cut off both my feet,” he told the dean. The frightened dean pulled it down himself.
cards.callout: A mill was an engine and a monopoly

levels.title: Medicine and the Four Humors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain medieval ideas about health and healing.
levels.summary: Medieval medicine sought balance among four humours. Physicians read urine and let blood to remove an excess; bloodletting was later discredited.

cards.headline: A medieval physician might hold your urine up to the light and study it.
cards.body: He was hunting for clues about four liquids that, he believed, ran your whole body: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Welcome to the four humours.

cards.headline: Four liquids in balance
cards.body: The theory was ancient. Hippocrates championed it, and Galen, Rome’s leading medical authority in the 2nd century CE, built on it; it was still current throughout the Middle Ages. The four humours were blood, phlegm, yellow bile (choler) and black bile (melancholy). The ideal person had them perfectly balanced, and illness meant one had got out of proportion. Health was a recipe, and sickness meant too much of one ingredient.

cards.headline: Reading the signs
cards.body: So how do you spot an imbalance you can’t see? Medieval physicians examined a patient’s urine: its colour, its consistency, its clarity and any sediment, all read as signs of the humours inside. A flask held up to the window was the medieval version of a lab test.

cards.headline: Letting out the excess
cards.body: If one humour was in excess, healers tried to remove it, by letting blood or applying leeches. After a church edict of 1163 barred clergy from bloodletting, barber-surgeons took it up alongside shaving and pulling teeth, a legacy you can still see in the barber’s pole. Bloodletting lost credibility in the 18th and 19th centuries, when studies showed it worked less well than claimed.
cards.callout: This is the history of an idea, not medical advice

mascot.line: Next time someone seems melancholic, remember: a medieval doctor would have blamed black bile.

cards.headline: Words that outlived the theory
cards.body: A person ruled by one humour was called sanguine (from the Latin for blood), phlegmatic, choleric or melancholic. The theory is long discredited, but the words stayed in English. To a medieval doctor, a sanguine friend was simply someone with plenty of blood.

levels.title: Women in the Middle Ages
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the lives, work and power of medieval women.
levels.summary: By class and region: Christine de Pizan wrote for a living, Margaret Paston ran estates, brewsters and Paris silkwomen worked in trade, and coverture limited wives.

cards.headline: In 1405 a French widow built a city out of words.
cards.body: Its citizens were famous women, and its author, Christine de Pizan, is a good guide to what medieval women could do, and what they couldn’t.

cards.headline: Living by the pen
cards.body: Christine de Pizan (1364 to about 1430) was widowed after ten years of marriage, with three children to raise. She took up writing to support them. In The Book of the City of Ladies (1405) she wrote of women known for heroism and virtue, and she defended women against misogynist satire. She argued back, in print, and it paid the bills.

cards.headline: Running the estate
cards.body: In England, the gentry had their own formidable women. Margaret Paston (about 1421 to 1484) was a Norfolk gentlewoman. She left the largest collection of personal letters from medieval England, many to her husband while he was away. While he was away she managed the family’s estates, and when attackers threatened their manor house she defended it and asked him for crossbows and armour.

cards.headline: Women at work
cards.body: In towns and villages, women worked for money. Women brewed and sold most of the ale drunk in medieval England; after 1350, men slowly took over the trade. In 13th- and 14th-century Paris, the silk industry even had some all-female guilds, and a few silkwomen did business with aristocrats and the king himself.

cards.headline: The legal limits
cards.body: The law set hard limits too. Under English coverture, rooted in Norman custom, a wife’s legal existence was suspended: she could not make contracts or sue in her own name, though a single woman could. So what a medieval woman could do depended heavily on her class, her region and whether she was married.
cards.callout: Class, place and marriage shaped a medieval woman’s options

levels.title: Songs, Games and Holidays
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how medieval people spent their free time.
levels.summary: "Holiday" means holy day. York’s guilds staged 48 plays on Corpus Christi, villages played football despite royal bans, and songs like "Sumer is icumen in" survive.

cards.headline: In 1314 England’s king banned football. It didn’t work.
cards.body: Medieval people worked hard, but they played hard too. So when did they get time off, and what did they do with it?

cards.headline: Holy days
cards.body: Free time followed the Church calendar. The word holiday comes from Old English haligdæg, “holy day”: a day set apart for religious observance. By the 14th century a holiday could also mean a day off work. Your summer holiday is, word for word, a holy day.

cards.headline: The whole town on stage
cards.body: On the summer feast of Corpus Christi, York put on a show. Its craft guilds performed a cycle of 48 plays, from the 14th century on, rolling them through the streets on pageant wagons. Each guild took a scene, sometimes one that suited its trade: the Shipwrights performed the Building of the Ark. Typecasting, medieval style.

mascot.line: Five royal bans in about a century, and the ball kept rolling.

cards.headline: Football with no rulebook
cards.body: Folk football was usually played at Shrovetide or Easter, village against village, across fields, through streams and down narrow streets. Everyone joined in: men and women, rich and poor, clergy too. Edward II banned it in 1314, and later kings banned it again in 1349, 1389, 1401 and 1423. All in vain. The game kept winning.

cards.headline: Sing, cuckoo
cards.body: Songs survive too. “Sumer is icumen in”, a round with the refrain “sing cuckoo”, was written down at Reading Abbey in the mid-13th century, and the manuscript is now in the British Library. A song about summer arriving, still singable after more than seven centuries.

cards.body: Not a lord, not a peasant, but someone who lived behind a town wall. Medieval France had a word for them, and you still use it.

cards.headline: The first bourgeois
cards.body: In medieval France, a bourgeois was someone who lived in a walled town, as distinct from a peasant. Picture the townspeople of this chapter: burgesses tempted by a rival windmill, brewsters selling ale, guild craftsmen climbing from apprentice to master, merchants at the weekly market. Their towns ran on charters from bishops, counts and kings. Today the bourgeoisie means the social order dominated by the middle class. The walled town handed the modern world a word.

levels.title: The House of Wisdom
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Baghdad became a center of learning.
levels.summary: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750; al-Mansur founded Baghdad as the Round City in 762. Al-Ma'mun sponsored Greek translation; the House of Wisdom's scope is debated.

cards.headline: In 762 a caliph built his capital as a circle. It became a city of translators.
cards.body: Under the caliph al-Ma’mun, Baghdad turned ancient Greek books into Arabic. At the heart of the story sits a famous name, the House of Wisdom. What was it, really?

cards.headline: A new family, a round city
cards.body: Remember Level 8’s Umayyad caliphs, ruling from Damascus? In 750 a new family, the Abbasids, overthrew them, and the capital later moved to a brand-new city. In 762 the caliph al-Mansur chose the site of Baghdad and built Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace, inside circular walls. Everyone called it the Round City. Most capitals grow; this one was drawn.

cards.headline: Greek books, Arabic words
cards.body: The caliph al-Ma’mun, who reigned from 813 to 833, encouraged the translation of ancient Greek works into Arabic. From about 800 to 1000, a large-scale translation movement carried Aristotle, Euclid and much more into Arabic. Picture a whole library learning a new language, one book at a time.
cards.callout: About 800 to 1000: Greek learning moves into Arabic

mascot.line: A famous building that might have been mostly a bookshelf. History loves a plot twist.

cards.headline: The House of Wisdom puzzle
cards.body: Bayt al-Hikmah, the House of Wisdom, was a royal library of the Abbasid caliphs, and it reached its peak under al-Ma’mun. It is often pictured as a great academy at the centre of everything. Historians are more careful: little evidence puts it at the centre of Baghdad’s scholarship, so its scope is debated. The translating itself is not in doubt. The legend may be bigger than the building; the books were real.

levels.title: Algebra and Numbers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how al-Khwarizmi and others shaped mathematics.
levels.summary: Al-Khwarizmi's al-jabr book named algebra and his Latin name gave us algorithm. The numerals came from India, through the Islamic world, to Europe.

cards.headline: Say “algorithm” and you’re saying a Baghdad scholar’s name.
cards.body: Say “algebra” and you’re quoting the title of his book. Meet al-Khwarizmi, and the numbers he helped carry west.

cards.headline: A book about balancing
cards.body: Al-Khwarizmi, who lived from about 780 to 850, worked at the House of Wisdom you met in Level 61. Around 825 he wrote a book on calculating by al-jabr and balancing. Al-jabr, “restoring”, meant moving a subtracted term to the other side of an equation; balancing cancelled what matched on both sides. Its Latin translation in the 12th century gave us the word algebra. If you’ve ever moved x to the other side, you’ve done al-jabr.

cards.headline: Numbers from India
cards.body: The digits you use every day originated in India in the 6th or 7th century. Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book of arithmetic with them, which survives in Latin as Algoritmi de numero Indorum, “Al-Khwarizmi Concerning the Hindu Art of Reckoning”. That Latin spelling of his name, Algoritmi, became our word algorithm. Hence “Hindu-Arabic” numerals: invented in India, carried by the Islamic world.

cards.headline: Into Europe
cards.body: Mathematicians of the Islamic world, especially al-Khwarizmi and al-Kindi, brought the numerals to Europe about the 12th century. Even so, when Fibonacci published his Liber abaci in 1202, few Europeans knew them. He had learned calculation from an Arab master in North Africa, and his book spread the system. Next time you do long division, thank a chain of scholars from India to Pisa.
cards.callout: India invented them; the Islamic world carried them; Europe adopted them
