options.label: It becomes the demand curve
options.rationale: Weather changes how much farmers can supply, not what buyers want.

questions.explanation: Weather is one of the production conditions held equal when the curve is drawn. Bad weather shifts the whole supply curve toward less.

levels.title: Demand
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why buyers want less of something when its price rises.
levels.summary: The law of demand: a higher price almost always cuts the quantity demanded, through the substitution and income effects. Income, tastes and related prices shift the whole demand curve.

cards.headline: When gas prices jump, people start carpooling.
cards.body: Nobody orders them to. They combine errands, take the bus and plan trips closer to home. Each person quietly buys a bit less. Add them all up and you get a law of economics.

cards.headline: The law of demand
cards.body: A rise in price almost always cuts the quantity demanded, the amount buyers want at that price. A fall in price raises it. It's Level 42's law in the mirror: when prices climb, sellers want to sell more and buyers want to buy less. Draw it and the demand curve slopes downward, because people buy more when things are cheaper.

mascot.line: Same paycheck, pricier gas. Your wallet just shrank without losing a cent.

cards.headline: Two reasons you buy less
cards.body: First, the substitution effect: when one thing gets pricier, you switch toward things that are now relatively cheaper, like the bus instead of the car. Second, the income effect: a higher price shrinks what your money can buy, even though your pay hasn't changed, so you buy less of most goods. Two effects, one direction.

cards.fact: Demand can change even when the price stands still.
cards.context: Like supply, the demand curve holds other things equal. Change them and the whole curve shifts: income, tastes, the prices of related goods, population, even expectations about the future. A change in the good's own price just slides buyers along the curve, exactly as Level 42's sellers slide along theirs.

cards.headline: Demand: understood
learned: Higher price, less wanted: the law of demand
Substitution and income effects explain it
The demand curve slopes downward
Income and tastes shift the whole curve

questions.prompt: What does the law of demand say?

options.label: When a price rises, sellers offer more
options.rationale: That's the law of supply.

options.label: When a price rises, buyers want less of it
Buyers always want the same amount
options.rationale: The amount buyers want changes with the price.

options.label: Higher prices make people want more
options.rationale: It works the other way for almost all goods.

questions.explanation: A rise in price almost always decreases the quantity demanded; a fall increases it.

questions.prompt: Gas prices jump but bus fares stay put, so you ride the bus more. What is this called?

options.label: The income effect
options.rationale: That one is about your money buying less overall.

options.label: The law of supply
options.rationale: That's about sellers, not your choice of transport.

options.label: The substitution effect
A price floor
options.rationale: No legal minimum price is involved here.

questions.explanation: Switching toward a good that is now relatively cheaper is the substitution effect.

questions.prompt: Your income rises and you buy more concert tickets, though ticket prices haven't changed. In Level 42's terms, what happened?

options.label: You moved along the demand curve
options.rationale: Moving along needs a change in the price itself.

options.label: The supply curve shifted
options.rationale: Nothing changed for sellers; it's your demand.

options.label: The law of demand stopped working
options.rationale: The law still holds; the whole curve moved.

options.label: The whole demand curve shifted

questions.explanation: A change in income is one of the other things held equal. When it changes, the whole demand curve shifts.

levels.title: Where Prices Come From
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how supply and demand together set a price.
levels.summary: The equilibrium price is where supply and demand cross. A surplus pushes prices down and a shortage pushes them up. Marshall called supply and demand the two blades of a pair of scissors.

cards.headline: Who decides what things cost?
cards.body: Most of the time, no single person. In markets, prices come from supply and demand pushing against each other. Put Level 42 and Level 43 on one chart and watch what happens.

cards.headline: Where the curves cross
cards.body: Supply climbs, demand falls, so the two curves cross at one point. That's the equilibrium price: the only price where the amount buyers want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell. At that price, every buyer willing to pay it finds a seller, and every seller willing to accept it finds a buyer.

cards.headline: The market's nudge
cards.body: Price too high? Sellers bring more than buyers want: a surplus. Rather than sit on unsold stock, some sellers cut their prices, because selling cheaper beats not selling at all. Price too low? Buyers want more than there is: a shortage, and sellers spot a chance to charge more. Either way, the price gets shoved toward the crossing point.

mascot.line: Next time someone says "it's all demand," hand them one scissor blade and some paper.

cards.fact: Supply or demand: which one sets the price? Both, like scissors.
cards.context: In his Principles of Economics, published in 1890, Alfred Marshall said that arguing over it is like arguing whether the upper or the lower blade of a pair of scissors does the cutting. One blade alone cuts nothing. Price comes from supply and demand working together.

cards.headline: Prices: explained
learned: Equilibrium is where supply meets demand
Surpluses push prices down
Shortages push prices up
Marshall: supply and demand are scissor blades

questions.prompt: What is the equilibrium price?

options.label: The highest price any buyer will pay
options.rationale: Some buyers would pay more; equilibrium is where the amounts match.

options.label: The price where the amount wanted equals the amount offered
A price fixed by law
options.rationale: Equilibrium comes from the market, not from a law.

options.label: The lowest price a seller can survive on
options.rationale: That is about costs, not where supply meets demand.

questions.explanation: Equilibrium is where the supply and demand curves cross: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

questions.prompt: A shop's price is above equilibrium, and unsold stock is piling up. What usually happens next?

options.label: Sellers raise the price further
options.rationale: Raising it would make the pile bigger.

options.label: Buyers start wanting more at that price
options.rationale: Buyers want less at a high price, not more.

options.label: Nothing: prices never move on their own
options.rationale: Unsold stock gives sellers a reason to move.

options.label: Sellers cut the price

questions.explanation: A surplus pushes some sellers to cut prices, since selling cheaper beats not selling at all.

questions.prompt: Why did Marshall compare supply and demand to the blades of a pair of scissors?

options.label: Price comes from both working together
Supply always cuts prices down
options.rationale: Neither blade works alone; that was his point.

options.label: Demand matters more than supply
options.rationale: He argued that neither one matters more.

options.label: Markets cut costs like tailors cut cloth
options.rationale: The picture is about two forces acting together.

questions.explanation: Asking which blade cuts is pointless, just like asking whether supply or demand alone sets the price.

levels.title: Shortages and Surpluses
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happens when prices are held too low or too high.
levels.summary: A price floor above equilibrium creates a surplus, like Europe's butter mountains. A price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage, like rent control.

cards.headline: In the 1980s, Europe had a butter mountain. And a wine lake.
cards.body: Those were the nicknames for giant stored surpluses of butter and wine. They grew out of a rule that stopped prices doing Level 44's job.

cards.headline: Floors make surpluses
cards.body: Governments sometimes regulate prices by law. A price floor is the lowest price anyone may legally pay. Set it above the equilibrium price and sellers offer more than buyers want: a surplus. Level 44's cure, cutting the price, is now against the rules. So the extra has nowhere to go.

mascot.line: A butter mountain sounds delicious until you realize someone has to store it.

cards.fact: Europe's farm policy held prices high, and farmers produced more and more.
cards.context: When the Common Agricultural Policy began in 1962, it supported farmers mainly by keeping their prices artificially high. That's a floor, and Level 42 predicts the rest: a higher price, more supply. By the 1980s, the result was huge stored surpluses of butter and wine. (The wine was actually industrial alcohol. No lake of fine vintage, sadly.)

cards.headline: Ceilings make shortages
cards.body: Now flip it. A price ceiling is the highest price anyone may legally charge, often set to keep necessities affordable. Set it below equilibrium and buyers want more than sellers offer: a shortage. This time the price can't rise to close the gap, so the shortage stays. Rent control is the classic case: it can leave fewer apartments to rent than there would be at market rates.

cards.headline: Price controls: tested
learned: A floor above equilibrium makes a surplus
Europe's butter mountains came from a floor
A ceiling below equilibrium makes a shortage
Rent control is the classic ceiling

questions.prompt: What is a price ceiling?

options.label: The lowest price anyone may legally pay
options.rationale: That's a price floor.

options.label: The price where supply meets demand
options.rationale: That's the equilibrium price.

options.label: The highest price anyone may legally charge
A tax added on top of a price
options.rationale: A ceiling caps the price; it adds nothing.

questions.explanation: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price, often meant to keep necessities affordable.

questions.prompt: Why did Europe's farm policy end up with butter mountains?

options.label: Prices held high made farmers produce more than buyers wanted
A bad harvest made farmers store butter for later
options.rationale: The surpluses came from too much production, not too little.

options.label: People in the 1980s stopped eating butter
options.rationale: The cause was the price policy, not a change in taste.

options.label: Prices were held so low that nobody would sell
options.rationale: Low prices would cause a shortage, not a surplus.

questions.explanation: Artificially high prices acted as a floor: farmers produced more and more, and the surplus had to be stored.

questions.prompt: From Level 44: in a free market, a shortage pushes the price up. What does a price ceiling below equilibrium do to that?

options.label: It speeds the rise up
options.rationale: A ceiling caps the price, so it cannot rise past it.

options.label: It turns the shortage into a surplus
options.rationale: Only a price held too high makes a surplus.

options.label: It has no effect on the shortage
options.rationale: It matters a lot: it stops the fix from happening.

options.label: It blocks the rise, so the shortage stays

questions.explanation: Normally sellers raise prices in a shortage. A ceiling forbids that, so the gap between wanted and offered doesn't close.

levels.title: Competition
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how competition pushes prices down and quality up.
levels.summary: In perfect competition, each seller is a price taker. Profits attract new rivals, which pushes prices down. Competition keeps prices down and quality up.

cards.headline: Try selling your corn above the market price. Watch what happens.
cards.body: Nothing happens. That's the problem: no buyers come at all. Meet the quiet force that works for you every time you shop.

cards.headline: Price takers
cards.body: In perfect competition, many firms sell identical products to many buyers, everyone knows the prices, and firms can come and go freely. A single corn farmer can't pick her price: supply and demand across the whole market set it. Ask more and buyers get the same corn from somebody else. Economists call her a price taker. The market names the price; she just takes it.

cards.headline: Profits attract rivals
cards.body: So what stops a whole industry charging a fortune? Newcomers. When sellers in a competitive market earn fat profits, new firms pile in. Their extra supply brings the price down, until the extra profit is squeezed away and nobody else wants to join. High profits are an open invitation.

cards.fact: Competition keeps prices down and quality up.
cards.context: That's how the US Federal Trade Commission puts it. When businesses must compete for your money, they have strong incentives to run efficiently, keep prices down and keep quality up. For shoppers, that adds up to lower prices, better products and services, more choice and more new ideas.

cards.headline: Competition: understood
learned: Competitive firms are price takers
Profits attract new rivals
Entry pushes prices down
Competition keeps prices down and quality up

questions.prompt: In perfect competition, what is a price taker?

options.label: A firm that must accept the market price
A buyer who always pays the asking price
options.rationale: The term describes sellers in a competitive market.

options.label: A government that sets prices
options.rationale: In perfect competition, nobody sets the price.

options.label: A firm that sets whatever price it likes
options.rationale: That's closer to a monopoly.

questions.explanation: With many sellers of identical products, one firm has to accept the price the whole market sets.

questions.prompt: Sellers in a competitive market are earning big profits. What does competition predict?

options.label: Prices rise even higher
options.rationale: Entry adds supply, which pulls prices down.

options.label: The government fixes the price
options.rationale: No law is needed; newcomers do the work.

options.label: New firms enter and the price falls
The existing sellers merge into one
options.rationale: Profits attract rivals; they don't create mergers.

questions.explanation: Profits attract new firms. Their extra supply brings the price down until the extra profit is gone.

questions.prompt: Why does a corn farmer who asks more than Level 44's equilibrium price find no buyers?

options.label: Corn has no equilibrium price
options.rationale: Every competitive market has one.

options.label: Buyers can get the same corn from many other sellers
The law forbids selling above equilibrium
options.rationale: No law is needed; competition does it.

options.label: Buyers only want corn when prices are rising
options.rationale: Buyers want less at higher prices, not more.

questions.explanation: With many sellers of identical corn at the market price, nobody pays extra to one farmer.

levels.title: Monopolies
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a monopoly is and why governments limit them.
levels.summary: A monopoly is one seller of something with no substitute, shielded by barriers to entry. It sells less at a higher price, so laws limit it: Standard Oil was broken up in 1911.

cards.headline: The board game Monopoly began as an economics lesson.
cards.body: It grew out of The Landlord's Game, which Lizzie Magie patented in 1904 to teach economic ideas about land and rent. Real monopolies are a lot less fun to play against.

cards.headline: One seller, no substitute
cards.body: A monopoly is a market with a single supplier of something that has no substitute. It can set its price without fear of competitors. What keeps rivals out? Barriers to entry: legal, technological or market forces that stop newcomers. Behind those walls, big profits no longer pull in Level 46's rivals, so nothing drags the price down.

mascot.line: No rivals, no pressure, no new ideas. A very comfortable nap.

cards.headline: Less stuff, higher prices
cards.body: Compared with a competitive market, a monopoly sells a smaller quantity at a higher price, so buyers lose out. It can get lazy, too: with no rival to fear, it can keep making the same old products in the same old way. In 1935, economist John Hicks summed it up: "The best of all monopoly profits is a quiet life."

cards.fact: Standard Oil once refined 90 to 95 percent of America's oil. Then came the breakup.
cards.context: That was its share by 1880. In 1890, the Sherman Act outlawed monopolizing a market, and in 1911 the US Supreme Court ordered Standard Oil broken up into separate companies. Governments limit monopolies to protect what Level 46 showed: competition is what keeps prices down and quality up.

cards.headline: Monopolies: understood
learned: A monopoly is one seller with no substitute
Barriers to entry keep rivals out
It sells less at a higher price
Antitrust laws broke up Standard Oil

questions.prompt: What is a monopoly?

options.label: Many firms selling identical products
options.rationale: That's perfect competition.

options.label: A price set by law below equilibrium
options.rationale: That's a price ceiling.

options.label: A board game about banks
options.rationale: The game is named after the idea, not the other way round.

options.label: A single seller of something with no substitute

questions.explanation: A monopoly is the exclusive possession of a market by a supplier of a product or service that has no substitute.

questions.prompt: Compared with a competitive market, what does a monopoly usually do?

options.label: Sells more at a lower price
options.rationale: That is what competition tends to do.

options.label: Sells less at a higher price
Sells the same amount at the same price
options.rationale: Without rivals, it can charge more and sell less.

options.label: Gives its product away to win customers
options.rationale: With no rivals, it has no need to.

questions.explanation: Without rivals, a monopoly sells a lower quantity at a higher price, and consumers lose out.

questions.prompt: Why do governments use laws like the Sherman Act to limit monopolies?

options.label: To set every price themselves
options.rationale: Antitrust laws protect competition; they do not set prices.

options.label: To help the biggest firm grow faster
options.rationale: They do the opposite: they stop one firm dominating.

options.label: To protect the competition that keeps prices down and quality up
To collect more tax from large companies
options.rationale: That is a job for tax law, not antitrust law.

questions.explanation: Competition pushes businesses to run efficiently, keep prices down and keep quality up. Antitrust laws protect it.

levels.title: Incentives
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how incentives shape the choices people make.
levels.summary: Incentives are rewards and penalties that shape choices, and people respond to them. Hanoi's 1902 rat-tail bounty backfired: people bred rats for their tails. Prices are incentives too.

cards.headline: In 1902, Hanoi paid people for dead rats. Soon, people were farming rats.
cards.body: It's one of history's great backfires. And it shows just how seriously people take a reward.

cards.headline: Carrots and sticks
cards.body: An incentive rewards or penalizes a choice. Positive incentives are rewards, like a buy-one-get-one-free sale. Negative incentives are penalties, like a speeding ticket or a littering fine. Some come from governments, some from businesses. People respond to them, and usually in predictable ways. That's the whole point of having them.

mascot.line: Pay for tails, get tails. The rats kept everything else.

cards.headline: The rat-tail bounty
cards.body: In colonial Hanoi, the French authorities wanted fewer rats. They paid a few cents for each rat tail handed in to the police. A tail seemed like proof of a dead rat. It wasn't. People cut the tails off rats and let them go free to breed more. Officials even found people farming rats, and a network smuggling them into the city.

cards.fact: Every price is an incentive.
cards.context: Economic incentives involve a financial benefit or cost. That's Level 42 in one line: a higher price rewards producing more, so sellers bring more to market. Hanoi's bounty was simply a price for rat tails, and people supplied rat tails. The lesson: reward exactly what you want, because that's what you'll get.

cards.headline: Incentives: understood
learned: Incentives are rewards and penalties
People respond to them predictably
Hanoi's rat-tail bounty backfired
Every price is an incentive

questions.prompt: Which of these is a negative incentive?

options.label: A buy-one-get-one-free sale

options.label: A littering fine

options.rationale: A bonus is a reward, a positive incentive.

options.label: A discount for paying early
options.rationale: A discount rewards a choice, so it is positive.

questions.explanation: Negative incentives are penalties that discourage a behavior, like fines and speeding tickets.

questions.prompt: Why did Hanoi's rat-tail bounty backfire?

options.label: The bounty was too small for anyone to bother
options.rationale: People bothered a lot: they farmed rats.

options.label: The rats fled the city to escape the hunt

options.rationale: The payments were made, which is why it backfired.

questions.explanation: The reward was for tails, not for fewer rats. People responded exactly to what was rewarded.

options.label: A higher price is a penalty for selling
options.rationale: It is a reward, not a penalty.

options.label: Prices have nothing to do with incentives
options.rationale: A price is an economic incentive.

options.label: A higher price is a reward for producing more

questions.explanation: A price is an economic incentive. A higher one means more profit, which encourages firms to produce more.

levels.title: Scarcity
levels.objective: After this level you can explain scarcity as the basic problem that economics studies.
levels.summary: Scarcity means wants exceed what's available, for everyone. Economics studies how people choose under scarcity. It explains why water, vital but plentiful, costs less than diamonds.

cards.headline: Water keeps you alive. Diamonds don't. Guess which costs more.
cards.body: Adam Smith puzzled over exactly this in 1776. The answer is the problem at the heart of all economics.

cards.headline: Wants beat what there is
cards.body: Scarcity means people's wants for goods, services and resources exceed what's available. It doesn't mean rare. It means not enough to go round, and it hits everyone. The ultimate scarce resource is time: rich or poor, you get the same 24 hours a day. No billionaire can buy a 25th.

cards.headline: The study of choosing
cards.body: Because there's never enough of everything, people have to choose. That's what economics studies: how people make decisions in the face of scarcity. In 1932, Lionel Robbins put it this way: economics studies human behavior as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses. Translation: limited stuff, many possible uses, pick.

mascot.line: Stranded in a desert, you would swap every diamond you own for one glass of water.

cards.fact: Water is vital and cheap. Diamonds are useless and dear. Scarcity explains it.
cards.context: In The Wealth of Nations, Smith noted that nothing is more useful than water, yet it buys scarcely anything, while a diamond, of scarcely any use, trades for a great quantity of other goods. The standard answer: water is plentiful, so one more glass is worth little to you. Diamonds are scarce, so each one is worth a lot. Price follows scarcity, not usefulness.

cards.headline: Scarcity: understood
learned: Scarcity: wants exceed what's available
Time is the ultimate scarce resource
Economics studies choices under scarcity
Scarcity explains cheap water, dear diamonds

questions.explanation: Scarcity means human wants for goods, services and resources exceed what's available.

questions.prompt: Water is far more useful than diamonds. Why is it usually much cheaper?

options.label: Diamonds cost more to transport

questions.explanation: Price follows scarcity. Water is plentiful, so an extra unit is worth little; diamonds are scarce, so each is worth a lot.

levels.title: Milestone: How Markets Work
levels.objective: After this level you can connect money, banks, investing and markets into one picture of how an economy runs.
levels.summary: Prices are messages that tell people what's scarce, with nobody giving orders. Money makes them readable, and supply and demand run markets for goods, work and savings alike.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Time to see the whole machine.
cards.body: Money, markets, supply, demand, competition, incentives, scarcity. They aren't separate topics. They're one machine, and the price tag is where every part of it meets.

cards.headline: Prices are messages
cards.body: In 1945, economist Friedrich Hayek asked you to imagine tin becoming scarcer, from a new use or a lost source. Tin users don't need to know which. The price rises, and they economize. Hayek called the price system a mechanism for communicating information: it gets tens of thousands of strangers to use a material more sparingly, with nobody giving orders.

cards.headline: Money makes the message readable
cards.body: Those messages need Level 1's money. As a unit of account, it puts every price on one ruler, so tin, bread and a haircut can be compared at a glance. Radford's camp showed it in miniature: once prices were quoted in cigarettes, like cheese for seven, anyone could compare anything with anything.

mascot.line: Loans, jobs, cookies, tin: different goods, same scissors.

cards.headline: One machine, many markets
cards.body: The same machine runs markets you've met elsewhere in this tree. In labor markets, job seekers supply work and employers demand it. In financial markets, savers supply money and borrowers demand it, and they meet at a rate of return, like an interest rate. Banks, shares and paychecks have their own chapters, but underneath it's supply and demand, meeting at a price.

cards.headline: Milestone: markets mapped

levels.title: Taxes
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what taxes pay for and name the main kinds of tax.
levels.summary: Taxes pay for what governments provide, about a third of GDP across rich countries. They fall on what you earn, buy and own; most countries use a VAT, the US does not.

cards.headline: In 1789, Benjamin Franklin named the only two sure things in life.
cards.body: One was death. The other was taxes. More than two centuries later, both are still going strong. So what do they actually pay for, and what exactly gets taxed?

cards.headline: What your taxes buy
cards.body: Taxes are how a government pays for the things it provides. In the US, the biggest federal items are national defense, Social Security, healthcare and interest on past borrowing. States and cities spend most on education, then on highways, libraries, parks, police and fire protection. So the fire truck racing down your street? You've already chipped in.

cards.fact: Across rich countries, taxes add up to about a third of the whole economy.
cards.context: In 2023, taxes averaged 33.9% of GDP (the value of everything a country produces in a year) across OECD countries. The range is wide: under a fifth in Mexico, over two-fifths in France and Denmark. How big that slice should be is a choice each country makes, and they choose very differently.

cards.headline: Three things to tax: what you earn, buy and own

items.label: What you earn

Payroll taxes on wages
Corporate income tax on profits

items.label: What you buy
points: Sales taxes and value-added taxes
Excise taxes on gasoline, tobacco and alcohol

items.label: What you own
points: Property taxes, a mainstay for US states and cities
Estate taxes on what people leave behind

mascot.line: A VAT is a relay race: every runner carries the tax a little further, and the shopper crosses the finish line.

cards.fact: The US is the only OECD country without a VAT.
cards.context: A value-added tax is a sales tax collected in slices. Each business along the chain, from lumber yard to furniture maker, pays tax on its sales and gets credit for the tax already paid on its inputs. More than 170 countries use one. The US relies instead on state and local sales taxes, added at the till.

levels.title: Who Pays What
levels.objective: After this level you can compare tax systems where the rate rises with income to systems with one rate.
levels.summary: Progressive taxes take a bigger share of bigger incomes, flat taxes the same share, regressive taxes a smaller share. Brackets tax only the extra dollars, so a raise never cuts your pay.

cards.headline: Could a raise push you into a higher tax bracket and leave you poorer?
cards.body: No. Only the extra dollars pay the higher rate, so your take-home pay still rises. Why that's true opens up the bigger question of this level: how should a tax bill be shared out?

cards.headline: Three ways to share the bill
cards.body: Picture three people earning very different incomes. A progressive tax takes a bigger share from the higher incomes; the US federal income tax works this way. A proportional, or flat, tax takes the same share from everyone, like the US Medicare payroll tax. A regressive tax takes a smaller share as income rises. In 1994, Estonia became the first country in Eastern Europe to swap its income tax for a flat one.

cards.headline: Brackets are buckets
cards.body: Progressive income taxes usually work in brackets. Picture your income pouring into a row of buckets. The first bucket is taxed at the lowest rate; only the money that spills into the next bucket pays the next rate, and so on. So when a raise tips you into a higher bracket, only the extra dollars are taxed at the higher rate. Your take-home pay goes up. Always.
cards.callout: A higher bracket taxes the extra dollars, not all of them.

cards.headline: The same rate, a different bite
cards.body: Remember Level 51's taxes on what you buy? A sales tax charges everyone the same rate at the till. But lower-income households spend a bigger share of their income on goods, while higher-income households spend a smaller share of theirs. So measured against income, a sales tax takes a bigger bite from lower incomes. That makes it regressive, even though the rate never changes.

cards.headline: One rate or rising rates? Both sides of the argument

Clears out deductions special interests exploit

items.label: Against a flat income tax
points: Less fair: shifts the burden toward lower and middle incomes

levels.title: Public Goods
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why things like roads and lighthouses are usually paid for by governments.
levels.summary: Public goods are nonexcludable and nonrival, so people can free ride and markets underprovide them. Taxes fix that. Coase found England's lighthouses were paid for by port dues.

cards.headline: Economists' go-to example for a century: the lighthouse. Then someone checked.
cards.body: From John Stuart Mill to Paul Samuelson, the lighthouse stood for something markets supposedly couldn't provide: how would you make a passing ship pay for the light? To see the problem, start with a fireworks show.

cards.headline: The fireworks problem
cards.body: Someone has to pay for the town's fireworks show. But once the rockets go up, anyone can watch from their own backyard. So each person has a reason to let others pay and enjoy the show for free. Economists call that free riding. If enough people do it, the money never comes in, and a show everyone would have enjoyed simply never happens.

mascot.line: Nonexcludable, nonrival: two clunky words for 'everyone gets it, and it never runs out'.

cards.headline: Public goods
cards.body: Fireworks are a public good, with two features. They're nonexcludable: it's costly or impossible to stop non-payers from enjoying them. And they're nonrival: your watching doesn't use up anyone else's view. National defense is the classic case, protecting everyone in a country at once. The usual fix is the one from Level 51: people agree through politics to pay taxes for it, and the free riders have nowhere to hide.

cards.fact: England's early lighthouses were often privately run, paid for by fees collected at ports.
cards.context: In 1974, economist Ronald Coase dug into the history. Ships that passed a light still had to dock somewhere, and there they paid light dues. Free riding solved? Critics point out that the right to collect those dues came from a royal patent, so government was still doing the enforcing. The lighthouse turned out to be a debate, not a textbook certainty.

learned: Public goods are nonexcludable and nonrival

levels.title: Government Budgets and Debt
levels.objective: After this level you can explain deficits, surpluses and national debt.
levels.summary: A deficit is one year's gap between spending and taxes; the national debt is the running total of borrowing plus interest. Economists weigh its risks and uses differently.

cards.headline: In 2015, Britain paid off debts from the 1700s.
cards.body: Some of the old bonds it repaid traced back to the South Sea Bubble crash of 1720 and to borrowing used for the Napoleonic Wars. How does a country end up owing money for nearly three centuries? Start with a single year's budget.

cards.headline: Deficit or surplus
cards.body: Every year, a government compares what it spends with what it collects in taxes. Spend more than it collects, and it runs a budget deficit. Collect more than it spends, and it runs a surplus. If the two match, the budget is balanced. Surpluses don't come around often: the US federal government last ran one in 2001.

cards.headline: The bathtub
cards.body: A deficit is one year's gap; the debt is the running total. To cover a deficit, a government borrows, largely by selling bonds. The national debt is all that borrowing added up, plus the interest owed. Think of a bathtub: the deficit is the tap running this year, the debt is the water level. Borrow $10,000 a year for four years and your yearly deficit is $10,000, but your debt is $40,000.
cards.callout: Deficit: this year's gap. Debt: the total so far.

cards.headline: How much debt is too much? Economists weigh both sides

items.label: The worry
points: Heavy borrowing soaks up savings
That can leave less for private investment ("crowding out")

items.label: The other view
points: Borrowing can pay for roads, water systems, education and research
Those can encourage long-term growth

levels.title: Central Banks
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a central bank does and why it is kept independent.
levels.summary: Central banks run monetary policy and watch over banks. Sweden's Riksbank (1668) is the oldest. They are kept independent from elections, though critics question unelected power.

cards.headline: The world's oldest central bank rose from the ruins of a failed one.
cards.body: Remember Level 5's Stockholms Banco, which issued Europe's first banknotes in 1661 and failed when the public lost confidence? Its founder, Johan Palmstruch, was sentenced to death, then reprieved. And in 1668, Sweden built a new bank from the wreckage. It still runs today as the Riksbank.

cards.headline: The bank at the center
cards.body: A central bank is the bank at the heart of a country's money. The US got one, the Federal Reserve, in 1913. Its jobs include steering interest rates and money (monetary policy), supervising banks, keeping the financial system stable and payments safe. Since 1977, Congress has told it to aim for maximum employment and stable prices. The goal is old: the Riksbank's law told it to keep the coinage at its 'right and fair value' from 1668.

cards.headline: Why keep it at arm's length?
cards.body: Imagine an election is coming. A government may be tempted to juice the economy with cheap money, even if prices rise later. So many countries put money decisions at arm's length. Federal Reserve governors serve staggered 14-year terms, and elected officials can't sit on its Board. A study of 155 central banks over 50 years found that greater independence helped keep inflation in check.

mascot.line: Independence cuts both ways: shielded from politics, but still answering to the public.

cards.headline: Independent, but answerable
cards.body: Not everyone is comfortable. Critics question whether unelected officials should hold so much power over everyone's money. Paul Tucker, a former Bank of England deputy governor, explored exactly that in his 2018 book, Unelected Power. The usual answer is accountability: the Fed's chair testifies to Congress, and it reports on its policy twice a year. Where to draw the line is still argued over.

levels.title: Interest Rates and the Economy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how central banks raise or lower interest rates to cool or boost the economy.
levels.summary: A central bank's key rate feeds into loan and savings rates. Raising it cools spending and price rises; cutting it boosts borrowing and hiring. Effects lag. Volcker's near-20% rates show the cost.

cards.headline: In 1981, America's key interest rate was near 20%. On purpose.
cards.body: Under chair Paul Volcker, the Federal Reserve let the federal funds rate approach 20% to fight high inflation. Why would a central bank make borrowing that painful? Follow what one interest rate does to a whole economy.

cards.headline: One rate, many ripples
cards.body: A central bank sets one core short-term interest rate: the Bank of England calls its version Bank Rate. It sounds like a number only bankers care about, but it ripples outward. Change it, and the rates banks charge on loans and mortgages, and pay on savings, tend to follow. Your mortgage, your car loan and your savings account all feel it.

cards.headline: The brake and the accelerator
cards.body: Raising the rate is the brake. Loan and mortgage payments go up and saving pays more, so people spend less, and businesses find it harder to raise prices. Cutting the rate is the accelerator. Borrowing gets cheaper, so households and businesses spend more, and businesses hire more workers to keep up.

mascot.line: We have all been that person frantically twisting the shower tap. Central bankers just do it with the whole economy.

cards.headline: A shower with a long pipe
cards.body: The catch is timing. In 1959, economist Milton Friedman told Congress that monetary policy works with a long and variable lag; in his study, the delay ran from 4 to 29 months. It's like a shower with a very long pipe: turn the tap, wait, and it's easy to overshoot into scalding or freezing before you feel the change.

cards.fact: Volcker's brake slowed prices, and it hurt.
cards.context: High rates hit industries that run on borrowing, like construction and autos. US unemployment reached nearly 11% late in 1982. But by October 1982, inflation had fallen to 5%. The brake worked on one goal while hurting another.

cards.headline: Rates: explained

levels.title: Printing Money
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why creating money too fast makes prices rise.
levels.summary: When money grows faster than the goods it buys, prices rise, as in Radford's camp and 16th-century Europe. The link holds over time but is not mechanical.

cards.headline: In Level 1's prison camp, a flood of cigarettes sent prices soaring.
cards.body: Economist R. A. Radford saw it happen. Big deliveries could bring several hundred thousand cigarettes within a fortnight. Prices soared, then fell as stocks ran out. The camp's money had suddenly multiplied. What does that do to prices?

cards.headline: More money, same stuff
cards.body: Why would more money push prices up? Picture a market with the same bread and jam as yesterday, but everyone holding twice the cash. The quantity theory of money says that when money grows faster than the goods and services it can buy, the extra money bids up prices rather than conjuring more stuff. Milton Friedman's answer was a rule: if output grows 2% a year, let money grow 2% too, and prices stay put.

cards.fact: In the 1500s, a flood of American silver helped push up European prices.
cards.context: From 1550, silver from mines like Potosí arrived in Spain in huge volumes and spread across Europe. Over the century, prices rose about sixfold, in what historians call the price revolution. They also point to a growing population needing food and housing, and still debate how much each cause mattered.

mascot.line: Money growth and prices: a strong link over time, but a wobbly one month to month.

cards.headline: Not a simple dial
cards.body: The link isn't a machine. In the 1980s and 1990s, how fast money changed hands became unstable, and many economists dropped strict money-growth rules. Most still agree prices can't keep rising indefinitely without more money. And today's 'printing' rarely needs a press: remember Level 8, where 97% of the money UK people hold is bank deposits.

levels.title: Rules for Business
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why governments set rules for banks and businesses.
levels.summary: Rules help where sellers know more than buyers, as The Jungle showed in 1906, and make banks hold capital to absorb losses. Every rule also has costs, which is why the right amount is argued over.

cards.headline: A 1906 novel turned readers' stomachs and changed the law that same year.
cards.body: Upton Sinclair's The Jungle showed filthy conditions in Chicago's meatpacking plants. On June 30, 1906, President Theodore Roosevelt signed both the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act. Why did buyers need a law to protect them?

cards.headline: You can't see inside a sausage
cards.body: The seller knows how it was made; you don't. Economists call this asymmetric information: one side of a deal knows more about quality than the other. Rules help close the gap. The 1906 food law banned adulterated and mislabeled food and drugs from being shipped between states. US advertising rules let sellers exaggerate, but a claim presented as a fact must be true.

mascot.line: Capital is the airbag: you hope never to need it, and you really want it there when you do.

cards.headline: A cushion for banks
cards.body: Banks get rules too. Regulators make them hold capital: the owners' own money, which works like a cushion. If some loans go bad, the losses hit that cushion first, so the bank can still repay its depositors. The aim is to make bank failures, and government bailouts, less likely.

items.label: What rules can buy
points: Safer food and honest labels
Claims you can trust
Sturdier banks

items.label: What rules can cost
points: Licenses reassure customers but can make it harder to enter a trade
Higher capital requirements may slow lending and growth

levels.title: Safety Nets
levels.objective: After this level you can explain unemployment insurance, pensions and other safety nets.
levels.summary: Germany created old-age social insurance in 1889. Unemployment insurance replaces part of lost wages. US Social Security is pay-as-you-go, strained as workers per beneficiary fall.

cards.headline: The world's first state pension started at age 70.
cards.body: In 1889, Germany, under Chancellor Otto von Bismarck, became the first nation to adopt old-age social insurance. It gave workers basic security from age 70, and workers, employers and the government all paid in. It was a net stretched under ordinary life.

cards.headline: Insurance for losing your job
cards.body: A safety net catches you when income suddenly stops. Unemployment insurance gives temporary, partial wage replacement to workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own. Temporary, because it runs out; partial, because it covers only part of your old pay. In between, it helps people keep paying the rent and the bills while they look for work.

cards.headline: Today's workers, today's retirees
cards.body: US Social Security is one of Level 51's biggest federal items, and it works pay-as-you-go. The taxes today's workers pay fund today's beneficiaries; nobody's contributions sit in a personal pot. That makes one ratio matter a lot. In 1965, about four workers paid in for each beneficiary. By 2023, there were 2.7.
cards.callout: 1965: about 4 workers per beneficiary. 2023: 2.7.

cards.headline: How should a net be designed? The trade-offs

levels.title: Checkpoint: Governments and Money
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how taxes, spending and central banks shape an economy.
levels.summary: Fiscal policy is spending and taxing by elected governments; monetary policy is the central bank steering rates and money. Chapter 6 in two levers.

cards.headline: Two sets of hands steer an economy, and they sit in different buildings.
cards.body: In the US, one set belongs to Congress and the President, the other to the Federal Reserve. Chapter 6 has shown you both at work. Time to give them their names.

cards.headline: Fiscal policy: spending and taxing
cards.body: Fiscal policy means a government's spending and taxing decisions; in the US, Congress and the administration make them. It covers most of this chapter: Level 51's taxes, Level 52's question of who pays, Level 53's public goods, Level 54's deficits and debt, and Level 59's safety nets.

mascot.line: Fiscal: who taxes and spends. Monetary: who steers rates. Different hands, one economy.

cards.headline: Monetary policy: rates and money
cards.body: Monetary policy is what a central bank does, mainly with interest rates, to pursue goals like stable prices and maximum employment. That was Levels 55–57. The two jobs are kept apart. The Federal Reserve plays no role in setting taxes or government spending.

levels.title: What Inflation Is
levels.objective: After this level you can explain inflation as a general rise in prices over time.
levels.summary: Inflation is a broad rise in prices that shrinks what money buys. Its causes include demand-pull, cost-push and expectations; economists disagree on how much money supply matters.

cards.headline: In Level 1's prison camp, a flood of cigarettes sent prices soaring.
cards.body: Radford watched it happen: several hundred thousand cigarettes might arrive in a fortnight. Prices soared, then fell back as stocks ran out. The camp had just lived through a small, smoky bout of inflation.

cards.headline: Prices, plural
cards.body: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise over a period of time. The key word is broad: it tracks the overall rise in prices across a country, not one item. If only coffee gets pricier after a bad harvest, that's coffee news. When the whole shopping list creeps up together, month after month, that's inflation.

mascot.line: Same note, smaller shopping bag. Sneaky, isn't it?

cards.fact: Inflation shrinks your money without changing the number on it.
cards.context: Economists call it lost purchasing power: as prices rise, each unit of money buys less. That's a blow to Level 1's third job, store of value. A banknote in a drawer shows the same amount next year; it just buys less. And if your pay rises more slowly than prices, you can afford less, even after a raise.

cards.headline: Why prices rise, and why economists argue
cards.body: Textbooks name three culprits. Demand-pull: spending outgrows what the economy can produce, "too much money chasing too few goods." Cost-push: a shock like pricier oil raises the cost of making things. Expectations: if everyone expects higher prices, wages and contracts build them in. How much each matters is argued over. Milton Friedman said inflation is "always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon"; Keynesians put more weight on spending and demand.

cards.headline: Inflation: defined

levels.title: Measuring Inflation
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a basket of everyday goods measures the cost of living.
levels.summary: The consumer price index tracks the cost of a spending-weighted basket of what households buy. The basket is updated as habits change, and a fixed basket tends to overstate how fast living costs rise.

cards.headline: In 2024, air fryers were officially promoted into Britain's inflation basket.
cards.body: Vinyl records got back in too. Hand sanitiser got dropped. To measure inflation, statisticians track a whole basket of what people buy, and they keep repacking it.

cards.headline: A country-sized shopping cart
cards.body: The consumer price index, or CPI, tracks the cost of a representative basket of goods and services that households buy. Its rise is how inflation gets measured. In the US, data collectors record the prices of about 80,000 items every month. Each item counts in proportion to what households actually spend on it, so housing, the biggest slice, far outweighs clothing.

mascot.line: A basket that tracks your habits better than your own shopping list.

cards.headline: The basket gets repacked
cards.body: A basket frozen in time would slowly stop looking like real life. So the UK updates its basket, 744 items in 2024, every year. That year, air fryers went in, prized for their energy savings, and vinyl records returned after more than thirty years away. Hand sanitiser came out as the pandemic faded. The basket is a portrait of how people live, redrawn every year.

cards.headline: Why a fixed basket runs hot
cards.body: Say beef gets pricey, so you switch to chicken. A fixed basket assumes you kept buying beef, so it overstates how much your living costs rose. That's substitution bias. A fixed basket also misses quality: a new phone that does more for the same price looks like no change at all. Both quirks make a fixed basket overstate the rising cost of living, which is why US statisticians now use methods that allow for some switching.

levels.title: Hyperinflation
levels.objective: After this level you can describe hyperinflation in Weimar Germany and Zimbabwe and explain what caused it.
levels.summary: Hyperinflation is inflation above 50% a month. Weimar Germany in 1923 and Zimbabwe in 2008 both printed money to pay the government's bills until their currencies collapsed.

cards.headline: In 1914, a dollar cost just over four German marks. By late 1923: trillions.
cards.body: About 4.2 trillion, to be exact. That isn't prices creeping up. That's money dissolving, and economists have a name for it.

cards.headline: When inflation runs wild
cards.body: In 1956, economist Phillip Cagan drew the line: hyperinflation means prices rising more than 50% in a single month. It usually starts the same way. A government creates new money to pay for its spending, faster than the economy can produce. Then trust breaks. People rush to spend money before it loses more value, or swap it for foreign currency, and prices race even faster.

cards.headline: Germany, 1923
cards.body: After World War I, Germany's government printed more and more money to pay its bills, including war reparations. In early 1923, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr region, coal output there stopped, and prices climbed further. Savings were wiped out. Historians still debate the blame: how much lies with reparations, and how much with Germany's own choices, such as printing money rather than raising taxes.

mascot.line: A price tag that needs rewriting before lunch. Imagine doing the shopping.

cards.fact: In 2008, Zimbabwe's prices were doubling roughly every day.
cards.context: After land reforms crippled farm output, Zimbabwe's government printed money aggressively. By mid-November 2008, monthly inflation hit about 79.6 billion percent. In January 2009, a 100 trillion dollar note went into circulation. That same year, the country gave up its own currency, and people paid in foreign money, mainly US dollars.

levels.title: Deflation
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why falling prices can hurt an economy.
levels.summary: Deflation is a general fall in prices. It usually comes from collapsing spending, and it hurts by making people delay purchases and making debts heavier.

cards.headline: Prices that keep falling sound like a never-ending sale. Economists dread them.
cards.body: Level 1's camp got a taste. When cigarette deliveries stopped, stocks ran out and prices fell. Trade slid back toward barter. Some sale.

cards.headline: Deflation, defined
cards.body: Deflation is a general decline in prices, and as Fed governor Ben Bernanke stressed in 2002, the key word is general. TVs getting cheaper because factories got more efficient is generally no problem for the economy as a whole. Real deflation is almost always a side effect of a collapse in spending so severe that producers must keep cutting prices to find buyers.

cards.headline: Why buy today?
cards.body: If prices will be lower next month, why buy now? When prices are falling, people delay purchases if they can. Multiply that across a whole country and you get less economic activity, less income for the businesses selling things, and slower growth. A sale that makes everyone wait turns into a stall.

mascot.line: The number on your loan never changes. What it's worth quietly does.

cards.fact: Under deflation, debts get heavier while you sleep.
cards.context: A loan is a fixed amount of money. When prices fall, each dollar is worth more, so borrowers repay dollars of ever-increasing real value. Japan showed how stubborn this can be: by 2002, a mild fall in consumer prices, about 1% a year, had come with years of painfully slow growth.

cards.headline: Deflation: defined
learned: Deflation is a general fall in prices

levels.title: GDP
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what GDP measures and what it misses.
levels.summary: GDP adds up the market value of the final goods and services a country produces. Real GDP strips out price changes, and GDP misses unpaid work, pollution, leisure and how income is shared.

cards.headline: Cook dinner at home and GDP ignores it. Buy the same meal, and it counts.
cards.body: Same food, same full stomach. The economy's headline number sees only one of them. What it counts, and what it skips, is this level's story.

cards.headline: Everything a country makes, in one number
cards.body: Gross domestic product, or GDP, is the market value of the final goods and services a country produces in a period, such as a quarter or a year. "Final" matters: flour sold to a baker is an input, and only the bread counts. You can add GDP up three ways: the value added at each stage of production, the spending of final buyers, or the incomes everyone earns making it all.

cards.headline: Real GDP: more stuff, not just pricier stuff
cards.body: Remember Level 61? If a country made exactly the same things this year but prices rose, its GDP in money terms would still grow. That's why economists watch real GDP, which adjusts for price changes. Real growth means the economy actually made more, not that the price tags got bigger.

mascot.line: A great ruler for output. A wobbly one for happiness.

cards.fact: The first US national accounts came with a warning label.
cards.context: In 1934, economist Simon Kuznets presented them to Congress, and warned that the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from national income. GDP leaves out unpaid work like housework and volunteering, and ignores pollution, lost leisure and how income is shared. It measures how much a country produces, not how well its people live.

levels.title: The Business Cycle
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why economies go through booms and recessions.
levels.summary: Economies swing irregularly between expansions and recessions, which the NBER dates after the fact. Economists debate whether spending swings or productivity shocks drive the cycle.

cards.headline: The US spent a whole year in recession before it was made official.
cards.body: On December 1, 2008, the referees announced that a recession had begun back in December 2007. Economies rise and fall, but the turns are only clear in the rear-view mirror.

cards.headline: A rollercoaster without a timetable
cards.body: Economies go through expansions, or booms, when activity grows, and recessions, when it declines. The peak is the last month of an expansion; the trough is the last month of a recession. It's called a cycle, but it keeps no schedule: expansions and recessions arrive at irregular intervals and last for different lengths of time.

cards.headline: Who calls a recession?
cards.body: In the US, the referees are the National Bureau of Economic Research, or NBER. Its definition: a significant decline in economic activity, spread across the economy, lasting more than a few months. The popular rule of two straight quarters of falling real GDP isn't the NBER's test, though most recessions fit it. Recessions vary a lot: the 2020 one lasted about two months.

mascot.line: Same rollercoaster, different theories about the engine. Both sides have evidence to argue over.

cards.headline: Why the ride? Economists split
cards.body: Economists still disagree about what drives the cycle. Many see swings in spending as the main engine: a surge in private or public spending fuels a boom, and a pullback brings a recession. Central banks can push too, by raising or lowering interest rates. Economists in the new classical tradition argue instead that cycles come largely from shocks to productivity and tastes, not changes in demand.

levels.title: Unemployment
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how unemployment is measured and name its main causes.
levels.summary: The US measures unemployment with a monthly household survey: you must lack a job, have looked for work and be able to start. Unemployment can be frictional, structural or cyclical.

cards.headline: You can have no job and still not count as unemployed.
cards.body: Retirees don't count. Neither do full-time students. In official statistics, "unemployed" means something precise, and the fine print changes the story.

cards.headline: Asking 60,000 households
cards.body: The US doesn't count the jobless one by one. Each month, the Current Population Survey asks about 60,000 households who is working. You count as unemployed if you have no job, have actively looked for work in the prior 4 weeks, and are available to start. Why not just count benefit claims? Many jobless people aren't eligible or never apply.

mascot.line: Stop looking for work, and the statistics stop looking at you.

cards.headline: The rate, and who vanishes from it
cards.body: The labor force is everyone who is employed or unemployed, and the unemployment rate is the unemployed as a percentage of it. Retirees, students and discouraged workers, who want a job but have stopped looking, sit outside the labor force. So give up looking and you vanish from the unemployment rate, even though you're still out of work.

levels.title: Bubbles
levels.objective: After this level you can explain speculative bubbles, from Dutch tulips to dot-com stocks.
levels.summary: A bubble is a price far above what fundamentals justify, kept up by buyers hoping to sell higher. Tulip mania was smaller than its legend; the dot-com bubble burst in 2000.

cards.headline: In February 1637, the Dutch market for tulip bulbs cracked.
cards.body: It has long been called the first recorded speculative bubble. But what is a bubble, and was this really one? The legend and the archives disagree.

cards.headline: What makes a bubble
cards.body: A bubble is when an asset's price sits far above what its fundamentals justify, and stays there for a long time. Why would anyone overpay? Because they expect to sell to someone even more optimistic. The catch: bubbles are hard to spot while you're inside one, and many are only called bubbles in hindsight.

cards.headline: Tulips: a virus, a crash, a myth
cards.body: Dutch collectors prized "broken" tulips with striped petals. The stripes came from a virus, which made those bulbs rare and unpredictable. In February 1637 the market cracked, as many buyers said they couldn't pay the prices they had agreed. Charles Mackay's 1841 book told of everyone from merchants to chimney sweeps joining in. Historian Anne Goldgar searched the archives: few people were involved, and she couldn't find anybody who went bankrupt.

mascot.line: Spotting a bubble from the inside is hard. Economists still argue over how.

cards.headline: Dot-com: a bubble with a stock ticker
cards.body: In the late 1990s, money poured into internet start-ups, many with little to show in products or profits. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index peaked in March 2000, and by October 2002 it was down more than 78%. Were bubbles like this obvious? Economists still argue. In 2013, the Nobel went to both Robert Shiller, who argues prices can drift far from fundamentals, and Eugene Fama, pioneer of the view that markets are efficient.

levels.title: The Great Depression
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what caused the Great Depression and how it changed economic policy.
levels.summary: From 1929, US output fell by a third and prices fell. Economists still debate the cause (the crash, a shrinking money supply, the gold standard). It reshaped economic policy.

cards.headline: In 2002, a Fed official apologized for the Great Depression.
cards.body: At a conference honoring Milton Friedman, Ben Bernanke told Friedman and Anna Schwartz: "Regarding the Great Depression. You're right, we did it. We're very sorry." Not every economist agrees on who "did it".

cards.fact: Between 1929 and 1933, US output fell by about a third.
cards.context: Unemployment reached about 25% of the labor force, and thousands of banks failed, more than 1,000 a year from 1930 to 1933. Prices fell about 10% a year: Level 64's deflation at full strength. The slump lasted until about 1941, the longest and deepest downturn in US history.

cards.headline: Who did it? Economists still argue
cards.body: Economists still disagree about the cause. One story starts with the 1929 stock market crash, which destroyed wealth and scared consumers and firms into spending less. Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed a shrinking money supply: as banks failed and the Fed failed to step in, money fell by nearly 30%, and spending fell with it. Others stress Level 7's gold standard, which helped spread the slump from country to country.

cards.headline: The Depression rewrote the rulebook
cards.body: The Depression sparked fundamental changes in economic institutions, policy and theory. The US got federal deposit insurance, securities regulation, Social Security and its first national minimum wage. And the Fed took the lesson personally: Bernanke's apology ended, "But thanks to you, we won't do it again."

levels.title: Checkpoint: Booms and Busts
levels.objective: After this level you can connect inflation, bubbles and recessions, using the 2008 financial crisis as the example.
levels.summary: In 2008, a US housing bubble burst, Lehman Brothers failed and the Great Recession followed, with doubled unemployment and briefly falling prices. Economists still debate why the boom happened.

cards.headline: In 2008, a bubble, a bust and a recession arrived as a package deal.
cards.body: Chapter 7's ideas don't take turns. The 2008 financial crisis put nearly all of them into one story. Time to follow it.

events.label: US home prices more than double, the sharpest rise on record
Home prices start falling; recession begins in December
Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy
Consumer prices are lower than a year before
The recession ends after 18 months

cards.headline: Chapter 7, all in one story
cards.body: Level 68's bubble: risky mortgages, packaged into securities, widened credit and pushed home prices up; then prices fell by over a fifth, bringing defaults and foreclosures. Level 66's cycle: the longest US recession since World War II. Level 67's cyclical unemployment: the jobless rate more than doubled, from under 5% to 10%. Even Level 64's worry appeared, as consumer prices fell over a year for the first time since 1955.

cards.headline: Still argued over
cards.body: Why did the housing boom happen? Economist John Taylor argued that the Fed kept interest rates low for too long. Ben Bernanke answered that this explains only a small part, and pointed to a flood of global savings that pushed interest rates down worldwide. Like the Great Depression, the Great Recession left a clear story of what happened and an open argument about why.

levels.title: Why Countries Trade
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why trade can leave both sides better off.
levels.summary: Voluntary trade happens only when both sides expect to gain, and countries trade because their resources and climates differ. A country gains overall, but some of its workers and firms lose.

cards.headline: Scotland could make fine wine. It would just cost about 30 times as much.
cards.body: Adam Smith pointed it out: with glass, hotbeds and heated walls, very good grapes will grow in Scotland. So why import wine at all? Answer that, and you know why countries trade.

cards.headline: Both sides win, or it doesn't happen
cards.body: Nobody forces a voluntary trade. It happens only if it makes both parties better off: you hand over something you value less for something you value more. Economists call that positive-sum. The swap doesn't just move value around; it creates some. The logic is the same in a school cafeteria and in the global marketplace. Countries don't trade to beat each other. They trade because each side comes out ahead.

mascot.line: Copper for coffee: less romantic than wine, but the very same idea.

cards.headline: Copper for coffee
cards.body: Countries are dealt different hands. Chile has copper; Guatemala's climate suits coffee. So Chile provides copper, Guatemala grows coffee, and they trade. Money makes the swap easy: exports bring money into a country and imports send it out. That's Level 1's medium of exchange, working across borders. Chile doesn't need a Guatemalan who wants copper, just buyers who pay.

cards.fact: Trade makes a country better off overall, not every person in it.
cards.context: Shoppers get lower prices and more variety, and exporters reach bigger markets. But some firms fail against cheaper foreign rivals, and their workers lose jobs. The gains are spread thinly across millions of people and are hard to see; the costs land hard on particular companies and workers. That's why trade can be good for a country and still be fiercely argued about.

levels.title: Comparative Advantage
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why countries gain by specializing, even when one is better at everything.
levels.summary: Ricardo showed in 1817 that Portugal and England both gain by specializing, though Portugal was better at both goods. What counts is comparative advantage: the lowest cost in goods given up.

cards.headline: Portugal was better at making both wine and cloth. It should still buy cloth.
cards.body: That was David Ricardo's claim in 1817: specialization and free trade benefit all trading partners, even the less efficient ones. It sounds backwards. Let's check his numbers.

cards.headline: Ricardo's numbers: workers needed for a year

items.label: England
points: Cloth: 100 workers
Wine: 120 workers

items.label: Portugal
points: Cloth: 90 workers
Wine: 80 workers

cards.headline: Better at everything, cheaper at one
cards.body: Portugal has an absolute advantage in both goods: it can make more of each than England. But costs are relative. In Portugal, wine takes fewer workers than cloth (80 against 90), so wine is its bargain. In England, cloth takes fewer than wine (100 against 120), so cloth is England's. That's comparative advantage: making a good at a lower cost in terms of the other goods you give up.

mascot.line: Being worse at everything still leaves you something you're least worse at. Oddly comforting.

cards.fact: Specialize and swap, and both countries end up with more of both.
cards.context: If Portugal makes only wine and England only cloth, then they trade, each can consume more wine and more cloth than by making both itself. Real life is messier than two countries and two goods: resources are limited, and workers and jobs don't always switch industries neatly. But the core idea holds: you don't have to be the best at something to gain from trading it.

levels.title: Imports and Exports
levels.objective: After this level you can explain imports, exports and the balance of trade.
levels.summary: Exports are sold abroad and imports are bought from abroad; travel spending counts too. Exports minus imports gives the trade balance, and whether a deficit matters is debated.

cards.headline: Buy a souvenir on holiday abroad, and your country just imported something.
cards.body: No ship, no container, no customs form. Yet the statisticians count it. What foreign visitors spend in a country counts as its exports, and what its residents spend on trips abroad counts as imports.

mascot.line: Next time someone asks about your trip, tell them you were supporting Italian exports.

cards.headline: Out the door, in the door
cards.body: An export is a good or service a country sells to other countries; an import is one it buys from them. Exports bring money in, and imports send it out. Goods like cars and coffee count, but so do services: finance, software, consulting and design. So does your holiday. A tourist eating pasta in Rome is, technically, an Italian export.

cards.headline: Keeping score
cards.body: Take exports, subtract imports, and you get the trade balance. Export more than you import and you run a trade surplus. Import more and you run a trade deficit. The United States has run a deficit year after year since the mid-1970s. So is it losing?

cards.fact: Is a trade deficit a loss? People disagree.
cards.context: Some policymakers see a deficit as proof that a country is losing at trade. Most experts say a deficit, or a surplus, is in itself neither good nor bad. Remember Level 71: each trade happens because both sides expect to gain. Whether a country's overall deficit is a problem is a separate, and still debated, question.

levels.title: Tariffs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what tariffs are and who ends up paying them.
levels.summary: A tariff is a tax on imports, paid by the importing company, and its cost often reaches shoppers, as with 2018's US washer tariffs. Supporters and critics weigh jobs against costs.

cards.headline: In 2018, the US put a tariff on imported washers. Dryers got pricier too.
cards.body: Dryers had no tariff at all. To see why their prices moved, you need to know what a tariff is and who ends up paying it.

cards.headline: A tax at the border
cards.body: A tariff is a tax on goods as they cross a national border, usually charged by the importing country. The foreign country doesn't pay it. The importing company does, handing it to the customs authority. Then the cost moves: the importer can pass it on to shoppers as higher prices or absorb it, and foreign exporters may accept thinner profit margins to keep selling.

mascot.line: The dryer never saw a tax bill. It just stood next to the washer.

cards.fact: Washer prices rose about 12%. Dryers, with no tariff, rose about the same.
cards.context: Economists Aaron Flaaen, Ali Hortaçsu and Felix Tintelnot studied the 2018 tariffs. People often buy washers and dryers together, so sellers raised dryer prices too. The tariffs did create about 1,800 US jobs. The study put the cost to consumers at roughly $815,000 a year for each of those jobs.

levels.title: Exchange Rates
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how currencies are traded and why their values change.
levels.summary: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. Floating rates move with interest rates, inflation and expectations; a stronger currency makes imports cheaper and exports pricier.

cards.headline: Every day, $9.6 trillion of money is traded for other money.
cards.body: That was the daily average in April 2025, up from $7.5 trillion in 2022. It's the foreign exchange market, where people and firms use one currency to buy another. Every price in it is an exchange rate.

cards.headline: A price tag on money
cards.body: An exchange rate is how much one currency is worth in terms of another. Swap dollars for euros before a trip and you're a buyer in this market. So are firms paying foreign suppliers and investors buying assets abroad. If your currency buys more euros than last year, it has appreciated, or strengthened. If it buys fewer, it has depreciated, or weakened.

cards.headline: What pushes rates around
cards.body: Most big currencies float: their rates are mainly set by the market, through supply and demand. Relatively high interest rates pull in money from abroad, so the currency tends to rise. Relatively high inflation eats away at what a currency buys, so it tends to fall. And expectations feed themselves: if people expect a currency to rise, they buy it, and that can push it up.

mascot.line: Same dollar, same day: great news for your holiday, bad news for your country's exporters.

cards.headline: Strong isn't simply good
cards.body: A stronger dollar helps Americans buying imports or traveling abroad, but a weaker one helps US exporters and foreign tourists visiting the US. Every move has winners and losers. Some countries skip the ride and fix, or peg, their rate against another currency, as the world did under Level 7's Bretton Woods system, when other currencies were fixed to the dollar.

levels.title: From Caravans to Containers
levels.objective: After this level you can trace how trade routes grew from the Silk Road to container ships.
levels.summary: The Silk Road linked China and the West, with goods passed along by middlemen. In 1956, Malcolm McLean's containers made loading ships far cheaper than handling loose cargo.

cards.headline: Silk crossed Asia for centuries, yet almost nobody made the whole trip.
cards.body: On the Silk Road, few people traveled the entire route. Goods moved in stages, handed from middleman to middleman. This level follows how goods traveled, from camel caravans to steel boxes.

cards.headline: The Silk Road
cards.body: The Silk Road was a caravan route of about 6,400 km linking China with the West, carrying goods and ideas between China and Rome. Silk went west; wool, gold and silver went east. Religions traveled it too, and so did diseases. After years as an unsafe, little-used route, it revived under the Mongols. That's when Marco Polo went east, and came home describing Level 5's Chinese paper money.

mascot.line: All that way across the ocean, and the slowest part was the dock.

cards.headline: One sack at a time
cards.body: Ships carried goods much farther than camels, but loading them stayed slow. Sacks, barrels and crates were handled one by one. This loose, break-bulk cargo could take several days to load, so ships often sat in port for long periods. Picture packing for a house move one sock at a time.

cards.fact: April 26, 1956: 58 boxes set sail, and loading got cheap.
cards.context: Trucking entrepreneur Malcolm McLean sent his ship, the Ideal X, from Newark to Houston carrying 58 metal containers. Instead of loose cargo, whole boxes went aboard. Loading a ship the conventional way cost more than $5.80 a ton. Loading McLean's containers cost about 16 cents.

levels.title: Globalization
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how supply chains stretch across many countries.
levels.summary: About half of world trade runs through global supply chains, like the iPhone 3G's. Globalization lowered prices and helped poor countries grow, while job losses piled up in particular places.

cards.headline: In March 2021, one stuck ship held up about $9 billion of trade a day.
cards.body: The Ever Given ran aground in the Suez Canal on March 23 and wasn't refloated until March 29. How could one ship matter so much? Because much of what you buy is pieced together across many countries.

cards.headline: Made in many places
cards.body: About half of global trade now happens inside global supply chains: networks that build products from parts and services sourced around the world. Take the iPhone 3G. Its parts came from firms in Japan, South Korea, Germany and the US. Then it was all assembled in China.

mascot.line: "Made in China" turns out to mean "finished in China". Labels are short; supply chains are long.

cards.fact: Assembly in China added $6.50 to an iPhone that cost $178.96 to make.
cards.context: That's about 3.6% of the total, by economists Yuqing Xing and Neal Detert's 2010 count. Yet trade statistics recorded all $178.96 as a Chinese export. Remember Level 73's trade balance, exports minus imports? With supply chains, the country on the label isn't always where most of the value was made.

cards.headline: Two sides of the same story
cards.body: Supporters point to prices and growth: globalization lets countries specialize, which lowers prices, and more open economies helped once extremely poor countries grow and cut poverty. Critics point to who paid. Economists David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson found cheap Chinese imports had cost the US about 2.4 million jobs by 2011, concentrated in places that stayed worse off for years. Meanwhile, consumers nationwide got slightly cheaper goods. Both are true at once.
