levels.title: Rich and Poor Countries
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the main reasons some countries are richer than others.
levels.summary: The richest fifth of countries are about 30 times richer than the poorest. Nobel winners link this to institutions; Jeffrey Sachs adds geography and disease; all paths run through productivity.

cards.headline: One town, one fence, two very different lives.
cards.body: Nogales is cut in half by the US–Mexico border fence. People on the Arizona side are generally much better off than their neighbors in Nogales, Sonora. Same town, same weather. So what makes the difference?

cards.fact: The richest 20% of countries are about 30 times richer than the poorest 20%.
cards.context: And the gap is stubborn: the poorest countries have grown richer, but they aren't catching up. Economists offer several explanations, and Nogales is a clue to one of them.

cards.headline: The rules of the game
cards.body: Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson won the 2024 economics Nobel for studying how institutions, a society's rules, affect prosperity. Inclusive institutions, with secure property rights and the rule of law, support long-run growth. Extractive ones benefit a small elite at everyone else's expense. Both halves of Nogales share a climate, ancestors, food and music. So, they argue, the difference is institutions.

mascot.line: Big questions rarely come with one-word answers. This one keeps economists busy.

cards.headline: Other pieces of the puzzle
cards.body: Not everyone thinks rules explain it all. Economist Jeffrey Sachs argued in 2003 that institutions matter, but not for everything: disease such as malaria and geographic isolation also hold poor countries back. Whichever story you favor, it runs through productivity, the value each worker produces. Productivity rises with education and better technology, and it underpins a country's standard of living.

levels.title: Global Institutions
levels.objective: After this level you can describe what the IMF, the World Bank and the WTO do.
levels.summary: Bretton Woods (1944) created the IMF, which lends in crises with conditions, and the World Bank, which funds development. The WTO (1995) runs trade rules and disputes. Each has critics.

cards.headline: July 1944: the war wasn't over, yet 44 nations planned the postwar economy.
cards.body: Delegates met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. Level 7 showed you the currency system they built. They also created two institutions that still exist: the International Monetary Fund and what is now the World Bank.

cards.headline: The IMF: help, with strings
cards.body: The IMF was set up to watch over exchange rates and lend to countries short of foreign currency to pay their international bills. It still lends in a crisis, with conditions: the borrower agrees to change its economic policies to fix the problems that led it to ask. Critics argue that austere conditions can slow growth, deepen crises and hurt the poorest people.

mascot.line: Same conference, two jobs: the IMF is the fire brigade, the World Bank the construction crew.

cards.headline: The World Bank: a builder
cards.body: The Bank's first loan went to France, for rebuilding after the war. When the Marshall Plan took over rebuilding Europe, the Bank turned to power, irrigation and transport projects around the world. Today, part of it gives grants and low-interest loans to help low-income countries invest and develop.

cards.fact: The WTO referees trade among 166 members.
cards.context: The World Trade Organization began on 1 January 1995, succeeding the 1947 General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. It runs trade agreements, hosts negotiations and handles disputes between members, which together account for 98% of world trade. Critics say it favors large corporations and raise concerns about the environment, labor rights and national sovereignty.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Trade and the Global Economy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why countries trade and how tariffs and exchange rates affect it.
levels.summary: The Big Mac index tests purchasing power parity with burger prices. One imported washer ties the chapter together: comparative advantage, containers, tariffs, exchange rates, trade balance.

cards.headline: What can a hamburger tell you about a currency?
cards.body: Since 1986, The Economist has compared the price of a Big Mac around the world, as a lighthearted lesson in exchange rates. It's also a good way to pull this chapter together.

mascot.line: Economics you can eat. Possibly the tastiest index ever invented.

cards.headline: The burger test
cards.body: The idea behind it is purchasing power parity: exchange rates should drift toward the rate that makes the same goods cost the same in different countries. If a Big Mac costs less abroad, in dollars, than in the US, that currency may be undervalued; if it costs more, overvalued. Take it with a pinch of salt: one burger can't capture local wages, taxes and other costs of doing business.

cards.headline: One import, the whole chapter
cards.body: Follow an imported washing machine home. Countries specialize where their costs are relatively lowest (Level 72), so it may well be made abroad. Containers made shipping it cheap (Level 76). A tariff can raise its price, as importers pass the cost on (Level 74). A stronger home currency makes imports cheaper; a weaker one, pricier (Level 75). And it arrives as an import, counted in the trade balance (Level 73).

levels.title: What a Company Is
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how companies are owned and organized.
levels.summary: Sole proprietors and partners owe business debts personally. A corporation is a separate legal person with limited liability, as the Salomon case showed. Shareholders elect its board.

cards.headline: A bootmaker's company went bust. Did he have to pay its debts?
cards.body: Aron Salomon made leather boots in London. In 1892 he turned his business into a limited company, and soon afterwards it failed, owing money. The fight over who should pay went all the way to Britain's top court. Its answer still shapes what a company is.

cards.headline: Three ways to own a business
cards.body: The simplest business is a sole proprietorship: one owner, who in law is the business. If it runs up debts, the owner owes them personally, with no limit. A partnership is the same deal shared by two or more owners, and in a general partnership every partner is on the hook. Before 1892, Salomon was a sole proprietor. His boots, and his debts, were all his.

mascot.line: A person made entirely of paperwork, who can own things, owe things and go to court. Company law is stranger than fiction.

cards.headline: A person made of paperwork
cards.body: A corporation is different. In law it's a separate person: it can own property, sign contracts, and sue or be sued. Its owners have limited liability, so they can lose what they put in, but no more. That was the whole case. Salomon's company failed, and its liquidator argued that Salomon should pay its debts himself. The House of Lords said no: the company was a separate person in law, even though he held nearly all its shares.

cards.headline: Owning isn't running
cards.body: In a corporation, owning and running are split. The owners are shareholders, and they elect a board of directors. The board sets the big goals and policies, then hires officers, like the chief executive officer (CEO), to run the firm day to day. So you can own a slice of a company without ever setting foot in it.

levels.title: Starting a Business
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what an entrepreneur does and what it costs to start a business.
levels.summary: An entrepreneur organizes a business and carries its risk. HP began in a garage with $538. Start-ups face one-time and ongoing costs, and about half last five years.

cards.headline: Two friends, a garage and $538. That's how HP started.
cards.body: Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard began working part-time in a Palo Alto garage. California now honors it as the "Birthplace of Silicon Valley". On day one, though, it was just two people and an idea that might not work.

cards.headline: What an entrepreneur does
cards.body: An entrepreneur is someone who organizes a business, runs it and carries its risk. The word comes from the Old French entreprendre, "to undertake", and that's the job: taking on something that might fail. Hewlett and Packard made it official on January 1, 1939, as a partnership, Level 81's two-owner model. Even the company's name was settled by a coin toss.

cards.headline: What it costs to begin
cards.body: Their $538 of working capital even counted the value of Packard's used drill press. Every start-up has costs. Some are one-time, like equipment, permits and licenses. Others keep coming, like rent, salaries and utilities. The money usually comes from the founders' own savings, from loans, or from investors, who put in cash in return for a share of ownership.

mascot.line: Brave, not reckless: knowing the odds is part of the entrepreneur's job.

cards.fact: About half of new US businesses are gone within five years.
cards.context: Government statisticians tracked every US business location that opened in March 2013. A year later, 79.6% were still going. After five years, 50.6% were left; after ten, 34.7%. That's the risk hiding inside "undertake". A garage that grows into HP is the famous exception, not the rule.

levels.title: Revenue, Costs and Profit
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a business makes a profit.
levels.summary: Revenue is price times quantity sold; profit is revenue minus total cost. Fixed costs stay put while variable costs move with output. Amazon lost money in 2002 despite billions in sales.

cards.headline: In 2002, Amazon sold about $3.9 billion of goods. It still lost money.
cards.body: Shoppers were buying and the orders kept coming, yet the year ended in the red. How? Because the money coming in is not the money you get to keep.

cards.headline: Revenue in, profit left
cards.body: Revenue is what a business takes in from selling: the price of each item times how many it sells. Profit is what's left after paying all the costs: revenue minus total cost. If costs are bigger than revenue, the answer is negative, and that's a loss. Amazon's 2002 revenue was huge, but its costs were bigger still, leaving a loss of about $149 million.

cards.headline: Two kinds of cost
cards.body: Costs come in two kinds. Fixed costs, like the rent on a shop or factory, machinery and advertising, stay the same whether you make one thing or a million. Variable costs, like workers' hours and raw materials, rise and fall with how much you make. Sell more and revenue grows, but variable costs grow right along with it. Only the fixed costs sit still.

mascot.line: Revenue is the size of the pizza. Profit is the slice you actually get to eat.

cards.fact: In 2003, Amazon finally made a full-year profit: about $35 million.
cards.context: Its net sales that year were about $5.26 billion. So the profit was a sliver of the revenue: less than a penny for every dollar of sales. The lesson: a big revenue number tells you how much a business sells, not how much it keeps.

cards.headline: Profit: calculated

levels.title: Economies of Scale
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why making more of something can make each one cheaper.
levels.summary: Making more spreads fixed costs over more units, so each costs less: economies of scale. Ford's Model T fell from $850 to $260. Firms that grow too big hit diseconomies of scale.

cards.headline: In 1908, a Model T cost $850. Later it sold for as little as $260.
cards.body: Same basic car, a fraction of the price. The trick wasn't a clearance sale. Ford built more than 15 million of them.

cards.headline: Spreading the fixed costs
cards.body: Remember Level 83's fixed costs? A factory's rent and machinery cost the same whether it turns out ten cars or ten thousand. Divide total cost by the number made and you get the average cost of each one. Make more, and the fixed costs are spread thinner, so each unit's share shrinks. It's like splitting a delivery fee: the more friends sharing it, the less each one pays.

cards.headline: Economies of scale
cards.body: When making more lowers the cost of each unit, economists call it economies of scale. Ford rode them hard. Mass production let it sell the Model T cheaply, and from 1908 to 1927 the price fell from $850 to as little as $260. By the early 1920s, more than half of the registered cars in the world were Fords.

mascot.line: So there is a sweet spot: big enough to spread the costs, small enough to hear each other.

cards.fact: Bigger isn't always cheaper.
cards.context: A firm can grow so large that it's hard to manage. Layers of managers try to talk to workers and to each other, messages get garbled, and work and materials stop flowing smoothly. Then the cost of each unit starts climbing again. Economists call that diseconomies of scale.

learned: Average cost = total cost divided by units made

levels.title: Division of Labor
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Adam Smith's pin factory and why specializing raises output.
levels.summary: In Adam Smith's pin factory (1776), ten workers splitting about 18 operations made upwards of 48,000 pins a day. Specializing builds skill, saves time and leads to machines.

cards.headline: One worker alone: perhaps not one pin a day. Ten together: 48,000.
cards.body: That's Adam Smith's famous pin factory, from the first chapter of The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776. Same people, same wire. The difference was how they split up the work.

cards.headline: Eighteen small jobs
cards.body: Smith counted about 18 distinct operations in making a pin. One worker draws out the wire, another straightens it, a third cuts it, and so on down the line. Ten workers, each sticking to a few steps, could make upwards of 48,000 pins a day: about 4,800 each. Working alone, Smith reckoned, each could certainly not make 20, and perhaps not even one.

cards.headline: Why specializing works
cards.body: Smith gave three reasons. Practice: doing one task over and over makes you better at it. Time: nobody loses minutes switching from one kind of work to the next. Machines: dividing the work leads to machines that save labor. Same hands, far more pins.

mascot.line: Big output, tiny tasks. Smith wanted you to see both sides of that deal.

cards.fact: Smith also saw the dark side of dividing labor.
cards.context: Later in the same book, he warned that a worker who spends a whole life on a few simple operations "generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become." Harsh words from the man who made the pin factory famous. Specializing multiplies output; it doesn't promise interesting work.

levels.title: What Sets Wages
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what determines how much a job pays.
levels.summary: A wage is the price of labor. Productive, well-trained workers are in more demand and in shorter supply. Dirty or dangerous jobs pay extra: a compensating differential.

cards.headline: In Adam Smith's day, a coal miner could out-earn a skilled blacksmith.
cards.body: The blacksmith had the craft. The miner had the dirt, the danger and the dark. So what really sets how much a job pays?

cards.headline: A wage is a price
cards.body: A wage is the price of labor. In the labor market, employers are the buyers, demanding workers, and workers are the sellers, supplying their time. Employers want more workers when those workers produce more, for example because they're better trained, or when customers want more of what they make. On the other side, jobs that need more education or training have fewer people able to do them.

cards.fact: In 2024, US workers with a bachelor's degree earned a median $1,543 a week.
cards.context: That compares with $930 for those with only a high school diploma, counting full-time workers aged 25 and over. Both sides of the market are at work: training can make workers more productive, which raises demand for them, and fewer people have it, which limits supply.

mascot.line: So the least pleasant jobs can carry a bonus built into the pay. The dirt is part of the price.

cards.headline: Paying for the dirt
cards.body: Back to the coal miner. Smith noticed that wages vary with the ease or hardship, and the cleanliness or dirtiness, of the work. A journeyman blacksmith seldom earned in 12 hours what a coal miner earned in 8, because mining was dirtier, more dangerous and done underground. Economists call this extra pay a compensating differential: to fill an unpleasant job, employers have to make it worth someone's while.

levels.title: Unions
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what unions are and how collective bargaining works.
levels.summary: A union is workers acting together. It bargains collectively over wages, hours and conditions, and can strike. The 1936 to 1937 Flint sit-down strike won recognition of the UAW.

cards.headline: In 1936, autoworkers in Flint went on strike without leaving work.
cards.body: They sat down inside General Motors' plants and stayed put, for 44 days. Why would a strike work better from the inside?

mascot.line: Strength in numbers, written into a contract.

cards.headline: Bargaining as a team
cards.body: One worker asking for a raise is easy to turn down. A union is an association of workers who act together to improve their conditions. Through collective bargaining, the union's representatives negotiate with the employer over wages, hours and working conditions. If talks fail, workers can strike: a collective refusal to work on the employer's terms.

cards.headline: Why sit down?
cards.body: Strikers who walk out can be replaced by other workers. So from December 30, 1936, the Flint strikers occupied GM's plants instead of picketing outside, which kept them out of the weather and hard to replace. On February 11, 1937, General Motors agreed to recognize their union, the United Auto Workers. Sit-down strikes like theirs are now counted among illegal kinds of strike.

cards.fact: About 1 in 10 US workers belongs to a union.
cards.context: In 2025, 10.0% of US wage and salary workers were union members, about half the 20.1% of 1983. Where a union does bargain, Level 86's price of labor isn't settled one worker at a time: it's negotiated for the group.

levels.title: Automation and Jobs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how machines have changed work, from looms to robots.
levels.summary: Luddites smashed machines from 1811. Farm work fell from 41% of US jobs in 1900 to 1.9% in 2000, and ATMs changed tellers' work. Machines take over tasks; work shifts.

cards.headline: In 1811, English workers started smashing machines.
cards.body: They signed threatening letters in the name of "Ned Ludd", a leader who never existed. What were they really fighting?

cards.headline: Not against machines
cards.body: The Luddite attacks began near Nottingham in March 1811, on knitting machines called stocking frames. But the Luddites weren't against machines as such. They objected to owners using them to get around labor standards, turning out cheaper, lower-quality work. Parliament's answer was harsh: breaking a machine became a capital crime.

cards.headline: Where did the farmers go?
cards.body: The biggest shift came on farms. In 1900, 41% of American workers worked in agriculture; by 2000, just 1.9% did. Tractors replaced horses and mules, and more productive farms freed a huge share of the population for jobs outside farming. The farm jobs went. The workers moved on.

cards.headline: Machines take tasks
cards.body: ATMs were supposed to finish off bank tellers. Instead, each urban branch needed fewer of them: 13 instead of 20 between 1988 and 2004. But banks opened 43% more urban branches, so teller jobs didn't disappear. They changed, from counting cash toward helping customers with other services.

mascot.line: From stocking frames to robot arms, the question stays the same: which tasks, and who gains?

cards.fact: The first industrial robot clocked in at General Motors in 1961.
cards.context: Unimate, a robot arm, lifted and stacked hot die-cast metal parts. It's Level 85's third reason in steel: divide work into simple steps, and machines that save labor follow.

levels.title: Advertising
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how advertising shapes what people buy.
levels.summary: Advertising can inform (eyeglasses cost more where ads were banned) and persuade (brand loyalty, "A Diamond Is Forever"). Pigou argued rival ads may simply cancel out.

cards.headline: Four words from 1947: "A Diamond Is Forever."
cards.body: Copywriter Frances Gerety wrote them for De Beers. In 1999, Advertising Age named them the best advertising slogan of the 20th century. How can a few words change what people buy?

cards.headline: Ads that inform
cards.body: Some ads are simply news: this exists, here's what it does, here's the price. That helps you compare. In 1972, economist Lee Benham found that eyeglasses cost more in US states that banned advertising than in states that allowed it. When shoppers can't see prices, they can't easily compare them.

cards.headline: Ads that persuade
cards.body: Other ads work on feelings. Blindfolded, many people can't tell common ketchups apart, yet habit and advertising give them strong favorites. De Beers's four words helped make the diamond solitaire the standard engagement ring. Before, engagement rings often used colored gems, small diamonds or even pearls. The stone didn't change. The story around it did.

mascot.line: Next time two rival brands shout at you back to back, you're watching Pigou's point play out.

cards.fact: Rival ads can cancel each other out.
cards.context: In 1920, economist A. C. Pigou pointed out that when two competing firms each spend to lure customers from the other, the spending may simply neutralize itself, leaving both where they'd be if neither had advertised. Picture two neighbors in a shouting match: both get louder, and nobody hears anything new.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Companies and Work
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how businesses make profits, set wages and change with technology.
levels.summary: Coase (1937): firms exist because markets have transaction costs, so managers direct work inside. From pin factories to robots, companies turn costs into revenue and pay wages for labor.

cards.headline: If markets work so well, why do companies exist at all?
cards.body: In theory, you could hire a stranger for every single task, one deal at a time. In 1937, economist Ronald Coase asked why businesses don't simply do that.

cards.headline: The cost of using the market
cards.body: Coase's answer: markets aren't free to use. Every deal means finding out prices and negotiating a separate contract, costs now called transaction costs. A firm cuts them. Instead of a fresh contract for each task, managers direct the work inside. The idea helped earn Coase the 1991 Nobel Prize in economics, and it explains why this chapter's companies exist at all.

cards.headline: The chapter through Coase's eyes
cards.body: Look back through Coase's lens. A corporation is a legal person that can own property and sign contracts. An entrepreneur organizes it and carries the risk. Inside, work is directed rather than bargained task by task. Profit is revenue minus total cost, and economies of scale push the cost of each unit down. Wages are the price of the labor it hires.

levels.title: Adam Smith and the Invisible Hand
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Smith's idea that self-interest can serve the common good through markets.
levels.summary: Adam Smith argued in 1776 that self-interested trade can serve everyone, as if led by an invisible hand. He also gave government duties and distrusted collusion, and critics say the hand often fails.

cards.headline: Your dinner doesn't depend on the butcher's kindness. Adam Smith said so.
cards.body: In 1776, the Scottish philosopher published The Wealth of Nations. One idea in it became among the most quoted, and most argued over, in all of economics.

cards.headline: The butcher, the brewer and the baker
cards.body: Smith's point was down to earth. You don't get dinner because the butcher, the brewer or the baker feels generous toward you. You get it because selling to you serves their own interest. Nobody has to love you for the bread to show up. Each baker minds his own business, and the town gets fed anyway.

mascot.line: One sentence in a book of hundreds of pages, and it became the most famous hand in economics.

cards.fact: Smith used the phrase 'invisible hand' just once in The Wealth of Nations.
cards.context: In it, a person who "intends only his own gain" is "led by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention." The idea: good outcomes for everyone can grow out of many self-interested choices, with no one arranging them. Later writers stretched it, more controversially, into a claim that free markets always deliver the best possible result.

cards.headline: Smith's fine print
cards.body: Smith was no enemy of government. He gave it three duties: defense, justice, and public works like roads and bridges that help society but wouldn't pay a private builder. And he didn't trust business to police itself. People of the same trade, he warned, seldom meet without the talk ending in a conspiracy against the public, or some scheme to raise prices.

cards.headline: The critics
cards.body: Modern critics push further. In 2002, economist Joseph Stiglitz wrote that the invisible hand is invisible, at least in part, because it isn't there. So the question Smith raised stays open: how much good can self-interest do on its own, and where does it need help?

levels.title: Karl Marx and Capitalism's Critics
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Marx's critique of capitalism and how far it spread.
levels.summary: Marx argued owners keep the value workers create as profit and predicted workers would overthrow capitalism. Communism once ruled a third of the world; critics rejected his theory of value.

cards.headline: Smith saw a town fed by self-interest. Marx saw workers being shortchanged.
cards.body: In 1848, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published The Communist Manifesto. In 1867 came the first volume of Das Kapital. Marx's question: who really creates the value in what a factory makes, and who keeps it?

cards.headline: Where does profit come from?
cards.body: Marx built on concepts inherited from Adam Smith and David Ricardo, including the labor theory of value: a product's value is set by the labor it takes to make it. Follow that through and profit looks suspicious. If workers create the value, but owners pay them just enough to live on and keep the rest, that leftover is what Marx called surplus value. To him, profit rested on exploitation.

cards.headline: A prediction of revolution
cards.body: Marx saw history as a series of class struggles, and under capitalism that meant owners of capital against workers. He expected wealth to pile up in fewer hands, and he and Engels predicted the industrial working class would one day overthrow capitalism. He pictured that revolution in industrialized countries. The revolution that did come was in mostly agrarian Russia, under Lenin's version of his ideas.

mascot.line: Same starting point as Smith, opposite conclusion. Economics is like that sometimes.

cards.fact: For much of the 20th century, about a third of the world lived under communist governments.
cards.context: Leaders including Lenin and Mao built on Marx's writings to impose communism on more than twenty countries, and his ideas inspired labor and socialist movements in western Europe. Critics went after the foundation. The Austrian school argued that a thing's value comes from its ability to satisfy wants, not the labor used to make it, and labor itself varies so much in skill that value is hard to measure that way.

levels.title: Keynes and Spending in a Slump
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Keynes's argument for government spending during a slump.
levels.summary: Keynes argued unemployment comes from too little spending, so in a slump government should spend, even by borrowing. From the 1970s, monetarists led by Milton Friedman gained ground.

cards.headline: An economist once suggested burying banknotes in old coal mines.
cards.body: That was John Maynard Keynes, in his 1936 book The General Theory. It sounds like a joke. It was a serious answer to a serious question: what should happen when an economy stops spending?

cards.headline: Nobody buys, nobody hires
cards.body: Keynes's big idea was total spending in the economy, which economists call aggregate demand. Businesses won't hire workers to make goods that can't be sold. So when spending falls, jobs go with it. In Keynes's view, the root of unemployment was too little demand, and cutting wages wouldn't cure it. Something had to get people spending again.

cards.headline: Government steps in
cards.body: His fix: if households and businesses won't spend, government can, even if it has to borrow and run a budget deficit. Hence the coal mines. Bury banknotes in bottles, let firms dig them up, and the digging alone would put people to work. Then Keynes added the sensible part: "It would, indeed, be more sensible to build houses." Useful spending beats useless spending, but in a slump, both beat none.

mascot.line: Keynes shaped both the money system and the arguments about it. Busy man.

cards.fact: Keynes helped design Level 7's Bretton Woods system.
cards.context: At the 1944 conference, he was one of the architects of the postwar system of fixed exchange rates. His ideas guided most Western governments until the 1970s, when monetarism eclipsed them. Its leader was Milton Friedman, Level 6's Yap storyteller, who argued government should steady the economy only by growing the money supply at a steady rate. And Friedrich Hayek, who debated Keynes in the 1930s, never accepted that Keynes had won.

levels.title: Markets, Plans and Mixed Economies
levels.objective: After this level you can compare market, planned and mixed economies.
levels.summary: Markets spread decisions among buyers and sellers; command economies take goals from rulers. Hayek argued prices carry knowledge no planner can gather. Most real economies are mixed.

cards.headline: Tin gets scarce. Thousands of people use less of it. Nobody gave an order.
cards.body: Economist Friedrich Hayek posed that puzzle in 1945. Every economy has to decide what gets made. The real fight is over who decides: a planner, the market, or a bit of both.

items.label: Market economy
points: Decisions spread out among buyers and sellers
Built on private enterprise

items.label: Command economy
points: Goals handed down from rulers
Soviet Five-Year Plans began in 1928

items.label: Mixed economy

Most real economies today

cards.headline: Prices as messages
cards.body: Hayek's argument: the knowledge an economy runs on exists in no single mind. It's scattered, with each person knowing things about their own resources that no planner ever can. Prices gather it up. When tin gets scarce, users don't need to know why. The price rises, and they use less. Hayek compared the price system to a kind of telecommunications system.

cards.fact: The inefficiency of communist economies helped bring down the Soviet Union in 1991.
cards.context: Soviet planners at Gosplan turned the party's goals into national plans. Hayek had argued no planner could gather knowledge scattered across a whole society. But markets don't run on prices alone either. Even market economies rely on government to protect property, enforce contracts, prevent fraud and collect taxes. That's why most real economies are mixed: part market, part government.

levels.title: Behavioral Economics
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why real people don't always act rationally with money.
levels.summary: Behavioral economics tests whether people are perfectly rational. Loss aversion makes owners value things more, and mental accounting sorts money into jars. Experience may shrink these effects.

cards.headline: Hand someone a mug and it instantly becomes worth more. To them.
cards.body: In a 1990 experiment, economists gave mugs to randomly chosen people and let them sell to people who didn't get one. Theory said about half the mugs should change hands. Far fewer did.

cards.headline: Rational on paper
cards.body: Traditional economic theory assumes people have good information and process it perfectly. Behavioral economics checks that against how people really behave. One of its founders wasn't even an economist: psychologist Daniel Kahneman, whose work with Amos Tversky produced "Prospect Theory" in 1979. He won the 2002 economics Nobel for bringing psychological research into economics.

cards.headline: Losses hurt more
cards.body: So why did the mug owners hang on? Richard Thaler's answer is loss aversion: losing something feels worse than gaining the same thing feels good. Once the mug is yours, selling it feels like a loss. That's the endowment effect: we value things more simply because we own them. Anyone who has tried to clear out a closet knows the feeling.

cards.headline: Money in labeled jars
cards.body: Thaler also described mental accounting: we sort money into separate accounts in our heads and judge each decision on its own. Losing money even hurts less if you're still "in the black" in that mental account, which Thaler calls the house money effect. That work helped win him the 2017 economics Nobel for his contributions to behavioral economics.

cards.fact: Experience may shrink the mug effect.
cards.context: Not everyone thinks these quirks run the world. In 2003, economist John List studied real marketplaces and found that as traders gained market experience, the endowment effect faded. A real quirk, then, but maybe not a permanent one.

Endowment effect: we value what we own

levels.title: Game Theory
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the prisoner's dilemma and why cooperation is hard.
levels.summary: In the prisoner's dilemma, each player does better by betraying whatever the other does, yet both end up worse off. When the game repeats with no known end, cooperation can pay, as tit for tat showed.

cards.headline: Two shops cut prices to steal each other's customers. Both end up poorer.
cards.body: Neither gains a single customer, and both earn smaller profits. Why would two sensible owners do that? Game theory has a famous answer, and it starts in a police station.

cards.headline: The prisoner's dilemma
cards.body: Two suspects are questioned in separate rooms. If both stay silent, each gets a year. If both confess, five years each. If one confesses and the other stays silent, the confessor walks free and the silent one gets 20 years. Work it through: whatever your partner does, confessing leaves you better off. So both confess, and both serve five years instead of one.
cards.callout: Both silent: 1 year each · Both confess: 5 years each

mascot.line: The prisoners were a marketing decision. Good one, though.

cards.fact: The prisoner's dilemma was invented before it had any prisoners.
cards.context: Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher devised the game at the RAND Corporation in 1950. Albert Tucker added the prison story later, to make it easier to explain. The same trap turns up far from any jail: in an arms race, two nations keep buying weapons, neither gains an advantage, and both end up poorer. The price-cutting shops are in it too.

cards.headline: Play again, and trust can pay
cards.body: There's a way out: meet again. When the game repeats and nobody knows which round is last, cooperation can emerge. In Robert Axelrod's computer tournaments, Anatol Rapoport's tit for tat did famously well: cooperate first, then copy your partner's last move. Axelrod found that every "nice" strategy, one that never betrays first, beat every strategy that wasn't.

learned: Betraying is best for each, whatever the other does

levels.title: Inequality
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how income and wealth inequality are measured.
levels.summary: The Gini coefficient runs from 0 (everyone has the same) to 1 (one person has it all). Wealth is far more unequal than income: in OECD countries, the top 10% hold about half of wealth.

cards.headline: Ten friends split a pizza. How do you put one number on how fairly?
cards.body: Everyone gets a slice: that's one extreme. One friend eats the whole thing: that's the other. Economists measure how evenly a country shares its income on exactly that kind of scale.

cards.headline: The Gini coefficient
cards.body: Italian statistician Corrado Gini devised it in 1912. A Gini of 0 means perfect equality: everyone has the same income. A Gini of 1 means one person gets all of it and everyone else gets nothing. It's tied to the Lorenz curve, a chart from 1905 that plots what share of income goes to what share of the people.

cards.headline: Income isn't wealth
cards.body: Income is a flow: the money coming in. Wealth is a stock: what you own. And wealth is shared far less evenly. Across 28 OECD countries, the richest 10% of households held 52% of all household wealth, while the top 10% of earners got 24% of income. On average, wealth inequality ran about twice as high as income inequality.
cards.callout: Top 10%: 52% of wealth · 24% of income

mascot.line: Same number, different pizzas. Always ask what went into the measure.

cards.fact: Two very different countries can have the same Gini.
cards.context: The Gini shows how unequal a distribution is, but not why. Two countries with very different income patterns can land on the same score. And some countries measure consumption rather than income, which can miss how much wealth the richest households hold. One number is a starting point, not the whole story.

levels.title: Externalities
levels.objective: After this level you can explain costs like pollution that fall on people outside a deal.
levels.summary: An externality is the effect of a deal on someone outside it, like pollution. Pigou proposed taxing such costs; Coase argued that when deals are cheap to make, people can bargain their way to a fix.

cards.headline: An outdoor concert sells tickets. The neighbors hear every song.
cards.body: They never bought a ticket and never agreed to the noise, but the deal between the band and the fans lands on them anyway. Economists have a name for that.

cards.headline: Costs that leak out
cards.body: An externality is the effect of a deal on a third party who is outside it. Pollution is the classic negative one: a factory's costs cover its workers and materials, but not the harm its smoke does to the neighbors. Because nobody pays for that harm, the market makes too much of the product. Externalities can be good, too: research that others build on is a standard example.

cards.headline: Pigou: send the bill
cards.body: In The Economics of Welfare, published in 1920, economist Arthur Pigou proposed a fix. Tax activities that impose costs on others; subsidize ones that spread benefits. The tax puts the missing cost back into the price. A carbon tax is the modern example, ideally set equal to the social cost of carbon.

mascot.line: Pigou says tax it. Coase says talk it out. Both are asking who pays for the mess.

cards.fact: Ronald Coase asked: why not let the neighbors bargain?
cards.context: In his 1960 paper "The Problem of Social Cost", Coase challenged Pigou's approach. Picture a rancher whose cattle trample a farmer's crops. The farmer could simply pay the rancher to keep fewer cattle. If making a deal costs little, the two can bargain to an efficient fix without government, whoever the law favors. The catch: deal-making costs range from negligible to enormous. Coase won the 1991 economics Nobel.

cards.headline: Externalities
learned: A deal can affect people outside it

Pigou: tax the harm, subsidize the benefit
Coase: cheap bargaining can fix it too

levels.title: The Economics of Your Life
levels.objective: After this level you can apply the tree's big ideas to everyday choices about work, saving and spending.
levels.summary: Keynes's 15-hour week never came, but longer retirements added leisure. Defaults shape how people save, and the sunk cost effect shows spent money steering choices.

cards.headline: Big ideas, small choices: your job, your savings, tonight's ticket.
cards.body: Economics isn't only about nations and markets. Its ideas show up in how much you work, whether you save, and whether you sit through a play you're not enjoying.

cards.headline: Work: Keynes's 15-hour week
cards.body: In 1930, Keynes predicted that a century later, living standards would be four to eight times higher and people might work just 15 hours a week. Economist Nicholas Crafts concluded the short week won't arrive by 2030. But the free time turned up somewhere else: in the UK, expected lifetime hours of leisure and home production rose 58% between 1931 and 2011, reflecting longer lives and longer retirements.

cards.headline: Saving: the power of the default
cards.body: Behavioral economists find that small details shape big decisions. One is the default: what happens unless you actively choose something else. Another is timing. Promising to save more in the future, especially after a raise, feels easier than saving more today, and Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi built their Save More Tomorrow plan on that. Critics call such nudges paternalistic; supporters stress that joining is voluntary and you can opt out any time.

mascot.line: Paid full price, so you'd better go? The study suggests that's exactly how our heads work.

cards.fact: Paying full price made people go to more plays.
cards.context: In a 1985 study, Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer sold theater season tickets at full price or at random discounts. Over the next six months, the full-price buyers went to more plays, though the money was spent either way. That's the sunk cost effect: a greater tendency to keep going with something once money, effort or time has gone into it.

cards.headline: Economics, up close
learned: Keynes's 15-hour week never came, but retirement did
Defaults and timing shape how much people save
Sunk costs can steer choices they shouldn't

levels.title: The Animal Kingdom in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what makes an animal an animal and name the main groups.
levels.summary: An animal has many cells without walls, eats other living things and usually moves at some stage. Sponges qualify. The kingdom: five familiar groups and a vast crowd without backbones.

cards.headline: Sponges were long mistaken for plants.
cards.body: They have no muscles, and a grown sponge stays stuck to one spot for life. Only after someone noticed their small movements, in 1765, did people slowly accept sponges as animals. So what does it actually take to be an animal?

cards.headline: The animal checklist
cards.body: Biologists use a short checklist. An animal is built from many cells, and unlike plants and fungi, those cells have no cell walls. It can't make its own food, so it eats other living or dead things. And most animals can move, at least at some stage of life. Fur, legs and a face are all optional. Eating someone else's lunch is not.

mascot.line: Swim once, then sit still forever. Honestly, a very relaxing life plan.

cards.fact: A sponge does all its traveling as a baby.
cards.context: Sponge larvae can swim. Then they settle, attach and stay put for good. The adult feeds by pulling water through its porous body, where tiny hairlike flagella stir up currents that bring in bacteria to eat. Many cells, no cell walls, eats other living things, moved at one stage of life: a sponge ticks every box on the checklist.

items.label: Five groups you know
points: Mammals and birds

items.label: The crowd you overlook
points: Insects, spiders and crabs
Snails, clams and squid

levels.title: How Many Species?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how many animal species are known and how many may exist.
levels.summary: About 1.5 million animal species have been described (IUCN, 2025). A 2011 estimate by Mora and colleagues puts all animal species at about 7.8 million, so most are still unnamed.

cards.headline: Scientists have named about 1.5 million animal species. Easy part.
cards.body: Every named species has a description behind it: someone found it, studied it and published it. But how do you count the animals nobody has found yet? One team came up with a clever answer, and it's humbling.

cards.fact: Named so far: about 1.5 million animal species.
cards.context: That's the IUCN Red List's 2025 tally of described animal species, and about 1 million of them are insects. IUCN itself warns that the figures aren't always up to date. So treat it as a snapshot, not a final score.

cards.headline: Counting the ones nobody has seen
cards.body: In 2011, Camilo Mora and colleagues spotted a pattern. Every species sits inside bigger groups, and those bigger groups are much better known. The number of groups at each level followed a steady relationship with the number of species, so the team used it to predict the total: about 8.7 million species of complex-celled life, give or take 1.3 million, and about 7.8 million of them animals.

mascot.line: Somewhere out there, an animal nobody has named is having a perfectly normal Tuesday.

cards.fact: Most animals have never been named.
cards.context: By Mora's estimate, about 86 percent of species on land and 91 percent in the ocean still await a description. Naming them all the traditional way could take up to 1,200 years and more than 300,000 taxonomists. It's an estimate, not a head count, but the message is hard to miss: you live on a planet you've mostly never met.

levels.title: Backbone or Not
levels.objective: After this level you can tell vertebrates, which have backbones, from invertebrates.
levels.summary: Vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) have a backbone around the spinal cord. They are about 1 in 20 known species; invertebrates are the rest, many with outer skeletons.

cards.headline: Only about 1 in 20 known animal species has a backbone.
cards.body: Mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish: the animals on almost every poster. Together they're a thin slice of the kingdom. What exactly does a backbone do, and how does everyone else manage without one?

cards.headline: Your membership card runs down your back
cards.body: A vertebrate has a backbone: a column of bones called vertebrae, which partly encloses the central nervous system. Your spinal cord runs right through it. Vertebrates come in five familiar groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Run a finger down the middle of your back. Those bumps are your membership card.

cards.headline: No backbone, still sturdy
cards.body: Invertebrates are every animal without a backbone, from sponges and jellyfish to worms, snails, crabs and insects. Plenty of them still have a skeleton. They just wear it on the outside: most mollusks, crustaceans and insects have a hard outer skeleton that protects the body and gives muscles something to pull on. A beetle is a knight that never takes off its armor.

mascot.line: All those posters of lions and eagles, and the kingdom quietly belongs to the beetles.

cards.fact: About 95 percent of known animal species are invertebrates.
cards.context: Of about 1.55 million described animal species in IUCN's 2025 table, only about 76,000 are vertebrates. Britannica rounds more cautiously: more than 90 percent of living animal species have no backbone. Either way, we're the minority. And Level 2's million insects? Every one of them is on the other side of this line.

levels.title: Naming Animals
levels.objective: After this level you can explain scientific names and Linnaeus's system.
levels.summary: Linnaeus gave each species a two-part name, genus then species; animal names start from 1758. Species sit inside ranks from domain down, and close relatives share a genus.

cards.headline: Say 'robin' in London and in Boston, and you mean two different birds.
cards.body: Early colonists in America named their bird robin because its breast color reminded them of the smaller European robin. The American robin is about 25 cm long, the European one about 14 cm. Same word, different animals. Scientists needed a better system.

cards.headline: Two words, one animal
cards.body: In the 1700s, Carl Linnaeus replaced long descriptive phrases with a two-part name for each species: first the genus, then the species. The European robin is Erithacus rubecula; the American robin is Turdus migratorius. Biologists everywhere accept the system, so a scientific name points to one species, wherever you are. Yours is Homo sapiens, and Linnaeus picked it himself.

mascot.line: A whole kingdom, and it all starts with one very long book.

cards.fact: Official animal names start in 1758.
cards.context: That's the year of the 10th edition of Linnaeus's Systema Naturae, the starting point for naming animals. Plants got their starting line a little earlier, with his Species Plantarum in 1753. Think of 1758 as day one of the official animal register.

cards.headline: Boxes inside boxes
cards.body: Linnaeus also stacked species into ranks: kingdom, class, order, genus, species. Biologists later added more, and today's ladder runs domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Close relatives share the lower rungs. Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars all sit in the genus Panthera, so the tiger is Panthera tigris and the leopard Panthera pardus. The genus works like a surname.

levels.title: Warm- and Cold-Blooded
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how different animals control their body temperature.
levels.summary: Endotherms (mammals, birds) make their own heat; ectotherms take it from their surroundings and manage it by behavior. "Cold-blooded" is misleading, and inside heat costs food.

cards.headline: Some 'cold-blooded' lizards run hotter than some mammals.
cards.body: Britannica calls the words warm-blooded and cold-blooded imprecise and misleading, and that lizard is why. So if blood temperature isn't the real difference, what is?

cards.headline: Inside heat, outside heat
cards.body: The real difference is where the heat comes from. Endotherms make most of it inside their bodies and hold a steady temperature whatever the weather: about 37 °C for mammals and about 40 °C for birds. Ectotherms absorb most of their heat from their surroundings; that includes fish, amphibians, reptiles and invertebrates. Endo means inside, ecto means outside. The name tells you where the furnace is.

cards.headline: A lizard's working day
cards.body: An ectotherm isn't helpless. A reptile basks in the sun or lies on a warm surface to heat up, then moves between sun and shade, or turns its body, to control how much heat it gains or loses. Its temperature still rises and falls with its surroundings more than yours does. It runs its thermostat with its feet.

mascot.line: Next time you feel starving, you know who to blame. The furnace.

cards.fact: Your steady warmth is paid for at every meal.
cards.context: Because reptiles don't keep a constant inside temperature, they have a low metabolic rate and need less food than warm-blooded animals of the same size. Many can survive long stretches without eating. Your 37 °C is a furnace that never switches off, and food is its fuel.

cards.body: Up to 16 hours a day of it. So is a panda a carnivore or not? It depends on whether you're asking about its family tree or its dinner plate. Start with the plate.

levels.title: Food Chains and Webs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how energy passes along a food chain.
levels.summary: Energy enters food chains through producers and passes up through consumers, about 10 percent per step, so most ecosystems have at most five levels. Chains overlap into webs.

cards.headline: A blue whale's dinner starts with sunlight.
cards.body: In one ocean food chain, single-celled phytoplankton feed tiny shrimp called krill, and krill are the blue whale's main food. So how does sunlight end up inside a whale, and why does so little of it make the trip?

cards.headline: Who eats whom
cards.body: A food chain starts with producers, which make their own food, nearly all by photosynthesis from sunlight, carbon dioxide and water. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat the producers. Secondary consumers eat them, tertiary consumers eat those, and apex predators sit on top. Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria finish the job, turning dead plants and wastes into nutrient-rich soil.

mascot.line: A 90 percent tax at every step. No wonder the top of the chain is so exclusive.

cards.fact: Only about 10 percent of the energy climbs each step.
cards.context: On average, each level passes on about 10 percent of its energy. The rest is lost: some food can't be digested, a lot escapes as heat, and some living things die without being eaten. Start with 1,000 units in plants, and about 100 reach the herbivores and about 10 the animals that eat them. That's why most ecosystems top out at five levels.

cards.headline: Chains tangle into webs
cards.body: Real animals rarely stick to one chain. All the overlapping chains in an ecosystem make up a food web. Level 6's omnivores are one reason: a bear eats berries, like a primary consumer, and salmon, like a higher one. Draw every arrow, and your neat line turns into a net.

levels.title: Ecosystems
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how animals, plants and places form an ecosystem.
levels.summary: An ecosystem is living things plus nonliving parts working together. When Robert Paine removed sea stars from a shore, mussels took over: the sea star was a keystone species.

cards.headline: A scientist pried sea stars off rocks with a crowbar and tossed them in the sea.
cards.body: On purpose. It was an experiment on the coast of Washington State in the 1960s, and what happened next changed how ecologists think about the places animals live.

cards.headline: More than a list of animals
cards.body: An ecosystem is a place where plants, animals and other organisms work together with the nonliving parts around them, such as rocks, temperature and humidity. It can be enormous, or as small as a tide pool, which is a complete, tiny ecosystem of its own. Every part depends on every other part, directly or indirectly. That's the claim. Paine went to test it.

cards.headline: The shore without its sea stars
cards.body: Robert Paine's carnivorous ochre sea stars ate mussels on the rocky shore of Mukkaw Bay. Within two years of removing them from one stretch, California mussels took over rock that had held anemones, sponges, barnacles, chitons, limpets and seaweeds. On nearby shore where the sea stars stayed, the mix survived. One hungry predator had been keeping room open for everyone else.

mascot.line: One sea star, one crowbar, one idea that changed ecology.

cards.fact: Some species hold the whole arch up.
cards.context: Paine called them keystone species. A keystone is the wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch that keeps it from collapsing. Take out the sea star and the shore's variety fell apart. Think back to Level 7's food web: one predator near the top decided who got room at the bottom.

cards.headline: Ecosystems: explored

levels.title: The Smallest and the Largest
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the smallest and largest animals alive.
levels.summary: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have lived. The smallest known vertebrate is the Brazilian flea toad (about 7.1 mm); male fairyfly wasps are the smallest adult insects.

cards.headline: The biggest animal ever is alive right now.
cards.body: Not a dinosaur. According to NOAA, the blue whale, a mammal swimming in today's oceans, is the largest animal known to have lived. So how big is that, and how small does an animal get at the other end of the scale?

mascot.line: Six tons of shrimp a day. And you thought your grocery bill was bad.

cards.fact: Blue whales can grow to about 33 meters long.
cards.context: That's NOAA's figure for the biggest, in the Antarctic: up to about 110 feet, weighing more than 150 metric tons. Yet they live almost entirely on krill, and the biggest may eat up to 6 tons of it a day. The largest animal ever runs on some of the smallest food in the sea.

Line it up against the biggest blue whale and the whale is more than 200,000 times longer. Same kingdom, same checklist from Level 1, wildly different sizes.

levels.title: Checkpoint: What Makes an Animal
levels.objective: After this level you can sort animals by backbone, body temperature and diet.
levels.summary: Three questions sort most animals: backbone or not, inside or outside heat, and what it eats. Some answers change with age: gray tree frog tadpoles eat algae and debris, while adults eat insects.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: three questions sort almost any animal.
cards.body: Does it have a backbone? Does it make its own heat? What does it eat? This chapter gave you all three. Let's run a few animals through them, then meet one that changes an answer halfway through its life.

mascot.line: Salad as a kid, bugs as a grown-up. Every frog has a coming-of-age story.

cards.fact: A gray tree frog switches diets as it grows up.
cards.context: As tadpoles, gray tree frogs eat algae and bits of rotting debris in the water. Adults mainly hunt insects and their larvae. So the diet question depends on when you ask: algae and debris when young, insects when grown. The other two answers never change. A frog is an amphibian, so it has a backbone, and it takes its heat from outside.

levels.title: What Makes a Mammal
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the features all mammals share.
levels.summary: Mammals breathe air, make their own heat, have hair at some point and feed young milk, the feature Linnaeus named them for in 1758. About 6,800 living species (MDD, 2026).

cards.headline: Linnaeus named your whole class after milk.
cards.body: In 1758, in the same book that started Level 4's official animal register, Carl Linnaeus grouped you with cats, whales and bats. He called the group Mammalia, from the Latin mamma, the milk-producing breast. So what does it take to join the club?

cards.headline: The mammal checklist
cards.body: Every mammal breathes air with lungs, has hair at some point in its life and feeds its young on milk. It also makes its own heat: Level 5's endotherms, with mammals at about 37 °C. One more badge hides inside your head, where a chain of three tiny bones carries sound across the middle ear. Milk is the one that made the name.

mascot.line: A whale's baby pictures are its only hairy ones.

cards.fact: Many whales have hair only before they're born.
cards.context: Hair is a typical mammal feature, but in many whales it has disappeared except in the fetal stage. That still counts: the checklist says hair at some point in life, and a whale ticks that box before it's even born.

cards.fact: About 6,800 living mammal species
cards.context: The American Society of Mammalogists' Mammal Diversity Database lists 6,791 living species in its July 2026 version. Next to Level 2's roughly 1.5 million described animal species, that's less than half of one percent. It's a small club, and you're a member.

levels.title: Big Cats
levels.objective: After this level you can describe lions, tigers and the other big cats.
levels.summary: Panthera cats (lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars) often roar; small cats' hardened hyoid prevents it. Lions live in prides where lionesses hunt; tigers, the largest cats, live alone.

cards.headline: Your house cat will never roar. It isn't shy.
cards.body: A lion's roar can be heard up to five miles away. A house cat can't make that sound at all, however big its attitude. The difference comes down to one small bone.

mascot.line: All that attitude, and the house cat is stuck with a meow. Life isn't fair.

cards.headline: The roaring club
cards.body: Level 4 put lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars in one genus, Panthera. These are the big cats, and they often roar. Smaller cats have a fully hardened hyoid, a small bone in the neck, and that stiff bone prevents them from roaring. Same family, different hardware.

cards.headline: A roar is a property line
cards.body: A pride can hold as many as 40 lions, and it has ground to defend. Both males and females roar to mark their territory, and the sound carries up to five miles. The lionesses bring home the dinner; the roar tells every other lion whose ground this is. Think of it as a fence you can hear from the next town.

levels.title: Elephants
levels.objective: After this level you can describe elephants' trunks, memory and family life.
levels.summary: Elephants are the largest land animals. The trunk is a boneless nose and upper lip. African families follow a matriarch, and older matriarchs are better at spotting strangers.

cards.headline: Scientists played elephants recordings of other elephants.
cards.body: In Kenya's Amboseli National Park, researchers played recorded elephant calls to family after family, some from friends and some from strangers. How a family reacted depended on one elephant. To meet her, start with the most famous nose in the world.

cards.headline: A nose that works like a hand
cards.body: Elephants are the largest living land animals, in three species: African savanna, African forest and Asian. The trunk is a nose and upper lip fused into one, with no bones inside and about 150,000 muscle bundles. With it an elephant smells, breathes, trumpets, drinks and grabs things. Imagine your nose and top lip merging, then learning to pick things up.

cards.headline: Grandmother is in charge
cards.body: African elephants live in female-led herds. The matriarch, usually the biggest and oldest female, leads her related females and their young. Adult males tend to roam alone or in loose all-male groups. In an elephant family, the family tree and the chain of command are the same drawing.

mascot.line: Respect your elders. Especially the ones who weigh several tons.

cards.fact: Older matriarchs know a stranger when they hear one.
cards.context: In the 2001 Amboseli study, families led by matriarchs aged 55 or more were far better at telling strangers' calls from familiar ones. Those families also produced more calves. The saying goes that elephants never forget. The science adds: it pays to have a grandmother who remembers.

levels.title: Whales and Dolphins
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how whales and dolphins are mammals that live in the sea.
levels.summary: Whales and dolphins breathe air through blowholes, have some hair and nurse their young. Dolphins sleep half a brain at a time. Toothed whales include dolphins; baleen whales strain food.

cards.headline: Dolphins sleep with half a brain at a time.
cards.body: Scientists think it lets them keep coming up to breathe, even while they snooze. A dolphin spends its whole life in the sea and still has to breathe air. That's your first clue that it's a mammal.

cards.headline: The checklist, passed underwater
cards.body: Whales, dolphins and porpoises meet Level 11's mammal checklist, with no discount for living at sea. They breathe air, are warm-blooded, have hair at some point in life and feed their young milk. They breathe through blowholes, nostrils on top of the head. Every breath means a trip to the surface, and the nose is already on top: a snorkel they never have to pack.

mascot.line: Twenty months of milk. Try telling this one it's a fish.

cards.fact: A dolphin calf drinks milk for about 20 months.
cards.context: A bottlenose dolphin mother is pregnant for about 12 months. Her calf nurses for about 20 months and stays with her for 3 to 6 years. That's a long childhood on milk, and about as mammal as it gets.

levels.title: Bats
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how bats fly and find food with echolocation.
levels.summary: More than 1,300 bat species make up about one-fifth of mammal species. Bats are the only true flying mammals, on hand-shaped wings, and many hunt by echolocation.

cards.headline: About 1 in 5 mammal species is a bat.
cards.body: The U.S. Geological Survey counts more than 1,300 bat species. Pick five mammal species at random and, on average, one of them is a bat. Two tricks set bats apart: they fly, and many of them see with sound.

cards.headline: A wing made from a hand
cards.body: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight. The wing is a modified hand: a thin, flexible skin stretched between long finger bones. Spread your fingers and imagine the skin between them larger, thinner and stretched wide. That's a bat wing, and the order's name, Chiroptera, means 'hand wing.'

mascot.line: Loudest party in town, and you're not on the frequency list.

cards.headline: Seeing with sound
cards.body: In echolocation, a bat sends out calls that bounce off objects and come back to its ears. The echoes tell the bat what's out there. Most of those calls are ultrasound, too high-pitched for you to hear. After dark, the air above you may be full of bat shouts you'll never notice.

cards.fact: Closing in, a bat speeds up its calls.
cards.context: When a bat detects an insect it wants to eat, it fires off a rapid series of calls to pinpoint exactly where the prey is. More calls mean fresher echoes, the way you'd glance more often at something you were about to catch.

levels.title: Marsupials
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how kangaroos and other marsupials raise their young in a pouch.
levels.summary: Marsupials are born tiny and finish growing in a pouch; a red kangaroo is born after about 33 days at jellybean size. Most live in Australia and New Guinea; opossums in the Americas.

cards.headline: A newborn red kangaroo is about the size of a jellybean.
cards.body: Its mother is pregnant for only about 33 days. Then the tiny baby climbs, on its own, straight into her pouch. Welcome to the marsupials: mammals that finish growing up outside the womb.

cards.headline: Born early, finished in the pouch
cards.body: Marsupial young are born in an embryo-like state and keep developing outside the womb. The newborn makes its own way to the shelter, warmth and milk of the pouch. Not every marsupial has a full pouch; in some species the nipples are simply exposed. Either way, the milk is the point: part nursery, part kitchen.

mascot.line: Moved out, still coming home for meals. Sounds familiar.

cards.fact: A joey moves out at about 235 days, but keeps coming back for milk.
cards.context: A red kangaroo joey leaves the pouch for good at around 235 days old, then keeps suckling until about 12 months. Red kangaroos are the largest living marsupials, with males standing about 2 m tall. Not bad for a jellybean.

cards.headline: Not only in Australia
cards.body: Most marsupial species live in Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands. The rest live in the Americas, mainly South and Central America. The Virginia opossum is the only marsupial found north of Mexico. Its young are born after just 12 to 13 days, about 14 mm long, and climb into the pouch. Seen an opossum in North America? You've met a marsupial.

levels.title: Mammals That Lay Eggs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the platypus and the echidna.
levels.summary: The platypus and four echidna species are monotremes, the only mammals that lay eggs. They feed milk from fur-covered patches, not nipples. Young echidnas leave the pouch when spines grow.

cards.headline: The first platypus skin in Europe looked like a prank.
cards.body: Some naturalists suspected a hoax: a duck's bill attached to the body of a mole. George Shaw described the animal properly in 1799. The bill was real, and the platypus had a bigger surprise to come.

cards.headline: Mammals that lay eggs
cards.body: The platypus and the four living species of echidna are monotremes, the only mammals that lay eggs. The platypus lives only in Australia; the short-beaked echidna lives in Australia, and the long-beaked echidna comes from New Guinea. Every other mammal in this chapter is born alive.

mascot.line: Duck bill, eggs, and milk. The platypus refuses to pick a lane.

cards.fact: Milk, but no nipples
cards.context: A platypus mother usually lays one or two eggs and keeps them warm between her body and her tail; they hatch in about ten days. Monotremes have no nipples, so her milk seeps from two fur-covered patches on her belly, and the young suckle it there. Still milk, so still a mammal.

cards.headline: Moved out for being prickly
cards.body: A short-beaked echidna lays one egg at a time. It hatches after about 10 days, and the young suckles inside the mother's pouch for two or three months. Then its spines grow in and it becomes too prickly, so she moves it out to a burrow. Every parent has a limit. Hers is spines.

levels.title: Primates
levels.objective: After this level you can describe apes and monkeys and what we share with them.
levels.summary: Primates have forward-facing eyes, flat nails and big brains. Apes, unlike most monkeys, have no tail. Chimps and bonobos, our closest relatives, differ from us by about 1.2% of DNA.

cards.headline: Monkey or ape? Check for a tail.
cards.body: A chimpanzee has no tail, so it isn't a monkey. Neither are you. Primates come in famous kinds, and you belong to one of them. But first: what makes any of them a primate?

cards.headline: The primate toolkit
cards.body: Primates' eyes face forward, so the two fields of view overlap. They have flat nails where other mammals have claws or hooves. And for their body weight, primates have bigger brains than other land mammals. Look at your fingertips: nails, not claws. That's your primate badge.

mascot.line: Next family reunion: bring the bonobos.

cards.headline: Apes: the tailless branch
cards.body: Apes are tailless primates, while most monkeys have tails. The great apes are gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans, and humans belong to the same family, Hominidae. So when someone calls you a monkey, you can correct them: ape, please.

cards.fact: Your DNA differs from a chimp's by about 1.2 percent.
cards.context: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives, both about 1.2 percent different in DNA. Gorillas differ by about 1.6 percent, and rhesus monkeys by about 7. But you didn't evolve from any primate alive today: humans and chimps share an ancestor species that lived millions of years ago. Cousins, not grandparents.

levels.title: Wolves and Dogs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how wolves became dogs.
levels.summary: Dogs came from an ancient wolf population, at least 15,000 years ago; where and how often is debated. A puppy buried at Oberkassel about 14,000 years ago is the earliest known pet.

cards.headline: About 14,000 years ago, someone nursed a very sick puppy.
cards.body: It caught canine distemper at about 19 weeks old and was gravely ill. It lived to about 28 weeks, likely only because people cared for it. How did an animal descended from wolves end up in human arms?

cards.headline: Not today's wolves
cards.body: Dogs came from the gray wolf. But a 2014 genome study found dogs and today's wolves share a common ancestor that lived 9,000 to 34,000 years ago. Dogs came from an ancient wolf population that isn't well represented by any wolves alive now. Your dog and a modern wolf are cousins, not parent and child.

mascot.line: A mystery with fur, four legs and 72 ancient genomes. Detectives, fetch!

cards.headline: When and where? Still argued
cards.body: A 2022 study of 72 ancient wolf genomes put the change in the Ice Age, at least 15,000 years ago. Dogs matched ancient wolves from eastern Eurasia best: an eastern source fed all dogs, and a more westerly one fed some. Where it happened, and whether once or more, is still unknown. Humanity's oldest friendship has no birth certificate.

cards.fact: The oldest known pet was a puppy.
cards.context: The Oberkassel puppy was buried in Germany with a man and a woman about 14,000 years ago. Researchers call it the earliest known evidence of dogs being treated as pets. Someone sat up with a sick puppy long before anyone wrote a word. Some things haven't changed.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Mammals
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the main groups of mammals and how they live.
levels.summary: Mammals start life three ways: monotremes lay eggs, marsupials finish in a pouch, placentals grow in the womb fed by a placenta. Elephants carry young up to about 22 months.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: three ways to start a mammal's life.
cards.body: Every mammal in this chapter feeds its young milk. But they don't all begin the same way. Line up an echidna, a kangaroo and an elephant, and you're looking at an egg, a pouch and the longest pregnancy of any mammal.

mascot.line: Egg, pouch or placenta: three routes, one destination. Milk.

cards.headline: The placenta's trick
cards.body: In placental mammals, an organ called the placenta passes nutrients and wastes between the mother's blood and her unborn baby's. So the young can grow for a long time and be born well developed: an elephant carries her calf up to about 22 months, longer than any other mammal. Placentals are every living mammal except marsupials and monotremes: the lion, whale, bat, chimp and dog in this chapter, and you.

levels.title: What Makes a Bird
levels.objective: After this level you can explain feathers, beaks and hollow bones.
levels.summary: Feathers set birds apart from every other animal. Birds also have toothless beaks, lay hard-shelled eggs and make their own heat, and big fliers carry bones partly filled with air.

cards.headline: A frigatebird's skeleton weighs less than its feathers.
cards.body: That's a bird with a seven-foot wingspan, and its bones are outweighed by its coat. It sounds like a trick. It's actually a clue to what a bird is, and to how so many of them manage to be so light.

cards.headline: Feathers are the password
cards.body: Not every bird can fly, so flight can't be the test. The real password is feathers. Britannica calls them the major characteristic that sets birds apart from all other animals. A turtle has a beak, but no turtle has a single feather. If it grows feathers, it's a bird. Full stop.

cards.headline: The rest of the kit
cards.body: Every bird is a vertebrate, one of the five backbone groups from Level 3. Its beak is its upper and lower jaws wrapped in a horny sheath, and no bird has teeth. Every bird lays hard-shelled eggs. And like you, birds make their own heat (Level 5), holding steady at about 40 °C. Feathers, beak, eggs, inner furnace: that's the kit.

mascot.line: Light bones, heavy coat. It's the exact opposite of how I pack for a trip.

cards.fact: In big fliers, the bones are partly air.
cards.context: In the largest flying birds, part of the bone is replaced by air spaces. A hollow tube can buckle, though, so the big wing bones carry struts inside, like the cross-braces in a bridge. That's how a frigatebird with a seven-foot wingspan ends up with a skeleton lighter than its feathers.

levels.title: How Birds Fly
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how wings create lift.
levels.summary: A wing makes lift by turning the air flowing past it, which pushes back the opposite way. A bird's wing is also its propeller, and big breast muscles anchored to a keel drive it.

cards.headline: A bird's wing is a wing and a propeller at once.
cards.body: That's how Britannica puts it. One limb holds the bird up and drives it forward at the same time. So how does a feathered arm do two jobs, and where does the power come from?

cards.headline: Lift: turn the air down, go up
cards.body: Lift happens when a wing turns the air flowing past it. Bend that flow downward, and the air pushes the wing the opposite way: up. That's Newton's third law, action and reaction. Both the top and the bottom of the wing help turn the flow. Hold your flat hand out of a car window, tip it up a little, and you'll feel it.

cards.headline: Inner wing lifts, wing tip pulls
cards.body: A bird splits the two jobs along the length of the wing. The inner part, near the body, supplies most of the lifting surface. The wing tip supplies most of the propelling force, pulling the bird forward on every beat. Shoulder end: wing. Far end: propeller.

mascot.line: Flapping your arms won't work. You'd need a keel first. And, admittedly, feathers.

cards.fact: The power comes from the breast.
cards.context: Flying birds have a keel, a ridge on the breastbone that anchors the flight muscles. The big pectoralis pulls the wings down on the power stroke. A smaller muscle, the supracoracoideus, about one-fifth its size, raises them again. Feathers shape the wing; the breast makes it beat.

levels.title: Eggs and Nests
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how birds build nests and hatch their eggs.
levels.summary: Nests range from nothing at all to woven weaver homes. The warmth comes from the parent's bare brood patch, near 38 °C, and the chick breaks out with an egg tooth it soon loses.

cards.headline: Some bird nests weigh more than a ton. Some birds build none.
cards.body: Falcons, owls and many seabirds and shorebirds make no real nest at all. Weavers weave grass into elaborate flask-shaped homes. Every bird lays hard-shelled eggs, though. So what does an egg actually need from its parents?

cards.headline: A nest is a cradle, not a heater
cards.body: Birds build with whatever works: twigs, leaves, mud, feathers, even spiderwebs. Some swifts glue theirs together with saliva. Nests run from about 2 cm across for small hummingbirds to more than 2 m for large eagles. But a nest only holds the eggs. The warmth has to come from somewhere else.

cards.headline: The bare patch
cards.body: Near the end of egg-laying, a sitting bird loses the feathers from a patch of its belly. This brood patch grows extra blood vessels that bring hot blood right to the skin, pressed against the eggs. Most birds incubate at around 38 °C, raising or lowering their body to adjust, and they turn the eggs as they develop. If both parents sit, both may grow a patch.

mascot.line: A tooth you only need once, for the world's hardest front door. Very efficient.

cards.fact: A chick breaks out with a 'tooth' it soon loses.
cards.context: The egg tooth is a hard tip on the chick's bill; ornithologist William Yarrell discovered its role in 1826. The chick uses it to punch the first hole in the shell. In most birds it falls off a few days after hatching, and in perching birds like finches and sparrows it's absorbed into the bill. Remember, no bird has teeth. This one is a loaner.
