levels.title: Birds of Prey
levels.objective: After this level you can describe eagles, hawks and falcons.
levels.summary: Birds of prey share hooked beaks and talons. Eagles and hawks kill with their feet; falcons bite, using a notch on the beak. A trained peregrine was clocked at 242 mph in a 1999 dive.

cards.headline: In 1999, a falcon was clocked at 242 mph.
cards.body: Her name was Frightful, a trained peregrine, diving from nearly three miles up. She belongs to a group of birds built for one job: catching other animals. What turns a bird into a hunter?

cards.headline: Hooks and talons
cards.body: All birds of prey have hook-tipped beaks and sharp, curved claws called talons. The daytime hunters (hawks, eagles, vultures and falcons) are also called raptors. The night shift belongs to the owls, and they get the next level. Spot the hooked beak and the talons, and you've found a bird of prey.

cards.fact: Frightful's speed was measured by a chip on her tail.
cards.context: Falconer Ken Franklin skydived alongside her, and a small chip on her tail feathers recorded the dives. Some falcon experts called the setup artificial, since wild peregrines don't usually start that high. Audubon's field guide is more careful: in a power dive, a peregrine may possibly reach 200 mph. Even the cautious number is astonishing for a bird.

levels.title: Owls
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how owls hunt in the dark.
levels.summary: Barn owls can strike prey in total darkness by sound alone. Lopsided ears find a sound's height, a dish-shaped face funnels sound in, and muffled feathers keep the hunt quiet.

cards.headline: In 1958, an owl caught a paper wad in total darkness.
cards.body: Owls are the night shift of the birds of prey. Researchers Payne and Drury let a mouse tow a crumpled wad of paper through a pitch-dark room. The barn owl struck the paper. It couldn't see it, and paper doesn't smell like dinner. So how did it know where to strike?

cards.headline: Ears that aren't level
cards.body: It heard it. A barn owl's ears are lopsided, one slightly higher than the other. A sound from below comes in louder on one side, a sound from above on the other, so the owl can tell a sound's height as well as its direction. That pins prey down in three dimensions. Audubon says barn owls are better at finding prey by ear than any other animal tested.

cards.headline: A face shaped like a dish
cards.body: All owls have a facial disc, a ring of short feathers around the face. The barn owl's heart-shaped disc is especially prominent, and it works like a satellite dish, funneling sound toward the ears. That face you find so cute is mostly hearing equipment.

mascot.line: Shh. The best hunter in the room is the one you can't hear.

cards.fact: Owl wings are built to hush.
cards.context: Owl flight feathers have comb-like serrations along the front edge that break up the air, a velvety surface, and a soft fringe on the trailing edge. Together they damp the swoosh of flight. That may help twice: the prey can't hear the owl coming, and the owl can keep listening to the prey.

levels.title: Penguins
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how penguins survive the cold and swim.
levels.summary: Penguin wings became flippers, and dense, nearly airless bones cut buoyancy for diving. Waterproof feathers, fat and heat-saving feet keep them warm; emperor males fast on fat.

cards.headline: Penguins fly. Just not through the air.
cards.body: Penguins live only in the Southern Hemisphere, and their wings evolved into flippers that drive them through the water. So what does it take to rebuild a bird for swimming, and to stay warm doing it?

cards.headline: Heavy bones on purpose
cards.body: Remember Level 21's air-filled bones? Penguins went the other way. Their limb bones are denser than nearly any other bird's, with almost no air inside. Scientists usually read that as ballast: less buoyancy means diving costs less energy. Emperor penguins, the deepest-diving birds on Earth, reach about 550 m. A floaty skeleton would fight them all the way down.

cards.headline: Coat, blanket, heat-saving feet
cards.body: A penguin wears a dense coat of short, stiff, waterproof feathers that trap air. Under that sits a thick layer of fat. And its legs and feet carry a countercurrent heat-exchange system that keeps the heat it loses to ice and cold water to a minimum. Three layers of defense, and the feet are one of them.

mascot.line: Nine weeks, no snacks, Antarctic winter. Parenting, but on hard mode.

cards.fact: An emperor penguin dad fasts for 9 weeks in winter.
cards.context: Emperor penguins breed in the coldest, darkest months of the Antarctic winter. The male incubates the egg for 9 weeks without eating, living off a thick fat reserve. Penguins also huddle in large groups to share body heat and shelter from the weather. His fat is both his blanket and his pantry.

levels.title: Hummingbirds
levels.objective: After this level you can describe hummingbirds' speed and energy needs.
levels.summary: A flying ruby-throated hummingbird's heart tops 1,200 beats a minute, and hummingbirds are the only vertebrates that can hover for long. Tiny and poorly insulated, they save energy at night in torpor.

cards.headline: A hummingbird's heart can beat more than 1,200 times a minute.
cards.body: That's a ruby-throated hummingbird in flight, according to the Smithsonian's National Zoo. At rest it drops to about 225. A human athlete working hard reaches only about 150. What kind of life needs an engine like that?

cards.headline: The only true hoverers
cards.body: Hummingbirds are the only vertebrates that can hover for a sustained time, parked in midair in front of a flower. They can fly backward, and even upside down. A ruby-throated hummingbird beats its wings about 70 times a second in ordinary flight, and more than 200 times a second in a dive. That's a lot of flapping just to stand still.

cards.headline: A tiny furnace with a thin coat
cards.body: Hummingbirds weigh just 2 to 20 grams, their feathers are poor insulation, and their metabolic demands are enormous. Remember Level 5: making your own heat costs food, which is why a lizard can eat so much less than a warm-blooded animal its size. A hummingbird is the extreme case, a tiny bird with a thin coat and a racing engine.

mascot.line: Full throttle all day, power-saving mode all night. Honestly, relatable.

cards.fact: At night, a hummingbird can nearly switch itself off.
cards.context: When a night is cold or food is short, a hummingbird can drop into torpor: a deep, sleep-like state with its metabolism slowed to a minimum and its body temperature very low. In a study published in 2020, a black metaltail hummingbird in the Peruvian Andes cooled to 3.3 °C, the lowest body temperature recorded for any bird or non-hibernating mammal.

levels.title: Parrots and Crows
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why parrots and crows are so clever.
levels.summary: Wild New Caledonian crows make hook tools, and Betty bent a wire into one in 2002. Alex the parrot named objects, colors and numbers. Their small brains are packed with neurons.

cards.headline: In 2002, a crow named Betty bent a wire into a hook.
cards.body: She was in an Oxford lab, facing a small bucket of food at the bottom of a tube. Another crow, Abel, had taken the hooked wire, leaving her a straight one. It was only the crows' fifth time handling wire. So Betty bent her own hook and lifted the bucket out.

cards.headline: Toolmakers in the wild
cards.body: Betty's species already had a reputation. In 1996, biologist Gavin Hunt reported in Nature that wild New Caledonian crows make hook tools: hooked twigs, and stepped-cut tools snipped from the barbed edges of pandanus leaves. They use them to fish invertebrates out of dead wood. Hunt noted the tools were standardized, in distinct types. Not random sticks: a toolkit.

cards.fact: A parrot named Alex could name 7 colors.
cards.context: Scientist Irene Pepperberg worked with Alex, an African grey parrot, for about 30 years. Using English words, he learned to identify 50 objects, 7 colors, 5 shapes and quantities up to 6, plus a zero-like idea. He died in 2007, at 31. Not bad for a 'birdbrain.'

mascot.line: Small package, dense wiring. The bird brain was underrated all along.

cards.headline: Small brains, packed tight
cards.body: How do they do it with such small heads? A 2016 study counted brain cells in 28 bird species. Parrot and songbird brains held, on average, about twice as many neurons as primate brains of the same mass. Large-brained parrots and corvids (the crow family) matched or beat primates with much bigger brains in forebrain neurons. Calling someone a birdbrain may be a compliment.

levels.title: Migration
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how birds migrate thousands of miles.
levels.summary: In 2022 a young godwit flew about 13,560 km nonstop on stored fat. Tracked Arctic terns fly about 70,900 km a year. Migrants steer by the sun, the stars and magnetism.

cards.headline: A young bird flew for 11 days without landing once.
cards.body: In October 2022, a juvenile bar-tailed godwit tagged B6 left Alaska and flew nonstop across the Pacific to Tasmania, Australia. No stops for food, water or rest. How does any bird pull that off?

mascot.line: No snacks, no naps, no landing for 11 days. I get restless on a two-hour train ride.

cards.fact: About 13,560 km in one go: the longest nonstop flight on record.
cards.context: That's 8,425 miles, tracked by a 5-gram solar-powered satellite tag. The U.S. Geological Survey calls it the longest documented nonstop flight by any animal. The fuel was fat: B6 fattened up on Alaska's Kuskokwim Delta before leaving, and some migrating birds double their body weight before a journey. The fuel tank is the bird.

cards.headline: The tern that follows summer
cards.body: The Arctic tern goes farther, just not in one hop. In a 2010 study, scientists fitted 11 terns from Greenland and Iceland with 1.4-gram geolocators. On average, each flew 70,900 km a year between the Arctic and the Southern Ocean, with a stopover in the North Atlantic: the longest round-trip migration ever recorded electronically. In 2016, Newcastle University reported a Farne Islands tern with an estimated 96,000 km round trip.

cards.fact: A tern's lifetime of flying could take it to the Moon and back three times.
cards.context: Arctic terns can live more than 30 years, so the 2010 study estimated a lifetime of migrations may top 2.4 million km. And they don't get lost: migrating birds can tell which direction they're flying from the sun, the stars and Earth's magnetic field. Sun, stars and magnetism: three compasses in one small head.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Birds
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how birds' bodies are built for flight and survival.
levels.summary: A bird's body is a flying machine. The ostrich dropped the flying: no keel, no flight, but fast two-toed feet, the largest living bird and the largest egg of any living bird.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: a bird that traded flying for running.
cards.body: This chapter built a flying machine: feathers, air-filled bones, lift from turned air, and a keel for the flight muscles. Now meet a bird that dropped the flying and kept the rest.

mascot.line: Two toes, one very fast plan: leave.

cards.fact: The ostrich is the largest living bird.
cards.context: An adult male may stand 2.75 m tall and weigh more than 150 kg. It lives in open country in Africa, and it cannot fly. Instead, a frightened ostrich can run at about 70 km/h, on the only two-toed feet of any bird, the main toe built almost like a hoof. Its escape plan is its legs.

cards.headline: No keel, no flight
cards.body: Remember Level 22's keel, the breastbone ridge that anchors the flight muscles? Ostriches, emus and their relatives, the ratites, have a smooth, raftlike breastbone with no keel at all. With nowhere to anchor big flight muscles, they can't fly. Size still counts, though: the ostrich lays the largest egg of any living bird, about 15 cm long.

levels.title: What Makes a Reptile
levels.objective: After this level you can explain scales, eggs and cold blood in reptiles.
levels.summary: Reptiles wear keratin scales that hold water in and lay amniotic eggs that carry their own water, so they breed on dry land. Four living groups, mostly ectotherms.

cards.headline: A reptile egg carries its own pond.
cards.body: Most amphibians have to lay soft, jelly-covered eggs in water. Reptiles broke that rule, and it freed them to breed on dry land. Two inventions did it: a skin that keeps water in, and an egg that does the same.

cards.headline: A raincoat that keeps the water in
cards.body: Run a finger along a lizard and you'll feel scales, a continuous coat of them over most reptiles. Their main ingredient is keratin, the same tough family of protein that builds your fingernails and hair. Scaly skin with keratin and waxy fats cuts water loss, and it was one of the key adaptations that let reptiles live on land. A reptile keeps its moisture sealed in.

mascot.line: Why lug your eggs to a pond when you can pack the pond inside the egg?

cards.fact: A reptile egg is a private pond with a lid.
cards.context: Inside, the embryo floats in the amnion, a fluid-filled sac that gives it its own watery world. Around it, a leathery or hard, calcium-based shell holds in water and nutrients. That egg freed reptiles from needing water to breed, so they can lay on dry land, while most amphibians still lay soft, jelly-like eggs in water. Some reptiles skip laying and give birth to live young instead.

cards.headline: Four families, one thermostat
cards.body: Today's reptiles come in four groups: turtles, the tuatara, lizards and snakes, and crocodilians. Together they number more than 12,500 species. Remember Level 5? Most reptiles are ectotherms, taking their heat from outside: they bask in the sun or lie on warm surfaces to heat up, then slip into shade to cool down. Scales, shelled eggs and borrowed heat: that's the reptile kit.

levels.title: Snakes
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how snakes move, hunt and swallow their prey.
levels.summary: Limbless snakes move in four main ways, smell in stereo with a forked tongue and the Jacobson's organ, and swallow big prey whole because the halves of their lower jaw aren't joined at the chin.

cards.headline: A python can swallow a whole deer, with no hands to help.
cards.body: Snakes have no legs, no movable eyelids and no external ears. Yet in Everglades National Park, a wild Burmese python was found with an adult white-tailed deer inside it. Getting there, finding the meal and getting it down each take a different trick.

cards.headline: Four ways to go without legs
cards.body: Snakes have four main ways of moving. The classic is serpentine: the body bends into S-shaped loops, and each loop shoves against whatever it can find, like rocks, twigs or pebbles. Heavy snakes like boas often creep in a straight line instead, lifting, anchoring and pushing with their belly scales, caterpillar-style. Concertina and sidewinding, the one for sand, complete the set. Every pebble in the path is a foothold.

cards.headline: Smelling in stereo
cards.body: To find a meal, a snake flicks its tongue. Each flick grabs scent particles from the air or ground and delivers them to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of its mouth, which detects smells. The fork matters: each tip samples a different spot, so the snake can tell which side a smell is stronger on. It works like your two ears telling you where a sound came from. That flickering tongue is really half of a nose.

mascot.line: No knife, no fork, no chewing. Just very patient jaws.

cards.fact: A snake's chin comes apart.
cards.context: Unlike your lower jawbone, the two halves of a snake's lower jaw aren't joined at the chin, so they can spread wide and move independently. The snake walks its mouth over the prey, one side and then the other, while stretchy skin widens the gape. That's how most snakes swallow prey whole, even prey much larger than their heads. It's how that Everglades python fit a deer.

levels.title: Venom
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how venom works and how antivenom is made.
levels.summary: Venom is injected; poison harms when eaten or touched. Venom's toxins attack nerves or blood. Antivenom comes from antibodies horses make against small doses of venom.

cards.headline: Calling a cobra 'poisonous' is technically wrong.
cards.body: Poison and venom are both toxins, and people swap the words all the time. The difference is how the toxin gets into you, and it's the key to how this level's cure works.

cards.headline: Who bites whom
cards.body: Venom has to be injected: a fang, stinger or spine wounds you and delivers it. Poison works the other way round. It harms when it's eaten or absorbed through the skin, so a poisonous animal, like a pufferfish, just waits to be touched or tasted. The rule of thumb: if it bites you and you get sick, it's venomous. If you bite it and you get sick, it's poisonous.

cards.headline: What's in the cocktail
cards.body: Venom is made in special glands, and it's a mixture of toxic enzymes and other proteins. Some are neurotoxins, which attack the nervous system; in a snakebite that can mean paralysis that stops a person breathing. Others are hemotoxins, which attack the blood and blood vessels, causing bleeding or wrecking the blood's ability to clot. A venom isn't one weapon. It's a toolkit.

mascot.line: The horse does the hard part. Its immune system learns the venom so ours don't have to.

cards.fact: Antivenom is still made with the help of horses.
cards.context: In the 1890s the French scientist Albert Calmette made the first snake antivenom, against cobra venom, and in 1895 began producing it with horses. The method has barely changed: a horse, or sometimes a sheep, gets small doses of venom, its immune system makes antibodies, and those are collected from its blood. WHO estimates about 81,000 to 138,000 people die from snakebites each year and calls antivenom the most effective treatment. If anyone is bitten, get medical help.

levels.title: Turtles and Tortoises
levels.objective: After this level you can describe turtles and tortoises and their shells.
levels.summary: A turtle's shell is its own backbone and ribs, so it can't leave it. Tortoises are the land-only turtles. In sea turtles, nest temperature sets the hatchlings' sex.

cards.headline: You can't take a turtle out of its shell. The shell is part of the turtle.
cards.body: Cartoons show turtles slipping out of their shells like sleeping bags. Real turtles can't, and the reason is inside: the shell is built from the turtle's own skeleton.

cards.headline: A box made of ribs
cards.body: The shell has two halves: the domed carapace on top and the plastron underneath, joined along each side into a rigid box. The carapace is built from the turtle's backbone and ribs, fused to bony plates that form in the skin. So a turtle can never leave its shell, and it doesn't shed it the way some reptiles shed their skin. It isn't a house the turtle lives in. It's a ribcage worn on the outside.

cards.headline: Every tortoise is a turtle
cards.body: All tortoises are turtles, but not all turtles are tortoises. A tortoise is simply a turtle that lives only on land; other turtles live in fresh water or the sea. Together they make more than 350 species, found on every continent except Antarctica. Think of 'turtle' as the family name and 'tortoise' as the branch that never goes swimming.

mascot.line: The nest's thermostat is doing a job most animals leave to genes.

cards.fact: In sea turtles, the sand chooses boy or girl.
cards.context: Sea turtle eggs that incubate below 27.7 °C hatch as males; above 31 °C, as females; in between, a mix. That makes warming beaches a problem. A NOAA-led study published in 2018 found that 99.1 percent of young green turtles from the warmer northern Great Barrier Reef beaches were female. Hot sand, missing brothers.

levels.title: Crocodiles
levels.objective: After this level you can describe crocodiles and alligators and how to tell them apart.
levels.summary: Crocodilians lurk with eyes, ears and nostrils on top. Crocodiles: V-shaped snout, lower teeth showing. Alligators: U-shaped snout. Tongue salt glands let crocodiles go to sea.

cards.headline: Alligator or crocodile? Wait for it to close its mouth.
cards.body: Alligators, crocodiles, caimans and gharials are all crocodilians, and at a glance they blur together. But a closed mouth gives the game away. So does a trip into seawater.

cards.headline: Built to lurk
cards.body: Every crocodilian is shaped for ambush. Its eyes, ears and nostrils sit on top of its head, so they stay above the surface while the rest of the body hides underwater. It can watch, listen and breathe without showing much more than a bump. From the bank, a waiting crocodile looks like a log with eyebrows.

items.label: Crocodile

mascot.line: Snout shape, teeth and a salty tongue. Three clues, one confident identification.

cards.fact: A crocodile's tongue works as a salt pump.
cards.context: Alligators live mostly in fresh water and can handle salt water only briefly, because they have no salt glands. Crocodiles have salt glands in their tongues that get rid of the extra salt. That's how the saltwater crocodile, the largest living crocodilian at up to 23 feet (about 7 meters), can turn up far out at sea.

levels.title: Lizards and Chameleons
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how chameleons change color.
levels.summary: Chameleons are lizards that shift colour by tuning nanocrystals in skin cells (Geneva, 2015). Their big changes are social signals and help with heat, not background matching.

cards.headline: A chameleon's colour show isn't mainly about hiding.
cards.body: The idea that chameleons change colour to match their background is a popular misconception. Their fastest, brightest changes are meant to be seen. And in 2015, scientists worked out how the colours are made. The answer isn't paint.

cards.headline: Colour from crystals
cards.body: Chameleons are lizards, and like many animals they can move pigment around inside skin cells. But in 2015 a University of Geneva team showed their brightest shifts come from something stranger. Panther chameleons' skin cells, called iridophores, hold a lattice of tiny guanine crystals. Calm, the crystals sit close together and reflect blue. Excited, the chameleon loosens the lattice, and the skin reflects yellows and reds. The colour is tuned, not painted on.

cards.headline: Talking in colour
cards.body: So who is the show for? Panther chameleons make their fastest, most complex changes in social moments: a male facing a rival, or courting a female, often within a minute or two. Their colours also shift with light, temperature and mood, like fright, victory or defeat. What they don't do is repaint themselves to match whatever branch they're on. The fireworks are a message, not a disguise.

mascot.line: Blue for calm, bright for a rival, dark for a cold morning. A whole wardrobe in one skin.

cards.fact: A chameleon also dresses for the weather.
cards.context: Remember Level 5? Chameleons are ectotherms, so they rely on outside heat. Darker colours absorb more light, so a chilly chameleon can darken to warm up faster while it basks. Deeper in the skin, a second layer of larger crystals reflects much of the sun's infrared, which may help keep it from overheating. Its skin is a billboard and a thermostat at once.

levels.title: Amphibians
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how frogs and other amphibians live in water and on land.
levels.summary: Amphibians live a 'dual life' and lay shell-less eggs in water. Their moist skin drinks and breathes, which let in the chytrid fungus; IUCN (2023) found 41% of species threatened.

cards.headline: A frog drinks through its skin.
cards.body: An amphibian takes in most of its water through its skin rather than by drinking, and it breathes through that skin too. That open, living skin is the group's great trick. It also turned out to be their weak spot.

cards.headline: A double life
cards.body: Amphibian loosely means 'dual life' in Greek, a nod to the metamorphosis many frogs and salamanders go through, starting life in one shape and ending in another. Most amphibians lay soft, jelly-covered eggs with no shell, in water or damp places: none of Level 31's packed pond. The class has three branches: frogs, salamanders and the legless caecilians.

cards.headline: Skin that drinks and breathes
cards.body: An amphibian's skin stays moist and permeable, kept wet by mucus glands. Water soaks in across it, and it's one of the animal's three breathing surfaces. Where a lizard wears a raincoat, a frog wears something closer to a wet lung. That works beautifully in damp places, and it leaves the skin wide open to whatever lands on it.

mascot.line: The very skin that lets a frog drink and breathe was the door the fungus walked through.

cards.fact: In 2023, IUCN found 41 percent of amphibian species threatened with extinction.
cards.context: That makes amphibians the most threatened class of vertebrates. From 1980 to 2004 the leading cause of worsening risk was disease from the chytrid fungus, which infects the skin and upsets the salts it moves into the body until the heart stops. A 2019 study linked chytrid to declines in at least 501 amphibian species, including 90 presumed extinctions. Since 2004, climate change has taken the lead.

levels.title: From Tadpole to Frog
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a tadpole turns into a frog.
levels.summary: A tadpole has gills, a finned tail and no legs. Hind legs come first, then lungs and front legs; the tail is absorbed. Gudernatsch (1912) showed thyroid hormone drives it.

cards.headline: A tadpole never drops its tail. Its body absorbs it.
cards.body: Somewhere between two months and three years, a swimming larva with gills rebuilds itself into a frog with lungs and legs. Here's the order of the work, and the chemical that gives the orders.

cards.headline: Barely a frog at all
cards.body: A young tadpole looks nothing like its parents. It usually has gills, a long, finned tail and no limbs at all, and it's often a plant-eater. Everything about it is built for life underwater: it breathes with gills where its parents will use lungs. To become a frog, almost every part has to be rebuilt.

mascot.line: One gland, one hormone, a whole new body. The thyroid is the site foreman.

cards.fact: In 1912, tadpoles fed horse thyroid changed early.
cards.context: Friedrich Gudernatsch fed tadpoles bits of several horse organs. Only the thyroid gland sped up their metamorphosis. Later, removing a tadpole's own thyroid stopped the change entirely: without thyroid hormone, the rebuild never happens. Level 10's gray tree frog, algae-eater as a tadpole and insect-hunter as an adult, goes through this same hormone-driven makeover.

levels.title: Dinosaurs Were Reptiles
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what dinosaurs were and how we know about them.
levels.summary: Dinosaurs were reptiles, named by Owen in 1842. They stood on pillar-like legs; pterosaurs and sea reptiles were not dinosaurs. Maiasaura's nests show eggs laid on land.

cards.headline: The first dinosaur was named mostly from a jawbone.
cards.body: In 1824, William Buckland described Megalosaurus from fossils made up mainly of a lower jawbone with a few teeth. Nobody yet had a word for the kind of animal it was. So what were these creatures, and how can we tell?

cards.headline: Terrible reptiles
cards.body: In 1842, Richard Owen studied the remains of three giant extinct animals and proposed a new group: Dinosauria. He built the name from Greek deinos, 'terrible' or 'fearfully great', and sauros, 'reptile' or 'lizard'. The reptile part was right. Dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles, in the same class as the turtles, lizards and crocodilians earlier in this chapter. Don't let 'lizard' fool you, though. Look at the legs.

cards.headline: Legs like pillars
cards.body: What set dinosaurs apart was how they stood. They held their legs straight under the body like columns, the way elephants do, instead of sprawled out to the sides like a lizard's. Their hip sockets even had a hole right through. Flying pterosaurs and sea reptiles like plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs were reptiles too, but on separate branches. Reptiles, yes. Dinosaurs, no.

mascot.line: Eggshells, tiny bones and worn baby teeth. The clues add up to a caring parent.

cards.fact: One dinosaur left a whole nesting ground.
cards.context: In 1978, a nesting site turned up near Choteau, Montana: nests with clutches of eggs, broken eggshells and baby dinosaurs. The babies were too young to walk, yet their teeth were worn, so someone was feeding them. Jack Horner and Bob Makela named the animal Maiasaura, 'good mother lizard'. Eggs in nests on land: the reptile plan from Level 31, preserved in stone.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Reptiles and Amphibians
levels.objective: After this level you can compare reptiles and amphibians.
levels.summary: Reptiles: dry scales, shelled eggs on land. Amphibians: moist skin, jelly eggs, often metamorphosis. Both ectotherms. A salamander looks like a lizard: no scales, no claws.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: it looks like a lizard, but it's a salamander.
cards.body: Long body, four legs, a tail. Is it a reptile or an amphibian? This chapter gave you everything you need to tell. Let's line the two classes up, then meet a mountain range full of lookalikes.

cards.headline: Check the toes
cards.body: A salamander and a lizard can share a silhouette, so look closer. The lizard has dry, scaly skin, claws on its toes and ear openings, and lays eggs in a leathery shell. The salamander has smooth, moist skin, no claws and no ear openings, and its eggs are wrapped in clear jelly. Same outline, different class.

mascot.line: No lungs, no scales, no claws. Just one very hard-working skin.

cards.fact: Many salamanders have no lungs at all.
cards.context: Great Smoky Mountains National Park has more salamander species than anywhere else on Earth, more than 30, and most of them are lungless. They breathe through tiny blood vessels in their skin and the linings of their mouths and throats. Level 37's skin that breathes, taken all the way.

levels.title: What Makes a Fish
levels.objective: After this level you can explain gills, fins and scales.
levels.summary: Fish breathe oxygen dissolved in water through blood-rich gills, steer with paired fins and wear bony scales that grow all their lives. Most are cold-blooded; the opah is the warm exception.

cards.headline: A fish needs oxygen as much as you do. It just never comes up for air.
cards.body: Chapter 5 heads underwater, and the first animal to explain is the obvious one. A fish spends its whole life submerged, yet it breathes oxygen all day long. The trick is its gills. So what else, besides gills, makes a fish a fish?

cards.headline: Breathing water, sort of
cards.body: Water carries a little oxygen dissolved in it, the way soda carries its fizz. A fish takes water in through its mouth and sends it over its gills: fleshy filaments packed with blood vessels. As the water flows past, oxygen slips into the blood and carbon dioxide slips out. A fish doesn't drink its air. It sieves it.

cards.headline: Steering fins and bony armor
cards.body: Fins do the driving. The pectoral fins, the pair on a fish's sides, are crucial for steadying and steering, working with the fins on its back and tail to keep it balanced. Scales are the armor. On a bony fish, each scale is a thin plate of bone overlapping the next like roof shingles, and it keeps growing for the fish's whole life. The armor gets upgraded as the owner grows.

mascot.line: A warm-blooded fish. Somewhere, a biology textbook just sighed.

cards.fact: Most fish are cold-blooded. The opah breaks the rule.
cards.context: Remember Level 5? Fish sit with the ectotherms, taking their heat from the water around them, like reptiles and amphibians. Most fish species do. The opah doesn't: it is warm-blooded, and a heat-exchange system in its gills helps keep it warm. So even "fish are cold-blooded" is a rule with a footnote.

levels.title: Sharks
levels.objective: After this level you can describe sharks and their senses.
levels.summary: Sharks are boneless, cartilage-framed fish older than trees. NOAA counts eight senses, from a sharp nose to a lateral line that feels pressure changes. Bites are rare: 65 unprovoked worldwide in 2025.

cards.headline: Sharks are older than trees.
cards.body: Sharks have been around for about 400 million years. The earliest trees showed up around 350 million years ago. So sharks were cruising the seas before the first forest cast a shadow. What is an animal that old built from, and how does it find its food?

cards.headline: A skeleton you could bend
cards.body: Sharks are fish, but they have no bones at all. Remember Level 41's bony fish, with scales of bone? Sharks are the other kind: cartilaginous fishes. Their whole skeleton is cartilage, the lightweight, flexible stuff that shapes your ear. Fold your ear over and let go. That's shark skeleton material.

cards.headline: Eight senses
cards.body: NOAA counts eight shark senses. Five are ones you have too: sight, hearing, smell, touch and taste. A shark's nose is famously sharp; it can smell blood in the water from a long way off. Then there's the lateral line, a row of tiny pores running from snout to tail. As water flows through them, sensory cells pick up changes in pressure. A shark feels the water around it move.

mascot.line: Older than trees and still not very interested in people. Honestly, fair.

cards.fact: Shark bites are rare: 65 unprovoked bites worldwide in 2025.
cards.context: That count comes from the International Shark Attack File, which tracks bites around the world. The 2025 total was in line with the average of 61 a year from 2020 to 2024, and the File calls the number extremely low. Eight senses tuned for finding food, 400 million years of practice, and people are still very rarely on the menu.

levels.title: The Deep Sea
levels.objective: After this level you can describe animals that live in the dark deep ocean.
levels.summary: Below about 1,000 meters no sunlight reaches, and food is scarce so far from the sunlit plankton. Most deep animals make their own light; female anglerfish fish with a lure lit by bacteria.

cards.headline: Below 1,000 meters, the sun never shows up.
cards.body: No dawn, no dusk, just dark water all the way down. Yet the deep sea isn't pitch black. Something down there is making its own light. Who lives in a place like that, and what do they eat?

cards.headline: A long way from lunch
cards.body: Remember Level 7? Every food chain starts with producers, and producers need sunlight. In the ocean, that means plankton near the bright surface. Down in the midnight zone, it's dark, cold and crushed by pressure, and it's a very long way from the bottom of the food chain. That distance limits how much life the deep can hold. Down here, nobody can afford to miss a meal.

cards.fact: In one deep-sea survey, three quarters of the animals could glow.
cards.context: In 2017, MBARI scientists Severine Martini and Steve Haddock tallied the animals in Monterey Bay, from the surface down to 4,000 meters. Three quarters of them can make their own light, a trick called bioluminescence. In water the sun never reaches past 1,000 meters, the animals bring their own lamps.

mascot.line: Bring your own light and your own bait. The anglerfish packs for every occasion.

cards.headline: A fishing rod with a night-light
cards.body: Meet the anglerfish. Adult females of most species carry a lure, the esca, dangling from a "fishing rod" above the mouth. The glow comes from bioluminescent bacteria living inside it. Prey drift toward the light and find a big mouth of sharp, backward-pointing teeth waiting. It's fishing, with the bait built in.

levels.title: Octopuses
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why octopuses are so intelligent.
levels.summary: The common octopus has about 500 million neurons, two thirds of them in its arms, and it solves puzzles and remembers the answers. It also has three hearts and blue, copper-based blood.

cards.headline: Most of an octopus's neurons aren't in its head.
cards.body: About two thirds of them are in its arms. Imagine your hands holding most of your thinking. How does an animal built like that end up so clever?

cards.headline: Brains in the arms
cards.body: The common octopus has about 500 million neurons, roughly as many as a dog. About two thirds of them sit in its arms, not its head. That lets an arm work on a problem while the central brain handles other tasks. Every arm gets its own assistant, and the boss gets some peace and quiet.

cards.headline: What a clever octopus can do
cards.body: Scientists have watched octopuses figure out how to open a clamshell that was wired shut. They find their way through mazes, solve problems, and remember the solutions afterward. Once an octopus has cracked a puzzle, it keeps the answer. That memory is the difference between lucky and smart.

mascot.line: Three hearts and blue blood. The octopus is basically royalty with a backup plan.

cards.fact: Three hearts, and blood that runs blue.
cards.context: Two of an octopus's hearts pump blood past its gills. Remember Level 41? That's where blood picks up oxygen from the water, just as it does in a fish. The third heart sends the oxygen-rich blood to the organs and muscles, and it stops beating when the octopus swims. The blood is blue because its oxygen carrier, hemocyanin, uses copper instead of the iron in your hemoglobin.

levels.title: Jellyfish
levels.objective: After this level you can describe jellyfish and how they sting.
levels.summary: A jellyfish is about 95 percent water, with no brain, heart or blood: a nerve net and one opening do the job. It stings with nematocysts, harpoons that fire in about 700 nanoseconds.

cards.headline: A jellyfish is about 95 percent water.
cards.body: No brain. No heart. Not even blood. It's close to a bag of seawater with a plan. So how does something that simple catch its dinner?

cards.headline: Simple, not sloppy
cards.body: A jellyfish senses its world with a nerve net, a simple web of nerves instead of a brain. Its gut is just as minimal: one cavity works as both stomach and intestine, and a single opening serves as both mouth and anus. Everything goes in and out the same door. Economical, if not elegant.

cards.headline: Harpoons on a hair trigger
cards.body: The hunting happens in stinging capsules called nematocysts. Each holds a tiny harpoon, coiled up and waiting. Trigger them and hundreds fire at once. Each jab lasts about 700 nanoseconds and hits hard enough to pierce a crustacean's shell. That's how an animal without a brain gets through armor.

mascot.line: Proof that a very short to-do list can still get the job done.

cards.fact: No brain, no heart, still an animal.
cards.context: Run a jellyfish through Level 1's checklist. Many cells, no cell walls: check. Eats other living things: check, caught with harpoons. Level 1 put jellyfish on the animal map for exactly these reasons. The checklist never asked for a brain, a heart or blood.

levels.title: Coral Is an Animal
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that corals are colonies of tiny animals.
levels.summary: A coral is a colony of tiny polyps that build limestone skeletons and catch food with stinging cells, so they are animals. Their algae are food and color; stressed corals expel them and bleach.

cards.headline: A coral is not a plant. It's a crowd of tiny animals.
cards.body: Corals stay fixed to the ocean floor, so plenty of people take them for plants. Remember Level 1's sponges, long mistaken for plants too? Corals pull the same trick. Here's who really lives inside.

cards.headline: A colony the size of nickels
cards.body: Most of what we call a coral is hundreds to thousands of tiny animals called polyps. Each is soft-bodied, most no thicker than a nickel, and each builds a hard outer skeleton of limestone. Polyps catch food with tentacles armed with nematocysts, the same stingers you met on Level 45's jellyfish, their relatives. They catch their food instead of making it. That's what makes them animals.

cards.headline: Roommates that pay rent in food
cards.body: Most corals share their tissues with microscopic algae called zooxanthellae. The coral gives them shelter. The algae photosynthesize and hand over food, so much that they are the coral's main food source. They also give the coral its color. Those famous reef colors come mostly from the tenants.

mascot.line: White doesn't mean dead, but it does mean trouble. Think of a coral running on empty.

cards.fact: Stressed corals throw out their algae and turn completely white.
cards.context: That's coral bleaching. Changes in temperature, light or nutrients can cause it, and NOAA names rising ocean temperature from climate change as the leading cause. Without its algae, a coral loses its main food and its color. A bleached coral isn't dead yet: if the stress eases, it can recover. If the stress drags on, the coral eventually dies.

levels.title: Salmon Runs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how salmon return to the rivers where they hatched.
levels.summary: Sockeye hatch in fresh water, grow at sea, then swim upstream to spawn where they were born, guided by the remembered smell of home. They die within weeks, and their bodies feed the river.

cards.headline: A sockeye salmon swims many miles upstream to spawn where it was born.
cards.body: It hatched in fresh water, spent years at sea, and now it's heading home, usually to the very stream or lake where its life began. It has no map and no one to follow. How does it find the way?

events.label: Hatches in a freshwater stream, river or lake
Grows up in fresh water
Heads out to the ocean to feed and grow
Swims back upstream, turning bright red
Dies, as every sockeye does

mascot.line: Imagine finding your childhood home by smell alone. Salmon never need to ask for directions.

cards.headline: Following its nose home
cards.body: Before a young salmon leaves for the sea, it learns the particular smell of its home stream. Scientists call this imprinting. Years later, the grown fish uses those odor memories to steer home. Salmon also imprint on Earth's magnetic field at the spot where they first reach the sea, a second clue for the long trip back. Home, for a salmon, is a smell it never forgets.

cards.fact: A salmon's last trip feeds the next generation.
cards.context: All sockeye die within a few weeks of spawning. Bears and eagles feast on them along the way; Level 6's bears are omnivores, eating berries and salmon. What's left of the dead fish gives energy and nutrients to the river, helping newly hatched salmon grow and survive. Bear, salmon, river, young salmon: one strand of Level 7's food web.

cards.headline: Salmon runs: explained
learned: Hatch in fresh water, grow at sea

Guided by the remembered smell of home
All sockeye die after spawning; their bodies feed the river

levels.title: Tide Pools
levels.objective: After this level you can describe tide pool animals like starfish and crabs.
levels.summary: Tide pools sit in the intertidal zone, flooded and drained twice a day. Residents seal up or move to stay wet; hermit crabs reuse shells. Sea stars walk on tube feet and eat with an outside stomach.

cards.headline: Twice a day, the sea leaves. Some animals stay behind.
cards.body: On a rocky shore, the tide floods the middle of the beach and then drains away, twice every day. The animals that live there have to survive two worlds: underwater, then out in the air. How do they do it?

cards.headline: Life between the tides
cards.body: The intertidal zone is the strip where ocean meets land, between high tide and low. Level 8 called a tide pool a complete tiny ecosystem, and its residents each have a low-tide plan. Some close up inside their shells to stay moist and keep predators out. Others move down to water that stays put. Hermit crabs reuse empty shells as homes. Nobody here wastes a good shell.

cards.headline: The star that isn't a fish
cards.body: Sea stars live in the middle zone, beside the anemones. Despite the nickname "starfish," they aren't fish: no gills, no scales, no fins. (Check them against Level 41.) They glide on tiny tube feet on their undersides, which also grip their prey. And if a sea star loses an arm, it can grow a new one.

mascot.line: Bringing your own stomach to the restaurant. Bold, efficient and a little rude.

cards.fact: A sea star eats with its stomach outside its body.
cards.context: Remember Paine's ochre sea stars in Level 8, eating mussels? Here's how. A sea star grips a closed mussel with its suction feet and pulls on the shell until it opens. Then it slips its own stomach inside and digests the mussel right there. Dinner is served in the shell.

levels.title: Ocean Food Webs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how tiny plankton support life in the ocean.
levels.summary: Plankton are drifters: phytoplankton make food from sunlight near the surface, and zooplankton such as krill eat them and rise each night to feed. The ocean makes roughly half of Earth's oxygen.

cards.headline: Every night, the biggest migration on Earth happens, and you've never seen it.
cards.body: Tiny drifting animals rise from deeper water to the ocean's surface to feed, then sink back down by day. Who are these drifters, and why does the whole ocean depend on them?

cards.headline: The ocean's drifters
cards.body: Plankton are living things carried by tides and currents, too weak to swim against them. The name comes from the Greek for "drifter." Phytoplankton are the plant drifters. Zooplankton are the animal ones: krill, young fish, and weak swimmers like Level 45's jellyfish. Most plankton are microscopic, but size doesn't decide it. Swimming does.

cards.headline: Level 7's chain, zoomed in
cards.body: Remember Level 7's ocean chain? Phytoplankton feed krill, and krill feed the blue whale. Phytoplankton make food from sunlight, so they stay near the surface. Most zooplankton graze on them, rising at night to eat. With only about 10 percent of the energy climbing each step, the base has to be enormous. The largest animal known to have lived depends on life too small to see.

mascot.line: Next time you see the sea, say thanks. Quietly. The plankton are working.

cards.fact: About half of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean.
cards.context: Scientists estimate that roughly half of the planet's oxygen production happens in the sea, mostly by photosynthesizing plankton. Like plants, phytoplankton take in carbon dioxide and give off oxygen. Marine life uses about as much as the ocean makes, but half of the world's oxygen factory is floating out there, too small to see.

levels.title: Milestone: Animals With Backbones
levels.objective: After this level you can connect mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish into one family tree.
levels.summary: Five vertebrate groups share one backbone; mammals and birds make their own heat, the rest mostly take it from outside. Fish are the biggest branch: about 37,000 of about 76,000 described species.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Five groups, one backbone.
cards.body: Back in Level 3 you ran a finger down your spine: your membership card. Mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish all carry one, a column of vertebrae around the spinal cord. This chapter spent its time with the biggest branch of that family. Time to see the whole backbone family at once.

cards.headline: One backbone family, sorted by heat

items.label: Make their own heat
points: Mammals, about 37 °C
Birds, about 40 °C

items.label: Take heat from outside
points: Fish (the opah is the exception)
Amphibians and reptiles

items.label: No backbone at all
points: This chapter's jellyfish and sea stars

mascot.line: Everyone photographs the lions, and meanwhile the fish quietly win the headcount.

cards.fact: Nearly half of all vertebrate species are fish.
cards.context: IUCN's 2025 table counts about 76,000 described vertebrate species, and about 37,000 of them are fish. Put every mammal, bird, reptile and amphibian species together and they only just outnumber the fish. From Level 41's gills to Level 47's salmon, this chapter covered the backbone family's biggest branch.

levels.title: Insects
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what makes an insect an insect.
levels.summary: Insects have three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs on the thorax and an outer skeleton. About 1 million species are named; about 10 quintillion are alive at once.

cards.headline: Right now, about 10 quintillion insects are alive.
cards.body: That’s the Smithsonian’s estimate: a 1 followed by 19 zeros. Beetles, flies, ants, moths: they look wildly different, yet every one of them is built on the same simple plan. Learn the plan, and you can spot an insect anywhere.

cards.headline: Count to three, then count to six
cards.body: Every adult insect’s body comes in three parts. The head carries the eyes, the mouthparts and one pair of antennae. The middle part, the thorax, carries three pairs of legs and, in most adults, one or two pairs of wings. The abdomen holds the digestive and reproductive organs. So count to three, then count to six. Anything that fails either count isn’t an insect, however buggy it looks.

cards.fact: An insect wears its skeleton on the outside.
cards.context: Remember Level 3’s beetle, the knight that never takes off its armor? Every insect has an outer skeleton like that. It protects the soft body inside and gives the muscles something to pull on. Your skeleton holds you up from the inside; an insect’s holds it together from the outside. Armor this good has one catch, and Level 58 will show you what it is.

mascot.line: Somewhere near you, an ant is reading this over your shoulder. Statistically, several.

cards.fact: About 1 million insect species have names.
cards.context: Level 2 counted about 1.5 million described animal species, and about 1 million of them are insects. Then there are the individuals: the Smithsonian’s 10 quintillion. Treat both numbers as estimates, since nobody can census every ant in every forest. But whichever way you count, kinds or bodies, insects fill the animal kingdom.

levels.title: Ants
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how ant colonies work.
levels.summary: An ant queen lays the eggs; sterile female workers do the rest; males only mate. Scent trails lead workers to food, and leafcutter ants farm a fungus on cut leaves.

cards.headline: Every worker ant you’ve ever seen was female.
cards.body: The ant hauling a crumb across your kitchen floor? She’s a sister, not a brother, and so is every worker in her nest. An ant colony runs less like a crowd and more like a family business. So who does what?

cards.headline: One mother, a nest full of daughters
cards.body: The queen’s main job is reproduction: she lays the eggs, and she may live for many years. Her daughters, the workers, are sterile, so they put all their effort into everyone else. They build, repair and defend the nest and feed the young, the other adults and the queen. Males turn up only to mate, and after mating, a male dies. It’s less a kingdom than a very busy nursery.

cards.headline: Follow the smell
cards.body: How does a whole line of ants find the same crumb? Some ants leave scent trails made of chemicals called pheromones, and their nestmates follow the trail to the food. That’s why ants so often march in single file: each one is following the path the ants before her marked. A trail of ants is basically a smell you can see.

mascot.line: Leaves in, lunch out. Tiny farmers with no tractors and a very long head start.

cards.fact: Leafcutter ants are farmers.
cards.context: They carry cut leaves home, but they don’t eat them. The leaves feed a fungus the ants grow in their nest, and the fungus feeds the colony. Their crop is found only with the ants, never in the wild. And they got there first: ants were farming fungus tens of millions of years before people began farming, about 12,000 years ago.

levels.title: Bees
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how bees make honey and pollinate plants.
levels.summary: Honeybee workers turn nectar into honey with enzymes and wing-fanning, and build comb from their own wax. Pollen caught in a bee’s hairs rubs off on the next flower.

cards.headline: Honey is flower nectar that bees have dried out.
cards.body: A bee doesn’t find honey. She makes it, from nectar, using her own chemistry, her wings and wax from her own body. And while she’s out shopping for nectar, she does the flowers a favor they can’t do for themselves.

cards.headline: The honey recipe
cards.body: Back at the hive, enzymes break the complex sugars in nectar into simpler ones. Then the bees beat their wings to help the extra water evaporate, and when it’s ready, they seal each cell with wax. Finished honey is only about 18 percent water. It’s the world’s smallest drying room, powered by wings.

cards.fact: Beeswax comes out of the bee.
cards.context: The wax workers make comes from four pairs of wax glands on the underside of the body. With it, they build comb: two layers of six-sided cells, where the colony keeps its honey. And the builders are all daughters again. Like Level 52’s ants, honeybee workers are females that never reproduce.

mascot.line: Paid in nectar, delivers pollen, never asks for a tip. Best courier in the garden.

cards.headline: Pollen hitchhikes on fuzz
cards.body: Flowers can’t walk, so they need a courier to move pollen from a flower’s anther to a stigma. That’s pollination. A bee is a fuzzy courier: her dense coat of branched hairs catches pollen as she feeds, and some rubs off on the stigma of the next flower. Honeybee workers also pack pollen into baskets on their hind legs to take home. She gets food; the flower gets its pollen delivered.

levels.title: Butterflies
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a caterpillar becomes a butterfly.
levels.summary: Butterflies pass through egg, larva, pupa and adult. In the chrysalis most caterpillar tissue dissolves, and imaginal discs build the wings, legs and eyes.

cards.headline: Inside a chrysalis, a caterpillar digests itself.
cards.body: It releases enzymes that dissolve most of its own body into what scientists call caterpillar soup. Out of that soup comes an animal with wings, new legs and new eyes. So how do you build a butterfly from soup?

events.label: Egg: a monarch egg hatches about four days after it’s laid
Larva, the caterpillar: grows from under 1 cm to about 5 cm
Pupa, the chrysalis: the body is rebuilt inside
Adult: the winged butterfly climbs out

cards.headline: Soup with a blueprint
cards.body: The meltdown isn’t chaos. While the caterpillar was still inside its egg, it grew small groups of cells called imaginal discs, one for each adult part it would need: eyes, wings, legs and more. In the chrysalis, the discs survive, feed on the soup around them and divide fast. In a fruit fly, a wing disc can grow from about 50 cells to more than 50,000. The caterpillar carried the plans for its future the whole time.

mascot.line: Imagine carrying your grown-up self around as a tiny folded plan. Caterpillars just do it.

cards.fact: Four stages add up to complete metamorphosis.
cards.context: Going through all four, egg, larva, pupa and adult, is what biologists call complete metamorphosis. The caterpillar and the butterfly look like two different animals, but they’re one insect at two ends of the same process. The wings you admire were packed away as tiny discs inside the caterpillar.

levels.title: Spiders
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how spiders make silk and spin webs.
levels.summary: Spiders are arachnids: two body parts, eight legs, no antennae. Silk is a liquid protein that hardens as it leaves the spinnerets; many orb weavers eat and rebuild their webs.

cards.headline: A spider is not an insect. Count its legs.
cards.body: Eight, not six. Level 51’s insect test fails on the legs, and it fails on the body parts too. Spiders are arachnids, a different group altogether. And every one of them carries a silk factory in its abdomen.

cards.headline: Liquid in, thread out
cards.body: Spider silk starts as a liquid protein made in glands in the abdomen. It leaves through the spinnerets, small silk-making organs usually on the underside of the abdomen, and hardens as it’s drawn out. Not every spider builds a web; some go hunting instead. But nearly all spiders are predators, feeding mostly on insects. Silk is their fishing line.

mascot.line: Eat the leftovers, then rebuild the kitchen. Honestly, admirable housekeeping.

cards.fact: Many orb weavers eat their own webs.
cards.context: Many orb weavers that hunt at night take down their web toward dawn, eat it, and build a fresh one each night. Eating the old silk sends its protein back to the silk glands to make new silk. An orb web takes about 30 to 45 minutes to build. It’s a fishing net you swallow every morning and knit again every evening.

levels.title: Snails and Slugs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe snails, slugs and their relatives.
levels.summary: Snails and slugs are gastropods, the largest mollusk group. They glide on one muscular foot over mucus and eat with a radula of tiny teeth. Slugs lost their shells.

cards.headline: A slug is a snail that lost its shell.
cards.body: Not in an accident: over the course of evolution. In slugs, the shell has shrunk to a small leftover inside the body, or vanished completely. Snails and slugs are the same kind of animal, a gastropod, and they share some very strange equipment.

cards.headline: Meet the mollusks
cards.body: Snails and slugs are mollusks: soft-bodied invertebrates, usually wrapped wholly or partly in a shell made by a layer of tissue called the mantle. Gastropods, the snails and slugs, are the largest group of mollusks. Their relatives include clams, mussels and oysters, and also squids and octopuses. A garden snail and a squid are family, which shows how much you can do with “soft-bodied.”

cards.headline: Life on one foot
cards.body: A snail travels on its foot, a single muscular organ that ripples with waves of contraction. Land snails and slugs glide along on a track of mucus. That shiny trail across your garden path is the road a snail builds for itself as it goes.

mascot.line: Thousands of teeth and not one toothbrush. Snails really commit to the salad.

cards.fact: A snail eats with a ribbon of teeth.
cards.context: Snails and slugs eat with a jaw and a radula, a flexible band of thousands of microscopic teeth. The jaw cuts off a piece of leaf, and the radula rasps it down; covered in rows of tiny teeth, it’s coarse like sandpaper. So when a snail eats your lettuce, it isn’t biting it. It’s sanding it.

levels.title: Earthworms
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how earthworms help the soil.
levels.summary: Earthworms breathe through moist skin, open burrows for air, water and roots, and leave rich casts. Darwin estimated they move over ten tons of earth per acre a year.

cards.headline: In 1881, Charles Darwin wrote a book about worms. It was a hit.
cards.body: It sold 6,000 copies within a year, and at first it sold far faster than On the Origin of Species had. Why would anyone rush to buy a book about earthworms? Because Darwin showed what they do to the ground under your feet.

cards.headline: Breathing through skin
cards.body: An earthworm has no lungs. It breathes through its skin, and that only works while the skin stays moist, so worms need damp soil. Its body is a chain of ringlike segments, as many as 150 in one common species. Most of the time you never see them. They’re noticed mainly after heavy rain, when they come up to the surface.

cards.headline: Plowing without a plow
cards.body: Earthworms eat decaying plants and swallow plenty of soil along the way. Their burrows open passages for air, water and roots, and they drag plant material down into the ground. What comes out the other end, the worm’s casts, is richer than the surrounding soil, with nutrients in forms plants can use more easily. Every worm is a tiny tiller and a fertilizer factory in one.

mascot.line: No lungs, no plow, and still the hardest-working farmhands around.

cards.fact: More than ten tons of earth per acre, every year.
cards.context: That was Darwin’s estimate for many parts of England: more than ten tons of dry earth passing through worms’ bodies and brought up to the surface on each acre of land, every year. His conclusion was a lovely one. Long before people existed, the land was already being plowed, by earthworms.

levels.title: Crabs and Lobsters
levels.objective: After this level you can describe crustaceans and their armor.
levels.summary: Crustaceans have two pairs of antennae and shells stiffened with calcium carbonate. Armor can’t grow, so they molt and hide while the soft new shell hardens.

cards.headline: A lobster often eats its own old shell.
cards.body: Right after climbing out of it. It sounds like a strange snack, but it’s a smart move for an animal whose armor can’t grow. So how does a crab or a lobster get bigger inside a suit of armor?

cards.headline: Armor with minerals added
cards.body: Crabs, lobsters, shrimps and even wood lice, the pill bugs of the garden, are crustaceans. Like insects, they wear their skeleton on the outside, but a crustacean’s is stiffened with calcium carbonate for extra rigidity. Look at the head, too: crustaceans carry two pairs of antennae in front of the mouth, where an insect has just one pair. A pill bug is a land-going cousin of the lobster on your plate.

cards.headline: Growing means getting undressed
cards.body: A rigid outer skeleton can’t grow, so crabs and lobsters shed it now and then. That’s molting. The animal climbs out wearing a new skeleton that’s soft and flexible, stretches it by taking in water or air, and then it hardens. An American lobster molts about 20 to 25 times in its first 5 to 8 years, before it’s old enough to breed. Growing up, for a lobster, is mostly changing clothes.

mascot.line: Waste not, want not: the old shell becomes the building material for the new one.

cards.fact: A fresh soft-shell crab has to hide.
cards.context: Just after molting, a crab is extremely vulnerable to damage and predators, so it stays hidden or buried for a few days while its new shell expands and starts to harden. The shell keeps hardening for two to three months. A lobster speeds up the job by eating its old shell, which replaces lost calcium and helps harden the new one. Armor is great, until the day you change it.

levels.title: Mosquitoes
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why mosquitoes kill more people than any other animal.
levels.summary: Only female mosquitoes bite, for egg-making blood. Bites carry germs such as malaria parasites; WHO estimated 610,000 malaria deaths in 2024.

cards.headline: The CDC calls the mosquito the world’s deadliest animal.
cards.body: Not a shark, not a snake: a small insect. Mosquitoes spread malaria, dengue, West Nile, Zika and more. The bite itself isn’t what kills. What rides along with it is.

cards.headline: Only the mothers bite
cards.body: Only female mosquitoes bite people and animals. They need a blood meal to produce eggs. The rest of the time, females and males alike sip flower nectar and fruit juices. So every mosquito that has ever bitten you was a female getting ready to lay eggs. The males were off somewhere, drinking juice.

cards.fact: A mosquito starts life in water.
cards.context: Female Anopheles mosquitoes, the kind that spread malaria, lay their eggs right on water. The larvae that hatch live in the water, and so do the pupae, which don’t eat at all. Only then does the adult emerge, and only the adult female bites. From egg to adult takes about 10 to 14 days.

cards.headline: The needle is shared
cards.body: Mosquitoes pick up germs, such as viruses and parasites, when they bite infected people or animals, and spread them with later bites. Malaria works this way. It’s caused by Plasmodium parasites, which reach people mainly through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. The mosquito is the delivery van; the parasite is the cargo.

mascot.line: Small animal, big consequences. This one is worth taking seriously.

cards.fact: Malaria killed an estimated 610,000 people in 2024.
cards.context: That’s the World Health Organization’s estimate, from about 282 million cases. About 95 percent of the deaths were in WHO’s African Region, and there, children under 5 were about three-quarters of them. That toll is why a tiny insect heads the CDC’s list.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Insects and Other Invertebrates
levels.objective: After this level you can compare insects, spiders, mollusks and crustaceans.
levels.summary: Insects, spiders and crustaceans are arthropods, with jointed legs and outer skeletons: about 84% of described animal species. Snails and earthworms are built another way.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: one word links the bee, the spider and the crab.
cards.body: They look nothing alike. Yet all three share a family name that means “jointed feet.” The snail and the earthworm don’t make the cut. Let’s line them up and see why.

cards.headline: Jointed feet, and a crowd
cards.body: All three are arthropods: animals with a jointed outer skeleton made of chitin bound to protein, and a segmented body whose segments carry jointed legs. The name says it: arthropod means “jointed feet.” By Britannica’s count, about 84 percent of described animal species are arthropods, most of them insects. If you picked an animal species at random, you’d very likely land on one.

mascot.line: Joints, shells, slime or segments: the backbone-free crowd has tried every design.

cards.headline: Two outsiders without joints
cards.body: A snail has no jointed legs at all. It’s a mollusk: a soft body, often inside a shell its mantle makes, carried on one muscular foot. The earthworm has no jointed legs either: it’s a chain of ringlike segments that breathes through its skin. Same kingdom, same missing backbone, very different ways to build a body without one.

levels.title: Adaptation
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how animals are adapted to where they live.
levels.summary: An adaptation fits living things to their home. The desert fennec fox's huge ears shed heat; the Arctic fox's small ears keep it in. Populations adapt over generations; individuals don't.

cards.headline: Two foxes, two very different pairs of ears.
cards.body: The fennec, a desert fox, has the biggest ears for its size of anyone in the dog family. The Arctic fox has short, rounded ones. Same family, opposite ears. That's no accident, and the reason is where each fox lives.

cards.headline: Radiators and lids
cards.body: Like every mammal, a fox makes its own heat and keeps about 37 °C inside. In the desert, the danger is too much of it: the fennec's huge ears help release body heat and keep it cool. In the Arctic, the danger runs the other way: the Arctic fox's small ears reduce heat loss, because less of it is exposed to the cold. One fox wears radiators on its head. The other keeps the lid on.

cards.headline: What an adaptation is
cards.body: Biologists call this fit an adaptation: an adjustment to the environment that improves an animal's chances of surviving there. It can be a body feature or a behavior, and the fennec has both. Thick fur on its paws protects its feet from hot sand, and it spends the heat of the day in a burrow, hunting at night. Ears, paws and timetable, all tuned to the same desert.

mascot.line: Wishing really hard for bigger ears has never worked. Believe me, I've checked.

cards.fact: No fox ever grew its own ears bigger.
cards.context: Individual animals can't adapt. Adaptation happens in populations, over several generations, as the result of natural selection acting on inherited differences. That process gets its own chapter later. For now, the result is what counts: animals that fit their homes.

levels.title: Camouflage
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how animals hide in plain sight.
levels.summary: Camouflage hides animals: background matching copies color, shape or movement; countershading (dark back, pale belly) flattens a body; Arctic foxes change coats by season.

cards.headline: Some leaves go for a walk.
cards.body: A leaf insect doesn't just look like a leaf. When it moves, it rocks back and forth, like a leaf blown by the wind. Hiding, it turns out, is about more than color.

cards.headline: Match the background
cards.body: The simplest disguise is background matching: an animal hides by resembling its surroundings in color, shape or movement. Earth-toned deer and squirrels do it among trees, a flounder does it on the seabed, and walking sticks and walking leaves copy the plants they sit on. A predator scanning for dinner sees only more scenery.

cards.headline: Paint out the shadow
cards.body: Countershading is sneakier. The animal's back is darker than its underside, which evens out light and shadow so the body looks flat and harder to spot. Sharks use it in open water, where there's nothing to hide behind. Seen from above, a shark's dark back blends with the deep water. Seen from below, its pale belly blends with the bright surface. No background? Bring your own.

mascot.line: A new outfit every season, and it's still just trying not to be noticed.

cards.fact: The Arctic fox changes its disguise with the seasons.
cards.context: Remember Level 61's small-eared Arctic fox? Many are white in winter and grayish brown in summer, so the coat matches whichever season it's in. The white coat that hides a fox in the snow would stand out on summer ground, so it doesn't keep it.

levels.title: Warning Colors and Mimics
levels.objective: After this level you can explain bright warning colors and why some animals copy them.
levels.summary: Warning colors advertise poison. Batesian mimics are harmless copies of dangerous species; Müllerian mimics are all harmful and share a pattern. The viceroy proved Müllerian (1991).

cards.headline: The viceroy butterfly was long called a harmless fake.
cards.body: It looks like a smaller monarch, and for a long time biologists thought that was a bluff: a tasty butterfly borrowing a poisonous one's look. Then someone asked the birds.

cards.headline: Bright means back off
cards.body: A monarch caterpillar feeds on milkweed, a poisonous plant, and the butterfly keeps the poisons in its body. Its bold pattern is warning coloration: a signal to predators that this animal is toxic or dangerous. A bird that has a bad experience learns to avoid the pattern, and then avoids other species that look similar too. Camouflage says "nothing here." Warning colors say "you'll regret this."

items.label: Batesian mimicry
points: A harmless species copies a dangerous one
The scarlet king snake copies the coral snake
Described by Henry Bates, 1862

items.label: Müllerian mimicry
points: Harmful species share one pattern
Predators learn to avoid it, for all of them
Proposed by Fritz Müller, 1878

mascot.line: Sometimes science is just asking a bird, "So, how did that taste?"

cards.fact: The viceroy wasn't bluffing.
cards.context: In 1991, Ritland and Brower offered red-winged blackbirds butterfly bodies with the wings removed, so taste alone decided. The birds found viceroys about as distasteful as monarchs. So the viceroy isn't a Batesian fake but a Müllerian partner: two bad-tasting butterflies sharing one warning.

levels.title: Hibernation
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how animals survive winter by hibernating.
levels.summary: Hibernation is a long, deep drop in metabolism and temperature; torpor is the short version. Arctic ground squirrels cool below 0 °C; bears cool a little, so their status is debated.

cards.headline: This squirrel spends winter colder than ice.
cards.body: A hibernating Arctic ground squirrel lets its core temperature fall as low as −2.9 °C, and it doesn't freeze. A black bear in its den cools by only about 5 to 6 °C. Both are famous winter sleepers. So which one is hibernating?

cards.headline: Turning the furnace down
cards.body: Remember Level 5: making your own heat costs food, and winter is short on food. Hibernation is the fix, a state of greatly reduced metabolism and lowered body temperature. A true hibernator can cool to near 0 °C, take only a few breaths a minute and slow its heart until the beat is barely detectable. It lives on stored fat in a protected den, and every few weeks it warms up and wakes briefly before settling back down.

cards.headline: Torpor: the short version
cards.body: Torpor is the same slowdown on a smaller scale: body temperature falls and the body's cells slow their work. White-footed mice and shrews use daily torpor that lasts just a few hours. A hibernator returns to torpor after each brief wake-up, again and again, for weeks. One is a nap. The other is the whole season off.

mascot.line: Five months without a snack or a bathroom break. Whatever you call it, I'm impressed.

cards.fact: Does a bear truly hibernate? Scientists still argue.
cards.context: Britannica says no: a bear's temperature doesn't drop much, and it wakes fairly easily. But in 2011, a University of Alaska Fairbanks team found hibernating black bears cut their metabolism to about 25 percent of normal, and called it hibernation. The bears go 5 to 7 months without eating, drinking, urinating or defecating. Judge by temperature and bears fall short; judge by energy saved and they pass.

levels.title: Desert Survivors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how camels and other animals survive with little water.
levels.summary: A camel's hump is fat, not water; it drinks up to about 30 gallons at once and can go nearly a week without. A kangaroo rat gets water from dry seeds and wastes almost none.

cards.headline: A camel's hump holds no water at all.
cards.body: It's fat. So how does a desert animal get enough water, and hang on to it? The desert has two famous answers, one very large and one very small.

cards.headline: The camel: fill up, then go
cards.body: The hump is a food store: fat to live on when food is scarce. Packing the fat into one hump also means the rest of the body isn't wrapped in insulation in the heat. Water is a separate trick. A camel can drink up to about 30 gallons (about 114 liters) in one sitting, then go nearly a week without drinking. It doesn't carry a tank. It just refills like a bathtub.

cards.headline: The kangaroo rat: barely drink at all
cards.body: A kangaroo rat eats mostly dry seeds, yet it has almost no need to drink. Digesting a gram of seeds gives it about half a gram of water, roughly one drop for every two seeds. Its breakfast is also its water bottle.

cards.headline: Spend almost nothing
cards.body: Making water only works if you don't waste it. A kangaroo rat neither sweats nor pants, and its kidneys concentrate its urine to an almost crystal-like consistency. It also spends the hot day in its burrow and comes out at night. The camel refills big; the kangaroo rat hardly spends any.

levels.title: Polar Survivors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how polar bears and penguins survive the cold.
levels.summary: Polar bears: thick fur over black skin, a fat layer, furred soles. Penguins: tight feathers trapping air over fat, and legs whose arteries and veins swap heat so the feet lose little.

cards.headline: Under its white coat, a polar bear is black.
cards.body: Its skin is black, and its fur isn't really white either: each hair is clear, with no pigment. The white look comes from light scattering in those clear hairs. So what actually keeps a polar bear warm?

cards.headline: Coat, fat and boots
cards.body: Layers. Thick fur is the outer coat, and under the skin lies a layer of insulating fat, topped up by eating seal blubber. Even the soles of its feet are furred, for warmth and for grip on the ice. A polar bear is dressed for the Arctic from head to paw.

cards.headline: The penguin's down jacket
cards.body: Penguins solve the same problem with feathers. Short, stiff feathers packed tightly together trap a layer of air next to the skin, and that still air does most of the insulating. Beneath it lies a thick layer of fat. Feathers outside, fat inside: the same two-layer plan as the bear.

mascot.line: Cold feet, warm heart. For once, that's a compliment.

cards.fact: A penguin keeps its feet cold on purpose.
cards.context: In a penguin's legs, arteries carrying warm blood down run right beside veins bringing cold blood back up, so heat passes across before it reaches the feet. An emperor penguin's foot skin stays near 0 °C, cold enough that it doesn't melt the ice it stands on. Warm body, cold feet, and very little heat wasted in between.

levels.title: Shells, Spines and Stings
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the ways animals defend themselves.
levels.summary: Animals defend themselves with armor (the three-banded armadillo rolls into a ball), spines (porcupine quills detach in an attacker) and chemicals (a skunk warns, then sprays about 10 feet).

cards.headline: A porcupine can't throw its quills.
cards.body: It's a popular idea, but the quills are never thrown or shot. So how do they end up stuck in an attacker? This level's defenders don't hide or run. They make themselves very hard to eat.

cards.headline: Armor: become a ball
cards.body: The southern three-banded armadillo is covered in plates of leathery armor, and it can roll completely into a ball, shielding its soft belly inside. Only one other armadillo can do the same: the Brazilian three-banded armadillo. A predator that finds one is left holding a sealed box.

cards.headline: Spines: let the attacker take them
cards.body: A North American porcupine carries about 30,000 quills, attached so lightly that they come off easily in anything that grabs it. Cornered, it raises its quills, turns its back and lashes its tail. Once in a predator's skin, a quill keeps working its way deeper, about 1 mm an hour. The lesson lasts.

cards.headline: Spray: warn first, then fire
cards.body: A striped skunk gives notice: it stomps its feet and raises its tail. Ignore that, and it can spray about 10 feet (3 meters) with startling accuracy. The warning makes sense, because refilling takes about a week. Its white stripes are warning coloration, the same "back off" signal as Level 63's monarch.
