levels.title: Why Bread Rises
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how yeast and baking soda make dough rise.
levels.summary: Yeast ferments sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol; gluten traps the gas and the oven expands it. Baking soda and baking powder make the same gas without yeast.

cards.headline: The holes in your bread were blown by yeast.
cards.body: Slice a loaf and look at the crumb, full of little holes. Each one was a bubble of gas. In yeast bread, that gas came from tiny yeast cells having lunch.

cards.headline: Fermentation: yeast's lunch
cards.body: Yeast feeds on the sugars in dough and turns them into two things: carbon dioxide gas and alcohol (ethanol). This is fermentation. The gas is the part bakers want. As the yeast works, bubbles of carbon dioxide build up and the dough slowly rises. Every hole in your sandwich started as a yeast burp.

cards.headline: Gluten: the balloon skin
cards.body: Gas escapes easily unless something holds it. In wheat dough, that something is gluten, a stretchy network of proteins that traps the bubbles, so the dough expands instead of leaking. Remember Level 2's balloon: it grows because gas is matter and takes up space. Think of dough as a sponge of tiny balloons, each one filled with carbon dioxide.

cards.headline: The oven's last push
cards.body: In the hot oven, the trapped gas expands and the dough rises one more time. Then the heat kills the yeast, and most of the alcohol evaporates. The yeast made alcohol all along; the oven just sends most of it off into the air.

cards.headline: No yeast? Use baking soda
cards.body: You can get the gas without yeast. Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) releases carbon dioxide when it's moistened and heated, and much more when the batter has an acidic ingredient such as honey, molasses or cocoa. Baking powder packs sodium bicarbonate together with its own acids, so it brings its own partner. Same gas, no yeast required.

levels.title: How Soap Works
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how soap lifts away grease.
levels.summary: Oil and water don't mix, so water alone can't lift grease. A soap molecule has a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail; soap wraps grease in micelles that rinse away. Soap itself is made from fats.

cards.headline: Water alone can't get grease off a pan.
cards.body: Rinse a greasy pan and the water runs right over the grease. Oil and water don't mix; together they make a heterogeneous mixture, like Level 6's Italian salad dressing. Add a squirt of soap and the grease lets go. What does soap know that water doesn't?

cards.headline: A molecule with two ends
cards.body: Each soap molecule has two very different ends. Its head is attracted to water. Its long tail is attracted to oil and grease, and avoids water. So one soap molecule can hold on to both at once, the one thing water can't do on its own. It's a go-between with a foot in each world.

mascot.line: Tails in the grease, heads in the water. Everybody gets the seat they like.

cards.headline: Micelles: grease, gift-wrapped
cards.body: In soapy water, the tails dig into a grease droplet while the heads stay out in the water. Soap molecules surround the grease and form tiny clusters called micelles: grease locked inside, water-loving heads facing out.

cards.headline: Down the drain
cards.body: Now the rinse water has something to hold on to: the heads on the outside of each micelle. The clusters stay suspended in the water, and the rinse carries them away, grease and all. Water never learned to dissolve grease. Soap just wrapped it up so water could carry it.

cards.headline: Soap starts as fat
cards.body: The twist: soap itself is made from fats and oils. Reacting a fat or oil, such as tallow or vegetable oil, with a strong alkali turns it into soap, a reaction called saponification. The grease fighter began life as grease.

levels.title: Cleaning Safely
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why some cleaners must never be mixed.
levels.summary: Bleach plus ammonia makes toxic chloramines; bleach plus acids like vinegar releases chlorine gas. Health agencies say never mix bleach, ventilate, and get fresh air after exposure.

cards.headline: Two cleaners that are safe alone can be dangerous together.
cards.body: Picture the cabinet under a sink: bleach, glass cleaner, a bottle of vinegar. The CDC's rule about them is blunt: never mix bleach with any other cleaner. The reason is a chemical change you already know how to spot.

cards.headline: Bleach plus ammonia
cards.body: Household bleach is sodium hypochlorite dissolved in water. Mix it with ammonia, found in some glass cleaners, and toxic gases called chloramines form. That's Level 9's chemical change: at least one new substance appears. This time the new substance is a gas, and it goes straight into the air you breathe.

cards.headline: Bleach plus acid
cards.body: Bleach mixed with acidic products releases chlorine gas. The acids hide in plain sight: vinegar, some toilet bowl cleaners, rust removers. Chlorine and chloramine gases irritate the eyes, nose and throat and cause coughing and trouble breathing. Higher exposures can damage the lungs.
cards.callout: Never mix bleach with ammonia or with acids

cards.headline: The second chemical isn't always in a bottle
cards.body: Urine contains ammonia. That's why Washington State's health department warns people to take care using bleach on litter boxes, diaper pails and toilets. A dangerous mix can happen with only one bottle in your hand.

mascot.line: One bottle at a time, window open. Some experiments are best left on the screen.

cards.headline: The habits that keep cleaning boring
cards.body: The CDC's advice is simple: never mix bleach with any other cleaner, keep the room well ventilated, and follow the label. If someone does breathe fumes from a mix, Poison Control says to leave the area right away for fresh air and call a poison center (1-800-222-1222 in the US). In cleaning, boring chemistry is the best chemistry.

levels.title: Dyes and Colors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how dyes give cloth its color.
levels.summary: Dyes absorb some colors of light and reflect the rest; mordants help some stay put. Dyes came from plants and snails until Perkin's 1856 mauve, the first synthetic dye sold.

cards.headline: In 1856, a teenager went looking for a medicine and found purple.
cards.body: William Henry Perkin was 18 and trying to make quinine, a malaria drug, from chemicals taken from coal tar. The medicine never appeared. A purple dye did: mauve, the first synthetic dye ever sold.

cards.headline: Before Perkin: plants and snails
cards.body: Until then, dyes came from plants and animals. Blue indigo came from plant leaves. Red came from the roots of the madder plant. Tyrian purple came from the glands of a sea snail. Purple, in other words, came from snail glands. Try scaling that up.

cards.headline: How a dye makes color
cards.body: A dye gives cloth a color that isn't easily changed by washing, heat or light. The color itself is about light. An object's color depends on which colors of light it absorbs and which it reflects. A red shirt reflects red light and absorbs the rest; black cloth absorbs all colors. What you see is the leftovers.

cards.headline: Making color stick
cards.body: A color that washes out is no use. Some dyes need a helper called a mordant, a metal salt that the fiber takes up. It reacts with the dye to make a less soluble form, held fast to the fabric. The word comes from the Latin mordere, to bite. The mordant gives the dye teeth.

cards.headline: Color from a flask
cards.body: Mauve came from a flask, not a snail. Perkin patented it in 1856, at 18, and it became the first commercialized synthetic dye: color made from coal-tar chemicals instead of harvested from plants and animals. A failed malaria medicine turned into a new way to make color.

levels.title: How Smells Travel
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how smell molecules reach your nose.
levels.summary: Smelling is detecting airborne chemicals, so only volatile substances have a smell. Warmth frees more molecules, and diffusion spreads them in a slow zigzag because they keep colliding.

cards.headline: You can smell a pizza before you see it.
cards.body: The delivery box is still closed in the hallway, yet the smell is already in the room. Something real traveled from the pizza to your nose: molecules. Smell is the detection of chemicals carried in the air.

cards.headline: Only escapees have a smell
cards.body: If smelling means catching chemicals from the air, a substance can only have a smell if some of its molecules get into the air. Odor molecules are volatile: they vaporize readily. Anything you can smell right now is quietly sending bits of itself your way.

cards.headline: Warmth launches more molecules
cards.body: Remember Level 4: heating makes particles move faster. As a liquid warms, more of its molecules have enough energy to escape into the air. So a steaming bowl of soup sends more smell molecules into the room than the same soup straight from the fridge.

mascot.line: Imagine crossing a crowded party by bumping into every guest. That's a smell molecule's evening.

cards.headline: Fast molecules, slow journey
cards.body: Gas molecules zip along at hundreds of meters per second. So why does a smell take time to cross a room? Each molecule keeps colliding with other molecules and bouncing off in a new direction. The overall spreading, from where molecules are crowded to where they're sparse, is called diffusion. It's a zigzag commute, not a sprint.

levels.title: Recycling Plastic
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happens to plastic when it is recycled.
levels.summary: Thermoplastics remelt; thermosets don't. Recycling sorts, grinds, washes and melts plastic into pellets, sorting flakes by density. Broken polymer chains lower the quality.

cards.headline: Heat one plastic and it melts. Heat another and it never will.
cards.body: Thermoplastics soften and can be remelted. Thermosets can't. That single difference decides whether a plastic can be melted down and made into something new.

cards.headline: Melters and non-melters
cards.body: Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be remelted and reshaped, which makes them readily recyclable. Thermosets, such as epoxy and polyurethane, cross-link as they harden. Once set, they can't be remelted; old thermosets are usually ground up and used as filler. As an analogy: one is chocolate, the other is a baked cake.

cards.headline: From bottle to pellet
cards.body: Mechanical recycling runs like a production line. Plastic is sorted by type, ground into small flakes and washed with hot water and detergent. Then the flakes are melted and formed into pellets, the raw material for new products.

cards.headline: Sorted by floating
cards.body: One step is pure Level 8. Flakes go into a water tank and separate by density. PET flakes from bottles sink, while flakes from caps, made of polypropylene or HDPE, float. Denser than water sinks; less dense floats. Density does the sorting, no robot needed.

cards.headline: Why recycled isn't quite new
cards.body: The heat and grinding of recycling break some of plastic's long polymer chains. So recycled plastic usually doesn't match new plastic, and it often goes into less-demanding products. Every trip through the melter costs it a little.

levels.title: Glass From Sand
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how glass is made from sand.
levels.summary: Glass is sand (silica) melted with soda, which lowers the melting temperature, and lime, which stops it dissolving in water. Cooled fast, it becomes an amorphous solid; it doesn't slowly flow.

cards.headline: Your window started out as sand.
cards.body: Everyday glass is made from sand plus two helpers, limestone and soda. Turning a gritty beach into something you can see through takes serious heat and a little clever chemistry.

cards.headline: Sand is hard to melt
cards.body: Sand is silicon dioxide, also called silica, and it melts only above 1,700 °C. So glassmakers add soda (sodium carbonate), which works as a flux: it lowers the melting temperature dramatically. Soda is the shortcut.

cards.headline: The catch: glass that dissolves
cards.body: Silica and soda alone make a glass that dissolves in water. Not ideal for a window in the rain. So glassmakers add a third ingredient, lime (calcium oxide, from limestone), which makes the glass insoluble again. Sand, soda and lime: soda-lime glass.

cards.headline: A solid with no pattern
cards.body: Molten glass is cooled quickly enough that crystals never form. Remember Level 3: in a solid, particles are tightly packed, often in a regular pattern. Glass skips the pattern. Its particles freeze in a jumble, making it an amorphous solid: rigid, but without a crystal's long-range order.

mascot.line: Checked the windows. Still solid. Still not dripping.

cards.headline: The flowing-window myth
cards.body: You may have heard that glass is a very slow liquid, because some old windows are thicker at the bottom. It isn't. Those panes were made uneven to begin with. Room-temperature glass would take longer than the age of the universe to sag noticeably. Your windows aren't dripping; they're just old.

levels.title: Fuels
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how gasoline and natural gas store energy.
levels.summary: Fuels store chemical energy in their bonds and release it as heat. Gasoline and natural gas are hydrocarbons; natural gas is mostly methane, and gasoline is distilled from crude oil.

cards.headline: Natural gas has no smell. The smell is added on purpose.
cards.body: Natural gas is colorless and odorless, so gas companies add mercaptan, a chemical with a strong, unpleasant smell. That way a leak announces itself: Level 86's airborne chemicals, drafted as an alarm. And that gas is a remarkable way to store energy.

cards.headline: Energy stored in bonds
cards.body: Fuels hold chemical energy: energy stored in the bonds of atoms and molecules. Petroleum and natural gas are packed with it. Burning converts it to heat, whether it's a gas flame under a pot or gasoline in a car engine. A full tank is really a tank of stored bonds.

cards.headline: Hydrocarbons: carbon and hydrogen
cards.body: Petroleum and natural gas are made mainly of hydrocarbons, compounds of only carbon and hydrogen. Natural gas is mostly methane (CH4), the simplest one: one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. When hydrocarbons burn, they form carbon dioxide and water, the same products as Level 9's burning candle.

cards.headline: Made from ancient life
cards.body: Where did all that stored energy come from? Oil and natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals, buried and changed by heat and pressure. Filling a tank means burning very old leftovers.

cards.headline: Gasoline: distilled from crude oil
cards.body: Gasoline is made from crude oil at refineries, and the first step is Level 7's trick on a giant scale: distillation. Heated crude oil separates into fractions by boiling point inside a tall tower. The lightest fractions, gasoline among them, rise to the top.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Chemistry at Home
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the chemistry behind cooking, cleaning and everyday materials.
levels.summary: Hard water's calcium and magnesium turn soap into scum; detergents don't. One kitchen holds the chapter: flame, toast, bread, glass, soap, and bleach kept from vinegar.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: why soap sometimes leaves a scum.
cards.body: In some homes, soap leaves a gray scum on the tub and seems to clean less well. The water is to blame. Then step into one kitchen and find the whole chapter at once.

cards.headline: Hard water fights soap
cards.body: Hard water carries calcium and magnesium. They react with soap to form an insoluble scum, soap scum, which weakens its cleaning. The soap that should be wrapping grease in Level 83's micelles ends up as crud on the tub instead.

mascot.line: Same two-ended trick, better manners around calcium.

cards.headline: Detergents: soap's synthetic cousins
cards.body: Detergents work like soap, with a charged head and a long oil-attracting tail. But they're made from petroleum products instead of natural fats, and they don't form scum with calcium and magnesium. So they keep cleaning in hard water.

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one kitchen
cards.body: Stand in one kitchen. The gas flame is hydrocarbons turning stored chemical energy into heat. The toast browns as sugars react with amino acids, and the bread rose on yeast's carbon dioxide. The window is sand, soda and lime. In the sink, soap wraps grease in micelles. And the bleach stays far from the vinegar, because together they release chlorine gas.

levels.title: Alchemy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what alchemists tried to do and what they got right.
levels.summary: Alchemists chased gold and long life and never caught either. Along the way they built the tools of the lab, like the alembic still, and gave chemistry its very name.

cards.headline: Isaac Newton wrote about a million words on alchemy.
cards.body: The man who explained gravity spent some thirty years on it, mostly in secret. So what were alchemists chasing, and was any of it worth the effort?

cards.headline: The dream: gold, and a longer life
cards.body: Alchemists tried to turn base metals, such as lead or copper, into silver or gold. Many hoped to make the philosophers' stone, a material that was supposed to do the transforming for them. A second dream ran alongside: a cure for disease and a way to extend life. Big goals. As it turned out, what they built while chasing them mattered far more.

mascot.line: Filtering, subliming, distilling. The alchemists had the moves; they just wanted the wrong prize.

cards.headline: The toolkit they left behind
cards.body: Alchemists described apparatus for distillation, sublimation and filtration in careful detail. Their alembic was a still in three parts: a vessel to heat the mixture, a head to catch and cool the vapor, and a receiver for the liquid that dripped out. Remember Level 7? Distilling works because the parts of a mixture boil at different temperatures. Three Chapter 1 moves were already on the alchemist's bench.

cards.headline: Words that stuck around
cards.body: The word alchemy comes from the Arabic al-kimiya, and the word chemistry grew out of alchemy. Arabic alchemy handed down alcohol, elixir and alembic too. And an ancient alchemist named Maria is credited with gentle heating in a bath of hot water instead of an open flame. Her name survives in the cook's bain-marie. The gold never came. The lab did.
cards.callout: Chemistry's name, tools and techniques all passed through the alchemist's workshop.

levels.title: Robert Boyle
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Boyle's work on gases.
levels.summary: Boyle found a trapped gas's volume is inversely proportional to its pressure: half the space, twice the push. He championed experiment, and was still an alchemist.

cards.headline: Block the end of a syringe and push. The air pushes back.
cards.body: Press the plunger in and the trapped air resists harder the further you go. Squeeze it into half the space and it pushes back twice as hard. In 1662 Robert Boyle published the rule behind that push.

cards.headline: A pump, a partner and a rule
cards.body: In 1659 Boyle and Robert Hooke finished building an air pump and used it to study air. From those experiments came the rule Boyle published in 1662, now called Boyle's law: at a constant temperature, a gas's volume is inversely proportional to its pressure. Double the pressure and the volume halves. Halve the pressure and the gas swells to twice its volume.
cards.callout: Boyle's law: more pressure, less volume, at the same temperature.

mascot.line: Breathe in. Congratulations, you just ran Boyle's experiment.

cards.headline: Why gases give way
cards.body: Level 3 explains why this works for gases. Their particles are far apart and move freely, so there is room to crowd them closer. Liquids and solids have almost no room to spare: their volume barely changes under pressure. You use Boyle's law with every breath. Your chest expands, the volume in your lungs grows, the pressure inside drops, and air flows in.

cards.headline: The skeptical chemist
cards.body: Boyle's 1661 book The Sceptical Chymist attacked the old Aristotelian ideas about what matter is made of. His work leaned on experiment and observation, and he argued so hard for chemistry that he was later called the father of chemistry.

cards.headline: A founder with a secret hobby
cards.body: Yet Boyle, like Newton in Level 91, pursued alchemy all his life, still hoping to turn base metals into gold. Science didn't switch on overnight. Its founders carried one foot in the old workshop and one in the new lab.

levels.title: Lavoisier
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Lavoisier founded modern chemistry.
levels.summary: Lavoisier showed burned metals gain oxygen, ending phlogiston, named oxygen and hydrogen, helped create chemistry's naming system and listed 33 elements, light and heat among them.

cards.headline: In 1789, Lavoisier listed 33 elements. Light and heat made the list.
cards.body: It was the best list anyone had, and it still had two entries that aren't substances at all. How did Antoine Lavoisier earn the title father of modern chemistry, and what did he get wrong?

cards.headline: Goodbye, phlogiston
cards.body: Before Lavoisier, many chemists believed that burnable things, like charcoal and metals, contained phlogiston, which they released into the air as they burned. But metals such as lead and tin weigh more after burning, not less. Lavoisier showed why: oxygen from the air combines with the metal. Level 2 told you air has mass. Take some in, and you get heavier.

mascot.line: "Dephlogisticated air" versus "oxygen". I know which one I'd rather spell.

cards.headline: Names that say what's inside
cards.body: In 1787 Lavoisier and three colleagues published a new method for naming chemical substances. Out went old names like dephlogisticated air and inflammable air. In came oxygen, meaning acid former, and hydrogen, meaning water former, because Lavoisier had shown that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. With small changes, that system is still the basis of chemical names today.

cards.headline: The list, the partner, the guillotine
cards.body: His 1789 textbook listed 33 substances he considered elements, starting with light and caloric (heat), which aren't elements at all. Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier worked beside him, drawing his laboratory for the book and translating English research. His day job undid him. He held a share in a tax-collecting company, and during the Reign of Terror he was guillotined, on May 8, 1794.

levels.title: Dalton's Atoms
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Dalton's atomic theory.
levels.summary: Watching the weather led John Dalton to atoms: every element has its own atom with its own mass, compounds join atoms in whole-number ratios, and reactions only rearrange atoms.

cards.headline: For 57 years, John Dalton wrote down the weather every day.
cards.body: He started in 1787 and kept going until his death in 1844. That habit, of all things, led him to the atom.

mascot.line: 57 years of weather notes. And you thought your diary habit was impressive.

cards.headline: From weather to atoms
cards.body: Weather happens in the air, and Level 6 told you air is a solution of gases, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Dalton studied how those gases share the sky. He concluded that each gas in a mixture pushes independently, exerting its own pressure as if the others weren't there. Thinking about gases that way led him, by way of meteorology, to atoms.

cards.headline: The theory in four lines
cards.body: Starting in 1808, Dalton set out his theory in A New System of Chemical Philosophy. All matter is made of tiny atoms. Each element has its own kind of atom, with its own characteristic mass. Compounds are atoms of different elements joined in small whole-number ratios. And in a chemical change, atoms are never created or destroyed, only rearranged. Level 9's new substances? Same atoms, new partners.
cards.callout: Level 3 said matter is made of particles. Dalton is a big reason we say so.

cards.headline: Wrong formula, right idea
cards.body: Dalton wasn't right about everything. He wrote water as HO, one hydrogen atom joined to one oxygen atom. In fact water has hydrogen and oxygen in a 2 to 1 ratio: H2O. Notice what the fix kept, though. It's still atoms of two elements in a small whole-number ratio, just as his theory said.

levels.title: Marie Curie
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Curie's discovery of radium and polonium.
levels.summary: Marie Curie named radioactivity, found polonium and radium hiding in pitchblende, purified a tenth of a gram of radium from tons of ore, and won Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry.

cards.headline: Several tons of ore. One tenth of a gram of prize.
cards.body: That was Marie Curie's haul after thousands of rounds of purifying radium. Why would anyone go to such lengths for so little?

cards.headline: A rock that was too active
cards.body: Henri Becquerel had found that uranium gives off rays; Curie gave the effect its name, radioactivity. She found that pitchblende, a uranium ore, was much more radioactive than pure uranium itself. Something else in the rock had to be responsible. In 1898 she and Pierre Curie announced two new elements: polonium, named after her native Poland, and radium.

cards.headline: The hardest separation
cards.body: Level 7 separated mixtures by using differences between their parts. Curie's guide was radioactivity itself: each time she removed some of a known element, such as bismuth, what was left was more active. But to prove radium was a real element, she needed enough to show. After thousands of crystallizations from several tons of starting material, she had one decigram, a tenth of a gram, of almost pure radium chloride.
cards.callout: Her detector for the hidden element was the radiation it gave off.

cards.headline: Two prizes, two sciences
cards.body: In 1903 Marie Curie shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, becoming the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone, for discovering radium and polonium. She remains the only woman to win in two different fields. The radiation she studied also harmed her: she died in 1934 of aplastic anemia caused by radiation exposure.

levels.title: Rosalind Franklin
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Franklin's X-ray picture of DNA.
levels.summary: Rosalind Franklin used X-ray diffraction to photograph DNA. Her Photo 51 showed an X that meant a helix. It was shown to Watson without her knowledge, and she died before the 1962 Nobel.

cards.headline: One photograph took 62 hours to expose.
cards.body: In May 1952, Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling aimed X-rays at a thin fiber of DNA and waited. The picture they got, Photo 51, helped reveal the shape of DNA.

mascot.line: You can't see an atom. You can see the shadow of a whole army of them marching in step.

cards.headline: Seeing with X-rays
cards.body: Franklin was a chemist who, from 1951 at King's College London, studied DNA with X-ray diffraction. X-rays scatter off a crystal at angles that reveal how its atoms are arranged. Level 3 said the particles in a solid are often packed in a neat, repeating pattern. Order in, pattern out: the scattered X-rays leave a pattern on film that encodes the structure.

cards.headline: X marks the shape
cards.body: Photo 51 showed a bold X-shaped pattern. To Franklin, that X meant DNA's strands are helical, twisted like a spiral staircase (an analogy). The photo became some of the clearest evidence that DNA is a double helix.
cards.callout: The X in Photo 51 is the signature of a helix.

cards.headline: Who got the credit
cards.body: In early 1953, her colleague Maurice Wilkins showed Photo 51 to James Watson, without her knowledge or agreement. That April, Watson and Crick published their DNA model in Nature, and Franklin and Gosling's own paper appeared in the same issue. Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958, aged 37. In 1962 Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared a Nobel Prize, which is never awarded after death.

learned: X-rays scatter off a crystal at angles that reveal its atoms' arrangement

levels.title: New Materials
levels.objective: After this level you can describe inventions like nylon and nonstick coatings.
levels.summary: Nylon was invented on purpose, in 1935, as a synthetic silk. Teflon was found by accident in 1938, when a cylinder of gas turned into a slippery white solid that nothing sticks to.

cards.headline: Two everyday materials, one company: one found on purpose, one by accident.
cards.body: In 1935 a team at DuPont invented nylon. In 1938 a DuPont chemist opened a gas cylinder, and nothing came out. That was how Teflon began.

cards.headline: Silk you can make in a lab
cards.body: Wallace Carothers's team at DuPont invented nylon in 1935 as a synthetic silk. It was a useful fiber built by chemistry from compounds available from air, water, and coal or petroleum: no silkworms required. Nylon went into production in 1939, and nylon stockings were a sensation at that year's New York World's Fair. In World War II, nylon went into parachutes instead.

mascot.line: When the scale disagrees with your eyes, trust the scale.

cards.headline: The cylinder that wasn't empty
cards.body: In 1938 Roy Plunkett had stored tetrafluoroethylene gas in small cylinders. When he opened one, no gas came out, yet it weighed the same as before. Level 2 explains why that was a clue: the matter was still in there, mass and all. Inside he found a white powder. The gas had turned into a new solid substance, a chemical change straight out of Level 9.

cards.headline: Why nothing sticks
cards.body: Plunkett tested the powder. It resisted heat, reacted with almost nothing, and was so slippery that most substances wouldn't stick to it. We know it as Teflon. Its first uses were industrial; nonstick pans came years later. One discovery was planned, the other was noticed, and both started with a chemist paying attention.

levels.title: Green Chemistry
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how chemists make processes safer and cleaner.
levels.summary: Green chemistry designs out hazardous substances instead of cleaning them up later. Atom economy keeps starting materials in the product, as in a three-step ibuprofen route.

cards.headline: The cleanest way to handle hazardous waste? Never make it.
cards.body: That's the idea behind green chemistry. It changes the question from "How do we clean this up?" to "Why are we making it at all?"

cards.headline: Prevent, don't mop up
cards.body: Green chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use or generation of hazardous substances. That's different from cleanup, which treats waste after it's made, often by separating hazardous chemicals from everything else: a Level 7 job, on an industrial scale. Green chemistry works upstream, so there's less to separate in the first place.
cards.callout: Cleanup treats waste after it's made. Green chemistry avoids making it.

mascot.line: Waste few or no atoms. My new motto, and also my approach to cookies.

cards.headline: Twelve principles, starting with waste
cards.body: In 1998 Paul Anastas and John Warner set out the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry. The first: it's better to prevent waste than to treat or clean it up afterward. The second is atom economy: design reactions so the final product contains as much of the starting materials as possible. Picture a recipe where most of the ingredients go in the bin instead of the cake (an analogy). Atom economy keeps them in the cake.

cards.headline: The ibuprofen fix
cards.body: An older way of making ibuprofen, the everyday painkiller, took six steps, and under 40 percent of the atoms used ended up in the product. BHC Company found a route with three steps and about 80 percent. It also recovers and reuses its main byproduct. In 1997 the route won a US Presidential Green Chemistry Challenge Award.

cards.headline: Green chemistry: designed

questions.explanation: Atom economy means designing syntheses so the product keeps the maximum share of the starting materials, wasting few atoms.

levels.title: Chemistry Myths
levels.objective: After this level you can debunk myths, like "chemical-free" products.
levels.summary: Everything is made of chemicals, so nothing is chemical-free: a 2008 million-pound offer and a blank 2014 'overview' made the point. And a molecule is the same from fruit or factory.

cards.headline: In 2008, chemists offered a million pounds for anything 100% chemical-free.
cards.body: The Royal Society of Chemistry promised the money to the first member of the public who could hand over such a material. Why were they so relaxed about it?

cards.headline: Everything is chemicals
cards.body: Everything you eat, drink and live in is made of chemicals, natural and synthetic alike. Level 2 said matter is anything with mass that takes up space, and Level 1 said chemistry studies what matter is made of. A truly chemical-free product would have to be made of nothing at all. The Royal Society of Chemistry was reclaiming the word from advertising, where chemical had come to mean poison.

mascot.line: Fastest peer review of my life. I read the whole results section in zero seconds.

cards.headline: A paper with nothing in it
cards.body: In 2014 two chemists sent the journal Nature Chemistry "A comprehensive overview of chemical-free consumer products". They examined lotions, supplements, household cleaners, foods and drinks, then listed every product that truly deserved the label. The list was empty. The journal shared the paper on its blog.

cards.headline: Natural isn't a different molecule
cards.body: A related myth says synthetic versions are chemically different from natural ones. Vitamin C says otherwise: natural and synthetic vitamin C are chemically identical, with no known difference in how they act in your body. A molecule doesn't remember whether it came from fruit or a factory. What matters is which substance it is, not where it was made.
cards.callout: Same molecule, same chemistry, whatever the label says.

levels.title: Your Body in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can name the body's main systems and what each one does.
levels.summary: The body runs as 11 organ systems, each a team of organs with a big job: wrapping and moving, supplying and cleaning, controlling and defending. None works alone.

cards.headline: You're not one machine. You're a crew of 11.
cards.body: Anatomy textbooks split the body into 11 organ systems, each a group of organs sharing one big job. Here's the whole crew in one level, plus the rule they all live by: nobody works alone.

mascot.line: Eleven teams on one payroll, and you never have to schedule a single shift.

cards.headline: Eleven systems, three kinds of work

items.label: Wrap, hold up, move
points: Integumentary (skin, hair, nails): wraps you
Skeletal: the frame that holds you up
Muscular: moves you and helps keep you warm

items.label: Supply and clean up
points: Respiratory: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out
Digestive: processes food for the body to use
Cardiovascular (heart and vessels): delivers oxygen and nutrients
Urinary: filters waste from blood, balances water

items.label: Control, defend, continue
points: Nervous: senses and responds
Endocrine: sends hormones that regulate the body
Lymphatic: returns fluid, defends against germs
Reproductive: makes sex cells

cards.headline: One flight of stairs, five systems
cards.body: Climb some stairs and watch the crew. Your nervous system takes in where the steps are and sets off a response. Muscles pull on your skeleton to lift you. Meanwhile your respiratory system brings oxygen into your blood, and your cardiovascular system carries it to the muscles doing the work. One step, five systems, zero meetings.

cards.fact: Staying warm is a team job too.
cards.context: Your muscles help keep your body warm, and your cardiovascular system spreads that warmth around, evening out the temperature across your body. Neither system has 'heating' as its main job, yet between them they keep you at a steady temperature. Two systems, one thermostat.

levels.title: Cells
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a cell is and name its main parts.
levels.summary: A cell is the basic building block of life. Its membrane controls what gets in and out, cytoplasm fills it, the nucleus gives orders and mitochondria supply energy.

cards.headline: An oak, a mushroom and you are built from the same kind of brick.
cards.body: It's the cell, the basic building block of every living thing. Your body is made of trillions of them. So what does one cell actually do, and what's inside it?

cards.headline: Every cell runs its own small life
cards.body: Each of your cells takes in nutrients from food, turns them into energy and does a special job, from giving your body structure to work that only its kind of cell can do. Cells also carry your hereditary material and can make copies of themselves. Trillions of small lives, all running at once, add up to one big one: yours.

cards.headline: A town with a wall
cards.body: Picture a cell as a tiny walled town. The plasma membrane is the wall: an outer lining that separates the cell from its surroundings and decides what gets in and out. Inside the wall is the cytoplasm, a jelly-like fluid packed with working parts. Everything the cell does happens inside that wall.

mascot.line: A walled town with its own power grid, and you have trillions of them. That is a lot of tiny mayors.

cards.headline: A town hall and power stations
cards.body: In the middle sits the nucleus, the command center. It sends out directions telling the cell when to grow, mature, divide or die. Out in the cytoplasm, mitochondria are the power stations: they turn energy from food into a form the cell can use. Orders from the hall, power from the stations: that's a working town.

levels.title: How Many Cells?
levels.objective: After this level you can estimate how many cells make up a body and how many kinds there are.
levels.summary: A 2016 estimate gives a reference adult about 30 trillion human cells, mostly red blood cells. Counts vary with body size, and the cells come in about 400 types.

cards.headline: Counting your cells at one per second would take about 950,000 years.
cards.body: No sleep, no snacks, no weekends off. Nobody has ever counted them one by one, of course. So how did scientists arrive at a number, and how many different kinds of cell are in the pile?

cards.fact: You're built from about 30 trillion human cells.
cards.context: That's the 2016 estimate by Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo, for a 'reference man': a young adult weighing 70 kg. They didn't count cells one at a time. They combined estimates for each cell type, like red blood cells and platelets, and added them up. Red blood cells alone made up about 84 percent of the total.

cards.headline: Your number depends on your body
cards.body: A 2023 study by Ian Hatton and colleagues ran the count for different bodies: about 36 trillion cells in a reference man, 28 trillion in a reference woman and 17 trillion in a 10-year-old child. A smaller body is built from fewer cells. So 'about 30 trillion' is a fair round figure for a grown-up. Think of it as a ballpark, not a barcode.

mascot.line: Same body, same team, and some players are a shrew while others are a whale.

cards.headline: About 400 kinds, from shrews to whales
cards.body: The same study sorted the body's cells into about 400 types, and their sizes are wildly different. From a tiny red blood cell to the biggest muscle fibers, cell mass spans about seven orders of magnitude, like going from a shrew to a blue whale. So red blood cells win the headcount, while muscle cells, few but huge, make up about half your cell mass.

levels.title: From Cells to Organs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how cells form tissues, organs and whole systems.
levels.summary: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems. The four tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous, and the stomach wall uses all four.

cards.headline: Your stomach isn't made of 'stomach'.
cards.body: Its wall is a lining, packing, muscle and nerves: four different tissues stacked into one organ. Every organ is built from tissues like that. Here's the ladder from a single cell to a whole working body.

cards.headline: Cells, tissues, organs, systems, you
cards.body: Your body is built in levels. A tissue is a group of similar cells working together on one job. An organ is a distinct structure made of two or more tissue types. An organ system is a group of organs teaming up on a major job, and your 11 systems together make the whole organism: you. Each rung of the ladder is built from the one below it.

cards.body: Back to that stomach. Inside is an epithelial lining. Around it, connective tissue holds the layers together. Then come three layers of smooth muscle that churn food, with networks of nerves running through the wall. Four tissue types, one organ, and that organ is one member of the digestive system you met in Level 1.

levels.title: DNA, the Instruction Book
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what DNA is and where the body keeps it.
levels.summary: DNA is the hereditary instruction book, written in four letters (A, C, G, T). Nearly every cell keeps a copy, mostly in the nucleus, with a little in the mitochondria.

cards.headline: A single cell of yours holds about 2 meters of instructions.
cards.body: Stretch out the DNA from just one of your cells and it would reach about six feet. Yet it's packed into a nucleus so small you'd need a specialized microscope to see it. What is this stuff, and where exactly does your body keep it?

cards.headline: A four-letter alphabet
cards.body: DNA is your hereditary material: the instructions for building and running you. It's written in four chemical letters, A, C, G and T, and as with words in a sentence, the order carries the meaning. Your full set runs to about 3 billion letters, and more than 99 percent of them are the same in everyone. You and a stranger differ by a sliver.

cards.headline: Kept in the command center
cards.body: Nearly every cell in your body has the same DNA. Most of it sits in the nucleus, Level 2's command center, packaged into 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Its two strands twist into a double helix, a spiral ladder whose rungs are paired letters: A with T, C with G. A small amount of DNA also lives in the mitochondria, the cell's power stations.

mascot.line: Your body's most common cell, and it travels without the manual. Bold.

cards.fact: Your most common cell has no nucleus at all.
cards.context: Remember Level 3? Red blood cells make up about 84 percent of your cells. Mature ones have no nucleus, so they don't carry the nuclear instruction book. So when you read that 'nearly every cell' has your DNA, the 'nearly' is doing real work.

levels.title: Genes
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a gene does and how genes lead to proteins.
levels.summary: A gene is a stretch of DNA; about 20,000 of yours code for proteins. A cell copies a gene into messenger RNA, and a ribosome reads it to build a protein.

cards.headline: The recipes are kept in the nucleus. The kitchen is outside.
cards.body: Most of your DNA sits in the nucleus, but the machines that build proteins, called ribosomes, work out in the cytoplasm. So how does a recipe reach the kitchen? Follow one gene.

cards.headline: A gene is one recipe
cards.body: A gene is a stretch of DNA, the basic unit of heredity. Many genes are instructions for making a protein; many others act like switches that control other genes. You have about 20,000 protein-coding genes, and together they fill less than 2 percent of your DNA. If your DNA is a cookbook, a gene is one recipe.

cards.headline: Proteins do the work
cards.body: The dish is a protein, and proteins do most of the work in your cells. Some are enzymes that run chemical reactions, some carry messages between cells, and some give cells their structure. Each is a chain built from 20 kinds of amino acids, strung like pearls on a necklace. The order of the pearls sets the protein's shape, and the shape sets its job.

mascot.line: Photocopy the recipe, cook from the copy. Every good kitchen works that way.

cards.headline: From recipe to dish in two steps
cards.body: First, transcription: the cell copies a gene into messenger RNA, a working copy that carries the message out of the nucleus. Then translation: a ribosome in the cytoplasm reads that copy three letters at a time. Each three-letter codon usually calls for one amino acid, and the ribosome links them in order. The original recipe stays safely on the shelf.

cards.fact: A gene makes a protein, not a person.
cards.context: Most traits don't come down to one gene. Height, for example, is shaped by hundreds of gene variants, each with a small effect, plus things like nutrition. Genes supply the recipes; a whole body is more like a banquet.

levels.title: Water and You
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how much of the body is water and why that matters.
levels.summary: Water is about 75% of a newborn and 50 to 60% of an adult, less with age or more body fat. Almost two-thirds of it sits inside cells, and it cools, cushions and cleans.

cards.headline: How much of you is water? It depends on your birthday.
cards.body: A newborn is about three-quarters water. Most adults are closer to half, or a bit more. No single number fits everyone. So where is all that water, and what is it doing?

cards.fact: Water is about 75% of a newborn, 50 to 60% of an adult, and less in old age.
cards.context: The share changes because the body's mix of tissues changes over a lifetime. Fat tissue holds less water than lean tissue, so people with more body fat have a lower percentage of water. Any single 'you are this much water' figure is a rough average at best.

cards.headline: Most of it is inside your cells
cards.body: Almost two-thirds of your body's water sits inside your cells, where it's the main ingredient of the jelly-like cytoplasm from Level 2. The rest is outside them, around your cells and in your blood. So don't picture a water tank. Picture trillions of tiny water-filled bags.

mascot.line: Coolant, cushion and cleaning crew, all in one liquid. Water does not like to specialize.

cards.headline: Water's day jobs
cards.body: All that water is busy. It helps keep your temperature normal: when you sweat, the evaporating water cools your skin. It lubricates and cushions your joints, protects your spinal cord and other sensitive tissues, and carries waste out of your body. Less a statue, more a fountain.

levels.title: The Microbes on You
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the trillions of microbes that live on and in the body.
levels.summary: About 38 trillion bacteria, mostly in the colon, live alongside about 30 trillion human cells: roughly one to one. They weigh about 0.2 kg and help digest food.

cards.headline: Roughly half the cells in and on you aren't human.
cards.body: They're bacteria, and most of them live in your gut. For every one of your own cells there's about one of them. They aren't invaders, either: they're residents, and many earn their keep. Meet your microbiome.

cards.fact: About 38 trillion bacteria share your body with about 30 trillion human cells.
cards.context: That's the 2016 estimate from the team behind Level 3's cell count: about 1.3 bacteria per human cell, roughly one to one. For decades, textbooks claimed bacteria vastly outnumbered our own cells, a figure traced to a rough 1970s estimate. Almost all of the bacteria live in the colon.

mascot.line: Science has confirmed it: a trip to the bathroom changes who is in charge.

cards.headline: A little more human after the bathroom
cards.body: Bacteria are small, so all 38 trillion together weigh only about 0.2 kg. And the ratio isn't fixed. Each bowel movement flushes out roughly a quarter to a third of the colon's bacteria, enough to tip the count toward human cells for a while. You are, briefly, a little more human afterwards.

cards.headline: Tenants who pay rent
cards.body: Your gut microbes help break down proteins, fats and carbohydrates in food into nutrients you can absorb, and they make useful compounds, like vitamins, that your own genes can't. Between them, more than 10,000 species carry about 8 million genes, hundreds of times more than your 20,000. You provide the house; they bring the toolbox.

levels.title: How We Learned About the Body
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how dissection and microscopes revealed the body's inner workings.
levels.summary: Galen's anatomy came from animals. In 1543 Vesalius dissected humans himself. Microscopes let Hooke name cells (1665) and Leeuwenhoek see bacteria (1683).

cards.headline: For centuries, doctors learned human anatomy from apes and pigs.
cards.body: Europe's most trusted anatomy books came from Galen, a Greek physician in the Roman Empire, who couldn't dissect human bodies. His books were still the standard in the 1500s. Two new ways of looking changed that: opening up the human body, and magnifying it.

mascot.line: Galen wasn't careless. He just had the wrong patient on the table.

cards.headline: Vesalius looked for himself
cards.body: In 1543, Andreas Vesalius published On the Structure of the Human Body, built on human dissections he did with his own hands. It was more accurate than any description before it, and it caught Galen's slips. Galen had said the human lower jaw is two bones. That's true for a dog. In people, it's one.

events.label: Vesalius's book maps the body from human dissection
Robert Hooke names 'cells' after the boxes he sees in cork
Leeuwenhoek describes bacteria from his own teeth
Schleiden and Schwann: all living things are made of cells

cards.headline: Microbiology began with a set of teeth
cards.body: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own single lenses, magnifying up to about 300 times. In 1683 he looked at the plaque from his own teeth and saw 'little animalcules' moving about: bacteria, seen for the first time. The microbes you met in Level 8 had been living on people all along. It took a homemade lens to notice them.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Building Blocks
levels.objective: After this level you can connect cells, DNA, tissues and organs into one picture of how a body is built.
levels.summary: Systems, organs, tissues, cells, DNA: one zoom. About 330 billion cells are replaced daily, and each new cell comes from an old one with a full copy of the DNA.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: you're being rebuilt while you read this.
cards.body: Every second, millions of your cells are replaced. First, a quick zoom through everything this chapter built. Then, how the building blocks keep renewing themselves.

cards.headline: Zoom from you to a single gene
cards.body: Start with you: 11 organ systems. Zoom into the digestive system and pick one organ, the stomach, built from four tissue types. Zoom into a tissue: similar cells working together, part of about 30 trillion human cells. Open one cell and find the nucleus, holding 46 chromosomes of DNA. Read one gene, and a ribosome builds a protein from its message.

cards.fact: About 330 billion of your cells are replaced every day.
cards.context: That's roughly 1 percent of them, or about 3.8 million every second, according to a 2021 estimate by Ron Sender and Ron Milo. Blood leads the way: about 90 percent of the new cells are blood cells.

mascot.line: Billions of copies a day, and hardly a typo that matters. Best printing press you will ever own.

cards.headline: Every new cell gets the whole book
cards.body: New cells come only from existing cells, one of the rules of cell theory. When a cell divides, each new cell needs an exact copy of the old cell's DNA, and each of DNA's two strands serves as the pattern for a copy. So Level 5's instruction book is being copied all day long, and you never feel a thing.

levels.title: The Skeleton
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the skeleton does and how many bones an adult has.
levels.summary: An adult has 206 bones, 106 of them in the hands and feet. The axial skeleton guards the brain, heart and lungs; bones also anchor muscles, make blood cells and bank calcium.

cards.headline: Wiggle your fingers and toes. That's more than half your skeleton.
cards.body: Your hands and feet hold more bones than the whole rest of your body. Here's the count for an adult skeleton, how it splits into two teams, and the jobs bones do besides holding you up.

cards.fact: An adult skeleton has 206 bones.
cards.context: Each hand has 27 bones and each foot has 26, so your hands and feet hold 106 of them. That leaves just 100 for everything else: skull, spine, ribs, arms, legs and hips. Your body clearly thinks fingers and toes deserve the fine print.

cards.headline: Two skeletons in one
cards.body: Anatomists split the 206 into two groups. The axial skeleton, 80 bones, is your central column: skull, spine and rib cage. It wraps around your brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs, so its big job is protection. The appendicular skeleton, 126 bones, is your arms and legs plus the shoulder and hip bones that attach them to the column. A bony vault in the middle, limbs bolted on the sides.

mascot.line: A frame, a shield, a bank and a blood factory. Your skeleton has more side jobs than anyone I know.

cards.body: Level 1 met the skeletal system as the frame that supports you. That's only job one. Bones give muscles something to pull on, which is how you move. They shield your organs. Red marrow inside some bones makes blood cells, and yellow marrow stores fat. Bone is also a mineral bank for calcium and phosphorus: about 99 percent of your body's calcium is held in your bones and teeth.

levels.title: Inside a Bone
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what bones are made of and how marrow makes blood.
levels.summary: Bone is living tissue: collagen for flexibility, calcium phosphate for hardness. Compact bone outside, spongy bone inside, and red marrow in the spaces makes blood cells.

cards.headline: Your bones are alive, and some of them are making blood right now.
cards.body: The skeleton in a science classroom is dry and dead. Yours is living tissue, full of working cells. Let's cut one open and see what it's made of, and find the factory hidden inside.

cards.headline: Tough fibers, hard crystals
cards.body: Bone is built from two main materials. Collagen, a tough protein, forms fibers that make bone flexible instead of brittle. Crystals of calcium phosphate harden around those fibers and make bone hard and strong. It's a bit like reinforced concrete: a hard material wrapped around a tough framework. Hard enough to hold you up, with just enough give to take a knock.

cards.headline: Solid outside, spongy inside
cards.body: Cut through a bone and you'll find two kinds of bone tissue. Compact bone is the dense, strong outer layer. Inside is spongy bone: a lattice of thin struts called trabeculae, with open spaces between them. The struts form along the lines of stress the bone carries, like scaffolding placed exactly where the load goes.

mascot.line: Every time you sit down, you are sitting on a blood factory. It does not mind at all.

cards.headline: The blood factory
cards.body: Those open spaces in spongy bone hold red marrow, and red marrow makes your blood cells: red blood cells that carry oxygen, white blood cells that fight infection, and platelets that help blood clot. Your hip and thigh bones are among the places it works. Remember Level 10: about 90 percent of the cells your body replaces each day are blood cells. Yellow marrow, the other kind, is mostly fat, an energy store.

levels.title: Joints
levels.objective: After this level you can name the main kinds of joint and explain how they let us move.
levels.summary: A joint is where bones meet. Some never move (skull sutures), some move a little (between vertebrae), and synovial joints move freely, cushioned by cartilage and slick fluid.

cards.headline: Some of your joints never move. That's the point.
cards.body: A joint is anywhere two bones meet. Your knee bends, your shoulder swings in a circle, and the joints in your skull barely move at all. Same word, very different jobs.

cards.headline: Why a knee doesn't grind
cards.body: Freely movable joints share one clever design. The bone ends are capped with smooth cartilage and sealed inside a capsule. The capsule's lining makes synovial fluid, a thick, slippery liquid that lubricates the joint and cuts friction between the bones. Every time you bend a knee, cartilage glides over cartilage on a thin slick of fluid.

levels.title: Broken Bones
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a broken bone heals.
levels.summary: A fracture is a break in a bone, seen on X-rays because calcium-rich bone shows white. It heals in stages: clot, cartilage callus, spongy bone, then compact bone and remodeling.

cards.headline: A well-healed break can vanish without a trace.
cards.body: When a bone breaks, your body doesn't just glue the pieces together. It rebuilds real bone, and often, once the repair is finished, there's no outside sign the break was ever there. Here's how that happens.

cards.headline: Seeing the break
cards.body: A fracture is simply a break in a bone. Most come from injuries such as falls, car accidents and sports, though overuse and repeated motions can cause them too. To find one, doctors usually take an X-ray. Bones contain calcium, which absorbs X-rays readily, so bone shows up white while muscle and fat appear in shades of gray.

mascot.line: Clot, cartilage, spongy bone, compact bone. Your skeleton repairs itself like a very patient building crew.

events.label: Blood from torn vessels clots around the break
A callus of cartilage starts bridging the gap
Bone cells replace the cartilage with spongy bone
Compact bone forms and remodeling restores the shape

cards.headline: Why a broken bone is kept still
cards.body: Healing builds new bone around the pieces wherever they happen to be. A bone that isn't set back in line will heal in its bent position. That's why doctors put the pieces in place and use a cast or splint to keep the bone from moving while it heals. Children run through the same repair stages as adults, only much faster.

levels.title: Muscles
levels.objective: After this level you can name the three kinds of muscle and what each one does.
levels.summary: Skeletal muscle moves bones on your command; smooth muscle works the gut, blood vessels and bladder on its own; cardiac muscle, found only in the heart, never stops.

cards.headline: Three kinds of muscle are working right now. You're steering one.
cards.body: Your heart is beating. Your stomach may be churning. Your hand is holding this screen. All three are muscle at work, but only one of them takes orders from you. Meet the three kinds.

points: Attached to bones

cards.headline: The muscle you never have to think about
cards.body: Remember Level 4's stomach wall, with three layers of smooth muscle that churn food? You never tell them to. Smooth muscle and heart muscle work without conscious control. Skeletal muscle is different: it depends completely on signals from your nervous system. No signal, no movement. That's why your arm waits for you, and your heartbeat doesn't.

mascot.line: Few in number, huge in size. Muscle fibers are the heavyweights of your cell world.

cards.fact: Skeletal muscle cells make up about half of your body's cell mass.
cards.context: Yet, as Level 3 found, they're only a tiny fraction of your cells by number. The trick is size: the biggest muscle fibers are the heaviest cells you have, sitting at the far end of a range that starts with tiny red blood cells. A few heavyweights, doing the lifting.

levels.title: How Muscles Pull
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why muscles can only pull and so work in pairs.
levels.summary: Myosin heads pull actin filaments past them, shortening a muscle. A muscle can only pull, so muscles work in pairs: the biceps bends the elbow and the triceps straightens it.

cards.headline: Your muscles can't push. So how do you push a door?
cards.body: Every muscle in your body can only pull. Yet you push doors, shopping carts and elevator buttons all day. The answer is teamwork, and it starts deep inside each muscle fiber.

cards.headline: Tiny hands on a rope
cards.body: Inside a muscle fiber lie two kinds of protein filament: thick ones with myosin heads, and thin ones made of actin. When a signal arrives, the myosin heads grab the actin and pull it, sliding the thin filaments past the thick ones. Each head pulls only a tiny distance, lets go, re-cocks using energy from ATP and grabs again. Picture a crowd of hands hauling in a rope.

cards.headline: Pull only, so muscles come in pairs
cards.body: Sliding filaments can shorten a muscle, but a muscle can only contract, never push. So muscles work in pairs that pull in opposite directions. Your biceps pulls to bend your elbow; your triceps, on the back of your arm, pulls to straighten it. At the knee, the quadriceps straighten and the hamstrings bend. When one partner pulls, the other relaxes.

mascot.line: Push-ups are secretly pull-ups for your triceps. Please do not tell the gym.

cards.headline: Every push is a pull in disguise
cards.body: So how do you push that door? Your triceps pulls to straighten your elbow, and your arm drives forward while the biceps relaxes. No muscle pushed anything. Every push you'll ever make is a pull happening somewhere else.

levels.title: Tendons and Ligaments
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what tendons and ligaments connect.
levels.summary: Tendons tie muscle to bone; ligaments tie bone to bone at joints. Both are ropes of parallel collagen with little blood supply. The Achilles tendon is the body's thickest.

cards.headline: Your body's thickest tendon is named after a hero's weak spot.
cards.body: In Greek myth, Achilles' heel was the one place he could be hurt. Today his name belongs to the tendon at the back of your heel. So what is a tendon, and what's the thing people always mix it up with?

cards.headline: Muscle to bone, bone to bone

items.label: Tendons

Carry a muscle's pull to the skeleton

items.label: Ligaments

cards.headline: Built like rope
cards.body: Both are dense connective tissue, the binding-and-supporting tissue type from Level 4. They're packed with collagen, the same tough protein that keeps bone from being brittle, and the fibers are lined up in parallel. Like the strands of a rope, parallel fibers resist stretching in the direction of the pull.

cards.fact: The Achilles tendon is the thickest and most powerful tendon in your body.
cards.context: It connects your calf muscles to your heel. So the legend's famous weak spot is home to your strongest tendon.

mascot.line: Sprain: ligament. Strain: muscle or tendon. The t in strain is for tendon, if that helps.

cards.headline: Two injuries, two tissues
cards.body: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament. A strain is a stretched or torn muscle or tendon. They sound alike, but they hurt different tissues. And because tendons don't have a rich blood supply, they heal slowly.

levels.title: Getting Stronger
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happens inside muscles when you exercise.
levels.summary: Muscles grow by thickening fibers with more myofibrils, not by adding cells. Endurance exercise can add mitochondria and capillaries; unused muscle shrinks, but can often recover.

cards.headline: Lifting weights won't give you new muscle cells. It upgrades the old ones.
cards.body: When muscles grow, your body doesn't add new muscle cells. It remodels the ones you already have. What changes depends on how you use them, and on whether you use them at all.

mascot.line: Your muscles do not hire new staff. They promote from within.

cards.headline: Thicker fibers, same number
cards.body: Resistance exercise, such as lifting weights, makes muscle fibers build more myofibrils. Each myofibril is a chain of tiny units holding Level 16's actin and myosin filaments. With more of them packed in, each fiber gets thicker, and so does the muscle. This is called hypertrophy: same cells, more rope-pullers inside each one.

cards.headline: Endurance builds the power supply
cards.body: Long, steady exercise changes muscle in a different way. It can add more mitochondria, the power stations from Level 2 that turn energy from food into a form cells can use. It can also add capillaries, the tiny blood vessels threading through the muscle. More engines, more fuel lines.

cards.headline: Use it or lose it
cards.body: The upgrade runs in reverse, too. When a muscle isn't used, it loses structural proteins and shrinks. That's called atrophy. The good news: atrophy from disuse can often be reversed with exercise. Your muscles keep adjusting to whatever you ask of them.

levels.title: Babies Have More Bones
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how bones grow and fuse from birth to adulthood.
levels.summary: A newborn has roughly 270 to 300 bones. Many start as cartilage, skull gaps close in the first two years, growth plates lengthen bones until early adulthood, and fusion leaves 206.

cards.headline: A newborn has more bones than you do.
cards.body: Estimates put a newborn at roughly 270 to 300 bones. You have 206. Nobody loses bones growing up. They join. Here's how a baby's skeleton becomes yours.

cards.fact: A newborn has roughly 270 to 300 bones; sources vary.
cards.context: Many of them start as cartilage, a tough but flexible tissue. The cartilage doesn't turn into bone; it works as a template that bone gradually replaces. As the skeleton grows, many separate pieces fuse, until the count settles at Level 11's 206.

cards.headline: Soft spots, on purpose
cards.body: At birth the skull's bones aren't yet joined, so the head can change shape on the way through the birth canal. The gaps, called fontanelles, also leave room for the brain to grow. The one at the back usually closes by 1 to 2 months; the one at the front, sometime between 7 and 19 months.

mascot.line: Cartilage on one side, bone on the other. A growth plate is a construction zone that closes when the job is done.

cards.headline: Growth plates: where bones get longer
cards.body: Long bones grow at growth plates, layers of cartilage near each end. On one side of a plate new cartilage forms; on the other it's replaced by bone, so the shaft gets longer. This continues until early adulthood. Then bone replaces the plate entirely, leaving only a thin line, and growth in length is done.

cards.headline: Fusing into one
cards.body: Some bones merge late. Each hip bone starts as three separate bones, the ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse during the late teens. Your sacrum, at the base of your spine, is five vertebrae fused into a single bone.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Bones and Muscles
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how bones, joints and muscles work together to move you.
levels.summary: Bones are levers, joints are fulcrums and muscles supply the effort. The bent arm trades force for a big, fast movement, and one lift uses nerves, muscle, tendon, joint and ligament together.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: every move you make is a lever.
cards.body: Bones, joints, muscles, tendons: you've met all the parts. Now watch them work as one machine, the same one you use to pull a nail with a hammer.

cards.headline: Levers everywhere
cards.body: Pull a nail with the back of a hammer and you're using a lever: a stiff bar turning on a fixed point, the fulcrum. Your body works the same way. Bones are the stiff levers, joints are the fulcrums, and contracting muscles supply the effort. The load is whatever you're moving, even your own head when you lift it.

mascot.line: Your arm trades strength for speed. Handy for catching things, and for waving hello.

cards.headline: Built for speed, not strength
cards.body: Bend your arm. The elbow is the pivot, and the biceps pulls on the forearm closer to the elbow than the cup in your hand. That costs force: the muscle must pull harder than the load it lifts. In return, a small contraction swings your hand through a large, fast movement. Many of your muscle-and-bone pairs make the same trade.

cards.headline: One sip, the whole chapter
cards.body: Lift that cup. Your nervous system signals the biceps, skeletal muscle you control. Myosin pulls actin, the muscle shortens, and a tendon carries the pull to your forearm bone. The elbow, a hinge joint where ligaments connect the bones, bends. The triceps relaxes, ready to pull back the other way.

levels.title: The Heart
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the heart's four chambers pump blood.
levels.summary: The heart is a fist-sized pump with four chambers: atria receive blood, ventricles push it out. The right side feeds the lungs, the left the body, and four valves keep it one-way.

cards.headline: Your heart is two pumps sharing one body.
cards.body: It's a muscle about the size of your fist. Look inside, though, and you find four chambers working as two pumps, side by side. Why would one organ need two?

cards.headline: Four rooms: two upstairs, two down
cards.body: Your heart has four chambers. The two upper ones, the atria, are receiving rooms where blood arrives. The two lower ones, the ventricles, are the pumps that push it back out. Picture a house with a front hall above an engine room, on each side. Blood comes in upstairs, drops downstairs and gets shoved out the door.

mascot.line: Right goes to the lungs, left goes everywhere else. Two pumps, one heartbeat, zero arguments about who does more.

cards.headline: Right side to the lungs, left side to everything else
cards.body: The right side handles blood coming home from your body, low on oxygen. It arrives in the right atrium through two big veins, the venae cavae, and the right ventricle pumps it to your lungs. Refilled with oxygen, it returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. Then the left ventricle gives the big push that sends it to your whole body. That's why you need two pumps: one short hop, one very long haul.

cards.fact: Four valves keep your blood on a one-way street.
cards.context: The tricuspid, mitral, pulmonary and aortic valves open to let blood through, then close so it can't flow backward. You can even hear them: the "lub" of a heartbeat is the mitral and tricuspid valves closing, and the "dub" is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing. So the famous sound of your heart isn't the muscle. It's the doors shutting.

levels.title: A Lifetime of Beats
levels.objective: After this level you can explain heart rate and how much blood the heart pumps in a lifetime.
levels.summary: Each beat starts at the SA node in the right atrium. A resting adult heart beats 60 to 100 times a minute, about 100,000 times a day: nearly 2.9 billion beats in a 79-year life.

cards.headline: Press two fingers to your wrist. That tap is your heart at work.
cards.body: Each tap is one heartbeat, and the number in a minute is your heart rate. Now multiply that rhythm by a whole lifetime. How many beats is that, and how much blood gets moved?

cards.headline: Every beat starts with a spark
cards.body: Your heart has its own built-in drummer. Pacemaker cells in the sinoatrial (SA) node, in the right atrium, fire an electrical signal, and the heart muscle contracts in response. At rest, 60 to 100 beats a minute is normal for adults. Young children run faster (80 to 130 at ages 1 to 2), well-trained athletes can idle at 40 to 60, and exercise speeds everyone up. Same drummer, different tempo.

cards.fact: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day.
cards.context: Each beat pushes only about 70 milliliters of blood out of a ventricle, around 5 liters a minute at rest. But the beats never stop adding up: by bedtime your heart has moved about 7,000 to 8,000 liters of blood. Small sips, enormous total.

mascot.line: Nearly three billion beats and not a single sick day. I would like to meet its manager.

cards.headline: Now multiply by a lifetime
cards.body: Keep that pace for an average life of almost 79 years and your heart beats nearly 2.9 billion times. Over those years it pumps more than 200 million liters of blood. It never takes a weekend off, and it does all of it with a muscle about the size of your fist.

levels.title: Blood Vessels
levels.objective: After this level you can compare arteries, veins and capillaries.
levels.summary: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins bring it back at low pressure, holding about two-thirds of it. Capillaries, a single cell layer thick, are where delivery happens.

cards.headline: Arteries aren't the "oxygen" ones. They're the "away" ones.
cards.body: You might guess that arteries carry oxygen-rich blood and veins carry the rest. The real rule is simpler, and it's all about which way the blood is heading.

items.label: Arteries
points: Carry blood away from the heart
Thick walls; the big ones stretch with each push, then recoil

items.label: Veins
points: Carry blood back to the heart
Lower pressure, thinner walls
Many, especially in the limbs, have one-way valves

items.label: Capillaries
points: Link the smallest arteries to the smallest veins
Walls just one thin layer of cells

cards.headline: The artery that breaks the color code
cards.body: Here's the proof that direction is the rule. The pulmonary arteries carry blood from your right ventricle to your lungs, and that blood is low in oxygen. They're still arteries, because they lead away from the heart. And the slow, low-pressure veins? At any moment they hold roughly two-thirds of your blood. Arteries are the express lanes; veins are the parking garage.

mascot.line: Single file, no overtaking. The busiest lanes in your body are also the narrowest.

cards.headline: Capillaries: where the delivery happens
cards.body: Arteries and veins are only roads. The drop-off happens in capillaries, vessels so narrow (about 8 to 10 micrometers) that red blood cells squeeze through in single file. Their walls are a single thin layer of cells, so oxygen and nutrients cross out to your tissues and wastes cross in. All the pumping from Level 21 exists to get blood to this doorstep.

levels.title: What Blood Is Made Of
levels.objective: After this level you can name the parts of blood and what each one does.
levels.summary: Blood is over half plasma, a watery liquid, plus red cells (about 45 percent) that carry oxygen on hemoglobin, and a sliver of white cells and platelets. Adults have about 4 to 6 liters.

cards.headline: Spin a tube of blood and it splits into layers.
cards.body: Put a blood sample in a centrifuge and it separates: plasma on top, a thin pale layer in the middle, red cells at the bottom. Blood is plasma plus red cells, white cells and platelets. So what is each layer doing?

cards.fact: Over half your blood is plasma, and plasma is about 92% water.
cards.context: It's a watery liquid with salts and proteins dissolved in it, and everything else in blood rides along in it. An adult has about 4 to 6 liters of blood in all. Remember Level 7's water outside your cells? Part of that third is right here, flowing.

mascot.line: Bright red or dusky red, but never blue. Blood only comes in shades of red.

cards.headline: Red cells: the oxygen couriers
cards.body: Red blood cells make up about 45 percent of blood's volume, and Level 3 found they are about 84 percent of all your cells. Their job is delivering oxygen from your lungs to your tissues. The carrier is hemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that also gives blood its color. Fresh from the lungs, blood is bright red; after dropping off oxygen, it's a duskier red. Never blue.

cards.headline: The thin pale band
cards.body: That middle layer holds the rest: white blood cells, which fight infection, and platelets, which help blood clot when you cut yourself. Together they're less than 1 percent of a blood sample. The smallest share of blood, doing two of its most urgent jobs. Platelets get their moment in Level 28.

levels.title: Blood Types
levels.objective: After this level you can explain blood types and why they matter for transfusions.
levels.summary: In 1901 Landsteiner found blood groups by watching red cells clump. ABO type depends on A and B antigens on red cells; mismatched antibodies attack donated cells, so transfusions must match.

cards.headline: Giving someone blood used to be a gamble.
cards.body: Blood transfusions stayed risky until an Austrian physician, Karl Landsteiner, discovered the major human blood groups. It turns out your blood carries a label, and the label matters.

cards.headline: The clumping clue
cards.body: In 1901 Landsteiner published what he'd found: mix blood from two people, and sometimes the red cells clump together. The clumping wasn't random. It followed blood groups, the start of the ABO system we still use. The discovery earned him the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Not bad for watching blood misbehave.

cards.headline: Name tags on your red cells
cards.body: Your ABO type depends on two markers, the A and B antigens, sitting on the plasma membrane of your red cells (Level 2's outer wall). Type A has A, type B has B, type AB has both and type O has neither. Your plasma also carries antibodies against any marker you lack: type A blood carries anti-B, type B carries anti-A, type O carries both and type AB carries neither.

mascot.line: O negative: the red cells with no name tags at all, which is exactly what makes them welcome everywhere.

cards.headline: Why a mismatch matters
cards.body: Give someone red cells with a marker their antibodies target, and those antibodies latch on, making the donated cells clump and break apart. There's a second label too: Rh positive or negative, set by the Rh D antigen (about 85 percent of Americans are positive). Type O negative red cells carry no A, B or Rh D, so they can go to anyone in an emergency. Type AB positive people can receive any type.
