levels.title: Gene Editing
levels.objective: After this level you can explain in simple terms what CRISPR gene editing does.
levels.summary: CRISPR-Cas9, borrowed from bacteria, uses a guide RNA to find a DNA spot and Cas9 to cut it. Casgevy became the first approved CRISPR medicine in 2023; editing embryos remains widely rejected.

cards.headline: The scissors behind gene editing were borrowed from bacteria.
cards.body: Bacteria get attacked by viruses too, and they keep a memory of the attackers. They store small pieces of viral DNA in their own DNA, in patterns called CRISPR arrays. If the virus returns, they make RNA that recognizes it, and an enzyme called Cas9 cuts the virus's DNA apart. Scientists realized they could borrow the whole kit.

cards.headline: Find, cut, repair
cards.body: In 2012, Jennifer Doudna, Emmanuelle Charpentier and colleagues showed that CRISPR could edit genes. Scientists write a short guide RNA that matches the DNA they want to change. The guide leads Cas9 to that exact spot, and Cas9 cuts. Then the cell's own repair machinery takes over, and researchers use it to delete, add or change genetic material. Doudna and Charpentier shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

cards.fact: In late 2023, CRISPR became a medicine.
cards.context: In November 2023, the UK's medicines regulator authorized Casgevy, the world's first approved CRISPR therapy. On December 8, 2023, the US FDA approved it for sickle cell disease in patients 12 and older. Doctors take the patient's own blood stem cells, edit them to make more fetal hemoglobin, and return them after high-dose chemotherapy.

mascot.line: One patient, or every descendant after them. Same scissors, very different question.

cards.headline: Where to draw the line
cards.body: Casgevy edits body cells, so the change stays with one patient. Edit an egg, sperm or embryo, and the change could pass to future generations; that is illegal in the US and many other countries. In 2018, He Jiankui announced twin girls born from edited embryos, and in 2019 a Chinese court sentenced him to three years in prison. In 2023, the organizers of an international genome-editing summit, including the Royal Society, stated: "Heritable human genome editing remains unacceptable at this time."

levels.title: Fusion Power
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how fusion differs from fission and why it is so hard to achieve.
levels.summary: Fusion joins light nuclei; fission splits heavy ones. Because nuclei repel, fusion needs about 150 million °C. NIF's December 2022 shot gained energy on the target, not for the whole facility.

cards.headline: On December 5, 2022, a fusion experiment got out more than it put in.
cards.body: At the National Ignition Facility in California, 192 lasers delivered 2.05 megajoules of energy to a tiny fuel target, and fusion released 3.15 megajoules. More out than in! So why isn't fusion lighting your home? Start with what fusion is, then read the fine print.

cards.headline: Fusion joins; fission splits
cards.body: Fission releases energy by splitting heavy nuclei such as uranium. Fusion goes the other way: it joins very light nuclei into heavier ones, and it's what powers the Sun and the other stars. In the lab, the best reaction joins two kinds of hydrogen, deuterium and tritium, into helium. Fusion also can't run away: if control is lost, the reaction simply stops.

cards.headline: Why it's so hard: nuclei don't want to touch
cards.body: Remember Level 3: like charges repel. Nuclei are all positively charged, so they push each other away. To make them fuse, the fuel must be heated until the nuclei have enough energy to overcome that push. ITER says deuterium-tritium fusion needs 150,000,000 °C, 10 times hotter than the core of the Sun. At that heat the fuel is a plasma. Tokamaks hold it with magnetic fields; NIF squeezes its fuel with lasers.

mascot.line: Target gain and facility gain: two different scoreboards. Always ask which one a headline means.

cards.fact: NIF's gain was on the target, not the whole facility.
cards.context: The lasers delivered 2.05 megajoules and fusion released 3.15, a gain above 1.5 on the target. But making each shot takes about 300 megajoules of electricity from the grid, so the facility as a whole used far more energy than the fusion made. By Level 10's math, 3.15 megajoules is under one kilowatt-hour.

levels.title: Quantum Computers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what makes quantum computers different, without the hype.
levels.summary: A qubit can be 0, 1 or a mix until measured. Quantum computers are expected to help with specific jobs like simulating molecules, not replace ordinary computers; qubits are fragile and error-prone.

cards.headline: In 2019, a quantum computer did a job in 200 seconds. The argument took longer.
cards.body: Google researchers reported that their Sycamore processor finished a calculation in 200 seconds that they estimated would take a top supercomputer 10,000 years. IBM researchers replied that a better classical method could do it in 2.5 days. To judge claims like these, you need to know what a qubit is, and what it's good for.

cards.headline: A switch that isn't just on or off
cards.body: Remember Level 4's switch: open or closed, never both. An ordinary computer bit is the same, either 0 or 1. A qubit, a quantum bit, can be 0, 1 or a mix of the two, called a superposition. But the moment you measure it, you get a plain 0 or 1. The in-between only lasts until you look.

cards.headline: What they're good for
cards.body: Quantum computers aren't faster at everything. NIST expects them to help with particular problems, such as simulating the quantum rules that govern molecules, chemicals and materials. In 1994, Peter Shor described a quantum algorithm that could quickly factor the huge numbers that protect much of today's encryption. That's why, in August 2024, NIST released its first encryption standards designed to withstand quantum attacks.

mascot.line: When a headline says quantum, ask: which problem, and compared with what?

cards.headline: What they're not
cards.body: A quantum computer isn't a faster laptop: NIST sees the two kinds of machine working together, not one replacing the other. Qubits are fragile. Many must be kept near absolute zero, and today's machines make an error roughly once in every thousand operations. And that 2019 task? It was a benchmark, sampling random quantum circuits, chosen because it gets exponentially harder for ordinary computers.

levels.title: Space Tech on Earth
levels.objective: After this level you can name everyday technologies that came out of space research.
levels.summary: Phone camera sensors grew from 1990s JPL research and memory foam from 1966 NASA airplane seats. Tang, Teflon and Velcro are not NASA inventions; astronauts just made them famous.

cards.headline: The camera in your phone grew out of a NASA project.
cards.body: NASA calls space technologies that end up in everyday life spinoffs, and it has published a Spinoff report every year since 1976. Some spinoffs are hiding in your pocket and under you right now. Some famous ones aren't spinoffs at all.

cards.headline: A camera on a chip
cards.body: In the 1990s, NASA wanted smaller spacecraft cameras that used less power. Eric Fossum's team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory built CMOS image sensors: a whole camera on one chip, far smaller and far thriftier with power than the sensors of the day. Small and battery-friendly turned out to be exactly what cell phones needed. Fossum called phones the killer application. The camera built for spacecraft ended up in your pocket.

mascot.line: A crash-safety cushion that ended up in your shoes. Knowledge travels.

cards.fact: Memory foam began as an airplane seat cushion in 1966.
cards.context: NASA's Ames Research Center wanted seats that protected people better in a crash. Charles Yost, working with NASA, made a foam that slowly molded to whatever pressed on it, then sprang back once the pressure was gone: "slow spring back foam." Later it padded football helmets, helped prevent bedsores and cushioned shoe insoles.

cards.headline: Myth check: NASA didn't invent Velcro
cards.body: Some famous "space inventions" aren't. NASA itself says General Foods developed Tang in 1957, DuPont invented Teflon in 1938, and a Swiss engineer invented Velcro in the 1940s. Astronauts made them famous: John Glenn drank Tang in orbit in 1962, and Apollo missions used Velcro to anchor equipment. Using something in space isn't the same as inventing it.

levels.title: Judging New Technology
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh the benefits and risks of a new invention.
levels.summary: Leaded petrol boosted engines from 1922 and harmed health until 2021. Collingridge's dilemma: effects show late, when change is hard. Ask who benefits, who bears the risk and who supplies evidence.

cards.headline: For 99 years, the world put lead in its petrol on purpose.
cards.body: From 1922, a lead compound called tetraethyllead was added to petrol to make engines run better. It worked. It also harmed people's hearts and children's developing brains. The last country stopped selling it in July 2021. How do you judge a new invention before its costs show up?

cards.headline: A benefit at the pump, a cost in the air
cards.body: The benefit was easy to see: better engine performance. The costs landed on people's health, and acting on them took decades. Most wealthy countries had banned leaded petrol by the 1980s, yet as late as 2002 almost all low- and middle-income countries still used it. The UN Environment Programme estimates that ending it prevents more than 1.2 million premature deaths a year.

cards.headline: The Collingridge dilemma
cards.body: In 1980, David Collingridge described the trap in his book The Social Control of Technology. Early on, a technology is easy to change, but nobody can yet predict its effects. By the time the effects are clear, it's everywhere and hard to change. Leaded petrol fits neatly, and the trap is worth remembering for every technology in this chapter.

mascot.line: My favorite question: who gains if I believe this? It works on headlines too.

cards.headline: Questions worth asking
cards.body: Who benefits, and who bears the risk? What's the evidence, and who supplies it? Remember Level 9: Edison, whose Pearl Street station ran on DC, claimed AC was more dangerous and electrocuted animals to prove it. Lawmakers try to match rules to risk. The European Union's AI Act, in force since August 2024, bans a few uses such as social scoring, sets strict rules for high-risk uses like hiring, and leaves minimal-risk AI such as spam filters free of new obligations.

levels.title: Government in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what governments do and why nearly every society has one.
levels.summary: Government is how a community is run: laws, order, services and taxes. The word began as Greek for steering a ship, and governments grew where people shared something vital, like Sumer's rivers.

cards.headline: "Government" began as a sailor's word. It meant steering a ship.
cards.body: It comes, through Latin, from the Greek kybernan: to steer or pilot a ship. Keep that picture. A ship full of people needs someone at the helm, and this whole skill is about who steers, how, and why the rest of the crew goes along.

cards.headline: What a government is
cards.body: Britannica defines government as the political system by which a country or community is administered and regulated. In plainer words, it's how a group of people organizes itself and decides who gets the authority to make choices for everyone. A village council and a national parliament are different sizes of the same idea: someone steering.

mascot.line: Laws, protection, services, taxes. Four jobs, one steering wheel.

cards.headline: The job list
cards.body: So what does the steering involve? Governments make laws to keep order. They defend the country and keep the peace at home, with armies, police and fire services. They provide things a society needs, like schools, health care and roads. And they raise money through taxes to pay for it all. Each of those jobs gets its own level in this chapter.

cards.fact: The first big governments grew up around shared rivers.
cards.context: While humans were few, Britannica notes, there was hardly any government. Farming changed that. In Sumer, in today's Iraq, crops depended on irrigation, and the flow of water down the Tigris and Euphrates had to be coordinated by a central authority. Once lots of people share something vital, somebody has to steer.

cards.fact: Today the United Nations has 193 member states.
cards.context: They range from giants like India to tiny Tuvalu, and each one runs its affairs through a government of its own. Governments differ enormously, as Chapter 2 will show. Having one at all is the part nearly everyone shares.

questions.explanation: "Govern" comes, through Latin gubernare, from the Greek kybernan: to steer or pilot a ship.

questions.prompt: According to Britannica, why did Sumer come to need a central authority?

options.label: Its people spoke too many different languages
options.rationale: Language isn't the reason given; water is.

options.label: Its kings wanted workers to build pyramids
options.rationale: Pyramids belong to Egypt, and they aren't the reason given here.

options.label: Water from its rivers had to be shared out
Its traders needed one coin for every market
options.rationale: Coins came much later; the issue was sharing water.

questions.explanation: Sumer's farms depended on irrigation, so the flow of the Tigris and Euphrates had to be coordinated by a central authority.

questions.prompt: How does the ship picture behind the word "government" fit Sumer's rivers?

options.label: Shared water needed someone to steer its use
Sumerian rulers governed from boats on the river
options.rationale: The picture is a metaphor; nobody ruled from a boat.

options.label: The Sumerians invented the word "government"
options.rationale: The word comes from Greek, much later.

options.label: Rivers made any government unnecessary there
options.rationale: The opposite: shared water called for a central authority.

questions.explanation: Government means steering, and Sumer's shared water is exactly the kind of thing that needs a steady hand at the helm.

levels.title: Why Have Rules?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why groups need rules, from games to countries.
levels.summary: Rules let everyone play the same game. The Football Association formed in 1863 to set one code of rules, and in 1967 Sweden switched to driving on the right to match its neighbors.

cards.headline: Before 1863, English football had no shared rulebook. It showed.
cards.body: Schools and clubs each played their own version of the game. The Football Association's own history recalls "feverish" disputes over how it should be played. Hard to enjoy a match when the two teams disagree about what game it is.

cards.headline: One rulebook for everyone
cards.body: On 26 October 1863, clubs met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London and formed the Football Association, aiming for a definite code of rules. One founder, Ebenezer Morley, argued that football should have rules the way cricket did. Now teams who had never met could play each other by the same code. That's the first job of rules: they let strangers cooperate.

cards.headline: Left or right doesn't matter. Agreeing does.
cards.body: Countries face the same problem on a bigger field. Driving on the left works fine. So does driving on the right. The trouble starts when neighbors pick differently. Sweden drove on the left, while Denmark, Finland and Norway drove on the right, and the mismatch caused accidents for Swedes driving abroad and for visitors to Sweden.

mascot.line: Spare a thought for anyone who slept through the announcement.

cards.fact: On 3 September 1967, a whole country switched sides of the road.
cards.context: Swedes call it Dagen H, for högertrafik, right-hand traffic. Early that morning, traffic stopped, then every vehicle moved over to the right. The change had to happen everywhere at once, because a traffic rule only works when everyone follows the same one. Deciding a rule like that for a whole country is a job for Level 1's steering wheel: government.

cards.headline: Rules: agreed
learned: Before 1863, football clubs played by different rules
The FA formed to set one code for everyone
Sweden's neighbors drove on the right
Dagen H, 1967: the whole country switched at once

questions.prompt: Why did clubs form the Football Association in 1863?

options.label: To build London's first football stadium
options.rationale: Stadiums weren't the point; rules were.

options.label: To set one definite code of rules
To start paying professional players
options.rationale: Pay wasn't on the table; a shared code was.

options.label: To ban football from the public schools
options.rationale: Schools kept playing; they just needed common rules.

questions.explanation: The FA was formed to establish a definite code of rules, so everyone could play the same game.

questions.prompt: Before 1967, what was the problem with Sweden driving on the left?

options.label: Left-hand driving is always more dangerous
options.rationale: Either side works; the problem was the mismatch.

options.label: Swedish law had never set a side of the road
options.rationale: Sweden had a rule; it just differed from its neighbors'.

options.label: Its neighbors drove on the right, causing accidents
Swedish-made cars could only drive on the right
options.rationale: Swedes did drive on the left until 1967.

questions.explanation: Denmark, Finland and Norway drove on the right, so Swedes abroad and visitors to Sweden were caught out.

questions.prompt: What do the 1863 football rulebook and Sweden's Dagen H have in common?

options.label: Both were decided by a public vote
options.rationale: Neither card describes a public vote.

options.label: Both copied the rules of cricket
options.rationale: Only Morley pointed to cricket; Sweden was about traffic.

options.label: Both happened in London
options.rationale: The FA met in London; Dagen H was in Sweden.

options.label: Both got everyone following the same rule

questions.explanation: A rule works best when everyone shares it: one code for football, one side of the road for a country.

levels.title: Power and Authority
levels.objective: After this level you can tell power from authority.
levels.summary: Power is the ability to impose your will on others; authority is power people accept as legitimate. Max Weber named three kinds of authority: traditional, charismatic and legal-rational.

cards.headline: A robber and a traffic officer can both make you stop. Only one has authority.
cards.body: Both get you to do something you didn't plan to do. Yet you'd feel very differently about each. A German sociologist gave us the words for that difference, and they're some of the most useful words in politics.

cards.headline: Power: getting your way
cards.body: Max Weber, in work published in 1922, defined power as the ability to exercise your will over others. That's all it takes. The robber has power. So does a bully, or anyone with a big enough stick. Notice what the definition leaves out: whether anyone thinks you ought to have it.

cards.headline: Authority: power people accept
cards.body: Authority is accepted power: power that people agree to follow because they see it as legitimate. For Weber, being obeyed wasn't enough. The order had to be accepted as valid. You wave back at the traffic officer; you don't wave back at the robber. Same stop, very different reason.

mascot.line: Next time someone says "because I said so", ask which of Weber's three they're using.

items.label: Traditional
points: Rests on long-standing custom
Example: a monarch who inherits the throne

items.label: Charismatic
points: Rests on a leader's exceptional personal qualities
Examples: Napoleon, Martin Luther King Jr.

items.label: Legal-rational
points: Rests on laws and written rules
Belongs to the office, not the person

cards.headline: Power vs authority: sorted
learned: Power: the ability to impose your will
Authority: power people accept as legitimate
Weber's three roots: tradition, charisma, law
Legal-rational authority belongs to the office

questions.prompt: In Weber's terms, what turns power into authority?

options.label: Having more weapons than anyone else
options.rationale: Weapons give power, not authority.

options.label: People accepting it as legitimate
Being written in a very old book
options.rationale: Tradition is one root of authority, but acceptance is what counts.

options.label: Winning every argument
options.rationale: Winning arguments isn't the test; acceptance is.

questions.explanation: Authority is power that people accept as legitimate and agree to follow.

questions.prompt: A newly elected official is obeyed because the rules give that office its powers. Which kind of authority is that?

options.label: Traditional
options.rationale: Traditional authority rests on custom, like an inherited throne.

options.label: Charismatic
options.rationale: Charismatic authority rests on the leader's personal qualities.

options.label: Legal-rational
No authority, only power
options.rationale: People accept the office's rules, so it's authority.

questions.explanation: Legal-rational authority rests on laws and written rules, and it belongs to the office rather than the person.

questions.prompt: Level 1's Sumer needed a central authority to share its water. In Weber's terms, what did that authority need beyond power?

options.label: A bigger army than its neighbors
options.rationale: An army is power; authority needs acceptance.

options.label: A written constitution
options.rationale: Constitutions aren't part of Weber's test.

options.label: Control of the only boats
options.rationale: Controlling boats would be power, not authority.

options.label: People accepting its orders as valid

questions.explanation: Authority is power that people accept. Sharing water works far better when people accept who decides.

levels.title: What a Law Is
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what makes a rule a law.
levels.summary: A law is a rule a community recognizes as binding, enforced by a controlling authority. Around 1750 BCE, Hammurabi of Babylon set 282 rulings in stone, written as if-then laws.

cards.headline: About 3,800 years ago, a king had his laws carved into stone.
cards.body: Around 1750 BCE, Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 legal rulings engraved on a black stone slab more than 2.25 meters tall. You can see it today in the Louvre in Paris. Why go to all that trouble? Because it shows what turns a rule into a law.

cards.headline: Rules versus laws
cards.body: Your household might ban shoes indoors. That's a rule, but not a law. Britannica describes law as the rules of conduct that a community recognizes as binding, enforced through a controlling authority. Two things make the difference: the whole community is bound by it, and an authority (Level 3's accepted power) stands ready to enforce it.

cards.headline: If this, then that
cards.body: Hammurabi's laws follow one pattern: if someone does this, then that follows. Law 196 is the famous one: if a man puts out another man's eye, his eye shall be put out. An eye for an eye. Every law is a consequence spelled out in advance, not made up after the fact.

mascot.line: Written down, public and enforced: a big step. Fair to everyone: a later chapter's story.

cards.fact: The code invited wronged people to come and read it.
cards.context: Its closing words tell anyone oppressed who has a case at law to stand before the king's image and read the inscription. A law everyone can read is a law everyone can point to. Equal for all, though? Not quite. Penalties varied with the offender's social status.

cards.headline: Law: laid down
learned: A law binds a whole community
A controlling authority enforces it
Hammurabi set out 282 rulings around 1750 BCE
His laws ran on if-then, like law 196

questions.prompt: What did Hammurabi's great stone slab record?

options.label: A map of Babylon's canals
options.rationale: It holds laws, not a map.

options.label: A list of Babylon's kings
options.rationale: It's a law code, not a king list.

options.label: 282 legal rulings
The city's tax receipts
options.rationale: It records legal rulings, not receipts.

questions.explanation: Around 1750 BCE, Hammurabi had 282 legal rulings engraved on a black stone stela, now in the Louvre.

questions.prompt: Why is a family's "no shoes indoors" rule not a law?

options.label: No controlling authority enforces it on a whole community
It was never carved into a stone slab like Hammurabi's
options.rationale: Laws don't need stone; they need community recognition and enforcement.

options.label: It isn't written in if-then form like a real law
options.rationale: Wording isn't the test.

options.label: Only kings and queens are allowed to make rules
options.rationale: Kings aren't required; a controlling authority is.

questions.explanation: Law is the set of rules a community recognizes as binding, enforced through a controlling authority.

questions.prompt: Level 3 defined authority as accepted power. What role does it play in making a law?

options.label: It carves the law into stone
options.rationale: Carving was Hammurabi's choice, not what makes a law.

options.label: It decides which games people play
options.rationale: That's closer to Level 2's football rules.

options.label: It stands behind the rule and enforces it
It makes the law apply only to rulers
options.rationale: Laws bind the community, not only rulers.

questions.explanation: A law is enforced through a controlling authority: accepted power standing behind the rule.

levels.title: Public Services
levels.objective: After this level you can name the services governments provide, like clean water and schools.
levels.summary: Governments provide public services like schools, transport, police and fire. Public goods such as defense invite free riding, which taxes required by law overcome.

cards.headline: Turn on a tap and clean water comes out. For 1 in 4 people, it doesn't.
cards.body: In 2024, about 2.1 billion people still lacked safely managed drinking water, according to WHO and UNICEF. Services like this are easy to forget, right up until they're missing.

cards.headline: Services for everyone
cards.body: Public services are the things government provides for its people, usually open to all and paid for with taxes. Think public schools, buses and trains, the mail, police and fire departments, and food, housing and health care for people in need. Your walk to school or work probably passes half a dozen of them before you've had breakfast.

cards.headline: Why not just buy them?
cards.body: Some things are hard to sell one customer at a time. Economists call them public goods: it's hard to stop anyone using them, and one person's use doesn't leave less for others. National defense is the classic case. It protects you whether you paid or not. So why pay? Letting others pay while you enjoy the benefit is called free riding.

mascot.line: Free riding: great for one person, terrible if everyone tries it.

cards.fact: Free riders are beaten by a rule that everyone chips in.
cards.context: If people agree through the political process to pay taxes, the law can require everyone to contribute, and the public good gets made. It's Level 2's lesson again: a rule works when everybody follows the same one. How those taxes work is the next level.

cards.headline: Public services: listed
learned: Governments provide schools, transport, mail, police and fire
In 2024, 1 in 4 people lacked safely managed water
Public goods are hard to exclude people from
Taxes required by law beat free riding

questions.prompt: In 2024, about what share of people worldwide lacked safely managed drinking water?

options.label: 1 in 100
options.rationale: Far more than that: about 2.1 billion people.

options.label: 1 in 20
options.rationale: Still too low; it was about 2.1 billion.

options.label: 1 in 4
1 in 2
options.rationale: Too high; it was about a quarter.

questions.explanation: WHO and UNICEF found about 2.1 billion people, 1 in 4, lacked safely managed drinking water in 2024.

questions.prompt: Why is national defense called a public good?

options.label: It protects only the people who paid for it
options.rationale: It protects everyone, paid or not.

options.label: It protects everyone, and no one's share runs out
It is always run by private security companies
options.rationale: Who runs it isn't what makes it a public good.

options.label: It is paid for by selling tickets to each family
options.rationale: You can't sell tickets to something you can't keep people out of.

questions.explanation: Public goods are nonexcludable and nonrival: defense protects everyone at once, whether or not they paid.

questions.prompt: Level 2 showed that a rule works when everyone follows the same one. How does that help pay for public goods?

options.label: Everyone takes turns guarding the country
options.rationale: The solution is money through taxes, not turns.

options.label: People vote on which neighbors should pay
options.rationale: The law requires everyone to contribute, not a chosen few.

options.label: A law makes everyone pay taxes, so no one free rides
Public goods are sold only to rule-followers
options.rationale: Public goods can't be sold to some and not others.

questions.explanation: When a law requires everyone to contribute through taxes, nobody can free ride, and the public good gets made.

levels.title: Paying for It
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how taxes fund government.
levels.summary: Taxes are compulsory, unrequited payments on what people earn, buy and own. In 2024 they averaged 34.1% of GDP across OECD countries, from 18.3% in Mexico to 45.2% in Denmark.

cards.headline: A bus fare buys you a ride. What does a tax buy you?
cards.body: You hand over money either way. But the two deals work in completely different ways, and that difference is what makes a tax a tax.

cards.headline: Compulsory and unrequited
cards.body: The OECD defines taxes as compulsory, unrequited payments to government. Compulsory: you can't opt out. Unrequited: what you get back from government isn't in proportion to what you paid. A fare buys one ride. Your taxes buy nothing in particular, and help pay for Level 5's whole list.

items.label: What you earn
points: Taxes on income and profits
Social security contributions and payroll taxes on wages

items.label: What you buy
points: Taxes on goods and services
Such as value-added tax (VAT)

items.label: What you own
points: Taxes on property

mascot.line: Same idea, very different sizes. Why anyone should agree to pay at all is Level 7's question.

cards.fact: Across OECD countries, taxes come to about a third of GDP.
cards.context: GDP measures the value of everything a country produces in a year. In 2024, taxes averaged 34.1% of GDP across OECD countries, per the OECD's Revenue Statistics 2025. The range was wide: 18.3% in Mexico, 45.2% in Denmark. How big that share should be is a political choice, and countries make it very differently.

cards.headline: Taxes: explained
learned: Taxes are compulsory and unrequited payments
They fall on what you earn, buy and own
OECD average in 2024: 34.1% of GDP
From 18.3% in Mexico to 45.2% in Denmark

questions.prompt: In the OECD's definition, what does it mean that a tax is "unrequited"?

options.label: You can choose whether to pay it
options.rationale: That's the opposite of how taxes work.

options.label: It is paid only once in your life
options.rationale: Taxes are paid again and again.

options.label: What you get back isn't in proportion to what you paid
It must be spent on the thing that was taxed
options.rationale: Tax money isn't tied to what was taxed.

questions.explanation: Unrequited means the benefits government provides aren't normally in proportion to what each person pays.

questions.prompt: In 2024, taxes across OECD countries averaged about what share of GDP?

options.label: About a tenth
options.rationale: Even Mexico, the lowest, was near a fifth.

options.label: About a third
About a half
options.rationale: Even Denmark, the highest, was below a half.

options.label: About nine-tenths
options.rationale: Far too high; the average was 34.1%.

questions.explanation: The 2024 average was 34.1% of GDP, from 18.3% in Mexico to 45.2% in Denmark.

questions.prompt: Level 5's free riders enjoy public goods without paying. Which feature of taxes stops them?

options.label: Taxes are compulsory
Taxes are only on property
options.rationale: Taxes fall on earnings, spending and property.

options.label: Taxes are set by each person
options.rationale: Nobody sets their own tax; that would invite free riding.

options.label: Taxes buy one specific service
options.rationale: Taxes are unrequited: they don't buy a specific service.

questions.explanation: Because taxes are compulsory, everyone contributes, so nobody can free ride on public goods.

levels.title: The Social Contract
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the ideas of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau.
levels.summary: A social contract sets out the rights and duties of rulers and ruled. Hobbes traded freedom for protection, Locke grounded government in consent, and Rousseau in the general will.

cards.headline: You never signed a contract with your government. Some say you're in one anyway.
cards.body: A social contract is an agreement, real or imagined, between the people, or between the people and their rulers, setting out the rights and duties of each. Three thinkers used the idea to tackle one question: why obey a government at all? Each gave a different answer.

cards.headline: Hobbes: anything beats chaos
cards.body: Thomas Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651, after England's civil war. Picture life with no government, he said: a war of all against all, where life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short." To escape it, people hand their freedom to an all-powerful sovereign in exchange for peace and protection. His bargain: safety is worth a lot of freedom.

cards.headline: Locke: government works for you
cards.body: John Locke saw it differently. Even without government, he argued, people have natural rights to life, liberty and property. Government gets its legitimacy from the consent of the governed, and if rulers violate those rights, people may resist them. Remember Level 3's authority, power people accept? Locke made that acceptance the whole foundation.

mascot.line: Three thinkers, three bargains. Philosophers still argue over which one you'd sign.

cards.headline: Rousseau: rules we make together
cards.body: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, born in Geneva, opened The Social Contract (1762) with a famous line: "Man was born free, and he is everywhere in chains." His answer was the general will. People agree together to live by laws aimed at the common good, laws they make for themselves. Obeying those, he argued, is a kind of freedom.

cards.headline: Social contract: signed
learned: A social contract sets out rulers' and people's rights and duties
Hobbes: give up freedom to a sovereign for peace
Locke: natural rights, consent and a right to resist
Rousseau: laws made together by the general will

questions.prompt: According to Hobbes, what would life be like without any government?

options.label: Peaceful but boring
options.rationale: Hobbes pictured war, not peace.

options.label: Governed by the general will
options.rationale: The general will is Rousseau's idea.

options.label: Free, with natural rights respected
options.rationale: That's closer to Locke's view.

options.label: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short

questions.explanation: Hobbes pictured a war of all against all, with life "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short".

questions.prompt: In Locke's view, what may people do if their rulers violate their natural rights?

options.label: Resist them
Nothing: the sovereign's power is absolute
options.rationale: Absolute power is Hobbes's sovereign, not Locke's.

options.label: Hand over even more freedom
options.rationale: Locke's answer runs the other way.

options.label: Leave the country forever
options.rationale: Locke's answer is a right to resist, not exile.

questions.explanation: For Locke, government rests on consent, so people may resist rulers who violate their rights to life, liberty and property.

questions.prompt: In this social contract level, which thinker is correctly paired with an idea?

options.label: Hobbes: the general will
options.rationale: The general will is Rousseau's.

options.label: Locke: an all-powerful sovereign
options.rationale: The all-powerful sovereign is Hobbes's.

options.label: Rousseau: the general will
Hobbes: a right to resist rulers
options.rationale: The right to resist is Locke's.

questions.explanation: Hobbes: a sovereign for protection. Locke: consent, natural rights and resistance. Rousseau: the general will.

levels.title: Levels of Government
levels.objective: After this level you can explain national, regional and local government.
levels.summary: Government comes in layers. In Canada, the federal level handles defence, provinces run schools and hospitals, and towns handle water and waste. India's panchayats govern villages.

cards.headline: Who fixes the pothole on your street? Not your country's leader.
cards.body: Government comes in layers, from the whole country down to your town. Canada makes a tidy example: it has three levels of government, each with its own list of jobs.

cards.headline: The top layer: the whole country
cards.body: Canada's federal government handles matters like national defence, foreign affairs, currency, citizenship and passports, criminal law and the postal service. These are jobs where one answer for the whole country makes sense. Imagine every town printing its own money, or running its own army.

cards.headline: The middle and bottom layers
cards.body: Canada's provinces and territories run education, hospitals and health care, and social services. Municipal governments take the jobs outside your front door: fire protection, local police, public transit, parks, waste management, water supply and local roads. Level 5's public services, it turns out, are shared out between the layers.
cards.callout: Some responsibilities are shared between levels.

mascot.line: Three layers of government over one village. That's a lot of people steering one ship.

cards.fact: In India, even a village has its own elected government.
cards.context: In 1992, India's 73rd constitutional amendment declared panchayats, elected local councils, institutions of self-government alongside the Union and state governments. They work at three tiers: the village, the block and the district. So a farmer can have a village council, a state government and a national one, all at once.

cards.headline: Levels of government: layered
learned: Canada has federal, provincial and municipal levels
Federal: defence, currency, passports
Provincial: schools and hospitals; municipal: water, waste, fire
India's panchayats govern villages, blocks and districts

options.label: Made panchayats institutions of self-government

options.rationale: States remained alongside the Union and panchayats.

options.label: Created India's first national parliament
options.rationale: The amendment concerned local councils, not parliament.

options.label: Merged every village into a larger district
options.rationale: Villages kept their own panchayats as one of three tiers.

questions.explanation: The 1992 amendment declared panchayats institutions of self-government, working at village, block and district level.

questions.prompt: Your rubbish bins haven't been emptied in Canada. Which level of government handles that?

options.label: Federal
options.rationale: The federal level handles country-wide jobs like defence and passports.

options.label: Provincial or territorial
options.rationale: Provinces run schools and hospitals, not bins.

options.label: Municipal
None: it's a private matter
options.rationale: Waste management is on the municipal list.

questions.explanation: Waste management is a municipal job in Canada, along with fire protection, water supply and local roads.

questions.prompt: Level 5 listed public schools as a public service. In Canada, which level runs education?

options.label: Federal
options.rationale: The federal level handles things like defence and passports.

options.label: Provincial or territorial
Municipal
options.rationale: Municipalities handle local services like water and waste.

options.label: Village panchayat
options.rationale: Panchayats are India's local councils, not Canada's.

questions.explanation: In Canada, provinces and territories are responsible for education, hospitals and health care.

levels.title: Nations and States
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the difference between a nation and a state.
levels.summary: A nation is a people with a shared identity; a state has territory, laws and a monopoly of legitimate force. The Kurds are a nation without a state; the UK is one state of four parts.

cards.headline: Tens of millions of Kurds share a nation. They have no state of their own.
cards.body: Britannica estimated the Kurds at 36 to 46 million in the mid-2010s, living mostly in parts of Iran, Iraq, Syria and Turkey. In the modern era they have had no nation-state of their own. How can so many people share a nation but not a state? Because those are two different things.

cards.headline: Nation, state, nation-state
cards.body: A nation is a community of people who share an identity: often a culture, a language or a history. A state is a political organization with territory, laws and the means to enforce them. Put the two together and you get a nation-state. A nation lives in a sense of "us". A state lives in borders, courts and passports.

cards.headline: Weber's test for a state
cards.body: Remember Max Weber from Level 3? In 1919 he defined the state as a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory. Only the state gets to use force, through police and courts, and people accept that it's allowed to. It's Level 3's authority, stretched across a whole country.

cards.fact: Nations and states rarely line up neatly.
cards.context: In Britannica's words, the borders of states and the boundaries of nations usually only partly overlap. The Kurds are one nation across several states. It works the other way too: the United Kingdom is one state made of four historical parts, England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, each with its own customs and traditions.

cards.headline: Nation vs state: mapped
learned: A nation: a people with a shared identity
A state: territory, laws and enforcement
Weber: the state monopolizes legitimate force
The Kurds and the UK show they rarely match

options.label: They are two different words for the same thing

options.rationale: They live under the governments of the states they're in.

options.label: Charisma: a leader's exceptional qualities

options.label: Free riding on public goods
options.rationale: Free riding is Level 5's problem, not legitimacy.

The general will

questions.explanation: Legitimate force is force people accept: Level 3's authority, stretched across a whole territory.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Why Government?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what governments are for and how they are paid for.
levels.summary: Aristotle called humans political animals. Chapter 1's answers to why government: shared rules, accepted authority, laws, public services paid for by taxes, and layers of government.

cards.headline: Why government at all? A Greek philosopher had an answer long before Hobbes.
cards.body: Aristotle said human beings are by nature political animals. We don't just happen to live in groups; living together is part of what we are. Anyone who could live entirely outside a community, he said, would be either a beast or a god.

cards.headline: First life, then the good life
cards.body: Aristotle wrote that the city-state comes into being for the sake of life, but exists for the sake of the good life. That's this chapter in one line. First, survival: Sumer's shared water, Hobbes's escape from a life that's nasty, brutish and short. Then, living well: schools, clean water and rules that let strangers play the same game.

items.label: Why rules?
points: So everyone plays the same game, from football to traffic
Laws bind a whole community and are enforced

items.label: Who decides?
points: Authority: power people accept as legitimate
The social contract asks why we obey

items.label: Who pays, and who does what?
points: Compulsory taxes fund public services
National, regional and local layers share the work

mascot.line: Ten levels in, and you can already steer a conversation about government.

cards.headline: Back at the helm
cards.body: Level 1 began with a ship. Now you can name its parts. The rules of the voyage are laws. Whoever holds the wheel needs authority, and the social contract asks why the crew goes along. The cargo everyone shares is public services. Taxes pay for the fuel. And the crew works on several decks at once, from the national government to the village council.

learned: Humans are political animals, said Aristotle
Rules and laws let everyone play the same game
Authority is power people accept
Taxes fund public services, shared across layers

levels.title: Monarchy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how monarchies work.
levels.summary: Monarchy means rule of one: a monarch who is head of state, usually by inheritance. Malaysia elects its ruler; Louis XIV claimed absolute power by divine right.

cards.headline: Malaysia's king changes every five years. His fellow rulers elect him.
cards.body: Malaysia's head of state, officially the paramount ruler, is elected from among nine hereditary state rulers for a five-year term. That makes him unusual. In most monarchies, nobody votes for the monarch at all. So what makes a monarchy a monarchy?

mascot.line: No CV, no interview. For most thrones, the only application form is a birth certificate.

cards.headline: Rule of one
cards.body: The name gives it away. Monarchy comes from the Greek monarkhia, literally "ruling of one". Britannica defines it as a system based on the undivided rule of a single person. That person, the monarch, is head of state and usually gets the job by heredity. You don't apply for a throne. You're born next in line for it.

cards.headline: Why people went along with it
cards.body: Remember Weber's three roots of authority from Level 3? A monarch who inherits the throne was his example of traditional authority: power accepted because things have always been done this way. Many monarchs had something extra on their side. Britannica notes that successful and popular monarchs were believed to have a sacred right to rule.

cards.fact: Louis XIV of France is the textbook absolute monarch.
cards.context: Absolutism means unlimited, centralized authority, held especially by a monarch. Louis XIV, who reigned from 1643 to 1715, is Britannica's most familiar example. Its favorite defense was the divine right of kings: kings got their authority from God, so they answered to no one on Earth. That's more than seven decades of answering to no one.

cards.headline: Monarchy: crowned

levels.title: Kings Who Reign but Do Not Rule
levels.objective: After this level you can explain constitutional monarchy.
levels.summary: In a constitutional monarchy the monarch is a symbolic head of state who reigns but does not govern. Sweden made its King's role entirely ceremonial in 1974; Japan's Emperor is a symbol.

cards.headline: Sweden has a king. He has no political power at all.
cards.body: Under Sweden's 1974 Instrument of Government, the King is still head of state, but he has no political power; his role is entirely ceremonial. A king who can't govern sounds like a contradiction. It's actually one of the most common kinds of monarchy.

cards.headline: Reigns, but does not govern
cards.body: Britannica defines constitutional monarchy as a system where a monarch shares power with a constitutionally organized government and acts as a symbolic head of state. The French politician Adolphe Thiers put it in five words: the king "reigns but does not govern." Not every king liked the idea. France's Louis-Philippe, who took the throne in 1830, refused to settle for that symbolic role.

cards.fact: Sweden gave up royal power in two big steps.
cards.context: In 1809, Sweden abolished royal absolutism: the King and the Riksdag, Sweden's parliament, were meant to share power. The 1974 Instrument of Government finished the job. The King stayed head of state, with a role that is entirely ceremonial. Level 11's Louis XIV would have found the job description baffling.

cards.headline: Japan's Emperor: a living symbol
cards.body: Japan's constitution makes the Emperor "the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people" and gives him no powers related to government. Britannica lists Japan alongside the United Kingdom, Belgium, Norway and Thailand as constitutional monarchies. So a crown can mean very different things: Louis XIV's unlimited power, or a symbol a whole country shares.

cards.headline: Constitutional monarchy: explained

levels.title: Dictatorship
levels.objective: After this level you can explain dictatorships and how they keep power.
levels.summary: A dictatorship is absolute power without effective limits, kept by force, terror and propaganda. Rome's dictator was a six-month emergency job; totalitarian states want all of life.

cards.headline: In ancient Rome, "dictator" was a job with a six-month limit.
cards.body: The Roman Republic appointed a dictator only in a crisis: a temporary magistrate with extraordinary powers, for at most six months. Then the job ended. Britannica's verdict on the modern kind is blunt: today's dictators resemble ancient tyrants, not ancient dictators.

cards.headline: Power with no brakes
cards.body: Britannica defines dictatorship as government in which one person or a small group holds absolute power without effective constitutional limits. The Roman version had brakes built in: a crisis to solve and a clock running. The modern version removes them. Nothing on the list can actually stop the ruler, and no deadline sends him home.

cards.headline: How dictators hold on
cards.body: Modern dictators typically take power by force or fraud, Britannica notes, then keep it through intimidation, terror and the suppression of basic civil liberties. They also use mass propaganda to keep public support. Put that in Level 3's terms. Fear gives them power; propaganda is the effort to make it look like authority, power that people accept.

mascot.line: An ordinary dictator wants you quiet. A totalitarian one wants your hobbies, your clubs and your thoughts too.

cards.fact: Some dictatorships want your whole life, not just your obedience.
cards.context: That's totalitarianism: government that permits no individual freedom and tries to put every part of life under the state. Benito Mussolini coined the term for Italy's fascist state: "all within the state, none outside the state, none against the state." Stalin's Soviet Union and Nazi Germany are Britannica's other classic cases.

levels.title: Rule by the Few
levels.objective: After this level you can explain oligarchy.
levels.summary: Oligarchy is rule by a privileged few for their own ends. Venice's Great Council closed to a hereditary group; Michels argued every organization drifts toward rule by a few.

cards.headline: Venice called itself a republic. A closed club of families ran it.
cards.body: Over about a century from 1297, Venice's Great Council, the body where sovereignty lay, was closed to everyone outside a fixed hereditary group. From the 1390s, new families stopped getting in at all. Rule by one is monarchy. What do you call rule by a locked room of a few?

cards.headline: Rule of the few
cards.body: Oligarchy comes from the Greek oligos, "few", and arkhein, "to rule". Britannica defines it as government by the few, especially power used by a small privileged group for corrupt or selfish ends. Aristotle drew the line against aristocracy, rule by the best. When the few rule for themselves, it's oligarchy, and those few are typically the wealthy.

cards.fact: Venice's oligarchy lasted into the late 18th century.
cards.context: Its head of state, the doge, had immense prestige but was increasingly bound by his councils. Real power sat with the Great Council, and the Great Council belonged to the old families. Stable? For centuries. Open? Only if you were born into the right family.

mascot.line: Next time your group chat "votes" on a plan, count how many people actually chose it.

cards.headline: The iron law
cards.body: In the early 20th century, the sociologist Robert Michels made a bolder claim. His iron law of oligarchy says every organization, even one committed to democratic ideals, ends up ruled by an elite few. Leaders gain expertise, central authority and control of the bureaucracy and resources, and use them to dominate the members. Think of any club you've joined. Who actually decides?

levels.title: Rule by Religion
levels.objective: After this level you can explain theocracy.
levels.summary: Theocracy is government by divine guidance or divinely guided officials. The pope holds every branch of power in Vatican City; Iran's supreme leader is a jurist above an elected president.

cards.headline: The world's smallest country announces its new ruler with smoke.
cards.body: When cardinals elect a pope in the Sistine Chapel, they burn the ballots. Black smoke means no decision yet. White smoke means a new pope. And the winner doesn't only lead a church. He runs a country, with every branch of its government in his hands.

cards.headline: Government by divine guidance
cards.body: Theocracy comes from the Greek theokratia, "rule of God", a word attributed to the historian Josephus. Britannica defines it as government by divine guidance or by officials regarded as divinely guided. Often the leaders are clergy and the law rests on religious law. Level 11's divine right put God behind a king. Theocracy puts religion at the center of the state itself.

mascot.line: Smallest country, biggest job description: lawmaker, executive and top judge, all in one.

cards.fact: In Vatican City, one person holds all three powers.
cards.context: At 0.44 square kilometers, Vatican City is the world's smallest fully independent state. The pope holds absolute executive, legislative and judicial powers there: he makes the laws, carries them out and judges them. He gets the job by election. Cardinals under 80 vote, and a winner needs a two-thirds majority.

cards.headline: Iran: a religious leader above elected offices
cards.body: Britannica names three present-day theocracies: Saudi Arabia, Iran and the Vatican. Iran mixes religious and elected offices. Since 1979, its head of state has been a supreme leader, a jurist of Islamic law chosen by the Assembly of Experts, whose members are directly elected every eight years. Iran's president and legislature are directly elected too, but the supreme leader can approve or dismiss the president and commands the armed forces.

levels.title: Direct Democracy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain government where citizens vote on everything themselves.
levels.summary: In direct democracy citizens decide issues themselves, as in the Swiss Landsgemeinde and New England town meetings. Large states make it hard, so it mostly works inside representative systems.

cards.headline: Once a year, voters in two Swiss cantons make their laws by raising a hand.
cards.body: In the cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden, voters gather in the open air for the Landsgemeinde and vote on laws and taxes by a show of hands. No representatives in between. Just you, your neighbors and your right arm.

cards.headline: Cutting out the middle
cards.body: That's direct democracy: citizens make the decisions themselves instead of electing officials to decide for them. Britannica puts the contrast simply. In a representative democracy you vote for people; in a direct democracy you often vote on the issue itself. It's the closest thing to Level 7's Rousseau in practice: laws people make together, for themselves.

cards.fact: New England towns govern themselves the same way.
cards.context: A town meeting is an assembly of a town's qualified voters. Together they elect officials and school boards, and debate and vote on taxes and spending. Imagine your town's budget decided not by a council but by whoever turns up, one hand at a time.

cards.headline: The catch: size
cards.body: So why doesn't every country work this way? Britannica notes the long-standing argument that direct democracy can't work across the space and time of large modern states. Picture a whole country trying to fit into one town square. Today it mostly lives inside representative systems, as specific tools rather than the whole machine. And the square has another price: critics complain a secret ballot is impossible when everyone can see your hand.

levels.title: Republics
levels.objective: After this level you can explain representative government.
levels.summary: A republic, from res publica, is ruled by representatives of the citizens, with no hereditary monarch. Madison argued representation lets self-government reach a large country.

cards.headline: In 509 BCE, Rome swapped its king for two officials elected every year.
cards.body: Britannica dates the Roman Republic from 509 BCE, when the Romans replaced their monarchy with elected magistrates. At the top stood two consuls, elected each year. And the Romans gave their new state a name you still use.

cards.headline: The public thing
cards.body: That name was res publica, Latin for "the public thing", and it gave us the word republic. Britannica defines a republic as a state ruled by representatives of the citizen body. Today the word is used for any government whose head of state isn't a hereditary monarch. The idea in one line: the state belongs to the public, not to a royal family.

mascot.line: Direct democracy: everyone in the room. Republic: everyone chooses who goes in the room.

cards.headline: Why send representatives?
cards.body: Level 16 left a problem: a whole country won't fit in one square. In Federalist No. 10, in 1787, James Madison offered an answer. A republic, he wrote, delegates government to a small number of citizens elected by the rest, so it can stretch over far more people and territory than a pure democracy. He also hoped representatives would "refine and enlarge the public views". Representation is how self-government scales up.

cards.fact: A republic isn't automatically a democracy, and a democracy needn't be a republic.
cards.context: Res publica once covered any non-tyrannical state, oligarchies included. Level 14's Venice called itself a republic while a closed set of families ran it. And Level 12's Sweden became a parliamentary democracy with its King still on the throne. The label tells you there's no hereditary monarch in charge. It doesn't tell you who really decides.

options.rationale: Venice's Great Council was run by noble families, not clergy.

options.label: Res publica once covered any non-tyrannical state, oligarchies included

questions.explanation: Res publica once covered any non-tyrannical state, including oligarchies, and Venice's Great Council was closed to a hereditary group.

levels.title: Federal or Unitary?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how power can be split between the center and the regions.
levels.summary: Federal systems split power between center and regions under a hard-to-change constitution; unitary states keep it at the center and delegate it, as the UK does with Scotland.

cards.headline: The United States is federal. Yet each of its states, inside, is unitary.
cards.body: Britannica points it out: the federal United States is made of states that each run as unitary governments, with counties and cities created by state law. How can one country be both? Because federal and unitary describe how power is shared out across the map, and you can do it differently on each floor.

cards.headline: Federal: power split by contract
cards.body: Federalism unites separate states or regions in one system while each keeps its own integrity. The split is usually written into a constitution that can be changed only by extraordinary procedures, so neither level can simply grab the other's powers. The United States, Switzerland, Canada, Australia, Germany, India and Brazil work this way. Level 8's Canadian provinces running schools and hospitals? That's federalism at work.

cards.headline: Unitary: power on loan from the center
cards.body: In a unitary state, most or all governing power sits with the central government. It delegates authority to regions and towns and channels decisions down to them. Britannica calls France the classic example of a centralized administrative system. Local councils still exist and still matter. Their powers are simply on loan.

mascot.line: Devolved power is a bit like a borrowed bike. You ride it every day, but the owner still has the spare key.

cards.fact: The UK hands power to Scotland but stays a unitary state.
cards.context: The UK Parliament's Scotland Act 1998 set up the Scottish Parliament, which opened in 1999. Yet the UK Parliament can still legislate for all parts of the UK, including devolved areas. Britannica's summary: Britain decentralizes power in practice though not in constitutional principle. Remember Level 9's UK, one state made of four parts?

cards.headline: Federal vs unitary: mapped
learned: Federal: power split by a hard-to-change constitution
Unitary: the center holds power and delegates it
France is the classic centralized state
The UK devolves power but its Parliament stays sovereign

questions.prompt: In a federal system, what usually protects the split of power between the center and the regions?

options.label: A written constitution that only extraordinary procedures can change
The central government's goodwill
options.rationale: In a federation neither level can simply take the other's powers.

options.label: A yearly vote in each region
options.rationale: The split is fixed in the constitution, not re-voted each year.

options.label: The monarch's personal decision
options.rationale: Federalism rests on a constitution, not a ruler's choice.

questions.explanation: Federal power-sharing is usually written into a constitution that can be changed only by extraordinary procedures.

questions.prompt: Scotland has had its own parliament since 1999. Why is the UK still a unitary state?

options.label: Scotland's parliament can overrule the UK Parliament
options.rationale: It's the other way round.

options.label: The UK has no regional governments at all
options.rationale: Scotland's parliament is a regional body.

options.label: The UK Parliament can still legislate for all parts of the UK

options.rationale: That guarantee is what a federation has, and the UK doesn't.

options.label: Federal

questions.explanation: Canada is federal: its provinces hold their own responsibilities, like schools and hospitals.

levels.title: When Government Fails
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happens when a state collapses.
levels.summary: A failed state loses control of its territory and the monopoly of legitimate force and can barely provide services. Somalia collapsed in 1991; the Fragile States Index tracks the pressures.

cards.headline: In 1991, Somalia's government fell. No government replaced it.
cards.body: That year President Mohamed Siad Barre was overthrown in a popular uprising. What followed, in Britannica's words, was state collapse under rival warlords, and more than three decades of civil war. Every kind of government in this chapter assumes a state that works. What happens when it doesn't?

cards.headline: Flunking Weber's test
cards.body: Britannica describes a failed state as one that can't project authority over its territory and people, or protect its borders. It can't keep a monopoly on the legitimate use of violence, and it provides only minimal public services. Remember Weber's definition of the state from Level 9: the monopoly of legitimate force within a territory. A failed state is what losing that monopoly looks like.

cards.headline: What failure costs
cards.body: Level 7's Hobbes imagined life without government as a war of all against all, "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short." Failed states show the real costs. Britannica lists crumbling infrastructure, flourishing corruption, and worsening basic measures such as infant mortality and literacy. Level 5's public services, it turns out, are what a working state quietly delivers every day.

cards.fact: Failure comes in degrees, and it can be spotted early.
cards.context: The Fund for Peace's Fragile States Index scores countries on twelve indicators, including state legitimacy, public services, and refugees and internally displaced people. The point isn't a pass-or-fail stamp. It's spotting the pressures pushing a state toward the brink, while there's still time to act.

cards.headline: Failed states: examined
learned: Somalia's state collapsed in 1991
Failed states lose the monopoly of legitimate force
Services, infrastructure and basic health suffer
The Fragile States Index tracks twelve pressures

options.label: Madison's

levels.title: Checkpoint: Kinds of Government
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the main kinds of government.
levels.summary: Aristotle sorted governments by who rules and for whose benefit. Chapter 2's systems fit his grid, and modern questions add limits, federalism and whether the state works at all.

cards.headline: Aristotle sorted every government with two questions. They still work.
cards.body: Who rules: one person, a few, or the many? And for whose benefit: everyone's, or only the rulers' own? Cross the two questions and you get six kinds of government.

items.label: Rule by one
points: For the common good: kingship
For the ruler's own good: tyranny

items.label: Rule by a few
points: For the common good: aristocracy
For their own good: oligarchy, usually the wealthy

items.label: Rule by the many
points: For the common good: polity
For their own good: "democracy", in his sense rule by the poor

mascot.line: Ten levels, a whole shelf of governments. You can now sort a history book's rulers by type.

cards.headline: This chapter on his grid
cards.body: Place the chapter on Aristotle's grid. Louis XIV and Malaysia's paramount ruler are rule by one. Venice's Great Council is rule by a few. Glarus's raised hands are rule by the many. Aristotle's twist is that numbers aren't everything: a government is just, he argued, when it aims at the common advantage. Modern systems add questions he didn't ask. Is power limited, as in a constitutional monarchy? Is it split across the map, as in a federation? Does the state work at all?

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: Aristotle: who rules, and for whose benefit?
Rule by one: monarchy, absolute or constitutional, and dictatorship
Rule by a few or by religion: oligarchy and theocracy
Rule by many: direct democracy and republics
Federal or unitary, and what happens when states fail

levels.title: Democracy's Roots
levels.objective: After this level you can trace democracy from Athens to today.
levels.summary: Democracy is Greek for rule by the people. Cleisthenes' Athens (508-507 BCE) tied rights to where you lived, though only free adult men took part; Lincoln restated the idea in 1863.

cards.headline: Every time you say "democracy", you're speaking ancient Greek.
cards.body: The word is a two-part sentence about who's in charge, and it has been in use for about 2,500 years. This level follows it from the city that coined it to a famous speech that put it into plain English.

cards.headline: People plus rule
cards.body: Democracy comes from the Greek demokratia, coined in the middle of the 5th century BCE from demos, "people", and kratos, "rule". Level 1 said government is about who gets the authority to decide for everyone. Democracy's answer is right there in the name: the people do.

cards.headline: Cleisthenes redraws the map
cards.body: In Athens, the statesman Cleisthenes is regarded as the founder of democracy. His reforms, approved in 508–507 BCE, changed one big thing: political rights would depend on your deme, or township, not your family or clan. Ten new local tribes replaced four old kinship ones. Suddenly what counted was your address, not your grandfather.

cards.fact: Athens' "people" meant only its free adult men.
cards.context: Britannica notes that democracy was historically a minority affair: in ancient Athens, all free adult males. Women, enslaved people and resident foreigners were excluded. The demos was real, but it was a club with a strict door policy.

mascot.line: Of, by, for. Three tiny words, and the old Greek one still fits inside them.

cards.headline: Of, by and for the people
cards.body: On 19 November 1863, dedicating a cemetery for Union soldiers at Gettysburg, Abraham Lincoln resolved that "government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth." That's demokratia unpacked into three little phrases: the people own it, run it, and are its point.

cards.headline: Democracy: rooted
learned: Democracy: Greek demos (people) + kratos (rule)
Cleisthenes tied Athenian rights to the local deme
Only free adult men counted as Athens' people
Lincoln: government of, by and for the people

questions.prompt: In the Greek word demokratia, what do demos and kratos mean?

options.label: Many and few
options.rationale: Those sound like numbers; the parts mean people and rule.

questions.explanation: Democracy comes from demos, "people", and kratos, "rule": rule by the people.

options.label: Which noble family they were born into
options.rationale: That's exactly what the reforms moved away from.

options.label: How much land they owned
options.rationale: Wealth isn't the basis the reforms set.

options.label: Their rank in the army
options.rationale: Military rank isn't the basis the reforms set.

options.label: Membership of their local deme, or township

questions.explanation: Cleisthenes based political rights on the deme, a township, instead of family or clan.

options.label: The people themselves hold it

levels.title: Magna Carta and Limits on Kings
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Magna Carta limited royal power.
levels.summary: On 15 June 1215 King John agreed to Magna Carta, putting the king under the law: no imprisonment without lawful judgment, no tax without consent, and 25 barons to enforce it.

cards.headline: In 1215, England's rebel barons made their king promise to obey the law.
cards.body: Chapter 1 showed rulers making laws, all the way back to Hammurabi. This level is about the harder trick: making a ruler keep them. It happened in a meadow by the Thames, and it wasn't the king's idea.

cards.headline: A king under pressure
cards.body: On 15 June 1215, at Runnymede beside the River Thames, King John agreed to Magna Carta, Latin for "Great Charter", under pressure from rebellious barons. Its 63 clauses wrote down the liberties of "free men". Britannica sums up the big idea: the sovereign is subject to the rule of law. The king makes laws, and the laws bind the king.

mascot.line: Clause 39 is the one people still quote. "Lawful judgment" is doing a lot of work there.

items.label: Clause 39
points: No free man seized, imprisoned, outlawed or exiled
Except by lawful judgment of his equals or the law of the land

items.label: Clause 40
points: "To no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice"
Justice isn't for sale, even from a king

cards.headline: No tax without consent
cards.body: Remember Level 6: taxes are compulsory. Clause 12 added a condition. No "scutage" or "aid", payments the king demanded, could be levied without the kingdom's general consent, apart from three customary cases such as ransoming the king. Compulsory, yes, but only after the kingdom had agreed. Hold that thought for the next level.

cards.headline: A charter with teeth
cards.body: Promises from kings were cheap, so clause 61 added enforcement. The barons would choose 25 of their number to watch over the charter. If the king broke it, they could seize his castles, lands and possessions until he made amends. A king who can lose his castles for breaking the rules is a king with limits.

cards.headline: Magna Carta: sealed
learned: 1215: King John agreed to Magna Carta at Runnymede
The king is subject to the rule of law
Clause 39: no punishment without lawful judgment
Clause 12: no scutage or aid without consent
Clause 61: 25 barons could enforce it

options.label: It let every free man vote for the king

options.label: It banned the king from owning castles

levels.title: Parliaments
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how parliaments work.
levels.summary: A parliament is a place for talking that makes laws, controls taxes and holds government to account. Iceland's Althing (about 930) has one chamber; the UK's Parliament has two.

cards.headline: Iceland's Althing met at the same site for more than eight centuries.
cards.body: Iceland's Althing was founded at Thingvellir around 930 and met there until 1798. Britannica counts it among the oldest national parliaments in the world. So what exactly is a parliament for? The name gives the first clue.

cards.headline: A place for talking
cards.body: Parliament comes from the Old French parlement, "a speaking, talk", from parler, "to speak". That's the core of it: a room (or, in Iceland's case, a site) where a country's representatives argue things out in the open before anything is decided. Kings could simply give orders; a parliament has to talk things through first.

mascot.line: Make the laws, hold the purse, question the government. That's the job description.

cards.headline: Laws, money, scrutiny
cards.body: Take the UK Parliament. Its main job is making laws. Its elected House of Commons has the sole right to impose taxes and decide funding for government services: Level 22's "no tax without consent", now given by elected members. And a prime minister must keep a Commons majority to stay in office, so the government's decisions face constant scrutiny and debate.

items.label: Two chambers (bicameral)
points: UK: the elected House of Commons
and the House of Lords, mainly appointed

items.label: One chamber (unicameral)

One house does all the work

levels.title: Presidents and Prime Ministers
levels.objective: After this level you can compare presidential and parliamentary systems.
levels.summary: Parliaments choose prime ministers and can remove them by a no-confidence vote, as in 1979; presidents are elected for fixed terms and are also head of state. France mixes the two.

cards.headline: On 28 March 1979, a British government lost a vote by one: 311 to 310.
cards.body: The House of Commons passed a motion of no confidence in Prime Minister James Callaghan's government, and he asked for a general election. A US president can't be sent packing by a vote like that. Why the difference? It comes down to where the leader's power comes from.

cards.headline: Prime ministers: chosen by parliament
cards.body: In a parliamentary system, the head of government, the prime minister, is selected by the legislature. Usually the party or coalition with the most seats forms the government. And what parliament gives, it can take away: a prime minister can be removed whenever they lose the confidence of a majority of parliament. That's the 1979 story.

mascot.line: Two hats: one for ribbon-cutting, one for running things. Some leaders wear both at once.

cards.headline: Presidents: elected for a fixed term
cards.body: In a presidential system, the head of government is popularly elected to a fixed term and doesn't depend on the legislature for power. The United States is the classic case. There's a second hat, too. The head of state is a ceremonial role; the head of government has real power. A president wears both. In parliamentary systems they're split, like Germany's president and chancellor.

UK, Germany, India, Japan

items.label: Presidential

levels.title: Separation of Powers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the three branches of government.
levels.summary: Separation of powers splits making, carrying out and judging laws among separate bodies. Montesquieu (1748) warned power tends to be abused; Bagehot (1867) noted Britain nearly fuses two of the three.

cards.headline: In 1748, a French thinker warned: anyone given power tends to abuse it.
cards.body: In The Spirit of Laws, Montesquieu wrote that every man invested with power is apt to abuse it, and to carry his authority as far as it will go. His fix wasn't to hunt for better rulers. It was to cut power into pieces.

cards.headline: Three jobs, three sets of hands
cards.body: Separation of powers divides government's three functions among separate, independent bodies: legislative (making laws), executive (carrying them out) and judicial (judging disputes about them). The aim, Britannica says, is to limit arbitrary excesses by government. Picture a game where one person writes the rules, enforces them and referees every dispute. You'd never win a call.

mascot.line: Not "find a good ruler" but "make sure no ruler has everything". A very different bet.

cards.headline: Montesquieu's warning
cards.body: When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person or body, Montesquieu wrote, there can be no liberty. Nor can there be liberty if the judicial power isn't separated from the other two. A ruler who makes the law, enforces it and judges it doesn't need to break any rules. They are the rules.

cards.headline: Britain's "efficient secret"
cards.body: Remember Level 24: a prime minister is chosen by parliament. In The English Constitution (1867), Walter Bagehot called the efficient secret of Britain's system the close union, the nearly complete fusion, of executive and legislative powers. The link is the Cabinet: a committee of the legislature selected to be the executive. So separation comes in degrees, not one blueprint.

cards.headline: Powers: separated
learned: Three powers: legislative, executive, judicial
Separating them limits arbitrary government
Montesquieu: united powers mean no liberty
Bagehot: Britain nearly fuses executive and legislature
