levels.title: Checks and Balances
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the branches limit each other.
levels.summary: Checks and balances let each branch block the others: power checking power. The Federalist No. 51 explains why; South Korea's 2016-2017 impeachment shows two branches checking a president.

cards.headline: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary."
cards.body: So says The Federalist No. 51, published in 1788 and generally credited to James Madison. People aren't angels, and neither are the people who govern them. The same essay offers a remedy in one line: "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition."

mascot.line: Angels would need none of this. Everyone else gets checks.

cards.headline: Power checking power
cards.body: Level 25 split government into branches. Checks and balances make the branches watch each other. Britannica defines it as separate branches empowered to prevent actions by other branches and induced to share power. Montesquieu put it in seven words: power should be a check to power. Nobody gets to be the only grown-up in the room.

cards.headline: A check in action: South Korea
cards.body: On 9 December 2016, South Korea's National Assembly voted by an overwhelming margin to impeach President Park Geun-hye. The decision then went to the Constitutional Court. On 10 March 2017 the court unanimously upheld it, and she became the first democratically elected South Korean president removed from office. Lawmakers acted, judges confirmed: two branches checking the third.

levels.title: Political Parties
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why political parties form.
levels.summary: Washington warned against parties in 1796, yet they formed: groups organized to win and use power that recruit candidates, organize voters, govern and oppose. Whig and Tory began as insults.

cards.headline: George Washington warned against political parties. Parties formed anyway.
cards.body: In his Farewell Address of 1796, Washington warned against "the baneful effects of the spirit of party". Yet in the 19th century, modern parties took shape across Europe and the United States. If they're so worrying, why do they keep appearing?

cards.headline: What a party is
cards.body: Britannica defines a political party as a group of persons organized to acquire and exercise political power. Remember Level 3: Weber called power the ability to exercise your will over others. A party is people deciding to pursue that together, in the open, under one name.

cards.headline: Why parties form
cards.body: One candidate can't run a country, and one lawmaker alone can't pass much. Parties recruit candidates, organize voters at elections, form governments and keep them going. And the side that loses doesn't vanish: parties give those out of power an organized opposition. Those are jobs somebody has to do, and parties grew up doing them.

mascot.line: Being called a bandit and replying "great, that's our name now" is a very political move.

cards.fact: Britain's first party names began as insults.
cards.context: "Whig" and "Tory" were terms of abuse, hurled in 1679 during the fight over excluding James, Duke of York, from the throne. Tory first meant an Irish outlaw or robber; Whig probably came from a Scottish word for a horse drover. The parties then adopted the insults as their own names.

levels.title: A Free Press
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a free press matters in a democracy.
levels.summary: Sweden's 1766 law, regarded as the first for press freedom, ended censorship and opened official documents. A free press informs the people who steer; Carlyle called it a Fourth Estate.

cards.headline: In 1766, Sweden became the first country to free its press by law.
cards.body: On 2 December 1766, Sweden's parliament, the Riksdag, passed what is regarded as the world's first law supporting freedom of the press and freedom of information. What does a free press have to do with democracy? Quite a lot.

cards.headline: Two freedoms in one law
cards.body: Sweden's act abolished censorship of printed publications, including imports (academic and theological works were the exception). It also guaranteed public access to documents drawn up by government agencies. Two ideas in one law: you can publish without asking permission, and you can see what your government writes down.

mascot.line: Voting without news is like reviewing a restaurant you've never eaten at.

cards.headline: You can't steer blind
cards.body: Britannica defines press freedom as the right of media outlets to report news without government control, and it matters because it gives people informed access to information and opinions about political matters. Remember Level 1's ship: government means steering. In a democracy the people are meant to steer, and nobody steers well in the dark.

cards.headline: The Fourth Estate
cards.body: Thomas Carlyle wrote that Burke said there were Three Estates in Parliament, "but, in the Reporters' Gallery yonder, there sat a Fourth Estate more important far than they all." The name stuck: the press is still called the Fourth Estate. Carlyle's point: the people reporting on Parliament held a power of their own.

levels.title: Protest and Free Speech
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the right to speak out and protest.
levels.summary: Speakers' Corner lets anyone speak lawfully, after 1866's torn-down railings. The 1966 UN Covenant protects expression (Article 19) and peaceful assembly (Article 21), within necessary laws.

cards.headline: In one corner of a London park, anyone can stand up and talk about anything.
cards.body: It's Speakers' Corner in Hyde Park. You can turn up unannounced and speak on any subject, as long as the police consider your speech lawful. That last condition is this whole level in miniature: a right to speak out, with edges.

cards.headline: Won by pulling down railings
cards.body: In 1866 the government suppressed a Reform League meeting in Hyde Park that was demanding a wider right to vote. Finding the park locked, demonstrators tore up hundreds of yards of railings to get in. Then in 1872 the Parks Regulation Act set out rules under which people could meet and speak freely in the park. The protest came first; the rules followed.

cards.headline: Written into international law
cards.body: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 16 December 1966, protects both halves of protest. Article 19: everyone has the right to hold opinions without interference, and to freedom of expression, including to seek, receive and impart information and ideas. Article 21: "The right of peaceful assembly shall be recognized." Speaking out, and gathering to do it.

mascot.line: A right with edges is still a right. The argument is always about where the edges go.

cards.headline: The edges
cards.body: Neither right is unlimited. Restrictions must be set by law and be necessary, for example to respect the rights or reputations of others, or to protect national security, public order, or public health or morals. Notice the key word in Article 21: peaceful. And remember Level 4: a law is a rule the community recognizes as binding. Here, law is what marks where the megaphone stops.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Democracy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how democracies share power and hold leaders to account.
levels.summary: Churchill: democracy is the worst form of government except all the others. Democracies share power (parliaments, branches, checks) and hold leaders to account (confidence votes, press, speech).

cards.headline: Churchill called democracy the worst form of government. Then came "except".
cards.body: On 11 November 1947, Winston Churchill told the House of Commons: "it has been said that democracy is the worst form of Government except all those other forms that have been tried from time to time."

cards.headline: Not perfect, and not pretending
cards.body: In the same remarks Churchill said no one pretends democracy is perfect or all-wise. And "it has been said" gives the game away: he was repeating a saying already going around, not coining it. This chapter has been a tour of that "except": the ways democracies avoid trusting anyone with everything, from a king bound by Magna Carta to Montesquieu's warning that united powers leave no liberty.

mascot.line: Ten levels on who holds power and who keeps an eye on them. Nicely done.

cards.headline: From a Greek word to a working machine
cards.body: The chapter began with demokratia, rule by the people, and Lincoln's government of, by and for the people. Everything since is machinery for making that phrase true: parliaments that talk before they decide, prime ministers who can lose parliament's confidence, presidents elected for fixed terms, parties that organize voters and opposition, and reporters in the gallery.

levels.title: What a Constitution Is
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a constitution does.
levels.summary: A constitution is a state's supreme law: it sets up government, divides and limits power, and protects rights. The US's is one document; the UK's is a collection.

cards.headline: Britain has a constitution. Just don't ask to borrow a copy.
cards.body: In the United States, the constitution is one specific written document. In the United Kingdom, it's a collection of documents, statutes and traditional practices that are generally accepted as governing political matters. There's no single booklet to hand you. So what makes something a constitution at all?

cards.headline: The rules for making rules
cards.body: Level 4 defined a law as a rule the whole community is bound by. A constitution sits one floor up. Britannica calls it the body of doctrines and practices that form the fundamental organizing principle of a state. International IDEA puts it more simply: a constitution is the supreme law of a country, and ordinary laws are made inside the framework it sets. It's the rulebook for the people who write the rulebooks.

mascot.line: Build it, share it out, fence it in. That's a constitution's whole to-do list.

cards.headline: Three jobs in one document
cards.body: What does that top-floor law actually do? Constitutions establish the system of government: who holds which office. They distribute and constrain power, so no office can do whatever it likes. And they protect the rights of citizens. In short, a constitution tells a government what it may do, and just as importantly, what it may not.

cards.fact: Aristotle's simplest definition of a constitution: "the arrangement of the offices" in a state.
cards.context: Remember Level 10's Aristotle, who called humans political animals? Britannica traces the whole idea of a constitution back to the ancient Greeks, and especially to him. By his definition, Britain qualifies easily. Its offices are arranged, with a collection of statutes, documents and practices saying how. The arrangement just isn't printed in one place.

cards.headline: Paper is the easy part
cards.body: Here's the catch. Britannica notes that virtually every state claims to have a constitution, but not every government conducts itself in a consistently constitutional manner. Writing "power is limited" on parchment doesn't limit anything by itself. The words only bite when the people holding power actually follow them.

levels.title: The U.S. Constitution
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the oldest written national constitution still in use.
levels.summary: Signed in Philadelphia in 1787 to replace the Articles of Confederation, the U.S. Constitution is the oldest written national constitution in use: seven articles, a supreme law.

cards.headline: The oldest written national constitution still in use fits on four pages.
cards.body: Britannica calls the U.S. Constitution the oldest written national constitution in use. All four pages of the original are on permanent display at the National Archives. And it opens with three words that say whose document it is: "We the People."

cards.headline: Plan B, written in one summer
cards.body: It wasn't the country's first try. It replaced the Articles of Confederation, which had denied the national government essential powers like direct taxation. Remember Level 6? A government that can't tax is a ship with no fuel. So in the summer of 1787, delegates in Philadelphia drafted something stronger, and 39 of them signed it on 17 September 1787.

cards.headline: Seven articles, one supreme law
cards.body: The Constitution has seven articles. Article I gives lawmaking power to Congress, Article II gives executive power to a President, and Article III gives judicial power to a Supreme Court and lower courts. Then Article VI adds the line that makes it a constitution in Level 31's sense: it shall be "the supreme Law of the Land."

mascot.line: Notice who's doing the establishing in that sentence. Not a king. The people.

cards.headline: Nine states to switch it on
cards.body: Signing wasn't enough. Article VII said the Constitution needed ratifying by nine states, and once they had, it took effect in 1789. Now look at that opening again. Level 7's Locke grounded government in the consent of the governed. This document begins with "We the People" and says they "do ordain and establish" it.

cards.fact: Its first ten amendments, ratified in 1791, are called the Bill of Rights.
cards.context: The original articles mostly build the machinery of government. The Bill of Rights added guarantees for people, starting with the First Amendment: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion," plus protections for speech, the press, assembly and petition. Several levels in this chapter start right there.

levels.title: Changing a Constitution
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how constitutions are amended.
levels.summary: Constitutions change by amendment, which most make harder than ordinary lawmaking. A 1789 US pay amendment was ratified in 1992 thanks to a student's C-grade paper.

cards.headline: In 1982 a student got a C on a paper. Then he helped amend the Constitution.
cards.body: Gregory Watson, a sophomore at the University of Texas at Austin, wrote about a congressional pay amendment proposed back in 1789. Congress had never set a deadline for ratifying it, he argued, so it was still pending. His professor wasn't convinced and gave him a C. So Watson started writing to state lawmakers.

cards.headline: Harder than a law, on purpose
cards.body: Constitutions must be able to change, but most make amending harder than passing an ordinary law. The usual hurdles: a supermajority in the legislature, a referendum, a double decision (sometimes with an election in between), or approval by the states or regions. Why bother? Too rigid, and needed reforms get stuck. Too flexible, and whoever holds power can wear away the rights and institutions the constitution protects.

mascot.line: Moral of the story: always check whether your homework is still pending ratification.

cards.headline: The American hurdle, and a two-century wait
cards.body: Under Article V, an amendment needs two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or a convention) to propose it and three-fourths of the states to ratify it. That bar has been cleared just 27 times. Watson's letters helped: the pay amendment, proposed on 25 September 1789, was ratified on 7 May 1992 as the 27th Amendment. In 2017 his university changed his grade to an A.

cards.headline: Some countries ask everyone
cards.body: Other countries set the bar differently. Some require a referendum for every amendment, however small: Australia, Denmark, Ireland and Japan among them. In Ireland, parliament passes a change the way it passes an ordinary law, and then a majority of voters must approve it. Remember Level 8's village panchayats? India gave them their status through its 73rd constitutional amendment in 1992.

cards.fact: More than 70 constitutions have parts that can't be amended at all.
cards.context: Examples include basic human rights in Germany. These locks are often the result of past traumas: countries coming out of conflict or dictatorship want to make sure the old oppression can never come back, not even through a perfectly legal vote.

levels.title: Human Rights
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
levels.summary: On 10 December 1948 the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with no votes against. Nonbinding at first, it inspired treaties and constitutions.

cards.headline: In 1948 the world wrote down rights for everyone. Not one country voted no.
cards.body: On 10 December 1948, meeting in Paris, the UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Eight countries abstained. None voted against. The promise was right there in the name: rights not for the citizens of one country, but for everyone.

cards.headline: A committee from many backgrounds
cards.body: The drafting was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. France's René Cassin wrote the first draft, with Lebanon's Charles Malik and China's Peng Chung Chang among the key figures. The Commission's 18 members came from various political, cultural and religious backgrounds. Getting that room to agree on one list was the achievement.

cards.headline: Article 1, in one breath
cards.body: The Declaration has 30 articles, and the first sets the tone: "All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights." Article 2 says the rights belong to everyone, without distinction of race, colour, sex, language, religion or opinion. Article 3 promises life, liberty and security of person. Sound familiar? Level 7's Locke argued for natural rights to life, liberty and property.

mascot.line: No teeth at first. Treaties and constitutions supplied them.

cards.headline: A standard, not a statute
cards.body: The UN proclaimed it as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations. It wasn't a binding law, and Britannica notes that its nonbinding status was first seen as a major weakness. Then it spread. In 1966 the UN adopted two covenants, on civil and political rights and on economic, social and cultural rights. The Declaration has inspired more than seventy human rights treaties, and many countries wrote it into their constitutions.

cards.fact: The Declaration is available in more than 500 languages.
cards.context: A common standard for all peoples only works if people can read it. That's the point of all those translations: whatever your language, the chances are good you can read Article 1 in it.

levels.title: Freedom of Religion
levels.objective: After this level you can explain freedom of religion and belief.
levels.summary: Freedom of religion covers belief, which can't be limited, and practice, which can be, but only for a few listed reasons. Countries arrange religion and state differently.

cards.headline: You can believe whatever you like. Acting on it is where the rules begin.
cards.body: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration gives everyone freedom of thought, conscience and religion. That includes the freedom to change your religion or belief, and to show it in teaching, practice, worship and observance. Two halves, then: what you believe, and what you do about it. International law treats them very differently.

cards.headline: Believing: no limits allowed
cards.body: The UN Human Rights Committee says no limitations are permitted on the freedom to have or adopt a religion or belief of your choice. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) adds that no one may be coerced in a way that would impair that freedom. A government can't make it illegal to believe something. Your mind is the one room it never gets a key to.

cards.headline: Practising: limits, but only a few
cards.body: Showing your religion is different, because it can affect other people. Under ICCPR Article 18, it may be limited, but only by law and only where necessary to protect public safety, order, health or morals, or the fundamental rights and freedoms of others. Think of it as a short list of permitted reasons. Any limit has to point to one of them.

mascot.line: Both sides were reading the same few words of Article 18. That's what makes it a real debate.

cards.headline: Where's the line? A live debate
cards.body: In 2004 France banned conspicuous religious symbols, such as Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and large Christian crosses, for pupils in public schools. The Stasi Commission and President Jacques Chirac backed it as applying laïcité, France's secularism. Human Rights Watch called it an unwarranted infringement on religious practice, arguing such symbols threatened no one's safety, order or rights. Underneath sits one question: when is a limit on practice truly necessary?

levels.title: Privacy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the right to privacy.
levels.summary: Warren and Brandeis called privacy 'the right to be let alone' in 1890. It's in the UN Declaration, built by US courts from the Bill of Rights, and extended to data by the EU.

cards.headline: In 1890, two lawyers warned that cameras were invading private life.
cards.body: "Instantaneous photographs and newspaper enterprise have invaded the sacred precincts of private and domestic life," wrote Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis in the Harvard Law Review. Their answer was a right with a wonderfully plain name: "the right to be let alone." Swap the camera for a phone and it could have been written this morning.

cards.headline: Written into the world's list
cards.body: Level 34's Declaration took the idea global. Article 12 says no one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with their privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to attacks on their honour and reputation. Notice the word "arbitrary." The promise isn't that nobody may ever look. It's that nobody may pry on a whim.

cards.headline: The missing word in the U.S. Constitution
cards.body: Search the U.S. Constitution for "privacy" and you won't find it. Courts built the right from parts of Level 32's Bill of Rights, especially the First, Fourth and Fifth Amendments. The Fourth protects people "in their persons, houses, papers, and effects" against unreasonable searches and seizures, and requires warrants based on probable cause. In 1965 the Supreme Court described a "zone of privacy" formed by these guarantees.

cards.headline: Your data, your rights
cards.body: Today much of your private life is data. In the European Union, data protection is a fundamental right under Article 8 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has applied since 25 May 2018. You can ask an organisation whether it holds personal data about you and, in some cases, have it erased: the so-called right to be forgotten.

mascot.line: Rights don't live alone. Sometimes they have to share the room.

cards.headline: When rights collide
cards.body: Privacy often has to be weighed against other things people value. The EU's right to erasure doesn't apply where processing the data is needed for freedom of expression, a legal obligation or legal claims. And Britannica points to the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001, which widened federal access to business records in terrorism investigations, as an example of the tension between privacy and national security.

levels.title: Who Gets to Vote
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the right to vote expanded over time.
levels.summary: Suffrage, the right to vote, once needed property in Britain and was denied by race in places. US amendments and the UN Declaration widened it; Austria now votes at 16.

cards.headline: For a long time, voting wasn't a right. It came with property.
cards.body: In 18th- and 19th-century Britain, you needed property or a certain income to vote. The argument was that only people with "a stake in the country" should have a voice in its public affairs. So how did the vote get from the propertied few to the rest?

cards.headline: Suffrage: who's in, who's out
cards.body: Suffrage is the right to vote, in electing public officials and, where a country allows it, on proposed laws. Every country draws a line around who has it. Some lines were drawn by race: South Africa at one time, and the Old South of the United States, did not permit their Black populations to vote. This level follows that line as it moved.

events.label: 15th Amendment: no denying the vote on account of race, color or previous servitude
24th Amendment: no poll tax as a condition of voting in federal elections
26th Amendment: no denying the vote on account of age to citizens 18 or older

cards.headline: A world standard: universal and equal
cards.body: Level 34's Declaration set a benchmark in 1948. Article 21 says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections by universal and equal suffrage, held by secret vote. Recall Level 3: authority is power people accept as legitimate. Article 21 names elections as the way that acceptance is expressed.

mascot.line: Property, race, age: each line on this card was once taken for granted.

cards.fact: In 2007 Austria lowered its voting age from 18 to 16.
cards.context: Austria's parliament says it was the first country in Europe to lower the voting age to 16 for all citizens. From property owners to 16-year-olds: the line is still moving.

levels.title: Women's Suffrage
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how women won the vote.
levels.summary: New Zealand gave women the vote in 1893 after Kate Sheppard's petition. Britain's suffragists and suffragettes split on tactics; the US and Switzerland followed in 1920 and 1971.

cards.headline: The first country where women won the vote? New Zealand, in 1893.
cards.body: On 19 September 1893, New Zealand women were granted the vote. That made New Zealand the first self-governing country in the world to give women the vote in parliamentary elections. It didn't happen by chance.

cards.headline: 31,872 signatures and a seven-year push
cards.body: Kate Sheppard of the Women's Christian Temperance Union led a seven-year campaign: public meetings, telegrams and letters to politicians, and a steady stream of pamphlets. Its climax was the 1893 petition, with 31,872 signatures, the largest ever gathered in Australasia. It was reportedly carried to Parliament in a wheelbarrow.

mascot.line: Same goal, two very different roads to it.

cards.context: More than 8 million of them. Men and women still voted under different rules, though. It took until 1928 for every man and woman over 21 to get the vote on equal terms: ten more years.

levels.title: Civil Rights
levels.objective: After this level you can explain civil rights movements and what they won.
levels.summary: Civil rights guarantee equal treatment under the law and usually need government action. The US movement won the 1964 and 1965 Acts; South Africa ended apartheid.

cards.headline: On 1 December 1955, a 43-year-old woman refused to give up her bus seat.
cards.body: Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger. What followed was the Montgomery bus boycott, which lasted about a year, led by an organisation that chose a young minister as its president: Martin Luther King Jr.

cards.headline: Rights that need the government to act
cards.body: Britannica defines civil rights as guarantees of equal social opportunities and equal protection under the law, regardless of race, religion or other personal characteristics. It draws a neat contrast. Civil liberties are secured by restraining government, like Level 32's First Amendment, which begins "Congress shall make no law." Civil rights usually need positive government action, often new legislation.

cards.headline: From a bus seat to a national law
cards.body: The boycott ended with a legal win: a federal court found segregation on publicly operated buses unconstitutional, and the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed it. Then came legislation. On 2 July 1964, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act, which banned discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin in places like restaurants and hotels, and at work.

mascot.line: A right on paper and a right in practice can be a lifetime apart.

cards.headline: A promise kept 95 years late
cards.body: Remember Level 37's 15th Amendment of 1870? Southern states had long kept Black citizens from voting anyway, with tools like literacy tests. After state troopers attacked peaceful marchers in Selma, Alabama, national attention helped persuade Congress to act. The Voting Rights Act, signed on 6 August 1965, outlawed literacy tests as a condition of voting. It enforced the 15th Amendment, 95 years after its ratification.

cards.fact: South Africa's apartheid laws were repealed in the early 1990s.
cards.context: Apartheid, Afrikaans for "apartness," was formally set up in 1948. Its laws classified people by race, and pass laws controlled where nonwhite South Africans could be. After repeal under President F. W. de Klerk, the 1994 elections produced a government led by Nelson Mandela. Level 40 picks up the story.

cards.headline: In 1996 Nelson Mandela signed a constitution at the scene of a massacre.
cards.body: In 1960, at Sharpeville, police opened fire on a crowd demonstrating against apartheid's pass laws. On 10 December 1996, President Mandela signed South Africa's new constitution into law in the same place. The date was International Human Rights Day, the anniversary of Level 34's Declaration, adopted on 10 December 1948.

cards.headline: Supreme, and meant to be
cards.body: The constitution is one written document of 14 chapters, and Chapter 2 is the Bill of Rights, which calls itself "a cornerstone of democracy in South Africa." Section 2 goes further: the Constitution is the supreme law, and "law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid." That's Level 31's idea with teeth. Under apartheid, the pass laws were law. Under this constitution, a law that discriminated unfairly by race would clash with the Bill of Rights, and so be invalid.

levels.title: How a Bill Becomes Law
levels.objective: After this level you can trace a bill from idea to law.
levels.summary: A bill is a proposed law. It passes readings and committee in both Houses, which must agree every word before Royal Assent makes it an Act; US chambers pass identical text.

cards.headline: A bill's "first reading" doesn't involve reading it.
cards.body: In the UK House of Commons, first reading is a formality: the bill's short title is read out, it's ordered to be printed, and that's it. No debate, no vote. So where does the real work happen? Follow one bill from idea to law.

cards.headline: Bill in, Act out
cards.body: A bill is a proposal for a new law, or for a change to an existing one, put before Parliament for debate. It isn't law yet. It's a draft asking permission. Only after it clears every stage and receives Royal Assent does it become an Act of Parliament. Think of the bill as the caterpillar and the Act as the butterfly.

events.label: The short title is read out; no debate
A debate on the bill's general principles

The same stages all over again

mascot.line: Ping-pong in Parliament: the only game where the ball is a bill.

cards.headline: Every word agreed
cards.body: Both Houses must agree the exact wording. If the Lords change something the Commons won't accept, the bill bounces back and forth between them, a process nicknamed ping-pong, until they settle. The US works the same way: the House and the Senate must pass a bill in identical form before it goes to the President to be signed. A law is born only when both chambers agree on every word.

levels.title: Debate
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how lawmakers debate a bill.
levels.summary: Second reading debates a bill's principles, under rules that keep argument on ideas. The US Senate's filibuster shows debate also needs a way to end: cloture.

cards.headline: In the House of Commons, MPs aren't allowed to call each other by name.
cards.body: Instead they say things like "the honourable Member for" someone's constituency. It sounds stuffy, but the rule has a job: to guard against personality in debate. Argue with the idea, not the person. That rule is a clue to what debate is for.

cards.headline: Arguing about the big idea
cards.body: Remember second reading from Level 41? That's where the big argument happens. The Commons debates a bill's general principles: should this law exist at all? The fine print waits for committee. A second reading debate is less about commas and more about whether the whole idea deserves to go further.

mascot.line: Wrong is allowed. Liar is not. A useful rule for family dinners too.

cards.headline: Mind your language
cards.body: Debate only works if people keep talking, so some words are off limits. Alleging that another member has lied is almost always out of order. The Speaker tells a member who uses unparliamentary language to withdraw it, and refusing can get them suspended. You can say a colleague is wrong as often as you like. Just not that they're lying.

cards.headline: How do you stop a talker?
cards.body: The US Senate allows extended debate, so senators can use long speeches to delay a bill. That's a filibuster, from a Dutch word for "freebooter" and the Spanish "filibusteros": pirates raiding the Caribbean. In 1917 the Senate adopted cloture, a way to end debate with a two-thirds vote. In 1975 it lowered the bar to three-fifths of senators, usually 60 of 100. Every chamber needs an answer to one question: when does talking stop and voting start?

levels.title: Committees
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what committees do.
levels.summary: Committees do lawmaking's detailed work. In Congress most bills die in committee; the rest get hearings and mark-up. In the UK, select committees also shadow each government department.

cards.headline: Want to see where laws are really made? Skip the big chamber.
cards.body: In 1885 Woodrow Wilson wrote: "Congress in session is Congress on public exhibition, whilst Congress in its committee-rooms is Congress at work." The speeches are the show. The committee room is the workshop.

cards.headline: Where bills go to wait
cards.body: No chamber can study every bill together, so each one is referred to a committee with its own area of policy, such as agriculture or education. And that's where most bills die. They're never reported out to the whole House or Senate. For a bill, getting introduced is easy. Getting out of committee is the hard part.

cards.headline: Hearings, then mark-up
cards.body: A bill that does get attention usually starts with a public hearing, where the committee hears witnesses representing different viewpoints. Then comes the mark-up session: members go through the bill and vote on amendments. Finally the committee reports the bill to the full chamber, or tables it, which ends the story. It's the line-by-line work Level 41's committee stage promised.

mascot.line: A committee for every department. Somebody is always taking notes.

cards.fact: In the UK, a committee shadows every government department.
cards.context: The House of Commons has a select committee for each department, examining its spending, policies and administration. Committees can question ministers and officials in public. So committees don't only shape new laws; they also keep an eye on how government runs.

levels.title: Lobbying
levels.objective: After this level you can explain lobbying and why it is controversial.
levels.summary: Lobbying, named after legislative lobbies, is trying to influence government. Supporters and critics disagree about it; rules mainly require registration and disclosure.

cards.headline: Lobbying is named after a room.
cards.body: People who wanted something from lawmakers used to wait in the lobbies outside the chamber to catch them. Britannica traces the word to constituents meeting their representatives in the lobby of England's House of Commons in the 17th century. Today the word covers far more than a hallway chat.

cards.headline: Who lobbies?
cards.body: Lobbying means trying to influence government decisions and public policy. It isn't only big companies. Trade associations, labor unions, charities, universities, religious organizations, local governments and citizen groups all lobby. So do you, in a small way, if you ever contact a lawmaker about a bill.

mascot.line: Same activity, two readings. Knowing both sides is how you join the argument well.

items.label: The case for
points: The OECD: it gives lawmakers valuable insights and data
Supporters: it's central to representative democracy

items.label: The case against
points: The OECD: abuse lets special interests monopolize influence
Critics: it can entrench access for elites

cards.headline: Letting in the daylight
cards.body: The OECD's answer is transparency: in 2010 it adopted the first international standard on transparency and integrity in lobbying. In the US, the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 makes lobbyists register with Congress and report on their lobbying. In the EU, since 1 July 2021, lobbyists must be in a transparency register before activities such as meeting Commissioners. The common idea: everyone should be able to see who is talking to whom.

levels.title: The Veto
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a veto works.
levels.summary: A veto, Latin for "I forbid", is an executive's power to reject a bill. The US President has 10 days to sign or veto; Congress can override by two-thirds. Override rules vary by country.

cards.headline: "Veto" is Latin for two words: "I forbid."
cards.body: In ancient Rome it was the term for a protest by a tribune of the people against a measure of the Senate or the magistrates. Presidents today still use the same word to stop a bill in its tracks. How much power does that give them?

cards.headline: Sign it or send it back
cards.body: A veto is an executive's power to reject a bill, preventing it from becoming law. In the US, the President has 10 days (Sundays excepted) to sign a bill or return it to Congress with objections. Congress can override a veto, but only by a two-thirds vote in each chamber. And if Congress adjourns so the President can't return the bill, it's a pocket veto, which can't be overridden at all.

cards.fact: Franklin D. Roosevelt vetoed 635 bills. Congress overrode 9.
cards.context: That's more vetoes than any other US president. Two-thirds of both chambers is a lot of agreement to find, and FDR's record shows it: nine overrides out of 635 tries.

mascot.line: One signature can change the math from half the room to two-thirds of it.

cards.headline: Different countries, different bars
cards.body: Override rules vary. Two-thirds is most common, in countries such as Mexico, Ghana and the Philippines. Poland needs three-fifths; Brazil needs only an absolute majority in both chambers. International IDEA points out what a veto really does: if the president backs a bill, an ordinary majority passes it. If the president opposes it, lawmakers need a supermajority.

levels.title: Regulations
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how government agencies write detailed rules.
levels.summary: Laws often leave details to ministers and agencies. UK secondary legislation fills in Acts; US agencies write regulations under authority from Congress through notice and comment, which is not a vote.

cards.headline: Parliament passes the Act. Then ministers write thousands of rules under it.
cards.body: In the UK, about 3,500 statutory instruments are made each year, and only about 1,000 of them need to be considered by Parliament. They're law too. So who writes them, and who keeps them in check?

cards.headline: Filling in the details
cards.body: An Act often sets out the big idea and leaves the fine print to someone else. That fine print is secondary legislation: law made by ministers or other bodies under powers given to them by an Act of Parliament. It fills in the details that make an Act work in daily life. If the Act is the recipe's title, the regulations are the measurements.

cards.headline: Where US agencies get the power
cards.body: The US works the same way. Agencies get their authority to issue regulations from laws enacted by Congress, and they must not go beyond it. The Administrative Procedure Act of 1946 sets an open process: an agency publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register, takes public comments, then publishes a final rule, which goes into the Code of Federal Regulations.

mascot.line: One good argument beats a thousand copies of the same one.

cards.headline: Comments count, but they're not votes
cards.body: Anyone can comment on a proposed federal rule. But it isn't a ballot: an agency may not base its final rule on how many comments are for or against. It must reason from the record. As the EPA puts it, one well-supported comment is often more informative than a thousand form letters.

levels.title: Local Laws
levels.objective: After this level you can explain city and town rules.
levels.summary: Byelaws are local laws a council makes for its own area, using powers from a higher government. Canada's municipalities are "creatures" of the provinces; US states follow Dillon's Rule or home rule.

cards.headline: Your city might have a law about ear piercing.
cards.body: Leeds, in England, does. Its council's byelaws cover hairdressers and barbers, ear piercing, pleasure fairs, the employment of children and the city's parks. So who gets to make rules like these, and how far can they go?

cards.headline: Laws with a postcode
cards.body: A byelaw is a local law made by a local authority, and it applies only within that area. The council doesn't invent the power to make it: it uses powers granted by Acts of Parliament. Sound familiar? It's Level 46's delegated power again, handed down one more floor, from Parliament to the town hall.

cards.headline: Creatures of the province
cards.body: Remember Level 8's Canadian municipalities, running water supply, parks and local roads? Their power comes from above. Canada's Constitution Act, 1867 gives provinces power over municipal institutions, and courts have called municipalities "creatures" of the provincial legislature. They have only the powers provincial law gives them.

mascot.line: Ask what a city may do, and the answer starts with who gave it the power.

cards.headline: Two American answers
cards.body: US states differ on how much power to hand down. Under Dillon's Rule, from two 1868 decisions by Iowa judge John F. Dillon, a local government may act only where the state has granted it the power. Home rule, which emerged in the early 1900s, delegates broader power from the state to its towns and cities. Either way, a local law lives inside a bigger government's law.

levels.title: Unjust Laws
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how laws can be unjust and how they get repealed.
levels.summary: Thinkers disagree about what to do with a law you believe is unjust. Thoreau and King argued for civil disobedience; Plato's Socrates chose to obey. The legal route out of a law is repeal.

cards.headline: In 1846, a writer spent a night in jail rather than pay a tax.
cards.body: Henry David Thoreau refused to pay his poll tax in Concord, Massachusetts, in protest against slavery and the Mexican-American War. His night in a cell opens a long argument: what should you do about a law you believe is unjust? Thinkers have given very different answers.

cards.headline: Thoreau: don't be the tool
cards.body: Thoreau turned the experience into an essay, "Resistance to Civil Government" (1849), later known as "Civil Disobedience." If a law requires you to be "the agent of injustice to another," he wrote, "then, I say, break the law." The essay went on to influence Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

cards.headline: King: break it openly
cards.body: In his Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963), King argued that people have a moral responsibility to obey just laws and to disobey unjust ones. But not in secret: one who breaks an unjust law, he wrote, must do so "openly, lovingly, and with a willingness to accept the penalty." He'd been arrested for parading without a permit. A permit rule is fine in itself, he argued; it becomes unjust when used to maintain segregation.

mascot.line: Thoreau, King and Socrates: three answers to one hard question. You get to weigh them.

cards.headline: Socrates: stay and obey
cards.body: In Plato's Crito, Socrates makes the opposite choice. Awaiting execution, he refuses a chance to escape, though he thinks his sentence unjust. By living in Athens all his life, he argues, he had implicitly agreed to obey its laws. Sound like Level 7's social contract? It's the same idea, told as a prison conversation.

cards.fact: South Africa's parliament repealed its race-classification law in 1991.
cards.context: The Population Registration Act of 1950 had classified all South Africans by race. It ended through the lawmaking process you've followed all chapter: a new act repealed it.

levels.title: Laws Around the World
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the main legal traditions of the world.
levels.summary: Civil law starts from written codes descended from Roman law; common law builds on precedent. Customary and Muslim law and mixed systems, like bijural Canada, complete the map.

cards.headline: Move from Ottawa to Montreal, and your contracts switch legal families.
cards.body: Canada is bijural. In Quebec, private law follows the civil law tradition, set out mainly in the Civil Code of Quebec. The rest of Canada uses common law. Same country, two ways of thinking about law. What's the difference?

cards.headline: Civil law: start with the code
cards.body: Civil law, the tradition of continental Europe, traces back to Roman law as compiled under Emperor Justinian. Its heart is a comprehensive written code. France's Napoleonic Code of 1804 became a model for many nations. Today civil law runs across continental Europe, much of Latin America, and parts of Asia and Africa. Like Hammurabi's stone from Level 4, the law starts as a written text.

cards.headline: Common law: start with the cases
cards.body: Common law grew up in medieval England from judges' decisions, recorded in reports of decided cases. Judges follow earlier decisions, called precedent, so similar cases are decided alike. It's the basis of law in the United States and most Commonwealth countries. In civil law, you open the code. In common law, you open the case reports.

mascot.line: Few countries fit one box neatly. The map of law is a patchwork.

cards.headline: Custom, religion and mixtures
cards.body: JuriGlobe, a University of Ottawa project, sorts the world's legal systems into five categories: civil law, common law, customary law, Muslim law and mixed systems. Most Muslim-majority countries use Western-style criminal codes but keep sharia mainly for family law, such as marriage, divorce and inheritance; Turkey replaced it with secular codes. And mixtures are common: South Africa and Scotland blend civil and common law, while Ghana and Kenya blend common and customary law.

levels.title: Milestone: How Power Is Shared
levels.objective: After this level you can connect kinds of government, rights and lawmaking into one picture.
levels.summary: A legislator is literally a proposer of a law. Making one law spreads power across legislators, committees, lobbyists, executives, agencies and councils, from Level 1's steering to your street.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Let's see how many hands shape one law.
cards.body: Level 1 said "govern" comes from a Greek word for steering a ship. This chapter showed that in lawmaking, nobody steers alone. Follow one law from a proposal to your street, and count the hands on the wheel.

cards.headline: The proposer of a law
cards.body: A legislator is, literally, a "proposer of a law": the word comes from the Latin legis lator, from lex, law, and lator, one who proposes, from a verb meaning to carry. So a lawmaker's first job isn't deciding. It's proposing, then persuading everyone else. That's why a bill faces readings, debate and committee before Royal Assent turns it into an Act.

mascot.line: Fifty levels in, and you can follow a law from an idea all the way to your street.

levels.title: Courts
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what courts do.
levels.summary: Courts settle disputes without force: they find the facts and apply the law. Valencia's Water Tribunal has done it at a cathedral door since al-Andalus.

cards.headline: Every Thursday at noon, a court meets on a cathedral doorstep.
cards.body: In Valencia, Spain, eight judges in farmers' blouses gather at the cathedral door to settle quarrels over irrigation water. The farmers who come before them elect them. The tribunal goes back to al-Andalus, between the 9th and 13th centuries, and UNESCO listed it as world heritage in 2009. Why do people keep bringing their fights to it? Because that is exactly what a court is for.

cards.headline: A referee instead of a fist
cards.body: Picture two farmers, one canal and a dry summer. Without a court, Britannica notes, people settle disputes by force. A court is a person or body with the authority to hear and resolve disputes, and its first job is keeping the peace as an impartial, authoritative judge. Remember Level 1's Sumer, where sharing river water needed a central authority? Valencia's farmers found theirs on a church step.

cards.headline: Two questions, in order
cards.body: Every trial court answers two questions: what happened, and what does the law say about it? It works out the facts, then applies the law to them. Did the farmer open his gate out of turn? That's a fact. What follows when someone does? That's law, Level 4's rule backed by authority. In Valencia it all happens out loud, in Valencian, with the verdict given on the spot. No paperwork required, and no time to lose your temper.

mascot.line: Nobody gets to judge their own canal. Hold on to that idea; it comes back more than once.

cards.fact: The judge from the farmers' own canal has to sit out.
cards.context: To keep the Water Tribunal impartial, the syndic of the canal the disputing farmers belong to takes no part in the deliberation. And there's no appeal: the sentence is final. Most court systems add a second layer instead, appeal courts, whose job is to check whether the trial court applied the law correctly.

levels.title: Judges
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what judges do and why their independence matters.
levels.summary: Judges keep trials fair, rule on the law and pass sentence. After James II replaced judges, the Act of Settlement (1701) made their jobs safe; the UN's 1985 principles went global.

cards.headline: In 1686, a king replaced judges until he got the ruling he wanted.
cards.body: James II of England wanted the power to excuse people from the Test Oath, which holders of public office had to take. After a number of judges had been replaced, the court in Godden v Hales found in the king's favour. The judges' names changed; the answer changed with them. That's the problem this level is about.

cards.headline: The referee, not a player
cards.body: What does a judge actually do? In an English Crown Court trial, the judge makes sure the trial is fair, resolves the legal questions, directs the jury on the law and, if there's a conviction, imposes the sentence. The judge doesn't take a side. A referee who is secretly on one team isn't a referee; he's a very well-dressed player.

cards.headline: 1701: the job becomes safe
cards.body: England's answer came in the Act of Settlement of 1701. Senior judges would now hold office during good behaviour, not at the monarch's pleasure, and only both Houses of Parliament together could remove them. Their salaries had to be fixed too, so nobody could squeeze them with money. A judge who can't be fired for the wrong answer can afford to give the right one.

cards.fact: Independent judges are now a worldwide standard.
cards.context: The UN's 1985 Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary say judges must decide impartially, on the facts and the law, free of improper pressures or threats from anyone. It's Level 51's Water Tribunal rule, scaled up: there, the syndic of the disputing farmers' canal sits out, so nobody judges their own case.

levels.title: Juries
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how juries work.
levels.summary: Juries of ordinary citizens, picked at random, decide guilt while the judge handles the law. Bushel's Case (1670) ruled jurors can't be punished for their verdict; Japan mixes citizens and judges.

cards.headline: In 1670, a London jury was locked up without food for saying "not guilty".
cards.body: The defendants were two Quakers, William Penn and William Mead, charged over preaching. The jurors acquitted them anyway. They were held without food, then fined and jailed for their verdict. One juror, Edward Bushel, refused to accept that. What he won still matters to every jury today.

cards.headline: Twelve people you've never met
cards.body: Here's how it works in England and Wales today. In a Crown Court trial, a jury of 12 members of the public decides whether the defendant is guilty. They're chosen at random from the electoral register; nobody volunteers. The judge handles the law, directs the jury and passes sentence. It's a lottery nobody enters on purpose.

cards.headline: Bushel's Case: the verdict is the jury's
cards.body: Bushel challenged his imprisonment, and in 1670 Chief Justice John Vaughan agreed with him: jurors cannot be punished for their verdict. The court judges the law; the jury judges the facts. Why does it matter? If jurors can be jailed for the wrong answer, the jury is just the judge with twelve extra chairs.

levels.title: Innocent Until Proven Guilty
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the presumption of innocence.
levels.summary: The accused doesn't have to prove innocence: the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Woolmington v DPP (1935) called it the golden thread; the UDHR made it a human right.

cards.headline: In 1935, a conviction fell because the judge put the burden on the wrong side.
cards.body: Reginald Woolmington said the gun that killed his wife went off by accident. His trial judge told the jury that, once the killing was proved, it was up to Woolmington to prove it was an accident. The House of Lords quashed his conviction. Not because anyone proved him innocent, but because nobody should have had to.

cards.headline: The golden thread
cards.body: Viscount Sankey's judgment gave the principle its famous name. Running through the web of English criminal law, he said, is one golden thread: it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the prisoner's guilt. The accused doesn't have to prove anything. Accusing is the easy part; proving is the prosecution's job.

cards.headline: Beyond reasonable doubt
cards.body: How sure must a jury be? In criminal cases, the prosecution has to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; if a reasonable doubt remains, the accused goes free. The system is tilted on purpose. In the 1760s William Blackstone put it in one line: it is better that ten guilty persons escape than that one innocent suffer.

mascot.line: Innocent until proven guilty isn't a guess about anyone. It's a rule about who has to do the proving.

cards.fact: It's written into the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
cards.context: Article 11 of the 1948 Declaration says everyone charged with a penal offence has the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty. The golden thread of an English courtroom is also a promise made to the whole world.

levels.title: Lawyers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what lawyers do on each side of a case.
levels.summary: A prosecutor brings the case for the state; a defence lawyer tests it. England's cab-rank rule keeps lawyers open to all; Gideon v Wainwright (1963) gave poor U.S. defendants a lawyer.

cards.headline: A prisoner's handwritten petition changed who gets a lawyer.
cards.body: In 1961 Clarence Earl Gideon was charged with breaking into a Florida pool hall. He couldn't afford a lawyer and asked the judge for one. Florida only appointed lawyers in capital cases, so Gideon defended himself, and lost. From prison he sent the Supreme Court a handwritten petition.

cards.headline: Two sides, two jobs
cards.body: A criminal trial has a lawyer on each side. The prosecutor brings the case for the state. In England and Wales that's the Crown Prosecution Service, independent of the police, which decides which police-investigated cases go to court and then prosecutes them. The defence lawyer represents the accused and tests every piece of evidence. Level 54's golden thread needs someone to pull on it.

cards.headline: The cab-rank rule
cards.body: How can a lawyer defend someone accused of something terrible? In England, barristers follow the cab-rank rule: like a taxi at the front of the rank, they must generally take a suitable case whatever they think of the client or the cause. The point, says the Bar Standards Board, is that everyone can get legal representation. Defending someone isn't endorsing them. It's making sure the case gets tested.

mascot.line: One handwritten letter, one retrial, one very different verdict.

cards.fact: Same man, same charge, different result.
cards.context: In 1963 the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that states must provide a lawyer to defendants in felony cases who can't afford one. Gideon got a retrial, this time with a lawyer, who discredited the prosecution's key witness. The jury acquitted him. The big difference was the person standing next to him.

levels.title: Criminal and Civil Law
levels.objective: After this level you can compare criminal and civil cases.
levels.summary: Criminal cases are brought by the state and can end in punishment; civil cases settle disputes between people or organisations, usually with damages, and need only 'more likely than not'.

cards.headline: Acquitted in 1995. Found liable in 1997. Same man, same two deaths.
cards.body: In 1995 a jury acquitted O.J. Simpson of murdering Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. In 1997 a different jury, in a civil trial, found him liable for their deaths and ordered him to pay $33.5 million in damages to the families. A contradiction? No. Two different kinds of case, asking two different questions.

cards.headline: Criminal: the state brings the case
cards.body: A criminal case is about an alleged crime. It comes to court when the state decides to prosecute; in England and Wales that decision is usually the Crown Prosecution Service's. If the accused is convicted, the sentence can be prison, community punishment or a fine. The victim isn't suing anyone. The state is the one asking for punishment.

cards.headline: Civil: people versus people
cards.body: A civil case is a dispute between people, businesses or organisations: damaged goods, say, or an unpaid debt. Nobody goes to prison for losing. The winner may get damages, meaning money, or a court order telling someone to do or stop doing something. It's less "you broke the law" and more "you owe me".

mascot.line: Higher stakes, higher bar. Liberty needs more proof than money.

cards.headline: Two different bars
cards.body: Here's the key. Criminal guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. A civil claim needs only to be more likely than not: the balance of probabilities, anything over 50%. So a jury can have a reasonable doubt that Simpson committed murder, while another decides it's more likely than not he was responsible. Same facts, two bars, two answers.

cards.headline: Criminal vs civil

Civil: parties settle a dispute

levels.title: Supreme Courts
levels.objective: After this level you can explain courts that decide what a constitution means.
levels.summary: Judicial review lets courts void unconstitutional laws: any U.S. court since Marbury v Madison (1803), special courts like Germany's. UK courts can only declare a law incompatible.

cards.headline: In 2024, Germany's top constitutional court received 4,640 new cases.
cards.body: About 96% were constitutional complaints. Any person in Germany can lodge one, claiming that a public authority has violated their fundamental rights, and about two-thirds of the 2024 complaints came without a lawyer. Fewer than 2 in 100 succeed. But when one does, the court can declare a law void. How can a court overrule a law?

cards.headline: Judicial review
cards.body: A constitution is the rulebook for the people who make the rules. Judicial review is the power of courts to examine laws and government actions and declare those that break the constitution null and void. In the United States it goes back to Marbury v Madison in 1803, when Chief Justice John Marshall claimed that power for the courts. Lawmakers write the laws; courts check them against the rulebook.

cards.headline: Every court, or one special court?
cards.body: Countries split the job in two ways. In the U.S., any court can hear a claim that a law breaks the constitution. Many European countries, such as Germany and Austria, give that job to a special constitutional court instead. Germany's is the one those 4,640 cases went to.

cards.fact: The UK's Supreme Court can't strike down an Act of Parliament.
cards.context: UK courts must apply Acts of Parliament even if they breach human rights. Higher courts can issue a declaration of incompatibility, but it doesn't change the law or stop it being enforced; Parliament decides whether to fix it. A German court can declare a law void. A UK court can raise a red flag, not show a red card.

levels.title: Police
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what police do and the limits on their power.
levels.summary: London's 1829 police were unarmed and deliberately unmilitary; British policing rests on public consent. The law limits police power: detention time limits, rights in custody, the Miranda warnings.

cards.headline: London's first modern police carried no guns and wore blue on purpose.
cards.body: In 1829 the Metropolitan Police Act, sponsored by Home Secretary Robert Peel, set up a professional police force for London. Its officers carried truncheons, handcuffs and a rattle to call for help. Their blue tailcoats and top hats were chosen to show they were not soldiers. Why work so hard not to look like an army?

cards.headline: Policing by consent
cards.body: Because the idea was to police with the public, not against it. The first of the British policing principles is to prevent crime and disorder, as an alternative to repression by military force. The UK Home Office calls it policing by consent: police power comes from the common consent of the public. In its words, the police are the public and the public are the police.

cards.headline: Powers, with limits
cards.body: Police have real power over people, so the law draws lines. In England and Wales, police can generally hold someone for up to 24 hours before they must charge or release them; longer needs approval for a serious crime. People in custody have the right to free legal advice and to tell someone where they are. In the U.S., Miranda v Arizona (1966) requires police to tell suspects in custody of their right to stay silent and to have a lawyer before questioning.

mascot.line: Different countries make different choices here. It's a policy, not a law of nature.

cards.fact: Only about 4 in 100 police officers in England and Wales are armed.
cards.context: Home Office figures show 6,558 armed officers on 31 March 2026, 4.0% of all police officers. The rest patrol without a gun, nearly two centuries after the first bobbies set out with a truncheon and a rattle.

levels.title: Prisons and Punishment
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the purposes of punishment and the debates about it.
levels.summary: About 11.7 million people were in prison in 2023. Punishment aims at retribution, deterrence, incapacitation or rehabilitation; Kant, Bentham and Beccaria argued over why.

cards.headline: About 11.7 million people were in prison worldwide in 2023.
cards.body: That's the UN Office on Drugs and Crime's count. Around 30 per cent of them, more than 3.7 million people, hadn't been sentenced: they were in pre-trial detention. So what is prison for? Your answer changes what a prison should look like.

cards.headline: Four reasons to punish
cards.body: Four aims come up again and again. Retribution: the offender pays for the wrong done. Deterrence: the threat of punishment discourages crime. Incapacitation: someone locked up can't reoffend outside. Rehabilitation: reform, so the person returns as a law-abiding citizen. A single prison sentence can try to do all four at once, and they don't always pull the same way.

cards.headline: Deserved, or useful?
cards.body: Philosophers split on the deepest question. Retributivists such as Immanuel Kant argue punishment is justified because the wrongdoer deserves it, whatever its effects. Jeremy Bentham took the other side: all punishment is in itself evil, he wrote, justified only as far as it prevents some greater evil. The debate is still going, and it shapes real sentences.

cards.fact: Getting caught matters more than the length of the sentence.
cards.context: That was Cesare Beccaria's argument in On Crimes and Punishments (1764): the certainty of punishment deters more than its severity. A speed camera you know is there changes your driving more than a huge fine you'll probably never get.

mascot.line: Same four aims everywhere. The argument is over the mix.

cards.headline: Norway's answer
cards.body: Norway's prison service follows a principle of normality: the punishment is the loss of liberty, and no other rights are removed by the sentencing court. Life inside should resemble life outside as much as possible. It's a system built around the rehabilitation aim. Countries weigh the four aims differently, and that's where the debate lives.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Courts and Justice
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how courts, police and punishment fit together.
levels.summary: Justice's symbols sum up the chapter: scales for impartial weighing (courts, juries, the burden of proof), a sword for the power to enforce (police, punishment), and a blindfold for independence.

cards.headline: Look up at London's Old Bailey and Justice is staring straight back.
cards.body: The gilded statue on the dome of England's most famous criminal court holds a sword in one hand and scales in the other. Unlike most statues of Justice, she wears no blindfold. Scales, sword, blindfold: three props. Between them, they sum up this whole chapter.

cards.headline: The scales: weighing the case
cards.body: Justice comes from a Roman virtue, and her scales came to stand for impartiality. That's Level 51's courts, weighing facts against the law. It's Level 53's jurors, weighing the evidence. And it's Level 54's rule for how the scales start: tipped toward the accused, until the prosecution proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

cards.headline: The sword: the power to enforce
cards.body: Her sword stands for power. A verdict is only words until someone can enforce it, and that's where Level 58's police and Level 59's punishment come in. But the sword answers to the scales: police work within legal limits, and a sentence follows only a conviction. Power first and weighing later is the order a fair system refuses.

mascot.line: Scales, sword, blindfold. You can now explain all three, and the court behind each one.

cards.fact: The blindfold arrived in the 16th century.
cards.context: From then on Justice was often shown blindfolded, and today the blindfold is read as a symbol of impartiality: she judges without looking at who stands before her. Level 52's independent judges wear it invisibly.

levels.title: Why Elections?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what elections are for.
levels.summary: Schumpeter: elections are a contest for votes that picks who rules. Popper: they let the ruled dismiss rulers without bloodshed. UDHR Article 21 bases authority on the will of the people.

cards.headline: Every few years, whole countries can fire their government. Nobody gets hurt.
cards.body: Swapping the people in charge of a country, peacefully and on a schedule, is an odd thing when you stop to think about it. So what exactly are elections for? An economist, a philosopher and the United Nations each gave an answer.

cards.headline: Schumpeter: a contest for your vote
cards.body: In 1942 the economist Joseph Schumpeter gave a blunt answer. Democracy, he wrote, is a method in which people win the power to decide through a "competitive struggle for the people's vote." Citizens don't really rule, in his view: elections are a fairly peaceful way of keeping or changing those who do. Think of a job interview where the whole country sits on the panel.

mascot.line: Hired by vote, fired by vote. Either way, nobody needs a sword.

cards.headline: Popper: the power to fire
cards.body: The philosopher Karl Popper, author of The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), shifted the question. "The people do not rule anywhere," he wrote; governments rule. What matters is that the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed, for example through general elections. For Popper, the test of a democracy isn't who wins. It's whether today's winners can be voted out tomorrow.

cards.headline: The UN: where authority comes from
cards.body: In 1948 the Universal Declaration of Human Rights put a third answer in writing. Article 21 says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections. Remember Level 3? Authority is power people accept as legitimate. Elections measure that acceptance again and again instead of assuming it. Locke's consent of the governed, on a timetable.

levels.title: The Secret Ballot
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why voting is secret.
levels.summary: Open voting invited intimidation and bribery. Victoria introduced the modern secret ballot in 1856 and Britain followed in 1872. John Stuart Mill argued voting should be public.

cards.headline: In 1843 New South Wales, you said your vote out loud. Often in a pub.
cards.body: At the New South Wales elections of 1843, voters told an officer, out loud, who they were voting for. Candidates handed out free drinks, and intimidation and bribery were everywhere. The fix came from Australia too.

cards.headline: Victoria's quiet revolution
cards.body: Victoria's secret ballot law took effect on 19 March 1856: the first modern secret ballot. The government printed the ballot papers, not the candidates. You marked yours in private, folded it and dropped it in a box. South Australia soon added a neat tweak: mark an X beside the candidate you want. That version is known as the Australian ballot.

cards.headline: No witness, no threat
cards.body: The logic is simple: if nobody can see your vote, nobody can intimidate you or punish you for it. Britain's Ballot Act of 1872 ended open voting there, a system that had become known for bribery, intimidation and drunken disorder. In 1948 the UDHR from Level 61 wrote secrecy in: elections held by secret vote or equivalent free procedures.

mascot.line: Mill trusted voters to be brave in public. The pubs of 1843 suggest why others preferred a folded ballot.

cards.headline: The great dissenter
cards.body: Not everyone cheered. John Stuart Mill, in Considerations on Representative Government (1861), argued that a vote is power over others, so it's a trust held for the public. Like any public duty, he said, it should be done "under the eye and criticism of the public." A secret ballot, he feared, invites people to vote for their own benefit instead.

levels.title: Voting Systems
levels.objective: After this level you can compare winner-take-all and proportional voting.
levels.summary: FPTP elects each district's top vote-getter; PR matches seats to votes; ranked systems transfer preferences. New Zealand moved to MMP. Arrow showed every system trades something.

cards.headline: In 1978, one New Zealand party won the most votes. The other one won power.
cards.body: It happened again in 1981. Both times Labour won more votes nationwide, but National won more seats and kept governing, and criticism of the voting system grew. How can that happen? It depends on how votes turn into seats.

cards.headline: First past the post
cards.body: In first-past-the-post, used in the UK, Canada, India and the United States, each district elects one member: whoever gets the most votes, majority or not. Win lots of districts narrowly and you can take more seats with fewer votes. In the 1950s the political scientist Maurice Duverger observed that this system tends to squeeze politics into two big parties.

cards.headline: Proportional representation
cards.body: Proportional representation aims straight at New Zealand's problem: a party's share of the votes becomes a matching share of seats. Districts elect several members; in Israel and the Netherlands the whole country is one district. New Zealand switched. A Royal Commission recommended Germany's mixed system (MMP) in 1986, and from 1996 voters got two votes: one for a local MP, one for a party.

cards.headline: Ranked choice
cards.body: Ranked systems ask for more than one choice. Australia's House of Representatives uses the Alternative Vote: rank the candidates, and if nobody has a majority, the least successful are eliminated and their votes pass to next preferences until someone does. Ireland's Single Transferable Vote uses rankings in districts that elect several members, keeping results fairly proportional.

mascot.line: The IDEA handbook's trade-offs plus Arrow's proof: choosing a voting system means choosing which flaw you can live with.

levels.title: Drawing the Map
levels.objective: After this level you can explain voting districts and gerrymandering.
levels.summary: District lines can decide results. Canada redraws after each census with independent commissions. Gerrymandering packs and cracks voters; geography alone can also create bias.

cards.headline: Same voters. Same votes. Move the lines, and you change the winner.
cards.body: Picture 100 voters, split 50-50 between two parties, divided into four districts. Draw the lines one way and each party wins two seats. Draw them another way and either party can win three. Nobody changed their vote. Only the map moved.

cards.headline: Why maps get redrawn
cards.body: Level 63's first-past-the-post elects one member per district, so where the lines fall matters. People move, so lines must move too. Canada redraws its federal districts after every 10-year census. Since 1964, independent commissions do the drawing, one per province, each chaired by a judge, and sitting lawmakers can't serve on them.

cards.headline: Meet the gerrymander
cards.body: In 1812, Massachusetts governor Elbridge Gerry signed a bill creating oddly shaped districts that helped his party. A cartoon in the Boston Gazette drew one as a salamander-like monster: the "Gerry-mander." The name stuck. Gerrymandering means deliberately drawing district lines to help or hurt a particular political interest.

mascot.line: Packing wastes votes in a pile. Cracking scatters them like crumbs.

cards.headline: Packing and cracking
cards.body: Two moves do most of the work. Packing crowds a group's voters into as few districts as possible, so they win a few seats by landslides. Cracking spreads them thinly across many districts, so they lose narrowly almost everywhere. Either way, that group ends up with fewer seats than its votes suggest.

cards.headline: Proving it is harder
cards.body: Nicholas Stephanopoulos and Eric McGhee (2015) proposed the efficiency gap: count each party's "wasted" votes, those for losers and those beyond what a winner needed, and compare. But Jowei Chen and Jonathan Rodden (2013) found that when one party's voters cluster in cities, even maps drawn without intent can short it seats. Geography can gerrymander by accident.

cards.headline: The map: drawn
learned: District lines can change who wins
Canada: independent commissions redraw after each census
Gerrymander: after Elbridge Gerry, 1812
Packing and cracking waste a group's votes

levels.title: Campaigns
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how election campaigns work.
levels.summary: Lazarsfeld's 1940 study found media changed few votes; people decided through conversations and opinion leaders. The UK caps party spending; Buckley v. Valeo struck down US spending limits.

cards.headline: In 1940, researchers set out to watch a campaign change minds. It mostly didn't.
cards.body: Paul Lazarsfeld and his team interviewed the same voters again and again in Erie County, Ohio, through a US presidential race. Their book, The People's Choice (1944), surprised even its authors, and it changed how people think about campaigns.

cards.headline: Your neighbor beat the radio
cards.body: Contrary to their expectations, the researchers found that radio and newspapers had only minor direct effects on how people voted. People mainly made up their minds by talking with those around them: family, friends, coworkers. The loudest broadcasts of the campaign were outvoted by the kitchen table.

cards.headline: The two-step flow
cards.body: So how do campaign messages travel? Lazarsfeld's answer was the two-step flow. Ideas move from the media to opinion leaders, the people who follow politics closely, and then from them to their followers through personal networks. Much of what you hear from a campaign reaches you secondhand, through someone you trust.

mascot.line: One question, two answers: is a spending cap fair play, or a cap on speech?

cards.headline: Rules for the race
cards.body: Level 61's Schumpeter called democracy a competitive struggle for the people's vote, and every competition needs rules. The UK caps how much each party may spend in the 365 days before a general election. In the US, the Supreme Court's Buckley v. Valeo (1976) upheld limits on contributions but struck down limits on spending as restricting free expression.
