levels.title: Polls
levels.objective: After this level you can explain opinion polls and their margin of error.
levels.summary: The 1936 Literary Digest poll's 2.4 million biased replies lost to Gallup's scientific sample. A plus or minus 3 margin needs about 1,067 random interviews; a lead's margin is about double.

cards.headline: In 1936, 2.4 million people answered a magazine's poll. It still got it wrong.
cards.body: The Literary Digest mailed about 10 million straw ballots, got 2.4 million back and predicted Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt won easily. How can so many answers be so wrong?

cards.headline: Big isn't the same as fair
cards.body: The Digest drew its names from phone lists, car registrations and club memberships. During the Depression, those leaned heavily toward the well-off, and only about a quarter of those mailed replied. George Gallup used more systematic, scientific sampling and publicly predicted that Roosevelt would win handily. A poll is only as good as who's in it.

cards.headline: The margin of error
cards.body: A well-chosen sample works like a spoonful from a well-stirred pot of soup. A simple random sample of 1,067 people has a margin of error of about plus or minus 3 points. That means if you ran the same survey 100 times, the result would land within 3 points of the true value about 95 times.

mascot.line: Next time a headline says "surges ahead by 2", check the margin before you believe the surge.

cards.headline: Read the lead, not just the number
cards.body: Here's the trap. The margin on the gap between two candidates is roughly double: a 3-point margin becomes about 6 points for the lead. So a 5-point lead could really be anywhere from -1 to +11. And sampling is only one source of error; question wording and who answers matter too.

cards.headline: Polls: read properly

The margin on a lead is roughly double

levels.title: Referendums
levels.objective: After this level you can explain direct votes on a single question.
levels.summary: A referendum puts one question to voters; an initiative starts with a citizens' petition. New Zealand chose MMP by referendum in 1993. Bulmer weighs benefits and risks; questions must be clear.

cards.headline: In 1988, Chile's ruler called a vote to keep himself in power. He lost.
cards.body: Augusto Pinochet, Chile's authoritarian ruler, held a referendum to extend his term. He unexpectedly lost, and his regime collapsed shortly after. One yes-or-no question turned out to be very powerful. So who gets to ask it?

cards.headline: One question, straight to the voters
cards.body: A referendum gives people a direct vote on a specific issue, sent to them by a parliament, president or government. A citizens' initiative works the other way round: the people start it, usually with a petition signed by a set number of people. Results can be binding or only advisory, though advisory votes are usually treated as binding in practice, especially if decisive.

cards.headline: Voters choose the rules
cards.body: Remember Level 63's New Zealand? It settled its voting-system argument by asking the voters. In a binding referendum in 1993, 53.9% chose MMP over first-past-the-post. The people chose the method that would count their own votes.

mascot.line: Try it: "Do you agree with the sensible plan to fix the roads?" The Venice Commission would send that one back.

cards.headline: Worth it? The debate
cards.body: Elliot Bulmer's primer for International IDEA weighs both sides. For: you vote on one measure on its merits, not a party's whole package. Against: voters may react to unrelated things, like how popular the leaders are; frequent votes cause fatigue; rulers can use referendums to fake legitimacy. The Venice Commission adds a rule: the question must be clear, not misleading, and must not suggest an answer.

levels.title: Counting the Votes
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how votes are counted and checked.
levels.summary: UK counts are watched by candidates' agents, recounts can be requested and ties go to lots. India's VVPAT slips and Philip Stark's risk-limiting audits let counts be checked.

cards.headline: In a UK election, an exact tie is settled by drawing lots.
cards.body: If two candidates tie and one more vote would decide it, the returning officer must decide between them by lot. But that only happens after every ballot has been counted, and checked, with witnesses watching. This level is about the witnesses.

cards.headline: Counting in the open
cards.body: At UK elections, each candidate can appoint counting agents to watch the verification and the count, and the process is meant to be transparent. If an agent doubts the result, they can ask for a recount. The returning officer must consider it, can refuse only an unreasonable request, and any recount happens in full view of everyone there.

cards.headline: A paper trail for machines
cards.body: Machines count fast, but can you check them? In India, a VVPAT printer beside each voting machine shows the voter a paper slip with their candidate's name and symbol for 7 seconds. Then it drops into a sealed box. Those slips can be counted, so the machine's tally has something to answer to.

cards.headline: Checking without recounting everything
cards.body: In 2007 the statistician Philip Stark developed the risk-limiting audit. Officials hand-check randomly chosen paper ballots. If the sample doesn't confirm the result, the audit grows, up to a full hand count that replaces the reported result. It has been tested in California, Ohio and Denmark. As Stark puts it, "unlike voters, ballots have to reply, and have to reply truthfully."

levels.title: Spotting Misinformation
levels.objective: After this level you can spot misleading claims about politics.
levels.summary: Misinformation, disinformation and malinformation differ by truth and intent. Fact checkers read laterally. Caulfield's SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace.

cards.headline: Who judges a website best: a historian, a Stanford student or a fact checker?
cards.body: Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew put 10 PhD historians, 10 professional fact checkers and 25 Stanford undergraduates in front of live websites on social and political issues. One group was far better and faster. Its trick works on any election claim you'll ever meet.

cards.headline: Three kinds of bad information
cards.body: First, some words. In a 2017 report for the Council of Europe, Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan separated three things. Misinformation is false but shared without meaning harm. Disinformation is false and shared knowingly to cause harm. Malinformation is genuine, but shared to cause harm. Same shape, different intent.

cards.headline: Read sideways
cards.body: The historians and students often fell for official-looking logos and domain names. They read vertically, staying on a site to judge it. The fact checkers read laterally: after a quick scan, they left the site and opened new tabs to see what others said about it. They reached better-founded conclusions in a fraction of the time. Don't ask a website whether it's trustworthy. Ask everyone else.

mascot.line: Four moves, a few minutes, and no need to be an expert. That's the whole point of SIFT.

cards.headline: SIFT before you share
cards.body: Mike Caulfield turned this into four moves, SIFT. Stop: when you hit a post, ask whether you know the source before reading or sharing. Investigate the source. Find better coverage. Trace claims, quotes and media back to their original context, because much of what we see online has been stripped of it, like a clip that leaves out what happened just before.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Elections
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how elections turn votes into power.
levels.summary: The IPU's 1994 Declaration on free and fair elections lists this chapter's ideas: authority from the people, a secret and equal vote, fair campaigns and an honest, observed count.

cards.headline: In 1994, the Inter-Parliamentary Union wrote a checklist for fair elections.
cards.body: On 26 March 1994 in Paris, the Inter-Parliamentary Council unanimously adopted the IPU's Declaration on Criteria for Free and Fair Elections. Read it now and it looks like this chapter's table of contents.

items.label: Where power comes from
points: Authority only from the will of the people
Elections at regular intervals (Level 61)

items.label: How you vote
points: The right to vote in secret is absolute (Level 62)
Every vote of equivalent weight (Level 64)

items.label: The race and the count
points: Campaigns on an equal basis (Level 65)
An honest count, with party agents and observers (Level 68)

mascot.line: Ten levels, and you can follow a vote from the ballot box all the way to power.

cards.headline: From a ballot to power
cards.body: Follow one vote through this chapter. It's cast in secret, turned into seats by a voting system and a district map, fought over in a campaign and counted in the open. What comes out is Level 3's authority: power people accept as legitimate. And Popper's point makes it complete: the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed, so next time the same vote can take that power away.

levels.title: Government Budgets
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a government plans its spending.
levels.summary: A budget, once a leather bag, is a government's plan for what it collects and spends. It runs through four overlapping stages: prepare, approve, carry out and audit.

cards.headline: In 1733, a pamphlet mocked Britain's top minister for opening his bag.
cards.body: The pamphlet was called The Budget Opened, and it attacked Robert Walpole's tax plans, likening him to a quack selling cures. The insult stuck. By the 1760s, 'budget' was simply the word for a government's money plans.

cards.headline: A plan in a bag
cards.body: The word comes from Old French bougette, a small leather bag: picture a finance minister opening his wallet to reveal his plans. Britain's chancellor still holds up a red box on Budget Day. Inside is a plan with two sides: the money the government expects to collect, much of it Level 6's compulsory taxes, and the money it intends to spend over the coming year.

events.label: The executive, the government of the day, puts the plan together
The legislature debates it, amends it and votes on it
The government collects the money and spends it
Auditors check what was actually spent, and whether it worked

mascot.line: Three budgets, one government, no days off. Somebody really should budget some rest.

cards.fact: At any moment, a government is juggling three budgets at once.
cards.context: While the executive prepares next year's budget, ministries are carrying out this year's, and the national audit office is checking last year's. It works like a school year: next year's timetable gets planned while this year's classes run and last year's exams are still being marked.

levels.title: Where Tax Money Goes
levels.objective: After this level you can describe what governments spend the most on.
levels.summary: OECD governments spent 42.6% of GDP in 2023. The biggest slice is social protection (pensions and benefits), then health; the size of that slice varies widely between countries.

cards.headline: If government spending were a pizza, which slice would be biggest?
cards.body: Defence? Schools? Roads? Take a guess before you scroll. In every EU country the answer is the same, and it's none of those.

cards.headline: First, the size of the pizza
cards.body: Across OECD countries, government spending averaged 42.6% of GDP in 2023. That's measured against GDP, the value of everything an economy produces in a year. Some countries go well past it: in 2024 Finland, France and Austria each spent more than half. Level 6's taxes, about a third of GDP, pay for much of it.

cards.headline: Ten standard slices
cards.body: To compare countries fairly, statisticians cut spending into ten standard functions, known as COFOG: general public services, defence, public order and safety, economic affairs, health, education, social protection and a few smaller ones. Social protection is the one nobody guesses. It covers pensions, plus benefits for people who are sick, disabled or out of work.

cards.fact: The biggest slice is social protection: 13.4% of GDP across the OECD in 2023.
cards.context: Health came second at 8.4%, and education averaged 4.9%. The smallest slice was environmental protection, at 0.5%. In the EU, social protection alone took 40% of all government spending in 2024. Governments spend more on looking after people than on anything else.

mascot.line: Same recipe, very different portions. That's why comparing countries is so revealing.

cards.fact: Same slice, very different sizes: from 7.9% of GDP to 25.7%.
cards.context: That was the range for social protection in 2023, from the United States to Finland. The OECD puts the gap down to different institutional models, meaning how much each country chooses to run through the state. How big the slice should be is a political choice, and countries make it very differently.

learned: OECD governments spent 42.6% of GDP in 2023

Social protection is the biggest slice, health next

levels.title: Public Schools
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how public schools are run and paid for.
levels.summary: Who runs a school and who pays for it are separate questions. Dutch private schools get equal state funding; countries also differ in which level of government pays.

cards.headline: Who runs your school, and who pays for it? The answers needn't match.
cards.body: In the Netherlands, the state funds public schools and private schools equally. The private ones are usually run by foundations based on a religion or other beliefs. So a Dutch school can be private and still paid for by taxes.

cards.headline: Run by whom, paid by whom
cards.body: The OECD sorts schools by who controls them. Public schools are typically funded and regulated by government. Private schools are run by a private body, and they come in two kinds. Government-dependent private schools get more than half their money from public sources; independent ones live mainly on fees and donations. Dutch private schools are almost all the first kind.

cards.fact: OECD governments spend about 2.2% of GDP on primary and lower secondary schools.
cards.context: That's the 2022 average; Iceland spent the most, 3.2%. Rich doesn't automatically mean a bigger share. Luxembourg spends among the most per pupil, yet less than the average share of GDP, because its GDP per person is among the highest.

mascot.line: Next time you see a school, ask two questions: who runs it, and who signs the cheques?

cards.headline: Which level of government pays?
cards.body: Remember Level 8's layers? For upper secondary schools, Greece, Iceland and New Zealand fund everything from the centre. In Spain, the regions provide and manage over 80% of the public money; in Switzerland, the cantons spend 94%. It's the same idea as Level 8's Canada, where the provinces run education. Same school corridors, very different paymasters.

levels.title: Healthcare Systems
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the main ways countries pay for healthcare.
levels.summary: Countries pay for healthcare through tax-funded government schemes, compulsory insurance or out of pocket, in different mixes. The US spent 17.2% of GDP on health in 2024; the OECD average, 9.3%.

cards.headline: Every country pays its doctors. The question is whose pocket pays.
cards.body: Nobody gets healthcare for free: nurses, scanners and medicines all cost money. What differs from country to country is the route the money takes, and the OECD sorts those routes into a few big pipes.

cards.headline: Three ways to pay the doctor

items.label: Government schemes
points: Care based on where you live, funded mostly by taxes
80%+ of spending in Sweden, Norway, Denmark, UK

items.label: Compulsory insurance
points: Funded by contributions from employers and employees
Over three-quarters in France, Germany, Japan

items.label: Out of pocket
points: Patients pay directly
Over a third of spending in Mexico, Chile, Latvia, Greece

cards.headline: Pipes, not boxes
cards.body: Most countries mix the pipes rather than pick one. In a government scheme, you're covered because you live there, and the bill goes to the taxpayer. In compulsory insurance, you're covered because contributions are paid for you, usually by you and your employer together. Neither is free; they differ in who writes the cheque and how. Out-of-pocket payments are the leftover, and in some countries it's a big leftover.

mascot.line: Different pipes, same patient. Compare what goes in and what comes out.

cards.fact: The United States spent 17.2% of GDP on health in 2024, the most in the OECD.
cards.context: The OECD average was 9.3%, and Germany came next at 12.3%. Across the OECD, health also took 15.1% of all government spending in 2023. Which system works best is argued fiercely. The WHO's stated goal for all of them is universal health coverage: the care people need, when they need it, without financial hardship.

levels.title: Pensions
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how pensions support older people.
levels.summary: Public pensions cost OECD countries 8.1% of GDP, about 18% of government spending. More older people per worker is pushing retirement ages up, as in Denmark's move to 70.

cards.headline: The world's first state pension started at 70. Denmark is heading back there.
cards.body: Germany's 1889 scheme set the pension age at 70, and lowered it to 65 in 1916. In May 2025, Denmark's parliament confirmed its pension age will reach 70 from 2040, the highest in Europe. Why would a country turn the clock back more than a century?

cards.fact: Public pensions cost OECD countries 8.1% of GDP on average.
cards.context: That's up from 6.7% in 2000, and it's about 18% of all government spending. Pensions are a big part of Level 72's biggest slice, social protection. The range is wide: Greece and Italy spend around 16% of GDP, Iceland and Ireland under 3%. In Iceland, as in Australia, compulsory workplace schemes carry much of the load.

cards.headline: More grandparents per worker
cards.body: Here's the squeeze. Across the OECD, there were 22 people aged 65 or over for every 100 aged 20 to 64 in 2000. By 2025 there were 33, and the projection for 2050 is 52. The OECD treats this ratio as a stand-in for potential pensioners per potential contributor. Each step up means fewer shoulders under each pension.

mascot.line: Bismarck's 70 is back in fashion. History does love a sequel.

cards.headline: Working longer, and arguing about it
cards.body: One response is a later retirement age. Under laws already passed, the OECD's average normal retirement age for men will rise from 64.7 to 66.4 for people starting work in 2024. Denmark shows both sides of the debate. Its government said the rise was needed to afford proper welfare for future generations; unions protested it as unjust.

learned: Germany's first pension age was 70, in 1889

options.label: Working-age people are paid more
options.rationale: The ratio says nothing about pay.

questions.explanation: The OECD uses this ratio as a stand-in for potential pensioners per potential contributor: 22 in 2000, 33 in 2025, 52 projected for 2050.

options.label: They are paid outside government

options.label: They are a big part of social protection

questions.explanation: Social protection covers pensions and benefits; public pensions alone take about 18% of government spending on average.

levels.title: Roads and Bridges
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how governments build and maintain infrastructure.
levels.summary: Genoa's bridge collapse showed that infrastructure must be maintained. Governments pay for roads with taxes, road-user taxes like the US fuel tax, or public-private partnerships.

cards.headline: On 14 August 2018, a motorway bridge in Genoa fell.
cards.body: The Morandi bridge had carried traffic since 1967. When it collapsed, 43 people died. A bridge is built once, but it has to be looked after for as long as it stands.

cards.fact: Genoa's new bridge came with its own robots.
cards.context: The San Giorgio bridge, designed by Renzo Piano, opened in August 2020. Four robots run along it, checking for weathering and erosion. It's maintenance built into the design: the dull, never-finished job that decides whether infrastructure lasts.

cards.headline: Who pays? Often, the drivers
cards.body: In 1956 the United States set up the Highway Trust Fund to help build the Interstate highways, paid for by taxes on road users, such as fuel taxes. The people who use the roads pay at the pump. The catch: the federal gas tax has been 18.4 cents a gallon since 1993, and since the late 2000s Congress has had to top the fund up repeatedly.

mascot.line: Build, pay, maintain, check. Every road you drive on went through all four.

cards.headline: Or bring in a partner
cards.body: Another route is a public-private partnership, or PPP. In the OECD's definition, it's a long-term deal in which a private company funds and delivers a public service, like a road, and shares the risks. The European Court of Auditors agreed in 2018 that PPPs can speed delivery and keep up maintenance. But when it checked 12 EU-backed PPPs, seven of nine finished projects ran late, by up to 52 months.

cards.headline: Infrastructure: maintained
learned: Genoa's 1967 bridge fell in 2018, killing 43
Its replacement has inspection robots
US highways run on road-user taxes like fuel tax

options.label: From profits of state-owned car makers

options.label: It bans drivers who haven't paid

options.label: It charges only people without cars

options.label: Drivers pay a little every time they fill up

levels.title: Corruption
levels.objective: After this level you can explain corruption and how countries fight it.
levels.summary: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. Hong Kong's ICAC, set up in 1974, fought it with enforcement, prevention and education; Transparency International measures perceptions.

cards.headline: In early-1970s Hong Kong, you might have to bribe an ambulance crew.
cards.body: Crews asked for 'tea money' before picking up a sick person. Bribes smoothed the way to public housing and school places too. A public service came with a private price tag.

cards.headline: Borrowed power, misused
cards.body: Transparency International defines corruption as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. Every word matters. Entrusted: the power was lent to an official by the public. Abuse: it was used for something it wasn't lent for. Private gain: the official pockets the benefit. Remember Level 3? Authority is power people accept. Corruption quietly turns it into a price list.

events.label: Police chief superintendent Peter Godber, under investigation, slips out of Hong Kong
Public outcry, and a judge-led inquiry
The Independent Commission Against Corruption is set up
Godber is brought back, convicted and jailed for four years

cards.fact: The ICAC fought corruption three ways: enforcement, prevention and education.
cards.context: Catch the corrupt, fix the systems that tempt them, and bring the public on side. It also stood apart from any government department, because corruption was worst in the police force itself. You can't ask the suspects to run the investigation.

cards.fact: Denmark tops the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, with 89 out of 100.
cards.context: Transparency International scores 182 countries and territories on perceived public-sector corruption, from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (very clean). In 2025 the global average fell to 42, and 122 countries scored below 50. It was Denmark's eighth year in a row at the top.

cards.headline: Corruption: exposed
learned: Corruption: abuse of entrusted power for private gain
Hong Kong set up the independent ICAC in 1974
Enforcement, prevention and education
CPI 2025: average 42; Denmark top with 89

options.label: Any law that people disagree with

options.label: The abuse of entrusted power for private gain
Spending more than the budget allows
options.rationale: Overspending is a budget problem, not in itself corruption.

options.label: Any gift between two friends
options.rationale: A gift between friends involves no entrusted power.

questions.explanation: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain.

options.label: Corruption was worst in the police, so they couldn't investigate themselves
The police had too few officers to spare

options.label: It was cheaper to run separately
options.rationale: Cost wasn't the point; trust was.

questions.explanation: Corruption was particularly serious in the police force, so an independent body was needed to investigate it.

options.label: Refuses to use any power at all
options.rationale: Corruption is misuse of power, not refusing to use it.

options.label: Hands their power back to the public
options.rationale: Giving power back isn't abuse.

options.label: Wins power in a fair election
options.rationale: Winning a fair election is how authority is gained, not abused.

options.label: Uses power the public entrusted to them for private gain

questions.explanation: Authority is power people accept; corruption abuses that entrusted power for private gain.

levels.title: Deficits and Debt
levels.objective: After this level you can explain government deficits and debt.
levels.summary: A deficit is spending above revenue in a year; borrowing to cover deficits builds debt. The IMF expects global public debt to pass 100% of GDP by 2029. Views on limits differ.

cards.headline: Global public debt is heading for its highest level since 1948.
cards.body: That's the IMF's projection: government debt worldwide rising above 100% of world GDP by 2029. How does a government end up owing more than a year's worth of everything its economy produces? One year at a time.

cards.headline: The yearly gap
cards.body: Level 71's budget has two sides. When spending beats revenue, the gap is a deficit; the reverse is a surplus. To cover a deficit, a government borrows, mostly by selling bonds: 79.3% of OECD public debt takes that form. Run deficits year after year and they pile up as debt.

cards.fact: In 2023, only six OECD countries ran a surplus.
cards.context: The average OECD government ran a deficit of 4.6% of GDP. Norway led the small surplus club at 16.5%.

mascot.line: Owing a lot isn't the same as being in trouble. Who lends to you, and at what price, matters.

cards.headline: Big debts, different risks
cards.body: Among the G20, Canada, China, France, Italy, Japan, the UK and the US have debts above 100% of GDP, or soon will. The IMF rates their risk as moderate, thanks to deep markets for their bonds. Meanwhile 55 countries are in or near debt distress, often with debts below 60%. The size of a debt isn't the whole story; its cost matters too.

cards.headline: How much debt is too much? Three answers

items.label: The IMF
points: Keep debt at safer levels
Build buffers for severe shocks

items.label: The OECD
points: Sustainable deficits can fund public investment
And cushion recessions, pandemics and disasters

items.label: Germany's rule
points: A 'debt brake' caps the structural deficit at 0.35% of GDP
Since 2025, defence above 1% of GDP is exempt

cards.headline: Debt: explained
learned: Deficit: spending above revenue in a year
Borrowing to cover deficits builds debt
IMF: global debt above 100% of GDP by 2029
The IMF, the OECD and Germany's rule differ on limits

options.label: When taxes are cut to zero
options.rationale: A deficit is about spending versus revenue, whatever the tax level.

questions.explanation: The fiscal balance is revenue minus spending; when spending is greater, it's a deficit.

levels.title: The Military
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what militaries do and who controls them.
levels.summary: Militaries carry the state's force for defence, under the control of elected civilians and parliaments. The world spent $2887 billion on them in 2025; how much is enough is debated.

cards.headline: Costa Rica has had no army since 1949.
cards.body: Its constitution abolishes the army as a permanent institution, and keeps the police forces needed for public order. UNESCO notes the money went into social development, especially health and education. So what are armies for, and who decides what they do?

cards.headline: The state's force, with a leash
cards.body: Remember Level 9's Weber? A state claims the monopoly of legitimate force within its territory. The military is the heaviest part of that force, and it provides Level 5's classic public good, national defence. That makes one question vital: who holds the leash?

cards.headline: Civilians in charge
cards.body: In a democracy, the armed forces answer to democratically elected authorities, overseen by the courts, the media and civil society. Civilians decide the military's missions, size, budget and purchases; commanders decide how to carry the missions out. Parliaments add laws, hearings and control of the purse, so Level 71's approval stage applies to tanks too.

cards.fact: The world spent $2887 billion on the military in 2025.
cards.context: That's SIPRI's count, equal to 2.5% of global GDP and 6.9% of the average government's spending. The five biggest spenders, the United States, China, Russia, Germany and India, made up 58% of it.

mascot.line: Watch the labels as well as the totals. What counts as defence is itself a choice.

cards.headline: How much is enough?
cards.body: Every country answers for itself, and NATO's members answered together. In 2014 they aimed for 2% of GDP by 2024; in June 2025 they agreed on 5% by 2035, at least 3.5% of it for core defence. SIPRI, which tracks the spending, warns the looser part of the target could invite 'creative accounting', with non-military projects relabelled as defence.

cards.headline: The military: controlled
learned: Costa Rica's 1949 constitution abolished its army
Elected civilians decide missions and budgets
World military spending: $2887 billion in 2025
NATO's target rose from 2% to 5% of GDP

levels.title: Checkpoint: Money and Government
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how governments raise and spend money.
levels.summary: Every budget ends with an audit. Independent auditors, backed by the 1977 Lima Declaration, check public money. Chapter 8: raise, plan, spend, check.

cards.headline: Every budget ends the same way: someone checks the receipts.
cards.body: Level 71's cycle had a fourth stage, audit, where the actual spending is checked. This chapter followed the money from taxes to pensions, bridges and tanks. This level follows the people who follow the money.

cards.headline: Auditors who answer to no minister
cards.body: Countries' top auditors are called supreme audit institutions. In 1977 they adopted the Lima Declaration, known as the Magna Carta of government auditing, and its chief aim is independent auditing. Level 76's European Court of Auditors shows the job: it asked not only 'was the money spent?' but 'did it deliver?', and found PPPs running up to 52 months late.

cards.headline: Follow one euro

The biggest share of spending goes on social protection, so it may well end up in someone's pension. If the government spent more than it collected, some of what it spent was borrowed. And after the year ends, an auditor checks that the money went where the budget said.

levels.title: Sovereignty
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what makes a country independent.
levels.summary: Sovereignty is a state's final say over its own affairs. Westphalia (1648) is seen as the start of the state system; Montevideo (1933) lists four tests for a state.

cards.headline: On 9 July 2011, the world gained a brand-new country.
cards.body: South Sudan became independent that day, the newest country on Earth, and five days later the UN admitted it as a member state. Remember Level 1's 193 UN members? South Sudan is the newest of them. So what exactly did it gain that day? In one word: sovereignty.

cards.headline: The final say
cards.body: Britannica defines sovereignty as the ultimate power or authority in a state's decision-making and in keeping order. Put simply, a sovereign state has the final say over its own affairs: which laws apply, who runs things, how order is kept. It's the difference between owning your house and renting a room in someone else's.

cards.fact: Modern sovereignty is often traced to a peace deal of 1648.
cards.context: The Peace of Westphalia, negotiated in the German towns of Munster and Osnabruck, ended the Thirty Years' War. It recognized the full territorial sovereignty of the empire's member states, including the right to make their own treaties. Many scholars see it as the foundation of the modern system of independent, equal states: lots of separate houses instead of one landlord.

mascot.line: Population, territory, government, relations: four boxes on one checklist.

cards.headline: A four-point checklist
cards.body: How do you recognize a state? The Montevideo Convention, signed in 1933, lists four qualifications: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. Level 9's state already had territory and laws; the fourth test looks outward. And Article 3 adds a twist: a state's existence doesn't depend on other states recognizing it.

levels.title: Diplomacy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how ambassadors and diplomats work.
levels.summary: Embassies represent, protect, negotiate and report. The 1961 Vienna Convention makes embassies inviolable and diplomats immune, but the host can send any diplomat home.

cards.headline: Police can go almost anywhere in a city. An embassy's door stops them.
cards.body: Under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, an embassy's premises are inviolable: the host country's officials may not enter without the consent of the head of the mission. Why would a sovereign country accept a door it can't open on its own soil?

cards.headline: What an embassy is for
cards.body: An embassy is one country's permanent office inside another. The Vienna Convention lists its jobs: represent its country, protect its interests and citizens, negotiate with the host government, report home on what's happening, and promote friendly relations. None of it is forced: diplomatic relations are set up by mutual consent. Level 81's fourth test for a state was the capacity to enter into relations with other states. Embassies are that capacity at work.

cards.fact: Protecting envoys is an ancient rule, written down in 1961.
cards.context: The Vienna Convention's preamble recalls that peoples of all nations from ancient times have recognized the status of diplomats. The Convention itself, signed on 18 April 1961, wrote down rules that had been stable for over 200 years, and almost all states are now parties. Diplomacy's rulebook was mostly copied out, not invented.

mascot.line: The host can't arrest a diplomat, but it can always show them the door.

cards.headline: Can't arrest you, can send you home
cards.body: A diplomat can't be arrested or detained, and is immune from the host country's criminal courts. That sounds like a license to misbehave, but the Convention says immunity isn't there to benefit individuals: it lets missions do their work without coercion or harassment. Diplomats must still respect local laws. And the host holds a trump card: it can declare any diplomat persona non grata, at any time, without saying why, and the sending country must recall them.

levels.title: Treaties
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how countries make treaties.
levels.summary: A treaty is a written agreement between states. Signing comes first; ratification binds. Then pacta sunt servanda: agreements must be kept.

cards.headline: A copy of the oldest known peace treaty hangs at the UN.
cards.body: Around 1269 BC, the Hittite king Hattusili III and Egypt's Ramesses II put peace in writing. They pledged lasting peace, nonaggression, extradition and mutual help. A replica now hangs near the entrance of the Security Council Chamber at UN Headquarters. Countries still make their biggest promises the same way: in writing.

cards.headline: Whatever you call it
cards.body: Pact, convention, protocol, agreement: the label doesn't matter. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969) defines a treaty as a written agreement between states, governed by international law, whatever its particular name. Working out the words is diplomats' work: negotiating with the host government was one of Level 82's embassy jobs. Think of a treaty as a contract, with countries as the signatures.

cards.headline: Sign first, bind later
cards.body: Signing is often not the last step. When a treaty needs ratification, a signature doesn't bind the state yet; ratification is the act by which a state consents to be bound. In between, a signer must not do anything that would defeat the treaty's purpose, unless it makes clear it won't join. The pen says "we mean to"; ratification says "we will".

mascot.line: A promise with a Latin motto and a UN filing cabinet behind it.

cards.fact: Pacta sunt servanda: agreements must be kept.
cards.context: That Latin phrase is arguably the oldest principle of international law. The 1969 Vienna Convention puts it in Article 26: every treaty in force binds its parties and must be performed in good faith. Article 27 closes the obvious loophole: a country can't point to its own laws as an excuse for failing to keep a treaty.

levels.title: The United Nations
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the UN does and does not do.
levels.summary: Founded in 1945 to prevent war, the UN gives every member one vote in the General Assembly; the Security Council's five permanent members hold a veto. It is not a world government.

cards.headline: The UN's founding document opens with a promise about war.
cards.body: Its first words set the mission: "to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, which twice in our lifetime has brought untold sorrow to mankind." Everything the UN does, and everything it can't do, makes more sense once you know it began with that sentence.

cards.headline: Signed in San Francisco
cards.body: Delegates from 50 countries spent two months in San Francisco in 1945 drawing up the UN Charter. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945, once China, France, the Soviet Union, the UK, the US and most other signers had ratified it. Ratified: Level 83's step, the one that turns a signature into a binding promise.

cards.headline: One country, one vote
cards.body: In the General Assembly, all 193 members sit together and each has one vote, so Tuvalu's vote counts exactly as much as India's. The Charter calls this the sovereign equality of all its members: Level 81's idea, written into the rules. The Assembly makes recommendations to states, and important questions need a two-thirds majority.

cards.headline: Fifteen seats, five vetoes
cards.body: Keeping the peace is mainly the Security Council's job. It has 15 members, 5 of them permanent: China, France, Russia, the UK and the US. Unlike the Assembly's recommendations, its decisions bind every UN member. A decision needs nine votes, including all five permanent members, so a single no from any one of them blocks it. That's the veto.

mascot.line: 193 captains, one meeting room, no admiral.

cards.fact: The UN is not a world government.
cards.context: In its own words, the UN is neither a supra-state nor a government of governments. It has no army and levies no taxes, and it depends on what its member states are willing to do. Back to Level 1's ship: the UN isn't a captain for every vessel. It's where the captains meet.

levels.title: The European Union
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the EU works.
levels.summary: The EU began with six countries pooling coal and steel to make war impossible. Today 27 members share lawmaking: the Commission proposes; Parliament and Council adopt.

cards.headline: It started with coal, steel and a plan to make war impossible.
cards.body: On 9 May 1950, French foreign minister Robert Schuman proposed pooling Western Europe's coal and steel industries. His aim was to make war between France and Germany "not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible." Today's European Union grew from that idea.

cards.fact: Six countries went first, in 1951.
cards.context: Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands signed a treaty to run their coal and steel industries jointly, so no single country could make the weapons of war to turn against the others. The goal was to end the bloody conflicts that had culminated in the Second World War. That first step led to today's European Union of 27 countries.

cards.headline: Laws made in a triangle
cards.body: Everything the EU does rests on treaties its member countries agreed to voluntarily and democratically. Lawmaking runs through a triangle. The European Commission proposes a law. Two bodies adopt it: the European Parliament, directly elected by EU citizens, and the Council of the EU, where ministers from each member government sit. The member countries then put it into practice, and the Commission checks that they do.

mascot.line: Not one house, not 27 separate ones: more like a shared kitchen with house rules.

cards.headline: Sharing the final say
cards.body: Remember Level 81: sovereignty means having the final say. EU members agreed, by treaty, to make some of their laws together, through a Parliament and a Council they all share, instead of each deciding alone. The final say hasn't vanished: in treaties they chose to sign, the members agreed to share some of it.

levels.title: War and Peace
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how wars start and how they end.
levels.summary: Clausewitz saw war as politics by other means. Rules on starting wars tightened from 1907 to 1945. An armistice stops a war; a peace treaty ends it.

cards.headline: On 11 November 1918, the guns fell silent. The war wasn't over yet.
cards.body: That day's armistice stopped the fighting on the Western Front, but the First World War formally ended only with the Treaty of Versailles, signed on 28 June 1919. Stopping a war and ending one turn out to be different steps. So is starting one.

cards.headline: Politics by other means
cards.body: Why do wars start? One classic answer comes from the Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz, whose book On War appeared in 1832, after his death. He argued that war is a continuation of state policy by other means. In his view, war isn't a break from politics: it's a tool governments pick up to pursue political goals.

The Charter keeps the right of self-defence if an armed attack occurs

mascot.line: Armistice: the guns stop. Peace treaty: the argument is settled on paper.

cards.headline: Stopping versus ending
cards.body: An armistice stops the fighting while the terms of peace are worked out. A peace treaty formally ends the war, as Versailles did after 1918's armistice. Sometimes the second step never comes: the Korean War armistice of 27 July 1953 stopped the fighting, but it was not a permanent peace treaty. Level 83's Kadesh tablet was the full kind: a peace treaty.

levels.title: International Courts
levels.objective: After this level you can explain courts that judge countries and war crimes.
levels.summary: Nuremberg held that people commit crimes against international law. The ICJ settles disputes between consenting states; the ICC tries individuals as a court of last resort.

cards.headline: In 1946, a court ruled that crimes are committed by people, not abstractions.
cards.body: The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, run by the US, UK, Soviet Union and France, tried 22 leading Nazi officials. Its judgment put it plainly: "Crimes against international law are committed by men, not by abstract entities." A state can't stand in the dock. The people who act in its name can.

cards.headline: Two courts, one city
cards.body: The Hague in the Netherlands hosts two very different international courts. The first is the International Court of Justice, which sits in the Peace Palace. It's the UN's principal judicial organ, and the only one of the UN's six main organs not based in New York. Its 15 judges are elected for nine-year terms by the General Assembly and the Security Council, Level 84's two big bodies.

cards.headline: Countries versus countries
cards.body: Only states can be parties in cases at the ICJ. And a state can't simply be dragged in: the Court's jurisdiction rests on the consent of the states involved. So the ICJ is where countries bring legal disputes with each other, and it also gives advisory opinions when UN bodies ask for one. Think of it as a court for arguments between sovereigns.

mascot.line: ICJ: country against country. ICC: a person in the dock. One letter apart, worlds apart.

cards.headline: People in the dock
cards.body: The second court, the International Criminal Court, works the other way round: it tries individuals. Set up by a treaty called the Rome Statute, it deals with genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and the crime of aggression committed since 1 July 2002. It's a court of last resort, meant to complement national courts, not replace them. Nuremberg set the precedent that people answer for such crimes.

levels.title: Refugees
levels.objective: After this level you can explain refugees and the right to asylum.
levels.summary: Nansen's 1922 passport helped refugees with no country. The 1951 Convention defines refugees and forbids returning them to danger. Most displaced people stay inside their country.

cards.headline: In 1922, a polar explorer created a passport for people with no country.
cards.body: In 1921 the League of Nations made Fridtjof Nansen its first High Commissioner for Refugees, to help people fleeing Russia after the revolution. Many had lost their nationality. His "Nansen passport" let them travel to other countries to look for work; about 450,000 people used one. Nansen received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922.

cards.headline: Who counts as a refugee
cards.body: Today's rule comes from the 1951 Refugee Convention. A refugee is someone outside their own country who can't or won't return to its protection because of a well-founded fear of being persecuted for their race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. And UNHCR says refugee status is declaratory: you're a refugee from the moment you meet the criteria, before any official says so.

cards.fact: The core rule: no sending refugees back into danger.
cards.context: It's called non-refoulement. Article 33 of the 1951 Convention says a refugee must not be expelled or returned to a territory where their life or freedom would be threatened, and UNHCR calls it one of the most fundamental principles of international law. Asylum is the protection a state grants to someone fleeing persecution or serious harm, and UNHCR says seeking it is a human right.

mascot.line: Same fear, same journey, different side of a border, different legal word.

cards.fact: Most people forced from home never cross a border.
cards.context: UNHCR's Global Trends report counted 117.8 million people forcibly displaced at the end of 2025. Of them, 41.6 million were refugees and 68.7 million were displaced inside their own countries. Because the 1951 definition requires being outside your own country, those 68.7 million aren't refugees in law, even though they fled home too.

learned: Nansen's 1922 passport helped people with no country

levels.title: Problems Without Borders
levels.objective: After this level you can explain problems no country can solve alone, like climate change.
levels.summary: Ozone and climate cross every border, and countries are tempted to free ride. The Montreal Protocol was ratified by all; under Paris each country sets its own plan.

cards.headline: One treaty has been ratified by every country. It's about the sky.
cards.body: The Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, set out to phase out the chemicals that were depleting the ozone layer. It became the first treaty in UN history to be ratified by every country. Why would a treaty about chemicals need the whole world on board?

cards.headline: Problems that ignore passports
cards.body: Some problems don't stop at the border. The UN calls climate change a global emergency that goes beyond national borders and needs international cooperation. As an OpenStax economics textbook puts it, no nation by itself can cut greenhouse gas emissions enough to solve global warming without the cooperation of other nations. The atmosphere has no customs checkpoint.

mascot.line: Level 5's free rider, now wearing a flag.

cards.headline: Free riders, planet-sized
cards.body: Remember Level 5's free riders, who enjoy a public good while letting others pay? Political scientists describe climate change the same way: a collective action problem, where a country can benefit from free riding on other countries' efforts. At home, a law can require everyone to chip in. Between sovereign countries there's no world government to do that (Level 84), so they make treaties instead.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Countries and the World
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how countries cooperate and settle disputes.
levels.summary: The 1959 Antarctic Treaty froze claims and kept a continent for peace and science. Countries talk through diplomats, promise by treaty and settle disputes in courts.

cards.headline: A whole continent is run by a treaty signed in 1959.
cards.body: On 1 December 1959, twelve countries whose scientists had taken part in the International Geophysical Year (1957–58) signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington. It came into force in 1961 and now has 58 parties. It's this chapter in a single document.

cards.headline: Sovereignty, parked
cards.body: Seven of the signers, including Argentina, Chile and the UK, had claimed parts of Antarctica, and some claims overlapped. The treaty didn't decide who was right. Article IV neither denies nor supports the claims, and allows no new or enlarged ones while the treaty is in force. Level 81's final say, put on hold by agreement.

mascot.line: Ten levels on how countries get along, and a whole continent to prove it can work.

cards.headline: Peace, science and open doors
cards.body: Article I says Antarctica shall be used for peaceful purposes only: no military bases, no nuclear explosions. Scientists keep the freedom to investigate and must share their results. And trust is backed by checking: every station is open to inspection at all times. Unlike Level 82's embassy door, nothing here stays shut.

levels.title: Citizenship
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what citizenship means.
levels.summary: Citizenship is a two-way bond with a state: allegiance for protection. Most people get it at birth by soil (jus soli) or blood (jus sanguinis); adults can naturalize.

cards.headline: You probably never applied for your first citizenship.
cards.body: If you hold one, a country's law may have settled it the day you were born, using one of two old rules: where you were born, or who your parents were. First, though: what exactly did you get?

cards.headline: A two-way deal
cards.body: Britannica defines citizenship as the relationship between an individual and a state to which the individual owes allegiance and in turn is entitled to its protection. Read that as a trade. You owe the state loyalty; the state owes you protection. Remember Level 9's state, with its territory, laws and means of enforcing them? Citizenship is your membership card for one.

items.label: Right of the soil (jus soli)
points: Born on the territory? You're a citizen, whoever your parents are
The basis in nearly every country in the Western Hemisphere

items.label: Right of blood (jus sanguinis)
points: Citizenship passes from a parent, wherever you're born
Japan: a child is Japanese if the father or mother is

mascot.line: Born into it or studied for it: both routes end with the same membership card.

cards.fact: Adults can join too. Canada asks for 1,095 days first.
cards.context: Becoming a citizen by applying is called naturalization. Britannica lists the usual requirements: a period of residence, language skills and knowledge of the country. Canada's version is at least 1,095 days (3 years) physically in Canada within the last 5, plus a citizenship test for applicants aged 18 to 54. Citizenship by birth is luck. Naturalization is homework.

levels.title: Rights and Responsibilities
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the duties that come with rights.
levels.summary: Rights come with responsibilities. Some are legal duties, like obeying the law and jury service when called; others are civic. Australia turned voting into a legal duty in 1924.

cards.headline: In Australia, skipping an election can land you a penalty.
cards.body: Since 1924, voting at Australian federal elections has been a legal duty, not just a right. Miss it without a valid and sufficient reason and you face a penalty. That raises a bigger question: what do citizens owe in return for their rights?

cards.headline: Rights come with responsibilities
cards.body: Canada's official citizenship guide puts it in one line: in Canada, rights come with responsibilities. It's an old idea. Level 7's social contract set out the rights and duties of each side, and Level 91's citizenship trades allegiance for protection. You don't just hold rights. You help keep up the system that protects them.

cards.headline: Must, and should
cards.body: The guide's list includes obeying the law, serving on a jury, voting in elections, helping others in your community, and protecting heritage and the environment. Some are enforced by law. If you're called for jury duty, the guide says, you are legally required to serve. Level 6's taxes belong with the musts too: they're compulsory. Voting is on the list as well. Whether the law makes you do it depends on the country.

mascot.line: Same duty on the list, two very different rules behind it.

cards.fact: Australia's turnout jumped from under 60% to over 91%.
cards.context: In 1922, fewer than 60% of eligible Australians voted in the federal election. Voting became compulsory in 1924, and at the 1925 election turnout rose to over 91%. Same country, same kind of election, one change to the rule. Whether voting should be a legal must or a civic should is a choice each country makes for itself.

levels.title: Speaking to Your Representative
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how to contact elected officials.
levels.summary: A UK MP represents everyone in the constituency, voters or not. Write with your address, visit a surgery, or sign a petition: 10,000 signatures earn a UK government reply, 100,000 a debate.

cards.headline: Your representative works for you, even if you voted for someone else.
cards.body: Take the UK. MPs are elected to represent the interests and concerns of all the people who live in their constituency, whether they voted for them or not. So the job includes you. The question is how to get their attention.

cards.headline: Step one: find your person
cards.body: In the UK, each MP represents one area, called a constituency, and can normally only take up issues raised by the people who live there, their constituents. So start with your address. Find out who represents it, then put that address in your letter or email. It tells the office you're one of theirs, not a stranger from across the country.

mascot.line: Bring your address, your problem and one clear ask.

cards.headline: Step two: go and talk
cards.body: Most MPs also hold surgeries in their constituency: sessions where you can meet them and talk through a problem. Remember Level 3's legal-rational authority, which belongs to the office and not the person? That's why this works. You're not begging a favor from a stranger. You're using an office that exists partly to hear you.

cards.fact: In the UK, 100,000 signatures get a petition considered for debate.
cards.context: UK Parliament petitions get a government response at 10,000 signatures and are considered for debate at 100,000. Canada's House of Commons sets a lower bar: an e-petition with at least 500 signatures is presented, and the government responds within 45 days. One letter speaks for you. A petition speaks for a crowd.

levels.title: Volunteering
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how volunteers help their communities.
levels.summary: Volunteering is unpaid, non-compulsory work, formal or informal. About 862 million people volunteer monthly, and some public services, like NSW's fire brigades, run largely on volunteers.

cards.headline: One Australian state's fire service runs on about 70,000 volunteers.
cards.body: The NSW Rural Fire Service in New South Wales has about 70,000 volunteer members and is widely described as the largest volunteer fire service in the world. Fire protection is on Level 5's list of public services. Here, a huge force of unpaid people helps provide it.

cards.headline: Unpaid, and unforced
cards.body: The International Labour Organization defines volunteer work as unpaid, non-compulsory work: time people give without pay, either through an organization or directly for others outside their own household. Compare Level 6's taxes, which are compulsory. Taxes are what everyone must give. Volunteering is what people choose to give.

cards.headline: Mostly without a uniform
cards.body: Formal volunteering happens through an organization, like a fire brigade. Informal volunteering is arranged directly between people: shopping for a sick neighbor, fixing a friend's fence. Worldwide, more than twice as many people volunteer informally as formally. So most volunteering happens without any roster or badge at all.

mascot.line: Not every public good comes out of a tax bill.

cards.fact: About 862 million people volunteer every month.
cards.context: That's the estimate in UN Volunteers' 2022 State of the World's Volunteerism Report, counting people aged 15 and over. By definition, nobody is made to give that time, and nobody is paid for it. It's a workforce no budget pays for.

levels.title: Reading the News Well
levels.objective: After this level you can judge whether a news story is reliable.
levels.summary: Many shared links are never read. Journalists' own codes give readers clues: headlines backed by the text, clearly identified sources, labeled opinion, and prompt corrections.

cards.headline: In one study, most shared news links were never even clicked.
cards.body: In 2016, researchers at Columbia University and France's Inria found that 59% of the news links shared on Twitter in their sample were never clicked. Plenty of headlines travel without their stories. So how do you judge the story itself? Journalists' own rulebooks offer clues.

cards.headline: Clue 1: the headline isn't the story
cards.body: The UK's Editors' Code, enforced by the press regulator IPSO, tells the press not to publish misleading information, including headlines not supported by the text. That rule exists because the problem does. A headline is a pitch, written short. Read far enough to see whether the story actually backs it up.

cards.headline: Clue 2: who says so?
cards.body: The US Society of Professional Journalists' Code of Ethics tells reporters to identify sources clearly, so the public can judge how reliable they are and why they're talking. A trustworthy story shows its workings: named people, documents, data. If you can't tell how the reporter knows something, you can't check it either.

cards.headline: Clue 3: news or opinion?
cards.body: Both codes draw the same line. The SPJ says to label advocacy and commentary. The UK code says the press, while free to campaign, must distinguish clearly between comment, conjecture and fact. Opinion isn't a flaw; it's a different product. Check the label before you treat an argument as a report.

mascot.line: Headline, sources, label, corrections. Four quick checks before you share.

cards.fact: A correction is a good sign, not a bad one.
cards.context: The SPJ tells journalists to correct mistakes promptly and prominently. The UK code says significant inaccuracies must be corrected promptly and with due prominence. An outlet that runs corrections is showing you it checks its own work.

options.label: Unclicked stories don't need to be accurate

questions.explanation: When headlines travel without their stories, a headline not supported by the text misleads many readers, which is why the code forbids it.

levels.title: Young People and Politics
levels.objective: After this level you can describe ways young people take part before they can vote.
levels.summary: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child gives children a right to be heard. Youth parliaments, letters to representatives and volunteering are ways in before voting age.

cards.headline: In 2009, teenagers took over the green benches of the House of Commons.
cards.body: On 30 October 2009, about 300 Members of the UK Youth Parliament debated in the Commons chamber. It was the first time a group other than MPs had used it. So what can you do in politics before you're old enough to vote?

cards.headline: A right to be heard
cards.body: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 1989, is the world's most widely ratified human rights treaty. It counts everyone under 18 as a child, unless the law sets adulthood earlier. Its Article 12 gives a child capable of forming views the right to express them freely in all matters affecting them, given due weight for age and maturity. Too young to vote isn't too young to be heard.

mascot.line: Candidates, ballots, campaigns: same moves, smaller pool.

cards.headline: Practice parliaments
cards.body: Youth parliaments turn that right into a habit. In the UK Youth Parliament, any young person aged 11 to 18 can vote or stand, members are elected, and once elected they run campaigns on issues that matter to young people. It's the real machinery in miniature. You learn politics the way you learn to swim: by getting in.

cards.headline: Tools that don't need a ballot
cards.body: This chapter has already handed you two more. Level 93: a UK MP represents all the people who live in the constituency, not only voters, so your letter counts. Level 94: volunteering is unpaid, non-compulsory work that anyone can choose to give. Neither one asks to see a voter card.

cards.headline: Young people: heard
learned: The Convention on the Rights of the Child: a right to be heard
Its Article 12 covers all matters affecting children
UK Youth Parliament: elected members aged 11 to 18
Letters and volunteering need no voter card

options.label: The right to vote from age 16
options.rationale: It's about being heard, not voting.

options.label: The right to stand for parliament
options.rationale: It doesn't cover standing for office.

options.label: The right to express their views in matters affecting them
The right to leave school at any age
options.rationale: Not what Article 12 covers.

questions.explanation: Article 12 gives a child capable of forming views the right to express them freely in all matters affecting them.

options.label: Its members are elected by and from 11- to 18-year-olds
It can pass laws that bind the whole country
options.rationale: It campaigns and debates; it doesn't make national law.

options.label: Its members are appointed by MPs
options.rationale: Members are elected, not appointed.

options.label: Only people over 18 may take part
options.rationale: It's for ages 11 to 18.

questions.explanation: Young people aged 11 to 18 vote and stand in its elections, and members run campaigns: an election system in miniature.

options.rationale: Her MP still represents her.

questions.explanation: UK MPs represent all the people who live in their constituency, whether or not they voted, and that includes people too young to vote.

levels.title: Local Government Up Close
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how a city or town council works.
levels.summary: Cities use designs like council-manager and mayor-council. English council meetings are public, agendas out five clear days ahead; India's gram sabha includes every village voter.

cards.headline: In an Indian village, every voter belongs to the local assembly.
cards.body: India's gram sabha is made up of everyone on the village panchayat's electoral roll, and it approves development plans before the panchayat carries them out. Remember Level 8's panchayats? This is the room they answer to. A big city can't fit every voter in one room, though. So how does an elected council run one?

cards.headline: Who runs the city day to day? Two US designs

items.label: Council-manager
points: Elected council makes policy and sets the budget
It appoints a professional city manager to run daily operations

items.label: Mayor-council
points: Mayor elected separately, often full-time
Mayor has major administrative and budget powers; council legislates

mascot.line: Five clear days is plenty of time to read an agenda. Few people do.

cards.headline: Open doors, published papers
cards.body: In England, the Local Government Act 1972 says a council meeting is open to the public, except when the public is lawfully kept out, for example for confidential matters. The agenda and reports must be open for inspection at least five clear days before. So you can read what's coming, then walk in and watch it being decided.

cards.headline: What's on the agenda?
cards.body: So what will you actually hear about? Level 8's list for Canada's municipal governments is a good guide: fire protection, local police, public transit, parks, waste management, water supply and local roads. National politics gets the headlines. Your council decides whether the bins get emptied on time.

cards.headline: Local government: up close
learned: Council-manager: the council hires a city manager
Mayor-council: a separately elected mayor runs things
English council meetings are open; agendas five clear days ahead
India's gram sabha includes every village voter

options.label: At least one clear day
options.rationale: Longer: at least five clear days.

options.label: At least five clear days
At least one month
options.rationale: Shorter than that: five clear days.

options.label: Only after the meeting
options.rationale: It must be open before the meeting.

questions.explanation: The Local Government Act 1972 requires the agenda and reports to be open for inspection at least five clear days before the meeting.

options.label: The mayor, elected separately from the council
options.rationale: That's the mayor-council form.

options.rationale: Residents elect the council; they don't run operations.

options.label: The state governor
options.rationale: City operations are run locally.

options.label: A professional city manager appointed by the council

options.label: It's the national parliament's village office
options.rationale: It's the village's own voters, not a national body.

options.label: A tax office that collects village taxes
options.rationale: Its role here is approving development plans.

questions.explanation: The gram sabha is everyone on the village electoral roll, and it approves development plans before the panchayat carries them out.

levels.title: Myths About Government
levels.objective: After this level you can debunk common myths about how government works.
levels.summary: Three myths checked against the rules: a higher tax bracket taxes only the income inside it; UK civil servants serve any elected government; MPs represent everyone in their area.

cards.headline: Get a raise, jump a tax bracket, take home less. Sound right?
cards.body: You may have heard it. It's wrong, at least for income tax in the US and the UK. This level checks three common beliefs about government against the actual rules.

cards.headline: Myth 1: a higher bracket taxes everything
cards.body: Income taxes in the US and the UK use brackets (the UK calls them bands). Each rate applies only to the part of your income inside its bracket. Cross into a higher one and only the income above the line pays the higher rate. Everything below is taxed exactly as before. Your earlier dollars and pounds never notice.

mascot.line: Rules differ between countries. Checking the actual rule beats repeating the rumor.

cards.headline: Myth 2: new government, new staff
cards.body: When a new party takes power, does it bring in its own officials? In the UK, the civil service is built on the opposite idea. Its code requires civil servants to serve the government, whatever its political persuasion, and to serve different governments equally well. They must not let their own political views decide their advice. The politicians at the top change; the code expects the staff to serve whoever wins.

cards.headline: Myth 3: your representative only works for their voters
cards.body: Level 93 already busted this one. UK MPs are elected to represent everyone who lives in their constituency, whether they voted for them or not. Winning an election puts someone in an office, and Level 3's legal-rational authority belongs to the office, not to its fan club.

cards.headline: Myths: checked
learned: A higher bracket taxes only the income inside it
UK civil servants serve any elected government
They keep their own politics out of their advice
MPs represent everyone in their constituency

questions.prompt: Under US or UK income tax brackets, what happens when your income crosses into a higher bracket?

options.label: All your income is taxed at the higher rate
options.rationale: That's the myth.

options.label: You stop paying tax on the lower part
options.rationale: The lower part is taxed as before.

options.label: Only the income above the line pays the higher rate
Your whole tax bill is cut in half
options.rationale: Nothing like that happens.

questions.explanation: Brackets are marginal: each rate applies only to the income inside its bracket.

questions.prompt: What does the UK Civil Service Code expect of civil servants when a new party forms the government?

options.label: To resign so the party can appoint its supporters
options.rationale: The code expects them to serve the new government.

options.label: To serve it as well as they served the last one
To follow their own political views in their advice
options.rationale: The code forbids that.

options.label: To wait until the next election before helping
options.rationale: They serve the government of the day.

questions.explanation: The code requires serving the government, whatever its political persuasion, and serving different governments equally well.

options.label: MPs represent only their party's members
options.rationale: They represent everyone in the constituency.

options.label: MPs represent the whole country equally
options.rationale: They represent their own constituency.

options.label: MPs represent only people over 18
options.rationale: All the people who live there.

options.label: MPs represent everyone living in their constituency

questions.explanation: UK MPs are elected to represent all the people who live in their constituency, whether they voted for them or not.

levels.title: How to Disagree Well
levels.objective: After this level you can argue about politics without falling out.
levels.summary: Mill: know the other side at its strongest. Dennett's Rapoport rules: restate, agree, credit, then criticize. Graham: aim at the central point, not the person.

cards.headline: "He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that."
cards.body: John Stuart Mill wrote that in On Liberty, in 1859. It's a bold claim: being sure you're right isn't the same as knowing why. This level is about arguing with people you disagree with, and still being on speaking terms afterwards.

cards.headline: Know their best case
cards.body: Mill's reasoning: if you can't answer the other side's reasons, or don't even know them, you have no ground for preferring either opinion. And he wanted those reasons heard from people who actually believe them, in their most plausible and persuasive form. A cartoon of your opponent is easy to beat. It's also not who you're arguing with.

cards.headline: Four steps before the rebuttal
cards.body: Philosopher Daniel Dennett, drawing on game theorist Anatol Rapoport, gave a recipe in 2013. First, restate the other view so well its holder says, "Thanks, I wish I'd thought of putting it that way." Second, list where you agree. Third, mention anything you learned from them. Only then, criticize. By step four, they're actually listening.

mascot.line: Next time you're tempted to mock the messenger, climb a rung.

cards.headline: Aim high on the ladder
cards.body: Paul Graham's 2008 essay How to Disagree ranks replies from worst to best. At the bottom: name-calling, then ad hominem (attacking the person), then responding to tone. At the top: refuting the central point. Low rungs are about the person. High rungs are about the argument.

cards.headline: Political animals, still
cards.body: Level 10's Aristotle said humans are by nature political animals: we live in communities, so we're bound to disagree inside them. The aim isn't a world without arguments. It's arguments that leave the community standing.

cards.headline: Disagreeing: done well
learned: Mill: knowing only your side means knowing little
Hear the other side at its most persuasive
Rapoport's rules: restate, agree, credit, then criticize
Graham: refute the central point, not the person

options.rationale: No vote; the steps are about understanding.

options.label: Restating their view fairly, noting agreement and what you learned
Pointing out the other person's tone
options.rationale: Tone-policing is low on Graham's ladder.

options.label: Quoting an expert who agrees with you
options.rationale: The rules start with the other person's view.

questions.explanation: Restate their view so well they wish they'd put it that way, list agreements, mention what you learned, and only then criticize.

questions.prompt: Why did Mill think you need to know the other side's reasons?

options.label: So you can quote them back as a joke
options.rationale: He wanted them heard in their strongest form.

options.label: Because the other side is always right
options.rationale: He didn't say that; he said you can't judge without them.

options.label: Because the law required it in 1859
options.rationale: It was an argument, not a law.

options.label: Without answering them, you have no ground to prefer your view

questions.explanation: Mill argued that if you can't refute the other side's reasons, or don't know them, you have no ground for preferring either opinion.

questions.prompt: Level 10's Aristotle called humans political animals. How does that fit this level's advice on disagreeing?

options.label: Living in communities means we will disagree, so do it well
Animals can't argue, so people shouldn't either
options.rationale: He meant we're made for community, not silence.

options.label: Only a beast or a god needs to argue
options.rationale: He said only a beast or a god lives outside a community.

options.label: Politics should be left to philosophers
options.rationale: Nothing in this level says so.

questions.explanation: If we're made to live in communities, disagreement comes with it; the point is to argue in ways that keep the community together.

levels.title: Mastery Challenge: How Government Works
levels.objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of How Government Works Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
levels.summary: Questions from why governments exist to your own part in one: authority, taxes, the social contract, citizenship, duties, local councils, news and the civil service. Every question can be corrected.
